en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Birth Stories (Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā) in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
(The Third Part) 4.
Catukkanipāta 1. Kāliṅgavagga
[301] 1. The Commentary on the Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka.
“Open this door of the month!”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the going forth of four female wanderers.
It is said that in Vesālī there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven [Licchavi princes] of the Licchavi kings.
And the Licchavis lived there. They were all intent on asking questions and receiving answers.
Then a certain Nigaṇṭha, skilled in five hundred points of debate, arrived at Vesālī; they received him with hospitality. Another such Nigaṇṭhī also arrived.
The two kings caused the two persons to engage in debate, and both were indeed equal. Then [the Licchavis... of the Licchavis...
It occurred to him: "A son born dependent upon these two will be capable.
Having arranged their marriage, he had them live together. Then, as a result of their cohabitation, four daughters and one son were born in succession.
They gave the daughters the names Saccā, Lolā, Avadhārikā, and Paṭicchādā, and [the name] for the boy...
“Saccaka. Those five persons, having reached maturity, learned a thousand arguments—five hundred from their mother’s side and five hundred from their father’s side.
Their parents thus instructed their daughters:
“If any householder should defeat your argument, you must become his handmaidens; if it is one who has gone forth...”
“He will break [this argument]; you should go forth in his presence.
Later on, her parents passed away. When they had died, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha remained right there in Vesālī, teaching the craft of the Licchavis.
Her sisters took a branch of a rose-apple tree and went out from the city for the sake of debate.

While wandering through the city, having reached Sāvatthī, they buried a branch at the city gate and said to the children, "Whether it be a householder or one gone forth, whoever is able to refute our argument, let him scatter this heap of dust with his feet and trample the branch with his feet.
Having spoken thus, they entered the city for alms. Then the Venerable Sāriputta—
Having swept the unswept places, set out water in empty jars, and attended to the sick, the Elder entered Sāvatthī for alms early in the morning.
Seeing that branch, he questioned the boys, and the boys explained what had happened to him.
The Elder had the boys themselves pull it down and crush it, saying, "By whomsoever this branch was placed [here]..."
"Let them come after they have finished their meal and see me at the gateway of the Jetavana," he said to the boys.
Having entered the city and finished his meal, he stood at the gateway of the monastery.
Those female wanderers, having returned from their alms-round, saw the crushed branch and asked, "By whom was this crushed? [The boys replied,] "By the Elder Sāriputta."
"If you wish to debate, go to the gateway of the Jetavana," the children said.
Having entered the city again, they gathered a great crowd of people, went to the gateway of the monastery, and asked the Elder a thousand questions.
The Elder answered them and asked, "Do you know anything else? "We do not know, Master," they replied.
"But I shall ask you something," he said. "Ask, Master; we shall answer if we know," they replied.
The Elder asked, "What is 'one'? They did not know. The Elder gave the answer.
They said, "Master, we are defeated; you have won. "Now what will you do? [They replied: "By our parents..."
“This is the instruction given: ‘If a householder should break with you, you should become his wives;
if he has gone forth, you should go forth in his presence. Therefore, grant us the going-forth.
The Elder said, “Very well,” and ordained them all in the presence of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā. Before long, they all attained arahantship.

They attained [the fruit]. Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, "Friends, the Elder Sāriputta, acting as a refuge for four female wanderers, led them all to Arahantship.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? and when they replied, "About this very matter," he said:
“Monks, it is not only now that he has been their refuge; in the past as well, he was their refuge.
But now he has caused them to receive the consecration of the going-forth, whereas in the past he established them in the position of chief queen. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while King Kāliṅga was reigning in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kāliṅga, in the city of Pāṭali in the kingdom of Assaka...
A king named Assaka ruled the kingdom. Kāliṅga possessed a full complement of troops and vehicles, and being himself as strong as an elephant, he saw no rival worthy of his match.
Desiring to wage war, he informed his ministers, "I am seeking battle, yet I see no opponent;
what shall we do? The ministers replied, "There is a certain means, Great King: you have four daughters."
"Adorned with the most excellent forms, let us have them beautified, place them in covered carriages, and surrounded by our forces, let us go through the villages, towns, and royal capitals.
Whichever king desires to take them for himself, with him we shall wage war," they said.
The king acted accordingly. Wherever they went, the kings, out of fear, [refrained from] entering their city.
They did not give [anything], but sent gifts and made them dwell outside the city.
Thus, having wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, they reached Pāṭalipura in the kingdom of Assaka. Assaka, for his part, had the city gates closed and sent a gift.
He had a minister named Nandisena, who was wise, competent, and skilled in means. He thought: "It is said that these..."
“The daughters of the king have roamed throughout the whole of Jambudīpa but did not find a rival;
such being the case, Jambudīpa has become empty. I shall fight with the King of Kāliṅga.
Having gone to the city gate and addressed the gatekeepers, he spoke the first verse in order to have the gate opened for them:
“Open this gate; let Aruṇarāja enter the city, well-guarded by Sīha, Susiṭṭha, Surakkhita, and Nandisena. In that context, “of Aruṇarāja”:
for when he was established in the kingdom, he became known by the name Assaka according to the name of his realm.
His name, however, was Aruṇa, given by his family; thus he said, "Of Aruṇarāja. By "Sīha" is meant the lion among men.
By "well-trained" is meant well-instructed by teachers. By "Nandisena" is meant by me, Nandisena by name.
Having spoken thus, he had the door opened, took them, and gave them to the king of Assaka, saying, "Do not be afraid."
"If there is war, I shall be victorious; therefore, make these princesses, who possess the most excellent beauty, my chief queens.

Having thus caused their consecration to be performed, he dismissed the men who had come with them, saying, "Go, and inform your king that the princesses have been appointed to the position of chief queens by the King of Assaka. They went and reported this.
Kāliṅga, saying, "Surely he does not know my strength," set out immediately with a great army.
Nandisena, learning of his approach, sent a message: "Let it be within his own royal domain;
let him not enter the royal domain of our king. Let the battle take place between the two kingdoms."
Thus, having heard the message, Sāsana remained within the boundaries of his own kingdom, and Assaka likewise remained within the boundaries of his own kingdom.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth as an ascetic, lived in a leaf-hut between those two kingdoms.
Kāliṅga thought: "These recluses might know something; who knows what will happen?"
"Whichever shall have victory or defeat, I will ask the ascetic.
Thinking thus, he approached the Bodhisatta in the guise of a stranger, paid homage, sat down to one side, exchanged pleasantries, and said:
"Venerable sir, Kāliṅga and Assaka both desire to fight, yet they remain each within their own respective royal boundaries; of these two, which one will be victorious?"
"Whose defeat is it? he asked. "O one of great merit, I do not know who will win and who will lose," [the deity] replied.
"However, Sakka, the king of the gods, is coming here; having questioned him, I shall tell you. Please come tomorrow.
Sakka came to attend upon the Bodhisatta and sat down; then the Bodhisatta questioned him regarding that matter.
“Venerable sir, the King of Kalinga will be victorious and Assaka will be defeated; these and those preliminary signs will appear.
On the following day, the King of Kalinga arrived and asked [the Bodhisatta], who explained it to him as well.
Without even asking, “What kind of preliminary sign could there be? he rose up, saying, “I shall indeed be victorious,” and departed in great joy. Such was the talk.
It spread widely. Having heard this, Assaka summoned Nandisena and said, "They say Kāliṅga will surely be victorious and we shall be defeated;

what indeed should be done? He [Nandisena] reassured the king, saying, "Who knows this, O Great King—whether there will be victory or defeat for either side? Do not worry," and then he approached the Bodhisatta.
Having paid homage, he sat to one side and asked, "Venerable sir, who will be victorious and who will be defeated?
"The King of Kāliṅga will be victorious and Assaka will be defeated. "Venerable sir, what will be the omen for the victor, and what for the vanquished?
"O one of great merit, for the victor, the protective deity will become a pure white bull."
“The other will be entirely black; the protective deities of both sides will fight and bring about victory and defeat.
Having heard this, Nandisena rose and went to fetch a thousand great warriors who were the king’s companions.
Taking them with him, he climbed a mountain nearby and asked, “Sirs, are you able to give our king his life? “Yes,” they replied.
“We shall be able,” they replied. “In that case, throw yourselves down this precipice! They began to throw themselves down.
Then, restraining them, he said, “Enough with throwing yourselves down here! Be well-disposed and fight without turning back to give our king his life. They accepted his words.
Then, when the battle was at hand, the King of Kalinga fell into complacency, thinking, "I shall surely be victorious.
His army also fell into complacency, thinking, "Victory is surely ours," and without donning their armor, they departed in groups as they pleased;
they did not exert effort when it was time to exert effort. Both kings, having mounted their horses—
Thinking, “We shall fight,” they approached one another. The protective deities of both went ahead;
the protective deity of King Kāliṅga became a pure white bull, while that of the other was entirely black.
Those deities also approached, displaying the manner of fighting with one another. However, those two bulls appeared as belonging to the two kings themselves.
Not for others. Nandisena asked the King of Assaka, “Is your protective deity visible to you, Great King? “Yes, he is visible,” he replied.

“In what form? “The protective deity of the King of Kāliṅga appears as a completely white bull, whereas our own protective deity stands there appearing as a completely black dog. “Great King, [it is so].”
"Do not be afraid; we shall conquer, and Kāliṅga shall be defeated.

Descend from the backs of your horses, take this spear, and pressing down on the belly of this well-trained Sindhava horse with your left hand, go swiftly with these one thousand men and strike down the protective deity of King Kāliṅga with a blow of this spear; then we—"
“A thousand of us shall strike with seven thousand spears; thus the protective deity of Kāliṅga will perish, and then Kāliṅga will be defeated, while we shall be victorious.
The king said, “Very well,” and having gone after receiving the signal given by Nandisena, he struck with a spear.
The thousand brave warriors and the seven thousand ministers also struck with their spears. The protective deity—
Right there he met his end, and at that very moment the King of Kalinga, having been defeated, fled.
Seeing him fleeing, about a thousand ministers cried out, "The King of Kalinga is fleeing!
Fleeing in terror of death, the King of Kalinga reviled the ascetic and spoke this second verse:
“Victory belongs to the Kalingas, who are capable of enduring the unbearable; defeat and misfortune belong to the Assakas.
Thus indeed was it spoken by you, O practitioner of the holy life; those who have become upright do not speak falsely.
In this context, “capable of enduring the unbearable” means capable of bearing what is difficult to bear. “Thus indeed was it spoken by you” [is said].
Thus she spoke, saying that by accepting a bribe, that false ascetic would defeat the defeated king and cause the victorious king to be defeated.
"Those who have become upright in body, speech, and mind do not speak falsehood.
Having thus reviled the ascetic, he fled and returned to his own city; even looking back, he did not turn around.
He was unable to do so. Then, after a few days had passed, Sakka went to visit the ascetic.
While conversing with him, the ascetic spoke this third verse:
“O Sakka, among the gods who have transcended false speech, truth is their supreme wealth.”
"That which you have spoken to me, O King of Gods, was a falsehood; on what grounds did Maghavā say this to Mahinda?
Therein, "that which you have spoken to me" means that by speaking words that destroy the welfare of others, you have uttered a lie.
"On what grounds did you speak thus?"—having heard this, Sakka spoke the fourth verse:
“Have you not heard, brahmin, while it was being recited: ‘The gods do not prevail over human prowess;
self-control, unbreakable concentration of mind, composure, and timely exertion;
firm energy and human effort—by these alone came the victory of the Assakas’?”
The meaning of this is as follows: "What is it, brahmin, that you have never heard before in those various statements being recited—that the devas do not envy or feel jealous of human prowess?

It is the self-taming known as 'taming' (dama) through the exertion of energy by King Assaka; the indivisibility of the mind through harmony, which is 'indivisible concentration' (abhejjasamādhi); [and] that of King Assaka..."
At the time of exerting effort among companions, there was non-distraction; just as the people of Kāliṅga retreated by breaking into separate factions,
so too, because they did not retreat and were of one accord with unbroken minds, their energy and human prowess became firm,
and for that very reason the Assakas achieved victory.
When Kaliṅga had fled, the horse-king Assaka, having caused a plundering, returned to his own city.
Nandisena sent a message to Kaliṅga, saying: "Send the portion of the inheritance belonging to these four princesses;
if you do not send it, we shall know what must be done in this matter. Having heard that message, he was terrified and trembling because of them.
He sent back the inheritance he had received, and from that time on they lived in harmony.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the daughters of King Kāliṅga were these young bhikkhunīs; Nandisena was Sāriputta; and as for the ascetic, it was I myself.
This is the first commentary on the Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka.
[302] 2. The Commentary on the Mahāassāroha Jātaka:
"Giving what is not to be given. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Ānanda.
The present-day story has already been told above. The Teacher said, "The ancient sages also, solely through the power of their own helpfulness..."
Having said, "They did so," he brought up a past event here as well.
In the past, the Bodhisatta, having been the King of Bārāṇasī, ruled his kingdom righteously and justly; he gave alms and observed moral virtue.
Thinking, "I shall pacify the rebellious border region," he went there surrounded by a great army and transport, but was defeated.
Having mounted his horse, he fled and reached a frontier village. There lived thirty royal servants.
At dawn, they would assemble in the center of the village and attend to their village affairs.
At that moment, the king, having mounted his saddled horse and being fully adorned and prepared, entered the village through its gate. They [asked], "What..."
Thinking, "What now shall we do?", they fled in fear and entered their respective homes. However, one man there did not go to his own house, but went out to meet the king and asked:
"It is heard that the king has gone to the borderlands; who are you—a royal official or a bandit?
He replied, "I am a royal official, sir. "Then come along," he said, and led him to the king's residence.
Having had him seated upon his own seat, he said, "Come, lady, wash your friend's feet," and had his wife wash his feet.
Then, having given him food according to his own means, he prepared a bed, saying, "Rest for a moment," and the king lay down.
The other, having removed the horse's armor, made it walk about, gave it water to drink, and [attended to its needs].

Having smeared his back with oil, he gave him grass. Thus, after attending to the king for three or four days, when the king said, "I am going, my good friend," he once again performed everything appropriate for both the king and the horse.
The king, being pleased, as he was departing, said: "My good friend, I am known as the Great Horse-Rider; our house is in the middle of the city."

"If you come to the city on any business, stand at the southern gate, ask the gatekeeper, 'In which house does the great horseman reside?', and having taken the gatekeeper with you, please come to our house," she said, and then she departed.
The army, not seeing the king, remained encamped outside the city; but upon seeing the king, they went out to meet him.
He surrounded [it]. As the king was entering the city, he stood at the gateway, summoned the gatekeeper, and had the great crowd withdraw, saying:
"Dear son, a certain inhabitant of a frontier village has come wishing to see me;
he will ask, 'Where is the house of Mahāassāroha? You must take him by the hand, bring him here, and show him to me. Then—"
“You shall receive a thousand,” he said. But he did not come. While he was not coming, the king caused the tax to be increased in the village where he lived;
yet when the tax was increased, he still did not come. Thus the king caused the tax to be increased a second and a third time, but he did not come at all.
Then the villagers gathered together and said, “Noble sir, for your friend, the great horseman—”
"From the moment you arrived, we have been so oppressed by the tax-collector that we cannot even lift our heads.
Go, speak to your friend, the great horseman, and have him remit our tax. "Very well, I shall go;
however, it is not possible to go empty-handed. My friend has two children, and for them and their wife..."
“Prepare robes, garments, ornaments, and so forth for both myself and my companion. “Very well, we shall prepare them,” they replied, and they prepared all the gifts.
He took those and the cakes he had baked in his own house, went there, and upon reaching the southern gate, he asked the gatekeeper:

“Friend, where is the house of the great horseman? He replied, “Come, I will show you,” and taking him by the hand, he went to the palace gate and announced, “The gatekeeper has arrived bringing a resident of a frontier village.
Upon hearing this, the king rose from his seat and went out to meet them, saying, “Let my friend and those who have come with him enter.”
Having done so and seeing her, he embraced her and asked, "Are my companion and children healthy?
Then, taking her by the hand, he ascended the great terrace, seated her upon the royal throne beneath the white parasol, and summoned the chief queen, saying, "Noble lady, wash my companion's feet.
She washed his feet, and the king, with a golden pitcher—
He poured water [over his feet]. The queen also washed his feet and anointed them with fragrant oil.
The king asked, "Friend, is there anything for us to eat? He replied, "There is," and had cakes brought out from a small bag.
Taking them with a golden platter, the king, showing him favor, said, "Eat what has been brought by my companion."
Having caused the queen and the ministers to eat, he himself also ate. The other presented another gift to the other as well.
For the sake of winning his favor, the king removed his own Kāsika garments and put on the pair of garments brought by him.
The queen also removed her Kāsika garments and her ornaments, put on the garment brought by him, and fastened the ornaments.
Then the king, having fed him with food worthy of a king, commanded a minister:

“Go, have his beard and hair trimmed according to my own custom, bathe him with scented water, clothe him in a Kāsī cloth worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], adorn him with royal ornaments, and bring him back.
He did exactly so. The king [had a drum beaten] in the city—
Having had this done and having assembled his ministers, he dropped a thread dyed with vermilion from his birth onto the middle of the white parasol and granted him half the kingdom.
From that time on, they ate, drank, and slept together;
their mutual trust became firm and could not be broken by anyone. Then the king, having summoned his son and daughter-in-law as well, established them in a residence within the city.
Having had it built, he gave it to them. They ruled the kingdom together, living in harmony and mutual affection.
Then the ministers, becoming angry, said to the prince: "Prince, the king has given half the kingdom to a certain householder;
he eats, drinks, and sleeps with him, and even has his children prostrate before him. By this king—"
“We do not know what deed has been done; we do not know what the king is doing, and we are ashamed. You must tell the king.
He consented, saying, “Very well,” and having reported all those words to the king, he said, “Do not act thus, Great King.
“Dear son, where did I dwell after being defeated in battle? Do you know? “We do not know, Your Majesty. “I—”
"Living in this man's house, I returned healthy and ruled the kingdom;
why then should I not grant prosperity to one who has been so helpful to me? Having said this, the Bodhisatta spoke these verses, demonstrating:
"My dear son, he who gives to one who does not deserve to receive and does not give to one who deserves to receive, finds no help at all when he falls into calamity."
“He who gives gifts to those unworthy of receiving them, and does not bestow them upon those worthy of receiving them,
meets with calamity when in distress and finds no companion.
But he who does not give gifts to those unworthy of receiving them, and who bestows them upon those worthy of receiving them— ”
When one falls into calamity in the midst of misfortunes, one finds a companion.
"The distinction between association and enjoyment perishes among ignoble, deceitful people;
yet even a tiny act done toward noble and upright persons becomes of great fruit."
“He who has previously performed what is good, and has done what is very difficult in this world—whether he should do so later or not—he is worthy of ultimate honor.

In this context, “toward those who have not rendered service” means toward those who have not previously performed a favor. “Toward those who have rendered service” means toward those who have previously performed a favor. “He does not bestow [favor]” means...
He does not let [the guest] enter, nor does he give [anything]. "In calamities" means in times of misfortune. "Calamity" means suffering.

"Showing the excellence of association and enjoyment" means showing the distinction between the association and the enjoyment provided by a friend; that is, showing the excellence of the virtues [thinking], "This person has done much for me.
All of this perishes because of its impure nature, because it belongs among ignoble qualities, and because of deceitfulness toward the crafty.

"Among the noble ones" (*ariyesu*) means among those who are purified by their own recognition of the virtues they have cultivated. "Among the upright" (*ajjavesu*) means for that very reason, among those who are straight and not crooked.
"Even the slightest" (*aṇumpi*) means even a small amount. "In such as these" (*tādisū*) refers to those persons who are noble and upright;
in them, even a small deed becomes of great fruit, of great radiance, and of great expansion, because it is planted in a fertile field.
The meaning is that [a deed] does not perish like a sown seed, whereas even a great deal of evil committed elsewhere perishes like a seed cast into fire. And this has been said:
"Just as a seed burned in fire does not sprout;..."
Thus what is done for an unworthy person perishes and does not flourish.
But in a person who is grateful, virtuous, and of noble conduct—
just as seeds in a good field— what is done for such a person does not perish.

"Having previously done what is good" means having stood by after first performing a service. "He did it" (*akā*) means he performed it; the sense is that he has done what is called "very difficult to do" in this world.

"Should he do it later" means whether he performs some other virtue later or not, by that very first virtue performed, he becomes worthy of ultimate honor; he is worthy of all respect and hospitality.
But having heard this, neither the ministers nor the prince said anything further.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the inhabitant of the frontier village, and I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī.
This concludes the second commentary on the Mahāassāroha Jātaka.
[303] 3. The Exposition of the Ekarāja-jātaka.
"When the unsurpassed qualities of sensual pleasure are perfected"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain servant of the King of Kosala.
The present-day account has already been told below in the Seyya-jātaka; however, here the Teacher...
"It was not only you who brought about your own ruin for no purpose; even the ancient wise men brought about their own ruin for no purpose. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, a minister who served as an attendant to the King of Bārāṇasī acted treacherously within the royal palace.
The king, having personally witnessed his misconduct, banished him from the kingdom. He then went to serve the King of Kosala, named Dubbhisena.

All of this has already been told in the Mahāsīlava Jātaka. Here, however, Dubbhisena had the King of Bārāṇasī, who was seated among his ministers on the great terrace, seized, placed in a swing-basket, and hung upside down by his head from the northern lintel.
The king, having cultivated loving-kindness (mettā) directed toward the robber-king and having performed the preliminary work for the kasiṇa, attained meditative absorption (jhāna).
The bonds were severed, and then the king sat cross-legged in the air. A fever arose in the body of the king of thieves, and crying out, "I am burning!
I am burning! he rolled back and forth upon the ground.
When asked, "What is this?", he replied, "Great King, you have had such a righteous king, who was innocent, hung with his head downward at the upper bolt of the gate."
They said, "In that case, go quickly and release him! The men went and saw the king sitting cross-legged in the air;
returning, they reported this to Dabbasena. He went in haste, paid homage to him, and in order to ask for forgiveness, he spoke the first verse:
“Having formerly enjoyed supreme sensual pleasures and ruled as a sole monarch, you are now cast into the difficult hell; yet you do not abandon your former beauty and strength.
Therein, *vasī* means “dwelt”; *ekarājā* is an address to the Bodhisatta by name; *so dāni* means “you, that very person, now.”
"Duggeti visame" means on uneven ground. "Narakamhīti āvāṭe" refers to a pit; this was said with reference to the place where he was suspended.
"Nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇaṃ" asks: even though you were cast into such an uneven place, did you not abandon your former complexion and strength?
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses:
“Formerly, indeed, patience and austerity were desired by me even at the cost of ill repute;
having now obtained that, O King, how could I abandon my former beauty and strength?
All these things, it is said, are thus brought to completion when they have overcome one who is illustrious and wise.”
“Having obtained former, sublime fame, one should not abandon one’s former reputation and strength.
O Lord of Men, having cast away happiness with suffering, or suffering with happiness, endure them both with fortitude;
for the virtuous, being fully extinguished in both states, remain the same in pleasure and in pain.”
In this context, "patience" (*khanti*) means patience as endurance. "Austerity" (*tapa*) means the practice of asceticism.
"Sought after" (*sampatthitā*) means desired or longed for. "By Dubbhisena"—with that name he addresses him. "Having now obtained that"—meaning having now obtained that aspiration.
"Should I abandon?"—for what reason should I abandon it? He points out that one who experiences either suffering or mental distress would indeed abandon it.
“‘All these duties have indeed been completed,’ he said, showing his own success by way of oral tradition.
This is what is meant: ‘All the duties to be performed by me—giving, virtue, meditation, and the Uposatha rites—have already been finished.
He is ‘renowned’ (*yasassin*) because of the excellence of his retinue, and ‘possessed of wisdom’ (*paññavant*) because of the perfection of his insight. (*Visayha* means capable of being overcome.)
"O wise ones, for the sake of accomplishing what was previously unaccomplished, [strive] for what is to be accomplished. Thus, these three are merely forms of address. Here, "na" is a particle;

it should be understood that the nasalization of the letter *n* is employed for the sake of the elegance of the phrasing (*byañjanasiliṭṭhatā*). "Yaso ca" means "and fame"; or rather, this very reading [is preferred].
"Laddhā purimaṃ" means having obtained what was previously unobtained in the past. "Uḷāraṃ" means...
"Great. He spoke thus with reference to the suppression of defilements, the development of loving-kindness, and the arising of jhāna. "I shall not abandon it":
having obtained such glory, for what reason would I give up my former complexion and strength? This is the meaning. "With suffering":
by the suffering of being cast into hell produced by you, having dispelled my royal happiness.
"Or by happiness as suffering": having dispelled that suffering by means of the happiness of jhāna. "Peaceful in both cases":
those who are peaceful like me are, in these two categories, of a nature thoroughly quenched;
they are equanimous toward both pleasure and pain, being identical and entirely unchanged.
Having heard this, Dubbhisena asked the Bodhisatta for forgiveness and said, "You yourselves should exercise your sovereignty;
I shall ward off your enemies. Having issued a royal command against that wicked minister, he departed.
The Bodhisatta, in turn, handed over the kingdom to his ministers, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and was destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Dubbhisena was Ānanda, and the King of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.
This concludes the third narrative, the Commentary on the Ekarāja Jātaka.
4. The Commentary on the Daddara Jātaka.
"These verses were spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain angry bhikkhu.

The background story has already been told below. At that time, when a discussion regarding that bhikkhu’s anger had arisen in the Dhamma Hall, the Teacher arrived and asked, 'Bhikkhus, about what talk are you gathered here now? [They replied: 'About this...'"
When he was thus addressed, the Buddha had him summoned and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are prone to anger?
When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, this man was prone to anger.
Because of his very nature of anger, even though these ancient wise ones remained in the state of a pure Naga king, for three years [he dwelt] in a cesspool filled with excrement."
Having said, "They dwelt [there]," he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was the son of King Daddara, who reigned over the Naga abode named Daddara on the foot of Mount Daddara in the Himalayan region. His name was Mahādaddara.
His younger brother was named Cūḷadaddara. He was irascible and harsh, wandering about reviling, abusing, and striking the young Nāgas.
When the Nāga king learned of his cruelty, he ordered him to be expelled from the Nāga realm.
However, Mahādaddara begged his father for forgiveness and restrained him. A second time...
The king was angry with him; he asked for forgiveness a second time. But on the third occasion, [the king said], "You prevented me from having this man of improper conduct expelled.
Go, both of you, leave this Nāga-abode and dwell for three years in a dung-heap in Bārāṇasī. He had them driven out of the Nāga-abode, and they went there and lived. Then...

While he was seeking his alms-round near the edge of a body of water on a dung-heap, village children saw him and, striking him and throwing clods, sticks, and other objects, reviled and abused him, saying, "Who are these broad-headed ones with needle-like toes? Are they water-urchins or frog-eaters? and so forth.
Cūḷadaddara, unable to endure that insult because of their fierce and harsh nature, spoke to his brother, saying: "Brother, these children despise us;
they do not know our true nature as venomous snakes. I cannot bear their contempt;
I shall destroy them with the blast of my nostrils. Speaking thus with his brother, he uttered the first verse:
“‘These harsh words spoken by people in the human world burn me, Daddara;
those who eat frogs and dwell at the water’s edge are biting me, though I am a non-venomous snake.

In this context, “burning” means causing suffering. Regarding the phrase “those who eat frogs and dwell at the water’s edge”: these village children, who call me a “frog-eater” and a “water-dweller,” are biting and reviling me as if I were a venomous snake, even though I am not.
Having heard his words, Mahādaddara recited the remaining verses:
"Exiled from his own kingdom, he has gone to another country;
He should build a great storehouse for the storing of insults."
“Where people do not know one by birth or by training,
there one should not exercise pride toward strangers who live under one’s authority.
Even while living abroad, one should remain like fire.”
"A wise person should forgive even a servant who has been rebuked.
In this regard, "the harsh words should be stored away" means that just as one might build a large granary for the purpose of storing grain,
fill it, and then utilize the grain when a need arises, even so, a wise person who has gone abroad [to a foreign land] should store the harsh words within his own heart.
One should construct a large storehouse for the purpose of storage. Having stored those harsh words there, one will act as appropriate when the time comes for oneself to be capable again.

Regarding the phrase "by birth or by discipline": this refers to cases where people do not recognize someone as such on account of their birth or discipline—such as thinking, "This person is a kṣatriya or a brāhmaṇa," or "He is virtuous, learned, and endowed with good qualities."
The meaning is as follows: "Mānaṃ" means they address me with such a lowly designation; they do not honor me, they do not respect me—thus one should not be proud (*mānaṃ na kareyya*).
"Vasamaññātake jane" means living in the presence of people who are ignorant of one's own birth, clan, and so forth.
"Vasato" means by one who lives; or this very reading (*vasatā*) is the text.
Thus they lived there for three years. Then their father summoned them, and from that time forth they became humble in spirit.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka;
at the conclusion of the Truths, the angry monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). "At that time, Cūḷadaddara was the angry monk."
"But the Great Daddara was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Daddara Jātaka, the fourth.
[305] 5. Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka.
"There is no such thing as privacy in the world. This was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the subduing of the defilements.
The story will be revealed in the *Pānīyajātaka* of the *Ekādasakanipāta*. Here, however, is the summary:
Five hundred bhikkhus, residing within Jetavana, gave rise to thoughts of sensual desire immediately following the middle watch of the night. The Teacher—
Just as a one-eyed man protects his eye, a man with an only son protects his son, or a yak protects its tail,
so too did he constantly watch over the bhikkhus. In the middle of the night, surveying Jetavana with his divine eye,
he saw those bhikkhus like thieves who had arisen within the residence of a universal monarch.
Having opened the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) and addressed the Elder Ānanda, he said:
“Ānanda, having assembled the bhikkhus who are staying in the Jeta Grove on their straw mats, prepare a seat at the door of the fragrant chamber.
He did so and informed the Teacher. The Teacher, having sat down on the prepared seat, addressed them by way of a general assembly.
“Monks,” he said, “in the past, the wise did not commit evil, thinking, ‘There is no such thing as secrecy in the doing of evil.
Having said this, at their request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity, he studied the craft right there in Bārāṇasī, becoming the eldest among five hundred young brahmins under a world-renowned teacher.
Now, that teacher had a daughter who had also reached maturity.
He thought, "I shall test the character of these young men and give my daughter only to one who is endowed with virtue. One day, he...
Having addressed his young men, he said: "Sons, my daughter has reached marriageable age; I shall arrange her wedding, and it is necessary for her to receive clothing and ornaments.
Go, each of you, and having stolen them from your own kinsmen while they are unaware, bring back the clothing and ornaments.
I will accept only what has not been seen by anyone; I will not accept anything brought after it has been shown."
He said: "Very well," they agreed, and from then on, they would steal clothes, ornaments, and other items from their relatives while they were not looking and bring them back.
The teacher set aside each item as it was brought. But the Bodhisatta did not bring anything at all.
Then the teacher said to him, "But you, dear boy, have not brought anything? "Yes, teacher. "Why?"
"Father! [he said]. "Do not accept what has been brought for you while anyone is looking on; however, I see no such thing as 'privacy' when it comes to performing evil deeds.
Demonstrating this, he spoke these two verses:

"There is no such thing as privacy in the world for one who performs an evil deed; there is no hiding place in the sky, nor in the depths of the ocean, nor in a mountain cave, where one could escape the King of Dharma."
Seeing the forested places, the fool imagines them to be secluded:
"I see no one secluded, nor does any emptiness exist;
wherever I do not see another, that place is not empty for me."
In this context, *raho* means a concealed place. *Vanabhūtāni* means those things produced in the forest.
*Taṃ bālo* means that the fool thinks, "This evil deed was committed by me in secret. *Suññaṃ vāpi* refers to whatever place might be empty or void of beings;
he says that even such a place does not exist.
The teacher, being pleased with him, said, "Dear son, it is not that there is no wealth in my house;
rather, desiring to give my daughter to one endowed with virtue, I acted thus while testing these young men. My daughter is truly worthy of you alone.
Having adorned his daughter, he gave her to the Bodhisatta. To the other young men he said, "Whatever you have brought back shall be yours."
“Take her home yourself,” he said.
The Teacher said, “Thus, monks, because of their own immorality those immoral youths did not obtain that woman, while the other wise youth obtained her because of his perfection in virtue.
Having spoken thus, and having become fully enlightened, he recited the other two verses:
“Dujjaca, Sujaca, Nanda, Sukhavaddhita, Vajja, and Addhuvasīla— they abandoned the Dhamma out of self-interest.
How could a brahmin who has reached the further shore of all phenomena abandon it?”
“He who upholds the Dhamma, steadfast and striving for truth.
In this context, the names of the six leading young men—beginning with Dujjaca—were mentioned;
he did not mention the names of the rest, but spoke generally of them all as “those young men who have abandoned the Dhamma. Therein, “those” refers to all those young men.
"Dhamma" means the state of obtaining womanhood. "Jahumatthikā" means those who desired [it] abandoned [it]; or this is the very reading [of the text].
The letter *m* is used for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*) between words and syllables. This is what is meant:
all those young men, though they were indeed desirous of that woman, abandoned that state of obtaining womanhood because of their own immorality.
"And the brahmin" refers, on the other hand, to another who is endowed with virtue (*sīla*). "How will he abandon? means by what cause will he abandon that inherent nature of obtaining womanhood?
"Of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammānaṃ*): in this context, the five mundane precepts, the ten precepts, and the three types of good conduct are called "all phenomena";
he has gone to the further shore of these, thus he is "one who has reached the further shore" (*pāragū*). "Phenomenon" (*dhamma*) refers to that very kind already mentioned.
“He who guards the Dhamma” means he who protects it. “Possessed of steadfastness” means endowed with the steadfastness that consists in guarding virtue.
“One who exerts himself for truth” means one who is endowed with exertion toward truth—that is, toward the nature of things as they are, namely, the aforementioned qualities of virtue.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, those five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
At that time, the teacher was Sāriputta, while I myself was the wise youth.
This concludes the fifth commentary, the Sīlavīmaṃsana-jātaka.
[306] 6. The Commentary on the Sujāta-jātaka.
“Kimaṇḍakā”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning Queen Mallikā.
It is said that one day a dispute arose between the king and her; some even say it was a “bed-quarrel. The king became so angry that he did not even know she existed.
Queen Mallikā, too, [realized] that the Teacher did not know the king’s state of anger toward her.
"He surely knows," he thought. The Teacher, perceiving this, decided, "I shall bring about harmony among these men.
Having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Sāvatthī accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus and went to the king's gate.
The king took the Tathāgata’s bowl, led him into his residence, and having had him seated on a prepared seat, [served him].
Having offered water for the hands to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he served rice gruel and solid food.
The Teacher covered his bowl with his hand and asked, "Great King, where is the Queen? "What of her, Bhante?
She is intoxicated by her own glory. "Great King, having bestowed glory upon herself, she has cast aside her womanhood; what was done by her..."
"It is not right not to tolerate an offense. Having heard the Teacher's words, the king summoned her;
she served the Teacher. The Teacher, saying, "It is fitting that you live in harmony with one another," spoke in praise of concord and then departed.
From then on, the two of them lived in harmony. The monks [discussed this] in the Hall of Truth.
"How did they report it? [They replied,] "Friends, the Teacher has made both sides harmonious with a single word.
The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now? When they said, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, I made these two harmonious by means of a single word. Having said this, to them...
Being requested, he related a past event.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister, providing him with counsel regarding both worldly affairs and the Dhamma.
Then one day, the king stood by an open window, looking out over the royal courtyard.

At that moment, a merchant’s daughter named Sujātā—beautiful and in the prime of her youth—was walking through the royal courtyard with a basket of jujubes on her head, crying out, "Take jujubes! Take jujubes!
When the king heard her voice, his heart became bound to her; and perceiving that she was unmarried, he summoned her.
Having appointed her to the position of chief queen, he bestowed great honor upon her. She became dear and pleasing to the king.

Then one day, the king sat eating jujube fruits on a golden platter. At that time, Queen Sujātā, seeing the king eating the jujube fruits, asked, "Great King, what indeed are you eating? and spoke the first verse:
“O King, what are these ‘kimaṇḍakas’ placed in this bronze bowl?
They are reddish and beautiful; please explain them to me when asked.

In this context, *kimaṇḍakā* means “what fruits are these? However, he calls them *aṇḍaka* because of their spherical shape. *Kaṃsamallake* means in a golden dish. *Upalohitakā* means red-colored. *Vaggū* means clean and stainless.
The king, becoming angry, said, "O merchant’s daughter, you do not even recognize the jujube fruits belonging to your own family," and spoke these two verses:
"Those jujube fruits which you, O Queen, formerly gathered with basket in hand while dressed in rags and tattered clothes—
of those, this is the Koliyan fruit for you."
“It is being carried off and does not delight; it abandons him of its own accord.
Bring this back right there, where they will cook the kola.
In that context, *bhaṇḍū* means one with a shaven head. *Nantakavāsinī* means clothed in worn-out rags. *Ucchaṅgahatthā* means carrying [the child] in her lap.
"Having entered the forest, you gathered [the fruit] by bending down a branch with a hook, and having repeatedly plucked it, you placed it in your lap;
thus, being 'lap-handed' (*ucchaṅgahatthā*), you gathered and plucked it.
As you were thus gathering and plucking it, this *koliya* fruit—which I am now eating—fell from you."
The meaning is that what was given to the family bears fruit.
"She is scorched and finds no delight" means that this wretched woman, while living in this royal family, is scorched and finds no pleasure, as if she were cast into a cauldron of molten iron.
"Wealth" refers to the king's wealth; it abandons this unfortunate woman. Where...
"Wherever they say she will go thinking, 'I shall cook *kola* fruits,' take her there so that she may earn her livelihood by gathering and selling only *badara* fruits," he said.
The Bodhisatta, perceiving that "no one other than myself will be able to reconcile these two," convinced the king and thought, "I shall ensure she is not driven out," and spoke the fourth verse:
“O Great King, such faults of negligence indeed occur even for a woman who has attained glory;
therefore, O Lord, forgive Sujātā, do not be angry with her, O Bull among Charioteers.
The meaning of this is: O Great King, such faults of negligence certainly happen even to a woman who has attained fame; this—
Having placed her in such a high position, he now said: "It is not fitting for you to be unable to endure such a transgression;
therefore, O King, forgive Sujātā. Do not be angry with her, O bull among charioteers, O foremost of charioteers.
At his word, the king forgave that offense of the queen and restored her to her former place. From then on, the two lived together in harmony.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was the King of Kosala, Sujātā was Mallikā, and the minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Sujātā Jātaka, the sixth.
7. The Commentary on the Palāsa Jātaka.
"O Brahmin, it is insentient and does not hear"—this the Teacher spoke while lying on his deathbed concerning the Venerable Ānanda.
That venerable one, having known, "Today at the time of dawn, the Teacher will attain final nibbāna," thought:
"I am still a trainee with tasks yet to be done, and the Teacher’s final nibbāna is imminent; [twenty-five...]"
“The service rendered to the Teacher for years will be fruitless.
Overcome by grief, he leaned against a monkey’s-head pillar in a garden hut and wept. Not seeing him, the Teacher asked, “Bhikkhus, where is Ānanda?
Having heard the reason for his absence, he had him summoned and said, “Ānanda, you have performed meritorious deeds; apply yourself to striving, for quickly—”
“You shall become free from taints; do not worry. For what reason would the service you have now rendered me be fruitless?
Even in the past, when you were still possessed of lust and other defilements, the service you rendered me was not without fruit. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity dwelling in a *palāsa* tree not far from Bārāṇasī.
Having made the offering, he was reborn there. At that time, the people living in Bārāṇasī were devotees of deities, constantly engaged in making offerings and other such rites.

Then, a certain poor Brahmin thought, "I too shall attend upon a deity," and having leveled and cleared the ground at the foot of a large Palāsa tree standing on a high spot, he surrounded it with sand.

Having scattered [flowers], swept [the area], applied five-finger marks of perfume on the tree, honored it with garlands, scents, and incense, lit a lamp, and said, "Sleep well," he circumambulated the tree clockwise and departed.
On the following day, having gone there early in the morning, he inquired after his comfortable sleep. Then one day, the deity of the tree thought: "This brahmin..."
"She is taking care of me exceedingly; having tested this brahmin, I shall show the reason why she takes such care of me.
At that moment, as the brahmin had arrived and was sweeping at the foot of the tree, she stood nearby in the guise of an elderly brahmin woman and spoke the first verse:
“O Brahmin, this leaf is insentient, not hearing, knowing yet not knowing;
you, being diligent, constant, and heedful, ask about a pleasant sleep—for what reason?
In that context, “not hearing” means not hearing precisely because it is insentient. “Knowing” means you, being one who knows, are “constant and heedful,” meaning always heedful.
Having heard that, the brahmin spoke this second verse:
“The tree is far-famed and vast, standing in its place with the form of a dwelling for living beings;
therefore, I revere this leafy tree, and whatever beings dwell here, may they be the cause of my wealth.”
In this context: "Famous from afar," O Brahmin, means this tree is renowned from a distance;
it is not merely well-known in its immediate vicinity. "And great" (*brahā*) means large. "Standing in a place" means standing on a high or level piece of ground.
"Having the nature of a dwelling for beings" means having the character of being a residence for deities; surely some deity of great power must dwell here. Of their wealth...
“Because of this tree and the spirits who dwell within it, I pay homage for the sake of wealth, not without cause.
Hearing this, the tree deity was pleased with the brahmin and said, “Brahmin, I am the deity reborn in this tree;
do not fear, I shall give you wealth. Having thus comforted him, she manifested her great divine power at the door of her own celestial mansion.
Standing in the air, he recited two other verses:
“I shall do for you according to my power, O Brahmin, seeing your gratitude.
For how could the efforts you made upon coming into the presence of the Noble One have been in vain?”
“Where there is a *pilakkhu* tree beyond the *tinduka* tree, surrounded by it, a great sacrificial post (*pubbayañña*) stands;
at its root a treasure is buried. Go, O heirless one, and dig it up!
In this context, “according to his power” means according to his capacity and according to his strength. “Gratitude” means the benefit performed for me by you.
"Knowing that [gratitude] exists within himself and beholding that gratitude," means: "Having come" (*āgamma*) means having approached.
"In the presence of the good" (*sataṃ sakāse*) means in the vicinity of virtuous persons.

"Those stirrings of yours shall be in vain"—how could those stirrings of speech, such as inquiring after your well-being, or those stirrings of body, such as sweeping the floor and so forth, be fruitless for you?

"Whatever *pilakkhu* tree is beyond the *tinduka* tree"—this she shows by extending her hand while standing right at the door of the celestial mansion (*vimāna*), indicating that this *pilakkhu* tree stands on the far side of the *tinduka* tree. Regarding the words "surrounded" (*parivārito*) and so forth:
at the foot of that *pilakkhu* tree, it is "surrounded" because it has been placed encircling the base of that tree; [and] by virtue of sacrifices (*yañña*) previously offered...
It is called a "former sacrifice" (*pubbayañña*) because it arose for former owners; it is "exalted" (*uḷāra*) because of its greatness due to the presence of many treasure-pots;
it is "buried" (*nikhāta*) because it was placed there after digging the ground; and it is "without heirs" (*adāyāda*) because there are currently no heirs to it. This is what is meant:
[he saw] those treasure-pots which, having surrounded the foot of that tree, were striking neck against neck.
"By its power, a great treasure has been buried without an owner; go, dig it up, and take it!
Having spoken thus, that deity said, "Brahmin, if you dig this up and take it, you will only exhaust yourself.
Go! I myself will bring it to your house and deposit it for you in such-and-such and such-and-such places."
"Enjoy this wealth for as long as you live, give gifts, and guard your virtue," he said, giving this advice to the brahmin;
then, by his own supernatural power, he established that wealth in the brahmin's house.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, but the tree deity was none other than myself."
The seventh is the Palāsajātaka Commentary.
[308] 8. The Sakuṇajātaka Commentary:

“We have done you no service,” this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning Devadatta’s ingratitude. Having said, “Monks, it is not only now; formerly too Devadatta was indeed ungrateful,” he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a woodpecker in a region of the Himalayas.
Now, while a certain lion was eating meat, a bone became stuck in his throat;
his throat swelled, he was unable to forage for food, and sharp pains arose. Then, that bird, intent on its own prey—
Seeing him, the bird perched on a branch asked, "Friend, what is your suffering? He explained the matter to him.
[The bird said], "Friend, I could remove this bone for you, but out of fear I do not dare to enter your mouth;
you might even eat me. [The other replied], "Do not be afraid, friend; I will not eat you, give me my life. [The bird said], "Very well," and he—
Having laid him down on his left side and thinking, "Who knows what he will do?", he placed a stick between the lion's upper and lower lips so that he could not close his mouth;
then, entering the mouth, he struck the tip of a bone with his beak. The bone fell out and was gone. Having caused the bone to fall, [he emerged] from the lion’s mouth.
As he was departing, the bird struck Daṇḍaka with its beak, knocking him down, and having emerged, it perched on the tip of a branch.
Once recovered from his illness, the lion one day killed a wild buffalo and was eating it.
Thinking, "I shall test him," the bird perched on a branch above him and, conversing with him, spoke the first verse:
“We have done you a service, for we were of some strength;
O King of Beasts, let there be homage to you, so that we too may receive something.

In this passage, “We have done you a service” means: “O lion, we too have performed a service for you. “For we were of some strength” means: by whatever strength we possessed, we have indeed acted without having deprived you of anything from that strength.
Having heard that, Sīha spoke this second verse:
“While you remain between my teeth, for me who subsists on blood and constantly commits cruel deeds— even though you live, it is much for you.”
Having heard that, the bird spoke these other two verses:
"To one who is ungrateful and does not act [for others], to one who does not repay what has been done for them;
to him in whom gratitude is absent, service is useless."
“He from whose presence one does not obtain the way of friendship because of what was done in his presence—without resentment or reproach, one should slowly withdraw from him.
Therein, *akataññu* means one who does not recognize a service rendered. *Akattāraṃ* means one who does nothing at all. *Sammukhaciṇṇena* means by what was done in his presence.

"By means of the virtue performed in his presence"—meaning that one who does not envy or revile that person should gradually withdraw from that wicked individual without envy or abuse. Having said this, the bird departed.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Devadatta was the lion, and I myself was the bird."
The eighth is the commentary on the Sakuṇa Jātaka.
[309] 9. The commentary on the Chava Jātaka:
"All this has been made final. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the group of six monks (Chabbaggiya).
He related the story. The background account has already been recorded in detail in the Vinaya; here, however, is the summary:
The Teacher summoned the group of six monks and asked, "Is it true, monks, that you sit on a low seat and teach the Dhamma to one sitting on a high seat?
When they replied, "It is so, Venerable Sir," he rebuked those monks, saying, "This is improper..."
“Monks, this is what causes you to show disrespect for my Dhamma; for in the past, wise men, sitting on low seats, even censured those who taught them outside doctrines.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
“In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of outcasts (caṇḍāla) and, having reached maturity...”
He established a household. His wife, having become pregnant with a longing for mangoes, said to him, "Husband, I wish to eat a mango.
He replied, "My dear, there are no mangoes at this time; I will bring you some other sour fruit.
She said, "Husband, I shall live only if I obtain a mango fruit; if I do not obtain it, I have no life. He, for her sake—
With his mind fixed upon it, he thought, "Where indeed shall I find mango fruit?
Now at that time, there was a mango tree in the king’s park at Bārāṇasī that bore fruit constantly. He thought, "I will bring some ripe mangoes from there and thus satisfy her craving.
In the middle of the night, he went to the park, climbed the mango tree, and hid among the branches.
He wandered about gazing at his mother’s branch. As he was doing so, the night turned to dawn.
He thought, "If I descend now and go, they will see me and seize me as a thief; I shall go during the night.
Then, having climbed up into a fork of the tree, he remained there hidden.

Then the King of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "I shall learn the mantras from the presence of the chaplain," entered the park, sat upon a high seat at the foot of a mango tree, had the teacher sit on a low seat, and learned the mantras.
The Bodhisatta, perched above, thought: "How unrighteous is this king, who sits on a high seat while learning the mantras!"
“This brahmin is also unrighteous, who sits on a low seat and recites the mantras.
I too am unrighteous, who, having fallen under the power of a woman and disregarding my own life, brought the mango.
As he was descending from the tree, he caught hold of a hanging branch and positioned himself between the two of them, saying, “Great King, I am lost!”
“You are deluded; the chaplain is dead,” he said. When the king asked him, “For what reason? he recited the first verse:
“All this has been done for the last time; both of you do not see the Dhamma.
Both have fallen from their natural state: he who is here causing the mantras to be forgotten, and [the one who is dead].”
"And he who studies the mantra.
In this regard, "all this was done at last" means that whatever has been done by us three people—all this task is wretched, lawless, and unrighteous.
Thus [he recognized] his own state as a thief and their lack of respect for the mantras.
Having censured [the first two], he spoke the words beginning with "Both do not see the Dhamma," while further censuring those other two.
Therein, "both" refers to these two persons who do not see the ancient Dhamma worthy of reverence;
they have therefore fallen away from the natural state of the Dhamma. For the Dhamma is called the "natural state" (*pakati*) by virtue of its being the primary origin. And this has also been said:
“Dhamma indeed appeared first;
afterwards, non-Dhamma arose in the world.
As for the phrase “he who”: this refers both to the one who, sitting on a low seat, causes [another] to recite the mantras, and to the one who, sitting on a high seat, studies them himself.
Having heard that, the brahmin spoke this second verse:
“I eat rice porridge, pure, with meat as a sauce;
therefore, I do not practice this Dhamma practiced by the seers.”
The meaning of this is: "For indeed, sir, I eat the king’s rice— pure, white,
and sprinkled with various kinds of meat preparations, with meat as its sauce— and because of that, being bound by my belly,
I do not practice this Dhamma which is practiced by seers who seek such qualities."
Having heard that, the other spoke two verses:
“Wander forth, O Great One! Other living beings are also cooking [you];
let not unrighteousness practiced by you split you apart like a jar.”
“Fie on that gain of fame, O brahmin, and on the gain of wealth, if one’s livelihood is through falling into ruin or through practicing unrighteousness.
In this context, *paribbaja* means go elsewhere from here. *Mahā* means this world is indeed great. *Pacantaññepi*... [the rest of the verse].
"Pāṇino" means that in this Jambudīpa there are other living beings (*pāṇino*) who are also cooked; it is not only this king alone.

"He strikes him like a pot with a jar" means a stone [strikes] a pot. This is what is meant: "May that very unrighteousness (*adhamma*), which you practice while dwelling here instead of going elsewhere, not shatter you when practiced in this way, just as a stone [shatters] a pot."
The brief meaning of the verse beginning with “Dhiratthu” is as follows:
O Brahmin, “dhiratthu” means “shame on this!”—we censure this acquisition of fame and this acquisition of wealth of yours. Why?
Because this gain obtained by you serves as the cause for falling into the states of misery in the future, and even now it constitutes a livelihood through unrighteous conduct; and as for this...
“Livelihood arises either from future rebirth in the lower realms or from practicing unrighteousness in this life; what is the use of that? Therefore, I speak to you thus.
Then, having gained confidence through his discourse on the Dhamma, the king asked, “Sir, what is your caste? “I am a caṇḍāla, Your Majesty.
The king said, “Sir, if you had been well-born by birth, I would have given the kingdom to you. From here—”

Then, saying, "From now on, I shall be king by day and you shall be king by night," he had the flower garland adorning his own neck placed around that man's neck and appointed him as the city guardian.
This is the tradition of placing red flower garlands around the necks of city guardians. From then on, the king, abiding by his advice, [honored] the teacher...
"Having shown respect, sitting on a low seat, he learned the mantras.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the Caṇḍāla’s son was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Chava-jātaka.
[310] 10. The Commentary on the Seyyajātaka.
"As far as the ocean's edge"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was despondent.
For while he was walking for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a woman who was beautiful and adorned with ornaments.
He was disenchanted with the Teaching and did not find delight in it. Then the monks informed the Blessed One. When the Blessed One asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are disenchanted?
he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir. When the Buddha asked, "Who has caused you to become disenchanted? he related the matter to him.
The Teacher said, "Why have you become disenchanted after going forth in such a Teaching that leads to liberation?"
"Even in the past, wise men, though they obtained the position of royal chaplain, renounced it and went forth into homelessness," he said, and then related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the chaplain’s Brahmin wife and was born on the same day as the king’s son. The king [thought], "Is there anyone..."
“Was he born on the same day as my son? he asked his ministers. “There is, Great King, the son of the family priest,” they replied.
The king had him brought, entrusted him to the nurses, and had him raised together with his own son.
The ornaments, food, drink, and other provisions for both were exactly the same. When they reached maturity, they grew up together.
Having gone to Takkasilā and mastered all the arts, they returned. The king gave the vice-regency to his son, and he became highly renowned.
From that time on, the Bodhisatta ate, drank, and slept together with the prince;
their mutual trust became firm.
In the course of time, after his father’s passing, the prince was established in the kingdom and enjoyed great prosperity.
The Bodhisatta thought: “My friend is ruling the kingdom; as soon as he perceives the right moment, he will surely grant me the position of state chaplain.
What is the use of my living the household life? Having gone forth, I shall cultivate seclusion. Thus, having paid homage to his mother and father, he departed.
Having obtained permission for his renunciation, he abandoned great prosperity and went forth all alone.

Entering the Himālaya mountains, he constructed a leaf-hut on a delightful spot of ground. Having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and dwelt there sporting in the play of *jhāna*. At that time, the king, remembering him, thought: "My friend..."
“He is not seen; where is he? he asked. The ministers informed him of his state of renunciation and said, “It is said that he dwells in a delightful grove.
The king, having inquired about his dwelling place, said to the minister Seyya, “Go, bring my friend back, and I shall grant him the position of chaplain. He replied, “Very well.”
Having given his assent, he departed from Bārāṇasī and, traveling by stages, reached a frontier village.
Having established his camp there, he went with forest-dwellers to the dwelling place of the Bodhisatta.
Seeing the Bodhisatta sitting at the door of the leaf-hut like a golden statue, he paid homage, sat down to one side, and exchanged greetings with him.
“Venerable sir, the king wishes to offer you the position of chaplain and desires your arrival,” he said.

The Bodhisatta replied, “Let alone the position of chaplain; even if I were to receive the entire sovereignty over Kāsī, Kosala, and Jambudīpa, or even the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, I would not go.
For the wise do not take up again the defilements they have once abandoned. Once—
"For that which has been abandoned is like spat-out phlegm," he said, and then spoke these verses:
"Though one should desire the earth bounded by the oceans, with the sea as its earrings, one should not desire it along with blame; know this, O Seṭṭha."
“Fie on that gain of fame, O brahmin, and fie on the gain of wealth,
if one’s livelihood is through falling into ruin or through practicing unrighteousness!
Even better, having taken a bowl, one should wander as a homeless renunciant.”
“That very livelihood is better than seeking it through unrighteousness.
Even if one were to wander forth as a homeless mendicant, taking up a bowl,
yet practicing non-violence toward others in the world— that is better even than sovereignty.”
In that context, "as far as the ocean's edge" (*sasamuddapariyāya*): *pariyāya* means a surrounding;
the meaning is together with the Cakkavāḷa mountain range standing encircling the ocean, or together with its surrounding known as the ocean. "The ocean earring" (*sāgarakuṇḍala*):

because it stands in the midst of the ocean like an island, it is like an earring; such is the meaning. "Regarding blame" (*nindāya*): [refers to] one endowed with the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhānasukha*).
"Having abandoned the going-forth, he has seized worldly power"—this is the censure [implied]. "Seyya" is an address by name.
"Vijānahi" means "understand the Dhamma. "Yā vutti vinipātena" refers to that livelihood consisting of the acquisition of fame, honor, and wealth obtained through the position of a royal chaplain;
having gone from here, for one intoxicated with the pride of power, there is a downfall (vinipāta) known as the ruin of oneself through the loss of meditative bliss.
Whether it be through unrighteous conduct, let that way of life be cursed!
"Taking the bowl" means having taken the alms-bowl. "A homeless one" means: may I too, free from a household, wander among other families.
"That very livelihood"—that indeed is my livelihood, better and more excellent than this seeking by unrighteousness.

"And that which is a search by means of what is not Dhamma. This is what is meant: "This very livelihood, even though it is obtained through what is not Dhamma, is more excellent than that [other way].

"Not harming" means not injuring. "Even with sovereignty"—even if I were to obtain sovereignty, this way of making a living for me, who carry an alms-bowl in hand while not harming others, is better and more supreme.
Thus, although he entreated him again and again, the other refused him. Seyya, failing to win his consent, paid him homage and departed; having gone, he reported to the King that he had not returned.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and many others likewise realized the fruits of Stream-entry and the higher stages.
At that time, King Ānanda was [the king], Sāriputta was the better [counsellor], and I myself was the son of the chaplain.
This is the tenth exposition, the Commentary on the Seyya Jātaka.
The first chapter, the Kāliṅga Vagga, is concluded.
2. The Chapter on the *Pucimanda* [311]. 1. The Commentary on the *Pucimanda-jātaka*.
"Arise, O thief!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
He related the story. It seems that while he was dwelling in a forest hut near Rājagaha, a certain thief broke into a house in a village at the city gate, took the household's valuables, and fled;
having entered the courtyard of the Elder’s hut, he lay down in front of the Elder’s leaf-hut, thinking, "I shall find protection here."
The Elder, realizing that he had been lying in front of him and suspecting him, thought, "Association with thieves is not permitted," and so he went out and drove him away, saying, "Do not lie here.
That thief, having departed from there, confused his tracks and fled.
People, taking torches and following the thief's footprints, arrived at that place and [observed] the places where he had come from, stood, sat, and lain down.
Having seen him, they thought, "The thief has come this way, stood here, sat here, departed by that path;
we did not see him," and having rushed hither and thither, they returned without even seeing him.
On the following day, at the time of the morning meal, the Elder, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from his almsround, went to Veḷuvana and [reported] that occurrence to the Teacher.
He reported this. The Teacher said, "Moggallāna, it is not you alone who has had reason to be suspicious; even the wise men of old were suspicious.
Having said this, at the request of the Elder, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was the deity of a nimba tree in the city's charnel ground.
Having offered the sacrifice, he was reborn there. Now one day, a thief who had committed a crime entered that charnel forest.
At that time, there were two senior trees there: a neem tree and a pipal tree.
The thief laid his bundle at the foot of the neem tree and lay down. At that moment, they were taking thieves who had been captured and impaling them on neem stakes. Then—
That deity thought: "If people come and seize this thief, they will cut off a branch from this very nimba tree, fashion it into a stake, and impale him upon it; if that happens, the tree will perish.
Come now, I shall remove him from here. Speaking with him, she uttered the first verse:
“Arise, thief! Why do you lie there? What is the use of your sleeping?
Let not the kings seize you, O evildoer in the village!
In this context, “the kings” is said with reference to the king’s men. “Evildoer” refers to one who commits the cruel and violent deeds of a thief.
Having spoken thus, he terrified him, saying, “Go elsewhere before the king’s men seize you,” and so made him flee. When he had fled, the deity of the Assattha tree spoke this second verse:
“What does it matter to the *pucimanda* tree, grown and standing in the forest, that they will seize a thief, a wrongdoer in the village?”

Regarding the phrase "standing there, born in the forest": the neem tree was both born and standing in the forest. However, because the deity had been reborn there, she addressed him using the conventional behavior associated with trees.
Having heard this, the neem-tree deity spoke the third verse:
"You do not know, O Assattha, the inner nature of me, the thief."
“Having seized a thief, kings place the evildoer in the village upon the neem-stake; my mind has doubt regarding that.
Therein, “assatthā” (is established) refers to the deity born there, addressed in the same manner as before. “Mama corassa” (of my thief)—
"They are singing together the reason for my dwelling and the thief's dwelling as one.
"They impale him upon the neem-stake" means that at this time, kings impale the thief upon a neem-stake. "In that my mind trembles" means that because of that cause, my heart trembles.
For if they impale him upon the stake, my celestial mansion (*vimāna*) will perish; otherwise, [it will remain] on the branch.
"They will hang [it] up; there will be the stench of a corpse in my mansion, and because of that, I shall drive them away"—this is the meaning.
While those deities were thus conversing with one another, the owners of the goods arrived following the footprints with torches in their hands;
seeing the place where the thief had lain down, they said, "Friends, the thief has just now risen and fled; he was not caught."

The robbers said, "If we catch him, we will go back after either impaling him on a stake of this very nimba tree or hanging him from its branch," and having spoken thus, they rushed hither and thither; but not seeing the robber, they departed.
Hearing their words, the deity of the Assattha tree spoke the fourth verse:
“One should suspect what is to be suspected, and guard against future danger;
the wise man, regarding future dangers, surveys both worlds.
In this context, “one should guard against future danger” refers to two types of future dangers: those pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to the future life.
Among those, by avoiding evil friends, one protects oneself regarding the present life;
by avoiding the three types of misconduct, one protects oneself regarding the future life.
Fearing the fear that arises from the causes of future dangers, the wise and learned person does not associate with evil friends and does not engage in misconduct through any of the three doors.
"Regarding both worlds": by reflecting thus, he surveys and looks upon both worlds known as this world and the world beyond.
While surveying them, out of fear of this world he avoids evil friends, and out of fear of the world beyond he does not commit evil.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the deity of the Assattha tree was Ānanda, while I myself was the deity of the Nimba tree."
The First Exposition of the *Pucimanda-jātaka*.
[312] 2. The Exposition of the *Kassapa-mandiya-jātaka*.
"O Kassapa, even if you are weary," etc.—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain elderly bhikkhu.
He related the story: It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain son of noble family, having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
Devoted to his meditation subject, he attained Arahantship before long.
Later on, after his mother passed away, he caused both his father and his younger brother to go forth as well. Having lived at Jetavana, at the time of the commencement of the rains retreat—
Having heard that the requisite of robes was easily obtained, they went to a certain village monastery;
there all three entered the rains retreat, and having completed the retreat, they returned to Jetavana. A young bhikkhu, at a place near Jetavana, said:
"Novice, you should go and bring the Elder after making him comfortable; I will go ahead and attend to the courtyard."
He entered the Jeta Grove. The elder monk was walking slowly, but the novice, as if pressing him repeatedly with his head, led him along by force, saying, "Go, venerable sir! Go, venerable sir!
The elder thought, "You have brought me under your own control," and turning back again, he walked from the very end. Thus they quarreled with one another.
While they were still working, the sun set and darkness fell.
