The other, having swept the courtyard and prepared water, not seeing them arrive, took a torch and went out to meet them; seeing them coming, he asked, "Why have you been so long? The elder—
He explained the reason for this. The man, having reassured both of them, brought him back slowly. On that day, he did not find an opportunity to attend upon the Buddha.
Then, on the second day, having come to attend upon the Buddha, paid homage, and sat down, the Teacher asked him, "When did you arrive?
"Yesterday, Bhante," he replied. "Having arrived yesterday, why do you attend upon the Buddha today?"
“Do you do this? he asked. He replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” and explained the reason. The Teacher rebuked the old man, saying, “It is not only now that he performs such an act;
he did so in the past as well. Now you have been wearied by him, but in the past he wearied the wise.
Having said this, at the request of the old man, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a market town of Kāsi.
When he reached maturity, his mother passed away. Having performed the funeral rites for his mother, and after the lapse of a month and a half, he gave away the wealth remaining in the house as alms;
then, taking his father and younger brother with him, he went to a region of the Himalayas.
Having taken the bark garment belonging to Devadatta and gone forth into the ascetic life, he lived in a delightful forest grove, subsisting on roots and fruits gathered by the practice of gleaning.

However, during the rainy season in the Himalayas, when the rain fell in unbroken torrents, it was impossible to dig for tubers and roots, and the fruits and leaves began to fall. For the most part, the ascetics [could not survive].
Having departed from the Himālayas, they lived along human pathways. Then the Bodhisatta, taking both his father and his younger brother, lived on human pathways;
subsequently, having taken them both back to the Himālayas where the trees were in full bloom and fruit, he was returning to his own hermitage in the mountains.
When the sun had set not far from the hermitage, he said, "You two should proceed slowly."
Having said, "I will go on ahead and look after the hermitage," he left them and went away.
The young ascetic, walking slowly with his father, led him by force, saying "Go! Go!", as if pressing him against the small of his back with his head.
The elder turned back, saying, "You are leading me according to your own whim! and [stood] at the end.
He set out and came back. While they were thus quarreling, darkness fell.
The Bodhisatta, having swept the leaf-hut and prepared water, took a torch and was coming along the path when he saw them and asked, "What have you been doing for all this time?
The junior ascetic told his father what had happened.

The Bodhisatta, having slowly led both of them away and put their belongings in order, bathed his father, performed services such as washing his feet and massaging his back, and prepared a charcoal couch;
then, sitting beside his father whose fatigue had subsided, he said:
"Father, young children are like earthenware vessels that break in an instant; from the moment they first break..."
"Once they have started, they can no longer be restrained; even if they revile and abuse them, the elders must endure them.
Having said this, he spoke these verses as an exhortation to his father:
"Even if, Kassapa, out of dullness, a youth should curse or strike you;..."
The wise person forgives all that; the sage endures it with patience.
Even if the peaceful ones should quarrel, they quickly return to peace again;
but fools, having reached a state of division, do not attain tranquility.
“These two come together more and more; their bond does not decay:
he who knows what has been undertaken and he who knows the teaching.
For he is the superior one, the bearer of the burden, the upholder of the yoke.”
“He who, when others are overcome by distress, is himself capable of reconciling them.
In this context, “Kassapa” is an address to his father by name. “Mandī” refers to being slow-witted due to youthfulness.
“A young man reviles and strikes” means that a young child both insults and hits [his parents]. “Dhīra” means one whose evil is censured; or else, *dhī* is said to mean...
"Paññā" means endowed with that [wisdom]. The other term, however, is a synonym for this very same thing.
By both terms, it is shown that an elder, a wise and learned person, endures—that is, patiently bears—all those offenses committed by foolish children.
"Sandhīyare" means they are again reconciled, joined, or restored through friendship. "Bālā pattāvā" means, moreover, the foolish ones...
Only their clay bowls break. "They have not attained peace" means that those fools, having engaged in even a trivial dispute, find no and do not attain the pacification of their enmity.
"These two [reunite] more" means that although these two persons have been divided, they come together again.
"Reconciliation" (*sandhi*) means a bond of friendship. "Of them" means that the bond of those very two does not decay.
"And one who knows [the offense] committed by oneself": this refers to one who knows the fault committed by himself, which has been transgressed and surpassed.
"And one who knows the confession": this refers to one who knows how to accept the confession of transgression uttered by that person who recognizes his own fault.
"And one who [knows] those committed by others": this refers to those who have committed offenses against others, being overcome by the fault of their transgression.

"He deserves to reconcile himself" means that even when those [friends] do not ask for forgiveness, he is capable of reconciling himself by saying, "Come, good sir, take up the recitation, listen to the commentary, apply yourself to meditation; why do you remain an outsider?
Thus he strives to restore friendship. Such a one, dwelling in loving-kindness, is superior because he carries the burden of friendship and the yoke of friendship.
"He is known as a 'bearer of burdens' and a 'bearer of the yoke.
Thus the Bodhisatta gave this counsel to his father, and from that time forth, he became tamed and well-tamed.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the father was the elder ascetic, the young ascetic was the novice, and I myself was the one who gave the father's counsel."
The second commentary: the *Kassapamandiyajātakavaṇṇanā*.
[313] 3. The commentary on the *Khantivādījātaka*:
"He who [strikes] your hands and feet... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain angry bhikkhu.

He related the story. The background of the case has already been told below. However, the Teacher said to that bhikkhu, "Bhikkhu, why do you give way to anger when you have gone forth in the teaching of the Buddha, who is free from anger?

In the past, even when thousands of spears were falling upon their bodies and their hands, feet, ears, and noses were being cut off, the ancient wise men did not give way to anger toward others. Having said this, he recounted the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Kalābu reigned.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family possessing eighty koṭis of wealth; having become a young man named Kuṇḍala-kumāra, he reached maturity, went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, established a household, and upon the passing of his parents, looked upon his heap of wealth.
Thinking, "My kinsmen took this wealth and departed without even taking it;
however, it is fitting that I take it and go," he sorted through all the wealth and gave whatever anyone brought to them.

Then, having entered the Himālaya mountains and gone forth into the homeless life, he lived for a long time subsisting on various fruits. Finally, for the purpose of seeking salt and sour flavors, he returned to the path of men.
Having arrived and reached Bārāṇasī by stages, he stayed in the royal park; on the following day, while wandering for alms in the city, he came to the gate of the general’s residence.

The general, being inspired with confidence by his deportment, invited him into the house, fed him the meal he had prepared himself, and having obtained his promise, had him stay right there in the royal park.
Then one day, King Kalābu, intoxicated by liquor and surrounded by skilled female dancers, went to the pleasure garden with great pomp.
Having had a couch prepared upon a auspicious stone slab, he lay down on the lap of a certain beloved and charming woman.
Female dancers, skilled in song, instrumental music, and dance, performed songs and other arts, just as if for Sakka, the king of the gods.
There was great prosperity, and the king fell asleep. Then those women thought, "He for whose sake we employ songs and the like has fallen into sleep;

what is the use of our singing and such? Having cast aside their lutes and other musical instruments right there, they departed for the park and took their delight in the garden, enticed by the flowers, fruits, and sprouts.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was sitting at the foot of a beautifully blossomed sāla tree in that park, enjoying the bliss of renunciation like a noble elephant in rut.
Then those women, while wandering in the park, saw him and said, "Come, ladies!
A renunciant is sitting at the foot of this tree; let us go and listen to something from his presence while the king is still asleep."
“Let us sit down,” they said; and having gone there, paid homage, and sat down surrounding him, they said, “Tell us something appropriate for us to hear.
The Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to them. Then that woman shook her lap and woke the king.
Having woken up and not seeing them, the king asked, “Where have those low-caste women gone? “These, Great King—” [he replied].
Having gone there, they sat down surrounding a certain ascetic. The king, becoming angry, took up his sword and went forward in haste, thinking, "I shall punish this rogue of a matted-hair ascetic.
Then those women, seeing the king approaching in a rage, the one most beloved among them went toward the king.
Taking swords in their hands, they sought to subdue the king. He came and stood before the Bodhisatta, asking, "What do you profess, ascetic?
"I am a teacher of patience, Great King. "What is this so-called 'patience'?
"It is the state of not becoming angry when others revile, abuse, or strike one. The king said, "Now I shall see!"
Thinking, "They possess the quality of patience," he summoned the executioner. The man, according to his custom, took up an axe and a thorny whip;
wearing a saffron robe and bearing a red garland, he approached, paid homage to the king, and said, "What shall I do, Your Majesty?
[The king replied: "Seize this thief, that wicked ascetic, drag him forward, and throw him down upon the ground."
“Take a thorny whip and give me two thousand lashes on each of the four sides—front, back, and both flanks.
He did so. The Bodhisatta’s outer skin was split; his inner skin was split; his flesh was cut; and blood flowed.
Again the king asked, “What do you profess, monk? “I profess patience, Great King. “But you—my...”
"You think my patience is in the skin," he said, "but there is no patience of mine in the skin;
rather, my patience is established within my heart, which you are unable to see. "Great King," [he replied]. Again, the executioner asked, "What shall I do?
"Cut off both hands of this fraudulent matted-hair ascetic. He took up an axe.
Having placed him upon the chopping block, he cut off his hands. Then the king said to him, "Cut off your feet," and he cut off his feet as well.
From the joints of his hands and feet, blood flowed out like liquid lac from the holes of a jar. Again the king asked, "What do you profess?
"I am a teacher of patience, Great King. "But you think that there is 'patience' in the joints of my hands and feet?"
“There is no fault here; my patience is established in profound matters,” he said.
The king replied, “Cut off his ears and nose. The other cut off his ears and nose, and blood flowed from his entire body. Again the king asked him, “What do you profess?
“Great King, I am one who professes patience (khantivādī). [The king said,] “But surely you will not—on the tips of your ears and nose...”
“If you think, ‘Patience is established,’ my patience is established within the depths of my heart.
The king said, “Kūṭajaṭila, sit here having yourself cast aside your patience,” and after striking the Bodhisatta’s chest with his foot, he departed.
When he had departed, the commander-in-chief wiped the blood from the Bodhisatta’s body, tied his hands, feet, ears, and the tip of his nose into the corners of his garment,
and having seated the Bodhisatta down gently and paid homage to him,
sat to one side and said: “Venerable sir, if you wish to be angry, you should be angry with the king alone for the offense committed against you, and not with others.”
Making this request, he spoke the first verse:
"O Great Hero, be angry with him who cut off your hands, your feet, and your ears and nose;
do not let the kingdom perish here."
In that context, "O Great Hero" means one of great prowess. "Do not let this kingdom perish" means: do not destroy this innocent kingdom of Kāsi.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
"He who cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose..."
“May that king live long; for those like me do not give way to anger.

In this context, “those like me” refers to wise persons endowed with the power of patience who, even when someone reviles, scolds, strikes them, or cuts and breaks them, do not become angry, thinking, “This person has abused, reviled, struck, cut, or broken me.
At the very moment the Bodhisatta was departing from the king’s pleasure garden and leaving the range of his vision, these forty-four thousand...
The great earth, two hundred thousand yojanas in thickness, split open like a leather bag bound at its seams;
flames emerging from the Avīci hell seized the king as if wrapping him in a red woolen blanket inherited from his family.
He entered the earth right there at the gate of the pleasure garden and was established in the Great Niraya of Avīci. On that very same day, the Bodhisatta also passed away.
The royal assembly and the citizens, with perfumes, garlands, and incense in their hands, came and performed the funeral rites for the body of the Bodhisatta.
However, some say that the Bodhisatta went back to the Himālayas again; this is untrue.
"In times past there was an ascetic who illuminated patience..."
While he remained steadfast in patience alone, the King of Kāsi cut him down.
"The ripening of that harsh deed was bitter;
it was what the King of Kāsi experienced when cast into hell."
These are two verses concerning the Fully Enlightened One.
Therein, "atītamaddhānaṃ" means in the past time. "Khantidīpano" is a praise of patience as endurance. "Achedayi" means he caused to be killed.
However, some say that the hands, feet, ears, and nose of the Bodhisatta were joined back together again.
What they say is likewise untrue. "Established" means firmly settled.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: at the conclusion of the Truths, the angry monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), while many others attained the fruits of Stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) and the rest.
At that time, King Kalābu was Devadatta, the general was Sāriputta, and the ascetic who preached patience was none other than myself.
The third: The Exposition of the Khantivādī Jātaka.
[314] 4. The Exposition of the Lohakumbhi Jātaka:
"I have lived a life ill-lived"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the King of Kosala.
At that time, it seems, the King of Kosala heard the voices of four beings in hell during the night.
One uttered the sound "du," another the sound "sa," another the sound "na," and another the sound "so. It is said that in their past lives, they had been princes in Sāvatthī who were adulterers;
having offended against the women of others who were protected and guarded, they indulged in mere mental dalliance.
Having committed much evil karma while playing, they were cut off by the wheel of death and reborn in four iron cauldrons on the outskirts of Sāvatthī;
after boiling there for sixty thousand years, they saw the rim of the opening of an iron cauldron rising up,
and cried out with a great sound in succession, "When indeed shall we be released from this suffering?"— thus did all four speak.
They cried out. Hearing their sound, the king, terrified by the fear of death, caused the dawn to rise while still sitting up.
At the time of sunrise, the brahmins arrived and asked the king if he had slept well.
The king said, "How could I have slept well, teachers? Today I heard four such terrifying sounds. The brahmins—
They shook their hands. “What is it, teachers? “It is the sound of a rash person, Great King.
“Is there a remedy for it, or no remedy? “There is certainly no remedy, Great King; however, we are well-trained, Great King. “By doing what will you ward it off?
“Great King, a remedy that is too great cannot be performed; however, we shall perform a sacrifice consisting of all fourfold sets.”

“We shall take them away. [The king said: “In that case, quickly take four elephants, four horses, four bulls, and four men—starting with the Laṭukika bird—and having seized four of each kind of living being, perform a sacrifice of all these sets of four and ensure my safety.
[They replied: “Very well, Great King,” and having accepted, they took whatever was required.
Having seized him, they brought him to the sacrificial enclosure; having driven many living beings toward the sacrificial posts, they stationed them there.

Having become emboldened with the thought, “We shall eat much fish and meat, and we shall obtain great wealth,” they moved back and forth, crying out, “O King, this must be obtained! This must be obtained!”
Queen Mallikā approached the king and asked, “Great King, why are the brahmins wandering about, inciting such great enthusiasm?
“Queen, what does this matter to you? You are intoxicated and heedless by your own prosperity;
moreover, you do not know our suffering. “What is it, Great King? “Queen, I have heard such things as ought not to be heard...”
I heard them; then, having heard these sounds, I asked the brahmins, "What will happen?
The brahmins replied, "Great King, a danger to your kingdom, your wealth, or your life is foreseen.
By performing a sacrifice with every fourfold set of offerings, we shall bring about your safety. Accepting their words, they [prepared] the sacrificial enclosure.
“Having done so, they come for whatever purpose each has, for the sake of that very thing.
“But Your Majesty, did you ask the foremost brahmin in the world with its devas about the origin of these sounds? “Who, O Queen, is this so-called ‘foremost brahmin in the world with its devas’?
“The Great Gotama, the Perfectly Enlightened One. “Queen, the Perfectly Enlightened One is not [my teacher].”
“Have you been asked? [The king replied: “In that case, go and ask.
Having accepted her words, the king, having finished his morning meal, mounted his excellent chariot and went to Jetavana.
There he paid homage to the Teacher and asked: “Venerable sir, last night when I heard four sounds, I questioned the brahmins; they—”
“‘Having performed the sacrifice of all fourfold animals, we shall bring about our safety,’ they said, and while they were performing the work in the sacrificial enclosure, I heard their sounds.
What will happen to me because of hearing those sounds? “Nothing at all, Great King.
Those beings in hell were crying out as they experienced suffering; these sounds were not heard by you alone now, for they were also heard by kings of old.”
“Even though they had heard [the advice], those brahmins, having consulted with them, desired to perform a sacrifice involving the slaughter of animals;

however, upon hearing the words of the wise, they did not do so. By interposing their speech between those [other] sounds, the wise caused the great multitude to be released and brought about their safety.
Having said this, being requested by him, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsi.
Having reached maturity and seen the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned such pleasures and went forth as an ascetic.
Having developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he sported in the play of jhāna within a delightful forest grove in the Himalayas.
He was living there. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, having heard these four sounds from the four hell-beings, became terrified and agitated.
When the brahmins said, "One of the three calamities must be occurring;
we shall pacify it with a sacrifice of all fourfold sets," the king consented. The domestic chaplain, together with the brahmins, prepared the sacrificial enclosure.
The great multitude had been led to the pillar. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having made the cultivation of loving-kindness his preliminary practice, surveyed the world with his divine eye;
seeing this situation, he thought, "Today it is fitting for me to go; there will be safety for the great multitude.
Then, by the power of his psychic potency, he rose into the air, descended into the royal park of the King of Bārāṇasī, and [stood] upon the auspicious stone slab.

He sat down like a golden statue. Then the preceptor’s eldest pupil approached his teacher and said, "Is it not true, teacher, that in our Vedas there is no such thing as performing a rite for safety after having killed another?
The chaplain replied, "You are protecting the king's wealth; we shall eat much fish and meat, and we shall obtain riches. Be silent."
“...will be,” he replied, and thus he turned him back.
Thinking, “I will not be a companion here,” he departed and went to the royal park. There, seeing the Bodhisatta, he paid homage to him;
after the customary greetings were exchanged, he sat down to one side. The Bodhisatta asked, “What is it, young man? Is the King ruling according to the Dhamma?”
“...is he ruling the kingdom? he asked. “Venerable sir, the king rules the kingdom according to the Dhamma;
however, having heard four sounds during the night, he questioned the brahmins. The brahmins said, ‘We shall perform a sacrifice of all fourfold animals and bring about his safety.
Desiring to ensure his own safety by performing the slaughter of animals, the king has brought a great multitude of people before the sacrificial post.”
“Venerable sir, is it not fitting for virtuous ones such as yourselves to explain the origin of those sounds and thus deliver the great multitude from the jaws of death?
“Young man, the king does not know us, nor do we know him;
however, we do know the origin of these sounds. If the king were to approach us and ask, we would [explain] to the king...”
“Having removed all doubt, I shall speak. “In that case, venerable sir, please remain right here for a moment;
I will bring the king. “Very well, young man,” he replied. He went and, having informed the king of the matter, brought the king back.
Then the king, having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, sat down to one side and asked: “Is it true, as I have heard, that you [know] the sounds...?”
“Do you know their final outcome? “Yes, Great King. “Tell me, venerable sir.
“Great King, these men, having committed misconduct with the wives of others who were protected and guarded in a previous existence, were reborn near the city of Bārāṇasī in four iron cauldrons.
There they boil for thirty thousand years, submerged in a mass of foam in boiling water of caustic molten iron.”
Having struck the surface of the cauldron and climbing upward, after a period of thirty thousand years, they saw the mouth of the cauldron;

looking outside, the four persons—desiring to speak the four verses in their entirety but being unable to do so—uttered only a single syllable each and sank back again into the iron cauldrons. Among them, [one uttered] the syllable *du*.
Having spoken thus, the being who had sunk [into hell] desired to say:
“We have lived a life ill-lived, we who, though possessing wealth, did not give;
while riches were available, we did not make an island for ourselves.”
Having said, "I was unable to complete that verse," the Bodhisatta, by means of his own knowledge, completed that verse and spoke it. The same method applies to the others as well.
Among them, this is the verse for one who wishes to speak after uttering the syllable *sa*:
"For sixty thousand years, in their entirety;..."
“When those being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?”—this verse was spoken by one who wished to say the word “no”:
“There is no end; whence could there be an end? No end is seen.”
"For then, O dear ones, evil was committed by me and by you.
Having uttered the syllable "so," this verse was spoken by one desiring to say more:
"Surely I, having gone from here and obtained a human birth..."
“Generous and perfected in virtue, I shall perform much wholesome merit.

In this context, “a life ill-lived” means that one who practices the three types of misconduct lives a life that is ill-lived, a base life; it is with reference to such a person that he said, “I have lived a life ill-lived.
“Those things being present which we did not give” refers to those objects worthy of being given (*deyyadhamma*)... [which we failed to give].
And we did not give gifts even though both [the donor] and the recipient were present.
We did not establish a lamp for ourselves—that is, we did not create our own support. "Complete" means neither deficient nor excessive. "In every way" means in all respects.
"While being cooked" means while we are being roasted in this hell.
“There is no end” means there is no delimitation of time such that one might think, “Our liberation will occur at such-and-such a time.
“From where is there an end? asks by what cause an end would be discerned. “There is no end” means that even for those desiring to see the end, the end of suffering does not appear.
For at that time, O sirs, it was our common lot—both mine and yours.
“Evil has been committed, done in great excess. There is also a reading, “*tathā hi pakatan*,” meaning “done for such a reason,” by which its interior cannot be seen.
“Mārisa” is a term of affectionate address used by me toward them, meaning “those like me.
“Nūna” is a particle expressing certainty; [it means] “having gone from here and obtained a human birth, I shall be generous.”
"Having been endowed with virtue, I shall perform much wholesome [deed] exclusively"—this is the meaning here.

Thus, after the Bodhisatta had spoken each verse, he said: "Great King, that being in hell, desiring to speak this verse in its entirety, was unable to do so because of the magnitude of his own evil; thus he—his..."
"Experiencing the ripening of his own karma, he cries out. There is no obstacle whatsoever for you on account of hearing this sound;

do not be afraid," he reassured the king. The king released the great multitude, caused a golden drum to be beaten throughout the land, and had the sacrificial enclosure demolished. Thus, the Bodhisatta brought safety to the great multitude.
Having stayed there for a few days and then departing from that very place, he was reborn in the Brahma-world without falling away from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the eldest pupil of the chaplain was Sāriputta, while the ascetic was none other than myself.
This is the fourth commentary on the Lohakumbhi Jātaka.
[315] 5. The Commentary on the *Sabbamaṃsalābha-jātaka*.

"Harsh indeed are your words!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning a bowl of alms-food containing oil given to the Elder Sāriputta after he had undergone a purgative treatment with oil.
At that time, it seems, some monks in Jetavana were using an oily purgative.
They drank it. Those monks had need of a meal with flavorful broth;

the attendants to the sick, thinking, "We shall bring flavorful food," entered Sāvatthī and, though they wandered for alms in the streets of the rice-sellers' houses, they returned without having obtained any flavorful food.
The Elder, entering for alms early in the morning, saw those monks and asked, "Friends, why so very early?"
“Turn back,” he asked. They reported the matter to him. The Elder said, “In that case, come along,” and taking them with him, he went down that very same street.
The people crowded around and gave them savory food. The attendants brought the savory food and gave it to the sick monks, who consumed it.
Then one day, in the Hall of Truth, the monks initiated a discussion.

“Friends, it seems that when the Elder, not receiving flavorful food from his attendants who had been given purgatives, took those leaving and went through the street of the rice-sellers’ houses, he sent back a great deal of flavorful alms-food.
The Teacher, having arrived and asked, “Monks, with what discussion are you sitting together here now? and being told, “With this one,” said, “No, monks...”

“Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta has obtained meat; in the past as well, he was one who was skilled and wise in speaking soft words and pleasant speech,” he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was the son of a merchant. Then, one day—
A certain deer-hunter, having obtained much meat and filled his cart, was coming toward the city thinking, "I shall sell it.

At that time, four sons of merchants living in Bārāṇasī had gone out from the city and were sitting at a place where the road met, conversing about various things they had seen or heard. Among them, one of the merchant's sons [saw] that cart of meat.
Seeing him, he said, "I will have this hunter bring a piece of meat. [The other] said, "Go and have it brought.
He approached the hunter and said, "Hey, hunter! Give me a piece of meat!
The hunter replied, "Sir, one who asks for something from another must use pleasant words; a piece of meat worthy of the speech you have uttered—"
Having said, "You shall receive [it]," he spoke the first verse:
"Truly harsh are your words, you who beg for flesh;
your speech is like a sinew, my friend, so I give you a sinew."
In that context, "resembling a caul" means it was rough like a caul. When he said, "I give you a caul, my dear; take it," [the other] replied, "Very well, take it.
Having lifted up a piece of fat—devoid of essence, flesh, and blood—that resembled his own words, he gave it to him.
Then another son of the merchant asked him, "What did you say when you begged for it? He replied, "'Are! I said. He [the other] said, "I too..."
Saying, "I will ask him for it," he went and said, "Elder brother, give me a piece of meat.
The other replied, "You shall receive a piece of meat worthy of your words," and spoke this second verse:
"This is the limb of humans, Which in the world is called 'brother';"
“A word similar to a limb; indeed, I give you a limb, my dear.
The meaning of this is: in this world, because they are like limbs to human beings, these—namely, a brother and a sister—are called “limbs”;
therefore, since this word of yours is similar to a limb, I give you a limb that is truly worthy of it. And so:
Having said this, he tore off a piece of flesh from his own limb and gave it to him.
Another son of the merchant asked, "What did you say when you begged for it?
He replied, "I said, 'Brother. He then said, "I too shall beg for it," and having gone there, he said, "Father, give me a piece of flesh. The hunter said, "In accordance with your words..."
Having said, "Will you accept? he spoke the third verse:
"When a son says 'Father,' it makes the father's heart tremble;
since your speech is like a father's heart, my dear, I give my heart to you."
Having spoken thus, he extracted some sweet meat along with a piece of heart-flesh and gave it to him.
The fourth son of the merchant asked, "What did you say when you begged for this? He replied, "I said, 'Father.
The other said, "Then I too shall beg," and having gone there, he said, "Friend, give me a piece of meat. The hunter said, "In accordance with your words..."
Having said, "Will you accept? he spoke the fourth verse:
"For one who has no friend in the village, that person is just like the wilderness.
Your speech is the same toward everyone; I give everything to you, my friend."

The meaning of this is as follows: For that man who has no friend reckoned as a companion because he does not walk with him through joys and sorrows in the village, even such a place for him becomes just like a wilderness inhabited by non-humans. Thus, this speech of yours is equal to all;
it is equal to one's own entire wealth and power. Therefore, all of this—
"I give you this meat-cart which belongs to me.
Having said this, he added, "Come, friend, let us carry this entire meat-cart to your house.
The merchant's son, driving the cart with him, went to his own home, unloaded the meat, and [gave it] to the hunter.
Having shown him honor and respect, he summoned even the hunter’s wife and children, removed them from their cruel occupation, and settled them within his own household.
Becoming an inseparable companion with him, he lived in harmony with him for as long as he lived.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the hunter was Sāriputta, and I myself was the merchant’s son who obtained all the meat.”
The fifth: The Commentary on the *Sabbamaṃsalābha-jātaka*.
[316] 6. The Commentary on the *Sasapaṇḍita-jātaka*:
"Seven red fish have I caught"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the gift of all one's requisites.
He related this story. It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain householder prepared an offering of all requisites for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having had a pavilion constructed at his house door and having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he had them sit on excellent seats arranged in the well-decorated pavilion.
After giving various kinds of choice and refined food as an offering, he invited them again for the following day for seven days.
Having invited them, on the seventh day he gave all the requisites to the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher, delivering a discourse of thanksgiving, said: "Lay follower, it is fitting for you to feel joy and gladness;
for this gift is indeed the lineage of the ancient wise ones. For the ancient wise ones, when supplicants arrived..."
"Having sacrificed their own lives, they even gave me their own flesh," he said, and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a hare and lived in the forest.
On one side of that forest was the foot of a mountain, on another side a river, and on the other side a frontier village.
He also had three companions: a monkey, a jackal, and an otter. These four wise ones lived together;
having each gathered food in their own respective feeding grounds, they would assemble together in the evening.
The hare-ascetic [would say]: "Alms must be given, virtue must be observed, and the Uposatha ceremony must be performed. To the three...
He taught the Dhamma by way of exhortation to the people. Having received his exhortation, they entered their respective tree-hollows and dwelt there.

As time passed in this manner, one day the Bodhisatta, looking up at the sky and seeing the moon, realized that the following day was the Uposatha day; he then said to the other three: "Tomorrow is the Uposatha."
"You three people should also observe the Uposatha by undertaking the precepts; for a gift given while established in virtue yields great fruit.
Therefore, when a beggar arrives, you should give from the food you yourselves were to eat.
Having accepted this with the words "Very well," they returned to their respective dwellings.
On the following day, early in the morning, the otter set out thinking, "I shall seek food," and went to the bank of the Ganges.
Now, a certain fisherman had hauled up seven rohita fish, strung them on a cord, and led them away;
having spread sand along the bank of the Ganges and covered [the fish] with sand, he was going downriver again to catch more fish. The otter, smelling the scent of the fish...
Having struck the fish, sifted through the sand, and seen a fish, he pulled it out and cried out three times, "Is there now anyone who owns these?
Seeing no owner, he bit the tip of a creeper, led the fish away, and placed it in his own dwelling-thicket.
Thinking, "I shall eat it at the proper time," he lay down reflecting upon his own virtue. The jackal, too, from his dwelling-place...
Having gone out and seeking almsfood, he saw two spits of meat, a monitor lizard, and a bowl of curd in the hut of a certain field-guard.
Shouting three times, "Is there perhaps an owner of these?", and seeing no owner,
he passed the rope used for lifting the bowl of curd through his neck and [took] the two spits of meat.
Having bitten the iguana with his mouth and carried it off, he placed it in his own dwelling thicket and lay down, reflecting on his own virtue, thinking, "I shall eat it at the proper time.

The monkey also emerged from his dwelling place, entered the forest grove, brought back a cluster of mangoes, and placed them in his own dwelling thicket, thinking, "I shall eat them at the proper time. His own...
He lay down reflecting upon his virtue.

But the Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall go out from my dwelling place at the very hour of dawn and eat the wild grass," lay down right there in his own thicket and reflected: "To give grass to the supplicants who have come to me..."
“It is not possible; I have not even sesame or rice. If a supplicant comes to me, I shall give him the flesh of my own body.
By the power of his virtue, Sakka’s Pandukambala stone throne manifested a sign of heat.
Reflecting on this, he perceived the cause and thought, “I shall test the king,” and first [sent] a lizard...
Having gone to the place where he lived, he stood there in the guise of a brahmin. When asked, "Brahmin, for what purpose have you stopped here?
he replied, "O Wise One, if I might receive some food, I would dwell here observing the Uposatha.
[The other] said, "Very well, I shall give you food," and while conversing with him, he spoke the first verse:
“Seven red fish have I, pulled from the water onto dry land;
this, O Brahmin, is what I have. Eat this and dwell in the forest.
In this context, *thalamubbhatā* means placed on dry land from the water, or drawn out by a fisherman. *Etaṃ bhutvā* means “having eaten this.”
“Having cooked and eaten this fish-food belonging to me, he sits at the foot of a delightful tree practicing the duty of a recluse and dwells in this forest.
The brahmin said, “Let it be so for now; we shall find out later,” and went into the presence of the jackal. By him also...
When asked, "For what purpose are you standing here?", he replied in that same manner. The jackal, thinking, "I shall give," spoke the second verse while conversing with him:
"The night’s meal for my field-guard was not brought by me:
two spits of meat, two iguanas, and one bowl of curd."
“Brahmin, I have this; having eaten this, dwell in the forest.
In that context, “dussa me” means “there is cloth for me”; “dussa amussa” is the meaning.
“Apābhataṃ” means brought or carried forth. “Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhā” refers to two spits of meat and one lizard, both roasted over coals.
*Godhā*: "Dadhivāraka" means a container for curd. "Idaṃ" means "this"; the sense is: "I have this much;

having cooked all of this with whatever kind of food one prefers and having eaten it, let me, being observant of the Uposatha, sit at the foot of a delightful tree and dwell in this forest grove while practicing the duty of a recluse."
The brahmin thought, “Let it be for now; I shall find out later,” and went into the presence of the monkey.

When the monkey asked him, “For what purpose have you stopped here? he said exactly the same thing. The monkey, thinking, “Very well, I will give it to you,” spoke the third verse while conversing with him:
“The mango is ripe, the water is cool, and the cool shade is delightful.”
“O Brahmin, I have this; having eaten this, dwell in the forest.
In this context, “mango-fruit” (*ambapakkam*) refers to the sweet mango fruit. “Cool water” (*dakam sītam*) refers to the cool water of the Ganges.
“Having eaten this, dwell in the forest” means: O Brahmin, having consumed this mango-fruit and having drunk the cool water...
Seated at the foot of a delightful tree according to his preference, practicing the duty of a recluse, he dwelt in this forest grove.
The brahmin thought, "Let it be for now; I shall find out later," and went into the presence of the Wise Hare.
When asked by him, "For what purpose have you come? he spoke exactly as before. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta was filled with joy and said, "Brahmin..."
"You have done well in coming to me for the sake of food; today I shall give a gift never given before.
As for you, being virtuous, you shall not commit the taking of life. Go, brahmin, gather various kinds of wood, make embers, and inform me;
I shall sacrifice myself in the midst of the embers."
“I shall give it to you. When my body has decomposed, you may eat the flesh and practice the duty of a recluse.
Speaking thus with him, he uttered the fourth verse:
“The hare has no sesame seeds, nor beans, nor rice;”
"Eat me, roasted by this fire, and dwell in the forest.

Therein, "eat me" means: "Having eaten me, who am the one for whom I said 'make a fire,' and who have been roasted by this fire, dwell in this forest; for the body of a single hare is sufficient to sustain a single man.
Having heard his words, Sakka, by his own supernatural power, created a heap of embers for the Bodhisatta.
He announced this. Rising from his bed of *dabba* grass, he went there and, thinking, "If there are insects within the pores of my body, let them not die," he shook his body three times.

Having placed his entire body as an object of sacrifice, he leaped into the heap of coals with a joyful heart like a royal swan landing in a lotus pond. That fire, however, [did not harm] the Bodhisatta.
He was unable to make even a single pore of his body warm; he felt as if he had entered the interior of a mass of snow.
Then, addressing Sakka, he said: "Brāhmaṇa, the fire produced by you is far too cold;
it cannot make even a single pore of my body warm. What is this? [Sakka replied: "O Wise Hare, I am not a brāhmaṇa; I am Sakka."
“I have come for the purpose of testing you. “Sakka, you may wait;
even if the entire world of living beings were to test me with gifts, they would not find in me any unwillingness to give,” the Bodhisatta roared like a lion.
Then Sakka said to him, “O wise hare, may your virtue be manifest for the duration of an entire aeon! and he pressed down upon the mountain.
Having taken mountain minerals and drawn the figure of the moon with its mark upon it, he brought the Bodhisatta and,
having laid him down upon the surface of young *dabba* grass within that very forest thicket in that same woodland,
he departed for his own dwelling place. Those four wise men, being in harmony and full of mutual affection, fulfilled their virtue, gave gifts, and performed the observance of the Uposatha.
Having done so, they departed according to their respective kamma.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder who had given the gift of all the requisites was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, Udda was Ānanda, the jackal was Moggallāna, the monkey was Sāriputta, Sakka was Anuruddha, and as for the wise hare, he was none other than myself.
The Sixth: The Commentary on the Sasa-paṇḍita Jātaka.
[317] 7. The Commentary on the Matarodana Jātaka.
"Weep only for the dead, the dead," said this while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain resident of Sāvatthī.
The Teacher spoke concerning a householder. It is said that his brother had passed away.
Overwhelmed by grief at his brother's death, he did not bathe, eat, or anoint himself; every morning he would go to the charnel ground and weep, consumed by sorrow.
At dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and, seeing that the householder possessed the necessary support for attaining the fruit of stream-entry, [thought]: "For this man..."
“Having brought forth the causes of the past and stilled his sorrow, there is no one else capable of bestowing the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) except me;

it is fitting that I should become his refuge. On the following day, after the meal, having returned from his almsround, he took his junior attendant and went to the man’s house door, announcing, “The Teacher has arrived.”
Having heard this, the householder prepared a seat and said, "Please enter," whereupon [the Teacher] entered and sat down on the prepared seat.
The householder also approached, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Householder, what are you thinking? "Yes, venerable sir, since the time my brother died, I have been thinking about it."
"Friend, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; that which is subject to breaking will break. One should not worry about it.
Even when their brother died, the ancient wise men did not worry, thinking, 'That which is subject to breaking has broken.
Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family possessing a wealth of eight hundred million.
When he reached maturity, his parents passed away.
After they had died, the Bodhisatta’s brother managed the household, and the Bodhisatta lived dependent upon him. Later on, in such a manner...
He passed away due to illness. His kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers gathered together, and raising their arms, they wept and wailed;
not a single one was able to compose themselves. Yet the Bodhisatta neither wept nor cried. People said, "Look, sirs!
Even when his brother has died, this man shows not even the slightest contraction of his face; he is exceedingly hard-hearted."
“‘I alone shall enjoy both portions,’ he thinks; surely he desires his brother’s death,” they reviled the Bodhisatta.
His kinsmen also reviled him, saying, “You do not even weep for your dead brother.
Hearing their words, he thought, “Out of your own blindness and folly, you who do not understand the eight worldly conditions, you say, ‘My brother is dead.’”
Weep! I too shall die, you too shall die; why do you not weep for yourselves, thinking, "We too shall die"?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*), having become impermanent, cease; there is not even a single phenomenon capable of remaining stable by its very nature.
You foolish fools, out of ignorance, weep without knowing the eight worldly conditions (*loka-dhamma*).
Having said, "For what purpose should I weep?", he spoke these verses:
"Weep for the dead indeed, but do not weep for him who is about to die;
for all who bear a body must, in due course, abandon their life."
“Devas and humans, quadrupeds, flocks of birds, and hooded serpents—none have mastery over their own bodies;
even while enjoying themselves, they must relinquish life.
Thus, observing that pleasure and pain among human beings are unstable and lack permanence,”
“Wailing and weeping are useless; why do you overwhelm yourselves with a multitude of sorrows?
‘They are rogues, drunkards, and untrained;
fools, yet they think themselves heroes, lacking in yoga’—so think those who are unskilled in the Dhamma.”
In that context, "the dead, indeed, are dead" means they are simply dead. "Successively" means that when their respective turn for death arrives, they relinquish life one after another;
they do not all die at once. If they were to die in such a manner [simultaneously], the continuity of the world would be cut off.
"Possessing wealth" means being endowed with a large physical body. "Delighting" means [delighting] here and there.
All these beings, such as the gods and others, having been born, abandon their lives while still finding delight in their respective places of birth and without being weary of them.
"Thus it is unstable" means that because there is an absence of both immobility and stability within the three realms of existence (*bhava*), it is unstable and lacks firmness.
"Why are you overwhelmed by a multitude of sorrows? means for what reason are you covered by a mass of grief?
They sprinkle and they overwhelm.

"Gamblers" refers to female gamblers—those who gamble with women, those who gamble with liquor, and those who gamble with dice—as well as those intoxicated by liquor and the like, and those who are "drunkards" (soṇḍā), meaning those who lack wisdom and are untrained.
"Fools" means those possessed of folly, the ignorant. "Brave men" refers to those who are not practitioners of yoga.
“By way of improper attention they are fools; by way of non-application to the yogas they are non-yogins.
There is also a reading, “ayodhino,” meaning those who are incapable of fighting against the Māra of the defilements. “Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma think a wise man is a fool”:
those such as gamblers and the like who are unskilled in the eightfold worldly conditions (lokadhamma), when faced with even a slight condition of suffering—
"When the eight worldly conditions have arisen, they themselves weep and wail;
yet, having understood this, they think of a wise and learned man like me—who does not weep or wail at the death of kinsmen and such things—thinking, 'This man is a fool; he does not weep.
Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught them the Dhamma, made them all free from grief."
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, I myself was the wise man who, by teaching the Dhamma to the great multitude, brought about a state free from sorrow."
The seventh is the commentary on the Matarodana Jātaka.
[318] 8. The commentary on the Kaṇavera Jātaka:
"When that time of spring... This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by a former wife.
He spoke concerning this. The background story will be made clear in the *Indriya Jātaka*.
The Teacher, however, said to that bhikkhu, "Bhikkhu, in the past you received the severing of your head by a sword because of this," and when requested by him, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of a householder in a village of Kāsī.
Born under the constellation Cora, he reached maturity and made his living by committing acts of theft;
he became notorious in the world as a hero with the strength of an elephant, such that no one was able to capture him.
One day, having broken into the house of a wealthy merchant, he carried off a great deal of wealth. The citizens approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, there is a great thief..."
"He is plundering the city; seize him! they said. The king ordered the city guard to apprehend him.
During the night, the guard stationed men here and there in groups, and having captured him together with his accomplices, he reported it to the king.
The king commanded the city guard alone, saying, "Cut off his head. The city guard—

Having had him bound with tight fetters behind his back, a garland of red *kaṇavīra* flowers hung around his neck, and brick-dust sprinkled upon his head, they led him to the execution ground to the beat of a harsh-sounding drum, striking him with whips at every crossroads.
"A thief who plundered this city has been caught! the entire city cried out in agitation.

At that time, in Bārāṇasī, there was a courtesan named Sāmā who was a favorite of the king; she charged a thousand pieces of gold and was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred beautiful female slaves.
Standing on the terrace of her palace with the window open, she saw him being led away.
He was handsome, pleasing, exceedingly beautiful, and possessed of a divine appearance; he appeared above the heads of everyone else. Sāmā [beheld] him...
Having seen him, her heart became bound to him, and thinking, "By what means might I make this man my own husband?", she thought, "There is a way.
She sent a thousand pieces of money in the hand of one of her female attendants to the city watchman, saying, "This thief is Sāmā’s brother; apart from Sāmā, he has no other support."
“Having taken this thousand pieces, you should release him,” she said. She went and did so.

The city guard said, “This thief is well-known; it is not possible to release him. However, having found another person and having had this man sit in a covered carriage, it will be possible to send him. She went and informed her [the thief].
At that time, however, a certain merchant’s son, whose heart was bound to Sāmā, gave her a thousand [pieces of gold] every day.
On that particular day as well, he took his thousand and went to her house at the time of sunset.
Sāmā, having taken the bundle of a thousand and placed it upon her thighs, sat weeping. When asked, "What is this?", she replied, "Master, this..."
"My brother is a thief; because he thinks, 'I am doing a lowly work,' he does not come near me.
He sent a message to the city guard saying, 'If I receive a thousand [pieces of gold], I will release him.
Now, I cannot find him going to the city guard's presence with this thousand. Because his mind was bound to her, he said:
“I shall go,” he said. “In that case, take only what has been brought by you and go,” [the city guard replied].
He took him and went to the house of the city guardian. Having placed the merchant’s son in a concealed spot and seating the thief in a hidden carriage, he sent word to Sāmā:
“This thief is notorious throughout the kingdom; therefore, during the darkness—”
"Let it be for now; I shall have him executed at the time when people are secluded," he said, making this pretext.

After waiting for a short while, once the people were secluded, he had the merchant’s son led with a great guard to the place of execution, cut off his head with a sword, impaled his body on a stake, and entered the city.
From that time on, Sāmā would not take anything from the hands of others;
she wandered about taking her pleasure only with him. He thought: "If this woman’s heart is bound to another, she will kill me as well and take her pleasure with him.
She is an extreme betrayer of friends; I must not remain here, but depart quickly."
"It is better to flee; moreover, rather than going with empty hands, I shall take her jewelry and depart," he thought.
Then, on one day, he said to her: "My dear, we always remain at home like chickens confined in a cage; let us go for a pleasure excursion to the park one day. She consented, saying, "Very well."
Having prepared all kinds of hard and soft foods, she adorned herself with every ornament,
sat with him in a covered carriage, and went to the park. While sporting there with her, he thought,
"Now it is time for me to escape," and as if wishing to enjoy the pleasure of defilement with her, he entered the midst of a *kaṇavīra* bush.
As if embracing him, she squeezed him until he lost consciousness, threw him down, stripped off all his ornaments, and bound them together with her own upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
Placing the bundle upon her shoulder, she leaped over the palace wall of the park and departed.
Having regained consciousness, she rose, went to her attendants, and asked, "Where is the noble son?"
“We do not know, noble lady. Thinking, “He must have fled out of fear, perceiving me to be dead,” she became displeased;
returning from that very spot to her home, she lay down on the floor, resolving, “From this moment on, as long as my beloved husband has not been seen, I shall not sleep upon a decorated bed.
From then on, she did not wear a pleasant garment, nor two... [two garments].
She did not eat her meals, nor did she use perfumes, garlands, and the like.

Thinking, "By whatever means possible, I shall seek out the noble son and have him summoned," she had actors summoned and gave them a thousand [pieces of money]. When they asked, "What shall we do, Noble Lady?
she said, "There is no place where you cannot go; while you are traveling through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, [perform] a festival..."
Having formed a circle at the festival grounds, you should sing this first song,” she said, teaching the actors the first verse.
Then, after speaking, she said: “When this song has been sung by you, if the noble son should be present within that assembly, he will converse with you;
then, having informed him of my state of health, you should take him and return.”
"If he does not come, you should send him a message. Having given them their travel expenses, he dismissed the actors.
They departed from Bārāṇasī and, performing their performances here and there, arrived at a certain frontier village.
That bandit was also living there, having fled thither. While they were performing there, they sang this little song first:
“That which you yourself pressed with your arm upon the lovely *kaṇavera* flowers in the springtime—that [flower] spoke of health to you.
In this context, *kaṇaveresu* means among the *karavīra* flowers. *Bhāṇusu* means endowed with the radiance of red-colored blossoms.
"O neighbor, [I am] such-and-such a name. "He oppressed her" means that, as if desiring to take his pleasure through the passion of defilement (*kilesarati*), he oppressed her while embracing her.
"That string" refers to that woman; she was healthy, yet you, fearing under the impression that "she is dead," fled. She spoke of her own health;
the meaning is that she informed [you].
Having heard that, the crow approached the actor and, conversing with him while saying, "You say 'Sāmā is alive,' but I do not believe it," he spoke the second verse:
"Alas! It would not be believable if the wind could carry away a mountain;
yet if the wind could carry away a mountain, it could carry away the entire earth."
"Where my wife has passed away, she told me she was well. The meaning of this is: "O actor, one should not believe this; it is not to be believed.
That the wind might carry away a mountain as if it were blades of grass or leaves—even if it were to carry away that mountain, it would carry away the entire earth. Just as...

"I would not believe this, nor that 'this is so. For how could I believe it when she says, 'Sāmā has passed away,' since Sāmā, having passed away, tells me she is healthy? One who is dead does not send a message to anyone.
Having heard his words, the actor spoke the third verse:
“She has not yet died, nor does she desire another;
being faithful, she eats but one meal a day, and she longs for him alone.
In this context, “she longs for him alone” means she does not desire any other man; she yearns for, desires, and aspires to him alone.
Hearing this, the thief said, "Whether she lives or dies, I have no need for her," and spoke the fourth verse:
"Though I am a stranger, Sāmā has married me, who am unstable, to one who is stable.
Yet Sāmā might marry another even more distant than I; from here, I shall go to a place far away."
In this context, *asanthutaṃ* means one with whom no association has been formed. *Cirasaṃthutena* means by one with whom an association has been established for a long time.
*Nimīnī* means she exchanged. *Adhuvaṃ dhuvena* means "she exchanged me, who am unstable, for him who is stable as her husband";
the meaning is that she gave a thousand [pieces of money] to the city guard and took me away. *Mayāpi sā mā nimineyya aññaṃ* means that Sāmā might also exchange me for another.
"Having changed my husband, I shall take him [with me]. I will go to a place even further than this, where it is impossible for her to hear news or any report of me;
I will go to such a distant place. Therefore, inform her that I have gone elsewhere.
Having said this, while they were still looking on, she dressed more heavily and fled with great speed.
The actors went and told her what he had done. She became remorseful and spent her time according to her own natural disposition.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: at the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.
At that time, the merchant’s son was this monk; the woman was his former wife; and the thief was none other than myself.
The eighth: The Commentary on the Kaṇavera Jātaka.
[319] 9. The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka.
"Truly happy indeed I live"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at the Badarika Monastery near Kosambī, concerning the Elder Rāhula.
He spoke concerning this. The background story has already been related in detail below in the *Tipallatthajātaka*.
In the Hall of Truth, the monks initiated a discussion, saying, "Friends, Rāhula is desirous of training, conscientious, and capable of receiving instruction.
When this discourse on that venerable one’s virtues had arisen, the Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion at present?"
Having asked, "Are you sitting together? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
even in the past, Rāhula was desirous of training, conscientious, and capable of receiving instruction. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā and, after mastering all the arts, he went forth into homelessness in a region of the Himalayas.
Having taken up the ascetic life of an *isi*, he developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
While dwelling in a delightful forest grove, enjoying the play of *jhāna*, he went to a certain frontier village to partake of salt and sour food. There, the people [saw] him...
Having seen him, with hearts full of faith, they had a leaf-hut constructed in a certain forest and, providing him with the four requisites, they settled him there.
At that time, in that village, a fowler caught a wild partridge, trained it thoroughly, and kept it in a cage.
He took the bird to that forest and, at its cry, [caught] all the other partridges that came near.
Having caught and sold them, he made his living. The partridge thought, "Because of me alone, many of my kinsmen are being destroyed;
this is my misfortune," and so he became silent. Knowing that he had become silent, the fowler struck him on the head with a bamboo splinter.
Distressed by the pain, the partridge cried out. In this way, that fowler [continued] because of him...
Having caught the partridge, he made his living from it.
Then that partridge thought: "I have no intention that 'these should die,' yet the act of dependence touches me;
for if I do not make a sound, they do not come, but only when I make one do they come. As they arrive..."
"By taking this, one brings about the end of life; is there, then, any evil for me in this, or is there not?
From that time forth, he wandered about seeking such a wise person who might cut through this doubt of his, thinking, "Who indeed could resolve this doubt for me?
Then one day, that fowler, having caught many partridges and filled a basket with them, thought, "I shall drink some water."
Having gone to the Bodhisatta’s hermitage and placed that cage near the Bodhisatta, he drank water and lay down on the sandy ground, falling asleep.
The partridge, perceiving that he had fallen asleep, thought, "I will ask this ascetic about my doubt;
if he knows, he will explain it to me," and while still sitting in the cage, he addressed him.
Questioning him, he spoke the first verse:
“Most happily indeed do I live, for I obtain and enjoy my food;
yet I stand by the wayside—what, O Venerable Sir, will be my destiny?”
"In this regard, 'I live very happily indeed,' venerable sir, means that by depending on this fowler, I live quite happily.
'I obtain' means that I am able to eat whatever food and delicacies I desire.
And 'I stand at the crossroads' means that furthermore, wherever my kinsmen perish upon hearing my cry as they arrive one after another, in that place..."
"I stand in the way. What, venerable sir, will be my destination? he asked, "What, venerable sir, will be my destiny, what will be my outcome?
Responding to his question, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“If your mind, O bird, does not incline toward evil action, then for you who are unoccupied [with evil] and auspicious, no evil will cling.
In this context, “toward evil action” means: if your mind does not incline for the sake of committing evil deeds.
"He does not incline toward it, lean toward it, or tend toward it.

"For one who is unoccupied"—meaning, while this is so, for you, O auspicious one, who remain pure and have not exerted yourself or made an effort to commit evil deeds, evil does not smear nor adhere to you.
Having heard that, the partridge spoke the third verse:
“Thinking, ‘Our relative is seated,’ many people come;
they commit an offense against the rule of dependence, and my mind is apprehensive regarding them.
The meaning of this is: Venerable sir, if I were not to make a sound, these partridge folk would not come; [they would commit an offense] toward me...
When many people come, thinking, "A relative of ours is sitting here," as each one arrives, the hunter seizes them and brings them to their death;
thus, depending upon and relying on me, he commits, acquires, and gains this kamma of taking life.
Regarding that evil committed in dependence on me, [I reflect]: "Is this evil mine?"—thus it occurs to me.
"The mind fears, suspects, and falls into remorse.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the fourth verse:
"If the mind is not corrupted, one does not experience the results of dependent action."
“Evil does not cling to one who is free from anxiety and auspicious.

The meaning of this is: if your mind is not corrupted by the performance of evil, and you do not lean toward it, incline toward it, or tend toward it—if that is so, then even an evil deed committed against the Venerable One by a hunter will not touch him.

"It does not adhere; for since you are one who is free from concern, without attachment, auspicious, and pure, the absence of the volition to take life means that evil does not defile you, and your mind is not stained by it.

In this way the Great Being convinced the partridge, and he too, relying on him, became free from remorse. When the hunter woke up, he paid homage to the Bodhisatta and departed, taking the cage with him.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Rāhula was the partridge, and the ascetic was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth narrative, the Tittira-jātaka. [320] 10. The Commentary on the Succaja-jātaka (The Birth Story of the Good Partridge)
"Alas, the dance is fleeting!"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain householder.
It is said that he thought, "I shall settle a debt in the village," and went there with his wife.
Having settled it and brought back the wealth, he thought, "I will take it later," and left it with one family. Then, as he was returning to Sāvatthī along the road, he fell ill.
He saw a mountain. Then his wife said to him, "Husband, if this mountain were made of gold, would you give me something from it?
"Who are you? I will not give you anything," he replied. She became displeased, thinking, "How hard-hearted he is!
Even if this mountain were made of gold, he would not give me anything."
Having arrived near the Jeta Grove, they thought, "We shall drink water," and entering the monastery, they drank.

At that very time at dawn, the Teacher, perceiving their underlying potential for the fruit of stream-entry and awaiting their arrival, sat in the courtyard of his fragrant chamber, emitting rays of six-colored light. They too, having drunk the water, returned.
Having paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down. After the Teacher had exchanged greetings with them, he asked, "Where have you been?
"To our village, venerable sir, to collect a loan," they replied. "What is it, lay sister?
Does your husband desire your welfare and do what is beneficial for you? "Venerable sir, I am full of affection for him."

"But this man has no affection for me; today, when I saw the mountain and said, 'If this mountain were made of gold, you might give me something,' he replied, 'Who are you? I will give you nothing. Thus, his heart is hardened.
"Laywoman, he speaks thus, yet when he remembers your virtue, then all his sovereignty—"
Having said, "He gives them," and being requested by them with the words, "Tell us, venerable sir," he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister, the performer of all his duties.
Then one day, seeing the crown prince coming to attend upon him, the king thought, "This..."
Thinking, "He might cause a rebellion in the inner palace," he summoned him and said, "Dear son, as long as I live, you shall not be permitted to dwell in the city;
dwell elsewhere and exercise sovereignty after my passing.
He replied, "Very well," and having paid homage to his father, departed from the city with his eldest wife, went to the borderlands, and entered the forest.
Having constructed a leaf-hut, he lived there, subsisting on forest roots and fruits. Later, the king passed away.
The crown prince, observing the constellations and learning of his death, was returning to Bārāṇasī when he saw a mountain along the way.
Then his wife said to him, "If, my lord, this mountain were made of gold..."
“If you have anything, give it to me. She replied, “Who are you? I will give you nothing.
She thought, “I entered the forest because I was unable to sever my affection for him, yet he speaks thus; his heart is exceedingly hard.
Even though he has become king, what good will he ever do for me? Thus she became displeased. He then returned and was established in the kingship.
He appointed her to the position of chief queen, but this was merely a matter of prestige;
there was no further honor or respect, nor did he even acknowledge her existence.
The Bodhisatta thought, "This queen was a benefactor to this king; disregarding hardship, she lived in the forest. This...
Disregarding her, he wandered about enjoying himself with others, thinking, "I shall act in such a way that she obtains all sovereignty.
One day, having approached her, he said, "Great Queen, we do not receive even a mere morsel of almsfood from you;
why have you neglected us? You are exceedingly hard-hearted!"
“There is,” he said. “Dear son, if I were to receive it myself, I would give it to you as well; but since I am not receiving it, what shall I give?
What indeed will the king give to me now? On the way, when he was asked, ‘Will you give me anything from this golden mountain that has arisen? he replied, ‘Who are you? I will give nothing.’”
“Even though he was capable of giving, he did not give. “But will you be able to speak this matter in the presence of the king?
“I shall be able, dear father. “In that case, while I stand before the king, I will ask him;
you may then speak. “Very well, dear father. When the Bodhisatta had come to the queen’s attendance upon the king and stood there, he said: “Is it not true, my lady...”
“Noble lady, we do not receive anything from you. “My dear, if I were receiving anything, I would give it to you;
but I myself receive nothing. Not receiving anything, how could I give to you? What indeed will the king give me now?
When he was returning from the forest, he saw a mountain and thought: ‘If this mountain were made of gold...’”
To illustrate this meaning—that when one is told, "If you have anything, give it to me," they say, "Who are you?
I will give nothing," and thus does not relinquish even what is easy to give—she spoke the first verse:
"Truly, she did not give what she promised to give; with her words she gave a mountain, but she did not actually bestow it."
"For what was there for him not to give, when he did not give the mountain upon my word?
In this context, "though it could easily be given" means that even though he was able to give it with ease, he did not give it. "Not giving" means not giving the mountain even by mere word.
"For what was there for him not to give? means: for what indeed was there for him not to give when he was thus entreated by me?

"What indeed would he have to give? If, when requested by me, he had given that mountain—even one made of gold—by his word alone, the meaning is that he would have granted it merely through his speech.
Having heard this, the king spoke the second verse:
“What one does, that one should say; what one does not do, that one should not say. The wise clearly recognize the one who speaks without acting.
Its meaning is this: whatever a wise person should perform with the body, that he should express with speech. Whatever he does not perform—
One should not say that; rather, one who *wishes* to give should say, "I give," not one who does not wish to give—this is the intended meaning. For what reason?
Because wise people recognize as merely speaking falsehood one who, having said "I will give," subsequently does not give.
This person speaks only the mere words "I will give" but does not actually give; for...
Moreover, even what has not been given becomes as if given by the mere utterance of words;
the wise understand his state of lying when they realize that it will be considered "already received" even before it is actually obtained, whereas fools are satisfied with the mere words.
Having heard this, the queen raised her hands in reverential salutation to the king and spoke the third verse:
“O Prince, let there be homage to you; you are established in truth and the Dhamma.
Even though you have met with misfortune, your mind delights in the truth.

In this context, “in truth and the Dhamma” refers both to verbal truth and to the nature of reality (sabhāvadhamma). “Even though you have met with misfortune” means that although you have encountered the misfortune known as banishment from your kingdom, your mind still finds delight only in the truth.
Having heard the queen speaking thus in praise of the king’s virtues, the Bodhisatta spoke the fourth verse while recounting her own virtues:
“She who is poor with the poor, and famous with the wealthy—
she indeed is his supreme wife, compared to the women of those possessed of gold.”
In this context, "famous" (*kittimā*) means "endowed with renown.
She is indeed "supreme" (*paramā*) because, when her husband is poor, she herself becomes poor and does not abandon him. When he is wealthy, she becomes wealthy and follows her husband alone;
she shares equally in his pleasure and pain. For she is his supreme and most excellent [consort].
"A wife," he said. "But for one who possesses wealth and stands in authority, there are indeed women; this is not at all surprising.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta praised the queen’s virtue, saying, "Great King, when you were suffering, she lived in the forest sharing your sorrow; it is right that you show her honor. At his words, the king—
Recalling the queen’s virtues, he said, “O wise one, through your words I have remembered the queen’s virtues,” and he gave her all her sovereignty.
Thinking, “I have been made to remember the queen’s virtues by you,” he also rendered great honor to the Bodhisatta.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, both the husband and wife were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti).
At that time, this householder was the King of Bārāṇasī, this female lay follower was the Queen, and I myself was the wise minister.
This concludes the commentary on the *Succaja Jātaka*, the tenth.
The second chapter, the *Pucimanda Vagga*.
3. The Chapter on the House-Destroyer [321] 1.

The Commentary on the Birth Story of the House-Destroyer "Your heads are like those of humans"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the one who had burned the leaf-hut of the Elder Mahākassapa.
This was spoken concerning a young bhikkhu. The incident, however, originated in Rājagaha.
At that time, it seems, the Elder was dwelling in a forest hut near Rājagaha, and two young men were attending upon him.
Of these two, one was helpful to the Elder, while the other was difficult to speak to; whatever the former did, the latter treated as if he himself had done it. Because of this—
When water for the face and other necessities have been prepared, he goes into the presence of the Elder, pays homage, and says, "Venerable sir, water has been set out;
wash your face," and so forth. Having risen early, he sweeps the Elder’s courtyard;
then, at the time of the Elder’s departure, he sweeps the entire courtyard himself while moving back and forth.
He acted as if he were doing so. Being perfect in his duties, he thought: "This man of evil speech acts toward me as if I had acted toward him;
I shall make his deception manifest.
Having eaten in that village and returned, while the others were still sleeping, he heated bathing water, placed it on a wooden shelf, and—
He placed another half-nāḷi measure of water on the hearth.

The other, having woken up and gone there, seeing steam rising, thought, "The water must have been heated and placed in the bathing shed," and went to the Elder, saying, "Venerable sir, bathing water has been placed in the bathing shed;
please bathe. The Elder said, "I shall bathe," and went along with him.
Having arrived, he did not give water at the gatehouse but asked, "Where is the water?
He hurried to the fire-hall and dropped his ladle into an empty vessel; the ladle struck the bottom of the empty vessel and made the sound "tatā.
From that time on, he became known by the name "Uluṅkasaddaka" (the Ladle-Sounder).
At that moment, the other [monk] brought water from a back-well and said, "Bathe, venerable sir.
Having bathed and reflected, the Elder, knowing the difficult-to-correct nature of Uluṅkasaddaka, exhorted him when he came for his evening attendance upon the Elder:
"Friend, for one who is called a recluse, it is proper to say only 'I have done what was to be done' regarding what he himself has accomplished; otherwise..."
“[This] is a deliberate lie; from now on, do not act in such a manner.
Having become angry with the Elder, on the following day he did not enter the village for alms together with the Elder. The Elder entered [the village] with the others alone.
