The one who made the sound of the water-pot went to the Elder’s supporter’s family, and when asked, “Venerable sir, where is the Elder? he replied, “Because of his indisposition...”
Having said, "I am sitting right here in the monastery," when they asked, "Venerable sir, what may we obtain for you? he replied, "Give me this and that.
Having taken [the food], he went to a place of his own choosing, ate, and returned to the monastery.
On the following day, the Elder went to that family and sat down. When the people asked, "Venerable sir, is there anything unwell with the noble one?"
When it was said, "Yesterday, while sitting in the monastery itself, we sent food in the hand of such-and-such a young man; has the noble one partaken?
the Elder remained silent. Having finished his meal duties, he went to the monastery and, at the time of the evening attendance upon the Elders, he addressed the one who had arrived:
"Friend, in such-and-such a village, in such-and-such a family, they thought, 'The Elder ought to receive this and that.'"
Having said, "It seems they ate after making a formal request," he added, "A formal request is not permitted; do not practice such improper conduct again.
Because of this, the man harbored resentment toward the Elder, thinking:
"Yesterday this man quarreled with me over a mere matter of water, and today he has eaten a handful of rice from the house of my own supporters!"
Unable to endure it, he started a quarrel again, thinking, "I shall know what this man ought to do.
On the following day, when the elders had entered for alms, he took up a club, broke the vessels used for consumption, set fire to the leaf-hut, and fled.
While still alive, he became a *manussapeta* (a hungry ghost among men); having withered away, he passed away and was reborn in the Great Niraya Hell of Avīci. He—
The misconduct committed by him became manifest in the midst of the great multitude.

Then, some bhikkhus went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī; having put away their bowls and robes in a suitable place, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged greetings with them.
“From where have you come? he asked. “From Rājagaha, venerable sir,” they replied. “Who is the teacher there who gives exhortation?
“The Elder Mahākassapa, venerable sir. “Is it well with Kassapa, monks? “Yes, venerable sir, it is well with the Elder;
however, his pupil, having become angry when the exhortation was given, set fire to the Elder’s leaf-hut.”
"He has fled. Hearing this, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is better to wander alone than to travel with such a fool as Kassapa," and he spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:
"If, while wandering, one does not find anyone better or even equal to oneself..."
“One should make a firm resolve for the solitary life; there is no companionship with fools.
Having said this, he further addressed those bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this Kuṭidūsaka was a defiler of huts;
formerly too he was a defiler of huts. And it is not only now that he is angry with one who gives him exhortation; formerly too he was angry.”
Having spoken thus, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a *siṅgila* bird.
Upon reaching maturity, he built a nest that was pleasing to him and sheltered from the rain, and lived in a region of the Himālaya. Then one...
At the time of the rains, while the sky was pouring down an unbroken torrent of rain, a monkey, oppressed by the cold and gnashing his teeth, sat not far from the Bodhisatta.
Seeing him thus suffering, the Bodhisatta conversed with him and spoke this first verse:
“Your head is like that of a human, yet your hands and feet are those of a monkey.”
"Now, by what reason is it that your house does not exist?
There, "by what reason" (*vaṇṇena*) means by what cause. "House" (*agāraṃ*): he asked, "By what cause is your dwelling-place not there?
Having heard that, the monkey spoke the second verse:
“Though my head is that of a human, and my hands and feet are those of a *siṅgila* bird, that wisdom which is said to be supreme among humans is not found in me.
In this context, he addresses that bird by the name *siṅgila*. “That which is said to be supreme among humans” means that which is the best among humans.

“They speak thus, yet I do not possess that wisdom of discernment. For in this world, the strength of the head, hands, feet, and body is indeed immeasurable, but the wisdom of discernment alone is supreme;
since I lack that, therefore a household life does not exist for me.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the following two verses:
“For one whose mind is unsteady, whose mind is fickle, who is treacherous,
and whose virtue is constantly inconstant— no state of happiness exists. Therefore,
exert your power and transcend mere virtuous conduct.”
"O monkey, build a hut to protect yourself from the cold wind.
In this context, "of one with an unsteady mind" means of one whose mind lacks a firm foundation. "A betrayer" means a betrayer of friends.
"Of one who is not constant in virtue" means of one who does not guard their virtue at all times. "He should exercise his power" means: O dear monkey, you should [act] with wisdom.
Exert power, strength, and means for the sake of arising. "Transcend *sīliyanti*":
having transcended the state of immorality known as *sīliya*, one becomes virtuous. "Make a *kuṭavaṃ kapī*":
make for yourself a *kuṭava*, a nest, a dwelling place capable of protecting against the cold wind.
The monkey thought, "This one is reproaching me simply because I am sitting in a place sheltered from the rain;

I will not let him sit in this nest. Then, wishing to seize the Bodhisatta, he leapt forward, but the Bodhisatta flew up and went elsewhere. The monkey, having destroyed the nest and reduced it to dust and fragments, departed.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the monkey was the one who set the hut on fire, while I myself was the Siṅgila bird.
This concludes the first commentary, the Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka.
2. The Commentary on the Duddubha Jātaka.
“Venerable sir, he trembles,” said this regarding certain non-Buddhist ascetics while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana.

It is said that those ascetics would prepare their beds on thorny mats in various places near Jetavana, practice the fivefold heat, and engage in various kinds of wrong austerities. Then, a number of bhikkhus in Sāvatthī...
Having wandered for alms and returning to Jeta’s Grove, they saw them on the road between villages;
going there and approaching the Teacher, they asked, "Venerable sir, is there any essence in the undertaking of vows by those of other sects?
The Teacher replied, "No, monks, there is neither essence nor distinction in their undertaking of vows; for when it is rubbed and scrutinized,"
“It sounds like a path to a dung-heap, like the cry of a *sasaka* or a *duddubha*,” he said.
When they requested, “We do not know its resemblance to a *duddubha*; tell us, venerable sir,” he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a lion and reached maturity.
He was dwelling in the forest. At that time, however, near the western ocean, there was a grove of palm trees interspersed with *beluva* trees.
There, a certain hare lived at the foot of a *beluva* tree, beneath a palm sapling.
One day, having returned from foraging and lying down beneath a palm leaf, he thought: "If this earth were to collapse..."
"Where indeed shall I go? At that moment, a beluva fruit fell upon a palm leaf.
Hearing its sound, he thought, "Surely the earth is collapsing! and leaping up, he fled without even looking back.
Seeing him fleeing with great speed, terrified by the fear of death, another rabbit asked, "What is it, sir? Why are you so—"
“You are fleeing in fear! “Do not ask me, sir! he replied. “What is it, sir? What is it?
the other cried, as he continued to run after him. The first man turned back and, without even looking, said, “The earth is collapsing here!
He too fled after him. Thus one saw the other, and the other saw another; in this way, a thousand hares fled together as one. They—
Even a single deer, upon seeing it, would flee after gathering together with others.
A boar, a gokanna, a buffalo, a gayal, a tiger, a leopard, a lion, and an elephant—each, having seen it, asked, "What is this?
When told, "The earth is collapsing here," they fled. In this manner, by degrees, there came to be a force of animals extending for a league.
Then the Bodhisatta, seeing that army fleeing, asked, "What is this? Upon hearing, "The earth is collapsing here," he thought:
"A collapse of the earth has never occurred before; surely these people have heard something false.
If I do not exert myself, they will all perish; I shall grant them their lives."
With the speed of a lion, he went ahead to the foot of the mountain and let out a lion’s roar three times.
Terrified by the fear of the lion, they turned back and stood huddled together. The lion entered among them and asked, "For what purpose are you fleeing?
"The earth is collapsing," they replied. "By whom was it seen collapsing? "The elephants know."
The elephant asked them. They replied, "We do not know; the lions know. The lions said, "We do not know; the tigers know.
The tigers said, "We do not know; the rhinoceroses know. The rhinoceroses said, "The gayals know.
The gayals said, "The buffaloes know. The buffaloes said, "The gavayas know. The gavayas [said], "The *gokaṇṇas* know. The *gokaṇṇas* also...
“The pigs know,” they said; the pigs also said, “The deer know”; the deer also said, “We do not know, the hares know.
When the hares were questioned, they pointed out that hare, saying, “This one tells.
Then he asked him, “Is it true, my friend, that you saw the earth being destroyed? “Yes, sir, I saw it. “Where were you living?”
"Do you know? "I live in a grove of *beluva* and *missaka* palm trees near the western ocean.
For there, lying at the foot of a *beluva* tree beneath a palm thicket, on the ground covered with palm leaves, I thought: 'If the earth were to collapse, where would I go?
Then, at that very moment, having heard the sound of the earth collapsing, I fled."
Sīha thought: “Surely a beluva fruit must have fallen upon that palm leaf and made a sound like a drum;
having heard that sound, he developed the perception that ‘the earth is collapsing’ and fled. I shall find out the truth of it.
Taking the hare with him and reassuring the great crowd, he said: “I [shall see] whether the earth is actually collapsing at this place where he saw it...”
“Having understood the state of non-dissolution as it truly is, I shall return; until my arrival, you must remain right here,” he said.
Placing the hare upon his back, he leaped forward with the speed of a lion, set the hare down in a grove of palm trees, and said, “Come, show me the place you have seen.
“I am not able to do so, Master,” [the hare replied]. “Come, do not be afraid,” he said. He—
Being unable to approach the Beluva tree, he stood at a short distance and,
saying, "This, Lord, is the place where Duddubha dwells," he spoke the first verse: "In this region, O Blessed One, where I dwell, Duddubha cries out."
“I too do not know this; what is it that sounds like a *duddubha*?
In this context, “sounds like a *duddubha*” means it makes the sound of a *duddubha*. “Venerable sir” (*bhaddante*) means “may there be welfare for you. “What is this? means:
in the place where I dwell, something there sounds like a *duddubha*; even I do not know, “What indeed is this that sounds like a *duddubha*?”
"Or for what reason does it thunder? Why did you hear only the sound of thundering?
When this was said, Sīha went to the foot of the beluva tree;
seeing the rabbit lying beneath a palm leaf and the ripe beluva fruit that had fallen onto the top of the palm leaf, he understood, as it truly was, that the earth had not been destroyed by fire.
Having understood this, he placed the hare upon his back and, with the speed of a lion, quickly went into the presence of the deer herds.
He announced the entire situation and, comforting the group of deer by saying, "Do not be afraid," he released them.
For had the Bodhisatta not been there at that time, they would all have entered the ocean and perished. But because of the Bodhisatta...
"Relying on him, all obtained life.
"Hearing that the beluva fruit had fallen, the hare rushed, crying 'duddubha!';
hearing the hare's words, the herd of deer was filled with agitation."
“Without having reached the consciousness of the path, following only the voices of others, these fools are intent on mere noise; they rely on the conviction of others.
But those who are endowed with virtue and delight in wisdom and tranquility—”
“The wise, far removed and detached, do not rely on the trust of others.
These are the three verses of the Fully Enlightened One.
In this context, *beluva* refers to the *beluva* fruit. *Duddubhanti* means making such a sound. *Santattā* means terrified.
“A herd of deer” (*migavāhinī*) refers to a multitude of deer numbering many thousands.
“The track of consciousness” (*padaviññāṇa*) means the station of consciousness; the meaning is that it has not reached the portion of auditory consciousness.

“They become dependent on others” means those fools, ordinary worldlings who follow the voices of others, imagining that very clamor known as the voice of another to be “supreme,” rely solely on the conviction of others because the track of consciousness has not been reached.
They act recklessly, doing this or that after placing their trust in the words of others.

"Endowed with virtue" means they are possessed of the virtue that has come through the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). "Delighting in tranquility through wisdom" means they delight in the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*) by means of the very wisdom that has come through the Path;
or alternatively, just as they are endowed with virtue, so too are they perfected in wisdom and delight in the pacification of the defilements.

The meaning is as follows: "The wise are far removed and abstinent" means that the wise, being far removed from and abstinent toward evil deeds—such stream-enterers who, by virtue of their distance from evil and their delight in the pacification of the defilements, have once penetrated the Dhamma through the knowledge of the path—even when others speak to them, they do not believe or accept it.
Why? Because it is evident to themselves. Therefore it was said:
“The man who is faithless and ungrateful, who severs the bond of continuity—he has destroyed his own opportunity, he has vomited out his hope; he is indeed the supreme person.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, I myself was the lion.”
The second [tale], the Commentary on the Duddubha Jātaka.
[323] 3. The Commentary on the Brahmadatta Jātaka:
"Two kinds of beggars"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at the Aggāḷava Cetiya near Āḷavī, concerning the training rule regarding the building of small huts (*kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada*).
He spoke with reference to this. The background story, however, has already been related below in the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka.
Here, the Teacher said, "Is it true, monks, that you live full of begging and full of requests?
When they replied, "Yes, venerable sir," he rebuked those monks, saying, "Monks, in the past, when the wise men were addressed by the King, the Lord of the Earth..."
"Even though they had been invited to a meal, they desired to ask for a leaf-parasol and a pair of single-layered sandals;
out of fear of breaking their sense of shame and modesty, they did not speak of it in the midst of the great crowd, but spoke of it in private. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while the King of Uttarapañcāla was ruling in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila, the Bodhisatta..."
Having been reborn in a brahmin family in a certain market town, he reached maturity and, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā,
later went forth into the ascetic life. After dwelling for a long time in the Himalayas, subsisting by gleaning on forest roots and fruits,
he wandered along the path of men to seek salt and sour flavors, eventually arriving at the city of Uttarapañcāla.
Having reached the royal garden and stayed there, on the following day he entered the city seeking alms and arrived at the palace gate.

The king, being pleased with his conduct and demeanor, had him seated upon a great terrace, fed him with choice food fit for a king, and having obtained his promise, settled him right there in the garden.
He continued to eat regularly at the royal residence itself.

At the end of the rainy season, desiring to go to the Himālaya mountains, he thought, "It is necessary for me to obtain a single-layered sandal and a leaf parasol as I travel on the road; I shall ask the king for them.
One day, having come to the royal park and seeing the king seated after paying his respects, [he requested] the sandals and the parasol.
Having thought, "I shall ask," he thought again: "When one asks another, 'Give me this,' one weeps;
and when the other says, 'There is none,' the former weeps in response. Now, let not the great multitude see us weeping, nor the king.
Therefore, in a secluded, hidden place, both of us shall weep and then remain silent. Then, to him—
“Great King, I desire privacy,” he said. Upon hearing this, the king withdrew his attendants.
The Bodhisatta thought, “If the king does not grant it when I ask, our friendship will be broken; therefore, I shall not ask.
Unable to take his name that day, he said, “Go now, Great King; I shall know on another day.”
On one day, when the king came to the park, twelve years passed while [the elder] was unable to request anything, even though he said, "Just so, just so. Then the king thought:
"My noble sir says, 'Great King, I desire privacy,' yet once the assembly has departed, he does not dare to say anything; it is clear he has something he wishes to say."
“Twelve years have passed; having lived the holy life for so long, he has become weary and, desiring to enjoy wealth, I suspect he longs for the kingdom.
Yet, being unable to utter the very name of kingship, he remains silent.
Today, beginning with the granting of the kingdom, I shall give him whatever he desires. He went to the pleasure grove.

Having gone and paid homage, he sat down. When the Bodhisatta said, "I desire to speak in private," and the assembly had withdrawn, [the king], being unable to say anything at all, was told by the Bodhisatta:
"For twelve years you said, 'I desire to speak in private,' yet even now that you have obtained privacy, you are unable to say anything.
I invite you to confess everything, beginning with your kingship."
“Being fearless, ask for whatever you desire. “Great King, will you grant me what I ask?
“I shall grant it, Bhante. “Great King, as I travel along the road, I require a single-layered sandal and a leaf parasol. “Bhante, have you had these for twelve years?”
“You cannot bring yourself to ask. “Yes, Great King. “For what reason, venerable sir, did you speak thus?
“Great King, one who begs, saying ‘Give me such-and-such,’ is said to weep; one who says ‘I have none’ is said to counter-weep.
‘If you do not give what I have asked for, let not the great multitude see this weeping and counter-weeping of ours.’”
“‘It is for this purpose, O King Brahmadatta, that I seek you in private,’ he said, and then spoke these first three verses:
“A beggar, O King, encounters two outcomes:
either failure or the gain of wealth; such indeed is the nature of begging.”
“Beggings, O bull among charioteers of the Pañcālas, are called weeping;
he who rejects a begging is called one who weeps in return.
Let not the well-assembled Pañcālas see me weeping.”
"Or you yourself, O King Brahmadatta, [will suffer] if you oppose him; therefore, I desire privacy.
In this passage, "O King Brahmadatta," both [the speaker and the listener] address the king. "Nigacchati" means he obtains or finds.
"Evaṃdhammā" means having such a nature. "Āhu" means the wise say. "Pañcālānaṃ rathesabha" refers to the bull among chariot-warriors of the kingdom of Pañcāla.
"O Lord, excellent chariot. "He who rejects a request" refers to one who refuses a petitioner by saying, "There is none.
"They call that 'counter-wailing'" means they say that such refusal is "paṭirodana. "'Lest they should see me' means:
'Lest the Pāñcālas, the inhabitants of your kingdom, gathered together, should see me weeping.'"
The King, having gained confidence in the Bodhisatta’s mark of reverence, spoke this fourth verse while granting him a boon:
“I give you, O Brahmin, a thousand Rohiṇī cows together with a bull;
for how could a noble man not give to a noble man after hearing your verses endowed with the Dhamma?”

In this context, *rohiṇīnam* means "of those that are red-colored. *Ariyo* means one who is endowed with noble conduct. *Ariyassa* means "to one who is endowed with noble conduct. *Kathaṃ na dajjā* means "for what reason would he not give? *Dhammayuttā* means "connected with reason" or "justified by cause.
However, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, I do not have need for sensual pleasures; give me only that which I ask for.
Taking a single-layered sandal and a leaf parasol, he said, "Great King, be heedful!"
"Give alms, observe the precepts, and perform the Uposatha rites," he advised the king; yet even as the king was still entreating him, he departed for the Himalayas.
There, having developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dharma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the king, while I myself was the ascetic."
The third *Jātaka* commentary, the Brahmadatta-jātaka.
[324] 4. The Commentary on the Cammasāṭaka-jātaka:
"He is indeed of beautiful form," this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a wandering ascetic named Cammasāṭaka.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that his only clothing consisted of a skin for both a lower garment and an upper robe.
One day, having departed from the wanderers’ park and wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he arrived at a place where sheep were fighting.
A sheep, seeing him and wishing to strike him, backed away. The wanderer thought, "This one is showing me respect..."
He did not retreat, saying, "I shall show you. A goat came rushing at him, struck him on the thigh, and knocked him down.
This incident of his failure to maintain self-control became well known throughout the Saṅgha of monks.
The monks raised the discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, "Friends, the wanderer Cammasāṭaka met with ruin because he failed to maintain self-control."
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?

When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, he met with ruin by employing those who were unworthy. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a certain merchant family.

Having reached maturity, he engaged in trade. At that time, a certain leather-clad wanderer (cammasāṭakaparibbājaka), while wandering for alms in Bārāṇasī, came upon a place where sheep were fighting.
Seeing a sheep backing away, he did not retreat, thinking, "It is showing me respect," [but rather thinking], "In the midst of all these people, this one sheep [is honoring us]..."
Knowing his virtue, he raised his joined palms in reverence and, while still standing, spoke this first verse: “Truly,
this four-footed creature is of noble form— both beautiful and very kind—
who honors a brahmin endowed with noble birth, he who is the excellent ram, renowned for his glory.”

In this context, "of beautiful form" means of noble birth. "Well-behaved" means one whose character is truly amiable. "Possessed of lineage and spells" means endowed with both noble birth and incantations.
"Famous" is a term for one who possesses a good reputation. At that moment, the wise merchant sitting in the marketplace, wishing to dissuade the wanderer, spoke the second verse:
"Do not, O Brahmin, place your trust in one who has seen only a little, based on his four feet."
"Desiring a firm blow, he approaches, thinking, 'He will give a good blow.
In this context, "with a fleeting glance" means with a momentary look.
Even as that wise merchant was speaking, the ram came rushing forward with speed, struck him on the thigh, and—
Right there, having caused him to feel intense pain, he threw him down. He lay there lamenting.
The Teacher, explaining the reason for this, spoke the third verse:
“The thigh-bone was broken, the load of thirty measures was overturned, and all the goods of the brahmin were shattered.”
“Both of them, raising their arms, cried out: ‘You are going too fast!
The celibate practitioner is being killed! The meaning of this is: “Monks, that wanderer’s thigh-bone was broken;
his carrying-pole was rolling back and forth. As it was rolling, whatever implements and goods the brahmin had there were also [thrown about].”
"Everything is broken. Raising both his arms and addressing the assembly standing around him, he cried out, wept, and lamented, saying, "Run forward! A celibate practitioner is being killed!
Then the wanderer spoke the fourth verse:
“Thus he lies struck down, who praises that which is unworthy of praise;
just as I today have been struck, O foolish one, by this ram.
In this context, *apūjaṃ* means that which is not worthy of worship (*apūjanīyaṃ*). *Yathāhamajja* means just as I today stand having made an improper exertion.
Struck by the ram with a powerful blow, he was killed right there. "Dummati" means one of poor wisdom.
Thus, whoever else shall exert effort toward what is unreal will experience suffering just as I have;
thus lamenting, he met his end right there.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the one wearing the skin-cloak was the present-day wearer of the skin-cloak, while the wise merchant was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the fourth Jātaka, the Cammasāṭaka Jātaka.
5. The Commentary on the Godharāja Jātaka.
"Thinking him to be a recluse"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical monk.

The background story has already been explained in detail above. Here too, the monks brought that monk before the Teacher and presented him, saying, "Venerable Sir, this monk is a hypocrite. The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, this one..."
Having said, "He is surely a deceiver," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a jackal;
having reached maturity and being endowed with physical strength, he lived in the forest. Not far from him, there was also a certain immoral ascetic who had built a leaf-hut.

Having built it, he made it his dwelling. While wandering for alms, the Bodhisatta saw it and, thinking, "This must be the leaf-hut of a virtuous ascetic," went there, paid homage to him, and returned to his own place of residence.
Then one day, that fraudulent ascetic obtained sweet meat prepared by a family of his supporters and thought, "What..."
Having asked, "What is this meat? and having heard it was "the meat of a monitor lizard," he was overcome by craving for its flavor.
Thinking, "I shall kill a monitor lizard that comes regularly to my hermitage, cook it as I please, and eat it," he took ghee, curd, pungent condiments, and other ingredients;
he went there, took a club, covered himself with his saffron robe, and waited for the Bodhisatta’s arrival.
Looking about, he sat at the door of the leaf-hut as if perfectly tranquil and composed.
Having approached and seen that his faculties were corrupted, [the monk] thought, "This man must have eaten the flesh of one of our own kin;
I shall investigate him. Standing downwind, he smelled the odor of the body and realized the state of having eaten the flesh of a kinsman.
Having recognized the ascetic, he did not approach him but turned back and went on his way. The ascetic, realizing that he had not returned, hurled a club;
however, the club did not strike his body but reached only the tip of his tail. The ascetic said, "Go away! I have missed you.
The Bodhisatta replied, "You may have missed me for now, but you shall not miss the four states of misery," and having said this, he fled.
Entering an anthill situated at the edge of the walking path, he thrust his head out through another opening and,
conversing with him, spoke these two verses:
“Thinking you were an ascetic, I approached you who are unrestrained;”
“Thus you have struck me with a staff, making me no longer a monastic.
“What use have you for matted hair, O dull-witted one? What use for your deerskin garment?
Your interior is a thicket, yet you polish only the exterior.”

In this context, "unrestrained" means that although he was not a recluse because his body and other faculties were unrestrained, I approached him thinking, "This is a recluse," imagining him to be a recluse due to his having stilled evil. "Pāhāsī" means I struck him. "With a deerskin garment" means:
what use have you for a deerskin robe worn draped over one shoulder? "The interior of your body" refers to the inside of your physical frame.
The thicket of defilements is like a gourd filled with poison, like a pit filled with dung, or like an anthill filled with venomous snakes.
You merely rub the exterior— the outside of the body— but because it is harsh within and smooth without,
it is like elephant dung or horse dung.
Having heard that, the ascetic spoke this third verse:
“Come, Godha, turn back; eat rice with fine grains.
I have oil and salt, and I have plenty of long pepper.”

"In this regard, 'I have plenty of *pippalī* (long pepper)' means that not only do I have rice and boiled milk-rice with oil and salt, but I also have many pungent condiments of various kinds, such as asafoetida, cumin, ginger, *lasuṇa*, garlic, black pepper, and *pippalī*; therefore, eat the rice boiled in milk prepared with these.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the fourth verse:
“I shall enter even further into this anthill a hundred fathoms high;
you praise oil and salt, but pepper is harmful to me.
In this context, “I shall enter” means I will go inside. “Harmful to me” means that this pepper, which you consider a pungent spice, is actually harmful and unsuitable for me.
Having spoken thus, he threatened him, saying, "Hey, you fraudulent ascetic!
If you stay here, I will have the people in the village where you go for alms seize you as a thief and bring you to ruin; flee quickly! Thereupon, the fraudulent ascetic fled.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the fraudulent ascetic was this deceitful bhikkhu, while I myself was the king of the herd."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Godharāja-jātaka.
[326] 6. The Commentary on the Kakkāru-jātaka.
"He who would not take by the body..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery, concerning Devadatta. Regarding him...
Indeed, after Devadatta had split the Saṅgha and departed, as his assembly defected along with the chief disciples, hot blood gushed from his mouth.

Then the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying, "Friends, Devadatta, having committed a falsehood and split the Saṅgha, now lies ill and experiences great suffering. The Teacher [heard this].
Having arrived, he asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting here gathered now?
When they replied, "With this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; even in the past this man was a liar.
And it is not only now that he experiences great suffering after committing a lie; in the past, too, he experienced it. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a certain son of the gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Now at that time, there was a great festival in Benares;
many nāgas, supaṇṇas, and earth-dwelling deities came and watched the festivities. From the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as well, four...
The sons of the gods, having adorned themselves with a head-ornament made of divine flowers called *kakkāru*, came to witness the festival.
The city of Bārāṇasī, twelve leagues in extent, was filled with a single scent by the fragrance of those flowers.
People wandered about, inquiring, "By whom were these flowers worn? Those sons of the gods—
Knowing, "They are observing us," they sprang up in the royal courtyard and stood in the sky by means of great divine power.
A great multitude gathered, and the king also went there together with the viceroy and his attendants.
Then they asked them, "From which divine world have you come, sirs? "We have come from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. "For what purpose have you come?"
“‘In order to show off their splendor. ‘What kind of flowers are these? ‘They are called celestial *kakkāru* flowers.
‘Master, you may wear other ornaments in the world of the gods; give these to us. The sons of the gods replied, ‘Celestial *kakkāru* flowers are of great power and are suitable only for the gods;
in the human world, they would be fit only for those who are base, of poor wisdom, and of low inclinations.’”
"These are not suitable for those who are immoral; however, these are suitable for those men who are endowed with such and such virtues," they said.
Having spoken thus, the eldest of the deva-sons recited the first verse:
“He who does not take another’s property with his body, nor speak falsehood with his speech, and who does not become intoxicated when receiving fame—he indeed is worthy of the *kakkāru* fruit.
The meaning of this is: he who, with his body, does not take even a blade of grass belonging to another, nor speaks a lie with his speech even while giving up his life...

He does not speak falsehood. This is merely a conventional way of teaching; however, the intended meaning here is one who, through the doors of body, speech, and mind, does not commit even the ten unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*).

Having obtained fame—that is, having gained power—one who, though intoxicated by the pride of power, does not abandon mindfulness and commit an evil deed: such a person as this, by these [qualities]...
“A person endowed with these qualities is worthy of this divine flower. Therefore, whoever is possessed of these qualities is worthy to ask for these flowers; I shall give them to him.
Having heard this, the chaplain thought: “I do not possess even one of these qualities; however, having spoken a falsehood...”
“Having taken these flowers, I shall wear them; thus the great multitude will know me as one endowed with virtues.
Thinking, “I am indeed possessed of these virtues,” he had those flowers brought and put on them, and then requested the second son of a god. The latter spoke this second verse:
“One should seek wealth by means of Dhamma, not take wealth through deceit;
having obtained riches, one should not become intoxicated—such a person indeed deserves the *kakkāru*.
Its meaning is as follows: one should seek wealth such as gold, silver, and so forth, by means of Dhamma, that is, by means of a livelihood purified [of wrong means]. “Not through deceit” means...
"One should not take wealth through deception; having obtained enjoyments such as clothing and ornaments, one should not fall into negligence—one such as this is worthy of these flowers.
The chaplain, saying "I am endowed with these qualities," had them brought and put them on, and then requested the third son of the gods. He spoke the third verse:
“He whose mind is not yellowed, and whose faith is undimmed—such a person should not eat savory food alone; he indeed deserves the *kakkāru* fruit.
The meaning of this is: for that individual whose mind is not yellowed—that is, like the dye of turmeric, it does not quickly fade.

It remains firm indeed. "Faith that does not waver" means that having placed one's trust in an action, its result, or the word of a person worthy of confidence, one does not become detached from or abandon it on account of even a trifling matter.
This refers to one who, rather than setting aside those who beg or other persons worthy of sharing, does not eat delicious food alone, but instead shares it with them.
“He who eats [this food] is worthy of these flowers.
The chaplain, saying, “I am endowed with these qualities,” had those flowers brought and put them on himself, and then requested the fourth son of the gods. He spoke this fourth verse:
“Whether face to face or behind one’s back, he who does not revile those who are virtuous;”
"One who acts as they speak is indeed worthy of these *kakkāru* flowers.

The meaning of this is: that person who, whether in the presence or absence of others, does not revile or abuse superior, wise men endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), but rather performs with their body exactly what they have spoken with their voice—that person is worthy of these flowers.
The chaplain, saying, "I am endowed with these qualities," had those flowers brought and put them on.
The four sons of the gods gave the four flower-cushions to the chaplain and returned to the world of the gods.
When they had departed, a great pain arose in the chaplain's head, as if it were being crushed by a sharp-pointed spike or bound with an iron band.
His head felt as if it were being crushed. Overcome by pain and tossing to and fro, he cried out with a great voice, "What is this?
When asked, he said, "I made a false claim, saying 'they exist' regarding qualities that do not even exist within me;
I begged these flowers from those sons of the gods. Take them away from my head! Even as they were taking them away...
They were unable to carry it away; it was as if they were bound by an iron band. Then, having lifted it up, they brought it to his house.
There, seven days passed while he was crying out.
The king summoned his ministers and said, "The unvirtuous brahmin will die; what shall we do? "Your Majesty, once more..."
"Perform a festival, O sons of gods; they will come again. The king performed a festival once more.
The sons of gods came again, made the entire city one with the scent of flowers, and stood just as before in the royal courtyard.
The great multitude gathered together, brought the immoral brahmin, and had him lie face up before them. He—
“Give me my life, masters! the son of a deity entreated them. The sons of the deities replied, “These flowers are utterly unsuitable for you, who are immoral and of evil character;
yet you were under the impression that you could deceive us. You have received the fruit of your own lying.
Having thus rebuked the immoral brahmin in the midst of the great multitude, they removed the flower-wreath from his head.
Having removed [the obstacle] and given counsel to the great multitude, they returned to their own places.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was Devadatta;
among those sons of gods, one was Kassapa, one was Moggallāna, one was Sāriputta, and the eldest son of the gods was [myself]."
"But I myself was he.
The sixth commentary on the Kakkāru Jātaka.
[327] 7. The Commentary on the Kākavati Jātaka.
"And this fragrance wafts from there"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.
At that time, the Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?
"It is true, Bhante," he replied. "Why are you dissatisfied? "Because of the defilements, Bhante. "Monk, regarding women..."

"A woman is not to be guarded; she cannot be guarded. Even in the past, when ancient wise men caused women to dwell in palaces made of *simbali* trees in the midst of the great ocean, they were unable to guard them. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta [was conceived] in the womb of his chief queen."
Having been reborn and reached maturity, he reigned after the passing of his father. His chief queen was named Kākavatī;
she was beautiful, like a celestial nymph. This is the summary here; however, the detailed account of the past will be revealed in the Kuṇāla Jātaka.
At that time, a certain king of the Supaṇṇas came in human guise and played a game of dice with the king.
With his mind bound by passion for the chief queen Kākavatī, he took her away, led her to the Supaṇṇa realm, and enjoyed himself with her.
Not seeing the queen, the king said to the Gandhabba named Naṭakuvera, "Search for her.
He, having surrounded the Supaṇṇa king, lay down in a reed forest on a certain lake; then, from that [place], the Supaṇṇa...
At the time of departure, he sat within the fold of a wing; having reached the abode of the Supaṇṇas, he emerged from the wing-fold and engaged in defiled contact with her.
Then, sitting again within that same wing-fold, he arrived at the time when the King of the Supaṇṇas was playing dice, took up his own lute, went to the gambling arena, and stood before the king.
Standing there, he recited the first verse by way of song:
“From here blows this fragrance, where my beloved dwells;
for Kākavati is far from here, where my mind finds its delight.”
In this context, "fragrance" (*gandha*) refers to the scent of her body, which is anointed with divine perfumes. "Wherever my beloved dwells" means:
from that Supaṇṇa abode where my beloved resides, the fragrance of her—due to the physical contact she has had with him—is wafting along with this wind;
such is the intended meaning. "Far from here" means far from this place. The particle *hi* is merely an expletive.
“‘Kākavatī’ means Queen Kākavatī. ‘Yattha me’ means that upon whom my mind is intent.
Having heard this, the Supaṇṇa spoke the second verse:
“How did you cross the ocean? How did you cross the Kepuka forest?”
“How did you cross the seven seas? How did you climb the *śimśapā* tree?

The meaning of this is: “How did you cross this sea surrounding Jambudvīpa, and beyond that, the river named Kepuka, and the seven seas situated among the mountains? By what means did you cross them—having traversed the seven seas?”
“While our abode and the *simbali* tree remain standing, how did you climb it?
Hearing this, Naṭakuvera spoke the third verse:
“With you we crossed the ocean; with you we crossed the *kepuka* forest.”
“By you the seven oceans were crossed; by you the *simbali* tree was climbed.
Herein, “by you” (*tayā*) means: by you acting as the instrument, I, sitting within your wings, performed all this—this is the meaning.
Then the King of Supaṇṇas spoke the fourth verse:
“Shame on me, so large of body! Shame on me, so devoid of consciousness!
For here I carry and bear the paramour of my wife.
Therein, saying “shame on me,” he spoke while censuring himself. “Devoid of consciousness” [refers to] the lack of lightness or heaviness due to his great body.
"Because of his lack of knowledge, he is unconscious. "Yattha" means "because. This is what is meant:
"Since I am bringing this Gandhabba—who is sitting between the leaves—to my own wife, leading him and carrying him away, therefore, 'Fie on me!
Having brought him and given him to the King of Bārāṇasī, he did not return to the city again.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the dejected bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, Naṭakuvera was the dejected bhikkhu, and I myself was the king.
The seventh is the Exposition of the Kākavatī-jātaka.
[328] 8. The Exposition of the Ananusociya-jātaka:
"O lady, there are many... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a householder whose wife had died.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that when his wife died, he did not bathe, drink, anoint himself, or eat;
nor did he engage in his work. Overwhelmed by grief, he went instead to the cremation ground and wandered about lamenting.
Yet, within him, the necessary condition for the path of stream-entry burned like a lamp inside a jar. At the time of dawn, the Teacher—
Surveying the world and seeing him, [the Blessed One] thought: "There is no one other than me who can remove his sorrow and bestow the path of stream-entry;
I shall be his support. Having returned from his almsround after the meal and taking his junior attendant monk, he went to the gate of that householder's home.
There, the householder, having heard of his arrival, performed honors such as going out to meet him, and [the Blessed One sat] on the seat prepared for him.
While he was seated, a householder approached, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha asked him, "Householder, what are you worrying about? He replied, "Yes, venerable sir, my wife has died, and I am worrying as I grieve for her.
The Buddha said, "Householder, that which is subject to breaking will indeed break; when it has broken, it is not fitting to worry. Even the ancient wise men..."
"Even when his wife died, they did not think, 'That which is subject to dissolution has dissolved,'" he said;
and being requested by him, he related a story of the past. The full account of this past event will be revealed in the *Cūḷabodhi Jātaka* of the *Dasaka Nipāta*, but here is the summary:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity and mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he went into the presence of his mother and father.
In this Jātaka, the Bodhisatta was a celibate from youth (komārabrahmacārī). Then his parents announced, "We shall seek a maiden for you.
The Bodhisatta replied, "I have no need for the life of a householder; after your passing..."
Having said, "I shall go forth," and being entreated by them again and again, he had a golden image made and said, "When I find a young maiden of such a form, I will take her.
His parents placed that golden image in a covered carriage and said, "Go, traveling throughout the land of Jambudīpa; wherever you see a young Brahmin maiden of such a form, [bring her back]."
"Give this golden image there and bring him back," they said, and sent men with a large retinue.

At that time, however, a meritorious being, having passed away from the Brahma-world, was reborn as a girl in the house of a Brahmin worth eighty crores in a market town in the kingdom of Kāsi; her name was Sammillahāsinī.
They gave her a name. When she reached the age of sixteen, she became beautiful, charming, like a celestial nymph, and endowed with all excellent physical traits.
Even in her, no thought of defilement had ever arisen before; she was one who practiced absolute celibacy.
People traveling with a golden statue arrived at that village. There, upon seeing her, the people [said], "Of such-and-such a brahmin..."
“Why is our daughter Sammillahāsini standing here? they asked. When the people heard this, they went to the brahmin family and asked for Sammillahāsini in marriage.

She sent a message to her parents, saying: “I shall go forth after your passing; I have no need for the life of a householder. They replied, “What are you doing, girl? and taking a golden image, they—
They sent him forth with a great retinue. And for both the Bodhisatta and Sammillahāsini, they performed the auspicious rites even though neither of them desired it.
Though they lived in the same chamber and lay upon the same bed, they did not look at one another out of defilement;
they dwelt together like two bhikkhus or two brahmins in a single place.
In the course of time, the Bodhisatta’s parents passed away.
Having performed the funeral rites for them, he summoned Sammillahāsini and said, “My dear, there are eighty crores of wealth belonging to my family and eighty crores belonging to yours;
taking this entire amount of money, look after this household, for I shall go forth into the religious life.”
“Noble son, since you have gone forth, I too shall go forth; I cannot bear to leave you. “In that case, come,” he said.

Then, having bestowed all their wealth upon the field of merit and abandoned their prosperity like a globule of spittle, they both entered the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life, and lived there for a long time subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
Having descended from the Himalayas to seek salt and sour condiments, they eventually reached Bārāṇasī and dwelt in the royal park.
While they were living there, a female wanderer who was delicate and accustomed to refined life contracted a dysentery while eating a meal mixed with unwholesome food.
Failing to obtain suitable medicine, she became weak. The Bodhisatta—
At the time for the alms-round, he took her, led her to the city gate, and having laid her down on a wooden plank in a certain hall, he himself entered the city for alms.

While he was still inside, she passed away. When the great multitude saw the beauty of the female wanderer, they surrounded her and wept and lamented. The Bodhisatta, having returned from his alms-round, arrived there.
Knowing that she had passed away, he said, "That which is subject to dissolution has dissolved; all conditioned phenomena are indeed impermanent and have such a destiny.
Having spoken thus, he sat right upon the wooden plank where she lay, ate the mixed food, and rinsed his mouth.
The great crowd standing around asked, "Venerable sir, what is this female wanderer to you? [He replied,] "In the time of her being a householder..."
“...she was my attendant. “Venerable sir, we at least cannot endure it; we weep and lament. Why do you not weep?
The Bodhisatta said, “As long as she was alive, she was something to me; now, because she has entered the other world, she is nothing to me.
She has fallen under the power of death; why should I weep? And while teaching the Dhamma to the great multitude, he spoke these verses:
“Many things exist for you, lady; what will those do for me?
Therefore, I do not grieve for her, my beloved who smiled so sweetly.
If one were to grieve for each and every thing that does not belong to him,”
One should grieve for oneself, always falling under the power of death:
"Neither for one standing, nor for one sitting, nor for one lying down, nor for one wandering;
as long as one breathes and blinks, even there old age cries out."
“In that state, where there is the wearing away of life, in separation and beyond doubt;
what has occurred is past, the rest should be endured, and what is gone should not be grieved over.
Herein, [the word] *bhotī* means "there exists for many," as in: "this one, having abandoned us, now belongs to the many other deceased beings."
“In between, it exists; it is found; it is perceived. [The question is: “What will come of these for me?”—meaning:
what will this woman, who is currently living with those deceased beings, be to me now? Or, by way of a special relationship with those deceased beings, what will she be to me?

What indeed will she be? Will she be my wife, or perhaps my sister? “What will come of these for me? means: what will she be to me? Or: what will come of them for me? “Te hi me kaṃ” (what to me because of them) is also [a possible reading].
The meaning is: "This corpse of mine shall become one with those other corpses.
Therefore—because this has been reckoned among the dead and is of no consequence to me—I do not grieve for it.
"Whatever is not found for him" means whatever is not present for that person who continues to grieve; he is dead and ceased.
The meaning is: "If he should grieve for this or that. There is also the reading "yassā," which means: "Whatever is not found in him, for that he should grieve.
Since they thus fall under the power of death, he should grieve only for himself who is constantly falling, going, and entering under the power of death;
the meaning is that by doing so, there would be no time at all for him to grieve for anything else.

In the third verse, the syntactical supplement is: “The life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*) does not follow after any being—neither one who is standing, nor one who is sitting, nor one who is lying down, nor one who is walking.
Here, *paddhaga* means “one who is walking,” having been substituted for *parivattentaṃ*. This is what is meant:
these beings dwell heedlessly in all four postures, yet the life-force [continues] both by night and by day.
And in all postures, being heedful, they perform only those actions that lead to their own destruction.
"As long as he opens" means as long as he blinks; for this is the conventional expression used at that time. This is what is meant:
as long as one opens and closes the eyes—even in such a brief interval as that, there is the passing away of these beings; among the three stages of life, it is that particular stage...
"Age indeed wanes, it does not increase.
Regarding "therein, alas, the self is ruined": therein, alas, the self is ruined. This is what is meant:
while that age is thus wasting away, this personal existence (attabhāva) which has come to be designated as "self" is ruined; it is impoverished by age.
It remains only half and incomplete. Thus, regarding this self that has been cast away, there is the certain and inevitable separation from those beings who have been born here and there;
and in the face of that certain and inevitable separation, whatever remains—living, immortal, and sentient—that which is living must indeed be cherished, loved, and treated with loving-kindness.
“May this being be healthy and free from affliction”—in this way, the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be practiced toward him.
But that which is departed, gone, dead, and deceased—that should not be mourned; it is not to be mourned.
Thus the Great Being taught the Dhamma, illustrating the aspect of impermanence with these four verses. The great multitude [and] the female wanderer...

He performed the bodily functions. The Bodhisatta, having entered the Himālaya mountains, developed the meditative absorptions (jhāna), the direct knowledges (abhiññā), and the attainments (samāpatti), and became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths (sacca) and identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
The householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Sammilla-hāsinī was the mother of Rāhula, and I myself was the ascetic.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the *Ananusociya-jātaka*.
[329] 9. The Commentary on the Kāḷabāhu Jātaka. “Whatever food and drink...
This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana monastery concerning Devadatta, who had lost his gain and honor.
For when Devadatta, having harbored groundless anger toward the Tathāgata, employed archers against him...
Through the release of Nāḷāgiri, his fault became manifest. Consequently, people no longer provided him with his regular meals and other offerings, and even the king would not look upon him.
With his gains and honor destroyed, he wandered about begging from families for food.
The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying: "Friends, Devadatta [craved] gain and honor..."
"I shall cause it to arise," yet he was unable to make even what had arisen firm.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, his gain and honor were destroyed. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Dhanañjaya was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a parrot named Rādha, large-bodied and with perfectly formed limbs;
his younger brother was named Poṭṭhapāda. A hunter captured both of them, took them away, and presented them to the King of Bārāṇasī.
The king placed them both inside golden cages and [fed them] with a golden dish.
He tended to him by feeding him honeyed parched grain and giving him sugar-water to drink. Great honor was shown to him, and they attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of fame.
Then a forest-dweller, having brought a large black monkey named Kāḷabāhu, presented it to the King of Bārāṇasī.
Because he arrived later, his gain and honor became greater, and those of the parrots declined. The Bodhisatta—

Because he possessed the characteristic of equanimity (*tādilakkhaṇa*), he said nothing; however, his younger brother, lacking that characteristic of equanimity and unable to endure that honor shown to the monkey, said:
"Brother, formerly in this royal family, they gave us alone the finest delicacies and foods.
But now we receive nothing; they give them only to the black-armed monkey. We [belonged] to King Dhanañjaya..."
Not receiving gain and honor from those nearby,
he spoke this first verse while conversing with him:
"That food and drink which we formerly received, that now goes only to the branches and the wild deer."
"Come now, Rādha, let us go to the forest; we have not been honored by Dhanañjaya.
In this passage, *yaṃ annapānassa* means "whatever food and drink [there was] from that king"; alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
*Dhanañjayāya* is the dative case used in the sense of the instrumental, meaning "by Dhanañjaya. *Asakkatā casmā* refers to the food and drink.
"We have not obtained [anything], nor have we been honored by him"—this is the meaning.
Having heard that, Rādha spoke this second verse:
"Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain;
“O Poṭṭhapāda, these conditions among humans are impermanent; do not grieve, why do you grieve?
In this context, *yasas* refers to the possession of power and retinue. *Ayasas* is the absence of that. “These” refers to these eight worldly conditions which are impermanent among humans;
even after having attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame, at a later time they become ones who have little gain and little honor.
They are not called "attainers of stability. The same principle applies to fame and the rest.
Having heard this, Poṭṭhapāda, unable to remove his resentment toward the monkey, spoke the third verse:
"Surely you are wise, Rādha; you know matters yet to come."
"How indeed shall we see that tree-monkey, driven out like a wretch from a royal family?
In this context, "how indeed" (kathaṃ nu) means by what means; "we shall see" (dakkhisāma) means we will see; "driven out" (niddhāvitaṃ) means expelled or cast out; "wretch" (jammaṃ) means miserable.
Having heard that, Rādha spoke the fourth verse:
“He winks his ear and makes a frown; again and again he terrifies the prince.
Kāḷabāhu will do that himself by which he will stand in want of food and drink.
Therein, “terrifies the prince” means he strikes terror into the royal prince. “By which he will stand in want of food and drink” means... [text fragment].
The meaning is: "By some cause he will stand far away from this food and drink; he himself will bring about that cause, so do not worry about him.
After only a few days, Kāḷabāhu stood before the princes and, by twitching his ears and other such gestures, terrified them.
Terrified and trembling, they raised a great outcry. The king asked, "What is this? and having heard the matter, [he acted].
“Drive him out! he said, and had the monkey driven away. The honor and gain of the fowlers returned to its former state.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Kāḷabāhu was Devadatta, Poṭṭhapāda was Ānanda, and Rādha was none other than myself.
This is the ninth commentary on the Kāḷabāhu Jātaka.
[330] 10. The Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka.
"Virtue alone is indeed beautiful"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a brahmin who was testing virtue.
Both previous accounts have already been told below. Here, however, the Bodhisatta was the royal chaplain to the King of Bārāṇasī.
He was there. Testing his own virtue, he took a kahāpaṇa coin from the money-changer’s tray for three days.
They seized him as a thief and presented him to the king. Standing before the king, he said:
“Virtue alone is indeed auspicious; virtue is unsurpassed in the world.”
“Behold the serpent of deadly venom; though he be virtuous, he is not slain.
Having praised virtue with this first verse and having obtained the king’s permission for his renunciation, he went forth to become a monk.
Then one day, a hawk seized a piece of meat from a butcher’s stall and soared into the sky. Other birds—
Surrounding him, they struck him with their claws, beaks, and other parts. Unable to endure that suffering, he dropped the piece of flesh;
another seized it. He too, being tormented in the same way, dropped it, and then yet another seized it.
Thus, whichever one seized it, the birds pursued him; whichever one dropped it, he became comfortable. The Bodhisatta—
Seeing him, he reflected: "These things called sensual pleasures are like lumps of meat; they bring suffering only to those who grasp them, but happiness to those who let them go.
Having thought this, he spoke the second verse:
"As long as they had anything at all, for that long they did not eat."
“Having gathered together, the hawks in this world do not harm one who possesses nothing.
The meaning of this is: as long as even a small piece of meat remained in his mouth, taken hold of by it, so long did the hawks gather and devour him in this world;
but when that was discarded, they did not harm him, for he was then without anything.
“Other birds do not harm a bird that is free from hindrances.
Having departed from the city, he lay down for the night in a certain house in a village along the way.
There, a female slave named Piṅgalā had made an appointment with a man, saying, “You should come at such-and-such a time.”
Having washed her husband’s feet, when he had lain down, she sat upon the threshold looking for his arrival, thinking, “He will come now;
he will come now. Thus she passed through both the first watch and the middle watch of the night.
But at the time of dawn, thinking, “He will not come now,” she lay down in despair and fell asleep.

Seeing this reason, the Bodhisatta thought: “This slave-girl sat for so long in the hope that ‘that man will return,’ but now, knowing he will not come, she sleeps peacefully with her hopes shattered.
For among the defilements, hope is indeed suffering; the state of being without hope is happiness. Having reflected thus, he spoke the third verse:
“One who is free from hope sleeps happily; hope that bears fruit is happy.
Having turned hope into hopelessness, Piṅgalā sleeps happily.
In this context, “fruit-bearing” means that for which a fruit has been obtained; it is “happy” because of the happiness inherent in that fruit.
"Having made it free from hope," means having made it desireless, having cut it off, and having abandoned it.
"Piṅgalā"—this slave girl Piṅgalā now sleeps in comfort.
On the following day, as he was entering the forest from that village, he saw a certain ascetic sitting in the forest, having entered into meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Having seen this and reflecting, "In this world and in the world beyond, there is no happiness superior to the bliss of jhāna," he spoke the fourth verse:
"There is nothing higher than concentration, In this world and in the world beyond."
“He who is concentrated harms neither another nor himself.
In this context, “there is nothing other than concentration” means that there is no other state of happiness superior to concentration.
Having entered the forest and gone forth as an ascetic, he developed the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges, and became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, I myself was the chaplain.
This concludes the tenth commentary, the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka.
The third section, the Kuṭidūsaka Vagga, is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Cuckoo [331] 1.

The Commentary on the Cuckoo Jātaka "Whoever, when the time has not yet arrived..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning Kokālika. The narrative background (vatthu) has already been explained in detail in the Takkarīya Jātaka.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his counselor and advisor;
the king, however, was a man of many words. The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall restrain his excessive talkativeness," wandered about contemplating a parable.
Then one day, the king went to the pleasure garden and sat upon an auspicious stone slab, and above him—
There was a celestial tree. In one of its crow's nests, a female cuckoo deposited her egg and departed.
The female crow tended to that cuckoo’s egg, and later, a cuckoo chick emerged from it.
Thinking, "This is my son," the crow brought food with her beak and nurtured him. He had not yet grown his wing-feathers.
The crow cried out at the very wrong time, making the sound of a cuckoo. The female crow thought, "He is crying out another sound right now;
what will he do when he grows up? She pecked him with her beak, killed him, and threw him from their nest.
He fell at the king's feet. The king asked the Bodhisatta, "What is this, friend? The Bodhisatta replied, "I [killed] one... to restrain the king.
"I am searching for a simile; now I have found it," he thought. Then he said, "Great King, those who are excessively talkative and speak much at the wrong time receive such a fate.
Great King, this young cuckoo, raised by a crow, had not yet developed its wings, yet it cried out the cry of a cuckoo at the wrong time.
Then the crow, realizing 'This is not my son,' struck it with her beak."
“Having killed them, he threw them out of their nests. Whether they be humans or animals, those who speak excessively at the wrong time receive such suffering.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“He who speaks excessively when the time has not arrived;”
Thus he lies slain, like a cuckoo’s offspring.
For a well-sharpened blade or even deadly *halāhala* poison does not strike one down when one is so close as ill-spoken words do.
“Therefore, whether at the right time or not the right time, a wise person should guard their speech;
they should not speak excessively, even to one who is equal to themselves.
But he who speaks measuredly at the right time, preceded by reflection and possessing discernment—”
"He takes in all enemies, just as a garuḍa [takes] serpents.
In this context, "when the time has not arrived" means when the time for one's own speech has not yet come.

"Exceeding the limit" (*ativela*) means speaking in an excessive measure by transgressing the proper occasion. "Like *halāhala*" means like the *halāhala* poison. "Immediately" (*nikaṭṭhe*) means at that very moment.
In a very short time. Therefore—because even more swiftly than a well-sharpened blade or deadly halāhala poison, it causes one to fall [into hell]—therefore.
One should guard one’s speech both at the proper time and at the improper time;
one should not speak excessively, even toward a person who is equal to oneself and makes no distinction. This is the meaning.
"Foremost in wisdom" means one who speaks having made wisdom his precursor. "Discerning" refers to a person who, having investigated with knowledge, finds the meaning;
such a person is called discerning. "Like a serpent-eater" means like a *uraga* (serpent). This is what is meant:
just as a *supaṇṇa* (garuḍa), having agitated the ocean, seizes and takes up a serpent of great size, and having taken it, at that very moment—

"Just as one who has climbed a *sīmbali* tree eats the flesh [of its fruit], even so, he who is guided by wisdom, discerning, and speaks measuredly at the proper time for speaking, wins over all his enemies, captures them, and brings them under his own control.
Having heard this Dhamma teaching from the Bodhisatta, the king from that time forth became moderate in speech; and having increased the Bodhisatta's fame, he granted him even greater honor.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the young cuckoo was Kokālika, and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the first narrative, the Commentary on the Cuckoo Jātaka.
2. The Commentary on the Chariot-Pole Jātaka.
"Even after killing, he says, 'I was killed. The Teacher spoke this while residing at Jetavana concerning the royal chaplain of the King of Kosala.
It is said that as he was traveling by chariot to his own estate village, driving his chariot along a narrow path, he saw a caravan of carts.
Saying, "Move your cart aside," he proceeded; but when the carts were not moved aside...
In his anger, he struck the front of the first cart on the chariot pole of the cart-driver.
Striking the chariot pole, it turned back and struck him right on the forehead. At that very moment, a swelling arose on his forehead.
He turned back and reported to the king, "I have been struck by the cart-drivers. Having summoned the cart-drivers, they proceeded to investigate the matter.

They saw that very fault. Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, it seems the king’s chaplain, while bringing a lawsuit on the grounds that 'I have been beaten by the carters,' has himself committed perjury.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting together here now? and [they replied], "With this..."
When he said, "Is this his name?", [the Buddha] replied, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, he did exactly this," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his very own judge-minister.
Then the king’s domestic priest set out in a chariot for his own village of property; everything else is just as before.
Then, when the matter was reported to the king, the king sat down in person at the court of justice.
He summoned the carters and, without even investigating the case, said, "You have beaten my chaplain and caused a boil to break out on his forehead," and he commanded, "Confiscate all their property!
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "Great King, you [have not investigated] the case..."
"Having investigated these matters, seize all their property; for some, even after striking themselves, say, 'We were struck by another.
Therefore, it is not right to act without inquiry. One who rules a kingdom must indeed perform his duties with careful consideration. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Having killed, he says ‘I have been killed’; having conquered, he declares ‘I have been conquered.
O King, one should not place trust in anyone who speaks thus about the past.
Therefore, a person of wisdom should listen even to another.”
Having heard the words of both, act according to the Dhamma:
“A householder who is lazy and devoted to sensual pleasures is not good; one who has gone forth who is unrestrained is not good;
a king who acts without reflection is not good; and a wise man who is prone to anger is not good.”
“A king should act with deliberation, not without deliberation, O Lord of the Earth;
for the fame and renown of a king who acts with deliberation increase.
In this context, “even having killed” means that even one who has killed himself says or declares, “I have been struck by another.”
"Having conquered," means either having conquered oneself or having conquered another, one says, "I have conquered.
"Aññadatthu" (O Great King), means that for one who has already gone to the royal court and proclaimed [the victory] beforehand, one would not believe the words of that prior proclaimer;
one would certainly not trust his word. "Tasmā" (therefore) means because the word of one who comes and speaks earlier is not to be trusted.
It should not be believed; therefore, one should act according to the Dhamma—that is, in accordance with the established nature of the judgment.
"Unrestrained" means one who is unrestrained in body and so forth, being immoral.

"That is not good" means that the anger—characterized as stubborn resentment—which belongs to that wise person possessed of knowledge due to their habit of holding onto things, is not good. "Not without reflection" means...

"Not without having investigated. "Lord of the Quarters" means the lord of the directions, O Great King. "Fame and renown" means that both his sovereign power and retinue, as well as his reputation, increase.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the king adjudicated according to the Dhamma; when adjudicated according to the Dhamma, it was found that the fault belonged to the brahmin alone.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was the brahmin of the present day, while the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the second commentary, the Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Pakkagodha Jātaka.
"This very thing is for me" was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain householder.

The story has already been related in detail below. However, on this occasion, as they were returning after having settled their debts, a hunter gave them a single cooked lizard on the road, saying, "Eat both of you. That man [went] to fetch water for his wife...
Having sent her away, he ate the entire lizard; when she returned, he said, "My dear, the lizard has escaped.
"Very well, master, what could one do against a lizard that is already on the run? She drank water at Jetavana and sat down near the Teacher.
The Teacher asked her, "What of this man, laywoman? Is he one who desires your welfare, is he affectionate toward you, and is he helpful to you?"
“Venerable Sir, I desire his welfare and am full of affection for him, but he is devoid of affection toward me,” she said. The Teacher replied, “Let it be;
do not worry. He acts in this very way. However, when he remembers your virtue, he will grant you all sovereignty.
Having said this, at their request, he related a story of the past.

The past account is exactly as described below. However, here, while they were returning, a hunter saw their state of exhaustion on the way and gave them a single wild lizard, saying, "Both of you eat this.
The princess tied it with a creeper, took it with her, and set out on the path. Seeing a lake, they left the road and went to the foot of an *assattha* tree.
They sat down. The prince said, "Go, Bhaddā; fetch water in a lotus leaf from the lake, and we shall eat the meat.
She hung the iguana on a branch and went for the water.
The other, having eaten the entire iguana, took its tail-tip and sat with his back turned. When she returned with the water, he [presented it to her].
“Lady, a lizard climbed down from a branch and entered an anthill; I ran after it and seized it by the tip of its tail.
Having grasped it at that spot, it broke off right in my hand and entered its hole,” he said. “Never mind, Your Majesty;
what can we do about a lizard that has fled? Come, let us go. Having drunk water, they went to Bārāṇasī.
When the prince attained the kingship, he appointed her to the position of chief queen alone, yet she received no honor or respect.
Desiring to show her honor, the Bodhisatta stood before the king and said, "My lady, do we not receive anything from you?
Why do you not look upon us? "Dear son, I myself am the one [who receives] from the king..."
“I receive nothing from those nearby; what shall I give to you? And what will the king give to me now?
When he returned from the forest, he ate the half-cooked lizard all by himself. “Noble lady, the King will not do such a thing;
do not speak thus. Then the queen said to him, “That was not known to you, dear one, but it was known to the King and to me.”
Having said, "It is clear," he spoke the first verse:
"It was you alone whom I recognized there in the midst of the forest, O bull among chariot-warriors—
you who were wearing your sword at your side, clad in armor, and dressed in a tirīṭa garment."
“From the branch of the assattha tree, flee like a lizard!”—therein, “at that very time” means you were known [by me] at that moment as “this one is not a giver to me”;
the meaning is that others, however, do not know your true nature. “Of the one with a sword girded” means of one whose sword is fastened. “Tirīṭin” means one clothed in a tirīṭa garment.
"At the time of traveling on the road. "The lizard roasted on coals" means: "The lizard, roasted on coals, fled.
Thus he made the fault committed by the king manifest in the midst of the assembly and spoke.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta said, "Noble lady, since the time the King became displeased with you, why have you both lived here making yourselves so uncomfortable? and he recited two verses:
“One should associate with one who associates, and do what is required for one who does what is required.
One should not do what is beneficial for one who desires no benefit, nor should one associate with one who does not associate.
One should abandon one who abandons, and harbor no resentment; one should not associate with one whose mind has departed.”
"Knowing that the tree has borne its fruit, the great world indeed looks toward another.
In this context: "To one who bows, he should bow"—meaning he should return the bow to one who bows to him with a gentle heart.

"To one who performs his duty"—meaning to one who performs the duty that has arisen for himself. "To one who does not wish for harm"—meaning to one who does not desire his own prosperity (avaḍḍhi). "Vanathaṃ" [is the term for] the thicket of craving.
"He should not make" means he should not produce craving or affection for that which is being abandoned. "With a mind departed" means with a mind that has moved away, a mind that is dispassionate.
"He should not associate" means he should not come together with it. "He should look toward another" means he should look toward something else;
just as a bird, knowing a tree's fruit is exhausted, goes to another tree laden with fruit.
The intention was: "Having known that this man's passion is exhausted, might I approach another who possesses affection?
Even as the Bodhisatta was speaking, the king recalled her virtue and said: "Bhadde, for all this time I did not perceive your virtue;
it was only through the speech of this wise man that I perceived it. This [is for you] who have endured my offense."
Having said, "I give the entire kingdom to you alone," he spoke the fourth verse:
"I shall do for you according to my power, O Kshatriya, out of regard for your gratitude;
I grant you all sovereignty, and whatever else you desire, that I shall give to you."

In this context, "he" refers to himself. "According to his power" means according to his capacity and according to his strength. "Whomever you wish" means: "To whomever you wish, beginning with this kingdom, whatever you desire, that I shall give.
Having spoken thus, the king gave all sovereignty to the queen, thinking, "By this I have reminded her of her virtue," and he also granted great authority to the wise man.
