The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, both the husband and wife were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
At that time, the husband and wife were none other than the husband and wife of today; as for the wise minister, he was none other than myself.
This is the third narrative, the *Pakkagodhājātaka*.
[334] 4. The Commentary on the Rājovāda Jātaka.
Regarding the verse beginning "If cattle while crossing... the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke concerning the "Instruction for a King.
The background story will be made clear in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka; however, here the Teacher said: "Great King, even ancient kings..."
"Having heard the words of the wise, they ruled their kingdoms with righteousness and equity, and thus went on to fill the city of heaven," he said;
and being requested by the king, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity and mastered all the arts, he went forth as an ascetic, developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
and dwelt in a delightful region of the Himalayas, subsisting on forest roots and fruits. Then the king, seeking out his own faults,
searched among his household, his subjects, and within the city, wondering, "Is there anyone who speaks of some fault in me?"
Having seen no one at all who spoke ill of him either in the city or outside the city, he wondered, "What is the talk about me in the countryside?

and traveled through the countryside in the guise of a stranger. There too, seeing no one who spoke ill of him and hearing only accounts of his own virtues, he wondered, "What is the talk about me in the region of the Himalayas?
and entering the forest, as he wandered about, he reached the hermitage of the Bodhisattva and paid homage to him.
Having performed the greetings, he sat down to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisatta had brought ripe *nigrodha* fruits from the forest and was eating them;
they were sweet, full of nutritive essence, and as delicious as sugar powder. He then addressed the king: "O one of great merit, these..."
"Having eaten a ripe *nigrodha* fruit, drink some water," he said.
The king did so and asked the Bodhisatta, "Venerable sir, why is this ripe *nigrodha* fruit so exceedingly sweet?
"O one of great merit, surely the king rules his kingdom with righteousness and justice; therefore it is sweet. In times when the king is unrighteous, it is not sweet."

“Is it so, Bhante? “Yes, Mahāpuñña; when kings are unrighteous, even the oils, honey, molasses, and so forth, as well as the roots and fruits of the forest, become tasteless and devoid of nutritive essence (*ojā*).
Not only these, but the entire kingdom becomes devoid of essence and coarse. But when they are righteous, all those things become sweet and full of nutritive essence.”
"The entire kingdom shall indeed become full of vitality. The king said, "So be it, Bhante," and without revealing his royal status, he paid homage to the Bodhisatta.
Having returned to Benares, thinking, "I shall test the words of the ascetic," he ruled the kingdom unrighteously.
Then, thinking, "Now I shall find out," he spent some time there before returning once more to that place.
Having gone there and paid homage to him, he sat down to one side.
The Bodhisatta spoke to him in the same manner and gave him a ripe *nigrodha* fruit; its taste was bitter for him.
The king, saying, "This is not sweet, it is flavorless," spat it out along with his saliva and said, "It is bitter, venerable sir. The Bodhisatta—

“O one of great merit, surely the king must be unrighteous. For when kings are unrighteous, everything beginning with the fruits and berries in the forest becomes insipid and devoid of nutritive essence,” he said, and then recited these verses:
“If, among cows crossing a ford, the lead bull goes astray;”
They all go crookedly when the leader has gone crookedly.
In the same way, among human beings, if he who is regarded as the best practices unrighteousness,
how much more so will the rest of the people?
The entire kingdom sleeps in misery if the king is unrighteous.
"When the lead bull goes straight as cattle are crossing [a ford],
all the cows go straight, because the leader has gone straight."
“In the same way, among human beings, whoever is regarded as the best—
if he practices the Dhamma, let alone the rest of the people—
the entire kingdom rests in happiness, provided the king is a righteous ruler.”
In this context, "cows" refers to cattle. "Hastening" means those descending into a river. "Crooked" means curved or bent.

"The leader" refers to the bull—the chief, the foremost—when he goes taking hold of the guide. "All the more so the other herd" means that other beings practice unrighteousness even earlier than that;
such is the meaning. "He lies in suffering" means that he does not merely lie down [at ease].
In all four postures, one experiences only suffering. "Unrighteous" means that if the king is unrighteous by way of falling into wrong courses such as favoritism (*chandādi*), [the people suffer].
"He sleeps in comfort" means that if the king, having abandoned wrong courses, becomes righteous, the entire kingdom attains comfort in all four postures.

Having heard the Dhamma from the Bodhisatta, the king announced his royal status and said, “Venerable sir, previously I myself made the *nigrodha* fruit bitter after it had been sweet; now I shall make it sweet again.
Having paid homage to the Bodhisatta and returned to the city, he ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma and restored everything to its original state.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the ascetic.
This concludes the commentary on the fourth Jātaka, the Rājovāda Jātaka.
[335] 5. The Commentary on the Jambuka Jātaka.
"Brahā pavaḍḍhakāyo so" (He has grown tall in body)—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana Grove concerning Devadatta’s construction of a dwelling for the Sugata.
The background story has already been explained in detail below; here, however, is the summary.
When the Teacher asked, "Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do upon seeing you?", the Elder replied, "Venerable Sir, imitating you..."
“Having placed a fan in my hand, he lay down. Then Kokālika struck him on the chest with his knee;
thus, imitating you, he experienced suffering. Having heard this, the Teacher said, “Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta experiences suffering by imitating me;
in the past, too, he experienced it. At his request, the Teacher related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a lion.
Living in a cave in the Himalayas, one day, after killing a buffalo, eating its meat, and drinking water, he returned to his cave.
A certain jackal, seeing him and unable to flee, lay down on his chest. "What is it, jackal? [the lion asked].

When this was said, he replied, "I shall attend upon you, venerable sir. Sīha said, "In that case, come," and having led him to his own dwelling place, he nourished him by bringing meat day after day.
As he grew to a stout body through the lion's leavings, pride arose in him one day. He approached the lion and said, "Master, I [serve] you at all times..."
“[This is] an obstacle; you should always bring meat and nourish me. Stay right here today;
I shall kill an elephant, eat some meat myself, and also bring some for you. The lion said, “Do not let this please you, jackal!
You were not reborn in the womb of a meat-eater to kill an elephant; it is I who [shall kill] the elephant for you.”
"I will kill it and give it to you. It is an elephant, massive in body and fully grown. Do not seize the elephant;
do as I say. Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
"O jackal, that one is tall and fully grown in body, with long fangs!"
"You were not born into that family where they seize elephants.
In this context, *brahā* means great. *Pavaḍḍhakāyo* means one whose body has grown tall. *Dīghadaṭṭho* means long-tusked;
with those tusks, he strikes those like you and brings them to the end of their life. *Yattha* means in which lion-lineage they were born.
They capture a rutting elephant; you were not born there, but rather you were born into a family of jackals—this is the meaning.

Having been thus forbidden by the lion, the jackal emerged from the cave, let out his characteristic "bukka-bukkā" cry three times, and standing upon a mountain peak, he looked down toward the foot of the mountain and saw a black wild elephant.
Seeing him approaching, [the elephant] leaped up, thinking, "I shall fall upon his jar," and turning around, he fell at the man's feet.
The elephant raised its forefoot and placed it upon his head; his head was shattered and reduced to fragments.
He lay right there groaning, while the elephant departed letting out a trumpeting cry. Thus did the Bodhisatta.
Having gone and stood upon the mountain peak, seeing that [jackal] had met his destruction, he recited three verses:
“He who, not being a lion, transforms himself through the pride of a lion; ... [the jackal] has been ruined by his own conceit.”
Having attacked the elephant, the jackal lies on the ground groaning:
“Though he is a famous and supreme being, with a well-formed body and great strength, this jackal,
having failed to consider the power and majesty [of his opponent], lies here struck down by the elephant.”
“He who here performs an action through negligence, having recognized within himself his own strength and power, may overcome that vast [evil] by means of prayer, incantation, and well-spoken words.
In this context, *vikubbati* means he transforms or turns it around. *Kotthūva* means like a jackal. *Anutthunam* means while lamenting.
This is what is meant: just as this jackal, having encountered a great elephant, lies on the ground groaning, so too is anyone else who, being weak, engages in a conflict with one who is powerful.
"Of illustrious fame" means possessing lordship. "Of the supreme person" means of the supreme person by virtue of both physical strength and the power of knowledge.
"Of one with a well-formed trunk" means of one with a well-proportioned great trunk. "Of great strength" means of great power.
"Without knowing the attainment of strength and power" means without knowing both the power consisting of the physical strength of such a lion and the birth as a lion;
the meaning is: without knowing the bodily strength, the power of knowledge, and the birth as a lion. "He lies down" [means] even himself [as if overcome] by the lion...
Thinking it was his equal, this jackal has been killed by the elephant and lies upon a bed of death.
*Pamāya*: having measured, that is, having scrutinized. There is also a reading *pamāṇā*; the meaning is:
"having taken one's own measure, he who performs an action according to his own measure. *Thāmabalaṃ*: strength known as fortitude, and bodily power.
The meaning is also "the power of knowledge. "By chanting" (*japena*) means by recitation (*ajjhena*). "By counsel" (*mantena*) means by acting after deliberating with other wise men.

"By well-spoken [words]" (*subhāsita*) means by blameless speech endowed with qualities such as truthfulness. "Possessed of requisites" (*parikkhava*) means one who is fully equipped with the necessary tools.
"He conquers extensively" (*so vipulaṃ jināti*) refers to one who, being of such a nature, performs whatever task he undertakes.
Having understood his own standing and strength, and having delimited them by means of his yearning and power, he speaks well-spoken words;
thus he wins a vast and great benefit and does not come to ruin.
In this way, through these three verses, the Bodhisatta explained the appropriate action to be performed in this world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Devadatta was the jackal, while I myself was the lion.
This concludes the commentary on the Jambuka Jātaka, the fifth.
[336] 6. The Commentary on the Brahāchatta Jātaka.
"He calls grass 'grass,'" said the Teacher while residing in Jeta’s Grove, speaking with reference to a hypocritical bhikkhu. The present-day account has already been told.
In the past, however, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister, advising him on matters of profit and righteousness.
The King of Benares, having marched against the King of Kosala with a great army, reached Sāvatthī.
Having entered the city by means of battle, he seized the king. Now, the Kosalan king had a son named Prince Citta.

He departed in disguise, went to Takkasilā, and having mastered the three Vedas and the eighteen arts, he left Takkasilā and, while training in all the crafts of every school, arrived at a frontier village.
He attained it. Relying upon him, five hundred ascetics lived in leaf huts in the forest.
The prince approached them, thinking, "I shall learn something from these as well," and having gone forth, he mastered everything they knew.
Later, he became the teacher of a community.
Then one day, having addressed the company of seers, he asked, "Worthy sirs, why do you not go to the Middle Country?
They replied, "Worthy sir, the people in the Middle Country are indeed wise; they ask questions, require expressions of thanks, and demand blessings to be recited.
If we are unable to do so, they reproach us. It is out of fear of this that we do not go. "Do not [be afraid]," he said.
“You need not fear; I shall do all of this myself. “In that case, let us go,” they said, and taking each their own various provisions for the journey, they gradually reached Benares.
The King of Benares, having brought the kingdom of Kosala under his own control, appointed royal officials there, and having taken whatever wealth was available there himself—
Having gone to Bārāṇasī, they filled iron cauldrons and buried them in a park, and at that time they were residing right there in Bārāṇasī.
Then those seers, having stayed overnight in the royal park, entered the city for alms on the following day and went to the king’s gate.
The king, becoming confident in their deportment, had them summoned and seated them upon a great terrace.
Having given him gruel and solid food, he questioned him on various matters until mealtime. Chattā, pleasing the king’s mind, answered all the questions;
at the conclusion of the meal, he delivered a wonderful discourse of thanksgiving.
The king, becoming even more deeply devoted, took his formal promise and had them all reside in the royal park.
Chatta knew the spell for extracting hidden treasures. While living there, he thought, "Where has this man hidden my father’s wealth?
Reciting the spell and looking about, he discovered that it had been hidden in the park.
Thinking, "Having taken this wealth, I shall seize the kingdom," he addressed the ascetics, saying, "Sirs,..."
“I am the son of the King of Kosala,” he said. “When our kingdom was seized by the King of Bārāṇasī, I went forth in disguise and protected my life for all this time.
Now that the family inheritance has been obtained, I shall take it and go to seize my own kingdom; what will you do? “We too—” he continued.
“We shall go together with her. Saying, “Very well,” he had large leather bags made;
during the night, having dug into the ground and extracted the jars of wealth, he placed the wealth into the bags and filled the jars with grass.
Then, having caused five hundred seers and other men to take the wealth, he fled.
Having gone to Sāvatthī, he had all the king’s officials seized, took possession of the kingdom, and ordered the repair of the city walls, watchtowers, and other fortifications.
Having ensured that the city could no longer be taken by war by his rival king, he resided within it.
The King of Bārāṇasī was also informed, “The ascetics have taken wealth from the park and fled. He went to the park and had the jars opened.
He saw only grass, and because of that loss of his wealth, a great sorrow arose within him.
He went to the city and wandered about, lamenting, "Grass! Grass!", and no one was able to extinguish his grief.
The Bodhisatta thought, "The king’s sorrow is great; he wanders about lamenting. But apart from me..."
“No one else is capable of dispelling his sorrow; I shall make him free from grief.
One day, while sitting comfortably with him, at the moment he was lamenting, [the king] spoke the first verse:
“You cry out, ‘Grass! Grass! Who indeed could bring you grass? What is this ‘grass’ that you speak of?”
"What need have you for grass that you speak only of grass?
In this context, "What need have you for grass" means: what task is there to be done by you with grass?
"You speak only of grass" means: for you merely say, "grass, grass," but do not specify, "this is such-and-such a kind of grass."
“He did not speak; rather, tell us the name of that grass—‘such-and-such grass is its name’—and we shall fetch it for you.
But if you have no need for the grass, do not prattle on without cause.
Having heard this, the king spoke the second verse:
“Here a celibate practitioner has come, tall, with a parasol, and very learned;
taking everything from me, he goes away after leaving behind a blade of grass.

In this context, *brahā* means tall. *Chatta* is his name. *Taking everything* means having taken all the wealth. “He goes away after leaving behind a blade of grass” is said thus to show that he went away after leaving a blade of grass in the jars.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
“Thus it is that one should act: by means of little, one desires much;
one should take nothing for oneself, and not even a blade of grass.”

The meaning of this is as follows: when one who desires much wealth from a mere blade of grass must act in this way—namely, taking all that belongs to one’s own father which is fit to be taken, while not taking the blade of grass which is unfit to be taken.
Thus, O Great King, that Brahmadatta took the wealth belonging to his father that was fit to be taken, but did not take that which was unfit to be taken.
“Having thrown grass into his mouth and gone on, what lamentation can there be for him?
Hearing this, the king spoke the fourth verse:
“The virtuous do not do such things; it is the fool who commits such acts against virtue.”
“Impermanent virtue is actually immorality; what wisdom can it produce?
In this context, “the virtuous” refers to those endowed with virtue who live the holy life (*brahmacārī*);

they do not perform such acts. “The fool performs virtues” means that the fool, being of bad conduct, performs for himself these so-called “virtues” which are in fact his own misconduct. “Impermanent virtue” [refers to...].
"Endowed with virtue that has not existed for a long time and has not been practiced for a long duration—what will such wisdom accomplish?
What will wisdom, even when cultivated by great learning, achieve or bring about for a person of such character?
It will only lead to his ruin. Having spoken thus in censure, he [the Bodhisatta]... [by that]... of the Bodhisatta.
Having become free from grief through this discourse, he ruled the kingdom with righteousness.
The Teacher, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the monk who was a hypocrite was Braḥāchatta, while the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Brahāchatta Jātaka, the sixth.
[337] 7. The Commentary on the Pīṭhajāataka.
“We did not give you a seat”—the Teacher spoke this while residing at Jetavana, concerning a certain bhikkhu.
It is said that he, having gone from the countryside to Jetavana, put away his bowl and robes, and paid homage to the Teacher.
He asked a young novice, "Friend, who are the benefactors for the visiting monks in Sāvatthī?
"Friend, the great merchant named Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay follower named Visākhā—these two are the benefactors of the Saṅgha of monks, standing in the place of mother and father.
Saying, "Very well," on the following day at dawn, before even a single monk had entered [the city], he...
He went to the gate of Anāthapiṇḍika’s house. Because he had arrived at an improper time, no one looked at him.
Having received nothing there, he went to the gate of Visākhā’s house. There too, because he had arrived too early, he received nothing.
Wandering here and there, as he was returning again, he found that the rice gruel had been finished; yet once more, he wandered here and there.
Having finished his alms-round when the meal was over, he went to the monastery. Having arrived at the vihāra, he walked about disparaging those families, thinking:
"Both families are indeed faithless and without confidence, yet these monks say, 'They are faithful and confident.
Then one day, the monks in the Dhamma hall raised this discussion: "Friends, it is said that such-and-such a person from the countryside..."
“A certain bhikkhu went to the door of a family very early in the morning; failing to obtain alms, he wanders about while disparaging those families.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he had that bhikkhu summoned and asked, “Is it true, bhikkhu, as they say? He replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir.”
When he said, "Venerable sir," [the Buddha] replied, "Why are you angry, monk?
Even in the past, before the Buddhas had arisen, ascetics did not become angry when they went to people's doors and failed to receive alms. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity and mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, the Bodhisatta later went forth into the ascetic life.
After dwelling for a long time in the Himalayas, he arrived at Bārāṇasī to partake of salt and sour gruel.
Having stayed in a park, on the following day he entered the city for alms. At that time, the merchant of Bārāṇasī was faithful and full of confidence. The Bodhisatta [thought], "Which..."
Having asked, "Is this the house of a noble family? and having heard, "It is the house of a merchant," he went to the door of the merchant's residence.
At that moment, the merchant had gone to attend upon the king, and the people did not see him; he was returning.
Then, seeing him as he was turning back from the royal palace, the merchant paid homage, took his alms-bowl, and—
Having led him home and had him sit down, he gratified him with water for washing the feet, oil for anointing, rice gruel, solid food, and other offerings;
then, without asking about any matter during the interval between meals, once the meal was finished, he paid homage and sat to one side, saying:
"Venerable sir, when beggars or righteous recluses and brahmins come to our door, they do not receive honor or respect..."

"‘There has never been such a thing before,’ they said; ‘but because you did not see our children today, you departed without receiving a seat, water for the feet, a foot-washing, or rice gruel and food—this is our fault, and it is right that you forgive us.
Having spoken thus, they recited the first verse:"
“We did not give you a seat, nor drink, nor food;
O practitioner of the holy life, forgive me, for I see this as a transgression.
In this context, “we did not give you a seat” means we did not even cause a seat to be given to you.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“I am neither provoked nor do I become angry, nor has anything displeasing happened to me;
yet there was this thought in my mind: ‘Surely such is the custom of this family.’”

In that regard, "I do not become attached" means I do not cling. "Of such a kind" means: "Surely this is the nature of this family; this will be a lineage of non-givers"—such a thought arose in my mind.
Having heard that, the merchant recited the other two verses:
"This is the custom in our family, ever since our father and grandfather;..."
“Seats, water, and foot-washing water—all these we offer respectfully.
‘In our family, this has always been the tradition since the time of our fathers and grandfathers:
we serve [our guests] with care, as if they were the most excellent of kinsmen.’”
In this context, *dhamma* means intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). *Pitupitāmaha* means belonging to both fathers and grandfathers.
*Udaka* means water for washing the feet. *Pajja* means oil for anointing the feet. *Sabbetaṃ* means all of this. *Nipadāmase*: here *ni-* and *pa-* are prefixes;
*dāmase* is the meaning, which is to say "I give. By this [offering], [the merit extends] as far as the seventh generation of the family circle.

This shows that "the lineage of donors is our lineage. "Like a kinsman of the highest kind" means that whenever we see a righteous ascetic or brahmin, we serve them respectfully with our own hands, just as we would toward a mother or a father.

However, the Bodhisatta, having stayed there for a few days teaching the Dhamma to the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī, returned once more to the Himālaya; there he developed the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and the meditative attainments (samāpatti), and became destined for the Brahmā-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the merchant of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, while the ascetic was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh narration, the Pīṭha Jātaka.
[338] 8. Thusajātakavaṇṇanā:
"Thus it is known" (viditaṃ thusaṃ). This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Ajātasattu.
It is said that when he was conceived in his mother’s womb, his mother—the daughter of the King of Kosala—developed a pregnancy craving to drink the blood from the right knee of King Bimbisāra.
Having conceived, she became pale. When questioned by her attendants, she explained the matter to them.
The king, having heard this, summoned the fortune-tellers and asked, "It is said such a pregnancy craving has arisen in the queen;
what will be its outcome? The fortune-tellers replied, "The being born from the queen’s womb will kill you and seize the kingdom."
They said: "The king thought, 'If my son kills me and takes the kingdom, what fault is there in that?
He had his right knee opened with a blade, had the blood caught in a golden bowl, and made the queen drink it.
She thought, 'If the son conceived in my womb kills his father, what use have I for him? For the sake of causing an abortion, she had her belly massaged."
The king, having learned of this, summoned her and said, "Bhadde, it seems my son will kill me and seize the kingdom.
However, I am neither ageless nor immortal; let me see the face of my son, and from now on, do not commit such an act.
From that time forward, she went to the pleasure grove and had her womb massaged. The king, having learned of this...
From that time forth, he forbade her from going to the pleasure garden. When she had reached full term, she gave birth to a son.
On the day of his naming, because his father was an enemy even while he was yet unborn, they gave him the name Ajātasattu (Unborn Enemy).
As the boy grew up being raised with princely luxuries, one day the Teacher, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus, went to the king’s residence and sat down.

The king, having served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods, paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to listen to the Dhamma. At that moment, they adorned the prince and presented him to the king.
With intense affection, the king took his son, seated him on his lap, and out of love for his son, cherished him alone as his own.

He did not listen to the Dhamma. The Teacher, knowing his state of negligence, said, "Great King, in the past, kings, fearing their sons, had them kept in concealment and commanded them, 'After our passing away, you must bring them out and establish them in the kingdom.
When the king requested him, he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā, where he taught various crafts to many princes and young brahmins. When the son of the King of Benares reached the age of sixteen, he went into his presence;
having mastered the three Vedas and all the arts, he became proficient in every craft and [approached] the teacher.
He took leave. The teacher, observing him by means of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*), thought: "A danger is foreseen on account of this boy's son;
I shall remove it through my own power. Having composed four verses, he gave them to the prince and spoke to him thus:
"Dear one, having established yourself in the kingdom, [recite] the first verse for your son..."
“You should speak while eating your meal at the age of sixteen; a second time during the great festival of attendance;
a third time while ascending the palace, standing at the head of the stairs; and a fourth time while entering the bedchamber, standing upon the threshold.
Having accepted this with the words “Very well,” he paid homage to his teacher and departed. After being established as the viceroy, following the passing of his father—

He was established in the kingdom. When his son was sixteen years old, seeing the royal splendor as his father went out for pleasure excursions in the garden and other outings, he desired to kill his father and seize the kingdom; thus, he spoke to his own attendants.
They said, "Very well, Your Majesty! What is the use of sovereignty obtained in old age? By whatever means possible, [let us remove] the king..."

“It is fitting to kill him and seize the kingdom,” they said. The prince, thinking, “I will kill him by having him eat poison,” sat down with his father while eating the evening meal, taking the poison with him.
Before even touching the rice in the food-bowl, the king first spoke this verse:
“The husk is known by mice, and the grain is likewise known;
avoiding husk after husk, they eat only the grain.
In this context, “known” means that even in the darkness of a black thicket, the husk is recognized as such by the mice, and the grain is likewise [recognized].
It is known as rice (*taṇḍula*) and is indeed manifest as such. Here, however, by way of a change in grammatical gender, it is said:
"husk is rice" (*thusaṃ taṇḍulaṃ*). "They eat" means they eat only the rice, having discarded each husk. This is what is meant:
"Dear prince, just as for mice, even in the dark, the husk is known as husk and the rice as rice..."
"It is evident; just as people discard the husk and eat only the grain, so too is my act of sitting here after taking your poison evident.
The prince, thinking "I am discovered," was terrified; unable to bear putting the poison into his bowl of rice, he rose, paid homage to the king, and—
He went. Having informed his own attendants of this matter, he asked, "Today I have been discovered; how now shall I kill him?
From that time on, they remained hidden in the park and consulted in whispers, saying, "There is a certain plan:
having girded our swords, when he goes for the great audience, we shall stand among the ministers..."
"Knowing the king’s state of negligence, it is fitting to strike him with a sword and kill him," they decided.
The prince, accepting this by saying "Very well," went forth at the time of the great audience, armed with a sword, and watched from here and there for an opportunity to strike the king.
At that moment, the king spoke the second verse:
“The whispering in the forest, and the whispering in the village behind the ear, and that which is ‘thus’ and ‘so’—all this too is known by me. In this context, “in the forest” means in the park.
“Whispering behind the ear” means whispering into the root of the ear. “And that which is ‘thus’ and ‘so’” refers to [the conventional designations].
"And as for this present search of mine for an opportunity to strike"— this is what is meant: "Dear prince,
both that secret whispering of yours with your own attendants in the park and in the village,
and this current preparation of 'thus' and 'so' for the purpose of killing me— all of this has been known by me."
Thinking, "My father knows my hostile intent," the prince fled from there and informed his attendants.
After seven or eight days had passed, they said to him, "Prince, your father does not know your hostile intent; you have come to this perception through mere suspicion.
Do not kill him. One day, taking a sword, he stood at the top of the stairs by the door of the inner chamber.
He stood there. Standing at the top of the stairs, the king spoke this third verse:
“Indeed, for one born according to the Dhamma, even while still a youth, his father—a monkey—bit off fruit with his teeth.”
In this context, "by way of nature" means by way of its own inherent character. "The father is a monkey to the son" means that the father is a monkey to the son, who is a young monkey.

This is what is meant: just as a monkey born in the forest, fearing the loss of his own troop, destroys the masculinity of a young monkey cub by biting off its teeth with his own teeth, so too [is it for you] who are excessively desirous of sovereignty.
“Having had the fruits plucked, I shall cause him to lose his manhood.
The prince, fearing that his father wished to have him seized, fled and reported to his attendants, “I have been threatened by my father.
When half a month had passed, they said, “Prince, if the king had known, he would not have tolerated this for so long.”

They said, "What you have spoken is mere conjecture; do not kill him. One day, taking his sword and entering his bedchamber on the upper palace, he sat on a lower couch, thinking, "I shall kill him as soon as he arrives.
Having finished his evening meal and dismissed his attendants, the king entered the bedchamber, intending to lie down.
Standing on the threshing floor, he spoke the fourth verse:
“Whatever you crawl about like a one-eyed goat among mustard seeds—
and that which lies beneath you— all this is known to me.”
In this context, *parisappasi* means you crawl here and there out of fear. *Sāsapeti* means in a field of mustard seeds.
*Yopāyanti* means even this [person]. This is what is meant:
even though you have entered this mustard-plant grove like a blind goat and are crawling here and there out of fear, having first come taking poison, and secondly with a sword—
"Thinking you had come wishing to strike me, you stood at the top of the stairs taking up your third sword;
now you lie on the lower couch, thinking 'I shall kill him. I know all this; I will not release you now.
Having seized you, I shall cause the king's command to be carried out. Thus, even as he remained unaware, each verse revealed its respective meaning to him.
The prince, seized by fear, thinking, "I am known by my father;
now he will have me executed," emerged from his bedchamber, cast his sword at the king’s feet, and prostrated himself with his chest at the king's feet, saying, "Forgive me, Your Majesty!
The king rebuked him, saying, "Did you think that no one knew of my deed? and bound him with iron shackles.
Having had him bound and imprisoned, he placed guards over him. At that time, the king recognized the Bodhisatta’s virtue.
Later, when the king passed away, they performed the funeral rites for his body, released the prince from prison, and established him in the kingdom.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I myself was the world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā.
The eighth explanation of the Thusa-jātaka [339].
9. The Explanation of the Bāveru-jātaka.
"By not seeing the peacock," said the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, referring to the heretics whose gains and honor had been lost.
For when the Buddha had not yet arisen, the heretics were recipients of gain and honor;

but once the Buddha had arisen, they became like glowworms at the rising of the sun, their gains and honors vanished. Regarding this conduct of theirs, the monks were discussing it in the Hall of Truth.
How did they originate this discussion? The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "For this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
even in the past, as long as those possessed of virtue had not arisen, those devoid of virtue attained the highest gain and the highest fame. But when those possessed of virtue have arisen..."
Having said, "We have become devoid of virtue and deprived of gain and honor," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a peacock;
having reached maturity and attained great beauty, he roamed in the forest. At that time, certain merchants, having taken a directional crow with them, set out by ship for the kingdom of Baveru.
They arrived. It is said that at that time there were no birds in the kingdom of Bāveru.

As the various inhabitants of the kingdom arrived and saw him sitting in the cage, they praised the crow alone, saying, "Look at the color of his plumage! Look at the end of his neck! Look at his beak!
His eyes are like round jewels! Then they said to those merchants, "Sirs, this bird..."
“Give it to us; we have need of this. You will obtain something else in your own kingdom.
“In that case, take it for its price. “Give it to us for a *kahāpaṇa* coin. “We will not give it.

Gradually increasing the amount, when they said, “Give it for a hundred [coins],” [the other replied], “This is a great benefit to us; let there be friendship with you,” and he gave a hundred *kahāpaṇa* coins.
They took him and gave him [to them]. They led him away, placed him in a golden cage, and tended to him with various kinds of fish, meat, and fruits.
In a place where other birds were not found, the crow—possessed of the ten unrighteous qualities—attained the highest gain and the highest fame.

On another occasion, those merchants took a peacock king and, having trained him so that he would dance to the sound of clapping hands and cry out at the sound of snapping fingers, they went to the kingdom of Bāveru.
When the great crowd had assembled, he stood at the prow of the ship, shook his wings, let out a sweet cry, and danced. When the people saw him, they...
Filled with joy, they said, "Noble ladies, give us this king of birds, who has attained such great fortune and is so well-trained.
[The messengers replied: "A crow was brought by us first, and you took it; now we have brought a peacock-king—ask for him as well!
It is not possible for anyone to come to your kingdom having captured a bird. [They said: "Very well, noble ladies..."
“You will obtain another in your own kingdom; give this one to us! they said, increasing the price, and took her for a thousand [pieces of gold].

Then, having placed her in a cage variegated with the seven precious gems, they attended to her with fish, meat, fruits, and various foods, as well as honey, parched grain, sugar-cane drinks, and so forth.
Thus the peacock king attained the pinnacle of gain and the height of glory; from the moment she arrived, [it was so].
The crow’s gain and honor declined; no one wished even to look at him.
Not obtaining any solid or soft food, the crow went crying out "Caw! Caw! and descended onto a dung heap to seek his prey.
Having joined these two instances together, the Teacher, as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke these verses:
“Because they did not see the peacock,
the crested one of melodious voice, they honored the crow there with meat and fruit.
But when the peacock, endowed with beauty, arrived at Bāveru— ”
Then his gain and honor diminished like that of a crow:
"As long as the Buddha, the King of Dharma, the Light-maker,
has not arisen, so long do people pay homage to various other ascetics and brahmins."
“And when the Buddha, endowed with grace, taught the Dhamma, then gain and honor departed from the sectarians.
Therein, *sikhino* means one possessed of a crest (*sikhā*). *Mañjubhāṇī* means one of sweet voice. *Apūjesuṃ* means they honored.
They honored him with meat and fruit—that is, with various kinds of meat and diverse fruits.
"He came to Bāveru" means he arrived at the Bāveru district; there is also a reading, "Bhāverū. "Ahāyatha" means he was deprived [of his life]. "Dhammarāja" (King of Dhamma):

he is a King of Dhamma because he delights the assembly by means of the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). "Light-maker" (*pabhaṅkara*): [he is so called] in relation to the world of beings, the world of space, and the world of formations.
“Because he has created light, he is the Maker of Radiance (Pabhaṅkara). ‘Endowed with beauty’ means he was possessed of the Brahma-voice.
‘He taught the Dhamma’ means he proclaimed the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
Having spoken these four verses, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the crow was Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, while I myself was the peacock king.”
The ninth: The Commentary on the Bāveru Jātaka.
[340] 10. The Commentary on the Visayha Jātaka.
"He gave gifts"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Anāthapiṇḍika. The narrative background (vatthu).
This has already been explained in detail below in the *Khadirangaṅgāra Jātaka*.

Here, however, the Teacher addressed Anāthapiṇḍika, saying, "Householder, even the ancients gave gifts, warding off Sakka, the lord of the devas, who stood in the sky trying to prevent them, saying, 'Do not give!
Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past."
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a merchant named Visayha, possessing a fortune of eight hundred million.
Endowed with the five moral precepts, he was inclined toward giving and delighted in charity.
He had constructed halls for almsgiving at six locations: at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the door of his own house.
He practiced giving, bestowing six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] day after day. The food provided for the Bodhisatta and for the mendicants and beggars was exactly the same.

As he gave alms, making the whole of Jambudīpa free from the plow, by the power of that generosity, the palace of Sakka trembled, and the pale-white woolen stone throne of Sakka, the king of the gods, manifested signs of heat.
Sakka, reflecting, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from my position? saw the Great Merchant.
He thought, "This Visayha gives gifts by spreading them out so extensively that he makes the whole of Jambudīpa free from plows.
Because of this giving, he will likely displace me and become Sakka himself. I shall destroy his wealth and reduce him to poverty."
Thinking, "I shall act in such a way that he does not give alms," he caused all his wealth, grain, oil, honey, ghee, sugar, and so forth—even down to his slaves, laborers, and servants—to disappear.
Then, those occupied with the distribution of alms came and said, "Master, the distribution of alms has ceased; there is nothing left in any place where it was set out."
"We see it," they announced. "Bring provisions from here; do not cut off the offerings," he said, and having summoned his wife, he told her, "My dear, cause the giving of alms to proceed.
She searched throughout the entire house and, finding not even half a māsaka coin, said, "Noble sir, apart from the garment we are wearing, I see nothing else; the whole house—""
"It is empty," he said. Having caused the doors of the inner chambers of the seven precious gems to be opened, he saw nothing;
except for the merchant and his wife, not even any other slaves or laborers were to be found. Then the Great Being addressed his wife:
"My dear, it is not possible to cut off the giving of alms; search throughout the entire residence and see if you can find anything."
He said: "At that moment, a grass-cutter abandoned his sickle, his carrying-pole, and the rope for binding the grass at the doorway and fled.
When the merchant’s wife saw this, she said, 'Master, I see nothing else here but this,' and having brought it, she gave it to him.
The Great Being said, "My dear, for all this time I have never before cut grass myself."
"Today, however, having gathered grass and brought it back, I shall sell it and give a fitting gift.
Fearing the interruption of his almsgiving, he took a sickle, a carrying-pole, and a rope, went out from the city, and proceeded to a grass-field.
Having gathered the grass, he thought, "One portion will be for ourselves; with the other, I shall give a gift," and so he tied two bundles of grass together and hung them on the carrying-pole.
Having taken it and gone to the city gate, he sold it and received a single māsaka coin; he gave one portion to the beggars.
Since there were many beggars, and as they cried out, "Give me too! Give me too!", he gave away the other portion as well.
On that day, he passed the time without food together with his wife. In this manner, six days passed by.

Then, on the seventh day, while he was gathering grass, his eyes rolled because of the heat of the sun striking his forehead—he being so extremely emaciated from having gone without food for seven days.
Unable to maintain his mindfulness, he fell down without spreading out the grass.
Sakka wandered about, observing his actions; at that very moment, he...
Having arrived and stood in the air, he recited the first verse:
“In former times you gave gifts with great effort, yet for you who were giving, there was the exhaustion of wealth.
If from now on you should not give gifts, your riches would remain while you practice restraint.”

The meaning of this is as follows: "O Visayha, previously, while there was wealth in your house, you gave gifts until the whole of Jambudīpa was left with its ploughs raised (i.e., until the entire land was cultivated for giving).
And for you who were giving in such a manner, there came the nature of exhaustion, the inherent quality of depletion;
all your property was exhausted. Even if you were not to give anything further from now on, to anyone whatsoever—"
“If you do not give, your wealth shall remain exactly as it is even though you are restrained from giving.
Therefore, give me your promise: ‘From now on, I will not give. I will restore your wealth to you.
Having heard his words, the Great Being asked, “Who are you? “I am Sakka,” he replied. The Bodhisatta said, “Sakka...”
"Indeed, by giving gifts himself, undertaking moral discipline, performing the Uposatha rites, and fulfilling the seven rules of conduct, Sakka attained his sovereignty;
but you, for the sake of your own power, have withheld gifts—you are truly acting ignobly!
Having said this, he spoke three stanzas:
“O thousand-eyed one, they say that even for one in extreme distress, it is unrighteous to do what is unworthy.
O King of the Gods, let us not lose that wealth—our faith—which we might abandon for the sake of enjoyments.
Where one chariot goes, there another chariot follows.”
“An ancient practice has been established, O Vāsava, and it continues even now:
‘If there will be [to give], we shall give; if there is nothing, what can we give?
Even when things have come to such a state, we shall still give; let us not neglect the act of giving.’”
In this context, "ignoble" (*anariya*) means base or evil action. "By the noble" (*ariyena*) means by one of noble conduct.

"Even by one who is very destitute" (*suduggatena*) means even by one who is extremely poor. "They say it is not to be done" (*akiccaṃ āhu*) means that the Buddhas and other noble ones declare it is something that should not be performed;
the intention is: "But you have instructed me in an ignoble path. *Vā* is merely a particle. "On account of which wealth" (*yaṃ bhogahetu*) refers to whatever riches.
"Because of using [it], we would abandon and relinquish our commitment to giving; let that wealth not even exist, for we have no need for that wealth"—this is what he indicates.
"A chariot" refers to any kind of vehicle. This is what is meant: by whichever path one chariot travels, another chariot [may also travel].
"This is the path taken by the chariot," thinking thus, he goes by that very same path. "Let the ancient practice continue" means:
let the practice formerly established by me continue while I am still living; let it not cease—this is the sense. "Being such as we are" means:
even though we are grass-gatherers, as long as we live, we shall surely give. For what reason? So that the gift may not be forgotten.
For one who does not give is said to be negligent; he neither remembers nor reflects upon it.
"But I do not wish to forget giving while I am alive; therefore, I shall certainly give," thus he explained.
Unable to dissuade him, Sakka asked, "For what purpose do you give this gift? The Bodhisatta replied, "Neither..."
"I do not give seeking the status of Sakka or Brahmā; rather, desiring omniscience, I give," he said.
Hearing his words, Sakka was delighted and rubbed the Bodhisatta’s back with his hand.
At that very moment, as soon as it was rubbed, the Bodhisatta’s entire body became fully restored. And by the power of Sakka, all his wealth and possessions—
He returned to his former state. Sakka said, "Great merchant, from this day forward, give alms by distributing twelve hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every single day.
Having thus made the wealth in his house inexhaustible, he sent him away and returned to his own place.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the merchant’s wife was Rāhula’s mother, and the merchant Visayha was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Visayha Jātaka, the tenth.
The fourth chapter, the Kokila Vagga, is finished.
5. Cūḷakuṇālavagga [341] 1. Kaṇḍarījātakavaṇṇanā:
The detailed exposition of this Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Those who make men delight in sensual pleasures," will be revealed in the Kuṇāla Jātaka.
The First Explanation: The Kaṇḍarī Jātaka [342].
2. The Second Explanation: The Monkey Jātaka.

"I was indeed able to save myself"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to bring about his own death. The background story has already been related in detail above.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a monkey womb in the Himalayan region;
having reached maturity, he lived on the banks of the Ganges.

Then, a female crocodile in the middle of the Ganges conceived a craving for the heart-flesh of the Bodhisatta and told her husband, the male crocodile. He said, "Having caused that monkey to sink into the water..."

Thinking, "Having killed him and taken his heart-flesh, I will give it to Saṃsumāri," he said to the Great Being, "Come, friend, let us go to the intermediate island to eat fruits. "How shall I go, friend? [the Great Being asked].
"I will carry you by placing you on my back," he replied. Not understanding his intention, the Great Being leaped up.
He sat upon his back. After the crocodile had gone a short distance, he began to submerge.
Then the monkey said to him, "Sir, for what reason are you making me submerge in the water? "I shall kill you and give your heart-flesh to my wife.
"Foolishly do you imagine that my heart-flesh is in my chest? "Then where is it?"
"Has it been set aside? "Do you not see it hanging from that *udumbara* tree? "I see it; will you give it to me?
"Yes, I shall give it. Because of his slowness, the jackal took hold of it and went to the foot of the *udumbara* tree on the riverbank.
The Bodhisatta, having leaped behind him, sat upon the *udumbara* tree and spoke these verses:
“I have indeed succeeded in lifting myself from the water onto dry land;
I shall no longer come under your power, O lotus-born one.
“Enough with these mangoes, and with the rose-apples and breadfruit trees!”
"Better for me an udumbara tree on the far shore of the ocean than one who does not quickly realize a matter that has arisen;
he falls under the power of his enemies and later regrets it."
“But whoever quickly understands a matter that has arisen, is released from the oppression of enemies and does not regret it later.
In this context, *asakkhiṃ vata* means “I was indeed capable”; *uddhātuṃ* means “to lift out”; and *vārija* refers to the crocodile.
"He addresses. By saying "those on the far shore of the ocean," he addresses the Ganges by the name "ocean," meaning:

"Those things which are to be eaten after going to the far shore of the ocean—enough with those! "And later he regrets" means that, failing to quickly recognize a matter that has arisen, he falls under the power of his enemies and later regrets it.
Thus, having explained the causes for the accomplishment of worldly duties with these four verses, he entered the forest grove itself.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Saṃsumāra was Devadatta, while the monkey was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Monkey Jātaka.
[343] 3. The Commentary on the Kuntinī-jātaka.
"We have dwelt in your house," the Teacher related this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a female *kuntinī* bird that had lived in the palace of the King of Kosala.
It is said that she served as the king’s messenger; she also had two chicks, and the king—
She had a bird-catcher take a letter for a certain king and sent it off.

When she had departed, the children in the royal household killed those young birds by crushing them with their hands. Upon her return, seeing the fledglings dead, she asked, "By whom have my little sons been killed?
They replied, "By such-and-such a person and such-and-such a person. At that time, there was a tiger in the royal household being raised for sport.
"He is harsh and cruel; he stands there by the power of his bonds. Then those children went to see that tiger.
The female bird also went along with them, thinking, "I shall treat these children exactly as they killed my sons.
She seized the children and threw them at the tiger's feet, and the tiger devoured them, making a *murāmurā* sound.
"Eat! she said. Thinking, "Now my heart's desire is fulfilled," she flew up and went back to the Himālayas.

Having heard this account, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Dharma: "Friends, it is said that in the royal palace there was a certain female hawk named Kuntinī who killed her own chicks;
having thrown those children at the feet of a tiger, she went back to the Himālayas herself."
“They have gone,” they replied. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?
When they said, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, she took her own children who had killed their own offspring, threw them at the feet of a tiger, and went back to the Himalayas. Having said this, he related the past event.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta ruled his kingdom with righteousness and impartiality.
In his palace, there was a certain female hawk who acted as a messenger; everything else was exactly as before. However, this is the difference:
that female hawk, having caused the child to be killed by a tiger, thought, "I can no longer live here; I shall depart."
"Furthermore, I will not go without informing the king; I shall go only after having informed him.
She approached the king, paid homage to him, and standing to one side, said: "Lord, through your negligence, they killed my two little children.
Overcome by anger, I in turn killed those children. Now, it is no longer possible for me to live here."
Having said, "It is possible," she spoke the first verse:
"We have lived in your house, always honored and revered;
you yourself have now done so; come, O King, let us depart."

"In this matter, you yourself have now brought this about," he said. "By having me sent away with a letter, and by failing to protect my dear children through your own negligence, you alone have now created this cause for my grief.
*Handā* is a particle used for emphasis. *Rājā* (the king) addresses the Bodhisatta. *Vajāmaham* means 'I am going to the Himavat.'"
Having heard that, the king spoke this second verse:
“Indeed, when one commits an evil deed and another returns an evil deed for it, in this way the enmity is settled. Stay there, Kuntī; do not come here.”

The meaning of this is as follows: when a person, against whom a grave deed such as the killing of one's own child has been committed by another, performs a counter-deed (*paṭikibbisa*) against that person in return, and recognizes, "I have retaliated against him"—in this way, "that enmity is settled" (*sammati veraṃ*);
by this much, that enmity is settled and pacified. Therefore, [the verse says]: "So dwell, O Kuntī, do not follow after it."
Having heard that, Kuntī spoke this third verse:
“Between one who has done wrong and the doer, friendship cannot be joined again;
my heart does not consent—depart, O bull among charioteers.”
In this context, "neither of one who has done nor of one who does" means that for two persons— one who has already acted and one who is currently being overcome, oppressed, or harassed—
the restoration of friendship is no longer joined or reconciled once the grammatical case has been changed to "he who does" (*yo kattā tassa*). For that reason, "the heart does not consent."
“My heart does not permit me to dwell here. ‘Go indeed, O bull among charioteers’—therefore, Great King, I shall certainly go.
Having heard this, the king spoke the fourth verse:
“Between one who has done a favor and the doer of it, friendship is joined once again.”
“O Kuntī, do not come under the power of either the wise or the foolish.
The meaning of this is: friendship is restored again between both the person who has been wronged and the one who committed the wrong;
however, that [restoration] occurs among the wise, and not among the foolish. For the friendship of the wise, even when broken, is joined together again, but that of the foolish—
“Once it is broken, it remains broken; therefore, dwell here, O Kuntinī, do not go away.
The female bird, thinking, “Even so, it is not possible for me to live here, my lord,” paid homage to the king, flew up, and went back to the Himālaya mountains.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the female Kuntinī was none other than the present Kuntinī, and the King of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”
The third *Kuntinījātaka* commentary.
[344] 4. The *Ambajātaka* commentary:
"He who adorns himself with indigo," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain elder who was a mango-guardian.
He related this story. It seems that after he had gone forth in his old age, he built a leaf-hut in an mango grove on the outskirts of Jetavana;
there he wandered about protecting the mango trees, eating the fallen mango fruits himself and giving some to his own kinsmen.
While he was away on his alms-round, mango-thieves would knock down the mangoes, eat them, and take them away.
And they departed. At that moment, four daughters of a wealthy merchant, having bathed in the Aciravatī River and been wandering about, entered that mango grove.
The old man arrived and, seeing them, said, "The mangoes have been eaten by you.
"Venerable sir, we have only just arrived; we did not eat your mangoes. "In that case, take an oath."
“Do you do so? “We shall do so, venerable sir,” they replied, and they made the oath. Having had them make the oath and having put them to shame, the elder released them.

When the monks heard of this deed of his, they raised the discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, “Friends, it is said that a certain elder, when the daughters of a merchant entered the mango grove where he was staying, made them take an oath...”
“Having made them feel ashamed, he dismissed them. The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
formerly, while acting as a mango-guardian, he also made four daughters of a wealthy merchant take an oath, made them feel ashamed, and dismissed them. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta served as the King of the Devas (Sakka).
At that time, a certain fraudulent ascetic, having built a leaf-hut on the bank of a river in a mango grove near Benares, lived there guarding the mango trees;
he ate the fallen ripe mangoes himself and gave some to his associates, living by various kinds of wrong livelihood.
He wandered about making his living. At that time, Sakka, the king of the gods, while surveying the world, thought: "Who in the world now attends upon their mother and father?
Who performs the duty of honoring their elders in the family? Who gives gifts, guards moral virtue, and observes the Uposatha rites?
Which renunciants dwell devotedly engaged in the duties of a recluse? And who are those who practice improper conduct? Thus he surveyed the world.
Seeing this mango-guardian, who was of improper conduct and a false ascetic, [the Elder] thought:
“This false ascetic wanders about guarding a mango grove, having abandoned his own duty as a recluse such as the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*;

I shall cause him to feel spiritual urgency. Thus, when he had entered the village for alms, by means of his supernatural power, he caused the mangoes to fall so that it appeared as if they had been plundered by thieves.
At that time, four daughters of merchants from Bārāṇasī entered that mango grove.
Seeing them, the shaven-headed ascetic Kūṭa detained them, saying, "The mangoes have been eaten by you. They replied, "Venerable sir, we have only just arrived;
we did not eat those mangoes. He said, "In that case, take an oath. They asked, "And having taken it, will we be allowed to go? He replied, "Yes."
“You shall obtain it. “Very well, venerable sir,” said the eldest among them, and making an oath, she recited the first verse:
“He who adorns himself with indigo is tormented by the tongs;
may that woman come under his power who plucked those mangoes from you.”

The meaning of this is as follows: May that [old age] prevail over such an elderly man who, for the sake of turning his grey hairs black, applies blue fruits and the like to create a dark dye, and who is distressed and exhausted by pulling out with tweezers the grey hairs that have grown amidst his black locks; may she obtain such a husband.
“O Mother, that which you brought for me...
Having said, “You stand to one side,” the ascetic made the second daughter of the treasurer take an oath. While making the oath, she spoke this second verse:
“Twenty or twenty-five, or even twenty-nine of my births;”
“May you not find such a husband as he who carried off your mangoes.
Its meaning is this: women indeed become dear to men at the age of fifteen or sixteen;
but she who carried off your mangoes, having failed to obtain such a husband despite being in the prime of youth, has reached twenty or twenty-five years by birth.
Or, having reached twenty-nine years—being deficient by one or two years—she thought, "Even though I have reached such a mature age, I have not obtained a husband.
While she stood to one side after having sworn an oath, he spoke the third verse for the third time:
"Let her go a long journey alone as a woman seeking a lover."
"Do not go to the rendezvous, O innocent one, she who carried off your mangoes.

Its meaning is this: "Let her who carried off your mangoes—having become an *abhisārikā* (a woman going to meet her lover) out of a desire for her husband, traveling alone and unaccompanied for a long distance of a league or two leagues—go [to him]."
And even after she had gone, when he made an appointment saying, "You should come to such-and-such a place," she did not see her husband.
While she stood to one side having sworn an oath, the fourth [man] spoke this fourth verse to her:
"Adorned, well-dressed, garlanded, and anointed with sandalwood paste..."
“Alone she lay upon her bed, she who brought you mangoes, O mother.”—the meaning of this is self-evident.

The ascetic said, “You have made very heavy oaths; others must have eaten the mangoes. Now, you may go,” and he dismissed them. Sakka, having displayed a terrifying form as an object of fear, caused the fraudulent ascetic to flee from that place.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, this old mango-guardian was the fraudulent matted-hair ascetic; these four daughters of the merchant were those very same women; and Sakka was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Amba Jātaka, the fourth.
[345] 5. The Commentary on the Rājakumma Jātaka.
"The forest that the fire burns"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain lazy bhikkhu.
It is said that this son of good family from Sāvatthī, having gone forth after pledging his heart to the Dispensation, was nonetheless lazy;
he remained outside the sphere of recitation, inquiry, systematic attention, and the performance of duties, being overcome by the hindrances. In his various sitting places and so forth...

It was exactly the same with his modes of deportment. On account of this state of laziness of his, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall, saying, "Friends, such-and-such a monk, having gone forth in this liberating dispensation, dwells lazy, indolent, and overcome by the hindrances. The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, what is it that you are discussing here?"
Having asked, "Are you sitting here now for this discussion? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
even in the past, this man was lazy," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his jewel among ministers.
The King of Bārāṇasī was by nature lazy. The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall awaken the king," wandered about contemplating a parable.

Then one day, having gone to the pleasure grove and wandering there surrounded by his retinue of ministers, the king saw a creature called a *rājakumbha*, who was lazy. Indeed, such lazy creatures [spend] the whole day...
Even when walking, they go only the distance of one or two finger-breadths. When the king saw this, he asked the Bodhisatta, "Friend, what is his name?
The Great Being replied, "Great King, this one is named Rājakumbha; he is lazy. For even though he walks all day long, he goes only the distance of one or two finger-breadths.
Having said this, he spoke in conversation with him: "O friend," he said.
“Rājakumbha, what are you doing with your slow progress while this forest fire has broken out in this wilderness?
Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
“The forest that the fire consumes, the flame whose path is black—”
“How do you act, O flickering one? Thus you are slow in effort.
In this context, *yadaggi* means when the fire is present. *Pāvako kaṇhavattanī* is a synonym for fire.
*Pacalaka* is how he addresses it; for it moves as it goes, or it is constantly flickering, and therefore it is called “the flickering one.”
It is said: "One of slow exertion" means one who possesses heavy effort.
Having heard that, Rājakumbha spoke the second verse:
"There are many clefts in trees, and fissures in the earth;"
“If we do not reach them, there will come a time for us.
The meaning of this is: “O wise one, there is no further destination for us beyond this point.
However, in this forest there are many gaps between the trees and openings in the earth. If we do not reach those, there will come a time for us—that is, death itself shall befall us.”
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke these other two verses:
“He who crosses when it is time to linger, and lingers when it is time to cross,
like one who tramples upon a dry leaf, destroys his own welfare.”
“He who hastens when there is time to hasten, and crosses over when one must cross over—like the moon dividing the night, his purpose is fulfilled.
In this context, “when there is time to hasten” refers to the time when various tasks ought to be performed slowly. “Crosses over” means he proceeds with great urgency.

He performs those actions with haste. "Like a dry leaf" means that just as a strong man might step on a palm leaf dried by wind and sun, crushing it right there into fine dust, even so he destroys his own welfare and prosperity.
"He delays" means he procrastinates; he performs those actions that ought to be done promptly only sluggishly.
"Tārayī" means that he performs with urgency those tasks that require urgent performance. "Sasīva rattiṃ vibhajanti":

just as the moon, illuminating the night of the bright fortnight, distinguishes the night from the night of the dark fortnight and becomes full day by day, so too it is said that the purpose of that man becomes fulfilled.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the king became diligent from that time forth.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, the King’s steward was the lazy bhikkhu, while the wise minister was none other than myself.
This is the fifth exposition of the Rājakumbha Jātaka.
[346] 6. The Commentary on the Kesava Jātaka:
"Having abandoned the Lord of Men"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning food given in trust.
It is said that in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika there was a regular meal for five hundred bhikkhus; his house was constantly...
It was a source of refreshment for the community of monks, radiant with the saffron robes, and fragrant with the scent of sages.
Then one day, as the king was making a ceremonial circuit of the city, he saw the community of monks at the house of a merchant.
Thinking, "I too shall provide regular almsfood for the Noble Saṅgha," he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and [approached] the five hundred monks.
He established a regular alms-round. From then on, a regular meal was given at the royal residence—exquisite food consisting of three-year-old fragrant rice.
There were no donors who gave with their own hands out of confidence or affection; rather, he had the king’s officials provide it.
The monks did not wish to sit down and eat; instead, they took various kinds of choice delicacies...
Having gone to their respective families who were their supporters, they gave that food to them and ate whatever was given by them, whether coarse or refined.
Then one day, people brought many kinds of fruits to the king. The king said, "Give these to the Saṅgha. The people...
Having gone to the dining hall and not seeing even a single monk, they reported to the king, "There is not even one monk here.

[The king asked,] "Is it not yet even time? [They replied,] "Yes, it is time; however, the monks have taken food from your house and gone to the houses of their own trusted supporters, giving it to them, and [now eat] what has been given by them—whether coarse or fine."
“...or eat elsewhere? The king thought, “Our food is exquisite; for what reason, then, do they not eat it and instead eat elsewhere?
I shall ask the Teacher. Having gone to the monastery, he paid homage to the Teacher and asked him.
The Teacher replied, “Great King, food is supreme when it inspires confidence. Having established confidence in your household—”
Due to the absence of donors out of affection, the monks, having taken their alms-food, consume it at their own places of trust.

Your Majesty, there is no other flavor like that of trust; for even if a person who lacks trust offers the four sweets, it does not equal the value of a mere meal of *sāmāka* grain offered by one who has trust.
Even when illness arose, the ancient wise men [acted thus] for the sake of the King...
"Even when five families of physicians were consulted and medicines prepared, the disease did not subside;

however, after going to the presence of those who had inspired his trust, he ate saltless *sāmāka* and *nīvāra* gruel mixed with only water, as well as saltless leaf-vegetables, and thus became free from illness.
Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi;
they gave him the name Kappakumāra. When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he later went forth as an ascetic.
At that time, there was an ascetic named Kesava, who was surrounded by five hundred ascetics.
Having become the leader of a group, he dwelt in the Himalayas. The Bodhisatta went into his presence and lived there as the senior pupil among five hundred disciples;
he was well-disposed toward the welfare of the ascetic Kesava and possessed affection for him. They became exceedingly intimate with one another.
Later on, Kesava, taking those ascetics with him, [set out] for the purpose of partaking of salt and sour gruel.
Having traveled along the path of men and reached Bārāṇasī, he stayed in the royal park; on the following day, having entered the city for alms, he went to the king’s gate.
When the king saw the group of seers, he had them summoned, fed them within his residence, and having obtained their consent, he had them dwell in the park.
Then, when the rainy season had passed, Kesava took leave of the king.
The king said, "Venerable sir, you are advanced in years; please remain here depending on us for the time being, and send the young ascetics to the Himālaya.
He replied, "Very well," and having sent them to the Himālaya along with his senior pupil, he himself remained behind alone.
Kappa went to the Himālaya and lived there together with the ascetics.
Kesava, living apart from Kappa, became distressed and, longing to see him, could not find sleep.
Because he could not sleep, his food did not digest properly; he suffered from dysentery, and intense pains arose.
The king, having summoned five families of physicians, attended to the ascetic, but the illness was not pacified.
Keśava said to the king, “Great King, do you desire my death, or rather my state of health?
“His state of health, venerable sir,” he replied. “In that case, send me to the Himalayas.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the king said, and having summoned his minister named Nārada, he commanded him, “Nārada, taking our venerable one with you, by means of forest-dwellers...”
“Go to the Himavat together with him,” he sent [Nārada]. Nārada, having led him there, returned.
As soon as Kappa saw Kesava, his mental affliction was stilled and his longing subsided.
Then Kappa gave him a gruel of *sāmāka* and *nīvāra* rice along with leaves that had not been salted, smoked, or sprinkled with water. To him—
At that very moment, the hemorrhage subsided.
Again, the king sent Nārada, saying, "Go and find out the condition of the ascetic Kesava.
He went and, seeing him healthy, said, "Venerable sir, the King of Bārāṇasī has summoned five families of physicians and is having you treated."
Having said, "He was unable to make you healthy; how did he tend for you? he spoke the first verse:
"Having abandoned the lord of men, who is enriched with all desirable things, how indeed, O Blessed One, does Kesi delight in Kappa’s hermitage?"

In this context, "the lord of men" refers to the king of Bārāṇasī. [The king thought: "How indeed does the Blessed One know Keśin? By what means does our Blessed One find delight in the hermitage of the ascetic Keśava?
Thus, as if conversing with others, he asked about the cause of Keśava’s delight. Having heard that, Keśava spoke the second verse:
"The fragrant, delightful, and charming Vakula trees are there."
“O Nārada, the well-spoken words of Kappa delight me.
Therein, “trees” means *vakkhā*. However, in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it is written simply as “trees” (*rukkhā*). “Well-spoken words” means that the well-spoken words uttered by Kappa delight me.
Having spoken thus, [he said]: “While he was thus making me rejoice, Kappa [offered] saltless, unsmoked, leaf-mixed food moistened with water...”
When he was given gruel made of *sāmāka* and *nīvāra* rice to drink, he said, "O uncle, the disease in my body has been pacified; I have become healthy.
Having heard this, Nārada spoke the third verse:
"I eat the boiled rice of *śāli*, pure, with meat as a sauce."
"How do they cover over the millet and wild rice that is without salt?
In this context, *bhuñjeti* means "you eat"; or rather, *bhuñjasi* is the reading. *Chādayanti* means "they cover," "they nourish," or "they satisfy.
The nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) has been added for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition. This is what is meant: you, who [prefer] pure meat with sauce...
"In the royal palace you eat rice fit for a king; how can this millet and wild rice, without salt, nourish and satisfy you?
How is it that this is pleasing to you?
Having heard that, Kesava spoke the fourth verse:
“Whether delicious or not delicious, whether little or much;
where one may eat with confidence—confidence is the supreme flavor.
In this context, *yadi vā asāduṃ* means “or whether it is not delicious. *Vissattho* means being free from apprehension, having attained a state of trust. *Yattha*...
"He should eat" means that in whatever residence one should eat in such a manner, whatever food is eaten there is indeed delicious.
Why? Because "trust is the supreme flavor. Trust is the supreme, the highest among these; thus they are called "those for whom trust is the supreme flavor.
Indeed, there is no other flavor like trust. For even the fourfold sweetness [of honey, ghee, sugar, and molasses], when given by one who lacks trust...
"Soup made from sour gruel given by one who trusts you is not worth anything.
Having heard his words, Nārada went into the presence of the king and reported, "Kesava said this.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the king; Sāriputta was Nārada; the Brahmā Baka was Kesava; and I myself was Kappa."
The sixth is the *Kesava-jātaka* commentary.
[347] 7. The *Ayakūṭa-jātaka* commentary:
"All iron..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning his conduct for the benefit of the world. The story will be made clear in the *Mahākaṇha-jātaka*.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity and having mastered all the arts, he ascended the throne upon his father’s passing and ruled the kingdom with righteousness.
At that time, people, acting as royal sacrificers (*devamaṅgalika*), slaughtered many goats, sheep, and other animals for the deities.
They performed a sacrificial offering (*balikamma*). The Bodhisatta caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming: "No living being is to be killed.
Unable to obtain their sacrificial offering, the *yakkhas* became enraged at the Bodhisatta;
they went to a gathering of *yakkhas* in the Himalayas and dispatched a fierce *yakkha* to kill the Bodhisatta. He [the *yakkha*] carried a great iron club, as large as a cartwheel and ablaze.
