Having seized it, thinking, "I will strike him with this and kill him," he returned and stood at the head of the Bodhisatta’s bed just after the middle watch of the night.
At that moment, Sakka’s throne manifested a sign of heat.
Reflecting on this, he understood the reason; taking his thunderbolt, he went and stood over the yakkha. The Bodhisatta [saw] the yakkha...
Seeing him, he thought, "Is this man standing there to protect me, or rather, does he wish to kill me?
Speaking with him, he uttered the first verse:
"Having taken up an iron spear of excessive size, you stand there in the sky;..."
"Have you been appointed today for my protection, or do you intend to kill me?
Therein, "vihito nu sajja" means "have you indeed been appointed today.
However, the Bodhisatta saw only the *yakkha*, not Sakka. Out of fear of Sakka, the *yakkha* [addressed] the Bodhisatta...
He was unable to strike him. Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, he spoke the second verse, explaining the matter as follows:
“Great King, I did not stand here for the purpose of protecting you; rather, I came thinking, ‘Having struck him with this flaming iron mace, I shall kill him.
It is out of fear of Sakka that I am unable to strike him.”
“I am a messenger of the Rākṣasas, O King; I have been sent here for your execution.
But Indra, the king of the gods, protects you; therefore, I shall not split your head.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke two other verses:
“If the King of the Gods, Maghavā, the Lord of Devas and husband of Sujā, protects me, then let all the piśācas cry out as they wish; I shall not be terrified by the race of rākṣasīs.
Let all the kumbhaṇḍas and the dust-piśācas cry out as they wish.”
“Goblins are not capable of fighting; that was a great deception.
In this context, “of the race of ogresses” means of the race designated as ogresses; the meaning is “of the ogress-beings.
“Kumbhaṇḍas” refers to those yakṣas who have bellies the size of jars and large stomachs. “Dust-goblins” refers to goblins in places of refuse. “Not capable” means...
The so-called *pisācas* are not capable of fighting with me.
As for that great terror which these *yakkhas*, having assembled, display—it is merely a great terror, a mere sight intended to cause fear;
the meaning is that I am not afraid.
Sakka, having driven away the yakkha and exhorted the Great Being, said, “Do not fear, Great King; from this day forward, your protection rests with me,” and he returned to his own abode.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: “At that time Sakka was Anuruddha, and the King of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.
This is the seventh commentary on the Aya-kūṭa Jātaka.
[348] 8. The Commentary on the Arañña-jātaka.

"From the forest, having come to the village"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction of Thullakumārikā. The story will be made clear in the Cūḷanāradakassapa-jātaka.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity and mastered his craft at Takṣaśilā, he went forth as a seer-ascetic after his wife had died.
While living in the Himalayas with his son, whom he had placed in the hermitage, he would go out for the sake of various fruits.
At that time, while bandits were plundering a frontier village and carrying off the tax-collectors, a young girl fled.
Having reached that hermitage, she seduced the young ascetic and brought about the ruin of his virtue, saying, "Come, let us go.

"First let my father come; having seen him, I will go," he replied. "In that case, come after you have seen him," she said, and having departed, she sat down on the path. When the father arrived, the young ascetic spoke the first verse:
“Having come from the forest to the village, what kind of virtue and what kind of conduct should I have?
To what kind of man, dear father, should I attend? Tell me this when I ask you.

In this context, “having come from the forest to the village” means: “Dear father, having gone from this forest to a human settlement for the sake of dwelling, and having reached the village where I am to live, what should I do?”
Then his father, giving him advice, spoke these three verses: “O dear son,
when you have gone from here, associate with one who would inspire confidence in you, who would forgive your lack of confidence, and who is both obedient and patient.”
“He who has committed no wrong by body, speech, or mind—
go from here and seek him out, as one would seek a treasure buried beneath the breast.
Seek that man whose heart is like turmeric-dyed cloth, who is fickle-minded, yet free from passion.”
"O dear one, do not associate with such a person, even if he were a non-human.
In this context, "he who would inspire confidence in you" refers to the man who would cause you to trust him and not harbor suspicion.
"And he who would endure your confidence" refers to one who, having attained your trust toward himself, would remain free from apprehension and tolerate it. "Desirous of hearing" means...
"And whoever wishes to hear your confidential words; and whoever is patient—that is, who forgives an offense committed by you—associate with him.
"You should associate with that man; you should attend upon him. "As if established on your breast":
just as one who has grown up being established on his breast is a breast-born son (*orasaputta*), so too you would be like a son established on the breast.
The meaning is: "Having sacrificed, one should associate with such a person.

"Like turmeric" (*haliddirāga*) means having an unstable mind, similar to the color of turmeric. "Monkey-mind" (*kapicitta*) means a mind like that of a monkey due to its quick shifting. "One who changes from passion to dispassion" (*rāgavirāgin*) means having a nature that becomes attached and detached in a mere moment.
"Even if he were without wealth" (*nimmanusso pi ce siyā*) means even if he should be destitute.
The entire surface of Jambudīpa might become devoid of humans due to the absence of a person free from bodily misconduct and the like;
nevertheless, my dear son, do not associate with such a fickle-minded person.
The meaning is that, having searched throughout the entire human world, you should associate only with one endowed with the qualities mentioned above.
Having heard this, the young ascetic said, "Father, where shall I find a man endowed with these qualities?
I will not go; I shall remain right here in your presence. Having spoken thus, he turned back. Then his father explained to him the preliminary practice for the *kasiṇas*.
Both of them, without falling away from their meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the son and the maiden were these very same persons; as for the father-ascetic, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narration, the Arañña-jātaka.
9. The Narration of the Sandhibheda-jātaka (The Breaking of the Joint)
“There is no commonality among women. The Teacher spoke this while residing at Jetavana, concerning the training rule on malicious talebearing (*pesuñña*).

It is said that on one occasion, having heard that “the group of six monks were engaging in malicious talebearing,” the Teacher summoned them and asked, “Is it true, monks, that you [are doing so] when monks have fallen into quarreling and strife?”
"Instigate slander against those who are engaged in disputes;
by that means, quarrels that have not yet arisen will arise, and those already arisen will increase further. Having asked this and being told "It is true," he rebuked those monks:
"Monks, slanderous speech is like the blow of a sharp spear; even firm trust is quickly destroyed by it."
"Having taken that [weapon], the person who breaks one's friendship becomes like a lion or a bull," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as his son.
Upon reaching maturity, having mastered the arts at Takkasilā, he ruled the kingdom righteously after his father’s passing. At that time, there was a certain cowherd...
While returning from tending the cows in the forest cow-pens, he failed to notice one pregnant cow and left her behind.
She developed a bond of friendship with a lioness, and the two became such close friends that they wandered about together.
Later, the cow gave birth to a calf and the lioness to a lion cub; both of them were of noble lineage.
As soon as they met, they became firm friends and wandered about together. Then a certain forest-dweller entered the forest;
seeing their mutual trust, he took some forest-grown goods, went to Bārāṇasī, and presented them to the king.
When the king asked him, "My good man, have you ever seen anything wonderful in the forest? he replied, "Your Majesty, nothing else..."
“I see nothing else, but I have seen a lion and a bull wandering together in one place, trusting in each other,” he said.
“When a third appears among them, there will be danger; when you see their third, then inform me.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” he replied.
When the forest ranger had gone to Bārāṇasī, a certain jackal waited upon both the lion and the bull.
The forest ranger went into the wilderness, saw this, and thinking, "I shall inform the king that a third has appeared," he returned to the city.
The jackal thought: "Apart from the meat of lions and bulls, there is no other food I have ever eaten before."
“There is no one here; having split these two apart, we shall eat their flesh. He [the forest-dweller] thought, “This one says this about him;
that one says this about him,” and having caused those two to split from one another, he soon brought them to the point of death through quarreling.
The forest-dweller also went and said to the king, “Your Majesty, a third has appeared among them. “Who is he? he asked.
“A jackal, Your Majesty,” he replied. The king said, “He will cause both friends to break apart and have them killed;
we shall arrive when they have met their death. Having spoken thus, he mounted his chariot and set out with a forest-dweller as his guide.
He arrived just as they had fallen into mutual strife and reached the end of their lives. But the jackal was joyful and elated.
At one time he ate the flesh of a lion, and at another time he ate the flesh of an ox.
Seeing that both had met their end, the king, while standing in his chariot, spoke these verses in conversation with his charioteer:
“O charioteer, there is no commonality among women, nor even among the foods you eat;”
Behold how well-considered was the thought of that betrayer of alliances:
"The sword is indeed sharp upon the flesh, yet slander turns back where even the lowest of beasts—
the bull and the lion— devour one another."
“On this bed he lies, O charioteer, which you see here:
he who listens to the speech of a backbiter and a slanderer.
Those people thrive in happiness, like men who have gone to heaven.”
“And those who do not understand the breach of the union of speech, O charioteer.
Therein, “neither among women” means: “O good charioteer, there is no commonality between these two beings regarding women, nor even regarding food.
For the lion frequents one kind of female, the bull another, and their food is yet another.”
The meaning is: "The lion eats; the other is the bull. As for the phrase *athassa*:

even though there was no cause for quarrel, nevertheless, look how well thought out—how truly well thought out—it was for this wicked jackal, a betrayer of friendships, who, having thought, "I shall eat the flesh of both," proceeded to kill these two. *Yattha* means *yasmiṃ* (in which).
While slander is circulating, jackals devour even the bull and the lion, the best of beasts;
this illustrates that such slander revolves about, cutting through friendship just as a sharp sword cuts through meat.
"That which you see here," friend charioteer, refers to this bed of the two who have died; furthermore—
The person who listens to and adopts the malicious speech of a slanderer who has broken the bond—such a one lies upon this very bed;
it is shown that they die in just this way. "They flourish in happiness" means they find and obtain happiness.

"Like men who have gone to heaven" means that like those men who have gone to heaven and possess divine enjoyments, they find happiness. "They do not understand" means they do not [perceive it] as being essential.
They departed; however, having heard such words, they reproached him, reminded him of his duty, and without breaking their friendship, returned to their former state.
Having spoken these verses, the king had the lion’s mane, hide, claws, and teeth taken away, and he went back to the city.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī.”
The ninth: The Commentary on the Sandhibhedajātakavaṇṇanā.
10. The Commentary on the Devatāpañhajātakavaṇṇanā.
"He slays with hands and feet"—this question of the deity will be made clear in the Umaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā.
The commentary on the Devatāpañha Jātaka is the tenth.
The fifth section, the Cūḷakuṇāla-vagga.
The summary (uddāna) of the Jātakas:
The Kāliṅga, the horseman, Ekarāja, and Daddara;
the Test of Virtue, Sujāta, Palāsa, the bird, and Chava;
and Seyya—these are the ten Jātakas.
Pucimanda, Kassapa, Khantivādī, Lohakumbhī,
the hare who obtained all the meat, Matāroda, Kaṇavera, Tittira,
and Saccaka— these are the ten.
Kuṭidūsa, Duddabha, Brahmadatta with his leather garment,
Godharāja, Kakkāru, Kākavatī— who indeed was not to be grieved for?
And Kāḷabāhu, the examiner of virtue— these are the ten.
Kokālika, the chariot-pole, the advice to the king of the spotted cows;
Jambuka, Brahmā, the umbrella, the bench, the flour, and Bāveru;
the merchant Visayha—these are the ten.
The Kinnarī, the Female Monkey, the Elephant’s Forehead, the Mango-Stealer, Keśava,
the Mountain Peak, the Forest, the Breach of the Junction, and the Questions of the Deity. This is the summary of the sections.
The Kāliṅga, the Pucimanda, the Kuṭidūsaka,
and the Kokila; and the Cūḷakuṇāla-vagga— these five chapters in the Catukka-nipāta constitute fifty Jātakas.
The commentary on the Catukkanipāta is finished.
5. Pañcakanipāta 1. Maṇikuṇḍalavagga (The Chapter on Jewels and Earrings)
[351] 1. The Commentary on the Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka.

"He conquered the chariot and the jeweled earrings"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a wicked minister who brought about total ruin within the palace of the King of Kosala.
The story has already been related in detail below. Here...

However, the Bodhisatta was the King of Bārāṇasī. A corrupt minister, having brought the King of Kosala and caused him to seize the kingdom of Kāsi, had the King of Bārāṇasī bound and cast into prison.
The King, having attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), sat cross-legged in the air; a fever arose in the body of the robber-king. He approached the King of Bārāṇasī.
He spoke the first verse:
“You have lost your chariot and your jeweled earrings, and likewise you have lost your children and your wife;
since you have lost all your possessions without exception, why do you not grieve at this time of sorrow?”

In that regard, "O Great King, you have lost the chariot, the horse, and the jeweled earrings"—that is, you have lost the chariot, the horse, and the jeweled earrings. There is also a reading: *jīno rathasse ca maṇikuṇḍale ca*. "With all your hair" means with every single hair.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke these two verses:
"Before death, possessions leave a mortal; or the mortal leaves them even earlier."
“Those who possess wealth and seek their desires are impermanent; therefore, I do not grieve in this time of sorrow.
The moon rises, waxes full, and wanes; the sun, having shone, sets.
These worldly conditions, Sattuka, are known by me; therefore, I do not grieve in this time of sorrow.”
In this context, "wealth leaves the mortal first" means that wealth departs from the mortal even before, or at the very outset; or else, the mortal abandons that wealth earlier.
"O seeker of pleasures" is an address to the king of thieves. "O you who desire sense-pleasures, O seeker of pleasures!
Wealth in this world is indeed impermanent; or rather, when wealth is lost, one becomes a non-possessor of wealth even while still alive."
The meaning is: "Even when wealth is lost or perishes of its own accord, I do not grieve even in times of sorrow for the great multitude.
"I have understood the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), O Sattuka," he says, addressing the king of thieves.
"O Sattuka, I have understood the worldly conditions such as gain and loss, fame and disrepute, and so forth. For just as the moon rises and waxes, and then again..."
Just as the sun, dispelling darkness and radiating great light, again sets in the evening, goes to its end, and is no longer seen; even so, wealth arises and perishes.
What is the use of grieving in that regard? Therefore, "I do not grieve"—this is the meaning.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the king of thieves, the Great Being now spoke, censuring that very thief:
"A lazy householder who indulges in sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained one who has gone forth is not good;
a king who acts without reflection is not good; and a wise man who is prone to anger is not good."
“A king should act with reflection, not without reflection, O Lord of the Earth;
for a king who acts with reflection, his glory and fame increase.
These two verses have already been explained in detail above. After the robber-king had asked the Bodhisatta’s forgiveness and handed over the kingdom, he returned to his own country.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Ānanda was the King of Kosala, while I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī.
This concludes the first exposition, the Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka.
2. The Exposition of the Sujāta Jātaka.
"Why do you hurry along?"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a householder whose father had died.
It is said that he wandered about lamenting after his father’s death and was unable to dispel his grief.
Then the Teacher, seeing that the man possessed the necessary conditions for attaining the fruit of stream-entry, went on alms-round in Sāvatthī with a junior monk as his attendant.
Taking [the boy] with him, he went to the man's house and sat on the prepared seat. Having paid homage to the man as he sat there, he asked, "Lay follower, why do you grieve?

When the man replied, "Yes, venerable sir," he said, "Friend, in the past, wise men did not grieve when their fathers passed away after hearing the words of the wise. At his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder’s family;
they gave him the name Sujātakaumāra. When he reached maturity, his grandfather passed away. From that time on, his father was overwhelmed with grief due to his father’s death;
having gone to the cremation ground and retrieved the bones from the pyre, he built an earthen stupa in his own park.
Having made those offerings and deposited them there, at every hour he went, he would worship the stupa with flowers and lament while gazing toward the shrine;
he neither bathed, nor anointed himself, nor ate, nor attended to his business. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta thought:
"Since the time my grandfather died, my father has wandered overcome by grief; but other than me, no one else..."
“Since he cannot be persuaded by this, I shall make him free from grief by some other means,” he thought.
Seeing a dead ox outside the village, he brought grass and water, placed them before it, and said, “Eat, eat! Drink, drink!
Those who came along saw him and said, “Friend Sujāta, what, have you gone mad? Grass and water for a dead ox?”
“...the local custom,” they said. He did not reply at all. Then, going to his father’s presence, they said, “Your son has become mad;
he is giving grass and water to a dead ox. Upon hearing this, the householder’s grief for his father subsided, and grief for his son took its place.
He came rushing forward and said, “Are you not wise, dear Sujāta? For what reason—”
Having said, "I shall give grass and water to my old ox," he spoke these two verses:
"Why do you, as if in great haste, pull up the green grass and say, 'Eat!
Eat! to this old ox whose life has departed?"
“For a dead ox does not rise up again by means of food and drink;
and you lament in vain, just as one who is foolish does.
In this context, *santaramāno* means acting as if in haste. *Lāyitvā* means having mowed. *Lapasī* means you lament. *Gatasattaṃ* [means one whose life has departed].
"An old ox" means one whose life has departed, a worn-out bull. As for the word "tanti," here it is merely a particle;
just as a foolish person of little wisdom might lament, so do you lament in vain.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke two verses:
“The head remains just as it was, as do the hooves and the tail;
the ears likewise remain—surely the ox must be rising up!
Yet neither the head nor the hooves of the ox are seen.”
"Is it not you yourself, O foolish one, who are weeping at the clay stupa?
In this context, "just so" means it remains exactly as it was previously situated.
"I think" refers to the thought that because these [limbs] such as the head remain just so, this ox might stand up. "Nor even the head of the grandfather," however—
The head and the hands and feet were not to be seen. (There is also a reading: “The back and the feet were not to be seen.
“Are you not yourself the one who is foolish? [He replied: “As for me, seeing the head and so forth, I act in this way; but you see nothing at all.
Having brought bones from the place where [the body] was burned and having made a mound of clay, you lament. Thus, compared to me, you are a hundredfold, a thousandfold—”

"Are you not yourself, O foolish one, a hundred thousand times more so? Indeed, conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are by nature subject to breaking; they break. What cause for lamentation is there in that?
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta’s father [thought]: "My son is wise; he understands the duties pertaining to this world and the world beyond. My..."
Thinking, "He performed this deed for the purpose of making me understand," he said, "Dear wise Sujāta, I have realized that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
From now on I shall not grieve; indeed, one must become such as a son who removes his father's sorrow.
Having spoken thus, he uttered words of praise for his son:
“While I was burning, like a fire fed with ghee,
you have extinguished all my distress as if sprinkling water.
You have indeed extracted the arrow that was lodged in my heart.”
“He who dispelled the grief for my father in me, who was overcome by sorrow—
‘I am now one whose arrow has been pulled out, free from grief and undisturbed;
I do not grieve nor do I weep, having heard you, young man.’”
“Thus do the wise act, those who are compassionate;
they turn one away from sorrow, just as Sujāta did for his father.
In this context, *nibbāpayeti* means he caused [the fire] to be extinguished. *Daraṃ* refers to the torment of sorrow. *Sujāto pitaraṃ yathā* means just as Sujāta [did for] his father.
"My son Sujāta, by his own wisdom, has turned me away from grief as my father;
likewise, others who possess wisdom turn others away from grief.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (Saccāni), the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). "At that time, I myself was Sujāta."
The second *Sujāta-jātaka* commentary.
[353] 3. The *Vena-sākha-jātaka* commentary:
"This must not be permanent"—this was said by the Teacher while staying at Bhesakaḷāvana near Saṃsumāragira in the country of the Bhaggas.
While dwelling there, he spoke concerning Prince Bodhi.

Prince Bodhi, the son of King Udena, while residing at Saṃsumāragiri at that time, summoned a carpenter of preeminent skill and, having had him construct a palace named Kokanada that was unlike anything built by other kings, he spoke thus after it was completed: "This carpenter..."
Out of envy, thinking, "Would that another king might have such a palace built," he had the man's eyes gouged out.
Consequently, the fact that his eyes had been torn out became well known throughout the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Therefore, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying:
"Friends, it is said that Prince Bodhi had the eyes of such a carpenter..."
...had them torn out, exclaiming, "Oh, how cruel, harsh, and violent he is!
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now? When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he was cruel, harsh, and violent. And not only now, but in the past he [was so] toward thousands of kṣatriyas..."
“Having had their eyes gouged out and having killed them, she caused an offering to be made with their flesh,” he said, and then related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā.
Young nobles and young brahmins from throughout the land of Jambudīpa studied the arts under him alone.
They mastered them. The son of the King of Bārāṇasī, Prince Brahmadatta by name, mastered the three Vedas under him.
However, he was by nature harsh, cruel, and violent. The Bodhisatta, having understood through the science of bodily marks that he was harsh, cruel, and violent, said:
"Dear son, you are harsh, cruel, and violent; because of this cruelty..."
“O Brahmadatta, the sovereignty one has attained is short-lived; when that sovereignty is lost, like a shattered ship in the ocean, one finds no firm footing.
Therefore, do not become such a person. Speaking thus to advise him, he uttered these two verses:
“This must not be considered permanent, O Brahmadatta: security, abundance of food, and physical well-being.”
May you not be utterly bewildered when your wealth is exhausted, like one whose raft has broken apart in the middle of the ocean.
Whatever a person does, that they see within themselves:
the doer of good sees what is good, and the doer of evil sees what is evil.
“As one sows such a seed, so one reaps such a fruit.

In this regard, O dear Brahmadatta, as for that security or abundance of food, or whatever such comfort there may be in the body—all this does not exist permanently or at all times for these beings. This—
But having been impermanent, it is subject to the nature of non-existence. Regarding "the cessation of one's own welfare" (*atthaccaya*):

when your sovereignty has vanished due to impermanence and your own welfare has come to an end, do not become bewildered—just as a man whose raft is broken or whose ship is wrecked becomes utterly confused, finding no foothold in the middle of the ocean. "He sees those [results] within himself" refers to those karmas.
Experiencing the ripening of that karma, he saw those very things within himself.
Having paid homage to his teacher, he went to Bārāṇasī, demonstrated his craft, was established as viceroy, and upon his father’s passing, attained the kingship.
His chaplain was named Piṅgiya, who was harsh, cruel, and violent.
Thus, out of greed for gain, he thought: "What if I were to have all the kings throughout the entire Jambudīpa seized by this king?
In this way, he will become the sole monarch, and I too shall become his sole court chaplain. He persuaded the king to adopt his plan.
The king, having set out from the city with a great army, besieged the city of a certain king.

He seized that king. By this means, having taken control of the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa, he set out surrounded by a thousand kings with the intention of seizing the kingdom of Takkasilā.
The Bodhisatta, having repaired the city, made it impregnable to others.

The King of Bārāṇasī, having had a curtain draped at the foot of a great banyan tree on the bank of the Ganges river, and having had a canopy erected above it and a couch prepared, took up residence there.
Although he had taken the thousand kings of Jambudīpa under his command and was engaged in battle, he was unable to capture Takkasilā; thus, he questioned his own chaplain: "Teacher,..."
“Even though we have come with so many kings, we are unable to take Takkasilā; what indeed should be done?

[The deity replied: “Great King, having plucked out the eyes of a thousand kings, having killed them, and having split open their bellies, take the meat of the five sweet flavors and perform an offering to the deity dwelling in this banyan tree.”
“By surrounding the tree with ant-hills and making five-fingered marks of blood, our victory will thus be swift,” they said.
The king, having consented by saying “Very well,” stationed the Mallas of great strength within the enclosure;
then, calling each king one by one, he caused them to be rendered unconscious by crushing, gouged out their eyes, and killed them.
Having taken flesh from his own body and washed it away in the Ganges, he had the aforementioned bali-offering performed, had the bali-drum beaten, and set out for battle.
Then, a certain yakkha came down from a watchtower, plucked out one of his right eyes, and departed; thereafter, a great...
Pain arose. Overcome by that pain, he returned and lay down on his back upon the seat prepared at the foot of the banyan tree.
At that moment, a vulture sitting at the top of the tree, having taken a bone with a sharp point, ate some flesh and dropped the bone;
the tip of the bone came and pierced the king’s left eye as if it were an iron stake.
Having fallen, he broke his eye. At that moment, he reflected upon the words of the Bodhisatta.

He said, "Our teacher, when speaking of how these beings experience results according to their karma—just as fruit corresponds to its seed—must have said this after seeing this very thing," and lamenting, he spoke two verses:
“This is that word of the Teacher which Pārāsariya spoke:
‘Do not, O good man, commit evil, lest what you have done later cause you remorse.
This very one, Piṅgiya, is that banyan branch upon which I caused a thousand kṣatriyas to be slain.”
“Though adorned and anointed with the essence of sandalwood, that very suffering has come back upon me.
In this regard, “this is the word of that teacher” means this is the speech of that teacher. “Pārāsariya” is a designation based on his clan.
“Done afterwards” means whatever evil was committed by you, that will later burn and torment you; do not [commit it].
"He gave me instruction, yet I did not follow his word"—thus he laments, pointing to the *nigrodha* tree.
"Venasākha" means one with spreading branches. "In whom they had me executed" refers to the tree under which he caused a thousand kṣatriyas to be killed.
"Adorned and anointed with the essence of sandalwood" means adorned with royal ornaments and anointed with the finest red sandalwood.
"This very tree where I had those kṣatriyas executed is now unable to provide even the slightest protection for me"—this he indicates.
"That very same suffering"—meaning the pain I inflicted upon others by gouging out their eyes—has come back to me in that very same way;
"now the words of our teacher have reached their ultimate fulfillment," he laments.
Thus lamenting, he called to mind his chief queen:
"Sāmā, with limbs anointed with sandalwood, tall as a *sobhañjana* tree—without seeing my noble lady pass away, I shall die;
that will be even more painful for me than this."
He spoke this verse.
Its meaning is as follows: My wife Suvaṇṇasāmā Ubbarī shines as she displays feminine grace;
just as a straight, upward-reaching branch of a *siggu* tree, swaying when stirred by a gentle breeze, is beautiful, so too does she shine. Her I—
"Now, because my eyes have been destroyed, I shall die without even seeing Ubbarī;
that failure to see her will be a suffering for me even greater than the pain of death itself.

While lamenting thus, he died and was reborn in hell. Neither could the chaplain, greedy for power, provide protection for him, nor did he exercise his own authority. As soon as he had died, the army broke up and fled.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was Prince Bodhi; Piṅgiya was Devadatta; and the world-renowned teacher was none other than myself.
This concludes the third commentary, the Vena-sākhā Jātaka.
4. The Commentary on the Uraga Jātaka.
“Like a snake’s slough, worn out”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a householder whose son had died.
The background story, however, is exactly like that of the husband and father who had died. Here too, the Teacher went to his residence in the same manner;
when the man had come, paid homage, and sat down, the Teacher asked him, “Friend, why do you grieve?”
When he said, “Yes, venerable sir, ever since my son died I have been grieving,” [the Buddha replied]:
“Friend, that which is subject to breaking breaks; that which is subject to perishing perishes. Moreover, this does not happen only in one family, nor only in one village;
rather, throughout the immeasurable world-systems and across the three realms of existence, there is no such thing as being exempt from death. Precisely because of that—”
"Even a single conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) capable of remaining is not called eternal;

all beings are subject to death, and all conditioned phenomena are subject to dissolution. Even the ancient sages, when their sons died, did not grieve, thinking: 'What is subject to death has died; what is subject to destruction has been destroyed.
Having said this, at his request, he related a story from the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a village near the gate of Benares.
Having established a household, he made his living by means of agricultural work.
He had two children, a son and a daughter. When his son reached maturity, he brought home a maiden from a family of equal status.
There were six people including that female slave: the Bodhisatta, his wife, their son, their daughter, the daughter-in-law, and the slave.
They lived together in harmony, affectionately and joyfully. The Bodhisatta gave this advice to the other five:
"Give alms according to whatever means you have obtained; observe moral virtue; perform the Uposatha duties."
“Practice it! Develop mindfulness of death; observe the nature of your own mortality.
For the death of these beings is certain, while life is uncertain. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to decay and destruction.
Be heedful by night and by day! Having accepted this instruction with the words, “Very well,” they became heedful and developed mindfulness of death.
Now one day, the Bodhisatta went to the field with his son and was plowing. The son gathered the refuse and set it on fire.
Not far from there, in an anthill, lived a venomous snake.
The smoke struck its eyes, and becoming enraged, it emerged, thinking, "It is because of this man that I am in danger," and sank its four fangs into him.

The ox was struck and, turning over, fell down. Seeing it had fallen after it had turned over, the Bodhisatta drove the other oxen away, went to the spot, and knowing it was dead, lifted it up, laid it down at the foot of a tree, covered it with his cloak, and neither wept nor lamented:
"That which is subject to breaking has broken; that which is subject to death is dead. All..."
“Formations are impermanent and result in death. Having thus observed their very nature of impermanence, he ploughed.
Seeing a neighbor passing by near the field, he asked him, “Sir, are you going home?
When the man replied, “Yes,” he said, “In that case, when you reach our house, please tell my wife: ‘It seems today, as before, for two—’”
“Without bringing food for all of you, you should bring food for only one person. Previously, a single female slave used to bring the food;
but today, all four of you should come dressed in clean garments, with perfumes and flowers in your hands.
He replied, “Very well,” and having gone there, he spoke to the brahmin lady exactly as instructed. She asked, “By whom, dear son, was this message given to you?”
"By the brahmin, noble lady," she replied. She realized, "My son is dead," yet not even the slightest tremor came over her.

Thus, with her mind so well-cultivated, dressed in clean garments and holding perfumes and flowers in her hands, she had a maidservant bring food and went to the field together with the others. Not even one person wept or lamented.
The Bodhisatta sat down and ate right within the shadow where his son was lying.
At the conclusion of the meal, they all removed the wood, placed him upon that funeral pyre, honored him with scents and flowers, and cremated him.
Not even a single drop of tears fell from anyone; they were all well-practiced in the mindfulness of death. By the power of their virtue, Sakka’s throne—
He manifested a state of heat. Reflecting, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from my position?

and perceiving the cause of that heat to be the power of their virtues, he became serene in mind and thought: "It is fitting for me to go into their presence, cause them to roar the lion's roar, and upon the conclusion of that roar, return after having made their residence complete with the seven treasures."
Having gone there with speed, he stood by the side of the cremation ground and asked, "Father, what are you doing?
"We are burning a human being, master," they replied. "You are not burning a human being; I think you have killed a deer and are cooking it.
"That is not so, master; we are indeed burning a human being. "In that case, this person will become your enemy."
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “He is our own legitimate son, my lord; he is not an enemy. “In that case, he must be your disliked son,” [the king asked].
“He is exceedingly dear to us, my lord,” [the Bodhisatta replied]. “Then why does he not weep?
As he explained the reason for his not weeping, he spoke the first verse:
"Just as a snake, casting off its worn-out skin, goes on to a new body,
so it is with the body when it is devoid of life, deceased, and passed away. Being cremated,
it does not know the lamentation of its kinsmen."
"Therefore, I do not grieve for this; he has gone to whatever destination belongs to him.
In this context, *saṃtanu* refers to one's own body. *Nibbhoge* means devoid of enjoyments due to the absence of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
*Pete* means one who has departed to the other world. *Kālakate* means "at the time of death"; the meaning is "one who has died. This is what is intended: [I do not grieve for him].
"Master, just as a snake might go its way after casting off its old skin— having severed it, looking back at it no more, and abandoning it without concern—
so too does my son go, having cast off his own body. Now that his body is devoid of the life-faculty and thus useless,
and since my son has passed away and returned to the state of death, who [is there to care for me]?"

There is no purpose in either compassion or lamentation. For just as one being impaled on stakes and burned does not perceive pleasure or pain, so too he does not perceive the lamentations of his kinsmen; for that reason, I do not grieve for him.
He has gone to whatever destination was his own.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, Sakka asked the brahmin woman, “Mother, what is he to you?
“He is my son, my lord,” she replied, “whom I carried in my womb for ten months, whom I suckled with milk, and whom I raised by tending his hands and feet.
“Mother, let the father not weep because of his manhood; but a mother’s heart is tender.”
“Others weep, so why do you not weep? She, explaining the reason for her lack of weeping, said:
“He came from there uninvited; he went from here unpermitted.
As he came, so he went; what lamentation can there be for that?”
“Burning, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to whatever destination is his. He spoke these two verses.
Therein, “uninvited” means: “O dear one, he came to our house uninvited by me from the world beyond. “He came” means: to our home.
"Has come": even as he departed from this world of humans, he went without my permission. "As he came":
just as he came by his own will, so too did he go. "Therein": regarding that departure of his from here, what cause for lamentation is there?
The verse beginning with "Being consumed" should be understood according to the method already explained.
Having heard the brahmin woman’s words, Sakka asked her sister, "Mother, what is he to you?
"He is my brother, master," she replied. "Mother, sisters are indeed affectionate toward their brothers; why then do you not weep?
As she explained the reason for her lack of tears—
“If I were to weep, I would become emaciated; what fruit would that bring me?
My kinsmen, friends, and companions would only feel even greater distress.
One who is burning with grief does not perceive the lamentations of their relatives.”
"Therefore, I do not grieve for this; he has gone to whatever destination is his.
She spoke these two verses. Therein, "If" means: if I were to weep for my brother who has died, I would become emaciated in body.
However, she shows that there is no growth for her on account of her brother. "For me" means: what fruit or what benefit is there for me while I am weeping?
[It] would be [so]. But it shows that my own lack of progress is apparent. "Of kinsmen, friends, and companions" means of kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers.
Or this very reading [is correct]. "Even more" means that for those who are our kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers, there might be even greater displeasure.
Having heard his sister's words, Sakka asked his wife: "My dear, what is he to you? "Husband."
“Master, [I am your wife]. “Women, when their husband has died, become widows and are without a protector; why do you not weep?
She then told him the reason for her not weeping:
“Just as a child cries out after the moon as it goes away...”
"This is exactly how it is for one who continues to mourn for the deceased:
'While burning, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore, I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to whatever destination belongs to him. Thus he spoke these two verses.

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as, for example, a foolish child sitting on his mother’s lap, not knowing what is appropriate or inappropriate, what is obtainable or unobtainable, might see the full moon moving through the sky on the night of the full moon and weep again and again, saying, “Mother, give me the moon!
Mother, give me the moon!”—this [case] is exactly like that.
Thus, the weeping of one who grieves for that deceased person is merely the result of such a process; it is even more foolish than that.
Why? Because he laments over a moon that still exists, whereas my husband, being dead, is now non-existent and would not know anything even if he were being impaled on stakes and burned.
Having heard his wife’s words, Sakka asked the slave girl, “Mother, what is he to you? “He is my master, sir,” she replied.
“Surely you must have been oppressed and beaten by him; that is why you do not weep, saying, ‘I am well freed.
“Sir, do not speak thus; this is not worthy of him. He is endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.”
“My noble son was like a son raised upon my breast. “Then why do you not weep?
As she explained the reason for her lack of tears, she said:
“Just as a water-jar that has been broken cannot be joined again;”
"It is only fitting that one who has passed away should be mourned.
'While burning, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore, I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to whatever destination is his.'"—thus he spoke these two verses.

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as a water-jar, when being lifted up, falls and breaks into seven pieces, and those shards cannot be reassembled or restored to their original state even if they were set in order and arranged again;
so too, the lamentation of one who grieves for such a person is likewise fruitless, because it is impossible to bring the dead back to life.
It might be possible for one possessing supernormal power (*iddhimant*) to reassemble a broken jar by means of the majesty of his power (*iddhānubhāva*) and fill it with water;
however, once someone has passed away, even by the power of supernormal feats, it is impossible to restore them to their former state. The other verses have already been explained.
Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma from all of them, Sakka was inspired with confidence and said: "By you, being heedful, mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*) has been cultivated."
"From this day forward, do not perform manual labor yourselves.
I, Sakka, king of the devas, shall provide immeasurable seven kinds of treasures in your houses. Give alms, guard your virtue, observe the Uposatha rites, and be heedful.
Having given them this exhortation and filled their homes with boundless wealth, he departed.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the female slave was Khujjuttarā, the daughter was Uppalavaṇṇā, the son was Rāhula, the mother was Khemā, and the brahmin was none other than myself.
The fourth: The Commentary on the Uragajātakavaṇṇanā.
[355] 5. The Commentary on the Ghaṭajātakavaṇṇanā.
"Others grieve and weep"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain minister of the King of Kosala.

He related [the Jātaka]. The story is exactly as told below. However, in this case, the king, having bestowed great honor upon his own benefactor minister, yet having accepted the words of those who sought to cause a rift, had him bound and cast into prison.
While sitting there, he realized the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). The king, recognizing his virtue, had him released.
So, taking perfumes and garlands, he went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Has some misfortune indeed arisen for you? When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir;

but through that misfortune, a benefit has come to me—the path of stream-entry has been realized," the Teacher said, "It is not only you, lay follower, who have brought about benefit through misfortune; even the ancient sages did so."
Having said, "They brought it," when requested by him, he related a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen;
they gave him the name Ghaṭakumāra. At a later time, he mastered the arts at Takkasilā.
He ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma. A certain minister in his inner court acted treacherously;
having learned of this through direct observation, the king banished him from the realm. At that time, a king named Dhaṅka was ruling in Sāvatthī.
He went into the presence of the former king, attended upon him, and—following the method described below—caused him to accept his proposal and [bestow] the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī.
He had him seized. Having taken the kingdom for himself, he had the Bodhisatta bound with chains and cast into prison.
The Bodhisatta, having attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), sat cross-legged in the air;
a burning fever arose in the body of the hawk. He went there and, seeing the Bodhisatta’s face, which was as beautiful as a golden mirror or a full-blown lotus—
Questioning the Bodhisatta, he spoke the first verse:
“Others grieve and weep; other people have tearful faces.
You have a bright and serene countenance; why, Ghaṭa, do you not grieve?”
In that context, "others" refers to the remaining people, excluding him.
Then the Bodhisatta, explaining the reason why he does not grieve, spoke these four verses:
"Grief does not bring back what is past, nor does it bring future happiness."
Therefore, O vulture, I do not grieve; there is no companion for one who grieves.
Through grief one becomes pale and emaciated, and food does not please him;
his enemies rejoice as he suffers, pierced by the arrow.
“Whether in the village or in the forest, in the lowlands or on the high ground—wherever I stand, he shall not come to me;
such am I, one who has seen the state.
He for whom even a single person is not enough to satisfy all the flavors of sensual desire.”
“Even the whole earth will not bring him happiness.
In this context, *nābbhatītaharo* means “one who does not take up what has passed”; or rather, this is the very reading [of the text]: *nābbhatītāhāro*.
Grief (*soka*) indeed does not take up again that which is past, transcended, ceased, and gone to its end. *Dutīyatā* means companionship. Or, by way of taking up the past or taking up the future...
Or, he says: "Sorrow is not the friend of anyone; for that reason as well, I do not grieve. "They grieve, while grieving":
the meaning is that when one is pierced by the dart of sorrow and is being tormented by it, one's enemies rejoice, thinking, "We have indeed seen the back of our adversary.
"The one pierced by the dart is afflicted" means that for one who has been struck by the dart of sorrow, they are distressed by that very same thing. "The enemies are glad" is the sense.
"Standing me, O noble King Dhaṅka, no calamity rooted in sorrow—such as the state of being pale and emaciated—will come to me, wherever I may stand among these villages and so forth.
"Thus I have seen the state": just as that calamity does not come, so too have I seen the state of *jhāna*. It is also called "the state of the eight worldly conditions."
They indeed say so. However, in the Pāḷi it is written, “*na mattaṃ nāgamissatī*,” which does not appear in the Aṭṭhakathā.

Because it brings forth the essence of all desires—namely, the bliss of *jhāna*—in the sense of fulfilling what is wished for and longed for in the concluding verse, it is called “the bringer of the essence of all desires” (*sabbakāmarasāharo*).
This is what is meant: that king who, having abandoned other companions, is himself alone the bringer of the essence of all desires.

It is not capable; one who is unable to bring forth the flavor of sensual pleasure known as all meditative absorption (*jhāna-sukha*) will find that even the entire earth does not bring happiness to that king. For there is no such thing as happiness for one who is afflicted by sensual desires.

However, that king who is capable of bringing forth the meditative happiness free from the distress of the defilements (*kilesa-daratha*) becomes happy. As for the meaning of this verse: "For whom... [the rest follows].
The reading “nālameko” is also found, but its meaning is not apparent.
Thus, having heard these four verses, Dhaṅka apologized to the Bodhisatta, handed over the kingdom to him, and departed.
The Bodhisatta, for his part, returned the kingdom to his ministers, went to the region of the Himālayas, and went forth as an ascetic.
Having gone forth, he did not fall away from his meditative absorption and became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Dhaṅka was Ānanda, while I myself was King Ghaṭa.
This concludes the commentary on the Ghaṭa Jātaka, the fifth.
[356] 6. The Commentary on the Koraṇḍiya Jātaka.
"In a certain forest..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the Dhamma-Senāpati (the General of the Dhamma).
It is said that whenever the Elder encountered those of immoral conduct, such as hunters, deer-trappers, fishermen, and others, he would immediately exhort them, saying: "Virtue..."
"Take the precepts! Take the precepts! he gave them the precepts. Out of respect for the elder, they were unable to contradict his words and took the precepts;
yet, having taken them, they did not guard them, but each went about their own business.
The elder addressed his co-residents: "Friends, these people have taken the precepts in my presence; having taken them..."
“...and yet they do not observe them,” he said. “Venerable sir, you give the precepts against their own wishes;
they accept them because they are unable to break your word. From now on, please do not give such precepts to those like this.
The Elder was displeased. When the monks heard what had occurred, they raised the matter for discussion in the Hall of Truth.
—“Friends, it is said that the Elder Sāriputta gives the precepts only to those who have already seen [the Truth].
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he gave the precepts only to those who had already seen [the Truth] and who did not ask for them. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he became the senior pupil named Koraṇḍiya under a world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā.
At that time, whenever fishermen and others came to see him, even without being asked, the teacher would say: "Take the precepts."
"Take the precepts," he said, and gave them the precepts. Although they had taken them, they did not guard them; the teacher reported this matter to his pupils.
The pupils said, "Venerable sir, you gave the precepts to these men against their will, and that is why they break them.
From now on, you should give them only to those who ask, and not to those who do not ask. He felt remorse.
Even though this was so, he still gave his blessing for the observance of the precepts whenever they were seen.
Then one day, people came from a certain village and invited the teacher to officiate at a Brahmin recitation ceremony.
He summoned the young man Koraṇḍiya and said, "Dear son, I will not go; you [must go] with these five hundred young men."
"Take this, go there, receive the oral instructions, and bring back the portion allotted to us," he sent him.
Having gone and returning on the way, he saw a mountain cleft and thought:
"Our teacher gives the precepts only to those who do not ask as they see fit; from now on, however, [I shall act] so that [he gives them] only to those who ask."

“I shall do so for you. While those young brahmins were sitting comfortably, he rose, lifted up massive boulders one after another, and hurled them into the ravine; he continued hurling them again and again.
Then those young brahmins rose and said, “Teacher, what are you doing? He said nothing to them, and they went in haste toward the teacher.
They reported this. The teacher, having arrived and conversing with him, spoke the first verse:
“Alone in the forest, in a mountain cave, you repeatedly pick up stones and throw them down;
again and again, appearing in a state of great agitation, Koraṇḍiya, what indeed is the purpose of your intent?”
"In that regard, what indeed is your purpose here in this cave by throwing stones?
Having heard his words and desiring to awaken the teacher, he spoke the second verse:
"I shall indeed make this ocean-shore level, just like the palm of my hand."
“I shall scatter the plateaus and the mountains; therefore, I cast this rock into the abyss.
In this context, “I shall [scatter] this” means I shall scatter this great earth. “Served by the oceans” means surrounded on four sides by the oceans.
“Just as with the hand” means I shall make it level like the palm of the hand. “Having scattered” means having dispersed [it].
“Sānūni ca pabbatāni ca” means both sand-mountains and stone-mountains.
Having heard that, the brahmin spoke this third verse:
“This earth does not deserve to be leveled by the hand by me alone, a mere mortal;”
"I think that this very cave alone is what you wish to conquer; O Koraṇḍiya, you have laughed at the world of the living.
In this context, "one is not able to do it for the sake of making" (*karaṇāya meko*) indicates that one person is unable to accomplish it.

"I think that this very cave alone is what you wish to conquer" (*maññāmi maññeva dariṃ jigīsaṃ*): I think—let alone the earth—that you wish to conquer this very single cave for the purpose of filling it.
“Exerting yourself, searching for stones, and even while devising a means, you will lose this world of the living—you will abandon it, meaning you will die.
Having heard that, the young man spoke the fourth verse:
“If it is not possible for a single man to level this earth-supporter for my sake, [what then]?”
“In the same way, Brahmā, you will not bring these people of various views under your control.

The meaning of this is: if even a single person is unable or incapable of making this earth, the supporter of beings, level, in the same way you will not bring these immoral people of various views under your control; for them, [virtue]...
If you say, "Take it! Take the precepts! he will not bring himself under your control;
for only wise men censure the taking of life as "unwholesome. But those such as the "Liberators from Saṃsāra" perceive it as wholesome;
how then will you bring them under your influence? Therefore, do not give the precepts to those who hold various views, but give them only to those who ask.
Having heard this, the teacher thought, “Koraṇḍiyā speaks rightly; I shall not act in such a way from now on. Realizing his own failure, he spoke the fifth verse:
“Lady Koraṇḍiyā, you have thus explained my purpose in brief form.
Just as it is impossible for a human being to level the earth, so too are human beings [in their nature].”
In this context, *samāyanti* means they come together (*samaṃ ayaṃ*). Thus the teacher offered praise to the young man (*māṇava*), and he too, having enlightened him, led him to his own home.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was Sāriputta, while the young man Koraṇḍiya was none other than myself.
This is the sixth commentary on the Koraṇḍiya Jātaka.
[357] 7. The Commentary on the Laṭukikā-Jātaka:
"I revere you, O elephant of sixty years. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta.
For one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, Devadatta..."
"He is harsh, cruel, and violent; he possesses not even a trace of compassion for living beings.

The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that he has been devoid of compassion;
in the past, too, he was just the same. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of an elephant.
Having reached maturity, he became a handsome and massive leader of a herd, surrounded by eighty thousand elephants, and dwelt in the regions of the Himālaya.
At that time, a certain little quail laid her eggs in the place where the elephants roamed; those [eggs...]
When the eggs had matured and hatched, the young birds emerged.
While they were still unable to fly because their wings had not yet grown, the Great Being, surrounded by eighty thousand elephants, arrived at that place while wandering in search of food.
Seeing him, the little quail thought: "This king of elephants will trample and kill my chicks; come now, [I must protect] them."
“I ask for righteous protection for the sake of my own safety. Having brought both factions together, she stood before him and spoke this first verse:
“I pay homage to you, O elephant, sixty years of age, the illustrious leader of the forest herd.”
"With my wings I shall make you pay homage with joined palms; do not kill my two feeble little sons.

In this context, "sixty years" refers to the decline of strength at the age of sixty. "Glorious" means endowed with a retinue. "With my wings I shall make you pay homage with joined palms" means that I, with my wings, shall cause you to perform the añjali gesture.
The Great Being said, "Do not worry, little bird; I will protect your two little sons," and [stood] over the young birds.
When eighty thousand elephants had passed by, she called out to Laṭukikā: "Laṭukikā, a solitary elephant is coming after us;
he will not heed our words. When he arrives, you must beg him as well and ensure the safety of my children.
Having said this, she departed. She [Laṭukikā] then went out to meet him.
Having done so, and having pressed his palms together with both hands, he spoke this second verse:
“I revere you, O elephant, who wander alone, a forest-dweller whose range is the mountain peaks;
I join my palms to you in reverence—do not kill my two young sons, for I am weak.”
In that context, "having its range on mountain ridges" means it takes its prey upon dense rocky mountains and sand dunes.
Having heard her words, he spoke this third verse:
"I will kill your little chicks, little bird; what can you do to me, for you are weak?"
“Even a hundred thousand such as these he would trample under his left foot.
In this context, “I will kill you” means: “Why have you placed these little children on my path of movement?
Since you have placed them there, therefore I will kill those children. “What can you do to me? refers to [the speaker] who possesses great power.
"You are weak; what can you do? You might as well try to fly! [The mother replied:
"I would crush even a hundred thousand such little birds with my left foot alone; as for my right foot, there is no need even to mention it.
Having said this, he crushed her two little chicks with his foot, flushed them out with urine, and roared.
He departed. The little lizard, having hidden in a tree branch, spoke the fourth verse while threatening him: "Now you go away bellowing like an elephant;
in just a few days you shall see my deed. You do not know the greatness of the power of knowledge over the power of the body; very well, I shall make you know it!"
“Force is not to be used everywhere; for force leads to the destruction of the fool.
O King of Nagas, I shall do you harm, you who have killed my two weak children.

In this passage, *balena* means by physical force. *Anatthaṃ* means misfortune or lack of prosperity. *Yo me* means "you who," referring to you who killed—that is, caused the death of—my two children when I was weak.
Having spoken thus, she attended upon a single crow for several days. When the crow was pleased and asked her, "What shall I do for you?
she replied, "Master, there is nothing else I need to have done; however, I request that you strike a solitary wandering elephant with your beak so as to break its eyes.
She was accepted by him with the words, "Very well," and [she went to] one...
She attended upon a blue fly. When she was asked by it, "What can I do for you?", she said, "When this crow has blinded the eyes of the solitary elephant, I wish for you to lay an egg there.
When she agreed, saying "Very well," she then attended upon a frog. When he was asked by it, "What can I do for you?", [she replied], "When the solitary elephant..."

“Having become blind, he searches for water; at that time, standing on the mountain peak, you should make a sound, and as he climbs up that mountain peak, you should descend into the abyss and make a sound. This much I expect from you,” she said.
He also accepted her words, saying, “Very well.”
Then one day, a crow pierced both the eyes of the elephant with its beak, and blue flies settled upon it like a swarm of gadflies.
Being devoured by worms, overcome by pain, and overwhelmed by thirst, he wandered about searching for water.
At that time, a frog standing on the mountain peak let out a cry. The elephant thought, "There must be water here."
He climbed to the summit of the mountain. Then the frog descended, stood on the precipice, and made a sound.
Thinking, "There must be water here," the elephant went toward the precipice, slipped, fell at the foot of the mountain, and met his death.
Knowing that he was dead, the little lizard thought, "I have seen the back of my enemy."
Joyful and delighted, they walked along his back and then departed according to their respective karma.

The Teacher said: "Monks, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone; for even this elephant, though endowed with such great strength, was brought to the end of its life by these four beings acting together.
"Behold the crow, the lizard, the frog, and the blue fly!"
"These have struck down the Naga; behold the enemy of the enemy!
Therefore, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone, even toward one who is disliked.
Having spoken this verse of Perfect Enlightenment, he identified the Jātaka.
In this context, *passa* is an unrestricted form of address; however, because it is spoken with reference to the monks, it means "look, O monks.
*Ete* means "these," referring to these four who have come together. *Aghātensuṃ* means "they struck him down.
*Passa verassa verinaṃ* means "look at the course of enmity for those who harbor enmity"—this is the meaning.
At that time, Devadatta was the solitary elephant, while I myself was the leader of the herd.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Laṭukikā-jātaka.
[358] 8. The Commentary on the Cūḷadhammapāla-jātaka.
"I alone am defiled, I am a murderer"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana grove concerning Devadatta’s attempt to bring about his own death.
In other previous births, Devadatta had not been able to do even as much as that to the Bodhisatta;
however, in this Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, when the Bodhisatta was seven months old, [Devadatta] [severed] his hands, feet, and head.
Having had [the flesh] cut off, he had a place called Asimālaka constructed. In the Daddara Jātaka, having seized him by the neck and killed him, he cooked the meat over a hearth and ate it.

In the Khantivādī Jātaka, after having him beaten with two thousand strokes of whips, having had his hands, feet, ears, and nose cut off, and having had him dragged along by his matted locks and laid down on his back, [he struck him] upon the chest...
Having struck him with his foot, he departed. On that very day, the Bodhisatta met his end. It was the same in the Cūḷanandiya Jātaka and the Mahākapi Jātaka;
he had indeed been seeking to kill him for a long time, and even during the Buddha’s lifetime, he continued to seek him out.
Then one day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth: “Friends, ...”
“Devadatta employs every means solely for the purpose of killing the Buddhas;
thinking, ‘I shall cause the Perfectly Enlightened One to be killed,’ he dispatched archers, hurled a stone, and let loose the elephant Nāḷāgiri.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, with what discussion are you sitting together here now? and they replied, “With this very one,” he said, “No.”
“Monks, it was not only now; even in the past he sought to kill me. But now he is unable to do even so much as that.
In the past, when I was Prince Cūḷa-Dhammapāla, though my son was still alive, he had me executed and had a sword-pavilion constructed. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when King Mahāpatāpa was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen, Candādevī;

they gave him the name Dhammapāla. When he was seven months old, his mother bathed him with scented water, adorned him, and sat down while playing with him. The king came to the place where she was staying.
While playing with her son, she was so overwhelmed by maternal affection that she did not rise even upon seeing the king.
He thought: "Right now she shows such pride because of her son; she does not respect me at all.
But when her son grows up, she will no longer perceive me as a 'human being. I shall have her executed right now."
So, having turned back and sat upon his royal throne, he summoned the executioner, saying, "Come according to your own custom.
Dressed in saffron-colored robes, wearing a red garland, and placing an axe upon his shoulder, the executioner arrived carrying a pillow-block and a staff for supporting his hands and feet;
he paid homage to the king and stood before him, asking, "What shall I do, Your Majesty? Then [the king] went with the queen to the inner chamber.
“Bring Dhammapāla! When the queen, having become angry with the king, realized he was turning back, she laid the Bodhisatta upon her breast and sat weeping.
The executioner went there, struck him on the back with his hand, snatched the boy from her arms, and taking him, returned to the presence of the king and asked, “What shall I do, Your Majesty?”
The king had a wooden plank brought and placed before him, saying, "Lay him down here. He did so.
Queen Candā followed behind her son, lamenting. Again the executioner asked, "What shall I do, Your Majesty?
[The king replied,] "Cut off the hands of Dhammapāla. Queen Candā cried out, "Great King, my son is only seven months old!"
Proclaiming this meaning—“The boy knows nothing; he is not at fault. But if there were any fault, it would be mine.
Therefore, have my hand cut off!”—she spoke the first verse:
“I alone am the one defiled, the destroyer of the fetus, of the king of great majesty.”
“Let him release this Dhammapāla; O King, cut off my hand.
In that context, *dūsiyā* means a corrupter (*dūsikā*); the meaning is: one who, upon seeing you, fails to rise and thus commits an offense.

There is also the reading *dūsikā*, which has the same meaning. *Bhūnahatā* means one whose prosperity (*bhūna*) has been destroyed; the meaning is: one whose growth has been ruined. The word *rañño* (of the king) follows from the phrase “*dūsiyā*.”
It should be construed with the word "pada. The meaning here is: "I am the one who committed the offense against King Mahāpatāpa, not this prince;
therefore, let him release this innocent boy Dhammapāla. Even if you wish to have hands cut off, O King, then cut off the hands of me, the perpetrator of the crime."
The king looked at the executioner. "What shall I do, Your Majesty? he asked. "Without making a fuss, cut off his hands," [the king replied].
At that moment, the executioner took up a sharp axe and cut off the prince's two hands as if they were young bamboo shoots.
As his two hands were being severed, he neither wept nor lamented; rather, he maintained patience.
Having preceded his actions with loving-kindness (*mettā*), he consented.
But Queen Candā, taking the severed hand-stump and placing it on her lap, wandered about lamenting, stained with blood.
When the executioner asked again, "What shall I do, Your Majesty?", she replied, "Cut off both feet as well. Hearing this, Queen Candā spoke the second verse:
“I alone am the one defiled and ruined by the king of great majesty;
let him release this protector of Dhamma, O King, and cut off my own feet.
The intended meaning here is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
The king again ordered the executioner. He cut off both of their feet.
Queen Candā, grasping even the tips of their feet and placing them on her lap, covered in blood and lamenting, cried out:
"My lord Mahāpatāpa, children whose hands and feet have been severed must be nourished by their mother; I shall work for wages and support my little son—give him back to me!"
The executioner asked, "What, Your Majesty? Has the royal command been carried out? Is my task finished? "It is not yet finished," [the King replied].
"Then what shall I do, Your Majesty? "Cut off his head. Upon hearing this, Queen Candā spoke the third verse:
"I alone am the one defiled, the destroyer of the embryo of the King of Great Splendor."
"Let him release this Dhammapāla; O King, cut off my own head!
Having said this, he presented his own head.
Again the executioner asked, "What shall I do, Your Majesty? "Cut off his head," [the king replied]. He then cut off his head.
“Is the king’s command carried out, Your Majesty? he asked. “It is not yet finished,” [the king] replied. “Then what shall I do, Your Majesty?
“Receive it with the tip of your sword and fashion what is called a ‘sword-hedge’ (asimālaka),” [the king said].
He threw the corpse into the air, caught it with the tip of his sword, fashioned what was called a ‘sword-hedge,’ and scattered it upon the great floor. Queen Candā [beheld] the Bodhisatta...
Placing him on her lap upon the great floor, weeping and lamenting, she spoke these verses:
"Surely this king has no friends or ministers who are well-wishers, Who do not say to the king: 'Do not kill your own biological son!'"
“Surely this king has no kinsmen or friends who are well-disposed toward him, since they do not say to the king:
‘Do not have your own son, your offspring, put to death’?
In this context, “surely there are friends and ministers who are well-disposed” means that surely there must be those who are his firm friends in all matters.
There are no ministers who live together with him, nor any dear friends because of their tender-heartedness.
As for those who do not speak—meaning those who have recently arrived and do not say, "Do not kill your own dear son," and thus restrain this king—I think there are none at all.
In the second verse, *ñātī* means kinsmen.
Having spoken these two verses, Queen Candā, holding the flesh of her heart with both hands, spoke this third verse:
“The arms of Dhammapāla, who is anointed with the essence of sandalwood, are being cut off;
O King, my life-breaths are being choked by him, the heir to the earth.”

Therein, he speaks thus, lamenting: "O heir, for the sake of the earth belonging to your father—the earth extending to its four boundaries—your hands, smeared with the essence of red sandalwood, are being cut off;
your feet are being cut off; and your head is being cut off. You have even been made a 'sword-garland' (asimālaka);
having severed your own lineage, you have now departed. Thus he says: "My life-breaths, O King, are being choked."
"Your Majesty, my life too is failing me, unable to bear this grief.
As she was thus lamenting, her heart burst like a bamboo stalk in the Veḷuvana grove while it was being scorched by fire;
there and then she met her end. The king, unable to remain on his couch, fell upon the great floor, [crashing] against the surface of the tiles.
It split in two, and he fell from there onto the ground.
Then even the solid earth, though it was two hundred and forty-four thousand *yojanas* thick, being unable to bear his weight, split open and gave way.
A flame from the Avīci hell rose up, as if wrapping him in a family heirloom blanket, seized him, and hurled him into Avīci. [Regarding] Canda:
The ministers of the Bodhisatta performed the funeral rites for his body.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Devadatta was the king; Candādevī was Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī; and Prince Dhammapāla was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narration, the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka.
[359] 9. The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka:
"Vikkama re haripādā. This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a daughter of a noble family in Sāvatthī.
It is said that she was the daughter of a family who were supporters of the two Chief Disciples in Sāvatthī.
She was endowed with faith and confidence, devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; she was perfected in conduct, wise, and delighted in the merit of giving and other virtues.
Her family, however, prevented her from marrying another of similar status within Sāvatthī who belonged to a family of wrong views.
Then her parents said, "Our daughter is faithful and confident; she cherishes the Three Jewels and delights in the merit of giving and other virtues, whereas you are holders of wrong views."

They said, "If you do not allow her to give alms according to her own wish, or to listen to the Dhamma, or to go to the monastery, or to observe the precepts, or to perform the Uposatha rites, we will not give her to you; rather, take a girl from a family of wrong view who is your own equal.
Being thus rejected by them, they said, "Your daughter [is coming] to our house..."
"Go and do all this according to your purpose; we shall not stop you—give him to us," they said.
When they were told, "In that case, take him," they took an auspicious day under a favorable constellation and led him to their own home.
She became one perfected in conduct and devoted to her husband, performing all the duties toward her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband.
One day she said to her husband, “Noble son, I wish to give alms to our family preceptors, the elders.
“Very well, dear lady; give alms according to your inclination.
She invited the elders, provided them with great honor, fed them excellent food, and sitting to one side, she said, “Venerable sirs, this family holds wrong views...”

"Lacking faith, he does not know the virtues of the Three Jewels; it would be well, noble sir, if this family were to come to know the virtues of the Three Jewels, so that you might receive alms right here for as long as that happens," she said.
The elders consented and began to eat there regularly. Again, she said to her husband: "Noble sir, the elders come here regularly; what is the reason for this?"
"Do you not see him? "Very well, I shall look," he replied. On the following day, at the conclusion of the elders' meal, she informed him.
He approached them, exchanged greetings with the elders, and sat down to one side.
Then the General of the Dhamma delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to him. As for his [reaction] to the elder's discourse and to their deportment...
Having gained confidence, from that time forward he prepared seats for the elders, strained drinking water for them, and listened to their Dhamma discourses between meals;
subsequently, his wrong view was destroyed.
Then one day, while the elder was preaching the Dhamma to both of them, he proclaimed the Truths; at the conclusion of the Truths—
Both husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
From that time forth, beginning with his parents and including even the slaves and laborers, everyone abandoned wrong view and became devoted solely to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
Then one day, the young woman said to her husband: "Noble son, what use have I for the household life? I desire—"

"Let us go forth. She said, "Very well, venerable sir, I too shall go forth. With a great retinue, he led her to the nunnery, ordained her, and then approached the Teacher himself to request ordination.
The Teacher ordained him as well. Both of them, having developed insight, attained arahantship before long.
Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall, saying, "Friends, a certain young bhikkhunī was born with the requisites for both herself and her husband;
having herself gone forth, she has even led him to attain Arahantship.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, what discussion are you currently seated around?"
