Having asked, "Is it indeed by her? and being told that it was, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that she has released her husband from the snare of passion;
in the past, she also released an ancient wise man from the snare of death. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a deer and, having reached maturity...
He was handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold;
he possessed a golden complexion, hands and feet as if finished with lac-dye, horns like strings of silver, eyes resembling precious gems, and a face like a ball of red wool.
His wife was also a young doe, beautiful and lovely to behold. They lived together in harmony.
They lived there, and eighty thousand variegated deer attended upon the Bodhisatta. At that time, hunters set snares along the deer trails.
Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was walking at the head of the herd, his foot became caught in a snare.
Thinking, "I will cut it," he pulled; the hide tore. As he pulled again, the flesh tore. Again—
His sinews were severed, and the noose remained fastened to his bone.
Unable to break the noose and terrified by the fear of death, he let out a loud cry. Hearing it, the herd of deer fled in fear.
His wife, however, having fled and looking among the deer, not seeing him, thought: "This danger must have arisen for my beloved husband."
Going to him with speed, weeping with a tearful face, she said the first verse, encouraging his resolve:
"Step forward, O you with lion-like feet! Step forward, O great deer! What, will you not be able to break this snare? Exerting your strength, cut it!"
"Cut the snare of the hunter; I do not delight in being alone in the forest.
In this context, *vikkama* means "exertion," with the sense of "drawing [the bow]. *Re* is a particle used for addressing. *Haripādā* means "one with golden feet.
Although his entire body was also golden in color, she spoke thus out of reverence. *Nāhaṃ ekā* means "I am not alone [with you]."
"Without [you], I shall not find delight in the forest alone; rather, failing to obtain grass and water, I shall wither away and die," she said, thus showing her intent.
Having heard that, the deer spoke the second verse:
"I am struggling, I cannot endure it; I am tossing the ground about with great force."
“The strong snare of Vārattaka is gnawing at my foot.
In this context, “I am struggling,” Bhaddā, means that I am exerting effort. “I cannot reach the end” means that I am not able to cut the snare.
“I am striking the ground” means that I even strike the earth with my foot, thinking, “Perhaps it might break.”
“Vegasā” means with speed. “Parikantati” means he cuts all around, cutting the hide and so forth.
Then the doe said to the Great Being: “Do not fear, my lord; by my own strength I shall entreat the hunter and bring back your life.
If I am unable to do so through entreaty, I shall give even my own life to bring back yours. Thus she spoke to the Great Being.
Having comforted the Bodhisatta, who was smeared with blood, she took hold of him and stood there.
The hunter, too, taking up his sword and spear, approached like the fire at the end of an eon. Seeing him, she comforted the deer, saying, "Husband, the hunter is coming;
I shall exert my own strength, so do not be afraid," and then went to meet the hunter face-to-face.
Having stepped back and stood to one side, she paid homage to him and, after describing the virtues of the Bodhisatta— saying, "My husband, my lord, is golden-hued,
endowed with virtue and good conduct, and is the king of eighty thousand deer"— she spoke the third verse while the king of deer remained standing,
requesting her own execution:
“Spread out the leaves, hunter, and draw forth your sword;
having first struck me, kill the great deer afterwards.
In this context, “spread out the leaves” means spread out the palāsa leaves for the purpose of placing the meat upon them. “Draw forth your sword” means take the sword out from its sheath.
Having heard this, the hunter thought, "Even when they were human beings, they did not sacrifice their own lives for the sake of their husband;
yet this animal now sacrifices her life and speaks in a sweet human voice.
Today, I shall grant life both to her and to her husband. With a mind full of faith, he spoke the fourth verse:
“I have neither heard nor seen, among human women speaking, such a female deer as you;
may you, Bhaddā, be happy, and so too this great deer.
Therein, “heard or seen” means: previously to this, nothing of this kind has been seen or heard by me.
"Speaking human speech, O deer"—for previously I had neither seen nor heard of a deer speaking human words.
However, for those whose text reads, "Neither have I heard nor seen a deer speaking human speech," the meaning is understood exactly according to that reading.
"Bhaddā" means one who is auspicious, wise, and skillful in means. Having thus addressed her, [he spoke].
Then, having comforted him by saying, "Both you and this great deer— may both of you be happy and free from suffering," the hunter went before the Bodhisatta,
cut the leather snare with his knife, and slowly extracted the loop caught in his foot;
he then untied the sinew from the sinew, the flesh from the flesh, and the skin from the skin, [and released] his foot.

He rubbed it with his hand. At that very moment, through the power of the Great Being’s fulfillment of the perfections, the power of the hunter’s heart of loving-kindness, and the power of the doe’s virtuous quality of loving-kindness, the sinews, flesh, and skin were joined together by their respective counterparts.
The Bodhisatta, however, remained happy and free from suffering.
Seeing the Bodhisatta happy, the doe was filled with joy and, expressing her appreciation to the hunter,
spoke this fifth verse: “O hunter, may you rejoice together with all your kinsmen,
just as I rejoice today, having seen the great deer set free.”
Therein, he addresses him as "hunter" by way of the name acquired through the performance of cruel deeds.
The Bodhisatta thought, "This hunter has become my refuge; it is fitting that I too should become his refuge.
Thus, giving him a cluster of jewels seen on his hunting ground, he said, "Friend, from now on, [abstain from] killing living beings and so forth."
"Do not do this; instead, establish a household, support your children, and perform meritorious deeds such as generosity and virtue.
Having given him this advice, he entered the forest.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the hunter was Channa, the doe was the young bhikkhunī, and the king of deer was none other than myself."
The ninth is the commentary on the Suvaṇṇamiga-jātaka.
[360] 10. The commentary on the Suyonandī-jātaka:
"The fragrance wafts from Timirā... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was despondent.
The Teacher related it. For after the Teacher had asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are weary? and having been told, "It is true," he asked, "What did you see?
When he replied, "A woman adorned with ornaments," the Teacher said, "Monk, this woman is impossible to guard;
even the ancient wise men, though they guarded her while staying in the abode of the Supaṇṇas, were unable to guard her."
Having spoken thus, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Tambarāja reigned. He had a chief queen named Suyonandī, who possessed supreme beauty.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a supaṇṇa; at that period, there were the island of the Nāgas and the island of the Sedus."
...was his name. The Bodhisatta lived in that island in the abode of the Supaṇṇas.

Having gone to Bārāṇasī, he played at dice with the King of Tambapaṇṇi in the guise of a young brahmin student. Seeing the perfection of his physical form, the female attendants reported it to Suyonandi, saying, "A young brahmin student such as this plays at dice with our king. Having heard this, she—
Desiring to see him, one day she adorned herself, went to the gambling hall, and while standing among her attendants, she gazed at him.
He too gazed at the queen. Both became bound to one another with mutual affection.
Through his own supernatural power, the king of the supaṇṇas raised a wind over the city; out of fear that their houses would collapse, the people [fled] from the royal palace.
They departed. By his own supernatural power, he created darkness, took the queen, and having come through the air, entered his own palace on Nāgadīpa;
those who knew the place where Suyonandi had gone were no more.
Delighting in her company, he went and played at dice with the king.
The king, however, had a Gandhabba named Sagga. Not knowing where the queen had gone, he addressed that Gandhabba and dispatched him, saying:
"Go, dear Gandhabba; having traversed every path by land and water, find the place where the queen has gone.
Taking his travel expenses, he began searching from the gateway village and eventually reached Kurukaccha.
He arrived there. At that time, merchants from Kurukaccha were traveling by ship to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. He approached them and said, "I am a musician;
having paid my fee for the ship, I will provide music for you. Please take me along as well.
They agreed, saying, "Very well," and having taken him aboard, they set sail. When the ship had traveled comfortably, they called out to him.
“Please perform the *gandhabba* for us,” they said.
“If I were to perform the *gandhabba*, while I am performing it, the fish would become agitated, and then your boat would break apart.
“When one performs the *gandhabba* at the level of a human being, there is no agitation of the fish; please do it. “In that case, do not be angry with me.”
Having tuned the lute, he performed music so that the melody of the song did not exceed the pitch of the strings, nor the pitch of the strings the melody of the song.
The fish, becoming enraptured by that sound, began to move about.
Then a certain sea-monster, leaping up and falling upon the ship, shattered it. Sagga, having lain down upon a plank, drifted with the wind.
As he was traveling, he arrived at Nāgadīpa, near the banyan tree belonging to the abode of the Supaṇṇas.
At that time, Queen Suyonandī had descended from her celestial palace while the Supaṇṇa king had gone to play dice;
wandering along the shore, she saw a heavenly Gandhabba, recognized him, and asked, "How have you come here? He told her everything. "In that case," [she said].

"Do not be afraid," he said, comforting her; then, taking her in his arms, he helped her up into the celestial mansion, laid her upon the couch, and when she was fully composed, he gave her divine food, bathed her with divine scented water, clothed her in divine garments, adorned her with divine fragrant flowers, and once again settled her upon the divine bed.
Thus she remained under his care for the duration of the day.
Having concealed herself at the time of the Supaṇṇa king’s arrival, she departed; when he had gone, she took her pleasure with him through the power of defilement.
Then, after the lapse of a month or half a month, merchants dwelling in Bārāṇasī arrived at the foot of a banyan tree on that island for the purpose of gathering firewood.
She boarded the ship with them, went to Bārāṇasī, and upon seeing the king, [she approached] him.
At the time for playing with the ball, having taken up his lute and performing music for the king, he spoke the first verse:
“The scent of the *timira* flowers wafts abroad, and the sea resounds with its roar;
far from here the *su-yonandi* bird cries out, yet copper-colored desires torment me.”

In that context, *timirānaṃ* means "of the *timira*-tree flowers. It is said that there are *timira* trees surrounding that banyan tree (*nigrodha*), and it is with reference to them that he speaks thus.
*Kusamuddo* means the "small sea. *Ghosavā* means "loud-sounding.
He says this with reference to the sea near that very banyan tree. *Ita* means "from this city. *Tamba* refers to the king.
She speaks. Or else, "tambakāmā" means those who desire the copper-colored [one]; thus she explains: "They pierce my heart.
Having heard that, the Supaṇṇa spoke the second verse:
"How did you cross the ocean? How did you see Sedima?"
"How was there a meeting in heaven between her and you?
Therein, "Seduma" refers to the island of Seduma.
Then Sagga recited three verses:
“The ship of the merchants from Kurukaccha, who were seeking wealth, was struck by sea-monsters; I escaped by means of a plank.
That ship, always fragrant with sandalwood, was smooth and soft to me.”
“Bhaddā rescued me with her limb, just as a mother rescues her own biological son.
‘With food and drink, with clothing and bedding,
and even with herself— O dull-eyed one, understand this thus,’ so she said, O Tamba.”

In that context, "she [comforted] me with gentle and soft [words]" means that having seen me who had crossed to the shore by means of a plank and was wandering on the seashore, she reassured me with gentle and soft speech, saying, "Do not fear.

"With her body" refers here to the pair of her arms, which are spoken of as "the body. "Bhaddā" means beautiful, lovely, and pleasing. "She [satisfied] me with food" means she [satisfied] me with this...

The meaning is that she satisfied [him] with food and so forth. "And by herself as well" indicates that it was not only with food and such, but that she also satisfied him with her own person, delighting me.
"Mandakkhī" means one of gentle appearance; it is said to mean one whose habit is to look with a soft expression.
There is also the reading "mattakkhī," which means one endowed with eyes that are as if intoxicated. Thus, "tambā."
"Know this, O King of Snakes.
Even as the Gandhabba was speaking, the Supaṇṇa became remorseful, thinking, "Though I dwell in the Supaṇṇa abode, I was unable to protect her;
what use have I for that unchaste woman? He brought her back, returned her to the king, and departed.
"From that time on, he did not return again.
Having delivered this Dharma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the king of the *supaṇṇas* was [the Buddha].
"But it was indeed I who was he.
This concludes the tenth commentary, the Suyonandī Jātaka.
The first section, the Maṇikuṇḍala Vagga, is finished.
2. The Chapter on the Ascent of Praise [361] 1. The Commentary on the Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka:
Regarding "By the Ascent of Praise," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the two chief disciples. For once, when...
At that time, both great elders, having requested permission from the Teacher, saying, "During this rainy season we shall cultivate ourselves in an empty dwelling," left the community behind;
taking their own bowls and robes, they departed from Jetavana and dwelt in the forest near a certain frontier village.
A certain man who lived on discarded food also attended upon the elders.
He lived there in seclusion. Observing the harmonious dwelling of the elders, he thought, "These men live together in great harmony;
is it possible to cause a rift between them? Having reflected thus, he approached the Elder Sāriputta and asked, "Venerable sir, do you have some grievance against the noble Elder Mahāmoggallāna?"

He asked, "What was it, friend? [The other replied: "Venerable sir, when I arrived, he spoke only of your faults, saying, 'What does this one called Sāriputta stand against me in terms of birth, lineage, family status, or in terms of learning, mastery of the scriptures, penetration, and supernormal powers?
The Elder smiled and said, "Go now, friend."
So on another day, he approached the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and spoke to him in the same manner.
He too smiled and said, "Go, friend," and then approached the Elder Sāriputta, asking, "Friend, this Vighāsāda has said something to you? "Yes, friend; he said it to me as well."
He preached [the Dhamma], saying, "It is fitting to remove this. When it was said, "Very well, friend, remove it," the Elder struck it with his finger, saying, "Do not dwell here," and removed it.
Both of them, having lived in harmony, went into the presence of the Teacher;
having paid homage, they sat down. The Teacher, having exchanged greetings, asked, "Have you spent the rains retreat in comfort?"
Having asked them, when they replied, "Venerable sir, a certain scavenger-eater, desiring to cause a schism among us,
fled because he was unable to do so," [the Buddha] said, "Sāriputta, it is not only now that he fled, being unable to cause a schism while intending 'I shall divide them';
and at their request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in the forest.
At that time, a lion and a tiger lived in a mountain cave in the forest.
A certain jackal, attending upon them, ate the remains of their meals until he became large-bodied. One day, he thought: "I have [eaten] the flesh of the lion and the tiger..."
“I have never eaten this before; it is right for me to cause a rift between these two people.

Then, having incited a quarrel between them, I shall eat the flesh of those who have died. He approached the lion and asked, “Master, do you have some enmity with the tiger? “Why so, good man? [The lion replied,] “Venerable sir, when I arrived, the tiger said, ‘The lion—’”

"He does not equal even a sixteenth part of me in terms of the color of his body, or his height and girth, or his birth, strength, and prowess"—thus he spoke only of your faults. Then the lion said to him, "Go;
he will not speak in such a manner. The tiger also approached [the elephant] and spoke using that very same method. Having heard this, the tiger too—
Having approached Sīha, he asked, "Friend, you say this and that," and spoke the first verse:
"By virtue of your complexion, stature, lineage, strength, and prowess, Subāhu is not superior to me;
thus you speak, 'O one with beautiful teeth'."
In that context, "and by the power of his departure" means both by the power of his body and by the power of his energy.

"Subāhu, there is no one superior to me"—this refers to the tiger named Subāhu; [the king says: "Is it true, O King of Beasts, you who are endowed with beautiful fangs, that you speak thus: 'By these reasons, this one called Subāhu is neither my equal nor my superior'?
"Yes, indeed," he replies. "O Sudāṭha (Beautiful-Fanged) King of Beasts, do you truly say this? Thus he speaks.
Having heard that, Sudāṭha spoke the remaining four verses:
“Regarding complexion, stature, birth, and prowess in battle,
Sudāṭha is not superior to me— thus you speak, Subāhu.”
“If you, Subāhu, thus revile me while I am living in this way,
I shall no longer take pleasure in living together with you.
One who would believe the words of others exactly as they are [spoken]...”
"One quickly breaks with a friend and engenders much enmity.
He is not a friend who is always vigilant, who suspects a rift and looks only for a flaw;
but he in whom one rests as if upon one's own breast—he indeed is a friend who cannot be divided by others."

In this context, *sammā* means "truly. *Dubbhasi* means: "If you take the word of a jackal and thus speak ill of me—who have lived in harmonious cohabitation with you—desiring to kill me, then from this day forward, I shall no longer delight in living together with you.
*Yathātathaṃ* means according to reality (*tathato*), as it truly is (*yathātathaṃ*), as it is in fact (*yathātacchaṃ*), without deception.
The word spoken by a noble one is to be trusted. Thus, the meaning is: one should trust the words of whoever those others may be.
"One who is always heedful" means that he who, being constantly heedful, does not place undue confidence in a friend, is not truly called a friend.
"Apprehensive of division" means [thinking], "It will break today," or "It will break tomorrow. Thus...
"He suspects only the breaking of friendship. "Observing only a flaw" means seeing only a defect or an opening.
"Like a son on his breast" refers to that friend upon whom one rests without fear or anxiety, as a son does upon his mother's heart.

Thus, when the lion had described the qualities of friendship with these four verses, the tiger, thinking "I have committed an offense," asked the lion for forgiveness. They lived together right there in harmony, while the jackal fled and went elsewhere.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the jackal was Vighāsāda, the lion was Sāriputta, and the tiger was Moggallāna;
as for the tree deity who lived in that forest and witnessed these events firsthand, she was none other than myself."
The First Exposition of the Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka.
[362] 2. The Exposition of the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka.
"Virtue is better"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain Brahmin who tested virtue.
He preached it. It seems that the king regarded him as superior to the other brahmins, thinking, "This man is endowed with virtue.
He thought to himself: "Does the king regard me as superior to others because I am 'endowed with virtue,' or because I am 'possessed of a retentive memory for what has been heard'?
I shall first investigate whether my greatness lies in virtue or in learning. Thus he...
One day he took a kahāpaṇa from the money-changer’s counter. Because of his high status, the money-changer said nothing the first time;
he said nothing the second time either. But on the third occasion, having had him seized as a "plunderer," he presented him to the king.
When the king asked, "What has this man done? he replied, "He plunders my household. "Is it true, brahmin? [the king asked.]
“Great King, I am not plundering your household; rather, I was troubled by the thought, ‘Is virtue greater, or is learning?
Thus, while investigating which of these two is greater, I took the coin three times.
He has had me bound and brought before you. Now, as for me, virtue is greater than learning.”
"I am well-known; I have no need for the household life; I shall go forth," he said.

Having thus obtained permission to go forth, and without even looking back at the door of his house, he went to Jetavana and requested ordination from the Teacher. The Teacher granted him both the going-forth and full ordination.
Not long after his ordination, having practiced insight meditation, he was established in the highest fruit.
The bhikkhus initiated a discussion in the Dhamma hall, saying, "Friends, the brahmin so-and-so, having tested his own virtue, went forth and, through insight, attained arahantship.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, about what talk are you gathered here now? When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now..."
"Indeed, in the past, the wise ones also tested their virtue, went forth into homelessness, and established their own footing," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā; returning to Bārāṇasī, he had an audience with the king.
The king gave him the position of court chaplain. He observed the five precepts. The king, regarding him as "virtuous," looked upon him with respect.
He thought, "Does the king look upon me with respect because I am 'virtuous,' or because I am 'endowed with the retention of what I have heard'?
Everything else was exactly as in the present story; however, in this case, that brahmin—
"Now I have learned from my own experience the greatness of virtue," he said, and spoke these five verses:
"Virtue is better, learning is better—such was my doubt.
Virtue alone is better than learning—of this I have no doubt."
“Birth and complexion are in vain; indeed, virtue alone is supreme.
For one who is not endowed with virtue, there is no purpose served by learning.
A kṣatriya who stands on unrighteousness, and a vaiśya who relies on unrighteousness...”
Having abandoned both worlds, they are reborn in an evil destination.
But kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas—
having practiced the Dhamma here— they become equal to those in the world of the thirty-three gods.
“Neither the Vedas, nor birth, nor kinsmen lead to the world beyond;
but one’s own perfectly pure virtue leads both to the world beyond and to happiness here.
In this context, the phrase “virtue alone is better than learning” means that virtue is superior by a hundredfold and a thousandfold compared to the mastery of what has been heard.
Having spoken thus, he established a table of contents—stating that "this virtue is of one kind by way of restraint; of two kinds by way of conduct and non-conduct;

of three kinds by way of bodily, verbal, and mental; and of four kinds by way of the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and dependence on the [proper] requisites"—and then spoke in detail on the praise of virtue.

“Mogha” means vain, fruitless, and empty. “Jāti” refers to birth in such families as those of the Khattiyas. “Vaṇṇa” refers to the physical complexion of the body, that is, the state of being handsome.
Since neither the perfection of birth nor the perfection of complexion can grant the happiness of heaven to one who is devoid of virtue, he therefore said that both of these are “vain.
He says, “Virtue alone indeed,” based on oral tradition, and not [on direct knowledge].

He knows for himself. "To one who has not approached" means to one who has not drawn near. "There is no purpose found in what is heard" means that for one devoid of virtue, there is no growth whatsoever—either in this world or in the next world—by the mere extent of what has been heard or mastered through study.
The two subsequent verses are spoken for the purpose of showing the futility of birth. Therein, "those who abandon both..."
Regarding the phrase "both worlds": those who are immoral, having abandoned both the world of gods and the world of humans, are reborn in a state of misery.
"Caṇḍālas and Pukkusas" refers to the Caṇḍālas who dispose of corpses and the Pukkusas who dispose of flowers.
"They become equal in the triple heaven" means that all these, by the power of their virtue, are reborn in the world of the gods as equals without distinction; they are reckoned simply as gods.
The fifth verse was spoken for the purpose of showing the futility of all [learning] such as the Vedas. Its meaning is this:
O Great King, these Vedas and so forth, setting aside the mere granting of fame in this world, are not able to grant either fame or happiness in the next world, in the second or third existence;
however, one’s own perfectly pure virtue alone is able to grant that.
Thus, having praised the virtues of moral conduct and obtained the king’s permission for his renunciation, the Great Being entered the Himalayas on that very day.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he developed the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
without falling away from his jhānas, he became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, it was I myself who, having tested my virtue, went forth into the ascetic life.
This concludes the second commentary, the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Hirijātaka.
“Crossing over with shame”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a frontier merchant who was a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika.
Both stories have already been related in detail in the ninth chapter of the Ekakanipāta in the Jātaka collection.
Here, however, [the story begins]: “The people of the frontier merchant had all their property confiscated, and of what belonged to them...”
When it was reported to the merchant of Bārāṇasī that they had fled after becoming masterless,
the merchant of Bārāṇasī said, “Those who do not do what ought to be done for those who have come to them receive no recompense at all,” and spoke these verses:
“[The one] who crosses over shame, who feels disgust [at wrongdoing], and who says, ‘I am yours’— ”
One who does not undertake such actions should be known as one who thinks, "This is not mine.
For what one would do, that one should speak; what one would not do, that one should not speak.
The wise clearly recognize one who speaks while not acting accordingly.
“He is not a friend who is always vigilant, who suspects division and looks only for flaws;
but he is indeed a friend who is unbreakable by others, in whom one rests as if upon one’s own breast like a son.
This is a state that produces joy, brings forth praise, and is blissful.”
One who bears the human burden develops the fruit as its reward:
“Having drunk the flavor of seclusion and the flavor of tranquility, one becomes free from distress and free from evil; drink the flavor of the joy of the Dhamma.”
In this context, "transgressing shame" means having overstepped a sense of moral dread. "Feeling disgust" means feeling revulsion toward the state of friendship.
"Saying 'I am yours'" means speaking merely with the words, "I am your friend.
"Superior deeds" refers to excellent actions corresponding to the promise, "I will give; I will do. "Not undertaking them" means not performing those actions.
One should recognize such a person as "this one is not my friend.
The bases for producing gladness are giving, virtue, meditation, and friendship with wise and virtuous friends.
However, here he speaks thus specifically with reference to the kind of friendship already described. For by a wise person...
Friendship with a virtuous friend produces joy and brings forth praise.
Because it is the cause of physical and mental happiness in both this world and the next, it is called "happiness.

Therefore, a clansman who perceives both the fruit and the benefit—considering the fourfold practice consisting of generosity, virtue, meditation, and friendship, which must be carried out by men—[should apply himself].

Bearing the human yoke, he develops and increases this state known as friendship—which produces joy, brings forth praise, and is a source of happiness—and it is explained that he does not break his friendship with the wise.
"The flavor of seclusion" refers to the flavor of physical, mental, and material seclusion; it is the flavor of gladness arising in dependence upon those forms of seclusion.
"And of tranquility" means of the joy obtained through the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"He is free from fever and free from evil" means he is free from fever because of the absence of the distress of all defilements, and he is free from evil because of the absence of defilements. "The flavor of the joy of the Dhamma" means the flavor known as the joy of the Dhamma;
the sense is that he drinks the joy of liberation (*vimutti-pīti*).
Thus the Great Being, apprehensive of association with evil friends, grasped the essence of the teaching by reaching the great Nibbāna, the deathless, through the flavor of seclusion.

Having delivered this Dhamma instruction, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "The border-dweller of that time was indeed the border-dweller of the present; the merchant of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.
This is the third commentary on the Hirijātaka.
[364] 4. The Exposition of the Firefly Jātaka.
"Who indeed shines while the light exists?"—this question concerning the firefly will be revealed in detail in the Mahā-Ummagga [Jātaka].
This concludes the fourth exposition, the Exposition of the Firefly Jātaka.
[365] 5. The Commentary on the *Ahituṇḍikajātaka*.
"I am a rogue," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning an elder bhikkhu.
The story has been related in detail below in the *Sālūka-jātaka*. Here too, that elder, having ordained a village boy, ...
He reviled him and struck him. The boy fled and left the order. A second time, having ordained him, he acted in the same manner.
A second time, having left the order, when he requested ordination again, [the elder] did not even wish to look at him. The monks raised this discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, such-and-such an old man, whether with his own novice or without him..."
“He is unable to walk; the other, having seen his fault, does not wish to look at him again; he is a kind-hearted boy.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you sitting here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this novice was kind-hearted; formerly too, when he once saw a fault—”
"Having seen him, he did not even wish to look at him again," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of grain-merchants;
having reached maturity, he made his living by trading in grain. Now, a certain snake-charmer, having caught a monkey and trained it—

While playing with the snake during a festival proclaimed in Benares, the snake-charmer left the monkey in the care of a grain merchant and wandered about for seven days playing with the snake. That merchant also gave the monkey various kinds of food and edibles to eat.
On the seventh day, the snake-charmer returned from the festive amusement and [took] that monkey with a bamboo scraper...
Having struck him three times and taken him with him, he went to the park, bound him, and fell asleep.
The monkey, having loosened his bonds, climbed an mango tree and sat there eating mangoes.
When the man woke up and saw the monkey on the tree, he thought, "It would be right for me to catch this one by coaxing it," and while conversing with it, he spoke the first verse:
“I am a rogue, my dear Sumukha, defeated at dice;
pluck down the mango fruits, for we shall eat them with your effort.
In this context, *akkhaparājito* means defeated by the dice. *Harehi* means pluck down; or rather, that is the very reading [of the word].
Having heard that, the monkey recited the remaining verses:
“O friend, you praise me falsely with what is untrue.
Who has ever heard of or seen a monkey named Sumukha?”
“Even today, O snake-charmer, I still bear in mind how you,
entering the grain shop while I was intoxicated, struck me when I was hungry.
Therefore, I would rather endure that painful bed and even rule as a king.”
“I would not give when asked, for I was driven by fear:
‘A wise man ought to maintain both his kin and his friends with one who is born of noble family, who is contented in the womb [with what he has], and who is free from stinginess.’”
In this context, *alikaṃ vata* means "indeed a falsehood. *Abhūtena* means "by what that does not exist.

*Ko te* means "where by you? *Sumukho* means "one with a beautiful face. *Ahituṇḍikā*—he addresses him thus (though there is also a reading, *ahikuṇḍikā*). *Chātaṃ* means "one overcome by hunger, weak, and miserable.
*Hanāsi* means "you struck [him] three times with a bamboo splinter. *Tāhaṃ* means "I, having seen that. *Saraṃ* means "remember."
“Suffering” means a painful sleep in that shop. “Even if you were to rule the kingdom”:
even if you were to take the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, give it to me, and have me rule the kingdom—even so, being asked by you, I would not give it;
I would not give you even that single mango fruit when asked by you. For what reason? Because I am terrified by fear.
For it means that I was thus terrified by that fear.
"Satiated in the womb" means being satiated right there in the mother’s womb with the flavor of excellent food, or indeed in a bedchamber prepared and adorned;
it refers to one who is not wretched due to the hope for enjoyments. "Both friend and companion" means both the state of a friend and the state of a companion, in such a manner...
"A wise man may well reconcile himself with one who is of noble birth, contented, not mean-spirited, and free from envy;
but as for you, what friendship could possibly be restored with such a wretched snake-charmer?
Having spoken thus, the monkey suddenly entered the forest.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the snake-charmer was the elder; the monkey was the novice; and I myself was the grain merchant.
This concludes the commentary on the *Ahituṇḍika-jātaka*, the fifth.
[366] 6. The Commentary on the *Gumbiya-jātaka* (The Story of the Tree-Stump)
"Like honey in color, like honey in taste"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk who was discontented.
The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?
When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "What did you see? He replied, "An adorned woman. The Teacher said, "Monk, these five..."
"Sensual pleasures are like honey placed on the road by a certain forest-dwelling *yakkha* who has mixed it with deadly *halāhala* poison," he said;
and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of caravan leaders.
Having reached maturity, he set out from Bārāṇasī with five hundred carts, taking merchandise for the purpose of trade.
Upon reaching the gateway of Mahāvattani-Āṭavī, he assembled his caravan and said, "Friends, there are poisonous leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth on this road;
if you eat anything you have never eaten before, do not eat it without asking me. There are also non-human beings [who are poisonous]."
Having placed honeycomb and madhuka fruits in a food-bag, they set it on the path;
and having given this instruction, "Do not eat those either without asking me," he set out on the road.
Then a yakkha named Gumbiya, having spread leaves upon the road in the middle of the forest and placed honey-balls mixed with halāhala poison, himself remained near the edge of the path.

He wandered about like one gathering honey, striking at the trees. Those who did not know [the truth] ate them, thinking, "These must have been set out for the sake of merit," and thus met their death;
non-human beings (amanussa) would come and devour them.
When the Bodhisatta’s own men saw those fruits, some of a greedy nature, unable to restrain themselves, ate them, while those of a wise nature said, "Let us ask..."
"We shall eat it," they said, and having taken it, they stood there. When the Bodhisatta saw them, he made them discard what was in their hands;
those who had eaten it first died. To those who had only half-eaten it, he administered emetics and purgatives, and once they had vomited, he gave them the "four sweets.
Thus, through his power, they regained their lives. The Bodhisatta—
Having reached his desired destination in safety, he sold his merchandise and returned to his own home.
While explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses of perfect enlightenment:
"Like honey in color, sweet in taste, and fragrant like honey, there was poison; ... [the rest of the verse follows] ..."
Gumbiya, while searching for grass, dropped poison in the forest.
Those who ate that poison, thinking it was honey, found it to be bitter;
they met their death because of it.
“But those who, having reflected, avoided that poison—
they are happy amidst the afflicted, extinguished amidst the burning.
In the very same way, among humans, the poisons of sensual desires lie hidden.”
“This is a bond of material things, the snare of Death dwelling in the cave.
Even so are these sensual pleasures;
those who always avoid them, like attendants to the sick, have transcended attachment to the world.”
In this context, *gumbiya* refers to a *yakkha* who had acquired that name by wandering in that forest thicket.
*Ghāsamesāno* means "seeking his own food," thinking, "Having eaten that poison, I shall eat those who have died.
*Odahī* means he placed down that poison, which was identical in color, fragrance, and taste to honey. *Kaṭukaṃ āsi* means it was pungent. *Maraṇaṃ* means death.
"Tenupāgaman" means that by means of that poison, those beings approached death.
"Āturesu" means those who, due to the force of the poison, were on the verge of death. "Ḍayhamānesu" means being burned by the very power of the poison.
"Visaṃ kāmā samohitā" means that just as poison was placed and hidden upon that great road at Vattani, so too among human beings.
These five objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), beginning with visible forms (*rūpa*), which are placed and fixed here and there, should be understood as "poison.
As for the phrase "bait and bondage": these five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are indeed the bait cast by Māra’s fisherman into this world that has become like a fish;
and because they do not allow one to escape from existence after existence (*bhavābhava*), they are the various types of fetters, such as the leather thong and so forth.
And various kinds of bondage. "The guise of Death dwelling in the cave" means the guise of death and Māra dwelling in the cave of the body.
"In this very way these sensual pleasures" means that just as poison is placed upon a well-trodden main road, so too are these sensual pleasures placed here and there.
"Afflicted" means that wise people are afflicted because they are subject to the certainty of death and are close to death. "Attendants."
"Those who always avoid the attendants of defilement and the bondages of defilement"—this refers to those wise persons of the aforementioned type who constantly shun such sensual pleasures.
"The attachment in the world" refers to the collection of defilements, such as lust and the rest, which is given the name "attachment" (saṅga) in the sense of being an attachment within the world.
"They have transcended" should be understood to mean that they have passed beyond; or, the meaning is that they are crossing over.

The Teacher, having proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. "At that time, I myself was the caravan leader.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the Gumbiya Jātaka.
[367] 7. The Commentary on the Sāḷiya Jātaka.
"This *sāḷiya-chāpoti* story" was told by the Teacher while staying at Veḷuvana, concerning the statement: "Friends, Devadatta was not even able to cause me fear.
At that time, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he was unable to cause me fear," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a village as a member of a householder family.
In his youth, he played at the foot of a banyan tree (*nigrodha*) by the village gate together with other children who were playing in the dust.
At that time, a certain weak physician, having received nothing in the village, was departing; upon reaching that spot, he saw a snake within the fork of a branch.

Seeing him sleeping after having removed his head, he thought, "I have gained nothing in the village; I will deceive these children, have them bitten by a snake, treat them, and thus obtain something.
Having thought this, he said to the Bodhisatta, "If you see a young *sāḷiya* deer, you should take it.
"Yes, I would take it," he replied. "You can see it within the branches of the tree."

“...lying there. Not knowing its true nature as a snake, he climbed the tree, seized it by the neck, and thinking, “It is a snake,” and not letting it turn back, he gripped it firmly and flung it with force.
It went and fell upon the physician’s neck, coiled around his neck, and biting him with the sound “kara kara,” it threw him down right there and fled. People gathered around.
The Great Being, teaching the Dhamma to the assembled multitude, spoke these verses:
“This one named Sāḷiya-chāpa, who seized the black snake— by that very snake he was bitten;
slain is the instructor of evil.”
“The man who desires to kill one who has not killed him,
he lies slain even as this man is slain. The man who desires to kill one who has not killed him and who has not caused him to be killed— ”
Thus he lies struck down, just like this man who has been killed.
"Just as if a man were to throw a handful of dust against the wind,
that very dust strikes him back— so too is this man struck down."
“He who offends an unoffending man, a pure person free from blemish—the evil returns to that very fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.
Herein, *yvāyaṃ* means “this one who”; alternatively, *ayam eva* is the reading. *Sappenāyaṃ* means “he is bitten by this snake. *Pāpānusāsako* means “one who instructs in what is evil.”
*Ahantāraṃ*: one who does not kill. *Ahantāraṃ*: one who does not cause death. *Seti*: he lies upon the bed of the dead. *Aghātentaṃ*:
one who does not cause hatred (does not kill). *Suddhassa*: of one who is innocent. *Posassa*: of a living being. *Anaṅgaṇassa*:
this too is said with reference specifically to the state of being innocent. *Pacceti*: it falls back, becoming a counterpart to the action.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the weak physician was Devadatta, while the wise boy was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh discourse, the Sāḷiya Jātaka.
8. The Commentary on the Tacasāra Jātaka.
"Fallen into the hands of enemies"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, concerning the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*).
At that time, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata was wise and skilled in means," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of householders in a village.

Everything should be told according to the method of the previous Jātaka. However, in this case, when the physician had died, the people living in the village, thinking those boys were "human-demons," bound them with thorny sticks and led them to Bārāṇasī, saying, "We shall present them to the king.
On the way, the Bodhisatta gave advice to the remaining boys: "Do not be afraid."
“Even upon seeing the king, you should remain fearless and with joyful faculties; the king will speak with us first, and from that moment on, I shall know.
They accepted this, saying, “Very well,” and acted accordingly.
When the king saw that they were fearless and joyful in their faculties, he thought: “These men, whom I brought bound with small sticks, thinking them to be ‘human demons,’ are such as these...”
“Even though they have fallen into suffering, they do not fear; their faculties remain joyful. What indeed could be the reason for their lack of sorrow?
I shall ask them. Thus, asking, he spoke the first verse:
“Having fallen into the hands of enemies, and being provided with nothing but skin and bone;”
“With such serene facial expressions, why do you not grieve?
In this context, “fallen into the hands of enemies” means they have been seized by the hands of enemies who are leading them away after binding their necks with thongs.
“Furnished with a core of bark” is said because they are bound with bamboo sticks. “Why? [is asked] because, even though they have met with such a calamity...
“Why do you not grieve? he asked.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses:
“No purpose whatsoever, even a slight one, is gained by grieving or lamenting.”
Seeing him anxious and distressed, his enemies become elated.
But when a wise man, knowing how to discern what is beneficial,
does not waver in the face of calamities, his enemies become distressed upon seeing his face unchanged from before.
“By means of incantations, spells, well-spoken words, by gifts, or by traditional lineage—
whenever and wherever one might obtain a benefit, one should strive in that very way.
But when one knows that this benefit cannot be obtained either by oneself or by another,”
"One should endure it without grieving, thinking: 'What can I do now? The kamma is firm.
In this context, "welfare" (*attha*) means progress. "The adversaries are delighted": having perceived that person as grieving and suffering, his enemies become joyful in heart.
It is not fitting for a wise person to do anything that causes them satisfaction.
He illuminates. "Yato" means when. "Na vedhati" means he does not tremble due to the fear of mental agitation.
"Atthavinicchayaññū" means skilled in the discernment of various meanings.
"Jappena" means by the recitation of mantras. "Mantena" means by the learning of mantras together with the wise. "Subhāsita" means well-spoken.
By pleasant speech. By "bestowing gifts" means by the giving of bribes. By "tradition" means by family lineage. This is what is meant:
"Great King, when calamities arise, a wise man indeed should neither grieve nor be distressed;
rather, he should overcome his enemies by means of one or another of these five methods. For if he is able, [he should employ] counsel..."
Even by whispering incantations and binding their mouths, they should be defeated;
if unable to do so, they should be defeated by consulting with wise men, observing a stratagem, and speaking kindly—those who can speak kindly should defeat them by speaking kindly;
if unable to do so, they should be defeated even by giving bribes to the judges.
If he is unable to do so in that way, he should speak of his family lineage, saying, "We have come down through such-and-such a line;
you and we share one and the same ancestor," and thus, by connecting with existing kinsmen even to the extent of ten million, he must still win them over.
Regarding the phrase "in whatever way": among these five methods, by whichever means and in whichever place he may obtain his own advancement.
"In such and such a way" means that for this or that reason one should exert effort in each respective instance;
the intention is that having exerted effort, one should conquer adversaries.
"And when he should know" means: but when he should know, "This purpose cannot be attained by me or by another in any other way."
"Even with effort, it cannot be obtained. Then, the wise man, neither grieving nor wearying, should endure it, thinking:
"The deed I committed in the past is firm and solid; it cannot be averted. What can be done now?
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s discourse on Dhamma, the king cleared his record and, knowing him to be innocent, [released] the petty officials.
Having caused [the prince] to be brought back and having bestowed great honor upon the Great Being, he made him his jewel-like minister who instructs him in matters of welfare and Dhamma;
likewise, having bestowed honor upon the other boys, he granted them various positions of authority.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda; the boys were the elder and younger Theras; but as for the wise boy, he was none other than myself."
The eighth: The Commentary on the Tacasāra Jātaka.
[369] 9. The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka.
"What have I done for the gods?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak to.
He related [the story]. The background of the matter will be made clear in the Mahāmittavindaka Jātaka. However, this Mittavindaka, having been cast into the ocean, became insatiable;

proceeding forward, he saw the Ussada Niraya, the place where beings destined for hell are tormented, and perceiving it as "a city," he entered it and took pleasure in the wheel of razors. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a son of the gods.
Having offered the sacrifice, he wanders through the Ussada hell. Seeing him, the king asked and spoke this first verse:
“What have I done for the gods? What evil deed have I committed, That a wheel, having struck my head, revolves upon my crown?”
Therein, he says: "What have I done to the gods, my lord, son of the gods? What indeed have I done to the gods that the gods are striking me?
Being overcome by the intensity of his suffering, he speaks thus while failing to perceive the evil deed he himself has committed, wondering, "What evil have I wrought?
He says, "By which [evil] of mine... referring to the evil by which, having struck and beaten my head, this...
"A wheel with spokes is spinning upon my head; what indeed is that?
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
"Having passed beyond Ramaṇaka, Sadāmatta, and Dūbhaka..."
"And the Brahmattara palace—on what account have you come here?
In this context, "Ramaṇaka" refers to the crystal palace; "Sadāmatta" refers to the silver palace; "Dūbhaka" refers to the gem palace;
and "Brahmattara palace" refers to the gold palace. "On what account" means: for what purpose have you [come] to these four, beginning with Ramaṇaka?
“Leaving behind these eight, sixteen, and thirty-two divine maidens, and passing by those palaces, for what reason have you come here?
Then Mittavindaka spoke the third verse:
“There will be even more wealth than this; I think it will be found right here.”
"Thus, because of this perception, see me fallen into calamity.
Therein, "more abundant than these" means they will possess more wealth than in these four palaces.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses:
“From four he attained eight, and from eight, sixteen;
from sixteen, thirty-two—thus the wheel of insatiable desire rolled over him.
For the person overcome by craving, the wheel revolves upon his head.”
“Vast above, difficult to fill, desire spreads far and wide;
those who greedily pursue it become the bearers of the wheel.
In this regard, Mittavindaka, this so-called craving (taṇhā), when cultivated, becomes vast above and expansive.
Like the great ocean, it is difficult to fill; it is spread out and expansive, following after whatever desire one has for various objects such as forms.
Therefore, those men who greedily pursue such craving, becoming greedy again and again and grasping at it—they are called "wheel-bearers," meaning they bear this razor-edged wheel.
But even as Mittavindaka was speaking, that razor-wheel sank down; consequently, he was unable to speak further. The son of the gods returned to his own celestial abode.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Mittavindaka was the monk of harsh speech, and I myself was the son of the gods.
This concludes the ninth narrative, the Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka.
[370] 10. The Palāsajātakavaṇṇanā: "The swan spoke to the palāsa tree.
This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the subduing of the defilements.
The story will be made clear in the Paññāsa Jātaka. Here, however, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus,..."
"Defilement (kilesa) is indeed to be feared; though it may be slight, it brings about destruction like a banyan grove.
Even the wise of old feared what was to be feared," he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a golden swan.
Having reached maturity, he lived in a golden cave on Mount Cittakūṭa; having eaten wild rice that grew spontaneously in a lake in the region of the Himālayas, he would return.
On his path to and from there was a great palāsa tree. Whether going, he would rest there before proceeding; whether returning, he would also rest there before coming back. Then, while he was there—

He had formed a friendship with a deity who had been reborn in that tree. Later on, a certain female bird, having eaten a *nigrodha* fruit from a *nigrodha* tree, came and sat upon that *palāsa* tree;
she dropped her excrement among the branches, and from it a *nigrodha* thicket grew. When it was only four finger-breadths high, because its sprouts and leaves were red—
"It shines. Seeing this, the king of swans addressed the tree deity: "Friend Palāsa, there is a tree called the *nigrodha* that grows upon it;
as it grows, it destroys its host. Do not allow it to grow, for it will destroy your celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
Uproot and cast it away beforehand; indeed, it is right to be wary of what is worthy of suspicion."
Speaking with the deity of the Palāsa tree, he recited the first verse:
“The swan said to the Palāsa: ‘O friend, a banyan tree is growing;
while you sit upon its branch, it will pierce your vital organs.’”
In this context, however, the first line was spoken by the Teacher after he had attained full enlightenment. *Palāsanti* means "they will strike" the deity of the tree.
*Samma* is a term of address meaning "friend. *Aṅkasmiṃ* means "in the fork" (of the tree). *So te mammāni checchati* means "he will cut your vital organs";
the sense is that he, who has been raised in your lap, will cut off your life like an enemy. For here, the "vital organs" (*mammāni*) refers to the formative forces of life (*jīvitasaṅkhārā*).
Hearing those words, the Palāsa tree deity, not accepting his speech, spoke this second verse:
“The banyan tree shall only grow; I shall remain its foundation.
Just as my father and mother are to me, so shall it be for me.”
The meaning of this is as follows: "Friend, you do not know that he is indeed growing up.
Just as parents are the support for their children during childhood, so shall I be his support;
and just as children who have been raised become the support for their parents in later old age, so too shall he be my support in my later years."
Then the swan spoke this third verse:
“That terrifying milk-tree which you have nurtured in your lap—bid it farewell, let us go; its growth does not please me.”
In this context, "since you" (*yaṃ tvaṃ*) means because you have nurtured this milk-tree like an enemy in your lap, which is terrifying due to its quality of instilling fear.
"Therefore we shall depart after addressing you" (*āmanta kho taṃ*) means that we shall go after having addressed you and made ourselves known.
"Its growth does not please me" (*vuḍḍhi massa*) means that its growth is not pleasing to me.
Having spoken thus, the swan-king spread his wings and returned to Mount Cittakūṭa itself; from that time forth, he did not come again.
Later on, the banyan tree grew large, and a tree deity was reborn within it.
As it grew, its foliage broke off, and along with the branches, the deity’s celestial mansion fell. At that time, she—
Having reflected on the words of the king of swans, lamenting, "The king of swans spoke this having seen this future peril,
yet I did not act upon his word," she uttered the fourth verse:
"Now indeed does it terrify me, the sight of the great ocean."
"Because I did not recognize the swan, a great fear has come upon me.
In this context, "Now indeed he makes me afraid" means that after winning him over when he was young, this Nigrodha now causes me fear and terrifies me.
"The sight of the great mountain" refers to the speech of the swan-king, which is as vast as Mount Sineru.
Having heard this but not understanding it—because he had not uprooted it while it was still young—a great fear came upon him, and he lamented, "A great danger has come upon me!
Meanwhile, as the banyan tree grew, it crushed all the foliage and reduced it to mere stumps; the celestial mansion of the deity vanished entirely.
“There is no growth praised by the wise for one who, while growing, consumes his own foundation;
suspecting such an obstruction, the wise man strives for the destruction of the root.
— This is the fifth verse on full enlightenment.
In this context, "praised by the wise" (*kusalappasatthā*) means praised by those who are skillful. "Devours" (*ghasate*) means he eats; the meaning is that he destroys.
"He stretches out" (*patārayī*) means he reaches out or exerts himself. This is what is meant:
"Monks, the growth of one who, while increasing, destroys his own foundation is not praised by the wise; moreover, for him who is [internally]..."

"Or, regarding an external danger, thinking 'from this my obstruction will come,' the hero endowed with wisdom, anticipating that obstruction and destruction, exerts himself for the destruction of the root.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, five hundred bhikkhus attained Arahatship. "At that time, I myself was the golden swan."
The Tenth: The Commentary on the Palāsa Jātaka.
The Second Chapter: The Section on Rising in Splendor. 3. The Third Chapter:
The Section on the Wealthy.
[371] 1. The Commentary on the Dīghīti Kosala Jātaka.
“For you who have become thus, O King”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning those who were quarreling at Kosambī.
For when they had come to Jetavana to ask for forgiveness, the Teacher addressed them, saying: “Bhikkhus,…”
"You are my own legitimate sons, born from my mouth; it is not fitting for sons to violate the advice given by their father.

Yet you have not followed my advice. In ancient times, even those wise men who had seized the kingdom by killing their own parents did not disregard the advice given by their mothers and fathers when bandits encountered them in the forest and came within the range of their hands."
Having said, "We shall not break [the army], we shall not kill," he related a past event.
In this Jātaka, however, there are two accounts; they will be revealed in detail in the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
That Prince Dīghāvu, having seized the King of Bārāṇasī—who was lying on his lap—in the forest by the crest of his hair...
Thinking, “Now I shall cut this thief who murdered his mother and father into pieces,” he raised his sword;
but at that moment, remembering the advice given by his parents, he thought, “Even if I must give up my life, I will not violate their advice;
I shall merely frighten him. Having thus reflected, he spoke the first verse:
“O King, for you who have come under my power in such a state, is there any means by which one might release you from suffering?
In this context, “under my power” means having come into my control. “Means” (pariyāya) refers to a cause or method.
Then the king spoke the second verse:
“O dear one, since I have come under your power in such a state,
there is no means whatsoever by which anyone might release me from this suffering.”
In that context, *no* is a particle meaning "not"; the sense is: "There is no other means whatsoever by which anyone might release me from this suffering.
Thereupon, the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses:
"O King, there is no other well-conducted life, Nor any other well-spoken word, O King; ... [that could free one from suffering]."
It protects one at the time of death, just as other wealth does.
“He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me”—
for those who harbor such thoughts, enmity is never stilled.
“He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me”—in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred subsides.
For hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world; rather, it is appeased by non-hatred alone.
"And by non-anger they are pacified; this is the eternal Dhamma.

In this context, "nothing else but good conduct" (*nāññaṃ sucaritaṃ*) means there is nothing other than good conduct; or rather, the reading is *nāññā sucaritā*, meaning "I see nothing else apart from good conduct.
Here, both "good conduct" (*sucarita*) and "well-spoken words" (*subhāsita*) refer specifically to the instruction given by one's mother and father.

He spoke with intentional meaning: "In this very way" means it is indeed useless. This is what is meant: O Great King, apart from well-conducted deeds and well-spoken words consisting of advice and instruction, there is nothing else at all capable of protecting or saving one at the time of death.
That other kind of wealth is likewise entirely useless; for even if you were now to give me as much as a hundred thousand million [of that], [it would avail nothing].
Even if one were to give away wealth, one would not thereby obtain life; therefore, this should be understood: "From wealth, well-conducted conduct and well-spoken words alone are superior.

This is the summarized meaning of the remaining verses as well: O Great King, those men who harbor enmity, thinking, "This person abused me, this person struck me, this person defeated me, this person took what belongs to me," and having thus bound themselves [to that grudge]...

Those who harbor such thoughts in their hearts do not find the pacification of their enmity; however, for those who do not harbor them in their hearts and do not keep them there, their enmity is pacified.
For enmities are never appeased by enmity; rather, they are appeased only by non-enmity.
This is the ancient law—this is the primordial law that has existed since time immemorial as the very nature of things.
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, I do not bear you ill will, yet you would kill me," and placed his sword in the king's hand.
The king also made an oath, saying, "I bear no ill will toward you," and went with him to the city.
There he showed him to his ministers, saying, "Sirs, this is Prince Dīghāvu, the son of the King of Kosala."
“By this man my life was given; it is not right for me to do anything against him,” he said, and having given his own daughter [to him], he established him in the kingdom belonging to his father.
From that time forth, both of them ruled the kingdom together, living in harmony and mutual affection.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the mother and father were the royal family, but Prince Dīghāvu was none other than I myself.”
The First Exposition of the Dīghīti-kosala-jātaka [372].
2. The Exposition of the Migapotaka-jātaka:
"Having departed from home"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning an elderly man.
It is said that he ordained a certain boy. The novice, having served him with great care, later passed away due to illness.
Upon his death, the elder was overcome by grief and wandered about wailing at a loud voice.
Unable to console him, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends,..."
“Such-and-such an elder is wandering about lamenting over the death of a novice; he will become one who is excluded from the cultivation of mindfulness of death.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what conversation are you having now, seated together?
When they replied, “This very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this man has been excluded from the cultivation of mindfulness of death; previously, too, he was so.”
Having said, "Wandering about, lamenting for my mother," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta served as the king of the gods (Sakka).
At that time, a certain brahmin living in the kingdom of Kāsi entered the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and lived on wild fruits.
He lived there. One day, seeing a dead fawn in the forest, he brought it to his hermitage, gave it fodder, and raised it.
As the fawn grew, it became handsome and attained great beauty. The ascetic treated it as his own son and cared for it.
One day, after eating a great deal of grass, the fawn died from indigestion.

The ascetic wandered about lamenting, "My son is dead. Then Sakka, the king of the gods, surveying the world, saw that ascetic and, thinking, "I shall cause him to be stirred," approached and stood in the air, reciting the first verse:
"For you who have departed from the home and have become a homeless one;..."
“That which you sorrow for the deceased is not good for a recluse.
Having heard that, the ascetic spoke this second verse:
“Indeed, Sakka, through living together, whether with a human or a wild animal,”
"Love arises in the heart; it is not possible not to grieve for that.
In this context, "it is not possible" means that it is not possible not to grieve for that person, whether human or animal; "I indeed grieve," he says.
Then Sakka spoke two verses:
“Those who weep and lament weep for one who is dead and about to die;
therefore, O seer, do not weep. The virtuous say that weeping is in vain.
For by weeping, O Brahmā, the dead spirit might indeed rise up.”
"All having gathered together, we weep for one another's kinsmen.
In this context, "will die" refers to whoever is about to die now. "And they lament" means they wail. This is what is meant:
those in the world who weep for the dead and for those who will die, they both weep and lament; for them—
There is no day when tears cease. Why? Because those who have died and those who are yet to die exist at all times.
Therefore, O seer, do not weep. Why? For the peaceful ones say that weeping is in vain;
the wise, such as the Buddhas and others, declare that weeping is "vain. As for this one who is called "dead" and "departed," if he—by means of weeping—...
"If they were to rise up, then why do we sit idle? Let us all come together and weep for one another's kinsmen.
However, because they do not rise up for the sake of weeping, he establishes the futility of weeping.
While Sakka was speaking thus, the ascetic, perceiving that "weeping is useless," spoke three verses in praise of Sakka:
“While I was burning, like a fire fed with ghee,
you have sprinkled me with water as it were and extinguished every dart.
You have indeed pulled out the arrow that was lodged in my heart.”
“He who dispelled the grief for my son while I was overcome by sorrow—by hearing your words, O Vāsava, I have had the dart extracted;
I am free from grief and undisturbed. I do not grieve, nor do I weep.”

In that context, *yamāsī* means "that which was mine. *Hadayassitam* means "resting in the heart. *Apānudī* means "he removed. Having given this exhortation to the ascetic, Sakka returned to his own place.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching here, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the ascetic was the elder, the deer was the novice, and Sakka was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Migapotaka Jātaka.
[373] 3. The Commentary on the Mouse Jātaka.
"Where has she gone? To what place has she gone?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Ajātasattu.
The story of the incident has already been related in detail below in the *Thusa Jātaka*. Here too, the Teacher likewise addressed the king regarding his son.
Seeing him playing together with [the prince] and listening to the Dhamma from time to time, and knowing that "through him a danger will arise for the king," he said,
"Great King, former kings, suspecting what was to be suspected, set their own sons aside in a secluded place, saying,
'May he rule the kingdom in our time of smoke (old age). Having said this, he related a story of the past."
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher.

There, the king of Benares’s son, named Yavakumāra, having mastered all the arts in his presence and received his formal dismissal, wished to depart and took leave of him. The teacher [said to] his son:

"Depending on this, there will be an obstacle for him. Having known this by means of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*), he began to consider a simile, thinking, "I shall take this away from him.
At that time, however, he had a horse; a wound appeared on its foot, and they kept it right in the house for the purpose of protecting the wound. Not far from it, there was a well. Then a mouse—
Having gone out from the house, he nibbled at the horse's wound; the horse was unable to prevent him.
One day, being unable to endure the pain, he struck with his hoof a mouse that had come to eat [the wound], killing it and throwing it into a well.
When the horse-keepers did not see the mouse, they said, "On other days, mice would come and nibble at the wound."
"Now she is no longer seen; where indeed has she gone? they said.
The Bodhisatta, having witnessed that event firsthand, thought: "Others, being ignorant, ask, 'Where has the mouse gone?
But I alone know that she was killed by me and thrown into the well. He then used this very incident as a simile.
Having composed the first verse and bound it [into a scroll], he gave it to the prince.
While searching for another simile, the prince saw that very same horse, with its wounds healed, emerge and go to a barley field;
seeing it thrusting its mouth through the gaps in the fence, thinking, "I shall eat the barley," he took that very incident as a simile and composed the second verse.
Having composed it, he gave it to him. But having himself composed the third verse by the power of his own wisdom, and having given that to him as well, he said:
"Dear son, once you are established in the kingdom, as you go in the evening to the bathing lotus-pond, you should go reciting the first verse as far as the main staircase;
and as you enter your residential palace, [you should recite] as far as the base of the steps."
"Go reciting the second verse; then, go reciting the third verse as far as the top of the staircase," he said, and sent him off.
That prince went and, having become the viceroy, ruled the kingdom after his father’s passing, and a son was born to him. He—
At the age of sixteen, out of greed for the kingdom, he thought, "I shall kill my father," and said to his attendants, "My father is young;
I shall become old and decrepit by the time I observe the end of his life.
At such a time, what is the use of even having obtained the kingdom? They replied, "Your Majesty, it is not possible to go to the borderlands and act as a bandit..."
“Kill your father by some means or other and seize the kingdom.
He replied, “Very well,” and went inside the palace to the edge of the king’s evening bathing pond. Thinking, “I shall kill him here,” he took his sword and stood waiting.
In the evening, the king said to a female slave named Mūsikā, “Go, clean the surface of the pond and come back; we shall bathe there.”
He sent her forth. Having gone there, she saw the prince while she was cleaning the surface of the lotus pond.
Out of fear that his own deed might become manifest, the prince cut her in two and threw her into the pond. The king went to bathe.
The other people said, "Even today the mouse-maiden has not returned; where has she gone? Where has she gone? The king—
“Where has she gone? To what place has she gone? thus the people lamented.
“I alone know: the mouse was killed in the well.
Speaking this first verse, he went to the edge of the lotus pond.
In this context, "where has she gone? and "to what place has she gone? are synonyms for one another. "Thus he laments" means he thus prattles on.

Thus, this verse [is spoken by the king]: "I alone know that the common people, not knowing, are prattling on, 'Where has the mouse-servant gone?'—that she was cut in two by the prince and thrown into the lotus pond. To the king...
He explained this matter to one who was indeed unaware of it.
The prince, fearing that "my father knows of the deed I have done," fled and reported the matter to his attendants.
After seven or eight days had passed, they spoke to him again: "Your Majesty, if the king were to know, he would not remain silent."
“It might be so; however, he must have said that out of a grasp for logic—do not kill him.
Then one day, sword in hand, he stood at the foot of the stairs and, as the king approached, looked here and there for an opening to strike. The king said:
“Why do you turn back this way and that, like a donkey?”
“Having killed a mouse at the well, you wish to eat barley.
Reciting this second verse, he went along. This verse also means:
“Since you turn back like a donkey, looking here and there for a place to strike with your weapons, therefore I know that on the previous day, in the lotus pond...”
“Having killed the mouse and the slave girl, you now wish to kill and devour me, the viceroy,” he said, making this point even while the king was unaware.
Terrified that his father had seen him, the prince fled.
After another half-month had passed, thinking, “I shall strike the king with a ladle and kill him,” he took a long-handled ladle, swung it about, and stood there. The king—
“You are still small, O witless one, a mere infant just born;
having encountered this long [snake], I shall not grant you life.
Reciting this third verse, he ascended to the top step of the staircase.

In this context, "one who has reached the first stage of life" means one who has entered [life] by way of the first stage; the meaning is that he stands in the first stage. "A youth" means one who is young.
"A long [spear]" refers to a weapon consisting of a spear with a long shaft. "Having seized" means having taken hold of;
the meaning is "you stand having leaned over. This verse also [means]: "O dull-witted one, you shall not obtain the enjoyment of your own [youthful] age."
“I will not give you life now, you shameless one! Having killed you and cut you into pieces, I shall impale you on a stake!
Thus she spoke this matter, threatening the prince while the king was unaware.
Being unable to escape that day, he fell at the feet of the king, saying, “Grant me my life, Your Majesty!”
The king, having rebuked him, had him bound with fetters, cast into prison, and seated beneath a white parasol upon a decorated royal throne;

then, joyful and elated, he uttered this inspired exclamation and recited the remaining verses: “My teacher, a world-renowned brahmin, seeing this obstacle for me, spoke these three stanzas. Thus he spoke, uttering the rest of the verses in a state of great joy and satisfaction.
“Neither by the realm of the sky-dwellers, nor by the multitude of sons of Aṅga;
though longed for by his son, he was indeed released by verses.
One should study all that has been heard—whether inferior, superior, or middling.”
"One should know the purpose of everything, but one should not employ everything;
there comes a time when learning brings about what is beneficial.
In this context, "not by dwelling in the sky" (*nāntalikkhabhavanena*): "dwelling in the sky" refers to a celestial mansion (*dibbavimāna*). Today, I—
"I have not even ascended to the celestial abodes; therefore, I am not liberated from death today even by the celestial abodes.
Nor am I liberated by the love for a son resembling Aṅga. For it was said, "I am desired [to be killed] by my own son";
thus, I am today sought to be slain by my very own son. "Liberated by verses"—that is, I [was liberated] by the teacher.
He was released by means of the verses that had been given after being bound.
"Suta" (heard) refers to the *pariyatti* (the scriptures). "Adhīyetha" (one should study) means one should take up and train in it.
By the phrase "whether inferior, superior, or middling," he indicates that everything—be it low, excellent, or intermediate—must indeed be studied. And yet, one should not employ all of it.
The meaning is: one should not employ a lowly or middling mantra or craft, but should employ only the supreme.

"At whatever time there is beneficial learning" means that at whatever time—just as when the wise Mahosadha engaged in the work of a potter—any learned craft becomes beneficial, such a time indeed exists. Later on...
After the king’s passing, the prince was established in the kingdom.
