Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, I myself was the world-renowned teacher.
This is the third narrative, the Commentary on the Mouse Jātaka.
[374] 4. The Commentary on the Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka.
"All quarrel," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by a former wife.
When that bhikkhu said, "Venerable Sir, my former wife is causing me distress," the Teacher—
“Monk, this woman has not only caused you harm now; in the past as well, because of her, your head was cut off with a sword.
Having said this, when requested by the monks, he related a story of the past.
Long ago, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta served as the king of the gods (Sakka). At that time, one...
A young brahmin residing in Bārāṇasī, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and attained perfection in archery, became known as the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha (the Junior Archer).
Then his teacher, thinking, "He has mastered a craft equal to my own," gave him his daughter in marriage.
Taking her, he set out on the road with the intention of going to Bārāṇasī.
On the way, a single elephant cleared a certain spot, and no one dared to ascend that place.
The wise Cūḷadhanuggaha, while the people were still holding him back, took his wife and ascended toward the mouth of the forest.
Then, in the middle of the forest, the elephant rose up; he pierced it in the frontal globe with an arrow. The arrow, having passed right through—
He departed by way of the rear. The elephant fell right there; the skilled archer, having made that spot safe, reached another forest ahead.
There too, fifty bandits were lying in wait to ambush the road.
Even there, though being restrained by his men, he mounted [the elephant], killed the deer belonging to those bandits, and cooked the meat near the path.
He reached the place where they were standing while eating.
Then, seeing him approaching together with his wife, who was beautifully adorned and dressed, the thieves made an effort, thinking, "We shall seize him!
The chief of the thieves was skilled in the characteristics of men; having merely looked at him, he [realized], "This is a supreme man..."
Realizing this, he did not allow even one of them to rise.
The wise archer sent his wife to them, saying, "Go and say, 'Give us one meat skewer as well,' and bring back some meat.
She went and said, "Please give me one meat skewer. The chief of the bandits, thinking, "This man is priceless," had a meat skewer given to her.
The thieves, thinking, "It seems we have eaten what was cooked," gave him a spit with raw meat on it.
The archer, full of self-importance, became angry with the thieves, saying, "They are giving me raw meat on a spit!
The thieves, becoming enraged and thinking, "Is he the only man here, while we are women?", rose up. The archer [pierced] forty-nine people with forty-nine arrows.
Having pierced [the elephant], he brought it down. There was no arrow left to pierce the chief robber. It is said that there were exactly fifty arrows in his quiver;
with one he pierced the elephant, and with the remaining forty-nine he pierced the robbers.
Having struck down the chief robber, he sat upon his chest and, saying, "I shall cut off his head," took [an arrow] from his wife's hand.
He had the sword brought. At that very moment, the woman, having instilled greed in the chief thief, placed the hilt of the sword in the thief's hand and the blade in her husband's hand.
The thief, grasping the handle of the staff and drawing the sword, cut off the archer’s head.
Having killed him, he took the woman and departed, asking for her birth and clan. She replied, "In Takkasilā, from a world-renowned teacher..."
“I am his daughter,” she said. “How did you obtain him? she asked. She replied, “My father was pleased that he had trained me in a craft equal to his own, so he gave me to him;
out of affection for you, I have caused my own husband, who was given to me by my family, to be killed.
The chief thief thought, “She has indeed killed her husband, who was given to her by her family, but what about another?”

Thinking, "Having seen me, he will surely do the same; it is best to abandon her," as he was walking along, he saw a small river with a shallow bed that was suddenly filled with water at that very moment. He said, "My dear lady, there are fierce crocodiles in this river;
what shall we do? She replied, "Master, let us make a bundle of all my jewelry and belongings with my upper robe."
“Having brought me to the other shore, come back again and take me with you as we go.
He replied, “Very well,” and taking all his jewelry and goods, he descended into the river. As if crossing over, he reached the opposite shore, abandoned her, and departed.
Seeing him, she said, “Husband, why do you go as if abandoning me? Why do you act thus? Come, take me with you as you go.”
Conversing with him, she spoke this first verse:
“Having taken all your goods, O Brahmin, you have crossed to the further shore.
Return quickly and swiftly; take me across as well from here.”
In this context, "quickly" means "swiftly"; "come back quickly" means "now, ferry me across as well.
Having heard this, the thief, while still standing on the opposite shore, spoke the second verse:
"Though we have not been acquainted, you, O lady, have united me—who am long-acquainted—with one who is unstable for the sake of the stable."
“I too, lady, will assign another [task] for you; I shall go much further than this.
She [was] as already explained above—however, the robber, saying, “I shall go much further than this; you stay,” while she was still crying out,
Taking her bundle of ornaments, she fled. Then that foolish woman, having met with such a calamity through her excessive greed, became destitute;
approaching a thicket of *eḷagalā* creepers nearby, she sat down weeping.
At that moment, Sakka, the king of the gods, surveying the world, saw her—stricken by her own immoderate desire, deprived of both husband and paramour, and weeping.
Having seen her, thinking, "I will go there after subduing and putting her to shame," he took Mātali and Pañcasikha with him, went to that place, and stood on the riverbank.
He said, "Mātali, you become a fish; Pañcasikha, you become a bird;
as for me, I shall become a jackal, take a lump of meat in my mouth, and go before her."
“Once I have gone there, you must leap out from the water and fall before me;
then, having cast away the lump of meat held in my mouth, I will spring forward to seize the fish.
At that moment, Pañcasikha, you must take that lump of meat and fly up into the air, while you, Mātali, fall back into the water,” he commanded. “Very well, Lord,” replied Mātali.
The fish became [the Bodhisatta], Pañcasikha became a bird, and Sakka, having become a jackal, took a lump of meat in his mouth and went to a spot in front of her.
The fish leapt from the water and fell before the jackal.
He dropped the lump of meat he was holding in his mouth and sprang toward the fish. The fish, having leapt up, [fell] into the water.
The husband, having taken a lump of meat, flew up into the air as a bird;
the jackal, failing to obtain either, sat with a dejected face looking at a cluster of *eḷagalā* creepers.

Seeing him, she laughed a great laugh like one breaking a water-jar, thinking, "This man, struck by excessive greed, has obtained neither meat nor fish. Hearing this, the jackal spoke the third verse:
“You make your body like a thicket of eḷagalā creepers, making a sound like a female jackal;
there is no dancing or singing here, nor any well-timed rhythmic clapping.
O beautiful one with lovely hips, since it is not a time for merriment, why do you laugh?”
In this context, *kāyanti* means "what is this? *Eḷagalāgumbe* means "in the *kamboji* grove.
*Ahuhāsiyaṃ* refers to a great laugh with bared teeth; he asks, "What is this that she is doing in this grove?

*Nayīdha naccagītaṃ vā* means "there is no dancing or singing here"—that is, there is no dance for anyone who might be dancing, nor song for anyone who might be singing, even though their hands are well-composed.
It indicates that for one who speaks while being well-composed, there is no clapping of hands; it asks, "Seeing whom would you laugh?
"Anamhikāle" means at the time of weeping. "Susoṇī" means one with beautiful hips. "Kiṃ nu jagghasī" means:
for what reason do you laugh with a great laugh, not even weeping, at a time when it is appropriate to weep? "Sobhane" is an address used in praise of her.
Having heard that, she spoke this fourth verse:
“O jackal, you are a fool, dull-witted, and lacking in wisdom;
having lost both the fish and the bait, you sit brooding like a beggar.”

In this context, *jīno* means having become one who has lost his wealth. *Pesim* means a piece of meat. "You brood like a pauper" means you brood, grieve, and worry like a pauper who has lost a thousand pieces of gold.
Then the jackal spoke the fifth stanza:
"The faults of others are easy to see, But one's own are difficult to see."
“I think you alone are burning with passion for both your husband and your lover. In this context, “you alone are burning with passion” means:
“O woman of evil character and immoral conduct, as for me, I shall certainly not find my prey;
but you, ruined by your excessive desire, have fixed your heart upon a thief seen only that moment—upon both him and your lover.”
"Having lived with a husband given to you by your family, now that you have taken me [as a wife], you have become a thousand times more wretched than before;
why do you brood, weep, and lament? Having thus put her to shame and brought about this distress, the Great Being spoke these words.
Hearing his speech, she recited this verse:
“‘So it is, O king of beasts, just as you say, jackal!
Surely, having gone from here, I shall become subject to the will of another husband.

In this context, *nūna* is a particle used in the sense of certainty. ‘Surely, having gone from here and finding another husband, I shall certainly become subject to the will and obedient to that husband.’”
Then, having heard the words of that woman of improper conduct and immoral character, Sakka, the king of the gods, spoke this final verse:
“Whoever steals a clay platter shall also steal one of bronze;
you have already committed evil, and you will do so again.”
The meaning of this is as follows: "What are you saying about improper conduct? He who carries away a clay bowl carries away even a bronze bowl of various kinds, such as those made of gold or silver;
and this evil deed was indeed committed by you—it is impossible for you to deny it—and you will surely do the same again.
Having thus put her to shame and brought about her downfall, he returned to his own place.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.
At that time, the archer was the despondent monk; the woman was his former wife; and Sakka, the King of the Devas, was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka, the fourth.
[375] 5. The Commentary on the Pigeon Birth Story (Kapotajātakavaṇṇanā).
Now, regarding the words "I am indeed [so]," the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain greedy monk.
The account of that greed has already been explained in detail many times. Then the Teacher asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are greedy?"
Having asked him, and the monk having replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Buddha said, "Monk, it is not only now;
in the past as well you were greedy, and through that greed you met your end. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a pigeon.
He lived in a nest-basket in the kitchen of the merchant of Bārāṇasī. Then, a certain crow, greedy for fish and meat, formed a friendship with him and lived right there.

One day, seeing a great deal of fish and meat, he thought, "I shall eat this," and lay down in the nest-basket itself while groaning; then the pigeon said to him, "Come, friend, for the sake of food."
Even when told, "Let us go," he replied, "I am lying down because of indigestion; you go on.
When the other had departed, he thought, "My thorn-like enemy has gone; now I shall eat fish and meat as I please," and spoke the first verse:
"Now I am happy and healthy, free from thorns and having escaped, like a pigeon."
“I shall now bring satisfaction to my heart, for thus this meat-and-vegetable dish strengthens me.
In this context, *nippatito* means gone out. *Kapotā* refers to a pigeon (*pārāvata*). *Kāhāmi dāni* means “I shall now do.
*Tathā hi maṃ maṃsasākaṃ baletī* means that indeed this meat and the remaining vegetables provide me with strength.
The meaning is that it encourages me, as if saying, "Arise and eat!

That [being], having had fish and meat cooked by the cook, emerged from the kitchen, caused sweat to flow from its body, came out from the cooking pot, settled upon a sauce-bowl, and let out the sound "kiri kiri. The cook—
Arriving in haste, he seized the crow, plucked off all its feathers, and ground fresh ginger and mustard seeds together.
He then crushed garlic with fermented rice-water and smeared it over the crow’s entire body.
Having struck a pebble until it was polished and pierced it with a thread, he tied it around the crow’s neck, placed it back into its very nest-box, and departed.
A dove, having arrived and seen her, thought, "Who is this crane lying in my companion's basket?
For he is fierce and might even kill me upon his arrival," and speaking thus in jest, he uttered the second verse:
"Who is this crested crane, a thief, the granddaughter of Laṅghī?"
"Come here quickly, Balāka; my friend the crow is fierce.
This has already been explained in meaning below.
Having heard that, the crow spoke the third verse:
“Enough of your laughing upon seeing me in such a state—shorn by the son of a cook and smeared with flour paste.
In this context, *alaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of prohibition.

*Jagghitāya* means “to laugh. This is what is meant: “Now that you see me in such a condition, having fallen into such suffering, it is enough for you to laugh; do not engage in joking and play at such a time.”
Thus, while still engaged in playful jesting, he spoke this fourth verse:
“Thou art well-bathed and well-anointed, satisfied with food and drink;
and a beryl adorns thy neck—didst thou come from Kajaṅgalā?”
Regarding that, "And that beryl upon your neck": this beryl gem of yours was fastened around your neck;
he spoke thus with reference to the skull, implying, "You did not show this to us for all this time. "Kajaṅgala":
here, Bārāṇasī itself is intended by the term "Kajaṅgalā. He asks: "Having departed from here, have you perhaps gone into the city?"
Then the crow spoke the fifth verse:
“Let neither friend nor foe of yours go to Kajaṅgalā;
having plucked their feathers there, they tie them around their necks as ornaments.”
In this context, "piñchāni" means feathers. "Having plucked them there" means having plucked them in that city of Bārāṇasī. "Vaṭṭanaṃ" means a round bowl.
Having heard that, the pigeon spoke this final verse:
"You will obtain it again, my friend, for such is your character."
"For human enjoyments are not fit to be enjoyed by a bird.
Therein, "you will again incur such [a fault]" means you will again incur a transgression of this kind. "For such is your nature" means that this is your character.
Having thus exhorted him, the hawk did not remain there but spread his wings and departed elsewhere; the crow, however, met his death right there.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

at the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy bhikkhu was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). At that time, the crow was the greedy bhikkhu, and the pigeon was none other than myself.
This is the fifth narrative, the Commentary on the Pigeon Jātaka.
The Third Chapter on the Fortunate.
The summary of the Jātakas:
Maṇikuṇḍala, Sujāta, Vena, Sākha, and Oraga;
Ghaṭa, Koraṇḍi, Laṭuki, and likewise Dhammapāla the deer;
Suyonandī, Vaṇṇāroha, Sīla, Hirī, Khajjopana;
Ahi, Gumbiya, Sāḷiya, Tacasāra, and Mittavinda.
The Palāsa, the Dīghiti, the Deerling, the Mouse, the Archer, and the Pigeon:
these are the twenty-five Jātakas.
The commentary on the Pañcaka-nipāta is finished.
6. The Chapter of Sixes (Chakkanipāta) 1.
The Section on the Unobstructed (Avāriyavagga) 1.
The Exposition of the Avāriya Jātaka (Avāriyajātakavaṇṇanā)
"Do not be angry, O lord of the earth"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain ferryman.
It is said that he was foolish and ignorant; he knew neither the virtues of the Jewels beginning with the Buddha nor those of other individuals;
he was fierce, harsh, and violent. Then, a certain monk from the countryside, thinking, "I shall pay my respects to the Buddha," [set out].
Coming in the evening, he reached the landing place on the Aciravatī River and said to him, "Lay follower, I wish to go to the other shore;
give me a boat. "Venerable sir, it is not the right time now; stay at some place here. "Lay follower, where shall I stay here?
Take me with you and let us go. Becoming angry, he said, "Come along, you ascetic! I will carry you! and so he seized the Elder.
Instead of boarding the boat and traveling straight ahead, he led the boat below, stirred up a great commotion, and soaked and exhausted his bowl and robes.
Then, having reached the shore at the time of darkness, he dismissed him.
Thereupon, having gone to the monastery and not obtaining an opportunity to pay his respects to the Buddha that day, he approached the Teacher on the following day and paid homage.
Sitting to one side, the Teacher exchanged greetings with him and asked, "When did you arrive? He replied, "Yesterday, Bhante.
When the Teacher asked, "Then why have you come for an audience with the Buddha today? he related the matter to him.
Having heard this, the Teacher said, "Monk, it is not only now; in the past, too, he was fierce, harsh, and violent. But now, by him..."
"You have indeed been exhausted; formerly, this one used to exhaust the wise," he said, and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, and having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, for a long time...
Having sustained himself with various fruits in the Himalayas, he arrived at Bārāṇasī for the purpose of consuming salt and sour gruel.
Staying in the royal park, on the following day he entered the city for alms. Then, seeing him reached the royal courtyard, the king was inspired by his dignified deportment;
he brought him to the inner palace, fed him, obtained his consent, and had him reside in the royal park, [providing] daily...

He went to wait upon him. To him the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, a king must rule his kingdom righteously, avoiding the four ways of wrong conduct, being diligent, and endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.
Having spoken thus, he gave him daily exhortation:—
"Do not be angry, O Lord of the Earth; do not be angry, O Bull among Charioteers.
A king who does not retaliate against one who is angry is honored by his kingdom.
Whether in the village or in the forest, whether in the lowlands or on the high ground..."
“I instruct you in all matters; do not be angry, O bull among charioteers!”—with these two verses he spoke.
Therein, “honored by the kingdom” means that such a king as this is worthy of honor by the kingdom. “I instruct you in all matters”:
O Great King, wherever I may dwell among these villages and so forth, it is by this very instruction [that I guide you].
"I instruct him" means that I instruct him, or that I instruct even a single being anywhere among these villages and so forth.
"Do not be angry with us, O bull among charioteers"—in this very way I instruct you; for it is not fitting for a king to be angry.
Why is that? Because kings have speech as their weapon; by the mere word of those who are angry, many meet their end.
Thus, on each day the king arrived, the Bodhisatta spoke these two verses.

With a mind full of faith due to this instruction, the king offered the Great Being an excellent village that yielded a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] annually; however, the Bodhisatta declined it.
Having thus lived right there for twelve years, he thought, "I have stayed too long; let me now go on a journey through the countryside."
"Having wandered about, I shall return. Without telling the king, he addressed the park-keeper, saying, "Dear friend, I am weary;
I shall wander through the countryside and then return. You should inform the king of this," and having said this, he departed and reached a ferry on the Ganges.
There, there was a boatman named Avāriyapitā. He was a fool who did not recognize the virtues of those possessed of virtue.
He does not know his own profit or loss; having ferried across first those people who wished to cross the Ganges, he later asks for his wages.
Engaging in quarrels with those who do not give him wages, he receives much abuse and blows, while his gain is meager—such is this blind fool.
Referring to him, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke the third verse:
“There was once a ferryman on the Ganges named Avāriyapitā;
having first ferried people across, he later demanded his fee.
Because of this, quarrels arose for him, and he did not increase in wealth.”
In that context, "Avāriyapitā" means that his daughter was named Avāriyā; it is by virtue of her that he became known as Avāriyapitā.
"Because of that quarrel" means that for that reason, or rather, because of that [incident], a quarrel arose between him and the people who later requested [the girl].
The Bodhisatta approached the boatman and said, "Friend, take me to the other shore. Hearing this, the man replied, "Ascetic, what fee will you give me for the boat?
"Friend, I shall tell you of the increase of wealth, the increase of prosperity, and the increase of Dhamma.
Hearing this, the boatman thought, "Surely he will give me something."
Having brought him to the other shore, he said, "Give me the fare for the boat. He [the boatman] replied to him, "Very well, friend," and first spoke of the increase of wealth:
"O father boatman, ask for payment while you have not yet crossed; ask for the far shore while it is still unattained."
"For the mind of one who has crossed over is indeed different from that of one seeking the further shore"—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, "O dear boatman, you should ask for wages from those people standing on this shore who have not yet crossed to the further shore;
having received what is given, place it in a secure spot and afterwards lead the people to the further shore."
In this way, there will be an increase in your wealth. For, dear father, the mind of one who has crossed over is different;
the mind of one who has reached the further shore is different, for he wishes to depart without giving anything.
But he who is called a "pāresi" (one who seeks the further shore), desiring the further shore, desires to depart even after giving more; thus, the mind of one seeking the further shore is different.
“...therefore you should ask for that which has not yet been crossed; this, for now, shall be called the increase of your wealth.
Having heard this, the boatman thought: “This will indeed be my instruction; now he will give me something else as well. Then the Bodhisatta said to him:
“Friend, this is the increase of your wealth; now listen to the increase of your welfare and Dhamma.”
Having said, "Listen," he spoke this verse while giving instruction:
"Whether in the village or in the forest, whether in the lowlands or on the high ground—I instruct you everywhere: do not be angry, O sailors!"
Having explained the increase in wealth and the increase in Dhamma through this verse, he said, "This is your increase in wealth and your increase in Dhamma.
But that dull-witted man, not considering that advice as anything at all, said, "This, ascetic, is the boat-hire fee given to me by you.
[The other replied], "Yes, friend. [He continued], "I have no further business with this; something else—"
“Give it to me,” he said. “Friend, I have nothing else besides this,” replied the ascetic. “Then why did you board my ship?
Having thus cast the ascetic down onto the bank of the Ganges, he sat upon his chest and began to strike him right on the face.
The Teacher said, “Monks, that is the very same ascetic who, having given such advice, received an excellent village from the king.”
Having given that very same advice to the blind and foolish boatman, he suffered the punishment of having his face beaten.
Therefore, one giving advice should give it only to a worthy person, not to an unworthy person. Having spoken thus, after attaining full enlightenment, he immediately thereafter recited this verse:
“By the very same instruction by which the king gave away a choice village, [the boatman received a beating].”
“By that very instruction, the boatman struck him on the face.
Even as he was striking him, his wife arrived carrying food; seeing the wicked man, she said, “Husband, this is a so-called ascetic who is a court favorite of the royal family;
do not strike him! He became enraged and said, “You [are protecting] this fraudulent ascetic for me...”
“I will not give you a blow,” he said; but rising up, he struck him and knocked him down.
Then the alms-bowl fell and broke, and the fetus from her heavy womb fell to the ground.
Then the people surrounded him, seized him as a “thief who has murdered a man,” bound him, and presented him to the king. After the king had investigated the case, he—
The king had it proclaimed. Having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher, explaining this matter, spoke the concluding verse:
“The meal was ruined, the wife was killed, and the fetus fell to the ground;
like a deer lured by gold, the smith did not achieve his purpose through that.”
In this context, "the food was broken" means the food-bowl was broken. "Struck" means beaten down. "On the ground" means upon the earth.

"Like a deer with gold" means that just as a deer—even if it were to trample gold, bullion, pearls, gems, and so forth, while walking or lying down upon them—is unable to increase or produce any benefit for itself by means of that gold; [so too is the case here].
In the same way, it is said that although that blind fool heard the advice given by the wise, he was unable to increase or accomplish his own welfare.
Regarding the phrase *abandhi su*, the meaning should be understood as *abandhi so*.
For in these words, *sa o* becomes the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) *su*.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the boatman was the present boatman; the king was Ānanda;
and the ascetic was none other than myself.
The First Exposition of the Avāriya Jātaka.
[377] 2. The Exposition of the Setaketu Jātaka.
"Do not be angry, dear one; for anger is not good"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a hypocritical monk. The story of the present will be made clear in the Uddāla Jātaka.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Benares, teaching the mantras to five hundred young brahmins. Among them was the eldest, a young brahmin named Setaketu, who had been born into a family of high-caste brahmins;
on account of his birth, he possessed great pride. One day, along with the other young brahmins—
While departing from the city together with [the Buddha], he saw a certain caṇḍāla entering the city; having asked him, "Who are you?
and being told, "I am a caṇḍāla," he struck his body. Fearing that the wind coming from him might touch his own body, he said, "Begone, caṇḍāla!
You ill-omened one! Go downwind! and quickly went upwind above him.
The Caṇḍāla went even faster and stood upwind of him. Then he reviled and abused him even more harshly, saying, "Begone, you ill-omened one! Hearing this, the Caṇḍāla asked, "Who are you?
"I am a young Brahmin," he replied. "Let him be a Brahmin; however, will you be able to answer the questions I ask? "Yes, I shall be able to do so."
“If you cannot do it, I will carry you on my shoulders. Having thus encouraged himself, he said, “Carry me.
The son of a caṇḍāla, having made him take hold of his retinue, asked the question: “Young man, what are called the directions?
“The directions are the four, beginning with the east. The caṇḍāla said, “I am not asking you about that direction.”
“Not knowing even this much, you feel disgust at the wind that has struck my body,” he said, and taking him by the backbone, he bent him over and passed him between his own feet.
The young men reported this occurrence to their teacher.
Upon hearing it, the teacher asked, “Is it true, dear one, that Setaketu was passed between the feet by a caṇḍāla? “Yes,” he replied.
“Teacher, you do not even know the mere direction in which that son of a Caṇḍāla slave-girl lives,” he said, and pushed him between his own feet.
Thinking, “Now that I have seen him, I shall know what must be done,” he, being angry, reviled and insulted the son of the Caṇḍāla.
Then the teacher said to him, “Dear Setaketu, do not be angry with him; the son of the Caṇḍāla slave-girl is wise; he does not [know] you.”

"He asks about this direction, yet he asks about another direction; for what you have not seen, heard, or known is far more abundant than what you have seen, heard, or known," he said, and while instructing him, he spoke these two verses:
"Do not be angry, dear one, for anger is never good; for you have not seen and have not heard much."
“Mother and father, O Setaketu, are said to be the honored directions;
the teacher is said to be the praised direction. ‘Householders who give food, drink, and clothing, and those who invite one [to teach]—they too call that a direction.
This is the supreme direction, O Setaketu, reaching which those who were suffering become happy.’”

In this context, "anger is not good" means that when anger arises, it does not allow one to distinguish between well-spoken and ill-spoken words, or between what is meaningful and meaningless, or what is beneficial and harmful; thus it is not good, nor is it something to be gained.

"Much more have you not seen" means that what has not been seen by your eye and what has not been heard by your ear is far more abundant. "Directions" refers to the quarters. Parents [are] prior to their children.
He says that it is called the eastern direction because it has arisen from the front.

Regarding the phrase "the teachers say the direction is praised," the teachers, however, say that because it is worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), the direction is praised as the "southern direction" (*dakkhiṇā disā*); thus the Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddhas, speak, declare, and illuminate this.

"Householders" (*agārino*) refers to laypeople. "Givers of food, drink, and clothing" (*annadā-pānadā-vatthadā*) means givers of food, givers of drink, and givers of clothing. "Invokers" (*avhāyikā*)...
“Come, accept this gift”—such are those who call out. They too speak of that direction:

the Buddhas and other noble ones (ariya) speak of that as one direction. By this, it is shown that laypeople who provide the four requisites are called "one direction" because they are to be approached by righteous recluses and brahmins on account of their requisites.
Another method: those householders who give food, drink, and clothing...

Because they are invoked higher and higher in the sense that they bestow the attainment of the six sensual heavens, those righteous recluses and brahmins who invoke them are also said to be that direction;
this explains that the Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddhas, speak of the "upper direction. And it is also said:
"The mother and father are the eastern direction, The teachers are the southern direction;..."
Wife and children are the western direction; friends and colleagues are the northern.
Servants and workers are below; ascetics and brahmins are above.
A householder who honors these directions is sufficient for his family.
"But this direction" is said with reference to Nibbāna.
For it is that which, having reached it, beings who are afflicted by the various kinds of suffering such as birth and so forth become free from suffering and happy;
and it is precisely this that is called "the direction not previously traveled by beings. For that very reason, Nibbāna is called "supreme. And this has also been said:
“As one would carry a bowl of oil filled to the brim and without spilling a drop, so should one guard one’s own mind, aspiring for the direction never before reached.
Thus did the Great Being explain the directions to the young brahmin. But he [the brahmin] thought, “I have been passed between the feet by a caṇḍāla!”
Having stayed in that place and gone to Takkasilā, he mastered all the arts in the presence of a world-renowned teacher.
Permitted by his teacher, he departed from Takkasilā and wandered about training in the arts of all philosophical schools.
Upon reaching a certain frontier village, he saw five hundred ascetics living in dependence on that village. To them...
Having gone forth in his presence and mastered whatever arts, mantras, and conduct they knew, he became a teacher of a group and, surrounded by them, went to Bārāṇasī.
On the following day, while wandering for alms, he entered the royal courtyard.
The king, being pleased with the ascetics' deportment, fed them within his residence and had them dwell in his own pleasure garden.
Thus, one day, after serving the ascetics their meal, he said, "Today, having gone to the park in the evening, I shall pay my respects to the noble ladies.
Setaketu went to the park, assembled the ascetics, and said, "Sirs, today the king will arrive;
it is possible to live happily for as long as one lives once one has pleased kings. Today, some [of you] should practice the *vagguli-vrata*..."
"Practice! Some of you should adopt the practice of sleeping on thorns; some should perform the five-fold austerity;
some should devote yourselves to the exertion of squatting; some should perform the ritual of descending into water; and some should recite the mantras.
Having thus instructed them, he himself sat upon a backrest at the door of a ripe *sāla* tree, with a single manuscript whose cover was radiant with five-colored dyes and adorned with various hues.
Having placed [the fire] upon the support, he answered each question as it was asked by four or five well-trained young men.
At that moment, the king arrived; seeing them performing false asceticism, he was pleased.
Approaching Setaketu and paying homage, he sat to one side and, conversing with the chaplain, spoke the third verse:

“Those with rough antelope skins, matted hair, and mud-stained teeth, who mutter mantras while their appearance is soiled—do these wise ones, through their human application, truly escape this state of misery?
In this context, *kharājinā* means those endowed with antelope skins complete with the hooves. *Paṅkadantā* [refers to those] because of the lack of tooth-sticks...

By not eating, their teeth are stained with grime. "Of ill-formed appearance" means those whose bodies are unanointed, unadorned, wearing coarse lower garments and upper robes, and devoid of garlands, perfumes, and ointments;
that is to say, they are of soiled appearance. "Those who mutter these" refers to those who recite these mantras.
"In human applications" means they are engaged in activities to be performed by humans. This [state] is what the wise are liberated from.
“*Apāyā*”: Having stood in this practice and having understood and made manifest this world, he asks, “Are these seers freed from the four states of misery (*apāya*)?
Having heard that, the chaplain spoke the fourth verse:

“O King, having performed evil deeds, even if one is very learned, if one does not practice the Dhamma, then even one who possesses a thousandfold knowledge will not, on that account, be released from suffering without attaining right conduct.
In this context, “having performed” means having done. “Right conduct” refers to the eight attainments together with virtue. This is what is meant.
“Great King, even if one possesses a thousand branches of knowledge and thinks, ‘I am very learned,’ yet if he does not practice the threefold dharma of good conduct, he will do only evil.

Having committed those evil deeds, because of that mere erudition, and failing to reach the ‘conduct’ defined as virtue and meditative attainment, he will not be released from suffering; indeed, he is not liberated from the suffering of the states of woe.”
Having heard that, the king conceived faith in the ascetics. Then Setaketu thought: "Faith in the ascetics has arisen in this king;
however, his domestic priest has cut it off as if striking with an axe.
It is fitting for me to speak with him. Speaking with him, he uttered the fifth stanza:
“Even one who knows a thousand Vedic hymns is not released from suffering by relying on that, so long as he has not attained right conduct (*caraṇa*).
I consider the Vedas to be fruitless; only conduct accompanied by self-restraint (*saṃyama*) is true.
Its meaning is this: even if one possesses a thousand Vedic hymns, if one relies on that great learning but does not attain right conduct, one is not released from suffering for oneself.
"If one does not release [the mind], then, such being the case, I think that the three Vedas are fruitless, and that only conduct accompanied by virtue and meditative attainment is true.
Having heard this, the chaplain spoke the sixth verse:
"The Vedas are certainly not fruitless; conduct accompanied by self-restraint is indeed true."
“For by mastering the Vedas one attains fame; by conduct, the self-controlled one wins peace.
The meaning of this is: the three Vedas do not become fruitless; rather, conduct accompanied by self-restraint alone is the truth, the better, the supreme, and the most excellent.
Why is that? “For by mastering the Vedas one attains fame”—that is, by mastering the three Vedas.
In this very life, one obtains a mere measure of fame, a mere measure of renown, and a mere measure of gain; beyond this, there is nothing else.
Therefore, those [practices] are not fruitless. By means of conduct, one "wins peace":

having established oneself in virtue (sīla) and generated meditative attainments (samāpatti), one increases insight (vipassanā) which has those attainments as its proximate cause, and thus reaches—that is, attains—that which is called Nibbāna, the ultimate peace.

Thus the chaplain, having broken the argument of Setaketu, had them all made into householders; having had them provided with shields and weapons and made into the king’s attendants, he appointed them as his subordinates. This, it is said, was the lineage of the high officials.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Setaketu was the deceitful monk, the Caṇḍāla was Sāriputta, the king was Ānanda, and the chaplain was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Setaketu Jātaka.
[378] 3. The Commentary on the Darīmukha Jātaka.
"Mud is desire," etc.—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation. The present-day account has already been told above.
In the past, in the city of Rājagaha, a king named Magadharāja reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was the chief queen of that king.
He was conceived in the womb, and they gave him the name Prince Brahmadatta.
On the very day of his birth, a son was also born to the family priest; his face was exceedingly radiant, so they gave him the name Darīmukha.
Both of them were raised in the royal court and became dear friends; when they reached the age of sixteen, they went to Takkaśilā.
Having mastered all the crafts, thinking, "We shall train in all the arts of every tradition and learn the local customs," they wandered through villages, market towns, and other places.
Upon reaching Bārāṇasī, they stayed at a temple and on the following day entered Bārāṇasī for alms.
There, in a certain family, having cooked milk-rice with the intention, "We will feed the brahmins and give them a recitation," [they were invited].

Seats were prepared. When people saw those two wandering for alms, they thought, "Brahmins have arrived," and having invited them into their homes, they spread a clean cloth upon the seat for the Great Being and a red woolen blanket upon the seat for Darīmukha.
Seeing that sign, Darīmukha thought, "Today my friend will become the King of Bārāṇasī, and I shall be the general."
He understood. Having eaten there, received the recitation, and pronounced blessings, they departed and went to that royal park.
There, the Great Being lay down upon a stone slab of auspicious proportions, while Darīmukha sat massaging his feet.
At that time, it was the seventh day since the death of the King of Bārāṇasī. The chaplain, having performed the funeral rites for the king, [proceeded].
On the seventh day after his accession to the kingdom, which was without an heir, he dispatched the Phussa-chariot.
The details regarding the dispatching of the Phussa-chariot will be made clear in the Mahājanaka Jātaka.

Having departed from the city, the Phussa-chariot, surrounded by a fourfold army and accompanied by the sounding of many hundreds of musical instruments, reached the gate of the pleasure garden. Darīmukha heard the sound of the musical instruments.
Upon hearing this, he thought, "Phussaratha is coming for my friend; today he will become king and grant me the position of commander-in-chief.
What need have I for the household life? I shall go forth and renounce the world.
Without taking leave of the Bodhisatta, he went aside and stood in concealment. The chaplain, having stopped the chariot at the gate of the park, [entered] the park.

Having entered [the cave] and seen the Bodhisatta reclining on the auspicious stone slab, he examined the marks on his feet and thought, "This meritorious being is capable of ruling over all four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands;
but what is the nature of his fortitude? He then had all the musical instruments played. The Bodhisatta, having awakened, from his mouth—

Having removed his garment and looked at the great multitude, he again covered his face with the garment, lay down for a short while, and then, rising with his fatigue allayed, sat cross-legged upon a stone slab.
The chaplain knelt on his knees and said, "Your Majesty, the kingdom has come to you. "A kingdom without an heir, you say? "Yes, Your Majesty."
“Very well,” he consented. They performed his consecration right there in the park.
Because of the greatness of his glory, without even looking at Darīmukha, he mounted his chariot and, surrounded by a great multitude, entered the city.
Having circumambulated it, he stood at the palace gate, assigned offices to his ministers, and ascended the palace.
At that moment, Darīmukha, thinking, "The park is now empty," arrived and sat down upon the auspicious stone slab.

Then, a withered leaf fell before him. Applying his mind to the decay and passing away within that very withered leaf and contemplating the three characteristics, he shook the earth as he attained Pacceka-bodhi. At that very instant, his lay appearance vanished.
It vanished; a set of robes and a bowl made of supernormal power descended from the sky and were fastened upon his body.

At that very moment, wearing the eight requisites and perfected in the four postures, appearing like an elder of sixty years standing, he rose into the air by means of his psychic power and went to the Nandamūlaka cave in the Himalayan region.
The Bodhisatta, for his part, ruled the kingdom with righteousness, owing to the greatness of his glory.
But having become negligent through indulgence in pleasure, he did not think of Darīmukha for forty years.
When those forty years had passed, however, he remembered him and desired to see him, thinking, "I have a friend named Darīmukha; where indeed could he be?
From that time on, whether in the inner palace or in the midst of the assembly, he would say, "Where indeed is my friend Darīmukha?"
“Whoever tells me where he dwells, I shall grant him great honor,” he said.
Thus, as he was repeatedly recollecting him, ten more years passed by.
The Paccekabuddha Darīmukha, too, after fifty years had elapsed, reflected and thought, “My friend is indeed remembering me.”
Knowing that "now this old man has reached an advanced age with sons, daughters, and others;
I shall go, preach the Dhamma to him, and cause him to go forth," he came through the air by means of psychic power, descended into the park, and sat upon a stone slab like a golden statue.
Seeing him, the park keeper approached and asked, "Venerable sir, from where have you come? "From the Nandamūlaka mountain cave," he replied.
“What is your name? “I am the Paccekabuddha named Darīmukha, friend.
“Venerable sir, do you know our king? “Yes, I know him; he was my companion in the life of a householder. “Venerable sir, the king wishes to see you.
I shall tell him that you have arrived. “Go and tell him. Saying “Very well,” he departed in great haste.
Having gone there, he informed the king that [the Paccekabuddha] was seated upon a stone slab. The king, thinking, "My friend has indeed arrived;
I shall see him," mounted his chariot and went to the park with a great retinue.

Having approached the Paccekabuddha, he paid homage, exchanged greetings, and sat down to one side. Then the Paccekabuddha said to him, "Brahmadatta, what [is it that you seek] by means of righteousness?"

Having established a friendly rapport by saying, "You have ruled the kingdom; you do not follow wrong paths; you do not oppress the world for the sake of wealth; you perform meritorious deeds such as giving," he said, "Brahmadatta, you are advanced in years;
now is the time for you to renounce sensual pleasures and go forth," and while teaching him the Dhamma, he spoke the first verse:
“Sensual pleasures are a mire and sensual pleasures are a swamp; this fear has been declared by me to have three roots.
Dust and smoke have also been made known by me. Having abandoned these, go forth into homelessness, O Brahmadatta!
In this context, “mire” (paṅka) refers to grasses, water-weeds, lotuses, thickets, and so forth, that grow in water. For just as water—
Just as those [mudbanks] cause one crossing over to stick and become entangled, so too, for the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) crossing the ocean of *saṃsāra*,
the five strands of sensual pleasure— or indeed all objects of desire (*vatthukāma*) and defilements of desire (*kilesakāma*)—
are called "mud" because they cause one to stick and become entangled. For gods, humans, and animals alike, being stuck and clinging fast in this mud, they suffer, weep, and lament.

"And stuck in the mire" (*palipo ca kāmā*): "mire" (*palipa*) refers to a great quagmire, in which even wild boars, deer, and the like, as well as lions and elephants, once stuck, are unable to extricate themselves and move on.

Because they resemble that [quagmire], both sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual defilements (*kilesakāma*) are called "the mire. For even wise beings, from the moment they become stuck in those sensual pleasures, [are held fast].
Having shattered sensual desires, they are unable to rise quickly and enter the delightful life of renunciation—which is without possessions and free from impediments.
"Bhayañca me taṃ": this means "this is fear"; the letter *m* is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
"Timūlaṃ": it is immovable, as if established upon three roots; this is the name for powerful fear. "Pavuttaṃ": uttered.
"Great King, these things called sensual pleasures are a powerful fear in the sense that they are the condition for the fear of self-reproach and so forth—
both in this present life and in future lives— and for the fear arising from the thirty-two types of tortures and the ninety-six diseases;
thus they have been proclaimed and spoken by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha, as well as by the omniscient Bodhisattvas."
The meaning is "illuminated. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: "And this fear is mine" means "and this three-rooted fear has been proclaimed by me.
And "dust and smoke"—because they resemble dust and smoke, they were described by me as "dust" and "smoke. Just as...
For when fine dust falls upon the body of a man who has bathed well, is anointed, and is adorned, it makes that body discolored,
devoid of luster, and soiled; even so, although they have come through the air by the power of psychic success and are renowned in the world like the moon and the sun,
from the very moment the dust of sensual desire once fell within them, [they were defiled].
Because their beauty of virtue, their splendor of virtue, and their purity of virtue have been impaired, they become ill-favored, devoid of luster,
and indeed defiled. Just as a wall, though perfectly clean, becomes black in color from the moment it is struck by smoke, so too those of extremely pure knowledge,
from the moment they are struck by the smoke of sensual desire, fall into the destruction of their virtues in the midst of the great multitude.
They appear as black smoke. Thus, because they resemble dust and smoke, these sensual pleasures were described by me to you as "dust and smoke.
Therefore, having abandoned these sensual pleasures, go forth into homelessness, O Brahmadatta—thus the Blessed One incited the king toward the life of renunciation.
Having heard this, the king spoke the second verse, describing his own state of being bound by the defilements:
“O Brahmin, I am obsessed with, enamored of, and infatuated by sensual pleasures; I am terrified of them.
For the sake of my livelihood, I cannot bear to abandon them; I shall perform abundant meritorious deeds.
In this context, *gadhitō* means bound by the bodily fetter of covetousness. *Ratto* means colored by lust through the alteration of one’s natural state.
"Adhimucchito" means excessively infatuated. "In both kinds of sensual pleasures" refers to both types of sense-desires;

"I" refers to myself. "Brāhmaṇa" is an address to the Paccekabuddha Darīmukha. "Bhiṃsarūpaṃ" means of formidable appearance. "Taṃ nussahemi" means I do not venture, nor am I able, to [engage in] those two kinds of sensual pleasure.
"Jīvikattho pahātuṃ" means that, being desirous of this livelihood, I have abandoned it.

He says, "I cannot abandon sensual desire. He thinks, "I shall perform meritorious deeds," meaning that now he will perform many and not a few meritorious acts consisting of giving, virtue, and the observance of the Uposatha.
Thus, this so-called "defilement-desire" (kilesakāma) cannot be removed from the moment it first adheres; by means of it, the mind becomes defiled.
Although the Great Man was told of the virtues of the renunciant life by the Paccekabuddha, he said, "I am not able to go forth.
This was because, at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, while searching for the qualities that produce a Buddha with the wisdom arising within himself,
he had seen the third perfection, renunciation.
“First, you must firmly undertake this third perfection, renunciation;
go forth to the perfection of renunciation if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as a man long imprisoned in a jail, afflicted by suffering,”
One does not generate passion for that, but seeks only liberation.
"In the same way, you should view all states of existence as if they were a prison;
by turning toward renunciation, you will attain full enlightenment."

Thus he praised the virtue of renunciation. Although the Paccekabuddha spoke in praise of the going-forth and said, "Cast off the defilements and become a recluse," he replied, "I am not able to cast off the defilements and become a recluse.
It is said that in this world there are eight types of people known as "madmen. As the ancients have said: "Eight kinds of persons acquire the designation of 'madman':
one mad with lust who has fallen under the power of greed; one mad with anger who has fallen under the power of hatred; one mad with views..."
"Under the sway of perversion, intoxicated by delusion and under the sway of ignorance; intoxicated by a spirit and under the sway of a spirit;
intoxicated by bile and under the sway of bile; intoxicated by liquor and under the sway of drink; and intoxicated by misfortune and under the sway of grief.
Among these eight types of intoxication, in this Jātaka, the Great Being became intoxicated with sensual desire and fell under the sway of greed.
Having gone forth, he did not recognize its true benefit.
But why are sentient beings unable to liberate themselves from this greed-born state, which causes harm and destroys virtue?
It is because throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, they have been bound together as one.
Even though this was so, the wise abandon it by means of many reflections, such as "sensual pleasures have little gratification.
For this very reason, although the Great Being said, "I am not able to go forth," the Paccekabuddha Darīmukha did not relinquish his responsibility,
but spoke two verses as further exhortation.
“He who, when exhorted by one who desires his welfare and acts out of compassion,
does not follow the instruction— thinking ‘this alone is better’— that dull-witted man enters the womb again and again.
He goes to a terrible hell, full of both the beautiful and the ugly, and filled with urine and excrement.”
“Beings who are greedy do not abandon their own bodies, those who remain with passion undiminished for sensual pleasures. In this context, “one who desires welfare” means one who desires growth.
“Compassionate for his welfare” means one who feels compassion through a mind that is well-disposed toward his benefit.
“Being exhorted” means being advised. “This alone is better” refers to that which one has grasped oneself, even if it is not good and is unsurpassed.
Thinking, "This is indeed better," that dull-witted person of ignorance does not pass beyond dwelling in the mother’s womb;
the meaning is that he enters the womb again and again.
"Of terrible form," O Great King, means that when that dull-witted one enters the mother’s womb, it is of a terrible appearance and a cruel nature.
It is indeed called "going to hell. For here, the mother’s womb is called "hell" in the sense that it is devoid of enjoyment;
thus it is referred to as the "four-walled hell. When asked, "What is the four-walled hell?", it is appropriate to say that it is the mother’s womb itself.
For a being reborn in the great Avīci hell certainly undergoes constant running back and forth; therefore, that [womb] is called the "four-walled hell."
It is not possible to speak; moreover, while in the mother’s womb for nine or ten months, one is unable to run here and there on all four sides.
In that extremely cramped space, one must remain with all four limbs tucked in and drawn together;
therefore, this is called the "Hell of the Four Walls."

"Beautiful and unbeautiful" means that for those noble sons who are practitioners and who fear *saṃsāra*, the mother’s womb is considered entirely unbeautiful among beautiful things. Therefore it was said:
"To one who does not see the noble form, Which is called 'noble' though it is ignoble, Unpure yet regarded as pure, And filled with various kinds of filth."
“Alas for this diseased, putrid body, loathsome, impure, and subject to sickness!
In it, people, being negligent and infatuated, miss the path leading to rebirth in the world of the Sugata.

“Attached” (*satta*) means clinging, adhering, stuck, and fastened; they do not abandon their own bodies, and thus they do not relinquish that mother’s womb. “Lustful” (*giddha*) means greedy. “Those who exist” refers to those who are not free from passion for sensual pleasures; they do not leave this dwelling in the womb.

Thus, after the Paccekabuddha Darīmukha had shown the suffering rooted in conception in the womb and the suffering rooted in its maintenance, he now spoke one and a half verses to show the suffering rooted in emergence from the womb:
“Smeared with filth, bespattered with blood, and plastered with phlegm, they emerge.
For whatever they touch with their bodies at that moment, all of it is unpleasant and entirely nothing but suffering.”
“Having seen this, I say that there is no hearing from another; I remember many of my former births.

In this regard, O Great King, “smeared with filth” means that these beings, when emerging from their mother’s womb, do not emerge having been anointed with the four kinds of perfumes or adorned with fragrant garlands; rather, they are smeared and obstructed by old excrement.
They emerge having offered [the sacrifice]. "Smeared with blood" means that they do not emerge even when anointed with red sandalwood paste;
rather, it is when they are smeared with actual blood that they emerge. "Coated with phlegm" means that they do not emerge even when anointed with white sandalwood paste;
rather, it is when they are coated with thick, viscous phlegm that they emerge. For at the time of the birth of women's offspring, [this is what occurs].
These impurities emerge. "Tāvadā" means at that very moment. This is what is meant:

Great King, when these beings emerge from the mother’s womb, smeared with filth and the like, whatever part of the path of emergence they touch—whether it be a hand or a foot—all of that is unpleasant and not sweet.
They experience only unmixed suffering; at that time, there is no such thing as pleasure for them.
Having seen this, O Great King, I say: "For they do not flow from elsewhere. When I speak thus, it is not because I have heard it from another;
I do not speak having heard it from some other ascetic or brahmin, but rather by means of my own knowledge of *paccekabodhi*.
The meaning is: "Having seen, having penetrated, and having made it directly manifest, I say.
By saying, "I remember many former births," he spoke thus to demonstrate his own power. This is what is meant:
"Great King, I indeed remember many former births, defined as the succession of aggregates in which I previously dwelt; I remember two incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand eons."
Now, having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher said, “In this way, that Paccekabuddha won over the king with well-spoken discourse,” and at the conclusion he spoke the half-stanza:
“With variegated verses, well-spoken, Darīmukha caused Sumedha to reflect.
Therein, “variegated” means endowed with manifold meanings; “well-spoken” means beautifully articulated. Darīmukha caused [him] to reflect.

"O monks, 'Sumedha'—that Paccekabuddha Darīmukha caused King Sumedha, who possessed beautiful wisdom and was capable of discerning what should and should not be done, to contemplate, to be convinced, and to accept his word; this is the meaning.
Thus, having shown the danger in sensual pleasures and having caused him to accept his word, the Paccekabuddha said: 'Great King, now..."
"Whether you go forth or not, I have explained to you the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit of renunciation;
you must be diligent," he said, and like a golden royal swan, he sprang into the air, crushing the womb of the clouds, and went straight to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.
The Great Being, with his ten fingers joined in a radiant salutation, [gazed after him].
Having placed [the child] upon his head and paid homage, once that [child] had passed from the range of his vision, he summoned his eldest son and entrusted the kingdom to him.
While the great multitude was weeping and lamenting, he abandoned sensual pleasures, entered the Himalayas, constructed a leaf-hut, and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Not long thereafter, he attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
Having been reborn there, at the end of his lifespan he went to the Brahma-world.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, many became Stream-enterers and others. "At that time, I myself was the king.
This is the third commentary on the Darīmukha Jātaka.
[379] 4. The Commentary on the Neru Jātaka.
“The ravens and the flocks of crows”—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu.
It is said that after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, he went to a certain frontier village.

People, having gained confidence in his deportment, fed him, obtained his promise, built a leaf-hut for him in the forest, and settled him there, showing him the highest honor. Then some eternalists (sassatavādins) arrived.
Having heard their words, they abandoned the Elder’s doctrine and adopted the doctrine of eternalism; they [then] remained with them alone.
They paid him honor. Then the annihilationists arrived; they abandoned the doctrine of eternalism and adopted the doctrine of annihilationism.
Then others, the naked ascetics, arrived; they abandoned the doctrine of annihilationism and adopted the doctrine of nakedness.

Having lived there with difficulty in the presence of those people who did not know the difference between their virtues and faults, he completed his rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and exchanged greetings, when asked, "Where did you spend the rains retreat?

he replied, "Near the borderlands, Bhante. When asked, "Did you live there happily? he said, "Bhante, I lived there in misery, being in the company of those who do not recognize virtue and non-virtue.
The Teacher said, "Monks, in the past, even wise beings in the animal realm..."

"Even though they were born [as birds], they did not dwell even for a single day with those who did not know their own virtues and faults; why then do you dwell in a place where you do not know your own virtues and faults?
Having said this, when requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a golden swan."
He also had a younger brother. While they were dwelling on Mount Cittakūṭa, they ate wild rice that grew naturally in the Himalayan region.
One day, after grazing there and returning toward Cittakūṭa, they saw a golden mountain named Neru along the way and sat down upon its summit. Now, those who dwell depending on that mountain—
On the feeding ground, the flocks of birds and the quadrupeds were of various colors;
however, from the moment they entered the mountain, they all became golden-colored by its radiance.
Seeing this, the Bodhisatta’s younger brother, not knowing the reason for it, spoke two verses in conversation with his brother, wondering, "What indeed could be the cause here?"
“The ravens and the flocks of crows, and we who are the best among those that fly—
all of us have become equal now that we have come to this mountain.
Here dwell lions and tigers, jackals, and the lowest of beasts.”
"All are indeed alike; what kind of mountain is this?

In this context, "crows" refers to forest crows. "Flocks of crows" refers to both ordinary flocks of crows and [other types]. "The best of those that fly" means the foremost among birds. "We are alike" means we are of similar color.
Having heard his words, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
“Men know this mountain, Neru, the most excellent of peaks;
here all living beings dwell, endowed with beauty.
In this context, “endowed with beauty here” means being endowed with beauty by means of radiance on this Neru mountain.
Having heard that, the younger brother spoke the remaining verses:
“Where there may be disrespect, or contempt for one’s own kin,
or even the honoring of the lowly— one should not dwell there for thirty years.”
“Where the lazy and the clever, the brave and the cowardly are all honored alike—
there the virtuous do not dwell, for that man makes no distinction.
This mountain does not differentiate between the low, the superior, and the middling.”
“Neru causes distinction; come, let us abandon Neru.

Herein, this is the meaning of the first verse: where there is disrespect and contempt—meaning disdain or humiliation—toward the continuity of wise ones endowed with virtue due to a lack of honor, or where there is honoring of the lowly and the immoral.
It might be that one would not dwell there. "Worthy of honor" means that these [persons] are here worthy of honor by a single, identical form of worship;

they receive equal respect. "Whether inferior, superior, or middling" means that he does not differentiate among them on account of birth, clan, family, locality, virtue, conduct, knowledge, and so forth—whether they be inferior, middling, or superior.
"Handa" is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation.
"Let us abandon it," they said. Having spoken thus, both those swans flew up and went back to Cittakūṭa itself.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka;
at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the younger swan was Ānanda, and the elder swan was [the Buddha].
"But it was I myself who was he.
The commentary on the Neru Jātaka is the fourth.
5. The commentary on the Āsaṅka Jātaka.
The story of the creeper named Āsāvatī was told by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, concerning the seduction of a former wife.
The background of this matter will be made clear in the Indriya Jātaka; however, here the Teacher asked that bhikkhu, “Is it true that you are dissatisfied?
When he replied, “It is true, Bhante,” the Teacher asked, “By whom have you been made dissatisfied?”
Having said this, when [the monk] replied, "Venerable sir, she was my former wife," [the Buddha] said, "Monk, this woman has brought you harm;
in the past as well, because of her, you abandoned a fourfold army and lived for three years in a region of the Himalayas, experiencing great suffering.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a village of Kāsi.

Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the arts at Takkasilā, went forth as an ascetic, and subsisting on forest roots and fruits, developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
He then dwelt in a region of the Himalayas. At that time, there was a certain man endowed with merit...
A being, having passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, was reborn in that place as a girl within the calyx of a single lotus in a lotus pond.
While the other lotuses withered and fell away, this one remained standing, possessing a great interior.
When the ascetic went to the lotus pond to bathe, he saw her and thought, "Even though the other lotuses have fallen away..."
Thinking, "This remains as something of great bulk;

what could be the reason for this?", he put on his bathing-cloth, went down into the water, and having approached, opened that lotus. Seeing the girl, he conceived the notion that she was his daughter, brought her to a leaf-hut, and looked after her.
Later, when she reached the age of sixteen, she became beautiful, possessing a most excellent form.
She had transcended human form but had not yet attained the form of a deity. At that time, Sakka came to attend upon the Bodhisatta;
seeing the girl, he asked, "Where has she come from? Having heard her history, he asked, "What does she require to obtain?
[The answer was: "A dwelling place, clothing, ornaments, and provisions for food, O Noble One."
Saying, "Very well, venerable sir," he constructed a crystal palace near her dwelling place and provided divine couches, divine garments, ornaments, food, and drink.
That palace would descend to the ground when she was about to ascend it, and once she had ascended, it would leap up and remain suspended in the air.
She lived in that palace, performing her duties and services for the Bodhisatta. Then a certain forest-dweller...

Having seen her, he asked, "Venerable sir, what is this? and upon hearing, "She is my daughter," he went to Bārāṇasī and reported to the king, "Your Majesty, in a region of the Himalayas, I saw such a daughter belonging to a certain ascetic.
Having heard this, the king became bound by the association of hearing [the news], and making a forest-dweller his guide for the way, with a fourfold army...
Having gone to that place with his army and caused the camp to be pitched, he took a forest guide and, surrounded by a host of ministers, entered the hermitage.
After paying homage to the Great Being, he sat down to one side and said, "Venerable sir, women are indeed a stain upon the holy life; I shall take care of your daughter. But the Bodhisatta—
Thinking, "What indeed is in this lotus? he felt apprehension; having descended into the water and brought it back, they gave that young woman the name Āsaṅkā (Apprehension).
He did not say directly to the king, "Take her and go," but said, "Great King, take her and go only after you know the name of this young woman. "I shall know it when you have told me."
“Venerable sir,” he said. “I will not tell you; go and take her name yourself once you have discovered it through the power of your own wisdom.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” from that time forth he consulted with his ministers as to what her name might be, wondering, “What indeed is her name?
He enumerated names that are difficult to discern, thinking, “She must be named so-and-so.”
He conversed with the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta rejected him, saying, "I am not of such-and-such a name.
As the king continued to investigate his name, a year passed by. At that time, lions and other wild beasts were seizing the elephant-riders, horsemen, and foot-soldiers;
there was danger from long-legged birds and danger from flies, and they were exhausted by the cold.
Many people were dying. Then the king, becoming angry, said, "What use have I for her? and departed after speaking thus to the Bodhisatta.
On that day, the maiden Āsaṅkā opened the crystal window and stood there showing herself.
When the king saw her, he said, "We cannot know your name; you must remain right here in the Himalayas. We—
“I shall go,” he said. “Where, O Great King, going, will you find a woman like me?
Listen to my words: in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in the Cittalatā Grove, there is a creeper named Āsāvatī;
within its fruit, a divine drink is produced. Having drunk of that once, they remain intoxicated for four months and lie upon celestial couches.”

"Furthermore, that tree bears fruit after a thousand years. Sons of the gods who are addicted to liquor, thinking 'we shall obtain fruit from this,' endure their thirst for divine drink and go there regularly for a thousand years, looking at the creeper to see if it is healthy.
Yet you have become despondent in only a single year. That which is called 'bearing fruit through hope' is happiness; do not be despondent," he said.
He spoke three verses:
“The creeper named Āsāvatī was born in the Cittalatāvana grove;
of it, only a single fruit ripens in a thousand years.”
“The gods wait upon that mindfulness whose fruit is so far-reaching;
O King, you are like a prayer—hope is fruitful and brings happiness.
That bird indeed hopes, that fowler indeed hopes.”
"And her hope was fulfilled, for her mindfulness had reached so far;
like a prayer, O King, your hope has borne fruit and is blissful.
Therein, "Āsāvatī" is her name. For because hope arose in her regarding its fruit, she received this name.
He obtains [it]. In the "Cittalatāvana" means in a park of that name.
It is said that in that park, the luster of the grasses, trees, creepers, and so forth, makes the bodies of the deities who enter it repeatedly variegated;
therefore, its name "Cittalatāvana" (Variegated Creeper Grove) arose. *Payirupāsanti* means they approach again and again. *Āsīseva* means by aspirations alone, by mere wishes.
"Do not cause her name to be cut off.
The king, captivated by her words, again assembled his ministers and had ten names prepared for her;
yet, searching for her name, he lived for another year. Even then, she had no name even among those ten, so they said, "She is simply 'Asukā' (So-and-so)."
When this was said, the Bodhisatta refused. Again the king thought, "What use have I for her? and mounting his horse, he departed.
She too, standing again at the window, showed herself.
The king said, "Stay, you; we shall go. "Why do you go, Great King? "I am unable to learn your name. "Great King, why?"
“You shall not fail to know its name; indeed, there is no hope that does not come to fruition.
It is said that once a certain crane, standing on a mountain peak, obtained exactly what he had prayed for. Why then will you not obtain it? Endure this, O Great King.
It is said that a certain crane, having gathered food from a lotus pond, flew up and perched upon the summit of a mountain.
Having stayed right there that day, on the following day he thought:

"I am sitting comfortably here on the summit of this mountain; if I were not to descend from here, but were to stay right here, taking my food and drinking water, and dwell for this day, that would indeed be excellent. Then, on that very same day, Sakka, the king of the gods—
Having crushed the Asuras and obtained divine sovereignty in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he thought:
"My own desire has indeed reached its fulfillment; is there anyone else whose desire remains unfulfilled?
While searching, he saw him and thought, "I shall bring this one's desire to its ultimate fulfillment. Not far from the place where Baka was sitting, there was a river.
“There was one; he filled that river with a flood and sent it over the mountain peak.
That crane, sitting right there, ate fish and drank water, and stayed in that very place for the rest of the day. When the water had run dry and gone away, [the king said]:
“In this way, Great King, even a crane obtained the fruit of his own hope; why will you not obtain yours? Having said this, he continued:
He said, “Or rather, he hopes,” and so forth.
Therein, “he hopes” (āsīsate) means he simply hopes or desires. “A bird” (pakkhī) is so called because of being endowed with wings;
“a twice-born” (dijo) is so called because of being born twice. “Awareness that has gone as far as that” refers to [the distance] from the mountain peak to the fish and the water.
"And see its distance; though it has gone so far away, by the power of Sakka, Baka’s hope was indeed fulfilled.
Then the king, having heard her words, became attached to her beauty, clung to her conversation, and being unable to depart, he assembled his ministers and had the name "Sata" inscribed.
While searching for the name according to that inscription, another year passed for him.
[This is] the past. After three years had passed, he approached the Bodhisatta and asked about the girl’s name, saying, "What will her name be? [The Bodhisatta replied,] "I do not know, Great King.
He said, "We shall depart now," and having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, he set out. As for Āsaṅkā and the maiden, they remained standing by the crystal window once again.
Seeing him, the king said, "Stay here; we shall go. "Why so, Great King?
"You have satisfied me with mere words, not with the delights of sensual pleasure.
Three years have passed while I have dwelt here, bound by your sweet speech; now I shall depart. And he spoke these verses:
“He addressed me with words, but did not act upon them;
like the fragrant *sereyyaka* flower, he was beautiful but scentless.
He who utters sweet speech toward friends, yet acts without fruit—”
“While giving away his wealth, he did not relinquish it; thus his connection with it decays.
For one should say what one would do, and one should not say what one would not do;
the wise clearly discern the one who speaks while not acting.”
“My strength has indeed failed me, and there is no provisions for the journey;
I fear I shall cause the death of living beings—come now, let us depart.
Therein, *sampesī* means he satisfied and refreshed them. *Sereyyakassa* refers to a golden *kuraṇḍaka* tree. This is merely a stylistic device of the teaching.

However, this was said with reference to any other flower whatsoever—such as the *suvaṇṇakuraṇḍaka*, the *jaya*, the *sumana*, and so forth—that possesses color but lacks fragrance. "Possessing color but lacking fragrance" means:

just as a garland of *sereyyaka* and other such flowers delights the eye through its possession of color, yet does not delight through its lack of fragrance, even so, you too [delight] by sight and by endearing speech...
And he gratified them, yet it is shown that this was not by means of action.
O Bhaddā, one who speaks with sweet words, saying, "I will give you such-and-such wealth," but then fails to give or bestow that wealth, performs only sweet words;
through that, the bond with that friend decays, and the intimacy of friendship does not endure. And as for provisions for the journey...
“Bhadde, having been bound by your sweet words, three years have passed while I have been living here;
my army—consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—is exhausted, and I have no provisions for men, consisting of food and wages.
I fear that there will be the taking of life; therefore, I suspect my own life will perish right here. Come now, I shall depart.”

Having heard the king’s words, the maiden Āsaṅkā said to him as she conversed with the king: “Great King, you know my name; it is indeed the very name spoken by you. Tell this to my father, take me, and go. She spoke thus:
“This indeed is my name, O bull among chariot-warriors, the name by which I am known.
Wait a moment, Great King; let us address my father.”
The meaning of this is: “Whatever my name may be, let that very thing be considered my ‘fear’ (āsaṅkā).
Having heard this, the king went to the Bodhisattva and said, “Venerable sir, your daughter’s name is Āsaṅkā.
[The Bodhisattva replied,] “O Great King, take her from the moment her name is known and depart. He then paid homage to the Great Being.
Having arrived at the door of the crystal palace, he said, "My dear, you have been given to me by your father as well; come now, let us go.
"Wait, Great King, let us inform our father," she said, and descending from the palace, she paid homage to the Great Being, wept, and asked for his forgiveness.
Having returned to the presence of the king, the king took her and went to Benares with his sons and daughters.
Increasing in prosperity, he lived in pleasant association. The Bodhisatta, without falling away from his meditative absorption (jhāna), was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths (saccāni), the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
