At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). At that time, the girl Āsaṅkā was the former wife.
The king was the monk who felt dejected, while I myself was the ascetic.
This concludes the commentary on the Āsaṅkajātakaya, the fifth.
[381] 6. Commentary on the Migālopa-jātaka.
"I do not like it"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak with.
The Teacher summoned that monk and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are difficult to speak with?

When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, it is not only now; even in the past you were indeed difficult to speak with, and regarding this state of being difficult to speak with—"
"But because you did not act upon the words of the wise, you have met with disaster in the face of the Veramba wind," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a vulture and became known as Apananda the vulture.
Surrounded by a flock of vultures, he lived on Vulture Peak Mountain. Now, his son—
There was one named Migālopa who was endowed with great strength and power;
he would fly higher than the limit of other vultures. The vultures informed the king of the vultures, saying, "Your son is flying too high.
He summoned him and said, "My dear, it seems you are going too high; by going too high, you will meet your death."
Having spoken thus, he recited these three verses:
“The deer’s flesh did not please me, for such is your destiny.
You fall, dear son, from what is high; you frequent, dear son, that which is no ground.”
“When the earth becomes for you like a four-cornered field, then, my dear, turn back; do not go further than this.
There are other birds as well, winged creatures that travel through the air.”
"Cast down by the force of the wind, they have perished along with their eternal companions.
Therein, "O Migalopa," he addresses his son by name. "Too high, dear one, you fly":
"Dear one, you go too high, overstepping the boundary of other vultures. By the phrase "like a four-cornered field," he [indicates] its boundary.
He explains: "This is what is meant—my dear, when this great earth appears as small as a four-cornered field, and you perceive it as such, then you should turn back from that point;
do not go beyond it. "There are others too" means: "It is not only you; other vultures have also acted in this way."
"He illuminates. "Carried away" means that those vultures, having crossed our boundary, were dragged off by the force of the wind and lost.

"Those equal to the eternal ones" (sassatīsama) means those who, considering themselves equal to the eternal earth, mountains, and so forth, perished in the interim without even completing their lifespan of a thousand years; this is the meaning.
Migālopa, because he was disobedient and did not follow his father’s word, leaped forward;
but seeing the boundary his father had described, he overstepped it, fell into a whirlwind, and having torn those too asunder, he soared up and plunged into the mouth of the Verambha wind.
Then the Verambha winds struck him. As soon as he was struck by them, he was broken into pieces and vanished right there in the sky.
“Having failed to carry out the command of his aged father Apananda,
and having transgressed the timely wind, he fell under the power of the Verambha winds.
His sons, his wives, and whoever else were his dependents— ”
All calamities shall befall those brahmins who do not accept advice:
"Thus, even here in this world, he who does not understand the words of the elders is one who transgresses the bounds,
arrogant, like a vulture that disregards the instruction."
"All encounter misfortune, having failed to follow the instruction of the Elder.
These are the three verses of the Fully Enlightened One.
Therein, "dependents" means those who live in reliance upon him. "To one who does not accept advice, he gave [the simile of] the vulture over the flock of deer."
Since they did not accept his advice, they all went beyond the boundary with him and met their destruction.
"In this way too," said the Blessed One, "monks, just like that vulture, whoever else— whether a householder or one gone forth—
does not accept the words of elders who are compassionate for their welfare, he too, by transgressing this boundary, is like a vulture intoxicated and arrogant."
"He meets with calamity.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher revealed the Truths and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Migālopa was the monk who was difficult to speak to, and Apananda was none other than myself.
This is the sixth commentary on the Migālopa Jātaka.
[382] 7. The Commentary on the Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka.
"Who indeed is dark of complexion?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Anāthapiṇḍika.
For from the time he was established in the fruit of stream-entry, he guarded the five precepts without flaw; his wife also...
Even his sons and daughters, as well as his slaves and laborers who worked for wages—all were protected.
Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, Anāthapiṇḍika lives surrounded only by those who are pure.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what kind of discussion are you having just now?"
Having asked, "Are you sitting together? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past, ancient wise men were likewise pure and surrounded by the pure. Being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having become a merchant, gave alms.
He guarded his virtue and observed the Uposatha rites; his wife also guarded the five precepts, and his sons, daughters, slaves, laborers, and servants likewise guarded the five precepts.
Thus, he became known as one whose retinue was pure and well-established in virtue.
Then, one day, he thought: "If anyone comes to me who is pure in conduct and virtuous like myself, to him..."
"It is not proper to give away a sitting mat or a couch for reclining;
it is permissible to give what is not leftover and has not been used. Having said this, he prepared an unused couch and a lodging on one side in his own dwelling place.
At that time, from the Cātumahārājika heaven, Virūpakkha the Great King’s daughter, Kāḷakaṇṇī—

Now, Dhatarattha the Great King’s daughter named Sirī and another named Cālā, taking many perfumes and garlands, went to the Anotatta bathing-place, thinking, "We shall sport at Anotatta. In that lake there are many bathing-places;
among them, only Buddhas bathe at the bathing-place of the Buddhas, and only Paccekabuddhas at the bathing-place of the Paccekabuddhas.
They bathe: at the bathing place for monks, only monks bathe; at the bathing place for ascetics, only ascetics bathe;
at the bathing places of the sons of the gods among the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure, beginning with those of the Four Great Kings, only the sons of the gods bathe;
and at the bathing places of the daughters of the gods, only the daughters of the gods bathe.
Then these two came there and, each saying "I shall bathe first! I shall bathe first!", they quarreled over the bathing place.
Kāḷakaṇṇī said, "I protect and govern the world; therefore, it is fitting that I bathe first.
Siri said, "I abide on the path that bestows sovereignty upon the great multitude; therefore, [I bathe first]."
"Are we worthy to bathe first? they asked. The women replied, "The Four Great Kings will know whether it is fitting for us to bathe first or not fitting.
They went into their presence and asked, "Among us, which one is worthy to bathe first in Lake Anotatta?
Dhatarattha and Virūpakkha said, "It is not possible for us to decide."
They entrusted the burden to Virūḷhaka and Vessavaṇa. They thought, "We too will not be able to manage this;
we shall send them to the presence of Sakka," and so they sent them to Sakka. Having heard their words, Sakka reflected:
"These two are also daughters of my own men; it is not possible for me to adjudicate this lawsuit. Then—
Sakka said, "In Bārāṇasī there is a merchant named Suciparivāra; in his house a bed is prepared that has never been used for eating from.
Whoever is permitted to sit or lie upon it is the one fit to bathe first.
Upon hearing this, Kāḷakaṇṇī at that very moment put on blue garments, smeared herself with blue ointment, and [prepared herself].
Having adorned herself with a necklace of sapphires, she descended from the world of the gods like a mechanical stone.
Just after the middle watch of the night, she emitted blue rays and stood in the air near the bed at the entrance hall of the merchant’s palace.
When the merchant looked and saw her, the very moment he beheld her, she became unlovely and disagreeable to him.
Thus, conversing with her, he spoke the first verse:
“Who is she who has a dark complexion, yet is not unpleasant to behold?
Who are you, whose daughter are you, and how may we come to know you?”
In this context, "black" (*kāḷena*) means dark blue (*nīlena*). "By color" (*vaṇṇena*) refers to the color of the body, clothing, and ornaments.
As it was said, "Monks, beings come together according to their elements," and since this celestial maiden was immoral and lacking in virtue, she became unlovely to him at the very sight of her;
therefore he spoke thus. "Who are you? (*kā vā tvam*); the reading is also "And who are you? (*kā ca tvam*).
Having heard that, Kāḷakaṇṇī spoke this second verse:
“I am the daughter of the great king Virūpakkha, the fierce one;
I am Kāḷī, the unfortunate one, known by the wise as ‘Kāḷakaṇṇī.’”
“Grant us the space we have requested; let us dwell in your presence.
In that context, *caṇḍī* means “wrathful”; for because of her state of anger, they gave me the name Caṇḍī. *Alakkhikā* means “devoid of wisdom.
*Maṃ vidū* means “they know me thus” in the deva-world of the Four Great Kings. *Vasemu* means “let us dwell today.”
“May we dwell for one night in your presence; give me space on this seat and bed that has not been used.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
“In what kind of character and what kind of conduct do you place your trust in a man?”
“O Kāḷī, being asked by me, tell us; how may we know you?
Therein, “you dwell settled” means you dwell and are established with your mind.
Then, speaking of her own virtues, she spoke the fourth verse:
“Deceitful, spiteful, contentious, envious, stingy, and fraudulent—he is the man I desire, who lets what he has gained go to waste. The meaning of this is:
that man who does not recognize the virtues he himself has performed, who is a concealer of his own virtues, regarding anything [of his own]...
When a reason is stated, one grasps it with stubbornness, thinking, "How could I not know this?
Upon seeing something done by others, one acts with malice to counter-act it;

one is not satisfied when others obtain gain, and guarding one's own prosperity with the thought, "May others have no power, but let it belong to me alone," one [acts] toward another even as little as a blade of grass...

He does not give even a drop of water; being possessed of the characteristic of a miser, he does not give what belongs to himself to another, but consumes only what belongs to others by various means. Whatever grain or wealth he acquires, it perishes and does not remain;
he becomes a drunkard, a gambler, or a libertine, and whatever he gains...
"Only destruction [is certain]; this person endowed with these qualities is dear, beloved, and pleasing to me;
it is in such a one that I establish my heart.
She then recited the fifth, sixth, and seventh verses:
“One who is angry and resentful, one who is malicious and divisive,
one whose speech is thorny and harsh— he is more pleasing to me than that [other person].
A person who thinks, ‘I will do it today’ or ‘I will do it tomorrow,’ does not realize his own true welfare.”
Being reviled, he becomes angry; he despises his own bed.
"A man addicted to passion falls away from all his friends;
that man is dear to me, and toward him I am free from ill-will."

These [terms] should also be expanded upon according to this same method. However, the concise meaning here is as follows: "One who is prone to anger" (*kodhana*) is one who becomes angry even at a slight matter.
"One who harbors resentment" (*upanāhī*) is one who, having kept another's offense in his heart, acts to their detriment for a very long time.

"A slanderer" (*pisuṇa*) is one whose speech is divisive. "One who causes division" (*vibhedaka*) is one who breaks friendships even over a slight matter. "One with thorny speech" (*kaṇḍakavāca*) is one whose speech is full of malice.
"Harsh" means stubborn speech. "More pleasant" means that man was more pleasant and dearer to me even than before.
"Today or tomorrow" means: "This task should be done today, this tomorrow, and this on the third day, etc.";
in this way, he does not perceive nor understand his own purpose or his own duty. "Being admonished" means being exhorted. As for "sleeping":

"He despises" means that he oversteps and treats with contempt a superior person—one who is more excellent in terms of birth, lineage, family, locality, virtue, conduct, and qualities—saying, "What can you possibly do for me?
"Addicted to sport" means being continuously infatuated, overcome, and brought under the sway of the sensual pleasures such as forms and so forth.
"He reviles" means saying things such as, "What have you done for me? and so on, [and] by everyone...
“He falls away and declines from his friends. ‘Free from affliction’ means: when these persons endowed with such virtues are present, I am free from suffering and grief;
having obtained them, I dwell elsewhere without attachment.
Then, reproaching him, the Great Being spoke the eighth verse:
“Go away from here, Kāḷī; this does not exist among us.
Go to another country, to the market towns or the royal capitals. In that context, *apehi* means “go away.
*Netaṃ amhesu* means “this—such as your slandering and so forth, which causes you to be dear [to others]—does not exist even among us.”
"Is not found; does not exist. By saying "in a market town or in a royal capital," he indicates:
"Go to other market towns and other royal capitals; go to wherever we do not see him.
Having heard this, Kāḷakaṇṇī became distressed and spoke the following verse:
“I too know that; this does not exist among you.
There are those in the world who are unfortunate, yet they amass much wealth;
both I and my brother, O Deva, shall scatter it away.”
In that regard, "This is not in you" means: I too know this—that which causes me to be held in affection, such as hypocrisy (*makkha*) and so forth, by which I am possessed, does not exist in you.
"There are those in the world who are unfortunate" means there are others in the world who lack virtue (*sīla*) and wisdom (*paññā*).
"They heap up" means that even while being devoid of virtue and wisdom, they accumulate much [demerit] through these [faults] such as hypocrisy.

They collect wealth and form it into a hoard. "Both of us shall destroy it"—that is, both he and my brother, the divine son named Deva, having joined together, shall scatter and ruin that wealth which has been collected and set aside by them.
Furthermore, we have many celestial enjoyments and divine couches in our own heavenly world; you should give [some] to us.
Having said, "Whether it be so or not, what use have I for her?", he departed.
At the moment of his departure, the divine daughter Sirī arrived, adorned with golden-colored garments, ointments, and golden ornaments;
she released a yellow radiance at the gate of attendance and stood firmly upon the level ground with even feet.
She stood there full of reverence. Seeing her, the Great Being spoke the first verse:
“Who is this with celestial beauty, standing so firmly upon the earth?
Who are you, whose daughter are you, and how may we come to know you?”
In that context, "divine" means distinguished and supreme.
Having heard this, Sirī spoke the second verse:
"I am the daughter of the Great King, the glorious Dhatarattha."
“I am Sirī and Lakkhī; the wise call me Bhūripaññā (‘Abundant Wisdom’).
Grant us the space we request; let us dwell in your presence.
Therein, “Sirī and Lakkhī” means: I alone am the one named Sirī and Lakkhī, and no other. “Bhūripaññā” means...
"Know me" means they know me as one endowed with vast wisdom equal to the earth in the realm of the Four Great Kings.
"May we dwell in your presence" means: "May we dwell for a single night on a seat not used by you and on a bed not used by you;
grant me this opportunity."
Thereafter, the Bodhisatta said:
"In what character and what conduct do you place your trust in a man?
O Lakṣmī, being asked by me, tell me; how may we recognize you?"
“Whether it be cold or even heat, wind and sun, gadflies and serpents;
having overcome all hunger and thirst, he who is constantly devoted day and night—
does not let the opportunity that has arrived pass by— he is pleasing to me and may enter into my service.”
“Free from anger, possessing friends, generous, endowed with virtue, honest and upright;
Inclusive, gentle, and soft-spoken, even when attained to greatness, he conducts himself with humility.
Toward such a person, I feel great affection, just as the ocean loves its own color amidst the waves.”
“Whether toward friends or enemies, toward the superior, the equal, or even the inferior;
whether one is acting for their benefit or for their harm, in public or in private, one should always behave with kindness.
One should never utter harsh speech, thinking, ‘May I be such a person to him, whether he be dead or alive.’”
Having obtained any one of these, the person of little wisdom wallows in sensual beauty;
such a one, with a deluded appearance and wandering in unrighteousness, I avoid like a place of excrement.
"One creates fortune for oneself; one creates misfortune for oneself."
"For neither fortune nor misfortune is created by one for another.
This is the merchant's question; the reply concerns glory (*sirī*).
In that context, "stinging insects and snakes": *ḍaṃsa* refers to brown flies, or indeed all species of flies.
Here, "stinging insects" (ḍaṃsa) is what is intended. "Reptiles" (sarīsapa) refers to those of long species. "Stinging insects and reptiles" means stinging insects and reptiles;

when these stinging insects and reptiles are present. This is what is meant: that great merchant, whether in cold or heat, or in wind and sun, or when stinging insects and reptiles are present—even while being oppressed by these things such as cold and so forth, and by hunger—[remains steadfast].

"And having overcome thirst"—having thus overcome and conquered all these perils, regarding them as no more than blades of grass, he conducts himself by constantly engaging and applying himself to his own duties, both in farming, trade, and so forth, and in giving, virtue, and other such practices, day and night.

"And when the time has arrived"—at times such as the season for farming and so on, he performs farming and the like; at times for the relinquishing of wealth, the guarding of virtue, listening to the Dhamma, and so forth.

And he does not fail to achieve the welfare that brings happiness in both this life and the future—consisting of such things as the relinquishing of wealth—but performs it whenever the proper time for application arrives;
such a person is pleasing to me, and in him I take my abode.
"Not given to anger" means endowed with the patience of endurance. "A friend" means endowed with virtuous friends. "Generous" means devoted to the relinquishing of wealth.
A gatherer is one who performs the gathering of friends, the gathering of material goods, and the gathering of the Dhamma. "Gentle" means soft-spoken.

"Of mild speech" means one whose words are sweet. "Even when he has attained greatness, he remains humble" means that even though he has reached a high position or vast power, he is not puffed up by his fame;
he conducts himself with modesty and follows the advice of the wise. In him, indeed, one places trust. In him...
"I am a person. "I become vast" means I become not small; for he is the foundation for great glory.

"Like a wave upon the ocean's surface": just as a wave appearing one after another to those looking at the color of the ocean seems vast, so too does he illustrate that "I become vast" in relation to that person.

"Open" means both in one's presence and in one's absence. "He practices only conciliation" means that toward this person—whether a friend or any other such category—he practices and maintains the fourfold method of conciliation.
"One who does not speak harshly" means one who would never at any time speak a word of abuse, but is instead sweet-spoken.
"Toward him, whether dead or alive" means that I shall remain devoted to that person even when he is deceased and while he is still living, both in this world...
This shows that one will experience exactly the same [consequences] even in the next world. Regarding the phrase *etesaṃ yo*:

the meaning is that whichever person, having obtained even a single one of these aforementioned qualities—such as overcoming cold and so forth—neglects it, forgets it, and does not apply himself to it again.

As for *kantasiriṃ*, there are three readings: *kantā sirī*, *kantasiriṃ*, and *kantaṃ sirim*. According to these, the construction of the meaning is as follows: * *Kantā sirī*: "Glorious beauty is desired. * *Kantasiriṃ*: "One who possesses desired glory. * *Kantaṃ sirim*: "Desired glory. Based on these, this is the application of the meaning.
—The person who, having obtained glory (*siri*), neglects one or another of these qualities, thinking, "My beloved glory remains in its proper place";
or the person who, desiring beloved and dear glory, neglects one or another of these qualities after having obtained it;
or the person who, having obtained glory, [neglects] that which is beloved and pleasing among these qualities...

"He is negligent. "Lacking wisdom" means devoid of wisdom. "That one of arrogant appearance, wandering unevenly"—I, being of pure birth, avoid from afar that person of arrogant nature and haughty disposition who wanders unevenly through the divisions of bodily misconduct and so forth, just as one would avoid a pit of excrement.

"One person is the maker of another's fortune"—if this were so, there would be no such thing as one man being the maker of another's fortune or misfortune; rather, everyone makes their own fortune or misfortune by themselves.
Having thus welcomed the queen’s words, the Great Being said: "This seat and bed are not leftovers;
they are suitable for you alone. Sit upon the couch and lie down upon the bed. She—
Having stayed there, he departed at dawn and went to the Cātumahārājika heaven, where he first bathed in Lake Anotatta.
Because that bed had been used by the goddess Siri, it became known as the "Siri-bed" (Sirīsayaṇa).
This is the lineage of the Siri-bed; for this reason, it is called "Siri-bed" even up to the present day.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the goddess Sirī was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the merchant Suciparivāra was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka.
8. The Narrative of the Kukkuṭa Jātaka.
“With a roof of variegated leaves”: this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was dissatisfied with the religious life.

The Teacher asked that monk, “Why are you dissatisfied? and when he replied, “Because of defilement, Venerable Sir, upon seeing a woman adorned and prepared for a festival,” the Teacher said, “Monk, women indeed deceive and entice...”
"Having come under one's own power, they bring about one's destruction; they become like a greedy cat," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the forest in the womb of a hen and lived in the forest with a retinue of many hundreds of hens.
Not far from him, there also lived a certain she-cat. Having set aside—
Having deceived the remaining hens by means of a stratagem, she ate the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta did not fall into her grasp.
She thought: "This cock is exceedingly cunning; he does not know our own deceitfulness nor our skill in stratagems.
Once I have enticed him with the words, 'I shall be your wife,' and brought him under my control—"
"It is proper for you to eat. Having gone to the foot of the tree where he was sitting, she addressed him with words preceded by praise and entreated him, reciting the first verse:
"O bird with a variegated-feathered roof, with a copper-colored crest; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“Descend to the branch of the tree; I shall become your wife for nothing.
Therein, *sucittapattachadanā* means a covering made of beautiful leaves. *Mudhā* means without a price; that is, without receiving anything at all, I shall become your wife.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta thought, “All my kinsmen have been eaten by her; now she wishes to eat me after luring me with sweet words. I will send her away,” and he spoke the second verse:
“You are four-footed, O beautiful one; I am two-footed, O delightful one.
A deer and a bird, we are unattached; seek another husband.
In this context, “deer” refers to the female cat. “Unattached” means they are unfit to be husband and wife, unrelated, and that no such bond exists between them.
Having heard that, she thought, "This man is exceedingly deceitful; by whatever means possible, I shall deceive him and eat him. Having reflected thus, she spoke this third verse:
"I shall be a maiden for you, sweet-voiced and speaking kindly.
Win me with noble love; let me hear from you what you desire."
In that context, "a young maiden" (komārikā) means she says: "I have known no other man for all this time; I shall become your wife as a young maiden.
"Gentle and sweet-spoken" (mañjukā piyabhāṇinī) means: "I shall indeed be sweet-spoken and pleasant in my speech to you.
"Find me" (vinda maṃ) means: "Receive me. "With noble acquisition" (ariyena vedena) means: with a beautiful manner of receiving. For I too, from here...
"Previously I did not know the touch of a man, and you likewise do not know the touch of a woman;
thus, being naturally celibate, receive me, who am also celibate, with a faultless gift.
If you desire me, yet do not believe my word, then have a drum beaten throughout Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent, and proclaim: 'This is my slave-girl.'"
“Make me your own slave and take me,” he said.
Then the Bodhisatta, thinking, “It is right to frighten this man and drive him away,” spoke the fourth verse:
“O eater of carrion, drinker of blood, thief, slayer of chickens! ... [the rest of the verse follows] ...”
“You do not desire me as your husband through noble knowledge. In this context, “not through noble [knowledge]” means:
“You do not desire me as your husband by means of attaining the noble life of celibacy;
rather, you wish to devour me after having deceived me. Begone, you evil woman! Thus he drove her away. She, however, fled and departed.
Furthermore, he was not even able to look at her.
“In this way, having seen a wealthy man,
even a clever woman leads him away with gentle words, like a female cat leading a cock.”
“He who does not quickly comprehend a matter that has arisen falls under the power of his enemies and later regrets it.
But he who quickly understands a matter that has arisen— ”
"He is released from the oppression of enemies, like a cock from a cat"—these are the verses of one who has attained full enlightenment (*abhisambuddha*).
In this context, *catura* means "endowed with cleverness. *Nārī* refers to women. *Nenti* means they lead [him] under their own control.
*Biḷārī viya* means: just as that female cat strives to lead away that cock, so too do other women likewise lead him away.
"A matter that has arisen" means some kind of matter that has occurred.

"He does not wake up to it" means he does not know it according to its true nature and later regrets it. "Like a cock" means that just as that wise cock was released when called out, so too one is released from the oppression of enemies; this is the meaning.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. "At that time, I myself was the cock-king.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka.
9. The Commentary on the Dhammadhaja Jātaka.
"Practice the Dhamma, O kinsmen"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain hypocritical monk.
For then the Teacher said, "Monks, this man is not a hypocrite only now; in the past, too, he was a hypocrite," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a bird.
Having reached maturity, surrounded by a flock of birds, he lived on an island in the middle of the ocean.
Then, some merchants dwelling in the kingdom of Kāsi, having caught a directional crow (*disākāka*), set out upon the ocean in a ship; in the middle of the ocean, the ship was wrecked.
That directional crow went to that island and thought: "This is a great flock of birds; I shall perform a trick."
“Having made their eggs and chicks into food, it is fitting to eat them one by one.
Having descended, he stood in the midst of the flock of birds with his mouth wide open, placing one foot upon the ground.
When asked by the birds, “Who are you, Master? he replied, “I am named Dhammika. [The birds asked], “But why [do you stand] on one foot?”
"Are you standing? "When I set down my second foot, the earth cannot support me.
"Then why do you stand with your mouth open? "I eat no other food; I eat only wind.
Having spoken thus, he addressed those birds, saying, "I shall give you a teaching; listen to it," and for the sake of instructing them—
He spoke the first verse:
“Practice the Dhamma, O kinsmen; practice the Dhamma, may it be well with you.
One who lives according to the Dhamma dwells happily in this world and in the next.”
In this context, "practice the Dhamma" means: perform the Dhamma consisting of the divisions such as good conduct of body and so forth.
"Relatives" is how he addresses them. "Practice the Dhamma; may it be well for you": having practiced once, do not slacken; practice again and again, and thus it will be well for you.
"He sleeps in peace" is merely the conclusion of the teaching; however, one who practices the Dhamma dwells in happiness.
It is shown that he is happy in all postures—whether walking, sitting, or lying down.
The birds, unaware that this crow was speaking thus out of deceit to eat their eggs, praised that immoral one and spoke the second verse:
“Blessed indeed is this bird, a twice-born one of supreme righteousness!”
“Standing on one foot, he teaches only the Dhamma.
In this context, “only the Dhamma” means only the true nature (sabhāva). “Teaches” means he spoke.
The birds, having placed their trust in that immoral one, said: “It is said, Master, that you take no other food, but only wind...”
"You eat them; therefore, you must watch over our eggs and chicks," he said, and they went out for their prey.
When they had gone, that wicked one ate his fill of the eggs and chicks.
Then, when they were returning, he became very peaceful and composed, opening his mouth and standing on one leg. The birds returned to their young...
Not seeing [the thief], they cried out with a great clamor, "Who is eating? and did not harbor even the slightest suspicion toward that crow, thinking, "This crow is righteous.
Then one day the Great Being thought, "Previously there was no obstacle here at all;
this has arisen only since his arrival. It is right to investigate him. He [then spoke] to the birds...
Acting as if he were going along with them for their alms-round, he turned back and stood in a concealed place.
The crow, thinking "the birds have gone," became free from apprehension; he rose up, went away, ate the eggs and the chicks, and then returned, opened his mouth, and stood on one leg.
When the birds had gathered, the king of the birds assembled them all and addressed the flock of birds, saying:
"Today, while watching for an obstacle to my young ones, I saw this wicked crow eating; come, let us seize him!
Having surrounded him and said, "If he flees, you must catch him," he spoke the remaining verses:
“You do not understand his virtue, yet you praise him without knowing it;
having eaten both eggs and young chicks, he speaks of ‘Dhamma, Dhamma.
One thing he says with his voice, another he does with his body.”
Neither by speech nor by body is one established in that Dhamma.
"One who is friendly in speech but whose mind is impenetrable, like a black snake hidden in a well;
such a person, though bearing the banner of the Dhamma, is difficult for a foolish man to know when he goes among villages and market towns."
“Tear at this with your beaks and wings; tear at this with your feet!
Destroy this corpse, for it is not worthy of living together.
In that context, *nāssa sīlam* means “it has no virtue. *Añaññāya* means “not having known. *Bhutvā* means “having eaten. *Vācāya*... [text fragment]
"And not with the body": for this person practices the Dhamma only by means of speech, but does not perform it with the body.
"He is not resolved upon that Dhamma": therefore it should be understood that while he speaks the Dhamma, he is not resolved upon it;
he is not resolved upon that Dhamma. "Gentle in speech" means soft in his words. "Difficult to fathom in mind" means difficult to fathom by the mind.
"Difficult to enter; uneven. "Covered" means covered by that very hole in which he lies. "Hole-dweller" means one who dwells in a hole.
"Dharma-bannered" means one who wanders having made the dharma of good conduct his banner.
"Virtuous in villages and market towns" means he is virtuous, excellent, and esteemed in both villages and market towns. "Hard to know" means that such a person is of immoral character.
One whose actions are concealed cannot be known by a foolish person of ignorance.
"Cimanti" means with their own feet; "viheṭhatha" means strike and kill. "Chava" means wretched. "Nāya" means:
"This one does not deserve to dwell in the same place as we do."
Having spoken thus, the chief bird leaped up himself and struck his head with his beak; the remaining birds struck him with their beaks, claws, feet, and wings. He met his death right there.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the deceitful crow was the deceitful bhikkhu of the present, while the king of the birds was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Dhammadhaja Jātaka, the ninth.
[385] 10. The Commentary on the Nandiya-miga-rāja-jātaka:
"If you go, O Brahmin," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who supported his mother.
For the Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you support a householder? and he replied, "It is true."
When he said, "Venerable sir," and [the Buddha] asked, "What do you have? and he replied, "My mother and father, venerable sir," [the Buddha] said, "Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
You preserve the lineage of the ancient wise ones; for the ancient wise ones, even after being reborn in the animal realm, gave their lives for their mothers and fathers.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while the King of Kosala was ruling in the kingdom of Kosala at Sāketa, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a deer.
Upon reaching maturity, he became a deer named Nandiya; endowed with virtuous conduct, he supported his parents. At that time, the King of Kosala was solely devoted to hunting.
Without allowing his subjects to perform agricultural work or other labors, he went out every day with a vast retinue.
He went out on a hunt. The people gathered together and said, "Sirs, this king is cutting short our work;

even our household livelihood is being ruined. What if we were to surround the Ārjuna grove park, set up a gate, dig a perimeter trench, plant grass [as a barrier], and then enter the forest with sticks, clubs, and other weapons in hand, [hiding] in the thickets?"
"Let us strike the deer, drive them out, surround them, and like cattle, lead them into the park with a fence;
then, having closed the gate and informed the king, we shall do our work," they deliberated.
"This is a good plan," they said, and becoming of one mind, they prepared the park, entered the forest, and surrounded an area of about one *yojana*.
At that moment, Nandiya had taken his parents and was lying on the ground in a small thicket.
People, with various shields and weapons in their hands, pressed arm against arm and surrounded the thicket.
Then some deer, looking about, entered the thicket. Seeing them, Nandiya thought, "Today, having renounced my life..."
Thinking, "It is right to give my life for my parents," he rose, paid homage to his mother and father, and said:
"Mother and Father, these people will enter this thicket and see all three of us. You should preserve your lives by some means;
life is better for you. Having given you the gift of life, I shall stand at the edge of the thicket with the people."
“As soon as the thicket is struck, I shall emerge; then, thinking ‘there will be only one deer in this small thicket,’ they will not enter the thicket.
You must remain vigilant! Having thus asked his parents for forgiveness, he stood ready to depart.
Then, while the people stood around the edge of the thicket and raised a great clamor, [he entered] the thicket.
As soon as it was struck, he emerged from there. Thinking, "There must be only one deer here," they did not enter the thicket.
Then Nandiya went and entered among the deer. The men surrounded them, led all the deer into the park, closed the gate, informed the king, and returned to their respective places.
From then on, the king himself would go and, having pierced a deer, would send someone else with the command, "Bring it here," and have it brought back.
The deer established a rotation; when a deer’s turn arrived, he would stand aside, and they would pierce and capture him.
Nandiya, however, drank water from the lotus pond and ate grass, yet his turn had not yet come.
He reached [the end]. Then, after the lapse of many days, his parents, desiring to see him, thought:
"Our son, King Nandiya the Deer, possesses the strength of a nāga and is endowed with fortitude;
if he is alive, he will surely leap over the fence and come to see us. We shall send him a message. Having thus reflected, they stood near the path.
Seeing a certain brahmin, they asked him in human speech, "Noble sir, where are you going?
When he replied, "To Sāketa," they sent a message to their son and spoke this first verse:
"If you go, brahmin, to the Ajjuna forest at Sāketa; [then speak thus to my son...]"
"You should speak to the one named Nandiya, our own biological son;
your mother and father are old, and they wish to see you.
The meaning of this is: "If you, O Brahmin, go to Sāketa, there is a park in Sāketa called the Ajjanavana..."
“There is a deer there named our son Nandiya; you should tell him:
‘Your parents are old and wish to see you before they die.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he went to Sāketa, entered the park on the following day, and [saw] the deer Nandiya.
“Who is it? he asked. The deer came forward, stood near him, and said, “It is I. The brahmin related the matter to him.
Having heard this, Nandiya said, “Brahmin, I would go; I would not fail to leap over the enclosure.
However, I have eaten the fodder, drink, and food belonging to the king, and that stands as a debt to me. And for these...”
"I have lived for a long time in the midst of these deer; it is not fitting for me to depart without having ensured the safety of both the king and them, and without displaying my own power.
But when my turn arrives, I shall ensure their safety and return in well-being. Proclaiming this matter, he spoke two verses:
“I have already eaten the fodder and the food and drink of the king;
I cannot, O Brahmin, endure to eat that royal alms-food.
I shall turn my gaze toward the arrow-heads of that king.”
"Then, happy and liberated, may I see my mother.
In this context, "pasturage" refers to the fodder provided in various places. "Drink and food" refers to water and the remaining grass.
"That royal provision" means that which belongs to the king, gathered together and formed into a single mass by way of being brought together. "To eat" means...
"To eat what has been poorly eaten. For one who fails to accomplish the king’s business is said to "eat what has not been eaten";

thus he says, "I am not able to eat in such a manner. Here, "Brāhmaṇa, be able" (*brāhmaṇa mussaha*) is an address, "Brāhmaṇa," with the letter *m* being used for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
“O Brahmin, when my own turn arrives, having fastened an arrow,
I will expose my own great flank to the king who has come out from the deer herd and is standing to one side,
saying, ‘Pierce me, Great King!’— I will expose it, I will offer it up. Thus I shall be happy.”
"Delivered," he thought, "I am now delivered from the fear of death; happy and free from suffering, and permitted by the king, perhaps I might even see my mother.
Having heard this, the brahmin departed. Later, on the day of his release, the king came to the park with a great retinue.
The Great Being stood to one side. The king, thinking, "I shall pierce the deer," drew his crescent-headed arrow.
He drew near. The Great Being, instead of fleeing as others do when terrified by the fear of death, remained fearless;
making loving-kindness his forerunner, he lay down on his broad flank and stood perfectly still.
By the power of his loving-kindness, the king was unable to discharge his arrow. The Great Being said, "Why, Great King, [do you not release] the arrow?"
“You have not released it; release it! he said. “I am unable, O King of Beasts,” he replied. “In that case, Great King, recognize the virtue of those who possess virtue.
Then the king, gaining confidence in the Bodhisatta, cast aside his bow and said, “Even this mindless scrap of wood and arrow recognizes your virtue;
yet I, though possessing a mind and being a human being, do not recognize your virtue.”
“I do not know, O King of Beasts; forgive me, and I grant you safety,” he said.
“Great King, you have granted me safety for now, but what will become of this herd of deer in the park? “I grant them safety as well.
Thus, according to the method described in the Nigrodha Jātaka, the Great Being [granted safety] to all the deer in the forest and to the birds dwelling in the sky.
Having granted safety to the aquatic fish and established the king in the five precepts, he said:
"Great King, it is fitting for a king to abandon going on wrong paths and to rule his kingdom righteously and equitably, without violating the ten duties of a king.
"Generosity, virtue, renunciation, Uprightness, gentleness, and austerity;"
“Absence of anger and non-cruelty, patience and non-opposition—
‘Thus I see these wholesome qualities established within myself;
from that, joy arises in me, and no small measure of gladness.’”
When he had thus taught the duties of a king by means of verses, he stayed for a few days in the presence of the king; then,
having caused a golden drum to be beaten throughout the city to proclaim the granting of safety to all beings, and saying, "Be heedful,
O Great King," he departed to visit his parents.
“In former times, I was a king of deer in the dwelling place of Kosala;
by name I was Nandiya, a handsome four-footed creature.
A hunter came there to kill me in the Ajuna forest.”
Having strung my bow and fixed an arrow to it, O Kosalan,
I aimed at the sight of that king’s razor-headed shafts;
thus I was released and happy, having come to see my mother.
These are the three verses of the Fully Enlightened One.
Therein, "in the abode of Kosala" means in the dwelling place of King Kosala;
the meaning is "in the forest in his vicinity. "In the grove" means in a park granted for the dwelling of deer. "Having committed an offense" means...
"Having joined together with Jiyā, having harnessed [the chariot]"—this is the meaning. "Sannayha" means having harnessed, having yoked. "Odahim" means I fastened [the reins].

"I have come to see my mother"—this is merely a formal opening of the teaching; the meaning is: "Having taught the Dhamma to the king and having caused the golden drum to be beaten for the sake of granting fearlessness to all beings, I have come to see my parents."
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the parents were members of a great royal family;
the Brahmin was Sāriputta; the king was Ānanda; and I myself was Nandiya, the king of the deer.
The Tenth: The Commentary on the Nandiya-miga-rāja-jātaka.
The First Chapter: The Section on the Unobstructed.
2. The Section on Kharaputta.
[386] 1. The Commentary on the Kharaputtajātaka.
“It is said that they spoke thus in truth”—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the seduction of an ex-wife.
For the Teacher questioned that bhikkhu, saying: “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are disenchanted? and so forth.
When he replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” [the Teacher] asked, “By whom were you made despondent? When he said, “By my former wife,” [the Teacher] said, “This woman has acted to your detriment;
formerly, too, by relying on her you were about to enter a fire and die, but by relying on wise men you regained your life.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when a king named Senaka was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was serving as the King of the Gods (Sakka).
At that time, King Senaka had a friendship with a certain Nāga king. It is said that this Nāga king would emerge from the Nāga realm and wander about on land seeking food.
Then, some village boys, seeing him, cried out, "This is a snake!"
They struck him with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons. Then, as the king was going to the park to play, he saw them and asked, "What are these boys doing?
Upon hearing that they were striking a snake, he said, "Do not strike;
drive them away," and had them dispersed. Having regained his life, the Naga king went to the Naga realm and took many jewels.
At the hour of midnight, having entered the king’s bedchamber and presented those jewels, he said, "Great King, it is by depending on you that I have obtained my livelihood.
Having thus established a friendship with the king, he went again and again and visited the king.
Among his own Naga maidens, he [chose] one Naga maiden who was unsated with sensual pleasures for the purpose of guarding her.
Having placed him near the king, [the teacher] gave him a spell, saying, "When you do not see this [king], then you should recite this mantra.
One day, he went to the park and played in the lotus pond together with a young Naga maiden.
A young female nāga, having seen a certain water-snake, cast off her own form and engaged in unrighteous conduct with it.
Not seeing her, the king recited his spells, asking, "Where has she gone? Upon seeing her committing the impropriety, he struck her with a bamboo splinter.
She became enraged, went from there to the nāga-abode, and was asked, "Why have you come?"
When questioned, she pointed to the wound, saying, "Your companion struck me on the back even though I would not accept his word.

Without knowing the truth of the matter, the Nāga king summoned four young Nāgas and sent them forth, saying, "Go, enter Senaka’s bedchamber and destroy him like chaff with the breath from your nostrils. They went there...
While the king was reclining on his royal couch, they entered the inner chamber.
At the very moment of their entry, the king said to the queen, "Do you know, my lady, where the young Naga maiden went? "I do not know, Your Majesty," she replied.
"Today, while we were sporting in our lotus pond, she abandoned her own form and [became] a water-snake..."
"He engaged in improper conduct with her; then, for the sake of instructing him, saying 'Do not do this,' I struck him with a bamboo scraper.
Fearing that she might go to the Nāga realm and break our friendship by telling my companion something else, I was seized with fear.
Upon hearing this, the young Nāgas turned back from there and went to the Nāga realm.

They reported this matter to the Nāga king. Overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he came to the king’s bedchamber at that very moment, explained the situation, and asked for forgiveness.

Saying, "This is my penance," he gave him the spell known as *Sabbarutajānana* (the Knowledge of All Sounds), saying, "Great King, this spell is priceless; if you were to give this spell to another, [it would bring ruin]."
“Having given [the kingdom], you should enter the fire and die,” he said. The king accepted, saying, “Very well.
From that time on, he could even distinguish the sound of ants.
One day, while he was sitting on the great terrace eating solid food with honey and molasses, a drop of honey [fell].
A drop of molasses and a piece of cake fell upon the ground. A single ant, seeing this, cried out as she wandered about, "The honey-trough on the king’s great terrace has been broken!
The cart of molasses and the cart of cakes have been overturned! Eat the honey, molasses, and cakes!
Then the king, hearing her cry, laughed. Standing near the king—
The queen thought, "What indeed did the king see that he laughed? At that time, after the husband had eaten solid food, bathed, and sat upon his couch, a fly appeared.
He said to her, "Come, my dear, let us take delight in the pleasure of the defilements. Then she said to him, "Wait a moment, husband;
now they will bring perfumes for the King. While he is anointing himself, at the soles of his feet—"
"The fragrant powder will fall upon me; having rolled there, I shall become fragrant, and then, reclining upon the king's back, we shall take our pleasure," she said.
Hearing that sound as well, the king laughed. The queen thought again, "What did he see that made him laugh?
Again, while the king was eating his evening meal, a single grain of rice fell to the ground.
The queen’s husband was the king. An ant cried out, “The food-cart at the royal palace has broken; eat the food!
Hearing this, the king laughed again. The queen, taking a golden spoon and serving the king, thought to herself, “Is it because he sees me that the king laughs?”
When she had ascended the bed with the king and was about to lie down, she asked, "For what reason, O King, did you laugh?
He replied, "What business have you with the reason for my laughter? Yet, being pressed again and again, he spoke.
Then she said to him, "Give me the secret of your knowledge," and although he refused, saying, "It cannot be given," she continued to press him repeatedly.
The king said, "If I give this mantra to you, I shall die. "Even if it means dying, give it to me, Your Majesty," she replied.
The king, being under the sway of his wife, consented, saying, "Very well. Thinking, "I will enter the fire after giving the mantra to her," he set out for the park by chariot.
At that moment, Sakka, surveying the world, saw this situation and thought, "This foolish king is going to enter the fire because of a woman;

I shall give him his life. Taking Sujā, the daughter of an Asura, he came to Bārāṇasī, turned her into a she-goat, and having himself become a goat, he resolved, "Let the great multitude not see us," and [approached] the king.
It stood in front of the chariot. Only the king and the horses harnessed to the chariot saw it; no one else saw it.
For the sake of initiating a conversation, the goat acted as if he were engaging in sexual intercourse with a she-goat right in front of the chariot.
Seeing this, one of the horses harnessed to the chariot said, "Friend King Goat, formerly..."
“We have heard that fools are indeed shameless, but we did not see it;
yet you commit an improper act in a secluded, hidden place right before us who are so many in number, and you feel no shame.
What we previously heard accords with what we have now seen. Having said this, he recited the first verse:
“Truly, the wise say this: ‘The goat is a fool.
Behold the fool who, while performing a secret act, does not realize he is being exposed.

In this context, *vasta* means a goat (*aja*). The wise—those endowed with knowledge—call him a fool, and they speak the truth indeed. *Passa* is an address meaning “behold”; its sense is “look, for indeed. *Na bujjhati* means he does not know that it is improper to act in such a manner.
Having heard that, Aja spoke these two verses:
“You too, my friend Kharaputta, are a fool; know this for certain:
For you are encircled by a rope, with your neck bent and your mouth hung down.”
“Furthermore, good horse, you are foolish in that, though set free, you do not flee;
and even more foolish than you, good Senaka, is he who carries you.
In this context, “you too, good horse” means: “Good steed, you are indeed more foolish than I. “The son of a donkey” refers to him.
It seems he was born as a donkey; that is why he spoke thus to him. "Vijānahi" means: "Know this:
'I am indeed a fool. "Parikkhitto" means: "encircled by the yoke around the neck. "Vaṅkoṭṭho" means: "having a crooked lip.
"Ohitomukho" means: "with the mouth covered by a muzzle. "Yo mutto na palāyasi" means: "you who, having been released from the chariot, do not flee."
That you did not flee into the forest at the time of urination—that failure to flee is another instance of your childishness;
and he who carries Senaka is even more childish than you.
The king understood the conversation between those two, and therefore, listening to them, he drove the chariot slowly. Having heard his words, the horse spoke a fourth verse once again:
“Is it, friend, that I am a fool, as you, O King, understand?
Or by what reason is Senaka a fool? Tell me that when asked.
In this context, *yaṃ* is a nominative singular used in the sense of the instrumental case. *Nū* is a particle used in the sense of tradition or hearsay. This is what is meant:
"Friend King Aja, you should understand the reason why I am a fool because of my status as an animal;
this is something you are capable of knowing. For it is precisely because I am an animal that I am a fool, and therefore you speak quite rightly when you call me 'the son of a she-ass' and so forth.
But for what reason is this King Senaka a fool? When asked, please explain that reason to me."
Having heard that, Aja spoke the fifth verse, explaining: “He who,
having attained the highest goal, reveals it to his wife,
will thereby abandon himself, and she shall no longer be his.”
In this context, "the supreme goal" refers to the end of knowing all sounds—that is, the mastery of mantras. "By that" means by reason of that gift of mantras;
having given it, he who enters the fire will abandon himself, and she will no longer be his wife.
Therefore, he is even more foolish than you, for he is unable to protect the glory he has obtained.
Having heard his words, the king said, "Aja, even if you were to bring about our safety, it would be you alone who would do so;
therefore, tell us first what ought to be done. Then King Aja replied to him, "Great King, among these beings there is nothing dearer than oneself;
for the sake of a single beloved object, one might even destroy oneself and lose one's reputation."
"It is not right to abandon him," he said, and then spoke the sixth verse:
"O Lord of Men, such a person as that does not truly love; having disregarded his own self, he pursues what is dear.
One's own self is better than anything else, and it is only through one who has cultivated the true goal that what is dear can later be obtained."
In this context, *piyamme* means "dear to me," or rather, the reading is simply *piyam*. This is what is meant:

O Lord of Men, such a person as yourself, established in the height of glory, does not—on account of even a single dear object—despise the self (*attaṃ*), cast aside the self, and then pursue those dear things. Why is that? Because the self alone is better, and the self is supreme.

Because one’s own self is better, more excellent, and supreme by a hundredfold and a thousandfold; it is the highest good and the highest excellence even compared to any other beloved object—this is the meaning.
For here, the particle *ca* should be understood as a grammatical particle (*nipāta*) used in the sense of *pi*.
It is possible for those who are beloved to be obtained later by a man who is accomplished in his purpose, that is, by one who has increased in purpose and is endowed with glory.
"Later, beloved ones can indeed be found; for their sake, one must not destroy oneself.
Thus did the Great Being give counsel to the king. The king, being pleased, asked, "O Aja King, from where have you come?
"I am Sakka, Great King; out of compassion for you, I have come to deliver you from death. "O King of the Gods, I..."
"I told her, 'I will give you the spell,' but now what shall I do? "Great King, there is no need for the destruction of either of you.
Say, 'This is the practice of the craft,' and have him struck with a few blows;
by this means he will not take it. The king agreed, saying, "Very well. The Great Being gave this advice to the king.
Having given it, he went back to his own place. The king, having gone to the park, summoned the queen and said, "Will you take the spell, lady?
"Yes, Your Majesty," she replied. "In that case, let us perform the preliminary ritual. "What is the ritual?
"It is not permitted to make a sound while a hundred blows are being struck upon the back. Out of greed for the spell, she consented, saying, "Very well."
The king summoned the executioner, had him seize her with a whip, and ordered him to strike her on both sides.
She endured two or three blows, but thereafter she cried out, "I have no need for the charm!
Then the king, thinking, "You wish to kill me in order to obtain the charm," had his back flayed and released her. From that time on—
From that point on, he was unable to speak further.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). At that time, the king was the discontented bhikkhu, and the queen was [the present queen].
The former wife was the horse Sāriputta, while Sakka was none other than myself.
This concludes the first commentary, the Kharaputtajātakavaṇṇanā.
[387] 2. Sūcijātakavaṇṇanā (The Needle Jātaka Commentary)
"Neither harsh nor cruel"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the perfection of wisdom.
The story will be revealed in the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka. At that time, however, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus, saying, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Tathāgata was wise and skilled in means," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a smith’s family in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Upon reaching maturity, he became a master of his craft. His parents, however, were poor;
not far from their village was another smith’s village consisting of a thousand huts, where there lived a chief smith with a thousand assistants who was a favorite of the king.

He was wealthy and possessed of great riches, and he had a daughter who possessed supreme beauty, resembling a celestial nymph (devaccharā) and endowed with the marks of a "Beauty of the Land" (janapadakalyāṇī).
People from neighboring villages, having gone to that village for the purpose of hiring laborers for axes, hatchets, plows, sickles, and other tools, would mostly see that young woman;
and having returned to their own respective villages, while sitting or standing in their dwellings and so forth—

They described her beauty to him. Having heard this, the Bodhisatta became captivated by the sound of it and, thinking, "I shall make her my foot-maid," he took a superior-quality iron, fashioned a fine, thick needle, pierced it with a hook, and cast it into the water.
He then made another similar casing for her and pierced it with the hook as well.
In this manner, he made seven sheaths for it; one should not ask, "How did he do it?
For, due to the greatness of the Bodhisattvas' knowledge, their undertaking is always successful.
He placed that needle in a tube, secured it with a cork, went to that village, asked for the street where the head of the workmen lived, and having gone there, stood at the door.
Standing there and praising the needle, saying, "Who wishes to buy such a needle as this from my hand for its price?", he stood near the door of the chief smith's house and recited the first verse:
"Akakkasaṃ apharusaṃ, kharadhotaṃ supāsiyaṃ; [It is smooth, not harsh, well-polished, and easy to handle.]
“Who would wish to buy a needle that is fine and sharp-pointed?
This is its meaning: because it lacks any film, blemish, or rust, it is not rough; because it is well-polished, it is not harsh;
because it has been washed with a hard stone, it is “hard-washed”; and because it is provided with a beautiful, well-bored eye, [it is excellent].
"Who wishes to buy from my hand this needle, well-guarded, fine because of its smoothness,
and sharp-pointed because of the keenness of its tip?
Having spoken thus, and further describing it, he recited the second verse:
“Who would wish to buy a needle that has been well-polished, well-whetted, gradually rounded, thick at the head, and stiff?
In this context, *sumajjañca* means well-polished with *kuruvindaka* powder. *Supāsañca* means [polished] with a smooth whetting-stone.
“Pierce the beautiful noose. That which, when struck, enters into the frame with a heavy blow is called “ghanaghātimā”;
the meaning is “of such a kind. “Paṭithaddhaṃ” means stiff and not soft.
At that moment, the young girl [placed her father], who had finished his breakfast, upon a small couch in order to allay his distress.
While fanning him with a palm-leaf fan as he lay there, she heard the Bodhisatta’s sweet voice;
struck in her heart as if by a lump of raw meat, and as if the heat of her distress were extinguished by a thousand jars of water, she thought:
"Who indeed is this who sells needles with such an exceedingly sweet sound in the smiths' village? By what business has he come? I shall find out."
Saying "No," she set aside her palm-leaf fan, went out from the house, stood in the outer porch, and conversed with him.
For the wishes of Bodhisattas are indeed fulfilled; he had come to that village for her very sake.
And as she was conversing with him, she said, "Young man, the inhabitants of the entire kingdom [have come] to this village for the purpose of needles and other such items..."
“They are coming; out of foolishness you wish to sell needles in a blacksmith’s village.
Even if you were to praise the quality of the needle all day long, no one will take a needle from your hand.
If you wish to obtain a profit, go to another village,” he said, and then spoke these two verses:
“From here they are spread out—needles and fish-hooks;
who is this that wishes to sell a needle in a village of smiths?
From here go forth weapons, various and manifold crafts.”
“Who is this who, in the smith’s village, wishes to sell needles?”— in this context,
“from here now” means that from this smith’s village in this kingdom,
needles, fish-hooks, and other implements are now being spread abroad and exported; they go forth, spreading out toward various directions.
"Koyanti: 'While this is so, who is there in this smith's village who wishes to sell needles?
'Caravans (satthāni)': various kinds of caravans going toward Bārāṇasī depart from here. 'Diverse and manifold (vividhā puthū)':
many diverse types of crafts belonging to the inhabitants of the entire kingdom proceed by means of the very implements taken from here."
Having heard her words, the Bodhisatta said, "Lady, you speak thus out of ignorance, not knowing," and spoke these two verses:
"A needle in the village of smiths may be sold by one who understands;
Only teachers know the work, whether it is well-done or ill-done."
“If your father, Bhaddā, had known this needle was made by me, and if he were to invite me to whatever other wealth there is in his house.
In this passage, a reversal of case endings has been made regarding the word *sūciṃ*. This is what is meant: [it refers to] that which is called a needle, by one who is discerning and wise.
It should be sold by a man right there in the smith’s village. For what reason? Only the teachers know whether a craft is well-done or poorly done;
only the teachers of each respective craft know whether the work in that particular craft is well-done or poorly done.
Therefore, if I were to go to the village of householders who do not understand the smith’s craft, how could they judge the quality of my needle—whether it is well-made or poorly made?
"How shall I make my strength known? But rather, I shall make my strength known in this village. Thus the Bodhisatta praised his own strength with this verse.
And as for the phrase "you should invite me," [he said]: "O lady, if your father were to see this needle made by me, thinking, 'It is like this...'"
Or he might know: "Thus it has been arranged," and he might invite me by saying, "I give this daughter of mine to you as a servant for your feet; take her.
Or he might invite me with whatever other wealth there is in the house, whether animate or inanimate. There is also a reading: "And whatever belongs to him."
And the meaning is that whatever other wealth he had in his house [was given].
Having heard all their talk, the head of the workmen called his daughter, saying "Amma," and asked, "With whom are you conversing?
She replied, "Father, there is a man who sells needles; I am conversing with him."
“In that case, summon him. She went and summoned him. The Bodhisatta entered the house, paid homage to the chief smith, and stood to one side. Then he asked him, “In which village do you live?
“I am a resident of such-and-such a village, the son of such-and-such a smith. “Why have you come here? “To sell needles. “Bring me a needle.”
“Let us see them. The Bodhisatta, wishing to manifest his own skill in the midst of everyone, said, “Is it not better to look upon [the work] in the midst of all rather than looking at it alone?
He replied, “Very well, dear one,” and having summoned all the smiths, surrounded by them, he said, “Bring it, dear one; we shall see your needle. “Teacher,…”
“Have one official and a bronze bowl filled with water brought here,” he said. He had them brought.
The Bodhisatta drew the needle-tube out from his earlobe and gave it to him. The chief of the craftsmen then drew the needle out and asked, “Dear sir, is this the needle?
“This is not the needle; this is the sheath. As he examined it, he could find neither the end nor the tip.
He saw it. The Bodhisatta had it brought, removed the sheath with his fingernail, and showing it to the great crowd, saying, "This is the needle;
this is the sheath," he placed the needle in the teacher's hand and the sheath at his feet.
When the teacher again said, "I think this is the needle," he replied, "This too is merely the sheath for a needle," and striking it with his fingernail, he [revealed] them in succession.
Having placed it at the feet of the chief smith, he set the needle in his hand, saying, "This is the needle.
A thousand smiths snapped their fingers and raised their robes in applause.
Then the chief smith asked him, "Dear boy, what is the power of this needle? "Teacher, it is powerful," he replied.
“Have a man lift up the anvil, place a water bowl beneath the anvil, and strike this needle through the middle of the anvil.
Having done so, he struck the needle with the point in the middle of the anvil.
It pierced right through the anvil and emerged from the surface of the water by no more than the breadth of a hair, neither upward nor downward.

Without being cast, it landed sideways. All the smiths, snapping their fingers and raising their garments in a thousand gestures, cried out, "For all this time, we have never heard of such things as 'smiths' even by report!
The chief smith summoned his daughter and, right there in the midst of the assembly, said, "This young woman belongs to you alone."

"It is suitable," he said, and having poured water [over the hand], he gave it to him. Later, upon the passing of the village headman of the smiths, he became the headman of the smiths in that village.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the daughter of the headman of the smiths was Rāhulamātā, and the wise son of the smith was none other than myself."
The second commentary: The Story of the Needle-Jātaka [388].
3. The Commentary on the Tuṇḍila-Jātaka: "Navachannake" (In the New Hut).
This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was afraid of death.
He related [this]. It is said that a son of good family living in Sāvatthī, having gone forth in the Buddha’s teaching, was terrified of death.

Upon hearing even the slightest rustling of a branch, the falling of a stick, the sound of a bird or a quadruped, or anything else of that sort, he would wander about trembling like a quail pierced in the belly, overcome by the fear of death. The bhikkhus...
In the Dhamma Hall, they raised this discussion: "Friends, it is said that such-and-such a bhikkhu is so afraid of death that upon hearing even the slightest sound, he trembles and flees.

Since death is certain for these beings and life is uncertain, should one not indeed attend to that very fact with wise attention? The Teacher approached and asked: "Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing now?"
Having asked, "Sitting for what discussion? and being told, "For this one," he had that bhikkhu summoned and said, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are afraid of death?
When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," [the Buddha] said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now;
even in the past he was indeed afraid of death," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a sow.
When the sow’s pregnancy had matured, she gave birth to two sons. One day, taking them with her, she lay down in a certain pit.
Now, there was an old woman living in a village near the gate of Benares who, having filled her carrying-pole with cotton from a cotton field—
Taking a stick, she came along striking the ground. Hearing that sound, the sow fled, abandoning her two young ones out of fear of death.
When the old woman saw the two piglets, she conceived the notion that they were her own children;
she placed them in a basket, brought them home, and gave the elder the name Mahātuṇḍila and the younger Cūḷatuṇḍila.

Having taken them in, she nourished them like her own children. Later, when they had grown up and their bodies became stout, the old woman was told, "Give these two to us for a price," yet she would say to no one, "They are my sons," and would not give them away.
Then, during a festival, some rogues who were drinking liquor found that their meat supply was exhausted; searching about, they wondered, "Where indeed shall we obtain meat?"
Having learned that there were pigs in the old woman’s house, they took some money, went there, and said, “Mother, take this money and give us one pig.
She refused, saying, “Enough, dear sons; these are my children. There is no such thing as giving away a child to those who buy meat for the purpose of eating it. The rogues said, “Mother, …”
"Boars are not the sons of human beings; give them to us. Although they entreated her again and again, they did not receive them.
Then, having made her drink strong liquor until she was intoxicated, they said, "Mother, what will you do with these boars?
Take the money and provide for yourself," and they placed coins in her hand.
Taking the kahāpaṇas, she said, "Father, I am unable to give Mahātuṇḍila; but take Cūḷatuṇḍila instead.
"Where is he? "He is going there; give him a call. "I do not see any food.
The rogues had a bowl of rice brought for the price. The old woman took it and placed it in the pig trough set at the door.
Having filled it, he stood near the granary. About thirty rogues with nooses in their hands also stood right there.
The old woman called out to him, saying, "Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, come here!
Hearing this, Mahātuṇḍila thought, "For all this time my mother has never before called out to Cūḷatuṇḍila; she calls to me first. Surely..."
“Today, fear will arise for us,” he realized. He addressed his younger brother:
“Dear son, my mother is calling for you; go and find out what it is.
Having gone out and seen them standing near the rice-bag, [the younger brother] thought, “Today my death has arrived,” and, terrified by the fear of death, he turned back.
Trembling, he came into the presence of his brother but was unable to stand still; shaking, he wandered about.
Seeing him, Mahātundaḷa asked, "Dear son, why are you trembling and wandering about today? You keep looking toward the entrance;
what is it that you are doing? Speaking of the matter he had seen, he recited the first verse:
“Freshly harvested grain is being given; the full trough stands before our mistress.
Though there are many people here with food in their hands, it does not occur to me to eat.
In this context, “freshly harvested grain is being given” means, brother, that formerly we had only broken rice gruel or burnt rice.
"Or else it was given [before], but today a gift of new cloth and ninefold requisites is being given.
'The bowl is full' means this bowl of ours for rice is full of pure rice. 'The mistress stands there' means our noble lady also stands near her.
'Many people' means not only the noble lady, but many other people as well, including those with dogs, are standing there. "No..."
"And yet it does not occur to me"—this means that even though they are standing right here, this food does not occur to me to eat; it does not please me.
Having heard that, the Great Being said, "Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, it seems my mother is actually raising pigs right here."
"For the sake of which you have supported [me], that purpose has today reached its fulfillment;
do not worry," he said, and then, teaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice and the grace of a Buddha, he spoke these two verses:

"You are trembling, you are wandering, you seek a refuge; you are without protection—where will you go? You are without a protector, without a support, and without a shelter; you are alone, friendless, and without a refuge."
“Eat without anxiety, Tuṇḍila, for we have been nourished for the sake of your flesh.
“Plunge into the lake that is free from mud; wash away all sweat and grime;
take up a fresh ointment whose fragrance never fades.”
In this context, "you tremble and wander" means you are terrified by the fear of death and, exhausted by that very thing, you wander about.
"You seek a shelter" means you look for a refuge. "You are without protection, dear one" means: formerly our mother was our resort, but today she has abandoned us without regard;
where will you go now? "Ogaha" means a plunge (ogāha), or rather, this is simply another reading for the same word.
"Carry away" (*pavāhaya*) means "carry off," that is, "take away. "It is not cut" means "it does not perish.

This is what is intended: "Dear son, if you are afraid of death, descend into a lotus pond free from mud, wash away all sweat and filth from your body, and anoint it with fragrant perfumes and ointments."

Having recollected the ten perfections (*pāramī*) and made the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) his precursor, as he uttered the first line, the sound spread over the entire city of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent.
At the very moment they heard it, the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, beginning with the king and the sub-kings, arrived; even those who had not yet come heard it while still standing in their homes.
The king’s men went and cut down the thicket, leveled the ground, and scattered sand over it. The intoxication from the strong liquor was broken within the ruffians;
they cast away their snares and stood listening to the Dhamma. The intoxication from the strong liquor was also broken within the old woman.
Then the Great Being began his teaching of the Dhamma to Cūḷatuṇḍila in the midst of the great multitude. Having heard that, Cūḷatuṇḍila—

“My brother says this: ‘In our lineage, there has never been at any time the practice of descending into a lotus pond to bathe, to remove sweat and impurities from the body, or to discard old ointments and apply new ones.
With what intention did my brother say this to me? Thus questioning, he spoke the fourth verse:
“What lake is free from mud? What is called ‘free from sweat and dust’?
And what is the fresh ointment whose fragrance never fades?
Hearing this, the Great Being said, “In that case, younger brother, listen with attentive ears,” and teaching the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, he spoke these verses:
“The Dhamma is a lake free from mud; evil is said to be its sweat and grime;
virtue is its fresh ointment, and its fragrance never fades.
Those who destroy the body rejoice, yet those who merely preserve the body do not rejoice.”
"And on the full moon day of Puṇṇā, they abandon life while still enjoying [pleasures].

In this context, "Dhamma" refers to all that is called Dhamma: the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the three types of good conduct, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the deathless Great Nibbāna.
"Free from mud" means free from the mud of the defilements of greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and the other afflictions.
“By its absence, there is no mud. By this, having distinguished it from all other phenomena, he shows that it is Nibbāna alone.
“Monks, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared the foremost among those phenomena;
that is to say, the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the round, the destruction of craving, dispassion.”
For it has been said: "Cessation is Nibbāna. Demonstrating that very point, he said: "Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, I speak of the Nibbāna-lake as a 'pond.
For birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth do not exist there. If you wish to be released from death, take up the path leading to Nibbāna.
It is said that the Bodhisatta spoke thus by way of the condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
“Evil, dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, is like sweat and dirt. Because it resembles sweat and dirt, evil was called “sweat and dirt” by the ancient wise ones.
Furthermore, this evil is of one kind, namely mental corruption;
