it is of two kinds: evil conduct and evil view; it is of three kinds: the three types of misconduct; it is of four kinds... [the four types of misconduct].
There are wrong courses of conduct; evil is fivefold through the five mental obstructions (*cetokhila*); evil is sixfold through the six types of disrespect (*agārava*);
evil is sevenfold through the seven unrighteous qualities (*asaddhamma*); evil is eightfold through the eight wrongnesses (*micchatta*);
evil is ninefold through the nine grounds for resentment (*āghātavatthu*); evil is tenfold through the ten unwholesome courses of action (*akusalakammapatha*); [and evil is] manifoldfold...
Evil—namely lust, hatred, and delusion—are unwholesome states analyzed according to single, dual, and triple categories;
thus, all this evil has been described by the wise as being "like the sweat and filth adhering to the body.

Virtue consists of the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the virtue of the fourfold purification. "This virtue, dear one, is like the anointing with the four kinds of fragrant ointment," it is said.
It says: "Of that [virtue], the fragrance—its scent—is never interrupted throughout the three stages of life;
it spreads and pervades the entire world.
'The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine;'"
The fragrance of the virtuous wafts against the wind; the person of integrity pervades all directions.
Whether it be sandalwood, tagara, blue lotus, or jasmine—among all these varieties of fragrance, the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed.
“Trifling is this fragrance, this tagara and sandalwood;
But the fragrance of those possessed of virtue Blows supreme even among the gods.
“They rejoice in killing the body,” said Cūḷatuṇḍila, dear father; these are ignorant men who think, “We shall eat sweet meat.”
They take delight and find satisfaction in committing the destruction of life, thinking, "We shall even cause our own sons and wives to be eaten.

When the destruction of life is practiced, cultivated, and frequently repeated, it leads to rebirth in hell; it leads to rebirth in the animal realm... [and] to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
Even the lightest result of the destruction of life leads to a short lifespan for one who has become human.
They do not understand this danger in the destruction of living beings. Not understanding it, they fail to realize:
"The fool thinks it is sweet as long as the evil does not ripen;
but when the evil ripens, the fool encounters suffering."
Perceiving [the result] as sweet:
"The foolish, the witless, go about with themselves as their own enemies,
performing evil karma that bears bitter fruit."
They do not even know this much:
"That action is not well done which, having been done, one regrets;
that for which one experiences the result while weeping with a tearful face."
"And they do not rejoice while bearing a body," O dear Cūḷatuṇḍila—
those beings who bear a body, when their own death approaches, with the exception of the lion, the king of beasts, the noble elephant, the noble horse,
and those whose taints are exhausted, there are none, beginning with the Bodhisatta himself, who do not tremble.
“All tremble at punishment; all fear death.
Making oneself the analogy, one should neither kill nor cause to kill.
“Puṇṇāya” means full of virtue. “Puṇṇamāsiyā” means joined with the full moon, or having remained for the completion of the month.
"It was, it seems, the full-moon Uposatha day at that time. 'They abandon life even while enjoying themselves,' O dear Cūḷatuṇḍila—do not grieve, do not lament.
Those who lack virtues such as moral discipline within themselves are indeed afraid of death.
But we are endowed with virtue and conduct and possess merit; therefore, beings like us abandon life even while enjoying themselves."
Thus the Great Being taught the Dhamma with a sweet voice and the grace of a Buddha.
The great multitude snapped their fingers and waved their garments, and the sky was filled with the sound of shouts of "Excellent!
The King of Bārāṇasī honored the Bodhisatta with the sovereignty and gave the glory to his mother; then, having bathed both of them with scented water, he...

Having had her anointed with perfumes and the like, and having had jewel-ornaments fastened around her neck, he led her home, established her in the position of a daughter, and tended to her with a great retinue.
The Bodhisatta gave the five precepts to the king;
all the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī and the inhabitants of the Kāsi kingdom observed the five precepts. On the days of the lunar phases, the Great Being [preached] to them...
He taught the Dhamma and, sitting in the court of justice, he adjudicated legal cases.
While he was alive, there were no such things as those who committed fraudulent lawsuits. Later on, the king passed away.
The Great Being, having performed the funeral rites for him, had the records of the court written down in a book and said, "Having consulted this book, you should adjudicate the cases."
Having taught the Dhamma to the great multitude and given them an exhortation on heedfulness, he entered the forest together with Cūḷatuṇḍila while everyone was still weeping and lamenting.
At that time, the Bodhisatta’s exhortation remained in effect for sixty thousand years.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu who had been afraid of death was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, King Ānanda was Cūḷatuṇḍila, the bhikkhu who feared death; the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and Mahātuṇḍila was none other than myself.
This concludes the third narrative, the Commentary on the Tuṇḍila Jātaka.
[389] 4. The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka Jātaka.
"Siṅgīmiga" (The Deer with the Golden Antlers): This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana Grove concerning the Elder Ānanda’s renunciation of his own life for the sake of another.
The background story, up to the employment of the archer, has been told in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka;
the dismissal of Dhanapāla is told in the Cūḷahaṃsa and Mahāhaṃsa Jātakas. At that time, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth.

“Friends, the Elder Ānanda, the Dhamma-treasurer, having attained the analytical knowledges of one still in training, sacrificed his life for the Fully Enlightened One when Dhanañjaya was approaching.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? and they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now.”
"Even in the past, Ānanda sacrificed his life for me," he said, and related a story of the past.
Long ago, on the eastern side of Rājagaha, there was a brahmin village named Sālindiya. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a farming brahmin family in that village;
having reached maturity and established a household, he [lived] in that village.
In a certain village field to the northeast, he had a thousand cartloads of manure plowed in.
One day, having gone to the field with his men and commanded the laborers, "Plow!
he approached a large pool at the edge of the field to rinse his mouth. Now, in that pool, there was one [creature] of golden color...
A crab lived there, handsome and pleasing to behold. After the Bodhisatta had chewed his tooth-stick, he descended into that pool.
While he was rinsing his mouth, the crab came near him.
Then, having picked it up and placed it within his upper garment, he took it with him as he went to perform the work to be done in the field.

Having thrown him right there into a pit, he went home. From that time on, whenever he came to the field, he would first go to that pit, lift out the crab, place it within his upper garment, and only afterwards attend to his work.
In this way, their mutual trust became firm.
The Bodhisatta used to come regularly to the field, and on his eyes, the five sensory faculties appeared clearly with their three circles perfectly pure.
Now, at the edge of the field, a female crow saw her eyes in a crow’s nest upon a palmyra tree and, desiring to eat them, said to the male crow:
“Husband, a craving has arisen in me. “What is this craving? [he asked.]
“What is his name? “We wish to eat this brahmin’s eyes. “A wicked craving has arisen in you;
who will be able to bring these? “You cannot,” [he replied]. “I know that too.
However, there is a termite mound not far from that palm tree where a black snake dwells. Attend upon it; it will bite him and kill him.”
“Then you shall pluck out his eyes and bring them to me. He agreed, saying, “Very well,” and from then on he waited upon the black snake.
When the crops sown by the Bodhisatta had reached the stage of ripening, the crab became large.
Then one day the snake said to the crow, “Friend, you wait upon me constantly;”
“What shall I do for you? [she asked]. “Master, this field-owner, my master’s slave, has developed a craving for eyes;
therefore, thinking that through your power I shall obtain those eyes for him, I am attending upon you.
The snake comforted her, saying, “Be at ease, this is no small matter; you shall obtain them,” and on the following day, along the path by which the brahmin was coming—
Leaning against the boundary of the field, he lay down, concealed by grass, watching for her arrival.

As the Bodhisatta was coming, he first descended into a pool, washed his face, showed his affection, embraced the golden crab, and having placed it between his upper garment and himself, entered the field. The snake—
Seeing him approaching, the crab sprang forward with speed, bit into the piece of meat, threw it down right there, and fled toward the anthill.

The Bodhisatta’s falling, the crab’s leaping out from within its shell, and the crow’s arrival and alighting upon the Bodhisatta’s chest occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after the other. Having alighted, the crow—
He struck the eyes with his beak. The crab thought, "Because of this crow, fear has arisen for my friend;

if he is caught, the snake will come. As if seizing him with a pair of tongs, he gripped the crow firmly by the neck with his claw, and after making him struggle, he loosened his grip slightly. The crow cried out, "Friend, why do you let me go and flee?"
Calling to the snake, "This crab is harassing me even more; come while I have not yet died," he spoke the first verse:
"The horned deer with long eyes and lashes, bone-skinned, water-dweller, hairless;"
"Overcome by him, I weep piteously; O deer, friend, why indeed have you abandoned me?
In this context, "siṅgī-miga" refers to a crab, either because of its golden (siṅgī) color or because of the presence of claws (siṅga) known as "aḷa.
"Āyata-cakkhu-netta" means one endowed with long eyes, which are called "netta" (eyes).
“Aṭṭhittaco” means “having skin as thin as a bone. “Hare sakhā” is a form of address, meaning “O friend!
When the snake heard this, he spread out his great hood and approached, consoling the crow. The Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke the second verse to illustrate this point:
“Exhaling with his great hood, the serpent, having reached the crab in the middle, [spoke thus].”
“A crab, seeking to protect its friend, seized a serpent.
In this context, *kakkaṭamajjhapatto* means having reached the crab. *Sakhā sakhāraṃ* means a companion [protecting] a companion.
There is also a reading, *sakaṃ sakhāraṃ*, which has the meaning of one’s own companion. *Paritāyamāno* means protecting. *Gahesi* means he seized.
With his second claw, he seized the snake firmly by the neck.
Then, having exhausted it, he loosened his grip slightly. Thereupon the snake thought, "Crabs eat neither the flesh of crows nor the flesh of snakes;
for what reason, then, has this one seized us? Having reflected thus, he—
Questioning him, he spoke this third verse:
“Neither a crow nor a black snake would a crab give to one seeking food;
I ask you, O one with long eyes and eyelashes, for what reason have we both been seized?”
In this context, "seeking food" means being desirous of nutriment. "He would take it" (*adeyya*)—by connecting it with the negative particle *na*, the meaning is "he did not take it.
Having heard that, the crab spoke two verses explaining the reason for his taking hold:
"This man is well-disposed toward me, who, having taken hold of me, leads me to the water."
"In that case, my suffering would not be slight; neither I nor he would exist.
Seeing my body fully grown, all people would surely wish to harm me;
even crows, seeing my meat—tasty, thick, and soft—would torment me."
In this context, *ayaṃ* refers to the Bodhisatta. *Atthakāmo* means desiring his welfare.
*Dakāya netīti* means that he, out of affection for me, takes me by the upper garment and leads me to the water, bringing me to the pool where he himself dwells. *Tasmiṃ mate* means:
if he should die in this place, then upon his death, there would be great physical and mental suffering for me.
He indicates that [the crab] will survive. "We both shall not be" means that neither of us two shall exist.
Regarding the verse beginning with "And seeing me," this is the meaning: there is also this further reason;
seeing me—helpless and without protection—with my body fully grown, everyone will think, "The meat of this crab is savory, thick, and tender," and they will kill me.
"I wish that not only people, but even crows who are creatures of the animal realm, would not harm, harass, or kill me upon seeing me.
Hearing this, the snake thought, "By some means I shall deceive him and thus liberate both the crow and myself. Then, desiring to deceive him, he spoke the sixth verse:
“If you have seized both of us for his sake, let him rise up; I shall swallow the poison.
Quickly release both me and the crow, before death reaches the man with the potent poison.
In this context, *sacetassa hetū* means “if for the sake of this [man]. *Uṭṭhātu* means “let him rise up,” that is, let him be free from the poison. *Visamāvamāmī* means “I shall swallow the poison.”
"I shall draw out his poison; I shall render it poisonless. For before death reaches this mortal in its full force, release both of us quickly while that death has not yet arrived.
"Before death reaches this mortal in its full force"—for if I were not to suck [the poison] from him, the poison would approach this mortal as something dense and powerful;
therefore, release both of us quickly while it has not yet reached him.
Having heard this, the crab thought: "This one wishes to escape by means of a stratagem, having caused both of us to be released;
he does not know my skill in means. Now I shall loosen my claw so that the snake can crawl away, but I will certainly not release the crow. Having thought thus, he spoke the seventh verse:
“I will release the snake first, not yet the crow; for the crow will act as a guarantor.
But when I see the man healthy and free from disease, I will release the crow just as I did the snake.

In this context, “guarantor” (paṭibandhaka) means a surety (pāṭibhoga). “Just as the snake”: just as I am releasing you, O snake, so too shall I release the crow; the only difference is that you must quickly suck the poison out of this brahmin’s body.
Having spoken thus, he made the opening wide and loose so that he might move about with ease.
The snake, having discharged its venom, rendered the Great Being’s body free of poison. He rose up, free from suffering, and stood there in his natural form.
The crab thought, "If these two people also become healthy, it will not be called a gain for my friend."

Thinking, "He will come; I shall destroy him," he cut off the heads of both [the snake and the crow] with his claws like a lotus bud with a knife, bringing them to their end of life. The female crow also fled from that place.
The Bodhisatta wound the snake’s body around a stick and threw it onto the top of a thicket. He released the golden crab into a pool.
Having heard this, he went to the village of Sālindiya. From that time forth, his friendship with the crab became even greater.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher, identifying the Jātaka, spoke this concluding verse:
“The crow at that time was Devadatta, and Māra was the black snake.”
“Ānandabhadda was the crab, and I was the brahmin teacher at that time.
At the conclusion of these words of truth, many became stream-enterers and others. As for the female crow, she was not mentioned in the verse; she was Ciñcā Māṇavikā.
This concludes the fourth narrative, the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka Jātaka.
[390] 5. The Commentary on the Mayhaka-jātaka.
"A bird named Mayhaka"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a visiting merchant.
Now, there was in Sāvatthī a certain visiting merchant who was wealthy and possessed of great riches; yet he did not enjoy those possessions himself.
He did not give to others; when choice, exquisite foods of superior flavor were brought to him, he would not eat them, but ate only broken rice with dregs as the second course.
When fine Kāsi cloths, perfumed and fumigated, were brought to him, he would have those removed and wear coarse, thick garments instead.
When a chariot yoked with noble steeds, adorned with jewels and gold, was brought to him, he would have that taken away and travel in a simple wooden cart.
He went along while a golden parasol was being held over him; then, having removed that, he went with a leaf parasol being held over him.
Having failed to perform even a single act of merit such as giving throughout his entire life, he died and was reborn in the Roruva hell.
His sonless inheritance was brought into the royal palace by the king’s forces within seven days and nights. Once it had been brought in—
The king, having finished his morning meal, went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.

When [the Teacher] asked, "Great King, why do you not pay your respects to the Buddha?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, seven days and nights have passed while the wealth of a merchant named Āgantuka-Setthi, who died in Sāvatthī and left no heirs, was being brought to our house; yet even after he had obtained this wealth, [he did not enjoy it]."
He neither enjoyed it himself nor gave it to others; his wealth was like a lotus pond possessed by a *rakkhasa*.
Without experiencing the taste of even a single day’s choice food and such, he entered the jaws of death.
Having done what, did this miserly man, a slave to demerit, acquire so much wealth? And by what means was his mind [turned away] from those riches?

"Do not take pleasure [in this]," he asked the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Great King, it was by him alone that both the acquisition of wealth and the reason for not enjoying the wealth once acquired were brought about.
When requested by him, the Teacher related a past event:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, there lived a merchant-chief in Bārāṇasī who was faithless and miserly."
He gave nothing to anyone and did not favor anyone.
One day, while going to attend upon the king, he saw the Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī wandering for alms. Having paid homage to him, he asked, "Venerable sir, have you received alms?
When the reply was, "We are indeed wandering, Great Merchant," he commanded a man, "Go, [give this...]"
“Bring him to our house, have him sit upon my couch, fill his bowl with the meal prepared for us, and give it to him.
He led the Paccekabuddha to the house, had him sit down, and informed the merchant’s wife.
She filled his bowl with food of various excellent flavors and gave it to him. Having taken the food, he departed from the merchant’s residence.

Having gone out, he set out along the street. As the merchant was returning from the royal palace, he saw him, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, have you obtained alms? "I have obtained them, great merchant," he replied. The merchant looked at the bowl and was unable to find peace of mind;
[he thought], "If my slaves or laborers eat this food of mine, even a difficult task—"
Thinking, "May they perform the deed; oh, may they know of me," he was unable to fulfill the subsequent volition.
For indeed, giving becomes fruitful only for one who is able to fulfill the three types of volition:
"Before the gift we are joyful; while giving, we are truly glad of heart."
“Indeed, having given, we do not regret it afterwards; therefore, even the young bow down to us.
“Before giving, one is joyful; while giving, one clarifies the mind;
after giving, one is glad at heart—this is the perfection of sacrifice.”
“Thus, Great King, by means of the requisites given to the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, the visiting merchant obtained great wealth;
yet, because he was unable to perform further refined acts of volition after having given, he was not able to enjoy his riches.
“But why, Bhante, did he not obtain a son? The Teacher said, “The reason for his not obtaining a son is also due to that very same [lack of further volition].”
"Thus it was said, O Great King," he said, and being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family possessing eighty crores of wealth.
Having reached maturity and following the passing of his parents, he took charge of his younger brother and managed the household."
Having had a hall for almsgiving constructed at the door of his house, he lived as a householder while distributing great gifts. Then a son was born to him.

When that son reached the age of walking on foot, [the father], seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, handed over all the household wealth to his younger brother and said, "Be diligent and continue the practice of giving."

Having given this advice, he went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and after attaining the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he dwelt in the Himalayan region.
His younger brother also obtained a son; seeing that boy growing up, he thought, "As long as my brother’s son lives, our family will be split in two. I shall kill my brother’s son."

Then one day, having thrown him into the river, he killed him. When his brother’s wife returned from bathing and asked, "Where is my son?", he replied, "He was playing in the water; then, while searching for him in the water, I did not see him.
She wept and wailed, and then became silent.
The Bodhisatta, having learned of this occurrence, thought, "I shall make this matter public.
He came through the air, descended at Bārāṇasī, and stood at the door of that man's house, well-clad and well-dressed.

Not seeing the hall of alms-giving, he thought, "Even the hall of alms-giving has been destroyed by this wicked man. His younger brother, learning of his arrival, came out and [saw] the Great Being...

Having paid homage to him and escorted him up to the palace, he fed him with excellent food. At the conclusion of his meal, while sitting in pleasant conversation, [the king] asked, "The boy is not to be seen;
where could he be? "He is dead, venerable sir. "By what cause? "I do not know, venerable sir;
it was at the place for water-sports, by such-and-such a cause. "How can you not know, you unvirtuous man?"
"It is evident that my purpose has been accomplished by her; surely you killed her for this very reason!
Could you possibly protect wealth that is being lost through kings and others? What difference is there between me, a mere bird, and you?
Then the Great Being, teaching the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, spoke these verses:
“There was a bird named Mayhaka, who roamed the mountain slopes and valleys;
having climbed a ripe *pipphali* tree, he cried out, ‘Mine! Mine!
As he was thus lamenting, flocks of birds gathered together.”
Having gathered the long pepper, they depart, while that brahmin merely laments.
"In the very same way, someone here, having accumulated much wealth,
does not provide for himself or his kinsmen according to his means."
“He does not enjoy clothing, food, garlands, or ointments even once; he does not support his kinsmen.
While he thus laments and guards them, thinking ‘This is mine, this is mine,’”
“Whether it be kings, thieves, or even unwelcome heirs,
they depart taking the wealth, while that man merely laments.
But the wise person, having acquired riches, supports his kinsmen.”
“By that he attains fame and rejoices in heaven after passing away.
In this context, *mayhako* is so named because of its habit of crying out, “Mine! Mine! It is called *girisānudarīcaro* because it roams among the mountain ravines.
*Pakkaṃ pipphaliṃ* refers to a certain ripe fruit found in a region of the Himālayas, laden with fruit.
The *pipphalirukkha* tree. "He cries out" means that, having surrounded that tree, he wanders about lamenting "Mine! Mine! in order to prevent the flocks of birds from eating the ripe fruits.
"While he was thus wailing" means while he was indeed wailing in this manner.
"Having eaten the *pipphali* and departing" means having consumed that *pipphalirukkha* tree and [going] to another tree abounding in fruit.
"They go to the tree. "Lamenting indeed" means that the brahmin was indeed lamenting.

"According to the portion" (yathodhi) means according to the respective shares; the meaning is that he did not give whatever portion was to be given for the use and enjoyment of his mother, father, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, and so forth.
"He does not experience it even once. There is also a reading "sakan," meaning "even what belongs to himself.
"He does not support them" means he does not support them by giving food, clothing, seeds, ploughs, and so forth. "That man merely laments":
when those people, such as the king and others, have taken the wealth and departed, that person merely laments. "The wise one" means the learned one.
"He gathers" means he gathers those weak kinsmen who come to his presence by giving them food, clothing, fans, ploughs, and so forth.
"By that" means that man, through that gathering of kinsmen, attains both fame and praise for himself in the midst of the four assemblies;
and after death, he rejoices in the celestial city of heaven.

Thus the Great Being, having taught him the Dhamma and restored his charity to its former state, went back to the Himālaya mountains; there, without falling away from his meditative absorption, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "In this way, Great King, because the visiting merchant killed his brother’s son, for so long a time he obtained neither a son nor a daughter," and then he identified the Jātaka by correlating the characters.
—“At that time, the younger one was the visiting merchant, while the elder one was none other than myself.
This concludes the fifth commentary, the Mayhakajātakavaṇṇanā.
[391] 6. The Commentary on the Vijjādharajātakavaṇṇanā.
“Of ugly appearance”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the practice for the welfare of the world.
The story will be made clear in the Mahākaṇha Jātaka. At that time, however, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Tathāgata practiced for the welfare of the world,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka.
At that time, a certain *vidyādhara*, having mastered his spells, would come at the hour of midnight and commit adultery with the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī.
The queen’s attendants became aware of this. She herself approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, a certain man..."
“At the hour of midnight, having entered the bedchamber, he defiles me,” she said. “But will you be able to leave some mark?

“I can, Your Majesty,” she replied; and having had a box of vermilion brought, she gave a five-fingered stamp on the back of that man as he departed after coming at night and enjoying himself, so that in the morning it would appear to the King.
He reported this. The king commanded his men: “Go, look in all directions and seize the man who has made a five-fingered mark with vermilion on his back.
The master of the spells, having committed an improper act at night, was standing on one leg by day in the charnel ground worshipping the sun.
When the king’s men saw him, they surrounded him. Thinking, “My deed has become manifest,” he [recited] the spell.
Having changed his appearance, he leapt into the air and departed.
When the king saw him, he asked the men who had arrived, "Did you see him? "Yes, we saw him. "Who is this?
"He is a renunciant, Your Majesty. [The king thought: "For he practices immoral conduct at night and lives during the day in the guise of a renunciant. The king—

Thinking, "These men, having wandered about during the day in the guise of ascetics, commit misconduct at night," he became angry with those who had gone forth, harbored a false accusation, and caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming:
"All these ascetics shall flee from my realm; wherever they are seen, let them be subject to the king's command.
Thereupon, all those throughout the kingdom of Kāsi, extending for three hundred leagues, fled away.
Those who had gone forth into homelessness departed for other royal capitals.
Throughout the entire kingdom of Kāsi, there was not even a single righteous ascetic or brahmin to give counsel to the people. Lacking instruction, the people became harsh;
turning away from generosity and virtue, they died and for the most part were reborn in the states of misery, while those reborn in heaven were non-existent.
Not seeing the new deva-sons, Sakka reflected, "What could be the reason?

Having discerned through his supernormal knowledge that they had been expelled from the kingdom after a false accusation was brought against them by the King of Bārāṇasī—who was incensed because they relied upon a master of the sciences—and had subsequently gone forth into homelessness, he thought:
"Apart from me, there is no one else capable of breaking this king's false accusation."

Thinking, "I shall become a refuge for the king and the inhabitants of the kingdom," he went to the presence of the Paccekabuddhas at Nandamūla Cave, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sirs, grant me one elder Paccekabuddha;
I shall bring glory to the kingdom of Kāsi. He received the Sangha Elder himself; then, taking his bowl and robes, [the Elder] stood before him.
Having done so, placing himself behind [the Paccekabuddha] and joining his palms at his head, he paid homage to the Paccekabuddha.
Assuming the form of a youth of supreme beauty, he walked three times over the heads of the entire city, arrived at the king’s gate, and stood in the air.
The ministers informed the king: "Your Majesty, a handsome youth has brought a certain ascetic..."
“Standing in the air at the king’s gate. The king rose from his seat, stood by the window, and, addressing the youth with the first verse as he conversed with him, said:
“O young man, why do you, though handsome yourself, stand here bowing and holding the bowl and robes of this ugly ascetic?”
“You, who possess the appearance of a noble one, pay homage with palms joined while standing before one of ugly form.
Is he indeed better than you, or are you similar to him? Tell me your name and his as well.
In this context, “possessing the appearance of a noble one” means having a beautiful form. “Is he indeed better than you? asks: is this ugly renunciant truly superior to you?
"Is he superior, or rather, is he equal? Tell me the name of both him and yourself"—thus he asks.

Then Sakka, saying to him, "Great King, those called *samaṇas* are worthy of great respect; therefore, it is not permitted for me to utter my own name, but I shall tell you my name," spoke the second verse:
“O King, the gods who have gone rightly and are upright do not take up names or clans;
yet I shall tell you my name: I am Sakka, the lord of the Thirty-three.
Therein, “O King, the gods who have gone rightly and are upright” means, O Great King, [those who have understood] all conditioned phenomena according to their true nature and essence.
Because they have attained the fruit supreme among all fruits—Arahatship—by means of right comprehension, they are "those who have gone rightly.

Because they have gone to Nibbāna by means of the straight Eightfold Path, they are "those who have gone straight. For those great ones whose taints are destroyed, who are purer than the gods of the sense-sphere (upapatti-devas), the gods of the sense-sphere do not know their names or clans.
When he says, "And I shall tell you my name," he means: furthermore, I shall tell you my own name.
Having heard that, the king asked about the benefit of bowing to a bhikkhu with the third verse: “O King of Devas, I ask you this matter:
what happiness does he obtain who, having seen a bhikkhu endowed with virtuous conduct, stands before him with palms joined in reverence and pays homage?
When he passes away from here, what bliss does he receive?”
Sakka spoke the fourth verse: “He who,
having seen a monk endowed with virtuous conduct, pays homage with hands joined in reverence while standing before him,
gains praise in this very life and goes to heaven upon the dissolution of the body.”
In this context, "a bhikkhunī" refers to a person who has shattered the defilements and is utterly pure. "Endowed with conduct" means possessed of the practice of virtue (*sīla*).
"In this very life" means that not only after passing away from here, but even in this present existence, she receives praise and experiences the happiness of being praised.
Having heard Sakka’s words, the king broke his own wrong perception and, with a joyful heart, spoke this fifth verse:
“Truly, prosperity has arisen for me today, that I have seen Vāsava, the Lord of Beings;
and having seen both you and the monk, Sakka, I shall perform abundant meritorious deeds.”
In this context, *lakkhī* means glory (*sirī*); some also say it means wisdom (*paññā*). This is what is meant:
"Today, even as I was listening to your words, the wisdom that knows the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome kamma has arisen in me. *Yaṃ* is a mere particle.
*Bhūtapatiddasāma* means we saw the Lord of Beings (*bhūtapati*).
Having heard this, Sakka, offering praise to the wise man, spoke the sixth verse:
“Truly, those who are wise and learned, who reflect upon many matters, should indeed be served.
Having seen both the bhikkhu and me, O King, perform abundant deeds of merit.”
In that context, "one who considers many points" means one capable of reflecting upon many reasons.
Having heard this, the king spoke the concluding verse:
"Becoming free from anger, with a mind always serene, and being devoted to all guests and supplicants;..."
“Having struck down my pride, I shall pay homage, having heard the well-spoken words of the Lord of Devas.
In this context, “having become one who is devoted to the granting of every request to guests” means:
having become one who is fit and appropriate for whatever all those guests—those who have arrived as visitors—request; [being one] for whom everything requested by them [is granted].
"Dadamāno" means "giving. "Having heard the well-spoken words, O Lord of Devas," he says this meaning: "Having heard your well-spoken words, I shall become such as you are.
Having spoken thus, he descended from the palace, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha, and stood to one side. The Paccekabuddha—
Sitting cross-legged in the air, he exhorted the king, saying: "Great King, a master of spells is not a true ascetic.
From this day forward, knowing that 'the world is not empty; there are righteous ascetics and brahmins,' give alms, guard your virtue, and observe the Uposatha rites.
Sakka also, standing in the air through his supernatural power, said: "From this day forward, be diligent..."
Having given this advice to the citizens, saying, "Let the runaway ascetics and brahmins return," he had the drum beaten, proclaiming, "Let those who have fled come back!
Then both of them returned to their own places. The king, abiding by that advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Paccekabuddha had attained Parinibbāna; the king was Ānanda, and Sakka was none other than myself."
The Sixth: The Exposition of the *Vijjādharajātakavaṇṇanā*.
[392] 7. The Exposition of the *Siṅghapupphajātakavaṇṇanā*.
"That which..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain bhikkhu. It is said that he...
Having departed from Jetavana and dwelling in a certain forest in the kingdom of Kosala, one day he descended into a lotus pond;
seeing a lotus in full bloom, he stood downwind and sniffed it.
Then a deity residing in that forest said to him: "Venerable sir, you are named 'Scent-thief'; this is one factor of theft for you."
He inspired him with a sense of spiritual urgency. Stirred by that inspiration, he returned once more to Jeta’s Grove; having paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down.
When asked, "Where, monk, did you dwell?", he replied, "In a certain grove named so-and-so; there a deity inspired me in this way.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Monk, it was not you alone whom the deity inspired while you were smelling the flowers..."
"Having been moved to spiritual urgency, and having said, 'Even the ancient sages were formerly moved to spiritual urgency,' he was requested [for a story], and so he related a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsī.
Having grown up and mastered his craft at Takkasilā, he later went forth as an ascetic."
While observing the fast near a certain lotus pond, he descended into the lake one day and stood there sniffing at a fully blossomed lotus.
Then, a certain goddess, standing in a hollow in the trunk of a tree, spoke this first verse to him in order to stir his sense of urgency:
“This lotus flower, which you are sniffing though it was not given to you;”
"This is one factor among thefts; you are a thief of scents, dear sir.
Therein, "this is one factor" means this is a single portion.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“I do not take it away, nor do I break it; from afar I smell the water-born flower.
By what reason, then, am I called a ‘thief of fragrance’?
In this context, “I smell from afar” means that standing at a distance, I inhale the scent. “By reason” (vaṇṇena) means by way of cause.
At that moment, a certain man was digging for lotus roots and breaking off white lotuses in that lake.

Seeing him, the Bodhisatta spoke to her, reciting the third verse as he conversed with her: “Standing far away, you call me a ‘thief’ even as I am sniffing at you; why then do you not say the same to this man?”
“He who digs up the lotus roots and breaks the white lotuses—
why is this man not called one whose actions are crowded (with evil)?
In this context, “one whose actions are crowded” means one whose actions are harsh and one whose actions are cruel.
Then, explaining the reason for her silence, the deity spoke the fourth and fifth verses:
“A man who is full of greed and cruelty, smeared with filth like a nurse’s garment—
there is no word for me to speak to him, nor is he worthy of my speaking.”
“For a person free from blemish, who constantly seeks purity,
even a hair’s breadth of evil appears as large as a cloud.
In this context, *dhāticelamiva* means a cloth worn by a nursemaid or slave-girl that has been smeared with spittle, mucus, urine, and excrement.
This man is as if smeared with evil; for that reason, my word has no authority over him.
But as for the ascetics, they are capable of receiving instruction and possess a dearable virtue; therefore, it is fitting to speak even to an ascetic who commits even a slight impropriety.
"To one without blemish" means to one like you who is free from fault. "He appears as large as a cloud" means:
“Having appeared with the magnitude of a great cloud, why do you now commit such a fault that is not even to be mentioned?
Stirred by this, the Bodhisatta, overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), spoke the sixth verse:
“Surely you know me, O Yakkha, and indeed you have compassion for me.”
"Furthermore, O Yakkha, you should speak when you see such a thing as this.
Herein, "Yakkha" is how he addresses the deity. "Vajjāsi" means "you should say. "When you see such as this" means: "When you see such a fault in me, then you should speak to me thus," he says.
Then that goddess spoke the seventh verse:
“I do not depend on you for my livelihood, nor am I your hired servant;
you alone, O Bhikkhu, should know by what means one may go to a happy destination.
In this context, “nor am I your hired servant” means we are not even your wage-earning laborers. For what reason? At all times...
She indicates: "I shall wander about while protecting [you]. "Whither you should go" means: "O Bhikkhu, as for the kamma by which you might go to a happy destination, you alone should know that.
Having thus given him this exhortation, she entered her own celestial mansion. The Bodhisatta, too, having attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), became destined for the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, the celestial maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ascetic was none other than myself.
This is the seventh commentary on the Siṅghapuppha Jātaka.
[393] 8. The Commentary on the Vighāsādajātaka:
"O, how happily indeed they live!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at the Eastern Monastery concerning certain monks of frivolous character.
For when those monks had been moved to spiritual urgency by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna after he had caused the palace to tremble, they gathered in the Hall of Truth (Dhammasabhā).
The monks sat there speaking of their faults. The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you sitting here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
even in the past these men were of a playful nature. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka.
Now, in a certain village of Kāsī, seven brothers, having seen the defects in sensual pleasures, went forth and took up the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Dwelling in the middle of the forest, they failed to apply themselves to their practice; instead, being preoccupied with physical strength, they wandered about engaging in various kinds of sport.
Sakka, the king of the gods, thinking, "I shall cause them to feel spiritual urgency," transformed himself into a woodpecker, went to their dwelling place, perched upon a tree,
and while inspiring them with a sense of urgency, spoke this first verse: "Happy indeed they live, those people who subsist on scraps;..."
"Praised in this very life, and in the future, a happy destination.
In this context, "those who eat leftovers" is said with reference to those who consume what remains after others have eaten.
"In this very life" means that those of such a kind are praised in this very life, and in the future they have a happy destination; he speaks with the intention that they will arise in heaven.
Then, one among them, having heard his words, addressed the rest and spoke this second verse:
“O wise ones, do not pay heed to what Sukka is saying!
Listen to this, brothers: it is us whom he is praising.”

In that context, "to him who is speaking" means to one who is speaking with human speech. "Do not listen" means do not hear. "Listen to this" means listen to these words of his. Addressing them as "uterine brothers" (sodariyā), he spoke thus because they had dwelt together in the same womb.
Then, rejecting them, Suvaṇṇasobhita recited the third verse:
"I do not praise you; you who feed on corpses, listen to me!"
“You are eaters of leavings, not scavengers.
There, with “kuṇapādā,” he addresses them as “eaters of corpses.
Having heard his words, they all recited the fourth verse:
“Seven years have we gone forth, peacocks in the middle of the forest;
subsisting on mere scraps, if we are censurable by you,
sir, who indeed would be praiseworthy?”

In this context, "crested" means those endowed with tufts of hair. "By the remains of food alone" means: if for such a long time—seven years—you have lived subsisting solely on the remains of the food of lions and tigers, and yet you are censurable to my lord, then who indeed are those who should be praised?
Causing them shame, the Great Being spoke the fifth verse:
"You [subsist] on the leftovers of lions, tigers, and wild beasts;..."
“Living on mere leavings, you imagine yourselves to be scavengers.
In this context, “the remains of what was left over by predators” refers to the leftover food remaining from other wild beasts.
Having heard that, the ascetics asked, “If we are not scavengers, then who indeed are the scavengers? Then, explaining the matter to them, he spoke the sixth verse:
“Those people who, having given to a brahmin, an ascetic, or any other mendicant, eat what remains, are called ‘eaters of scraps’ (vighāsādino).
In this context, *vanibbino* refers to one who begs for various goods. Having thus put them to shame, the Great Being returned to his own place.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the seven brothers were these monks of frivolous conduct, while Sakka was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Vighāsāda Jātaka, the eighth.
[394] 9. The Commentary on the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka.
"Exquisite. This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain greedy monk.
The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are greedy? When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, you were not only greedy now;
you were greedy even in the past. Because of your greediness, however, in Benares [you were reborn] amidst the corpses of elephants, cattle, horses, and men."
Having said, “Unsatisfied, thinking ‘I shall obtain something even better than this,’ you have entered the forest,” he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a quail and lived in the forest subsisting on coarse grass seeds.
At that time, there was a greedy crow in Benares who was unsatisfied with the carcasses of elephants and other such things.
Thinking, "I shall obtain something even better than this," he entered the forest and, while eating various fruits, saw the Bodhisatta.
He thought, "This quail has an exceedingly plump body; I suppose it eats sweet food.
Having asked what its food is, and having eaten that myself, I too shall become plump. Then, [standing] above the Bodhisatta...
Perching on a branch, he asked the Bodhisatta, "O partridge, what kind of choice food do you eat that you have become so plump?
Being thus questioned by him, the Bodhisatta, exchanging greetings with him,
spoke the first verse:
“You eat excellent food, uncle—ghee and oil as well.
For what reason, then, are you so thin, O crow?

In this context, *bhattaṃ* refers to food prepared according to the human custom of dining. He addresses him as “uncle” (*mātula*) out of affectionate courtesy. “Thin” (*kisa*) means having little flesh and blood.
Having heard his words, the crow spoke these three verses:
“For one living in the midst of enemies, seeking only their bait,
with a heart constantly agitated— whence can there be firmness for such a crow?”
“Crows and vultures are constantly anxious due to their evil deeds;
even when they find alms-food, it does not satisfy them, and so I am thin, O sparrow.
You eat coarse seeds of grass that contain little moisture.”
"Now, by what reason are you so stout and round?
In this context, "daḷhiyanti" means: from where could there be such stoutness in a crow like me? From where could there be stoutness? This is the meaning.
"Ubbegino" means possessed of agitation. "Dhaṅkā" is simply another name for crows. "Obtained through evil karma" refers to [the state] of a crow.
The alms-food obtained through the evil karma known as plundering what belongs to humans. "It does not satisfy" means it does not nourish.
"Therefore I am thus" means for that reason I am emaciated. "With little moisture" means lacking essence.
Although the crow perceived the Bodhisatta to be eating choice food, he spoke thus while asking about the food-gathering of the quails.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke these verses while explaining the reason for his own stoutness:
“By having few desires, by not brooding over things, and by not traveling far;
by subsisting on whatever is obtained or not obtained—it is because of this, O crow, that I am stout.”
“For the person of few desires, who finds happiness in having little concern,
whose pride is well-restrained, his livelihood is easily acquired. In this context,
“of few desires” means being free from craving due to having few desires regarding food, [seeking] only for the mere maintenance of the body.
The meaning is: "by means of taking food. "By lack of anxiety" means by the absence of such anxiety regarding food as, "Where shall I get food today? Where tomorrow?
"And by not going far" means by not traveling a great distance with the thought, "I shall obtain sweet food in such-and-such a place.
"Whether obtained or unobtained" means whether it be coarse or refined, whatever has been obtained.
"By that very [reason]. "I am stout by that"—by those four kinds of causes, I am stout. "O crow!"—he addresses the crow. "Of those with happiness free from anxiety":
one who desires the happiness of the noble ones (ariya) who are free from anxiety, being devoid of concern for food, is "one with happiness free from anxiety";
[the phrase refers to] one endowed with such happiness. "With a well-restrained mind": [thinking], "Having eaten this much, I shall digest it..."
"I shall be able [to do so]"—thus for one who has well-restrained their intake of food.
"A livelihood that is easy to procure" means that for such a person, the maintenance of life can be easily procured; it is "easy to procure" because it is well-accomplished.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths (*sacca*), the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
At that time, the crow was the greedy monk, while I myself was the quail.
This concludes the ninth narrative, the Commentary on the Quail Jātaka. [395] 10. The Commentary on the Pigeon Jātaka.
"Indeed, after a long time I see you!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a greedy bhikkhu. The present-day account is exactly as described above.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having become a dove, lived in a nest-basket in the kitchen of the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī.
A crow also made friends with him and lived right there as well.
Everything should be expanded in detail. The cook plucked out the crows’ feathers, smeared them with flour, pierced a piece of a skull, fastened it around his neck, and placed him in a basket.
When the Bodhisatta returned from the forest and saw him, he spoke the first verse in jest:
“After a long time indeed I see my friend, the bearer of the jewel;
truly my companion shines with his well-groomed beard.
In this context, “with his well-groomed beard” means by means of this act of shaving the beard.
Having heard that, the crow spoke this second verse:
"With my armpits and body hair grown long, I have been occupied with my work;
having finally found a barber after a long time, I am having that hair shaved off today."

"In that regard, 'I was occupied with duties' means: 'O friend pāravata, being occupied with royal affairs and finding no opportunity, my armpits and pubic hair grew long,' he says. 'Today I had it removed' means: 'Today I had it removed.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
'The hair which you did not remove today, though a barber—so difficult to find—had been obtained.'"
"Now then, my dear friend, what is this that is jingling at your throat?
The meaning of this is: "Since you have had your hair removed after finding a barber so difficult to obtain, let that be; but what is this now that is jingling at your throat, my friend?
Thereupon the crow spoke two verses:
“A jeweled ornament hangs from the necks of those delicate men;
I am training myself according to their example—do not think this was done in jest.
Even if you desire this well-fashioned trimming of my beard, [I shall do it].”
“Friend, I shall have it made for you; I will even give you a gem.
In this context, “a gem” refers to a jewel-ornament that hangs from the necks of such people. “Tesaṃ ahaṃ” means “I [will provide] for them.
“Mā tvaṃ maññī” means “but do not think, ‘This was done by me in jest. Even if this...
"You desire it" means: if you wish for this beard-grooming performed by me.
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the sixth verse:
"You alone are covered by the jewel, and by the well-fashioned beard."
“Indeed, I shall go to you; I long to see you.
Therein, “maṇinā” means “of the gem,” or rather this reading, “maṇino,” is correct. This is what is meant:
“O crow, you alone are a worthy match for this gem and for this well-made basket; but for me, it is simply the sight of you that I desire.”
"It is dear; therefore, having taken leave of it, I shall go.
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta flew up and went elsewhere. The crow met its death right there.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
The greedy monk was established in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). At that time, the crow was the greedy monk, while I myself was the pigeon.
This concludes the tenth discourse, the Commentary on the Pārāvata Jātaka.
The second chapter, the Kharaputta Vagga, is finished.
The Summary of Birth Stories (Jātaka-uddāna): Avāriya, Setaketu, Darīmukha, and Neru;
Āsaṅka, Migālopa, Kāḷakaṇṇī, and Kukkuṭa.
Dhammadhaja and Nandiya, Kharaputta and Sūci;
Tuṇḍila, Soṇṇakakkaṭa, Mayhaka, and Vijjādhara;
Siṅghapuppha, Vighāsāda, Vaṭṭaka, and Pārāvata.
The Great Elders recited twenty Jātakas in the sixth chapter.
The commentary on the Chakkanipāta is concluded.
7. The Sattakanipāta (The Chapter of Seven).
1. The Section on Cocks [396]. 1. The Commentary on the Cock Birth Story (*Kukkujātaka*).

"A cock and a half"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the *Rājovāda* (Advice to the King). The story of the present time will be made clear in the *Tesakuṇa-jātaka*.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister, advising him in matters of welfare and righteousness.
Having set out upon a wrong path, the king ruled unrighteously; he oppressed the countryside and gathered only wealth for himself.
Desiring to admonish the king, the Bodhisatta wandered about, reflecting upon a parable.
In the king’s park, a dwelling house was under construction with its roof yet unfinished; the wooden rafters had been set up and the cross-beams had merely been inserted.

The king, having gone to the park for recreation, wandered about there, entered that house, and while looking upward, saw the circular framework of the rafters. Fearing he might fall upon it, he went out.
Standing outside and looking again, he thought, "Upon what does the central pillar stand? Upon what do the rafters rest?
Then, questioning the Bodhisatta, he spoke the first verse:
"The central pillar rises one and a half *kukkūs* in height; eight spans (*vidatthi*) encircle it."
"That *siṃsapā* tree, made of heartwood and free of pith, standing where it does, does not shake from above.
Therein, "one and a half *kukkus*" means one and a half *ratanas*. "By height" (*udayena*) means by its vertical measure. "They surround it" means they encircle it;
for this [tree] is eight spans (*vidatthi*) in circumference, as it is said to be eight spans in measurement around.
"It exists. "Where is it situated? means: having been established where? "It does not collapse" means: it does not fall down.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta thought, "I have now obtained a simile for the purpose of the King's instruction," and he spoke these verses:
"That which consists of thirty straight beams of heartwood, Laid out evenly with cross-beams, stands firm; ... [the rest of the verse follows] ..."
Well-fastened by those [rafters] and pressed down with force, standing evenly, it does not collapse from above.
"In this same way, a wise man, well-supported by firm, incorruptible, and pure counselors,
does not fall from his prosperity, just as a central ridge-pole does not collapse when supported by rafters bearing its weight."
In that context: "The thirty made of heartwood" refers to those thirty rafters made of heartwood. "Encircling" means surrounding them.
"Standing level" means standing with equal parts. "Pressed by force" means pressed by the strength of those various rafters, being well-restrained and joined together as one.
"The wise one" refers to the king endowed with knowledge. "By the pure ones" means...
"With friends of noble character" means with those of pure conduct. "With counselors" means with those skilled in counsel.

"Like the ridge-pole bearing the weight of the rafters": just as the ridge-pole, bearing the weight of the rafters, does not collapse or fall, so too a king who is well-supported by such counselors—whose hearts are loyal—does not collapse, does not fall, and does not decline in his glory.
Even as the Bodhisatta was speaking, the king observed his own situation: "In the absence of the central ridge-pole (*kaṇṇikā*), the rafters (*gopānasi*) do not remain;
without being supported by the rafters, the central ridge-pole does not remain; when the rafters break, the central ridge-pole falls.
In exactly the same way, an unrighteous king [falls] from his friends and ministers, his army, and the brahmins and householders."
Furthermore, if he does not hold them together when they are breaking apart and is not supported by them, his sovereignty will fall away;
for a king must indeed be righteous. Then, at that moment, they brought a citron as a gift for him.
The king said to the Bodhisatta, "Friend, eat this citron. Having taken it, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, this..."

"Those who do not know how to eat make it bitter or sour; but the wise, knowing how, remove the bitterness without discarding the sourness and without adding the juice of *mātuluṅga*, and thus they eat.
Demonstrating to the king the means of accumulating wealth through this simile, he spoke these two verses:
“Just as a caravan leader makes bitter bell fruit palatable even without touching it, so too, O King, one who collects wealth makes it sweet;
but one who seizes it by force makes it tasteless.
Likewise, a wise man in villages and market towns, gathering royal revenues without violence,”
"Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, he would bring it to fruition without harming others.
In this context, *kharattacaṃ* means "rough bark. *Bellaṃ* means a citron (*mātuluṅga*). There is also a reading *belaṃ*, which has the same meaning.
*Satthavā* means "with a knife in hand. *Anāmasanto* means not touching even the thin outer bark; [thinking] "this is the fruit..."
It makes it bitter. One who gathers [the parts] together, while scraping the outer bark and not removing the inner sourness, makes it sweet.

"O King," he addresses the monarch. One who removes the thin band [of bark], yet removes only the thin bark and does not entirely eliminate the bitterness, would indeed make it unsweet. "Thus" means in this manner.
The wise king, too, not falling under the sway of reckless craving and abandoning the path to ruin,
protected his kingdom without oppression; he accumulated wealth by the method of ants building an anthill and by the method of bees gathering pollen.
“Generosity, virtue, renunciation, uprightness, gentleness,
austerity, non-anger, non-harming, patience, and non-opposition.”— Thus,
by practicing in accordance with these ten royal duties, acting as one who follows the Dhamma, he would increase the prosperity and welfare of both himself and others, without ever harming another.
The king, consulting with the Bodhisatta, went to the edge of a lotus pond.
Seeing a lotus in full bloom, with the color of the rising sun, standing untouched by the water, he said: "Friend, this lotus, though born in the water, stands there unsullied by the water.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him: "Great King, a king indeed ought to be like this."
Admonishing him, he spoke these verses:
“Just as a lotus born in lotus-pools, with its roots white and produced from pure water,
is not smeared by mud, nor by dust, nor by water— even when scorched by the heat of a fire— just so is the one who has abandoned all attachments.”

“Thus, one who is pure in conventional conduct, free from violence, whose actions are purified, and who has cast off evil—such a person is not smeared by the defilements of karma, just as a lotus born in lotus ponds is not.
Therein, *odātamūlaṃ* means having a white root. *Ambujaṃ* is a synonym for the lotus (*paduma*). *Agginikāsiphālitaṃ*... [text continues]
The meaning is that it is split open and blossomed by the sun, which has the appearance of fire.
"Neither mud, nor dust, nor water stains it" means that neither mud, nor dust, nor water stains or smears it.

Alternatively, the reading is simply "lippati," or these words are in the nominative case used in the sense of the locative; thus, it does not stain or adhere to those things, such as mud and the rest.
The meaning is as follows: "Pure in legal procedure" (*vohārasuci*) means pure in the judicial procedures established by ancient righteous kings after they had them committed to writing;
the meaning is that one who administers justice according to the Dhamma, having abandoned the path of wrong-doing.

"Free from violence" (*asāhasa*) means being devoid of violent action precisely because of standing firm in righteous adjudication. "Of purified conduct" (*visuddhakammanta*) [is so called] for that very same reason of being free from violence.
One whose conduct is pure, who speaks the truth, who is free from anger, impartial, and like a scale for the world—one who is "devoid of evil" means one whose evil karma has been removed.

"Such a one is not smeared by the defilements of karma": this defilement of karma—namely, killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech—does not adhere to such a king. For what reason? Because such a person is born [with such qualities].
Just as a lotus in ponds—just as the lotus born in ponds is unstained, so too is he called "unstained.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s advice, the king from then on ruled his kingdom according to Dhamma; performing meritorious deeds such as giving, he became destined for heaven.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the wise minister. This concludes the first narrative, the Kukkujātaka. 2. The Manojajātaka Narrative: The Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now that the Bodhisatta has been a wise counselor; in the past, too, he was a wise counselor. Then the monks asked the Teacher:

"Venerable Sir, when was the Bodhisatta a wise counselor? The Teacher replied: "In the past, monks, there was a king named Manoja. He had a wise counselor named Mahosadha. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Mahosadha. Once upon a time, monks, King Manoja ruled over the kingdom of Mithilā. He was wise, intelligent, and possessed of great discernment. He was skilled in the art of governance and capable of administering the affairs of state. His counselor, Mahosadha, was likewise wise, intelligent, and possessed of great discernment. He was skilled in the art of governance and capable of administering the affairs of state. One day, while the king was seated on the royal throne in the inner apartments, surrounded by his ministers, a messenger arrived from the frontier regions. He approached the king, paid homage, and sat down at one side. Seated thus, the messenger addressed the king: "Your Majesty, the border tribes have risen in revolt. The king, having heard this, became agitated and anxious. He summoned his ministers and said: "Sirs, the border tribes have risen in revolt. What shall we do? The ministers replied: "Your Majesty, the border tribes are fierce and difficult to subdue. We cannot overcome them by force alone. Let us send a messenger to them, requesting peace. The king agreed and dispatched a messenger with instructions: "Go to the border tribes and tell them: 'We wish for peace. The messenger went to the border tribes and delivered the message. They replied: "We will not make peace unless you send us a tribute of a thousand elephants. The messenger returned and reported this to the king. The king was distressed, thinking: "How can I provide such a tribute? He consulted his ministers, who advised him to seek the counsel of Mahosadha. The king summoned Mahosadha and said: "Friend, the border tribes demand a tribute of a thousand elephants. How shall we provide this? Mahosadha replied: "Your Majesty, do not worry. I shall find a way. With the king's permission, he went out of the city and stood at the crossroads. There he saw a man carrying a single elephant. He approached the man and asked: "Sir, why are you carrying this elephant? The man replied: "I am carrying it because I need its tusks for a medicine. Mahosadha said: "If that is so, I will give you a large sum of money; let me have the elephant. He paid the man a great price and took the elephant. He then sent word to the border tribes: "I have obtained a thousand elephants; come and collect your tribute. The border tribes were amazed and thought: "This must be some trickery. They sent a messenger back to ask: "Where are these elephants? Mahosadha replied: "They are in the city. Come and take them. The border tribes went to the city and found that there were indeed a thousand elephants. They were astonished and said: "This is truly a clever stratagem! They made peace with the king and departed. The Teacher, having related this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, King Manoja was Ānanda, and I myself was the wise counselor Mahosadha. This concludes the second narrative, the Manojajātaka.
The story of "Just as Water Flows Downward" was told by the Teacher while staying at Veḷuvana concerning a monk who associated with his adversaries.
The background of the story has already been related in detail below in the Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka. At that time, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past, too, this man was one who associated with his adversaries," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having become a lion, lived together with a lioness and obtained two cubs—a son and a daughter. The son’s name was Manoja;
when he reached maturity, he took a lioness for himself. Thus there were five individuals. Manoja [lived] in the forest among the wild buffalo and other animals.
Having killed [the animal], he brought the meat and supported his mother, father, sister, and wife.
One day, while on his alms-round, he saw a jackal named Giri lying on its chest, unable to flee;
asking, "What is it, friend? and being told, "I wish to serve you, Master," he said, "Very well, serve me," and took him along.
He brought him to his own dwelling cave. When the Bodhisatta saw him, he was unable to prevent him, saying, "Dear Manoja, jackals are indeed immoral and of evil nature;
they urge one toward what should not be done, so do not keep him near you.
Then one day, desiring to eat the flesh of the hermitage, the jackal said to Manoja: "Master, apart from us..."
“There is no horse meat that we have not eaten before; let us seize a horse. “But where, friend, are there horses? “In Bārāṇasī, on the riverbank.

Taking his word, he went with him to the horses at the time they were bathing in the river, seized one horse, mounted it on his back, and proceeded with great speed toward the entrance of his own cave.
He returned. Then his father, having eaten horse meat, said to him, "Dear son, horses are indeed the property of kings;
moreover, kings have many wiles and cause them to be pierced by skilled archers.
Lions that eat horse meat do not live long. From now on, do not take horses. But he did not heed his father's words and continued to take them. "The lion..."
Having heard, “He seizes [the horse] right there,” the king had a lotus pond for horses constructed within the city itself.
Even from there, Sīha would come and seize them. The king had a stable for horses built and provided fodder and water only inside the hall.
Sīha would go along the top of the wall and seize them even from inside the hall.
The king summoned a marksman who could hit a target at a distance of one *akkhaṇa* and said, "My son, will you be able to shoot the lion?
He replied, "I can," and having had a stand erected against the wall on the path by which the lion would come, he took his position there.
When the lion arrived, he left the jackal in the outer cemetery and leaped into the city to seize a horse. The archer—
On the way there, thinking, "The speed is too fierce," he did not shoot at the lion, but instead took hold of the horse.
On the way back, because of the heavy burden, the lion’s speed had slackened; [the hunter] then pierced the lion in its hindquarters with a sharp iron arrow (*nārāca*).
The arrow emerged from the front part of the body and soared into the sky. The lion cried out, "I have been pierced! Having shot it, the archer—like a thunderbolt—...
He struck the bowstring. Hearing the sound of both the lion and the bowstring, the jackal thought, "My friend must have been shot and killed by the archer;
there can be no friendship with one who is dead.
Now I shall go back to the forest where I usually dwell. Speaking thus to himself, he uttered two verses:
“Since the bow bends and the string twangs, Manoja,
the king of deer and my friend, must surely have been slain.
Come now, I shall depart from the forest depths as I please.”
“Guides such as these are true friends; while I live, a friend may indeed be found.

Herein, “in such a manner” means in whatever way the bow bends down. “Is surely slain” means he is certainly killed. “Guides such as these” means that those who have died are not called friends at all. “May I find” means it is possible for me, while living, to obtain a friend.
Then Sīha, having gone with a single bound and cast the horse down at the mouth of the cave, himself also died and fell. Then his kinsmen...
Having gone out, they saw him smeared with blood, with blood streaming from his wounds,
fallen into the end of life, frequented by wicked people; and having seen him, his mother, father, sister,
and wife spoke four verses in succession:
“One who does not associate with evil people attains ultimate happiness;
see how Giriyasī’s son attained mental joy by following his instruction.
One whose mother delights in associating with the wicked does not rejoice as a mother would for her own son.”
"Behold Manoja lying there, covered all over with blood.
Thus does a person come to ruin and fall into even greater evil—
he who does not act upon the words of those who wish him well and see his true welfare."
“And thus he becomes even worse than that, who, though excellent, serves base people;
behold the excellence of one who served base people, the lord of beasts, struck down by the forceful speed of the arrow.
In this context, “he prospers in ultimate happiness” means that he does not obtain happiness for long. “The instruction of Giriya” refers to this.
"Such is his instruction," he said, censuring him. "By one who is a companion in evil" means by one who is associated with evil, a companion in wickedness.
"Submerged" means sunk down. "He becomes even more wicked" means he encounters further evil. "Of those who desire his welfare" means of those who wish for his benefit.
"Of those who see the future benefit" means of those who perceive the purpose yet to come. "More wicked" means more evil. "One who serves base people."
One who associates with inferior people. "Superior" means one who is senior by virtue of physical strength.
The final verse of the Fully Enlightened One is as follows:
"A person who associates with the inferior declines; he who associates with equals never declines."
"One who approaches the best rises quickly; therefore, one should resort to that which is even more excellent.
In this context, "he is humbled" means, monks, that one who serves the inferior is humbled—just like the elephant Manoja—he declines, falls away, and meets with destruction.
"One who serves equals" means that by serving those equal to oneself in virtue and other qualities, one does not decline; there is only progress.
"‘He approaches the best’: he approaches that which is even more superior through such qualities as virtue (sīla). ‘He rises quickly’:
he rises swiftly indeed through qualities such as virtue; he attains growth.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (sacca), the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, Vipakkhasevaka was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
At that time, Devadatta was the jackal, Vipakkhasevaka was Manoja, Uppalavaṇṇā was the sister, the nun Khemā was the wife, Rāhulamātā was the mother, and my father was King Sīha—I myself was he.
This concludes the second commentary, the Manoja Jātaka.
[398] 3. The Commentary on the Sutanu Jātaka.

"Your Majesty, he is your servant"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the monk Mātuposaka (the Supporter of His Mother). The story will be made clear in the Sāmajātaka.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of poor householders;
they gave him the name Sutanūti. When he reached maturity, he worked for wages, supported his mother and father, and after his father passed away...
He supported his mother. At that time, however, the King of Bārāṇasī was fond of hunting.
One day, having entered the forest to the extent of one or two *yojanas* with a large retinue, he announced to everyone:
"Whoever causes a deer to flee by his very standing place shall be declared the winner of this prize. The ministers built a watchtower on the king's regular path.

They gave it to him after covering it up. When the men had surrounded the deer’s dwelling places and raised a great clamor, causing the deer to rise up, a single black antelope entered the place where the king was standing. The king, thinking, "I shall pierce him," discharged an arrow.
Having mastered the art of illusion, the deer, perceiving the arrow coming toward his great flank, turned around and [faced] the arrow.
Having become as if pierced, he fell down. The king, thinking, "I have wounded the deer," ran after it to seize it.
The deer rose up and fled with the speed of the wind; the ministers and others laughed at the king.
He pursued the deer until he was exhausted, then cut it in two with his sword, hung one half on a stick, and returned like one carrying a yoke.
Thinking, “I will rest for a short while,” he approached a banyan tree standing near the road, lay down, and fell asleep.
Now, a yakkha named Māghadeva had been reborn in that banyan tree; having entered it, he received permission from Vessavaṇa to eat anyone who went there.
Seeing the king rising and walking away, he seized him by the hand, saying, “Stop! You are my food.”
He seized him. “Who are you? he asked. “I am a yakkha born here; I am permitted to eat those who enter this place.
The king, establishing mindfulness, asked: “Will you eat me this very day, or will you eat me regularly?
“If I obtain them, I shall eat them regularly. The king said: “Eat this deer today and release me.”
“I will send one person from my own household to you, together with a single bowl of food.
“In that case, be careful; on the day he is not sent, we shall eat that very food ourselves.
“I am the King of Bārāṇasī; there is nothing that does not exist for me. Having obtained this promise, the yakkha released him. He entered the city.
Having told this matter to one of his ministers who was his personal attendant, he asked, "What should be done now?
[The minister replied,] "A time limit has been set, Your Majesty. "It has not been set," [the king said]. "You have acted improperly;
even so, do not worry, for there are many people in the prison. "In that case, you must carry out this task yourself; give me my life back!"
The friend, having agreed by saying "Very well," would daily bring a person out from the prison, take a bowl of food, and send it to the *yakkha* without anyone knowing.
The *yakkha*, having eaten the food, would devour the human being.
In time, the prisons became devoid of people. When the king could no longer find anyone to carry the food, he was overcome with the fear of death.
He trembled. Then the minister, having comforted him, said, “Your Majesty, the hope for wealth is stronger than the hope for life.
Let us place a bundle of a thousand coins upon the back of an elephant and have the drum beaten, proclaiming: ‘Who will take this wealth and go to bring food for the Yakkha?
Having said this, he had it done accordingly. Hearing that, the Bodhisatta thought, “I [will go] for the sake of wages...”
“By gathering even a māsaka or half a māsaka, I support my mother with great difficulty.
Taking this wealth and giving it to my mother, I shall go into the presence of the yakkha. If I am able to subdue the yakkha, that will be well;
if I am not able, my mother will live in comfort. Having reported this matter to his mother, he said, “Enough…”
“Father, I have no need for wealth,” he said, refusing twice;
but on the third occasion, without even asking her permission, he took a thousand [pieces], saying, “Bring a thousand, noble sir, I will carry the meal,” and gave it to his mother.
Then he said, “Mother, do not worry; I shall subdue the yakkha and bring safety to the great multitude. This very day, for you—”
“I will come after making her laugh,” he said, and having paid homage to his mother, he went with the royal attendants into the presence of the king. Having paid homage, he stood there.
Then the king asked, “Dear son, will you carry the food? “Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. “What have you received?”
“Is it appropriate? “Your golden sandals, O King. “For what reason? “O King, that yakkha is permitted to devour those who stand upon the ground at the foot of his own tree;
I shall not stand on ground belonging to him, but shall stand upon the sandals. “What else is appropriate to receive? “Your parasol, O King.”
“What is the purpose of this? [The king asked. “Your Majesty, a *yakkha* may eat anyone who stands within the shade of his own tree;
I shall not stand in the shade of that tree, but shall stand in the shade of your parasol. “What else would you like to have?
