“Your sword, Sire. “What use is this to you? “Sire, even non-human beings [fear] those with weapons in their hands.”
“They are indeed afraid. “What else should be obtained? “Your Majesty, fill a golden bowl and give us the food we eat.
“For what reason, dear ones? “Your Majesty, it is not fitting for a wise man such as myself to carry coarse food in an earthenware bowl.
“Very well, dear ones,” the king said, and having caused everything to be given, he [bestowed it] upon him.
He assigned them to attendants.
The Bodhisatta said to the king, “Great King, do not fear; today I shall subdue the yakkha and return after ensuring your safety.
Having paid homage to the king and had the necessary provisions gathered, he went there and stationed men not far from the tree.
Setting aside his golden sandals, having girded his sword, and holding a white parasol over his head, he took rice in a golden bowl and set out toward the presence of the yakkha.
The yakkha, watching the road, saw him and thought, "This man does not come according to the pattern of his arrivals on other days; what could be the reason? The Bodhisatta, too—
Having gone near the tree, he placed the bowl of food within the shade using the tip of his beak, and standing at the edge of the shade,
he spoke the first verse:
“The king has sent you this meal, pure, with meat as its sauce.”
“Come out and eat, you who dwell in the *maghadeva* tree!”—in this context, “he sent” means he dispatched [a messenger].
“In the *maghadeva* tree” refers to the deity dwelling in that tree; for the *maghadeva* is called a banyan tree (*vaṭarukkha*), and he addresses that deity.
Having heard this, the yakkha thought, “I will deceive this man and eat him once he has entered the inner shade,” and spoke the second verse:
“Come, young man, having taken alms that are well-prepared with broth;
both you, young man, and the alms-food, both shall become food.
In this context, “alms” refers to my regular supply of alms-food; “well-prepared with broth” means it is fully endowed with soup.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke two verses:
“By a small thing, O yakkha, you will lose a great matter;
people, perceiving death, will no longer bring you alms.”

“O Yakkha, having received your constant alms—pure, excellent, and endowed with the finest flavors—there will be no man here who brings you alms once I have been devoured; indeed, it will be very difficult for him to find food.
In this context, “thullamatthaṃ” means that by a small cause you will abandon a great purpose. “Nāharissantī” means they will not bring [alms].
"From now on, perceiving death, they will not bring [food]; then, like a tree with withered branches, you will become weak, deprived of food.
"Laddhāyaṃ" means "having obtained this," that is, having obtained the arrival. This is what is meant:
"O friend Yakkha, what I have brought today shall be your regular alms-food, pure and excellent."
"Endowed with the finest flavor, it shall come to you daily, having been obtained. *Āhariyo* means "one who brings.
This is what is meant: "If you eat me after I have come bringing this alms-food, then once I am thus eaten, another man to bring you alms will be very difficult to find here. For what reason?"
"For there is no other wise man like me in Bārāṇasī; moreover, when I was eaten, even Sutanu was eaten by a yakkha—of whom else would he be ashamed?
Thus you will not receive food to bring back, and from this point on, food will be difficult for you to obtain; nor will it be possible for us to seize the king.
"You will obtain it. Why? Because you are outside the tree. However, if after eating this meal you send me away, I shall inform the king and ensure that you receive a regular supply of food;
I shall not allow him to eat you, nor shall I remain standing near you—I shall stand upon my sandals—and I shall not even stay in the shade of the tree for you."
"I shall remain here; I shall remain within the very shade of my own parasol.
But if you oppose me, I will split you in two with my sword, for I have come today having prepared myself specifically for this purpose.
Thus, it is said, the Great Being rebuked him.
The yakkha, observing that "the young man speaks what is fitting," spoke with a clear heart these two verses:
"It is for my very sake, Sutano, that you speak thus, young man.
Permitted by me, may you see your mother in safety."
“O young man, taking your sword, umbrella, and bowl, go;
may your mother see you safely, and may you see your mother.
Therein, *sutano* addresses the Bodhisatta. *Yathā bhāsasi* means: “Just as you speak, so this matter which has been spoken by you is my very own matter; it is for my own prosperity.”
Having heard the yakkha’s words, the Bodhisatta—thinking, “My task is accomplished; the yakkha has been subdued by me;
much wealth has been obtained; and the king’s word has been fulfilled”—with a joyful heart, offered his thanks to the yakkha and spoke this concluding verse:
“Thus, O yakkha, may you be happy, together with all your kinsmen.”
"I have acquired wealth and I have carried out the king’s command.

Having said this, he addressed the yakkha: "Friend, because you previously committed unwholesome deeds, you were reborn as a harsh and cruel yakkha who feeds on the blood and flesh of others; from now on, do not commit the taking of life and other such acts."
Having thus explained the benefits of virtue and the dangers of immorality, he established the yakṣa in the five precepts.
Then, saying, "What is the use of your dwelling in the forest? Come, let us seat you at the city gate and make you a recipient of the first portion of alms," he went out with the yakṣa.
Having had the yakṣa take up his sword and other weapons, he proceeded to Bārāṇasī. "Sutanu..."
"A young man is coming, having seized a *yakkha*," they reported to the king. The king, surrounded by his ministers, went out to meet the Bodhisatta;
he had the *yakkha* seated at the city gate, appointed him to receive the first portion of the alms-food, and having entered the city, caused the drum to be beaten to assemble the citizens.
After proclaiming the Bodhisatta’s virtues, he [appointed him] to the position of general.
He gave [the gift]. And this man, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and became destined for heaven.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the bhikkhu who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the yakkha was Aṅgulimāla, and the king was Ānanda.
"But I myself was that young brahmin.
This concludes the third narrative, the Sutanu Jātaka.
[399] 4. The Commentary on the Mātuposaka Gijjha Jātaka (The Vulture Who Nourished His Mother).
"How will they manage?"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who supported his mother. The background story will be revealed in the Sāmajātaka.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a vulture.
Having reached maturity, he placed his aged and blind parents in a vulture cave and [provided for them] with beef and other such foods.
Having brought it back, he nourished them. At that time, in the charnel ground at Bārāṇasī, a hunter had set a snare for vultures without any restraint.
Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was searching for beef and other such food, he entered the charnel ground;
having caught his foot in the snare, he did not think of himself, but remembering his aged, sightless parents, [he thought: "How..."
“Will my parents indeed survive, not even knowing of my state of captivity?
I think they will perish, helpless and destitute, withering away right here in this mountain cave,” he lamented, and spoke the first verse:
“How indeed will they fare, those aged ones dwelling in the mountain cleft?”
“I am bound by the snare; I have fallen under the power of Nīlīya.
Therein, “of Nīlīya” means of the son of a hunter (nesāda) named thus.
Then, having heard the sound of the vulture-king’s lamentation, the hunter’s son spoke the second verse:
“Why do you lament greedily? What is this lamentation of yours?
For I have never heard or seen a bird speaking in human speech.
The vulture replied:
“I support my parents, who are old and dwell in a mountain cave;
how indeed will they fare when I have fallen under your power?
The hunter said:
“Since the vulture surveys carcasses for a hundred leagues,
why is it that you do not wake up even when encountering the net and the snare?
The king of vultures replied:
“When ruin comes upon a person at the end of life, then,
though encountering nets and snares, they do not wake up.
“Support your parents when they are old and dwelling in mountain caves;”
“I have given you my consent; may you see your kinsmen in safety.
“Thus, hunter, rejoice together with all your kinsmen;
I shall support my aged mother and father dwelling in the mountain cave.”
"The second [verse] was spoken by the son of a hunter, and the third by the vulture. These verses were spoken in sequence.

Therein, "What indeed" means that which is said in the world. "The vulture sees corpses even from a hundred leagues away" means that he sees corpses even though they are situated beyond a hundred leagues; if that is so, then why do you...
"Even though you have encountered this net and this snare, you do not wake up; even though you have come into my presence, you do not realize it.

"Parābhava" means destruction. Regarding the word "bharassu": having heard this Dhamma discourse from the Bodhisatta, he thought, "This wise vulture king, while lamenting, does not lament for himself; he laments for his parents. He will not kill me..."
Satisfied, he said, “It is well-fitted! and having spoken thus, with a heart of love and a gentle mind, he released the snare.
Then the Bodhisatta, freed from the jaws of death and made happy, offered words of thanksgiving; reciting the concluding verse, he took a mouthful of flesh and gave it to his parents.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the bhikkhu Mātuposaka was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.
At that time, Channa was the son of the hunter; his parents were members of a great royal family; and as for the king of vultures, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the fourth Jātaka, the Mātuposaka-gijjha-jātaka.
[400] 5. Commentary on the Dabbhapuppha-jātaka.
"O Bhante, he who wanders along the shore"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning Upananda the Sakyan-son.
For after going forth in the Dispensation, having abandoned qualities such as fewness of desires, he became one of great craving.
During the rains-retreat, having taken possession of two or three monasteries, he would keep his sunshade or sandals in one, and his staff in another.
Having set aside either a water-pot or a water-jar, he dwelt alone.

Having entered the rains retreat in a certain monastery in the countryside, as if raising the moon in the sky, he preached to the monks the practice of the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsa) which demonstrates contentment with the basic requisites, saying, "Monks, one must indeed be of few desires. Hearing this, the monks [prepared] delightful...
Having discarded their bowls and robes, they took up clay bowls and rag-robes.
He placed those at his own dwelling place, and having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā*, he filled a carriage and set out for Jetavana.
On the way, on the back side of a certain forest monastery, his foot became caught in a creeper; thinking, "Surely here..."
Thinking, "I shall obtain something," he entered that monastery. There, two elderly monks had entered the rains retreat.
Having received two coarse cloths and one fine woolen blanket, they were unable to divide them;
seeing him, they thought with joyful hearts, "The elder will divide these for us," and said, "Venerable sir, we [have these]..."
"We cannot divide the rainy-season robes; because of this, a dispute has arisen among us.

Divide this and give it to us," they said. He replied, "Very well, I shall divide them. Having divided two coarse cloths between the two groups, he took a woolen blanket, saying, "This belongs to our Vinaya experts," and departed.
The elders of Tepi, being attached to their woolen blankets, went with him to Jetavana.
Having informed the monks who were experts in the Vinaya of that matter, they asked: "Venerable sirs, is it permissible for those who are experts in the Vinaya to consume such plunder?
When the monks saw the heap of bowls and robes brought by the elder Upananda, they said: "You possess great merit."
"Friend, you have obtained much alms-bowl and robe," they said. He replied, "From where, friends, could I have merit?
I obtained this by means of such-and-such a stratagem," and he told them everything.
The monks raised the discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, Upananda the Sakyan-son has great craving and great greed. The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "What are you discussing?"
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked. When they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, Upananda has not acted in a manner befitting his own practice.
Indeed, a monk who wishes to advise another must first ensure that his own conduct is appropriate; only then should he advise another.”
"First, one should establish oneself in what is proper;
then one may instruct others, and thus the wise person shall not be defiled.
Having taught the Dhamma with this verse from the *Dhammapada*, [the Blessed One said]: "Monks, it is not only now that Upananda has done so; formerly too he was like this."
"Having great craving and great greed, and not only now, but even in the past, he used to plunder the property of these very people," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity living on the bank of a river.
At that time, a certain jackal named Māyāvin lived with his wife on a certain spot by the riverbank. Then one day...
The female jackal said to the male jackal, "My lord, a craving has arisen in me; I wish to eat fresh red fish. The jackal replied, "Do not worry;
I shall bring it for you. While wandering along the riverbank, he became entangled by a creeper wrapping around his leg and was carried right along with the current.
At that moment, two otters—one a deep-water dweller and the other a shore-dweller—[saw] the fish...

While searching, they stood upon the bank. Among them, one who dwelt in the deep waters, seeing a large rohita fish, quickly entered the water and seized it by the tail. The powerful fish went along, dragging him behind.
That deep-water crocodile, thinking, "This great fish will be enough for both of us; come, be my companion," spoke thus with the other.
He spoke the first verse:
“O noble one who wanders along the shore, run after my companion!
A large fish has been caught by me; it is carrying me away with great speed.”
In that context, "sahāyamanudhāva maṃ" means "run after me, my companion"; the letter *m* is used here by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
This is what is meant: "Just as I am not deprived of this fish, so you, having seized me by the tail, run after me.
Having heard that, the other spoke the second verse:
“O Venerable One, you who move in the deep, grasp firmly with strength!
I shall pull you out, just as a garuḍa pulls out a snake. In this context, “with strength” means by means of power.
“I shall pull you out” means I shall extract you. “Just as a garuḍa [pulls out] a snake” means like a *garuḷa* pulling out a serpent.
Then the two of them, having joined together, brought out the rohita fish, placed it on dry land, and killed it.
Quarreling over who should divide it, saying, "You divide it! You divide it!", they were unable to reach an agreement and sat there waiting.
At that time, a jackal arrived at that place. Seeing him, they both went forward to meet him and said, "Friend, this..."
“The Dabbhapuppha fish was caught by us together; because we were unable to divide it among ourselves, a dispute arose.
Divide it into equal portions for us and give it to us! Thus they spoke the third verse:
“A dispute has arisen among us; O Dabbhapuppha, listen to me!
"By means of conciliation, let the dispute be properly settled.
Therein, "dabbhapuppha" refers to addressing him because his color is like that of a *dabbha* flower. "Medhaga" means quarrel.
Having heard their words, the jackal, demonstrating his own strength—
“I was established in the Dhamma in the past; many lawsuits were settled by me.
I have properly quelled the strife; the dispute has been pacified.
Having spoken this verse, he distributed [the goods].
“The tail shall move along the bank, the head shall move deep within;
the middle section, being worn away, shall remain as it is for one who stands firm in the Dhamma.
Thus he spoke this verse.
In this regard, the meaning of the first verse is as follows: Formerly, I was a minister of judgment for kings;
sitting in the court of justice, I decided many legal cases for various brahmins, householders, and others.
Having thus decided and adjudicated their many disputes, why should I now fail to decide the dispute of four-footed creatures such as yourselves, who are of the same species?
"I shall not be able to settle your dispute; let your quarrel be properly settled by relying on me.
Having said this, he divided the fish into three portions: "You who frequent the shore, take the tail; let the head belong to the deep-water dweller;
and as for this middle section, it is for the one who frequents both. Furthermore, this is the middle portion.

Or else, *acca* means *aticca* (having passed beyond); "Having passed beyond these two sections, this middle portion shall belong to me, who am established in the Dhamma and am the master of the decision.
Having thus divided the fish, he said: "Do not quarrel; eat the tail and the head."
Having said this, he bit the middle section with his mouth and fled while they were still looking on.
Dejected like those who had been defeated by a thousand, they sat down and spoke this verse:
"Even for a long time we would have remained as food, had we not quarreled."
“Headless and without a tail, the jackal carries off the rohita fish.
Therein, “for a long time” is said with reference to two or three days.
The jackal, too, thinking, “Today I will have my wife eat a rohita fish,” went to her side with a joyful heart. Seeing him approaching, she greeted him with delight:
“Just as a kshatriya king would rejoice upon gaining a kingdom,
so do I rejoice today, having seen my husband with his face full.
Having spoken this verse, she asked about the means for attaining that state:
“How is it that you, being a land-dweller, seize a fish in the water?
Friend, being questioned by me, tell me: how was this attained by you?”—he spoke this verse.
In that regard, how is it "how indeed"? When pieces of fish were placed before her, [the jackal] asked, "How indeed did you, being a land-dweller, catch fish in the water?
The jackal, explaining to her the means by which she had attained this success, spoke the following verse:
"Through quarreling they become emaciated; through quarreling there is loss of wealth."
"O Rohita, those who are deceitful are wasted away by disputes; do not enjoy [this] through deceit.
In this context, "they become emaciated through dispute" means, O Bhadda, that these beings, while engaging in dispute and relying upon dispute, become thin, with little flesh and little blood.
"Through dispute there is loss of wealth" means through the depletion of riches such as gold, silver, and so forth.

They come to grief through quarreling alone. When two are at variance, one who is defeated suffers the loss of his wealth because of that defeat, while the other suffers by having to give the share of victory.
"The two hooks have caught him"—both hooks have indeed caught this fish through their very quarreling.
Therefore, do not ask me about the origin of what I have brought; simply eat this deceitful Rohita fish.
The other verses on full awakening are as follows:
“In the same way, wherever a dispute arises among humans,
they run to one established in the Dhamma, for he is their leader.”
“Even their wealth is exhausted there, yet the royal treasury increases.
In this context, “even so, monks,” means that just as these dogs perish,
even so among humans, in whatever place a dispute arises, those people run to one established in the Dhamma and approach the presiding judge.
What is the reason? For he is their leader; the meaning is that he is the one who pacifies the disputes of those who have fallen into contention.

"There, even by wealth" means that there those who have fallen into dispute are defeated even in terms of wealth—their own possessions diminish—while the royal treasury increases through both fines and the taking of the shares of victory.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Upananda was the jackal; the two old hounds were those two; and the tree deity who witnessed the event was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Dabbhapuppha Jātaka, the fifth.
[401] 6. The Commentary on the Paṇṇaka Jātaka.
“*Paṇṇakaṃ tikhiṇadhāraṃ* (a sharp-edged leaf)” — this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by a former wife.
For the Teacher, having asked that bhikkhu, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are dissatisfied?
and being told, “It is true, Bhante,” and having asked, “By whom were you made dissatisfied? and being told, “By my former wife,” said, “Bhikkhu...”

"This woman has brought you harm; in the past as well, through her you were on the verge of death from a mental affliction, but by relying on wise men, you obtained life," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while King Maddava was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family.

They gave him the name Senaka-kumāra. When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he returned to Bārāṇasī and became a minister who advised King Maddava on matters of profit and righteousness.

When the words "the wise man Senaka" were uttered, he was renowned throughout the entire city like the moon or the sun. At that time, the son of the king’s domestic priest went to attend upon the king.
Having seen the king’s chief queen—adorned with every ornament and possessing a most excellent form—he became infatuated with her.
Returning home, he lay down refusing food. When questioned by his companions, he explained the matter to them.
The king also, asking, "The son of the chaplain is not to be seen; where could he be? and having heard the reason, summoned him.
“I shall give you these seven days; having kept her in your house for seven days, you may take her away on the eighth day,” he said.
He agreed, saying, “Very well,” and taking her to his home, he took his pleasure with her.
Their hearts becoming bound to one another, they fled by the main gate without informing anyone and went to the territory of another king.
They returned, but no one knew where he had gone; it was as if his path upon the boat had vanished.
Although the king caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city and searched in various ways, he did not discover the place where he had gone.
Consequently, a powerful grief arose within him; his heart grew hot and blood flowed from it. From that time forth, he became ill.
Blood issued forth, and he fell into a great illness. Even the king’s eminent physicians were unable to cure him.
The Bodhisatta thought, “This king has no physical disease; rather, he is afflicted by a mental ailment because he cannot see his wife.
I shall treat him through a skillful means. Thus, he summoned two wise royal ministers, Āyura and Pukkusa, and addressed them.
“Other than a mental affliction caused by not seeing the queen, there is no other illness for the king;
moreover, our king has been very helpful to us. Therefore, we shall treat him through a stratagem:
having had a festival staged in the royal courtyard, we will have him swallow a sword—knowing how to do so—and then, placing the king within the lion-window, we will have him watch the festival.”
When the king sees you swallowing a sword, he will ask the question: "Is there indeed anything more difficult than this?
My dear Āyura, you should answer him: "The words 'I shall give such-and-such' are more difficult than this.
Then, my dear Pukkusa, he will ask you; at that time, when he says "Great King, I shall give" but does not actually give, you should [answer him].
“Such speech is fruitless; no one lives by such speech, nor eats or drinks because of it.
But those who act in accordance with his words, giving exactly what was promised, do something even more difficult than that.
Having spoken thus, he held a festival, saying, “Beyond this, I shall know what must be done.”
Then those three wise men went to the presence of the king and said, "Great King, a festival is taking place in the royal courtyard;
for those watching it, even suffering does not feel like suffering. Come, let us go. Having led the king there, they opened the lion-window and had him look upon the festival.
Many people displayed their respective crafts and skills. One—
Then a man swallowed a sword-jewel with a sharp edge thirty-three finger-breadths long. Seeing this, the king thought, "This man swallows this sword;
I shall ask these wise men whether there is anything more difficult than this," and addressing Āyura, he spoke the first verse:
“A man swallows in the midst of an assembly a leafy sword with a sharp edge and a well-finished hilt— what is more difficult than that?
Whatever other thing is more difficult, tell me that when I ask you.”
In this context, *paṇṇaka* means "produced in the Paṇṇaka region. *Sampannapāyin* means "one who drinks the excellent [blood] of others. Regarding *parisāya*, it means:
"In the midst of the assembly, out of greed for wealth, this man swallows it. *Yadaññaṃ* means:
"Apart from this swallowing of the sword, tell me, when asked by me, what other deed is more difficult to perform?"
Then, while speaking to him, he recited this second verse:
“A man might, out of greed, swallow a well-sharpened sword;
yet more difficult than that is for one who says, ‘I give,’ when he ought to say, ‘I do not.’”
"It is easy to attain omniscience; know this, O Maddava.
In that context, "vajja" means one should say. "That is more difficult to do" means that the mere word "I give" is more difficult than not being greedy.
"Omniscience" refers to setting aside the statement "I will give you such-and-such," and [attaining] every other cause.
"It is easy. "Gentle one," he addressed the king by his clan name.
Having heard the words of the king, who was unskilled in life-and-death matters, [the minister thought]: "It is indeed difficult to say the words 'I give this' when one's throat is constricted;
yet I said, 'I give the queen to the son of the chaplain. Oh, what an exceedingly difficult thing I have done!"
As he reflected, the sorrow in his heart diminished slightly.
Then, wondering, "Is there anything more difficult than this saying, 'I give this to another'? he spoke the third verse while conversing with the wise Pukkusa:
"You have explained the question concerning life, O one skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma."
"Now I ask Pukkusa: what is more difficult than that?
Whatever other matter is more difficult, tell it to me when I have asked.

In this context, "the meaning of the question" means he explained the purpose of the question. "Skilled in the Dhamma" means proficient in the scriptures that illuminate its meaning. "Than that" means more difficult than that which was previously stated.
Then, explaining this to him, the wise Pukkusāti spoke the fourth verse:
“They do not live by their speech alone; a word uttered that bears no fruit is of no avail.
But for one who, having given, should fail to speak [of it], that is even more difficult than that.”
“O Maddava, know this: it is easy to attain omniscience.
In that context, *datvā* means having given a promise, saying, “I shall give such-and-such.

*Avākayira* means that while giving that promised object, one should cast away greed for it—that is, one should cut it off—one should give that goods; this is what is meant. *Tato*... [the rest of the passage follows].
Therefore, because of the absence of secrecy and because of the statement, "I give this one named so-and-so to you," that very act was even more difficult to perform.
Upon hearing those words of the king, the King reflected, "Having first said, 'I give the queen to the chaplain's son,' and having made my word consistent with my speech, I gave her;
alas, a truly difficult task I have performed! As he pondered thus, his grief became somewhat lessened.
He was born. Then this thought occurred to him: "There is no one wiser than the wise man Senaka;
I shall ask him this question. Thereupon, asking him, he spoke the fifth verse:
"Pukkusa has explained the question, being skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma."
"Now I ask Senaka: what is more difficult than that?
Whatever other matter is difficult, tell it to me when I have asked.
Then, answering him, Senaka spoke the sixth verse:
“A person might give a gift, whether small or great;
yet for one who gives and does not feel regret, that is more difficult than that.
To attain the state of omniscience is easy—know this, O Maddava.”
In this context, "he does not regret" means that after giving to another a cherished object that is exceedingly attractive and dear to himself,
he does not later feel remorse or sorrow regarding that dear object, thinking, "Why was this given by me? This is more difficult than being insatiable,
more difficult than saying the words, "I give you such-and-such," and more difficult than the act of giving itself.

Thus the Great Being spoke, making the king understand. For once a gift has been given, the subsequent volition is indeed difficult to sustain; the difficulty of maintaining that volition is illustrated by the Vessantara Jātaka. Indeed, it is said:
"Taking up my bow and fastening my sword on my left side, I shall bring back my own children, for the slaughter of one's children is a bitter pain."
“It is impossible that these youths should suffer, once they have understood the Dhamma of the virtuous; for who, having given, would regret it?
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the king reflected: “I acted solely out of my own whim toward the son of the family priest...”
"Having given away the queen, I am unable to maintain my composure; I grieve and I am weary. This is not fitting for me.
If she had felt affection for me, she would not have fled after abandoning this sovereignty.
But what use is she to me now that she has fled without feeling any affection for me? As he was thinking thus, a drop of water [fell] upon a lotus leaf.
As if all his grief had turned back and departed, at that very moment his belly was completely pacified.
Being free from disease and happy, he offered praise to the Bodhisatta and spoke this concluding verse:
“The man Pukkusa has explained the question concerning life-span.”
"He surpasses all questions, just as Senaka speaks.

In this context, "just as he speaks" means that just as the wise man speaks, so too, having given this gift, one should not feel regret. Having offered this praise for him, [Senaka], being satisfied, gave much wealth.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths—
The discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the king’s chief queen was the former second wife;
the king was the discontented bhikkhu; the scholar Āyurapaṇḍita was Moggallāna; the scholar Pukkusapaṇḍita was Sāriputta; and the scholar Senakapaṇḍita was none other than myself.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the Paṇṇaka Jātaka.
[402] 7. The Commentary on the Sattubhasta Jātaka.
“With a distracted mind”—this the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning his own perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī). The story of the present will be made clear in the Umaṅga Jātaka.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Janaka reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.
They gave him the name Senaka Kumāra. When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he returned to Bārāṇasī and saw the king.
The king appointed him to the position of minister and bestowed great honor upon him.
He advised the king according to both worldly profit and the Dhamma; he was sweet-spoken and a preacher of the Dhamma.
Having made offerings, he established the king in the five precepts, and further established him in generosity, the observance of the Uposatha, and the ten courses of wholesome action;
by means of this noble practice, the entire kingdom became like the time when the Buddhas have appeared.
On the fortnightly days, the king, the viceroy, and all others would assemble together and prepare the Dharma hall. The Great Being...
In the Dhamma Hall, having ascended his excellent jeweled throne, he taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha;
his discourse was like the Dhamma-talks of the Buddhas themselves.
Then, a certain elderly brahmin, having wandered for alms and obtained a thousand kahāpaṇas, [approached] at one point...
Having deposited [the money] in the brahmin family, he went away again, thinking, "I shall go for alms. While he was gone, that family spent the coins.
When he returned, he had the coins brought back. Unable to give him the coins, the brahmin gave him his own daughter to serve at his feet. Taking her, the brahmin departed from Bārāṇasī.
He made his dwelling in a certain brahmin village not far away. Then his wife, being young and unsatisfied with sensual pleasures, engaged in sexual misconduct with another young brahmin.
For there are sixteen things that can never bring satisfaction. What are these sixteen?
The ocean is never satisfied by all the rivers; fire is never satisfied by fuel; a king...

A ruler is not satisfied with his kingdom; a fool is not satisfied with his evil deeds; a woman is not satisfied with these three things: sexual intercourse, ornaments, and childbirth; a brahmin is not satisfied with mantras;
a meditator is not satisfied with the attainments of the meditative abodes; one in training is not satisfied with the reduction of defilements;
one of few desires is not satisfied with the virtues of the ascetic practices; and one who has aroused energy is not satisfied with the exertion of energy.
One does not tire; the preacher of the Dhamma does not tire in discussion; the confident person does not tire in the assembly;
the faithful person does not tire in attending upon the Saṅgha; the donor does not tire in relinquishing; the wise person does not tire in hearing the Dhamma;
and the four assemblies do not tire in seeing the Tathāgata.
That brahmin woman, unsatisfied with the act of sexual union, sent that brahmin out and remained at ease, desiring to commit an evil deed.
One day, lying down dejected, she was asked, "What is the matter, madam?
and she replied, "Brahmin, I am unable to perform the work in your house; bring some male and female slaves. [He said,] "Madam, I have no wealth."
“What shall I give you so that I may take you? “Go and seek wealth by wandering for alms, and then bring it back.
“In that case, sir, prepare provisions for my journey. He filled a leather bag with both bound and unbound grain-measures and gave it to him.
Wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, the brahmin obtained seven hundred kahāpaṇas.
Thinking, "Enough of this much wealth for the sake of male and female slaves," he turned back and was returning to his own village.
At a certain convenient spot by the water, he unfastened his bag, ate some roasted grain, and without even tying the mouth of the bag, he stepped down into the water to drink.
Then, a black snake in a hollow of a tree, having smelled the scent of the grain—
Having entered his bag and arranged his belongings, he lay down eating the flour. The brahmin returned;
without looking inside the bag, he tied it up, placed it on his shoulder, and set out.
On the way, a deity dwelling in a tree stood upon its trunk and said, "Brahmin, if you stay along the road..."
"You yourself will die if you go home today; your wife will die as well," he said, and then vanished.
Looking about, the man did not see the deity. Terrified and seized by the fear of death, weeping and lamenting, he reached the gate of the city of Bārāṇasī.
At that time, it was the fifteenth day of the observance (Uposatha), the day on which the Bodhisatta, seated upon the decorated Dharma-throne, would deliver a discourse on the Dhamma.
A great multitude of people, carrying various perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, went there in groups to listen to the Dhamma discourse.
When the brahmin saw them, he asked, "Where are you going? They replied, "Brahmin, today the wise man Senaka teaches the Dhamma with a sweet voice and the grace of a Buddha;
do you not know this? Upon hearing this, he thought, "It seems Senaka is a wise man."
“He is a preacher of the Dhamma, and I too am terrified by the fear of death. Wise people are indeed capable of removing even great sorrow;
it is fitting for me to go there as well to hear the Dhamma.

He went there with them and sat down at the edge of the assembly, which was surrounded by the king and his retinue, where a crowd of seven hundred people were gathered with their arms around each other’s shoulders.
Not far from the Dhamma-seat, trembling with the fear of death, he stood weeping.

The Great Being preached the Dhamma as if descending from the celestial Ganges and as if raining down the rain of the Deathless. The great multitude, filled with joy, gave shouts of approval and listened to the Dhamma.

For those who are wise possess the eye that sees in all directions. At that moment, the Great Being opened his eyes, which were endowed with the five kinds of serene clarity, and looking all around at the assembly, he saw that brahmin and thought:
"This entire assembly, filled with joy, listens to the Dhamma while applauding; yet this one brahmin is overcome with dejection and weeps. What is the reason for this?"
“His inner mind must be filled with grief capable of producing tears;
having struck it with sourness like a copper stain, I shall draw out that grief just as one draws a drop of water from a lotus leaf.
Having made him free from sorrow and joyful right here, I will teach him the Dhamma. Addressing him, he said, “Brāhmaṇa, I am the wise man named Senaka. Just now—”
"I shall dispel your sorrow; speak with confidence," he said, and while conversing with him, he spoke the first verse:
"Your mind is distracted and your faculties are agitated; streams of tears flow from your eyes.
What have you lost, or what do you long for, that you have come here, O Brahmā? Pray, tell me this."
In that context, "you have agitated faculties" refers specifically to the eye-faculty; thus he said, "you have agitated faculties. "A flood of water" means teardrops.
"Iṅgha" is a particle used for the purpose of exhortation. For it was while exhorting him that the Great Being spoke thus:
"Brāhmaṇa, beings indeed grieve and lament for two reasons: toward some kind of beloved thing among the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras)..."
“Or [it may be] because something dear has been lost, or because you have not obtained something you were longing for.
In that case, what is it that you have lost, or what is it that you are longing for that you have come here? Tell me this quickly!
Then, explaining the cause of his own sorrow, the brahmin spoke the second verse:
“My wife would die today as I was going away, yet the *yakkha* said my death would come as I returned;
I am trembling with this grief. Explain this matter to me, Senaka.
In this context, “going” (*vajatō*) means going to the house; “returning” (*agacchatō*) means returning; and “*yakkha*” refers to one encountered on the road.

"A certain tree deity spoke thus," he says. It is said that this deity did not inform him, "O Brahmin, there is a black snake in your bag," for the purpose of manifesting the power of the Bodhisatta’s wisdom.
"By this suffering" means by the suffering of his wife's death if he goes, and by the suffering of his own death if he does not go; because of that, he was trembling and shaken.
"Kampito" means "trembling. "Etamatthaṃ" means "this reason. The meaning is: "Tell me that reason by which my wife’s death occurs if I go, and my own death occurs if I do not go.
Having heard the brahmin’s words, the Great Being cast out his net of wisdom, as if casting a net upon the surface of the ocean.
Having spread it out, he thought: "There are many causes of death for these beings. They die even when submerged in the ocean;
there they are seized by predatory fish. They die even when falling into the Ganges; there they are seized by crocodiles.
They die even when falling from trees, being pierced by thorns, struck by various kinds of weapons, having consumed poison, or having hanged themselves."
"Even if she falls from a precipice, or is afflicted by various kinds of diseases such as extreme cold and the like, she will surely die.

Thus, among so many causes of death, by what cause indeed will this brahmin himself die while staying on the road, and by what cause will his wife die as she enters his house? While he was thus reflecting, [he saw] the brahmin...
Seeing a bag on the shoulder, he thought: "There must be a snake that has entered this bag.

While entering, it must have done so because when this brahmin went to drink water—having eaten barley meal at the time of his morning meal without first tying the mouth of the bag—the snake entered due to the smell of the meal. And as for the brahmin..."
Having drunk water and returned, he will depart after tying up his bag without realizing that the snake had entered it.
If, while staying on the road, he should unfasten the bag at his evening lodging-place with the thought,
"I shall eat some flour," and insert his hand into it, then the snake will bite him on the hand and bring about the end of his life.
It will bring about his death; this is the cause of his death while staying on the way. But if he should go home, the bag will come into the hands of his wife;
thinking, "I shall look inside the goods," she will release the bag and insert her hand, whereupon the snake will bite her and bring about the end of her life. This is [the cause of his death].
He understood through his knowledge of skillful means that "today is the cause of my wife's death because [the snake] went into the house.
Then this thought occurred to him: "This black snake must be brave and fearless;
for even while striking the Brāhmaṇa’s great vital parts, it shows no movement or trembling in its own bag. Regarding such [a being]:
"He does not even reveal his own presence in the midst of the assembly; therefore, this black snake must be brave and fearless.
He understood this through the very knowledge of skillful means (*upāyakosalla-ñāṇa*), as if seeing with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
Thus, having seen the snake entering its bag in the midst of the assembly including the king, the man who stood there...
Having discerned [the answer] through his knowledge of skillful means (*upāyakosalla-ñāṇa*), the Great Being spoke the third verse while answering the brahmin’s question:
“Having reflected upon many points, that which I shall say here is the truth alone.
I think, O brahmin, that a black snake has entered your quiver while you were unaware.”
In this context, "many points" means many reasons. "Having reflected" means having penetrated [the truth], such that there is a penetration occurring by way of reflection.
"That which I shall speak here" means that among these reasons, I shall speak this particular reason.
"That alone is the truth" means that very thing will be as it truly is, like something seen with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), as if it were spoken [by one who has directly perceived it].
“He illuminates. “I think” means I observe. “A bag of meal” means a sack for meal.
“Not knowing” means thinking, “I think a single black snake has entered while [the owner] was unaware.
Having spoken thus, he asked, “Brāhmaṇa, is there meal in this sack? “There is,” [he replied].
“‘You are wise,’ [he said]. ‘Did you eat the groats this morning at the time for the morning meal? ‘Yes, I am wise. ‘Where did you sit while eating them?
‘In the forest, at the foot of a tree, O wise one. ‘When you went to drink water after eating the groats, did you tie the opening of your bag or not?
‘I did not tie it, O wise one. ‘After drinking the water and returning, [did you find] the bag...”
“Having looked, bind it,” [the king said]. “I bound it without even looking, O wise one,” [the brahmin replied].
“Brahmin, I suspect that when you went to drink water, while you were unaware, a snake entered the bag due to the smell of the flour;
thus you came here, and therefore, having taken down the bag and placed it in the midst of the assembly, you should unfasten the mouth of the bag.”
“Step back and stand still! Take a staff and strike the bag first;
then, seeing the black snake emerging with its hood spread wide and making a hissing sound, you will become free from doubt. Thus he spoke the fourth verse:
“Take up a staff and beat the bag; look at the blind, deaf, double-tongued serpent!”
"Cut off doubt and hesitations; behold the serpent and release the bellows!
Therein, "strike down" means strike. "Behold the serpent with a dripping mouth" means behold the double-tongued snake emerging from its skin-sack, its mouth dripping with saliva.
"Cut off doubt and hesitations" [means]: "Is there indeed..."
"Today, cut through these doubts and hesitations that arise again and again, wondering, 'Is there a snake in my bag, or is there not?
Have faith in me; for my explanation is not false. Look now at the serpent as it comes out; let go of the bag!"
Having heard the Great Being’s words, the brahmin was moved with emotion and, overcome by fear, did exactly as instructed.
When the snake was struck on the head with the staff, it emerged from the mouth of its basket and stood there looking at the great multitude.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke the fifth verse:
“Filled with agitation in the midst of the assembly, that brahmin released the snake-skin bag;
then a serpent of fierce power emerged, a venomous snake spreading its hood.
At the moment the snake emerged with its hood spread, it was like the prophecy of a Great Being who would become an omniscient Buddha.

"Has it been so? the great multitude raised thousands of hand-claps, thousands of finger-snaps resounded, a rain of the seven treasures fell like a thick downpour from the clouds, thousands of shouts of "Sādhu!
arose, and it was like the sound of the great earth splitting asunder. Yet, such an answering of a question through the grace of a Buddha is not at all due to birth...
It is the power of wisdom, not the power of lineage, clan, or region. Of what, then, is this the power? It is the power of wisdom.
For a person possessing wisdom, having increased insight (*vipassanā*) and opened the door of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), enters the great Nibbāna of the Deathless;

he penetrates the perfection of a disciple (*sāvaka-pāramī*), the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*paccekabodhi*), and even the perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). Among those things that lead to the attainment of the great Nibbāna of the Deathless...
For among all phenomena, wisdom alone is supreme; all the rest are its attendants. Therefore it was said:
“Wisdom is supreme, so say those who are skilled, Like the king of stars among the constellations;
Virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the good— These follow after one possessed of wisdom.”
When the Great Being had thus spoken these verses, a certain snake-charmer tied the snake’s mouth shut,
took it, and released it into the forest. Then the brahmin approached the king,
offered him victory, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke this half-verse in praise of the king:
“Great is the gain for King Janaka, who beholds Senaka of excellent wisdom.
The meaning of this is: he who, having opened his eyes, [beholds] the wise Senaka of excellent, supreme wisdom at whatever moment he desires—
"He is permitted to be looked upon with eyes of affection; for this King Janaka, it is indeed a great gain to obtain his sight at every moment he desires.
Among all gains obtained by him, these very gains are truly what are called 'well-obtained gains.
Having thus offered praise to the king, the brahmin again took seven hundred kahāpaṇas from his bag, and wishing to give a gift of joy by praising the Great Being, he spoke one and a half verses:
“Are you one who has cast off the veil and sees all? O Brahmin, is your wisdom truly formidable?
‘I have these seven hundred [men]; take them all, I give them to you.
For by you my life was saved today, and likewise you have brought safety to my wife.’”
In that context, “Are you one whose veil is rent, O All-Seer?”—this he asks by way of praise, [meaning]:
“Are you indeed one whose veil is rent regarding all modes of phenomena (*dhammākāra*), one whose nature is to be unveiled, an omniscient Buddha?
“Is your knowledge, O Brahmin, terrifying?”—or rather, even though you are not omniscient, is your knowledge exceedingly terrifying, powerful like the knowledge of an omniscient one?
"Indeed, it was by her that I received life today, for she gave it to me.
Furthermore, "It was you alone who brought safety to my wife.
Having said this, he added, "Even if there were a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], I would surely give them; such is all the wealth I possess."
"Take these seven hundred for me," he begged the Bodhisatta again and again.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the eighth verse:
"The wise do not accept wages for well-spoken verses of diverse beauty."
"Even from here, O Brahmin, let them give you wealth; taking it, go to your own abode.
In this context, *vetana* means *vettana*, or this very reading is used. "Even from here, O Brahmin" means, O Brāhmaṇa, let them give you wealth even from here, from the very base of my feet.
"Taking the wealth, you go" refers to three hundred [pieces] other than these.
“Take this thousand coins and go to your own home.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being had the brahmin given enough kahāpaṇas to fill the thousand, and asked him, “Brahmin, by whom were you sent to beg for wealth?
“By my wife, O Wise One,” he replied. “But as for your wife—”
“Are they old women or young? “They are young, but wise.
“In that case, she sent her because she thought, ‘I shall act without restraint with another while remaining fearless.
If you take these coins home, she will give those coins—obtained with such difficulty—to her own paramour. Therefore, go straight home yourself.”
"Go outside the village and, having placed the kahāpaṇas at the foot of a tree or wherever else you please, enter," he said, and then sent him off.
He went near the village, placed the kahāpaṇas at the foot of a certain tree, and returned home in the evening.
At that moment, his wife was sitting with her paramour at the door. The brahmin [arrived] at the door...

Standing there, he said, "Are you a lady? She, perceiving his voice, extinguished the lamp, opened the door, and once the brahmin had entered within, she led the other out, placed her at the threshold of the door, and went inside the house.
Finding nothing in her bundle, she asked, "Brahmin, what have you obtained by wandering for alms? "I have obtained a thousand," he replied.
“But where is it? [The man asked. “It was placed in such-and-such a spot; I will bring it back first thing in the morning, so do not worry.
She went and told her lover. He came out and took it as if it were his own.
On the following day, the brahmin went there and, not seeing the coins, went to the Bodhisatta and said, “What—”
When he was asked, "Brāhmaṇa?", he replied, "I do not see any kahāpaṇas, wise sir. "Did you tell your wife?
"Yes, wise sir. The Great Being, knowing that she had informed her lover, asked, "Brāhmaṇa, do you have a family priest for your wife? "I do, wise sir. "Do you have one as well? "Yes."
“You are wise,” [he said]. Then the Great Being, having caused the payment for seven days’ provisions to be given to him, said: “Go;
on the first day, invite and feed fourteen brahmins—seven for you and seven for your wife.
Starting from the following day, reduce the number by one each day until on the seventh day, there are two brahmins—one for you and one for your wife.”
“Having invited them, when you have invited the brahmins for seven days with your wife, find out whether the brahmin who has been invited will come regularly, and report it to me,” he said.
The brahmin did so and reported to the Great Being, “I have observed it, O Wise One; the brahmin comes regularly to eat.”

The Bodhisatta sent men with him, had that brahmin brought before him, and asked, "Did you take this thousand kahāpaṇas belonging to this brahmin from the foot of such-and-such a tree? "I did not take them, O wise one," he replied.
"You do not know my status as the wise Senaka; I shall have those kahāpaṇas brought back to me. Terrified, he said, "They were taken..."
“I accept,” he replied. “Where have they been kept? “They were kept right there, O wise one.
The Bodhisatta asked the brahmin, “Brahmin, shall that same wife be yours, or will you take another?
“That same one shall be mine, O wise one. The Bodhisatta sent men to bring the brahmin’s coins and his wife.
Having had the coins recovered from the hands of the thief-brāhmaṇa and having caused them to be given back to the [other] brāhmaṇa,
the king had the thief punished according to royal decree and expelled from the city; he likewise had the brāhmaṇī punished according to royal decree, granted great honor to the [innocent] brāhmaṇa,
and settled him in his own presence.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, many realized the fruit of stream-entry and other attainments. At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda; the tree deity was Sāriputta;
the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and the wise Senaka was none other than myself.
The seventh is the commentary on the Sattubhasta Jātaka.
[403] 8. The commentary on the Aṭṭhisena Jātaka:
"Those whom I do not know"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at the Aggāḷava Cetiya near Āḷavī, concerning the training rule regarding small huts (kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada).
He spoke with reference to this. The story of the present has already been told below in the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka.
However, the Teacher addressed those bhikkhus, saying: "Bhikkhus, in the past, when no Buddha had yet appeared, ancient wise men went forth into the ascetic life of outsiders;
even when invited by kings, they did not beg, thinking: 'Begging is indeed unpleasant and disagreeable to others. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a certain market town;
they gave him the name Prince Aṭṭhisena.
When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he later perceived the peril in sensual pleasures, left the household life, and went forth as an ascetic.
Having gone forth and attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), he dwelt for a long time in the regions of the Himalayas.
Then, descending to the path of men in order to partake of salt and sour food, he eventually reached Bārāṇasī.

Staying in the royal park, on the following day, while wandering for alms, he entered the royal courtyard. The king, becoming confident in his conduct and way of life, invited him up to the terrace of the palace.
Having seated him on a couch and fed him with excellent food, and having heard the words of thanksgiving at the conclusion of the meal, he became inspired with faith.
Having obtained his promise, he had the Great Being reside in the royal garden and went to attend upon him two or three times each day.
One day, being further inspired by a discourse on the Dhamma, he said, beginning with the gift of the kingdom: "Tell me whatever you require."
He invited [the Bodhisatta]. The Bodhisatta did not say, "Give me this or that.
Other beggars asked for whatever they desired, saying, "Give this," or "Give that," and the king gave it without hesitation. One day he thought:
"Other beggars and mendicants ask me, 'Give us this and that,' but the noble Aṭṭhisena, from the time he was invited..."
"Ever since he began, he has not asked for anything; yet he is wise and skilled in means. I shall question him.
One day, having eaten his morning meal, he went, paid his respects, and sat to one side.
Asking the reason why others were begging and the reason why he was not, he spoke the first verse:
“I eat, yet I do not know, O Aṭṭhisena, mendicant;
they gather together and beg from me—why do you not beg from me?
In this context, *vanibbaka* means a beggar. *Saṅgamma* means having come together. This is what is meant: “Noble sir, Aṭṭhisena...”
“I do not know these forest-dwellers by name, clan, caste, family, or region, nor do I know them as ‘these are such-and-such’;
yet they come together and ask me for whatever they desire. But why do you not ask me for anything?
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:
“A beggar is disliked; one who does not grant a request is disliked.
Therefore, I do not beg from you, lest there be a sense of being rejected by me.
In this regard, “a beggar is disliked,” O Great King, refers to that person who, saying “Give this to me,” acts as a beggar.
He becomes unpleasant and disagreeable even to his parents and his friends, ministers, and others.
His state of being unpleasant is to be illustrated by the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka. "They beg" means the goods requested. "Not giving" means not bestowing them. This is what is meant:
even one who does not give what is requested—that person who refuses to give, starting with his own parents—becomes unpleasant to the beggar. Therefore...
Since even a beggar becomes unpleasant to a donor if he does not give the requested goods, therefore I do not beg from you.
"Lest there be shame for me"—for if I were to beg, you would become ashamed;
that shame arising in you toward me would be mine, but if you were not to give, it would be mine.
"May you become a stranger, and may my state of being a stranger toward you likewise cease;
thus, in every way, let there be no state of estrangement between us, lest our mutual loving-kindness be broken"—contemplating this meaning, I do not ask anything of you.
Having heard his words, the king spoke three verses:
“He who lives by begging but does not beg at the proper time destroys the merit of others and does not sustain himself either.
But he who lives by begging and begs at the proper time— ”
Furthermore, he causes others to gain merit and sustains himself as well:
“The wise, seeing that supplicants have arrived, will not feel resentment;
‘You are dear to us, O practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī); speak, for you desire to hear.’”
In this context, "those who live by begging" means one who lives by begging; or rather, this is the reading itself.

This is what is meant: "Venerable Aṭṭhisena, whatever righteous ascetic or brahmin living by begging does not ask for anything at all when it is the proper time and occasion to ask, he destroys and causes the donor to fall away from merit, and he himself [is likewise lost]."
And one does not live happily. "One gains merit" means that when one asks at the proper time, by asking one causes another to attain merit and one also lives happily oneself.
"They will not find fault" refers to what you said: "May there be no finding fault on my part. Why do you say that?
For the wise, being learned, know both giving and the fruit of giving; they [do not find fault] with those who ask.
It is shown that upon seeing [him] arrived, they do not despise him nor do they become angry; rather, they are simply filled with joy.
In the phrase "yācakam-āgate," the letter *m* is used for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*byañjanasandhi*); the meaning is "when the beggar has arrived. Regarding "brahmacārī piyo me si":
"O noble Aṭṭhisena, you who lead a pure life and possess great merit, you are exceedingly dear to me; therefore—"
"Choose a boon; indeed, ask for it! Whatever you wish to say, 'Do you wish to hear?'—say it all, and I shall surely grant even my kingdom to you.
Thus, although the Bodhisatta was invited by the king even with his kingdom, he did not ask for anything at all. However, to the king who spoke thus to him...
When his intention had been stated, the Great Being, in order to demonstrate the practice of one who has gone forth, spoke the sixth verse, showing the way of the renunciant:
"Great King, this kind of begging is indeed customary for householders who enjoy sensual pleasures, not for those who have gone forth.
But from the very moment of going forth, a renunciant must live with a livelihood that is pure and unlike that of householders."
“The wise do not indeed beg, for the steadfast one is worthy of being known;
the Noble Ones stand with reference [to others]—this is the begging of the Noble Ones.
In this context, “the wise” refers to the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddha, those practicing for enlightenment, and those who have gone forth into the ascetic life.
All Bodhisattas are wise and virtuous; such wise ones do not beg, saying, "Give this and that to us.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the wise one ought to know":
the attendant who is wise and learned ought to know and understand for himself everything required, whether during the time of illness or when not ill. With reference to...
"The Noble Ones stand" means that the Noble Ones, without breaking their word, stand solely according to the practice of alms-gathering for the sake of those who need them;
they do not disturb either a limb of the body or a limb of speech.
For one who displays a bodily movement and makes a sign disturbs a limb of the body, and one who makes a verbal utterance disturbs a limb of speech.
Without performing either of those two, the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas remain.
"This is the begging of the Noble Ones" means that standing for almsfood without disturbing the members of the body or the members of speech is what is called the begging of the Noble Ones.

Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the king spoke the seventh verse, saying: "Venerable sir, if a wise attendant, knowing for himself, gives to his own family priest what ought to be given, I too shall give this and that to you."
“I give you, O brahmin, a thousand red cows together with a bull;
for how could a noble one not give to a noble one after hearing your verses endowed with the Dhamma?
In this context, *rohiṇīnaṃ* means of those that are red in color. *Gavaṃ sahassaṃ* means a thousand cows, for the purpose of enjoying the sweet flavors such as milk, curd, and so forth.
“I give you a thousand such oxen; please accept them from me. “Ariya” means one who is noble in conduct.
“Of the Ariya” means of one who is noble in conduct. “How would he not give? means for what reason would he not give?
When this was said, the Bodhisatta refused, saying: “Great King, I am a renunciant who possesses nothing; I have no need for oxen.”

Abiding by that advice, the king performed meritorious deeds such as giving and became destined for heaven. He too, without falling away from his meditative absorption (jhāna), was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (saccāni), the Teacher identified the Jātaka;
at the conclusion of the Truths, many were established in the fruits of stream-entry (sotāpatti) and the other stages. At that time, the king was Ānanda, while Aṭṭhisena was none other than myself.
The eighth: The Commentary on the Aṭṭhisiṅga Jātaka.
[404] 9. The Commentary on the Kapi Jātaka:
"Where an enemy dwells... This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning Devadatta’s sinking into the earth.
He spoke concerning this. For when he had entered the earth, they raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, Devadatta has perished along with his assembly.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now that Devadatta..."
"Having been lost along with his retinue, he was indeed lost even before," he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey and lived in the royal park with a retinue of five hundred monkeys.
Devadatta also was reborn in the womb of a monkey and lived in that very same place with a retinue of five hundred monkeys.

[The king] was dwelling [there]. Now one day, when the chaplain had gone to the garden, bathed, adorned himself, and was departing, a certain greedy monkey went ahead of him, sat upon the top of the gateway arch at the entrance to the royal garden, dropped a lump of excrement onto his head, and then, as he looked up, dropped another into his mouth.
The chaplain turned back and said, "Very well, I shall know about you."
Thinking, "This must be done," he frightened the monkeys and, having bathed again, departed.
Having taken up a grudge against him, they reported to the Bodhisatta that the monkeys had been terrified. He thought, "It is not fitting to dwell in a place inhabited by enemies;
let the entire troop of monkeys flee and go elsewhere," and he made this known to the thousand monkeys as well.
The ill-mannered monkey, taking his own retinue of monkeys with him, sat right there, thinking, "I shall find out later.
The Bodhisatta, taking his own retinue, entered the forest.
Then one day, while a certain ram was eating rice spread out in the sun by a female slave who was husking it, he received a blow from a pitchfork and his body burst into flames.
While fleeing, he brushed his body against the wall of a grass hut situated near an elephant stable. The fire caught the grass hut;
from there it spread to the elephant stable, burning the backs of the elephants within.
The elephant doctors were tending to the elephants.
The chaplain, too, wandered about considering a means to capture the monkeys.
Then, as he was sitting after having come to attend upon the king, the king said to him: "Teacher, many of our elephants have become wounded;
the elephant-doctors do not know how to treat them. Do you know any medicine? "I know it, Great King. "What is its name?"
“Monkey fat, Great King,” [he replied]. “Where shall we find it? “Are there not many monkeys in the park?
The king said, “Go, kill the monkeys in the park and bring their fat. The archers went and killed five hundred monkeys by shooting them with arrows.
However, one senior monkey, while fleeing, was struck by an arrow and remained right there.
Without falling, it reached the Bodhisatta’s dwelling place and fell there.
The monkeys, thinking, "He has died after reaching our dwelling place," reported his death to the Bodhisatta upon receiving the blow.
He went and sat in the midst of the troop of monkeys and said to them, "Those who dwell in the company of enemies, failing to follow the advice of the wise, are destroyed in this way."
Out of a desire to advise him, he spoke these verses:
“Where an enemy dwells, there a wise man should not live;
for one night or two nights, it is painful to dwell among enemies.”
“Truly, for a man of light mind who follows his own whims,
Because of one monkey, ruin was brought upon the whole troop.
Like a fool imagining himself wise, he acted as the protector of the herd.”
Having fallen under the power of his own mind, he lies down like a monkey.
It is not good for a strong fool to be the leader of a herd;
he becomes a source of harm to his kinsmen, just as the cetaka bird is to the other birds.
“Only the wise and strong one is truly good, the protector of the herd;
he is a benefactor to his kinsmen, just as Vāsava is to the Thirty-three Gods.
And he who perceives within himself both virtue, wisdom, and learning—”
He acts for the welfare of both: himself and others.
Therefore, a wise person should weigh themselves, as it were, against virtue, wisdom, and learning;
or else, the wise one should lead a group, or wander alone.
In this context, "of one with a fickle mind" means he would be of a fickle mind. This is what is meant:
when a person conforms to or follows the lead of a friend or a kinsman who is of a fickle mind, that person, by so conforming, becomes fickle-minded himself and performs the work of an enemy.
"Of one monkey"—behold, of one who is fickle-minded, blind, and foolish.
"This monkey is the cause of this entire troop’s misconduct, lack of progress, and great destruction.
One who "considers himself wise" is one who, being himself foolish, imagines "I am wise," and failing to follow the advice of the truly wise, falls under the sway of his own mind.
Having fallen under the sway of his own mind, he [perishes] just as this ill-behaved monkey [fell upon] the bed of death.
"Should lie down"—the meaning is "one should lie down in this manner.
"Not good" means that the one called a fool, though endowed with strength and acting as the protector of the herd, is neither good nor successful. For what reason?
Because he is harmful to his kinsmen and leads only to their destruction. "Like the Ceta bird among birds"—for just as [among] the Tittira birds...
The Dīpaka partridge, even when raining [on others] throughout the day, does not kill other birds;
he kills only his own kinsmen, and thus it is for their harm alone—this is the meaning. "He becomes a benefactor" means that he acts for the welfare of others through body, speech, and mind as well.
"He practices for the benefit of both" refers to the person here who perceives these qualities, such as virtue and the rest, within himself, thinking: "For me..."
Having understood according to reality that "there is conduct and virtue, and there is wisdom as well as learning and mastery," he leads the community;
thus, acting for the benefit of both himself and others who move about surrounded by him, he acts solely for the welfare of both.
"He should weigh himself" means he should examine himself. "He should weigh" means having examined. "As virtue, wisdom, and learning"—these [he should weigh].
Like virtue and the other [perfections]. This is what is meant:

because one who regards virtue and the rest as being within himself acts for the benefit of both, therefore a wise person, weighing his own self against those virtues and so forth—having investigated whether he is "established in virtue, wisdom, and learning," and having made his state of establishment directly evident—the steadfast one may lead a community.
"In the four postures, one should either wander alone or live as a companion;

even for one who attends upon others or lives in seclusion, he must be endowed with these three qualities. Thus, even while being the king of monkeys, the Great Being spoke on the duties of the Vinaya and the Pariyatti.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the ill-behaved monkey was Devadatta; his retinue was Devadatta’s retinue; and the wise monkey king was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Kapi-jātaka, the ninth.
[405] 10. Commentary on the Baka-jātaka.
“Seventy-two”: This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the Brahmā Baka. For this Brahmā developed the view:
“This is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change; there is no escape from the world other than this, which is called Nibbāna.
It is said that this Brahmā, who had been reborn in a lower realm, had previously cultivated meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Having been reborn among the Vehapphala devas, he spent there a lifespan measuring five hundred kappas;

having been reborn among the Subhakiṇha devas, he spent sixty-four kappas there; passing away from there, he was reborn among the Ābhassara devas with a lifespan of eight kappas, and it was there that this view arose in him.
For he neither witnessed his own death from the higher Brahma-world nor his rebirth there.

Not seeing either of those two, he adopted this view. The Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of that Brahmā, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, vanished from Jeta’s Grove and appeared in that Brahmā world. Then the Brahmā [addressed] the Blessed One:
Having seen him, he said: "Come, dear sir! Welcome, dear sir! It has been a long time, dear sir, since you made this occasion to come here.
For this, dear sir, is permanent; this is stable; this is eternal; this is absolute;
this is not subject to passing away; for this is neither born, nor ages, nor dies, nor passes away, nor reappears."
"Moreover, there is no other escape beyond this," he said.
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed the Brahmā Baka: "Brahmā Baka is indeed enveloped in ignorance!
Brahmā Baka is indeed enveloped in ignorance! For while it is actually impermanent, he says it is permanent... [and so on] ...while it is actually peaceful..."
"but there is no other higher escape; there is no other higher escape," he will say.
Having heard that, the Brahmā thought, "He says this to you, he says this to you; thus he pursues and hounds me.
Then, just as a weak thief, having received a few blows, thinks, "Am I the only thief? Is not so-and-so also one?"...
Pointing out all his companions, saying, "This one too is a thief, this one too is a thief," and likewise terrified by the fear of the Blessed One’s interrogation,
he spoke the first verse while pointing out his other companions:
"Seventy-two are they, O Gotama, who have performed meritorious deeds, who are masters of their own will, and have transcended birth and old age."
“This is our final attainment of the Brahma-state, O Veda-gone One; thus do many people pray for us.

Therein, “seventy-two” means: not only I alone, O Gotama, but we seventy-two persons in this Brahma-world, having performed meritorious deeds, are masters (vasavattino) by virtue of exercising control over ourselves above others, and [we have attained] birth...

"Having transcended old age, he has reached the goal through knowledge; therefore, he is a *vedagu*. O Gotama, this is our final attainment of Brahma-hood, our last birth, our attainment of the highest state.
Many people praise us with joined palms, saying: 'This venerable one is Brahmā, the Great Brahmā,' and so forth."
“They aspire and long for, thinking, ‘O, may we too become such as this!’—the meaning is that they desire it.
Having heard his words, the Teacher spoke the second verse:
“Truly small is this, Baka, not a long life, though you consider it a long life.”
“O Brahmā, I know your lifespan to be a hundred thousand *nirabbudas*.
In this context, “a hundred thousand *nirabbudas*” means a hundred thousand of those numerical units called *nirabbudas*.
For ten tens of years make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand; and a hundred thousands make a hundred thousand (*satasahassa*).

One hundred times one hundred thousand is called a *koṭi*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭis* is called a *pakoṭi*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is called a *koṭipakoṭi*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭipakoṭis* is called one *nahuta*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *nahutas* is called one *ninnahuta*.
A skilled calculator is able to count up to this point; beyond that is what is known as "reckoning" (*gaṇanā*).
This is the domain of the Buddhas alone. In that regard, one hundred thousand times one hundred thousand *sata-ninnahuta*s makes one *abbuda*; twenty *abbuda*s make one *nirabbuda*;
and one hundred thousand times those *nirabbuda*s is what is called an *ahaha*.
This much was the remaining lifespan for the Brahmā Baka in that existence; it was with reference to this that the Blessed One spoke thus.
Having heard that, the crane spoke this third verse:
“I am the Blessed One of infinite vision, who has transcended birth, old age, and sorrow.
What former vow or virtuous conduct do you speak of? Tell it to me so that I may know it.”
In this context, "Bhagavā" means: O Blessed One, while you say, "I understand your lifespan," you also say, "I am Anantadassī, one who has transcended birth, old age, and sorrow.
"Vatasīlavattaṃ" refers to both the undertaking of vows and the practice of virtue.
This is what is meant: if you are an omniscient Buddha, that being so, why do you ask me about my former vow?
“Tell me that virtuous conduct so that I may understand, exactly as it is in its true nature, what has been taught by you.
Then the Blessed One, bringing forward past instances, spoke these four verses to explain them:
“You gave drink to many people who were thirsty, exhausted by the heat of the summer;”
I recall that ancient practice of yours, your conduct and virtue, as one who has awakened from sleep might recall a dream:
"When people were seized on the banks of the Eṇī river and were being led away as captives,
you set them free— that ancient practice of yours, your conduct and virtue, I recall as one who has awakened from sleep."
“On the current of the Ganges, a ship seized by a fierce nāga that was in human form—you released it by force and power.
That is your ancient practice of vows and virtuous conduct;
I remember it as one who has awakened from sleep.”
“Kappa was your companion in the observance of vows; I did not recognize you as one possessing full awakening.
That ancient practice of your vows and virtuous conduct, I now recall as if waking from sleep.
In this context: *apāyesi* means “you caused to drink. *Ghammani samparete* means “when oppressed by heat,” that is, when excessively afflicted by heat.
"Tormented by heat. "As if awakened from sleep": at the time of dawn, having slept and seen a dream, I remember it as if it were that very dream.

It is said that the Brahmā Baka, having been an ascetic in a previous aeon while living in a desert wilderness, brought water and gave it to many travelers who had entered that wilderness. Then one day, a certain caravan leader...
He set out across the desert wilderness with five hundred carts. Unable to determine their direction, the men wandered for seven days until their wood and water were exhausted;

deprived of food and overcome by the heat, they thought, "Now there is no life left for us," so they turned the carts around, unyoked the oxen, and lay down beneath them. At that time, the ascetic, reflecting upon the situation—

Seeing them, he thought, "May they not perish while I am watching," and by the power of his own supernatural might, he caused the current of the Ganges to surge upward and turned it toward the caravan leader; not far away, he also created a forest grove.
