Having drunk water, bathed, and satisfied their oxen, the men gathered grass from the forest grove and took firewood.
Having observed the direction, they crossed the wilderness free from harm; it is with reference to this that it was said.
"On the bank of the Eṇī" means on the bank of the river named Eṇī. "Being led away as a prisoner" means being led away after having been seized for execution.
It is said that at another time, that ascetic lived in a forest thicket on the riverbank near a certain frontier village.
Then one day, robbers descended from the mountain, raided that village, and having seized a great multitude of people, they led them up the mountain.
Having stationed guards along the way and entered a mountain cave, they sat there preparing food.
The ascetic, hearing the great cries of distress of the oxen, buffaloes, boys, girls, and others, [reflected...]

Thinking, "May they not perish while I am looking on," he abandoned his physical form through the power of his supernormal abilities (*iddhi*) and went to that place as a king surrounded by a fourfold army, having had the war-drum beaten.
When the prison guards saw him, they informed the thieves. The thieves thought, "A conflict with the king is indeed not fitting," and [they returned] everything that had been seized.
Having abandoned their belongings and without even eating their meal, they fled. The ascetic brought them all back and settled them right in his own village;
it was with reference to this that it was said.
"A seized ship" means a ship held fast. "By the violent one" means by the cruel one. "In the guise of men" means with the desire to destroy human beings.
"By force" means by power. "Having overcome" means having conquered. At another time, that ascetic lived on the bank of the Ganges.

At that time, people would tie together two or three boats, construct a flower-pavilion atop the boats, sit upon the boats, and travel to their relatives' homes while eating and drinking. They would take the wine remaining after they had drunk...
The remnants of food, fish, meat, betel, and so forth that remained after they had eaten and consumed were thrown right into the Ganges.
The Naga King of the Ganges, becoming angry and thinking, "These people are throwing refuse upon me," resolved, "I shall seize all those people and drown them in the Ganges.
He then manifested a massive physical form, the size of a single-droṇa boat, and [plunged] into the water.
Having split open his hood, he advanced toward them. Upon seeing the Naga king, they were struck with the fear of death and simultaneously let out a great cry.
Hearing their lamentation and perceiving the king’s wrath, the ascetic thought, "Let them not perish while I am looking on," and by means of his own power and quick action, [he intervened].
Having quickly manifested himself in the form of a garuḍa, he departed. Seeing him, the nāga king, terrified by the fear of death, submerged himself in the water.
The people, having attained safety, went on their way; it was with reference to this that it was said.
"One who lives in bondage" means a pupil. They consider one who possesses wisdom to be a possessor of vows—one who is endowed both with wisdom and with the observance of vows.
And thinking of him as "an ascetic" (*tāpasa*). What does this show? O Great Brahmā, in the past, during your time as the ascetic Kesava, I was your pupil named Kappa;
acting as your attendant, I cured the illness of you who had been brought from Bārāṇasī to the Himalayas by your minister named Nārada.
Then, when Nārada came for a second time, [he found you] free from disease.
Having seen him, he spoke this verse:
“Having abandoned the lord of men, who is successful in all his desires,
how indeed, O Blessed One, do you take delight in Kesi’s hermitage?”
To him you said this:
"Sweet and delightful are the words of Vakkha, so pleasing to the mind;
the well-spoken verses of Kappa, Nārada, bring me joy."

The Blessed One spoke thus, pointing out how this [Brahmā], having become his own pupil, had brought about the subsiding of his illness. Furthermore, he related all that the Brahmā had done in the human world while making it known to the Great Brahmā.
Recalling the deed he himself had performed through the Teacher’s words, he uttered the final verse in praise of the Tathāgata:
“Surely you understand this lifespan of mine; you know even more, for you are a Buddha.”
"For thus he, possessing the power of radiance, stands illuminating the Brahma-world.
In this context, "for thus you are a Buddha" means that for you there is nothing unknown;
it shows that they are called "Buddhas" precisely because they have awakened to all phenomena. And furthermore, "for thus he"—because of his very state as a Buddha—...
"This radiance of your body is ablaze; it stands illuminating," meaning it stands illuminating this entire Brahma-world.
Thus the Teacher, making known his own Buddha-qualities, taught the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the minds of ten thousand Brahmās who had assembled were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging. Thus it was.
The Blessed One, having become a refuge for many Brahmās, returned from the Brahma-world to Jetavana;
there, after delivering that Dhamma teaching to the monks according to the same method he had used previously, he identified the Jātaka, saying:
"At that time, the ascetic Kesava was the Brahmā Baka, but Kappa the youth was none other than myself."
The Tenth: The Explanation of the Bakajātakavaṇṇanā.
The First: The Chapter on the Cocks (Kukkuvagga).
2. The Chapter on Gandhāra (Gandhāravagga).
[406] 1. The Commentary on the Gandhāra Jātaka.
"Having abandoned thousands of villages"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the training rule regarding the storage of medicines.
However, the story originated in Rājagaha. For the venerable Pilindavaccha [approached] a family of monastery attendants...
Having gone to the royal residence to release him, he used his supernatural power to turn the king’s palace into gold;
the people, being filled with faith, sent five kinds of medicinal requisites to the Elder. He distributed these among the assembly.
However, the assembly became excessive in its accumulation; whatever they received, they filled jars, pots, and even their bowl-bags and stored them away.
When people saw this, they complained, saying, "These recluses are full of greed; they are like those who keep their storehouses inside.
When the Teacher heard of this occurrence, he laid down a training rule, beginning with the words, "Now, regarding those things for sick bhikkhus...
and said, "Bhikkhus, in the past, when no Buddha had appeared, ancient wise men went forth into the ascetic life of outsiders and, even while observing merely the five precepts,"
“They censured those who would store even a mere measure of salt for the sake of the following day, saying:
‘But you, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, are doing what is improper by making provisions for the second and third days. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of the King of Gandhāra; upon his father’s passing, he was established in the kingship.”
He ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma. In the Middle Country as well, in the kingdom of Videha, a king named Videha ruled the kingdom.
These two kings, though never having met before, became firm friends with one another.
At that time, human beings were long-lived, living for thirty thousand years. Then, on one occasion, on the day of the full-moon Uposatha, the King of Gandhāra...
Having undertaken the moral precepts, he sat upon the excellent couch prepared for him on the great terrace,
looking toward the eastern world-system through the open lion-window and discoursing with his ministers on matters consistent with the Dhamma and the Truth. At that moment,
Rāhu eclipsed the full orb of the moon as it seemed to be crossing the vault of the sky, and the moonlight vanished.
The ministers, not seeing the moonlight, informed the king that the moon had been seized by Rāhu.
The king, looking at the moon, thought: "This moon has become defiled and lusterless due to an adventitious impurity;
this retinue of mine is likewise an impurity for me. It is not fitting for me to be like the moon seized by Rāhu."
"I would become lusterless; like the lunar orb shining in the pure firmament, I shall renounce the kingdom and go forth into homelessness.
What need have I for others to advise me? Unattached to family or faction, I shall wander about advising only myself;
this is what is suitable for me. Having thought thus, he said, "Make whoever you wish king."

He handed over the kingdom to his ministers. Having renounced the kingdom and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he developed the *jhānas* and higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), and dwelling in the delight of *jhāna*, he made his home in a region of the Himalayas.
King Videha, thinking, "Is my friend happy?", inquired of merchants and, having heard of his having gone forth, [proceeded accordingly].
Thinking, "Now that my companions have gone forth, what shall I do with kingship?",
he abandoned the filled storehouses in the city of Mithilā— seven yojanas in extent— and the Videha kingdom of three hundred yojanas, along with its sixteen thousand villages;
he also renounced his sixteen thousand female dancers and disregarded his sons and daughters, entering the region of the Himālayas to go forth into the religious life.
Living on fallen fruit and dwelling in a life of perfect composure, he wandered about. As the two of them were practicing their conduct in unison, they eventually met one another;
yet, they did not recognize each other. Greeting one another with joy, they lived together in a life of perfect composure.
At that time, the ascetic of Videha was attending upon the ascetic of Gandhāra.

On a certain full-moon day, while they were sitting at the foot of a tree and engaging in a discussion consistent with the Dhamma and the goal, Rāhu eclipsed the moon’s orb as it shone in the vault of the sky. The ascetic Videha, wondering, “Why has the moon’s radiance vanished?
looked up; seeing that the moon had been seized by Rāhu, he thought, “Who indeed is this?”
“Teacher, having eclipsed the moon, he has made it lusterless,” he asked. [The teacher replied: “Disciple, this one named Rāhu is an affliction of the moon;
he does not allow it to shine. And I too, seeing the lunar disk seized by Rāhu, thought:
‘This lunar disk, though naturally pure, has become lusterless due to an adventitious affliction; it is the same with me.’”

Thinking, "This kingdom is a defilement; as long as it does not render this [kingdom] lusterless like the moon's orb seized by Rāhu, so long shall I go forth," he took that very moon's orb seized by Rāhu as his object of meditation, abandoned his great kingdom, and went forth.
"Teacher, are you the King of Gandhāra? "Yes, I am. "Teacher, I too—"
“In the kingdom of Videha, in the city of Mithilā, there was a king named Videha; surely we were companions who had never seen one another.
“But what was your object [of perception], sir? “Having heard that you had gone forth, I thought, ‘Surely he must have seen some great excellence in the going-forth’;
thus, making you alone my object, I abandoned the kingdom and went forth. They...
From that time forth, they lived together in great harmony and mutual affection, subsisting on whatever fruit was available.
After dwelling there for a long time, however, they descended from the Himalayas to seek salt and sour condiments, and eventually reached a frontier village.

The people, having gained confidence in them through their dignified deportment, gave them alms, received their promise [to stay], and prepared for them dwellings and other necessities in the forest for day and night.
Having built [the dwellings], they settled them there. Along the way, they also had leaf huts constructed at convenient water sources for the monks to take their meals.
Having gone for alms in the border villages, those monks would sit in those leaf huts, eat, and then proceed to their own places of residence.
When those people were giving them food, sometimes salt would fall into their bowls.
Sometimes they gave it mixed in; sometimes they tied it in a leaf-wrapping;
and sometimes they gave food entirely without salt. One day, they placed a large amount of salt in a leaf-wrapping.

The ascetic of Videha took the salt, went on his way, and when it was time for the Bodhisatta’s meal, he gave him a sufficient portion, took an appropriate amount for himself, and placed the remainder back in the leaf-wrapping.
Having bound him, he placed him inside a bundle of grass, thinking, "It will be a day when salt is prohibited.

Then one day, when food without salt was obtained, Videha gave his alms-bowl to Gandhāra, brought salt from within the bundle of grass, and said, "Teacher, take some salt. "Today no one gave salt to people; where did you get it? he asked.
“Teacher, on the previous day people gave me much salt; therefore, thinking, ‘There will be a day without salt,’ I set aside some extra salt.

Then the Bodhisatta rebuked him, saying: “Foolish man, having renounced the kingdom of Videha which extends three hundred leagues, and having gone forth and attained the state of possessing nothing, you now generate a craving for salt crystals!”
Admonishing him, he spoke the first verse:
“Having abandoned sixteen thousand villages,
And flourishing storehouses full of provisions, Why do you now make a hoard?”
In this context, "storehouses" refers to storehouses for treasures such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls, as well as storehouses for clothing and storehouses for grain.
"Prosperous" means full. "Now you are making a hoard" means that now you are making a hoard even of a mere measure of salt, thinking, "It will be tomorrow; it will be on the third day."
Being thus reproached, Videha, unable to endure the censure, took a contrary stance and spoke the second verse, challenging him:
“Teacher, not seeing your own faults, you see only faults in me.
Did you not renounce your kingdom and go forth into homelessness thinking, ‘What is the use of instructing others? I shall instruct only myself’? Why then do you now instruct me? Thus he rebuked him.
“Having left the realm of Gandhāra, which abounds in wealth and treasures, you have now come forth from your own governance to govern here.
In this context, “from governance” means from the giving of exhortations and instructions. “Now here” means: why do you now exhort me here in the forest?
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:
“I speak the Dhamma, O Videha; unrighteousness does not please me.
As I speak the Dhamma, no evil defiles me.”
In this context, *dhamma* means intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), that very cause which has been described and praised by the Buddhas and others.
"Unrighteousness does not please me" means that what is called unrighteousness—that which is contrary to intrinsic nature—never pleases me at any time.
"Evil does not smear me" means that for one who speaks only of his own intrinsic nature and the [true] cause, evil does not smear or adhere to the heart.
This giving of exhortation is the tradition of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and Bodhisattvas.
Fools do not accept the exhortation given by them, yet there is no evil for the one who gives the exhortation.
"Just as one would see a guardian of treasures who points out their flaws..."
One should associate with such a wise person who speaks what is beneficial;
for one who associates with such a person, it becomes better, not worse.
One should advise and instruct them, and restrain them from what is unwholesome.
"For he is dear to the virtuous, but is disliked by the wicked.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the Videha ascetic said, "Teacher, even when speaking in accordance with the truth, it is not fitting to speak by provoking or angering another.
You have spoken to me with extreme harshness, as if shaving my head with a blunt razor."
Having said, "He spoke thus," he recited the fourth verse:
"In whatever way another may find cause for irritation,
a wise person should not utter even words of great significance."
In this context, "by whatever means" refers even to a reason connected with the Dhamma. "It receives affliction" means that it certainly receives impact, vexation, and provocation.

"One should not speak that" means: therefore, one should not speak to that other person any speech by which they are provoked, even if that speech is highly significant or based on a great purpose. This is the meaning.
Then the Bodhisatta spoke the fifth verse:
“Let it be crushed or not, let it be scattered like chaff;
no evil shall cling to me as I speak the Dhamma.”
In this context, "absolutely" (*ekamsena*) means as follows:
when a person who has acted improperly is being admonished, saying, "You have done what is improper," let him absolutely either become angry or not; or let him scatter like a handful of dust.
But for me, while speaking the Dhamma, there is no such thing as evil.

And having spoken thus, standing in accordance with this instruction of the Sugata— “Ānanda, I shall not exert myself toward you in such a way as a potter does toward unbaked clay; rather, Ānanda, I will strike it again and again,
and whatever is solid shall remain”— just as a potter [acts] toward his vessels, again and again...
"Having struck it again and again, one does not take up what is raw, but takes up only a vessel that is well-baked;
in the same way, after repeatedly advising and restraining him, a person who resembles a baked vessel should be accepted. Thus, advising him once more to demonstrate this, he said:
"If he possesses neither his own wisdom nor discipline well-trained..."
“Like a blind buffalo in the forest, many people would wander.
But because some here are well-trained in the teacher’s instruction,
they therefore wander with discipline mastered and well-composed.”— he spoke these two verses.

The meaning of this is as follows: O Vedeha, if these beings were not well-trained in their own intelligence, or in the instructions of the wise, or in the discipline of conduct and precepts, then it would be just as an elephant in rut wanders through a dense forest of grass and creepers, unable to distinguish between what is edible and inedible, or between a place that is dangerous and one that is safe. In the same way...
Many people like you should practice in this way. However, because some beings here, though lacking their own independent intelligence,
have been well-trained in the rules of conduct under a teacher, they— having been disciplined by their respective teachers according to the discipline appropriate for each—
practice as those who are "disciplined in discipline," being well-composed and single-minded.
By this he shows the following: a being, having become a householder, should train in training appropriate to his own family;

having gone forth, he should train in training appropriate to those who have gone forth. For householders too, having trained in occupations such as agriculture and cattle-rearing that are appropriate to their own families, live with a perfected livelihood and in a well-composed manner. Likewise, those who have gone forth [should train] in qualities that are inspiring and appropriate to those who have gone forth.

Trained in the higher training of virtue, the higher training of mind, and the higher training of wisdom regarding going forth and returning, they wander free from distraction and well-composed. For in this world:
“Great learning, craft, and discipline well-trained;”
“And whatever speech is well-spoken—this is the supreme blessing.
Having heard this, the ascetic of Videha said, “Teacher, from now on, instruct and advise me. Because I am by nature impatient, I spoke with you;
please forgive me for that. Having thus paid homage, he asked the Great Being for forgiveness. They lived together in harmony.
Having stayed there, they returned once more to the Himālayas. There, the Bodhisatta taught the ascetic Vedeha the preparatory exercises for the kasiṇas.

Having practiced them, he attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and the meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Thus, both of them, without falling away from their jhānas, became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Vedeha was Ānanda, and the King of Gandhāra was none other than myself.
This concludes the first commentary, the Gandhāra Jātaka.
2. The Commentary on the Mahākapi Jātaka (The Great Monkey)
"Making oneself a bridge," the Teacher spoke concerning the practice for the benefit of relatives while residing at Jetavana.

The story will be made clear in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka. At that time, they raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, the Perfectly Enlightened One acts for the welfare of his relatives. The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing?"
Having asked, "Are you sitting here now for this discussion? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Tathāgata acted for the welfare of his kinsmen," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey and reached maturity.
Endowed with height and circumference, possessed of strength and power, and measuring five times the strength of an elephant,
he dwelt in a region of the Himalayas surrounded by a troop of eighty thousand monkeys. There, by the bank of the Ganges, there was a banyan tree (*ambarukkha*)—
endowed with branches and foliage, providing abundant shade and thick leaves, rising up like a mountain peak— which some call the "Nigrodha tree."
Its fruits were sweet, possessing celestial fragrance and flavor, and were very large, the size of great jars.
From one branch, the fruits fell onto dry land; from another branch, they fell into the waters of the Ganges;
and from two branches, the fruits fell in the middle, at the foot of the tree. The Bodhisatta, taking a troop of monkeys with him, was eating the fruits there.
“Once, based on a fruit that fell into the water from this tree, a danger will arise for us.
Thinking thus, at the time of flowering, he had them eat and throw down every single fruit—even those on the branch right above the water—starting from the time they were the size of a pea.
Even so, there remained one hidden within a cocoon of ants, unseen by the eighty thousand monkeys.
A single ripe fruit fell into the river and became caught in the upper net of the King of Bārāṇasī, who was playing in the water after having the nets cast both upstream and downstream.
After the king had played all day, at the time of departure in the evening, the fishermen hauled up the nets;
seeing it, but not knowing what kind of fruit it was, they presented it to the king.
The king asked, "What is the fruit of this? "We do not know, Your Majesty," they replied. "Who will know?
"The forest-dwellers, Your Majesty. He had the forest-dwellers summoned;
having heard from them that it was "mango-fruit," he cut it with a knife, first made the forest-dwellers eat it, and afterwards ate it himself, as did his harem and his ministers.
He had it served. The taste of the ripe mangoes pervaded the king’s entire body.
Bound by craving for that flavor, he asked the forest-dwellers where that tree stood;
when they told him, "In the Himalayan region, on the bank of a river," he had many boat-fleets moored and traveled upstream along the path shown by the forest-dwellers.
He did not specify a limit, saying, "It will take this many days. However, having gradually reached that place, the forest-dwellers informed the king, "Sire, here is the tree.
The king moored his boat and, surrounded by a great multitude, went there on foot.
Having prepared a couch at the foot of the tree, he ate mangoes and various kinds of exquisite food.
Having eaten, he lay down; they established guards in all directions and kindled a fire.
When the people had fallen asleep, at the hour of midnight, the Great Being departed with his retinue.
Eighty thousand monkeys were moving from branch to branch, eating mangoes. The king woke up and, seeing the troop of monkeys, [awoke] the men.
Having raised them up, he summoned the archers and said, "Surround these fruit-eating monkeys so that they do not flee, and strike them; tomorrow we shall eat both mangoes and monkey meat.
The archers, having agreed by saying "Very well," stood encircling the tree with their arrows nocked. Seeing them, [the monkeys...]

The monkeys, terrified by the fear of death and unable to escape, approached the Great Being and asked, “Your Majesty, archers have surrounded the tree, intending to shoot us escaping monkeys; what shall we do? Trembling, they stood there.
The Bodhisatta comforted the troop of monkeys, saying, “Do not be afraid; I will give you your lives. Thus he reassured them.
Having climbed straight up a tree with branches rising upward and branches extending toward the Ganges, he went along them until reaching their end, leaped from there,
and after traversing a distance of about a hundred bow-lengths, he landed on the top of a thicket on the bank of the Ganges.
Descending from there, he demarcated the space in the air, thinking, "This much shall be the extent of the place where I have come," and [cut] a rattan vine at its base.
Having cut and cleared it, he defined these two locations, thinking, "This much space will be fastened to the tree, and this much will remain suspended in the air.
He did not, however, mark the place on his own waist where the binding was to be made.
Taking that creeper, he tied one end to a tree standing on the bank of the Ganges and the other end to his own waist.
Having bound himself, he leaped with such speed—like a cloud severed by the wind—that he covered a distance of a hundred bow-lengths.
Because he had not noticed the place where the binding was around his waist, he was unable to reach the tree;
instead, seizing a branch of the mango tree firmly with both hands, he gave a signal to the troop of monkeys: "Quickly, while trampling upon my back, [climb] the rattan vine..."
"Go on a safe journey. The eighty thousand monkeys, having paid homage to the Great Being and asked for his forgiveness, departed accordingly.
At that time, Devadatta was also among them, having been born as a monkey.
Thinking, "This is the time to see the back of my enemy," he climbed a high branch, gathered momentum, and leapt onto his back.
The Great Being’s heart broke and intense pain arose. He too, having caused him to experience that pain, departed.
The Great Being was left all alone. The king, without sleeping, saw everything that had been done by the monkeys and the Great Being, and thought:
"Though he is an animal, disregarding his own life, he has acted solely for the safety of the assembly."
Thinking, "He has done so," he lay down.
When the night had turned to dawn, being pleased with the Great Being, [the hunter] thought, "It is not right to destroy this king of monkeys;
I shall win him over by some means and look after him. He then set up a collection of boats within the Ganges and erected a platform upon them.
Having had the Great Being bound gently and led inside, they spread a yellow robe upon his back, bathed him with water from the Ganges,
gave him molasses-water to drink, and once his body was purified, had him anointed with oil refined a thousand times. Then,
having had a sheepskin spread upon the surface of the bed and having laid him down there gently, he himself sat upon a low seat.
He spoke the first verse:
“Having made yourself a bridge, you who have safely crossed over—
what do these great monkeys matter to them, and what do they matter to you?”
The meaning of this is: "O great monkey, you who made yourself a bridge, placed yourself on the scale,
and sacrificed your life to carry these monkeys across in safety— you were what to them, and they were what to you?"
Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses, exhorting the king:
“I am the king, the lord of them, the protector of the herd;
[I am here] for those who are overcome by grief and terrified, O subduer of enemies.”
“Having leaped over myself, with my bow cast aside,
I then fastened a strong binding of creeper-strings to my other feet.
Like a tree driven by the wind, I was carried away and approached a tree.”
Thus, being of little strength there, I grasped a branch with my hands.
While I was thus stretched out upon that branch and the creeper,
the deer, treading upon me with their feet as they passed by, went safely away.
“That bond does not torment me; once dead, it will not torment me.
Happiness was brought by those for whom I exercised sovereignty.
This is the simile for you, O King; listen to it, O subduer of enemies.”
“A wise Kṣatriya king should seek the welfare of the kingdom, the army, the city, and indeed of all;
he should desire the happiness of everyone.
In this context, “of them” refers to those eighty thousand monkeys. “Of you who are afraid” means for the purpose of piercing you.
"To those who stood there having been commanded, while they were afraid. "Arindama" is a term used to address the king;
for a king is called "Arindama" because he subdues enemies such as thieves and the like. "From the distance of a full arrow-shot of a drawn bow" means:
having leaped into the air and released himself from a position measuring one full arrow-length of an unstrung bow, and then having jumped from this tree, [he went] from the place where he had gone.
"On the other feet" means on the hind feet. This was said with reference to the region of the hips.
For the Bodhisatta, having bound that creeper-cord firmly around his hips and having stepped upon the ground with his hind feet, released it and leaped into the air with the force of the wind.
"He reached the tree, driven along" means that, like a cloud severed by the wind, he was driven by the force generated by himself.
"Driven by the wind": just as a cloud torn apart by the wind is driven by the wind, so too, having been driven by my own momentum, I approached this *amba* tree. "Unable to reach it":
the meaning is that, being unable to reach the tree in that portion of space, I seized its branch with my hands.
"Viyāyatanti" means with the body stretched out and drawn taut, like the string of a lute made from a tree branch and a rattan creeper.
"Samanukkamantā" means having been permitted by me, they paid homage to me and, stepping forward on foot, proceeded continuously;
thus they have gone in safety. "Taṃ maṃ na tapate bandho" means that this bond of the creeper does not distress me, nor...
Now he will experience death. For what reason? Because they brought me happiness. That is to say, for those over whom I exercised sovereignty, I brought happiness.
Indeed, these people made me their king, thinking, "O Great King, this one will take away our arisen suffering and bring us happiness.
And I too [thought], "I shall take away the suffering that has arisen for you."
The king was born among them. Today, having removed from them the suffering of death, I have brought the happiness of life;
therefore, neither imprisonment torments me, nor will execution torment me.
"This is the simile for you"—this, O Great King, is the simile for the deed performed by me. Listen to it. Therefore, by means of this...
Having illustrated this through a simile, listen to the advice being given to you: "O Great King, by a king,
as for the kingdom"— that is to say, O Great King, a king, having not crushed the kingdom like sugarcane in a mill,
but rather abandoning the fourfold course of wrong conduct, embracing it with the four bases of sympathy, and establishing himself in the ten royal duties, [should act] as I have done for myself.
Having renounced his own life, he thought: "How might the inhabitants of this kingdom, free from fear, with their gates open during the summer season, surrounded by kinsmen and attendants,
fanning their chests with their children, cooled by pleasant breezes,
and enjoying their respective possessions as they please, come to possess both physical and mental happiness?"— thus for the sake of the entire kingdom...
The meaning is that for the chariots, carts, and other such vehicles, for the draft animals suitable for them, for the army consisting of foot soldiers,
and for the towns and countryside known as "nigamas," the happiness of all these must be sought and pursued. By the term "a Khattiya who understands," it refers to one who,
by virtue of being the lord of fields, has received the name "Khattiya" and has surpassed all other beings.
"One who understands must be endowed with wisdom.
Thus the Great Being passed away while exhorting and instructing the king.
The king summoned his ministers and said, "Perform the funeral rites for this king of monkeys as you would for kings," and he also gave orders to the women of the harem.
“Dressed in red garments, with disheveled hair and carrying torches in your hands, go to the cremation ground surrounding the king of monkeys.

The ministers, having constructed a funeral pyre with about a hundred cartloads of wood and performed the funeral rites for the Great Being according to the royal custom, took his skull and went into the presence of the king. The king—

Having had a shrine constructed at the cremation site of the Mahāsatta, having lit lamps there, and having honored it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he had a golden-inlaid skull bowl fashioned.
Placing it upon the tip of a spear and carrying it before him while honoring it with perfumes, garlands, and the like, he went to Bārāṇasī.
Having stationed it at the inner gate of the royal palace and prepared the entire city, he performed a seven-day festival of worship for the relics.
Then, having taken that relic and having had a shrine constructed, he worshipped it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings for as long as he lived.
Established in the instruction of the Bodhisatta, performing meritorious deeds such as giving and ruling his kingdom righteously, he was destined for heaven.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Ānanda was the king; the wicked monkey was Devadatta; the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and I myself was the monkey king."
The second *Mahākapijātaka-vaṇṇanā*.
[408] 3. The *Kumbhakārajātaka-vaṇṇanā*:
"In the forest of Ambāhamadda," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the subduing of the defilements.
He related [the story]. The background of the matter will be made clear in the *Pānīya Jātaka*.
At that time, however, five hundred friends who had gone forth into homelessness were living in the Antokoṭisaṇṭhāra; at the hour of midnight, they gave rise to thoughts of sensual desire.
The Teacher, for his disciples, [observes] three times during the night and three times during the day—thus six times throughout the day and night—[examines their minds].
Watching over it like a hen her egg, or a yak its tail, or a mother her beloved child,
or as a one-eyed man protects his single eye, he suppresses any defilement that arises at that very moment.
On that day, while surveying Jetavana at the hour of midnight, he perceived the mental activity of those bhikkhus.
Knowing this, [the Buddha thought]: “If this defilement increases within these bhikkhus, it will destroy the cause for their attainment of arahantship;
therefore, I shall now suppress their defilement and grant them arahantship.

Having emerged from the Gandhakuṭi, he summoned the Elder Ānanda and said, “Ānanda, assemble all the bhikkhus who are staying in the innermost quarters of the monastery. Having had them assembled, [he spoke].
Having sat upon the excellent Buddha-throne that had been prepared, he said: "Monks, it is not fitting to live under the power of internal defilements;
for a defilement, when it increases, brings about great ruin like an enemy. Indeed, a monk must suppress even a slight defilement.
Regarding this, ancient wise men [dealt with] even a slight object..."
"Having seen this, he suppressed the defilements arising within him and brought forth the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (individual enlightenment)," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a potter’s family in a village near the gates of the city of Benares.
Upon reaching maturity, he established a household and had a son and a daughter.
Having obtained the work of a potter, he supported his wife and children by means of it.

At that time, in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, a king named Karaṇḍaka, while going to the pleasure garden with a great retinue, saw at the gate of the garden a mango tree laden with fruit and heavy with sweet fruit;
even while seated upon the back of his excellent elephant, he reached out his hand and [took] one.

Having taken a cluster of mangoes and entered the garden, he sat upon the auspicious stone; after giving what was appropriate to those who were entitled to receive it, he partook of the mango himself.
Thinking, "From the moment the King has taken [the fruit], the rest must indeed take it," the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others also shook down the mangoes and ate them.
Those who arrived later climbed the tree with clubs...
Having shaken it down and broken its branches apart, they ate even the raw fruit until nothing remained.
The king, having sported in the park throughout the day, sat upon a magnificent, adorned elephant-back at evening time and was proceeding along when he saw that tree.
Alighting from the elephant, he went to the foot of the tree, looked at it, and thought, "This [tree] this very morning..."
Thinking, "This tree stood beautiful, laden with the weight of its fruit, providing satisfaction to passers-by;
now, having lost its fruit, it stands unsightly, broken and shattered," he looked again in another direction and saw another mango tree that was fruitless.
Seeing it, he thought, "This tree stands beautiful like a mountain of shaven jewels because of its lack of fruit, whereas this one—"
"Because of possessing fruit, I have fallen into this calamity; this household life is like a tree bearing fruit, while the life of renunciation is like a fruitless tree.
Only one who possesses wealth has fear; for one who is destitute there is no fear.
I, too, must become like a fruitless tree. Having taken the fruit-bearing tree as his object of meditation, he remained right there at the foot of the tree.
Having observed the three characteristics, increased his insight, and realized the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi, he reflected:
"The hut of my mother’s womb is now demolished; rebirth in the three realms of existence is severed; the cesspool of saṃsāra is cleared away;
the ocean of tears has been dried up by me; the rampart of bones is broken; there shall be no further rebirth for me."
He stood there adorned with every kind of ornament.
Then the ministers said to him, "You have been standing far too long, Great King. "We are not Great Kings; we are called Paccekabuddhas," he replied.
"O Lord, those who are called Paccekabuddhas are not like you. "Then what are they like? he asked.

“O King, those who have shaved off their hair and beard, are clothed in saffron robes, and are unattached to families or groups—like clouds cut by the wind, or like the orb of the moon released from Rāhu—they dwell in the Nandamūla cave in the Himālayas; such, O King, are the Paccekabuddhas.
At that moment, the king raised his hand and touched his head; instantly his lay appearance vanished and the appearance of a recluse appeared.
“The three robes and the bowl, the razor, the needle, and the girdle;
together with the water-strainer—these eight belong to the bhikkhu devoted to yoga.

Thus, the requisites of a recluse mentioned therein remained fastened to his body. Standing in the air, he gave exhortation to the great multitude and departed through the path of the wind for the Nandamūlaka cave in the Northern Himalayas.
In the kingdom of Gandhāra, in the city of Takkasilā, King Naggaji, seated upon his couch on the upper terrace of his palace,
saw a woman sitting nearby who had fastened a single jeweled bracelet on each hand and was grinding perfumes.
Observing that these bracelets did not strike against one another nor produce any sound because they were solitary, he looked at them.
She sat down. Then, having transferred the bracelet from her right hand to her left hand, she began to grind the perfume with her right hand;
as the second bracelet came into contact with the first on her left hand, it made a clinking sound.
Seeing those two bracelets striking against each other and jingling, the king thought:
"Just as this bangle does not strike against itself at one time, but strikes and makes a sound when a second one comes near it, even so these beings do not strike one another nor quarrel when alone;
but when there are two or three, they strike one another and engage in strife.
As for me, however, I govern the inhabitants of the two kingdoms of Kaśmīra and Gandhāra."
"Since I too must live as one who is like a single bracelet, it is fitting that I dwell examining myself alone, without scrutinizing another," he said.

Taking his *saṅghaṭṭanavalaya* (clashing bracelet) as his object of meditation, while remaining seated as he was, he discerned the three characteristics, developed insight, and realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*. The rest is exactly as before.

In the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, a king named Nimi, having finished his morning meal and surrounded by his assembly of ministers, stood watching the street through the open bars of his lion-window.
Then a hawk, seizing a piece of meat from a butcher’s stall, soared into the sky.
It was surrounded on all sides by vultures and other birds, who, for the sake of food, [pecked at it] with their beaks.
Striking with their wings, pecking with their beaks, and trampling with their feet, they came upon him.
Unable to endure his own slaughter, he cast away that piece of meat. Another seized it; the birds released this one and pursued him instead.
When he too let go, another took hold of it, and they tormented him in the very same way. Seeing those birds, the king reflected: "Whosoever [takes] the piece of meat..."
Whoever grasps at this or that experiences suffering for that very thing; whoever relinquishes it experiences happiness for that very thing.
Likewise, whoever grasps at these five strands of sensual pleasure experiences suffering for them, while for another there is happiness. For these are common to many.
As for me, I have sixteen thousand women; yet these five [strands] are like a morsel of meat abandoned by a dog to a host.

"It is fitting to become happy by abandoning the strands of sensual pleasure. As he applied his mind thoroughly (*yoniso manasikaronto*), while remaining exactly as he was, he discerned the three characteristics (*tīṇi lakkhaṇāni*), increased his insight (*vipassanā*), and realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*. The rest is just as before.
In the kingdom of Uttarapañcāla, in the city of Kapila, there was a king named Dummukha, who, having finished his morning meal and being adorned with all his ornaments—
Surrounded by his circle of ministers, he stood in the royal courtyard looking out through the open lion-window. At that moment, the cowherds opened the gate of the enclosure;
the bulls emerged from the enclosure and, driven by their defilements, pursued a certain cow.
Thereupon, a great bull with sharp horns, seeing another bull approaching, was overcome by the stinginess of his defilements.
With his sharp horn, he struck the other ox in the intestines.
Through the opening of that wound, the entrails protruded, and he met his death right there. Seeing this, the king reflected:
"These beings, beginning with those in the animal realm, undergo suffering due to the power of the defilements; even this bull has met his end because of the defilements."
"Having attained this, other beings as well tremble because of their defilements; it is fitting for me to abandon these trembling defilements of beings.
While still standing, he discerned the three characteristics, increased his insight, and realized the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi.
The rest is exactly as before.
Then one day, four Paccekabuddhas, perceiving it was time for the alms-round, departed from the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.

Having chewed a nāga-vine tooth-stick at Lake Anotatta and performed their bodily ablutions, they stood upon a slab of ruby-colored stone, put on their lower garments, and took up their bowls and robes.
Then, by means of psychic power, they leapt into the air and proceeded while crushing five-colored clouds.
Having traveled and disembarked not far from a village at the gate of the city of Bārāṇasī, they put on their robes in a convenient spot,
took up their bowls, and entering the gate-village, went about for alms until they reached the door of the Bodhisatta’s house.
Seeing them, the Bodhisatta, with a joyful heart, invited them into his home and had seats prepared.

Having had them sit down, having offered water for the guest-offering, and having served them with excellent hard and soft foods, he sat to one side, paid homage to the senior of the Saṅgha, and said:
"Venerable sir, your renunciation shines exceedingly;
your faculties are serene, and the color of your skin is perfectly pure. What object did you see that led you to this life of alms-gathering and renunciation?"
"Have you arrived? he asked. And just as he had questioned the senior elder of the Saṅgha, he approached and questioned the others as well.

Then those four men, each describing his own circumstances for going forth according to the formula beginning with "I was the king named so-and-so in such-and-such a city and such-and-such a province," spoke one verse each in succession:
“In the middle of the forest, I saw an ambāhamadda tree, shining, laden with fruit, and grown to full maturity;
I saw it shattered for the sake of its fruit, and having seen that, I wander on my alms-round.
A well-polished stone slab, fashioned by a hero among men, was being carried by two women with little noise.”

And because of the second [incident], there was a cry: "Seeing one bird carrying off a carcass, many birds gathered together; for the sake of food, they struck it down. Seeing that, I wander on my alms-round.
"Seeing one bird carrying off a carcass, many birds gathered together;
for the sake of food, they struck it down. Seeing that, I wander on my alms-round."
“I saw a bull at the head of the herd, with trembling horns, endowed with beauty and strength;
I saw him pierced by the cause of sensual desire, and having seen that, I wander for alms.
Therein, *ambāhamaddaṃ* means “I saw a mango tree (*amba-rukkhaṃ*); *vanamantarasmim* means “within the forest,” that is, in the middle of a mango grove.
The meaning is as follows: *Saṃvirūḷhaṃ* means well-grown. *Tamaddasaṃ* means that having gone out from the park, he saw again that [tree] which had been broken for the sake of its fruit.

*Taṃ disvā* means having seen that [tree] broken for the sake of its fruit, he experienced a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*, and entered upon this life of mendicancy and renunciation;
therefore, he said, "I practice the life of a mendicant."
From the moment he saw this mango tree, which was distinguished by its fruit, he described his entire mental state.
The same method applies to the answers for the others as well. Here, however, is the commentary on the words not previously explained:
*sela* means a jeweled bracelet. *Naravīraniṭṭhitaṃ* means completed by heroic men; the meaning is "made by wise persons. *Yugaṃ*...

Having made one from each [of them], there was a single pair of bracelets. "The birds" (*dijā*) refers to the birds that had seized the lump of flesh; "the remaining birds" refers to those other than the one that had seized it.
"Carrying off the carrion" means carrying away the lump of flesh. "Having come together" (*samecca*) means having approached and assembled.

"They struck him down" (*paripātayiṃsu*) means they pursued him while striking him. "I saw a bull" (*usabhāhamaddaṃ*) means I saw a bull. "With quivering hump" (*calakkakuṃ*) means with a trembling hump.
Having heard each verse, the Bodhisatta praised each Paccekabuddha individually, saying, "Excellent, venerable sir; that object of meditation is truly worthy of you.

Then, after hearing the Dhamma discourse delivered by the four men, the Paccekabuddhas departed, indifferent to household life. Having eaten his morning meal and being seated comfortably, [the Bodhisatta reflected].
Having addressed his wife, he said: "My dear lady, these four Paccekabuddhas have renounced their kingdoms and gone forth;
being without possessions and free from impediments, they spend their time in the bliss of the renunciant life. I, however, maintain my livelihood by working for wages.
What use have I for the household life? You stay at home, caring for our two little sons. Having said this, he spoke two verses:
“Karaṇḍaka of the Kalingas, Naggaji of the Gandharas,
King Nimi of the Videhas, and Dummukha of the Pancalas— these,
having abandoned their kingdoms, went forth as those possessing nothing.”
“All these gods have assembled together, just like blazing fires;
I too shall wander alone, O Bhaggavī, having abandoned all sensual pleasures as if they were vomit.
The meaning of this for them was: “Bhadde, this senior monk, a Paccekabuddha named Karaṇḍaka, [resides] in the city of Dantapura.”
The first was the king of the Kalinga country named Kaliṅga; the second was the king of the Gandhāra country named Naggaji in the city of Takkasilā;
the third was the king of the Videha country named Nimi in the city of Mithilā;
and the fourth was the king of the northern Pañcāla country named Dummukha in the city of Kapila. These were such as these kingdoms.
Having abandoned all things and become nothing at all, they went forth into homelessness.
Indeed, all these here have come together as one, equal to the former Paccekabuddhas and the pure devas.
"Just as fire," means that just as a blazing fire shines, so too do these shine with the five qualities beginning with virtue (*sīla*). Just as they are, so shall I also, having gone forth...
"I shall wander alone" is the meaning. "O Bhaggavī" is how he addresses his wife. "Having abandoned sensual pleasures" means having abandoned objective sensual pleasures such as forms and so forth.
"According to their respective spheres" means as they exist according to one's own sphere (*odhi*). This is what is meant:

"Having abandoned sensual pleasures as they exist according to the sphere of forms and so forth, I too, having gone forth, shall wander alone. There is also a reading, "according to their respective limits" (*yatodhikāni*).
The meaning of this is as follows: "Those whose limit (odhi) has ceased" means those for whom the portions [of defilements] have ceased;

that is, the sections [of the defilements] have been brought to an end. For from the moment one thinks, "I shall go forth," one portion of the defilements of sensual desire is said to have ceased—that is, it has been suppressed—and the corresponding objective portion of sensual desire is likewise ceased.
Having heard his words, she said, "My lord, ever since the time I heard the Dhamma discourse from the Paccekabuddhas, my heart no longer finds rest in the household life," and she spoke this verse:
"This very moment is it, for there is no other; there would be no instructor for me later.
I too shall wander alone, Bhaggava, like a bird released from a man’s hand."
In this context, "there would be no one to instruct me hereafter" means that there would be no instructor or advisor, because such advisors are difficult to find;
therefore, he shows that "this very moment is the time to go forth, for there is no other.
"Like a bird released" means that just as among birds caught by a fowler and thrown into a cage, one might be released from his hand.

"Just as a female bird, having crossed the path of the wind, might go to whatever place she desires and wander all alone, so too shall I, released from your hand, wander alone. Desiring to go forth herself, she spoke thus.
Upon hearing her words, the Bodhisatta remained silent. But she, having deceived the Bodhisatta, went on ahead.
Desiring to go forth, she said, "Husband, I am going to the water-crossing; look after the children," and taking her water-jar, she fled as if departing.
Having gone to the presence of the ascetics on the outskirts of the city, she went forth.

The Bodhisatta, realizing that she had not returned, personally raised the children himself. Later, when they had grown a little and were capable of discerning what was fit and unfit for them, [he continued to care for them].
On one day, while cooking rice for them when they had gathered together, he cooked it with too little husked rice;
on another day, with too much moisture; on another day, perfectly cooked; on another day, over-moist; on another day, without salt;
and on another day, with too much salt. The children said, "Father, today the rice has too little husk; today it is over-moist."
"Today it is well-cooked; today it is over-soaked; today it lacks salt; today it is too salty," they said.
Hearing this, the Bodhisatta replied, "Yes, dear ones," and reflected: "These children now know what is raw, what is cooked, what is under-salted, and what is over-salted;
they will be able to live by their own nature. It is fitting for me to go forth. Then...
Having given those children to his kinsmen and entrusted them to them, saying, "O mother and father,
please raise these children well," he departed from the city even as his kinsmen were still lamenting; having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*,
he dwelt in the vicinity of that very city.
Then one day, as he was wandering for alms in Bārāṇasī, a female wanderer saw him, paid homage to him, and said, "Noble sir, I suppose your children have been driven away.
The Great Being replied, "I did not drive the children away; I went forth into homelessness at the time when they were unable to discern what was their own and what was not.
You, however, should disregard them and take delight in the life of renunciation," and having said this, he spoke the concluding verse:
“They know what is raw and what is cooked, as well as what is salty and what is unsalted;
having seen that, I went forth. You too, go about your alms-round;

I too shall go about my alms-round. In this context, “having seen that, I went forth” means: having seen that activity of the children, I went forth. “You too, go about your alms-round; I too shall go about my alms-round” means: you too should practice the wandering for alms, and I too shall practice the wandering for alms.
Having thus exhorted the female wanderer, he dismissed her. She too, having received his instruction and paid homage to the Great Being, departed for the place of her choosing.
Indeed, it is said that from that day forward, they never saw one another again.
And the Bodhisatta, having attained the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges, passed away to be reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, those five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
At that time, the daughter was Uppalavaṇṇā, the son was Prince Rāhula, the female wanderer was Rāhulamātā, and the male wanderer was none other than myself.
The third *Kumbhakārajātaka-vaṇṇanā*.
[409] 4. The *Daḷhadhammajātaka-vaṇṇanā*:
"If I were one of firm Dhamma... This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Ghosita’s Monastery near Kosambī concerning Udena.
He spoke concerning King Bhaddavatika’s female elephant.
The manner in which that female elephant was acquired, as well as the royal lineage of Udena, will be revealed in the Mātaṅga Jātaka.

One day, however, as she was leaving the city at early morning, that female elephant saw the Blessed One surrounded by a host of noble disciples, possessing the peerless splendor of a Buddha, entering the city for alms.
Seeing him entering, he prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and said:
"Blessed One, the All-Knowing One, the Savior of the entire world, King Udena—when I was young and capable of managing affairs—loved me and granted me great privileges, saying:
'It is by depending on this man that I have obtained my life, my kingdom, and my queen,' and he provided me with all manner of ornaments."
Having decorated the place where he stood, having had the surrounding area perfumed with incense, having had a canopy inlaid with golden stars fastened over his head,
having had it enclosed on all sides with variegated cloth, having had a lamp lit with scented oil, having had incense burners set up,
and having had a golden basin placed at the spot where dung was discarded, [he sat] upon me on a variegated carpet.

He established [me in my position] and had various foods of superior flavor provided for me, worthy of a king. But now, in my old age, at a time when I am unable to complete my work, he has revoked all those privileges.
Having become destitute and without support, I live in the forest eating *ketaka* flowers; I have no other refuge. O Udena, consider my merit!
“O Blessed One, having had this examined, please restore my former status to its original state,” she entreated the Tathāgata while lamenting.
The Teacher said, “Go; after I have spoken to the king, I shall restore your honor to its original state,” and he went to the gate of the king’s residence.
The king, having ushered the Tathāgata into his palace, [prepared for] the assembly headed by the Buddha...
He offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher, while giving a blessing, asked:
"Great King, where is Bhaddavatikā? "I do not know, Bhante," he replied.
"Great King, it is not right to bestow honor upon benefactors only to take it back when they have grown old; one ought to be grateful and mindful of what has been done."
“Bhaddavatikā is now old and decrepit; having become destitute, she lives in the forest eating *ketaka* flowers.
It is not fitting for you to leave her without support at such a time of decline.
Having thus spoken of Bhaddavatikā’s virtues, he said, “Restore all her former privileges to their original state,” and then departed. The king did accordingly. [The Tathāgata...]
It was rumored throughout the entire city that, after praising the virtues of Bhaddavatikā, the ancient bell had been restored to its original state;
this news also became well known within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion in the Dhamma Hall, saying:
"Friends, it is said that the Teacher, after praising the virtues of Bhaddavatikā, restored the ancient bell to its original condition."
“...was made. The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the Tathāgata, having praised her virtue, restored her lost reputation. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Daḷhadhamma reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of ministers;
having reached maturity, he attended upon that king. Having received great honor from him, he stood in the position of the minister-jewel.
At that time, the king had an elephant-cow named Oṭṭhī, who was endowed with strength and power.
She was very powerful. One day she would travel a hundred yojanas;
she performed the duty of carrying messages for the king and, having fought in battle, crushed the enemy.

Thinking, "She has been of great service to me," the king gave her all manner of ornaments and caused her to be granted every privilege, just as Bhaddavatikā had been given by Udena. Then, when she became old and weak—
The king took all the glory for himself. From that time on, she became destitute and lived in the forest, subsisting on grass and leaves.
Then one day, when there was a shortage of vessels in the royal household, the king summoned a potter and said, "It seems we do not have enough vessels.
[The potter replied: "Your Majesty, I cannot find oxen to yoke to the cart for bringing cow dung."
Having heard his words, the king asked, "Where is our elephant suffering from the *oṭṭhi* disease?
"He acts according to his own nature, Your Majesty," [the man] replied. The king said, "From now on, employ him to bring cow dung," and he gave him to the potter.
The potter said, "Very well, Your Majesty," and did accordingly.
Then one day, as she was leaving the city, she saw the Bodhisatta entering it;
having bowed down and prostrated at his feet, she lamented: "My lord, the king, perceiving that I was of great service in my youth, granted me great honor;
but now, in my old age, he has stripped me of everything and has not even a thought for me."
"He does nothing; as for me, I am helpless, living in the forest eating grass and leaves.
Thus, having fallen into such suffering, he has now given me to a potter to be yoked to a cart. Apart from you, I have no other refuge.
You know the service I rendered to the King; it would be well if you would now restore my lost reputation."
Having said, "Do so," she spoke these three verses:
"If I, though acting with great prowess in battle,
did not please the firm-minded one while bearing an arrow in my breast, yet still supporting him upon my chest."
“Surely the king does not know my prowess and manliness,
nor the deeds well-performed in battle, nor the messengers dispatched by me.
Surely I shall die, friendless and without refuge.”
"For at that time, the dung-collector was given to the potter.
In this context, "carrying" means carrying out errands, breaking enemy fortifications in battle, and thus carrying out and accomplishing various tasks.
"Bearing the dart upon her breast" means bearing a shaft, a sword, or a spear fastened to her chest.

Advancing against the enemies at the time of battle. "Moving with valor" means moving with stride and prowess, going forth with courage in battle through the defeat of the enemy forces. This is what is meant:
"If, O Lord, while performing these duties I did not please or satisfy the mind of King Daḷhadhamma, who else now [could do so]?"
"He will please his mind.
"My manly valor" means the human effort exerted by me. "Well-wrought threads" means well-wrought deeds.

For just as actions themselves are "action-ends" (*kammantāni*) and forests themselves are "forest-ends" (*vanantāni*), so too here it is well-wrought deeds themselves that are called "well-wrought threads" (*sukatantāni*).

"Sent" means those dispatched by messengers; that is, having tied a letter to my neck and been sent with the instruction, "Give this to such-and-such a king," I traveled a hundred *yojanas* in a single day and performed the tasks of a messenger. "Surely the king does not know" means:
surely this king of yours does not know these deeds performed by me. "Without refuge" means without support.
"Without refuge. *Tadā hi* means "for thus," or else this very reading (*tadā hīti*) is the text.
*Dinnā* means "I was given to the potter by the king, having been made a dung-collector.
Having heard her words, the Bodhisatta said, "Do not grieve; I shall speak to the king and restore your reputation."
Having comforted him with the words, "I shall do so," he entered the city; and having eaten his morning meal, he went into the presence of the king.

After engaging the king in conversation, he said: "Great King, was it not your own servant named Asuka who, having bound an arrow to his chest at such-and-such places, emerged victorious in battle? And on such-and-such a day, [he did so] around the neck..."
“Having tied a leaf and sent it off, it traveled for a hundred yojanas; you gave her great honor, so where is she now?
he asked. “I gave her to a potter to carry his cow dung,” they replied.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “It was indeed improper of you, Great King, to give her to a potter for the purpose of yoking her to a cart.”
Saying, "Give it," he spoke these four stanzas as an exhortation to the king:
"As long as a man has hope, so long does he boast;
when his wealth fails, they abandon him, just as a nobleman abandons a disease of the gums."
“He who has previously performed what is wholesome, but having accomplished his purpose does not realize it,
finds that those goals which were his aspirations fall away from him.
He who has previously performed what is wholesome, and having accomplished his purpose realizes it...”
"The goals for which they have aspirations will flourish for them.
Therefore, I say to you, O noble ones, as many as are gathered here:
Be grateful to all, and you shall long remain in heaven."

Regarding that, first, the meaning of the initial verse is as follows: Here, a certain person of ignorant nature, for as long as he has expectations—that is, for as long as he expects, "This person will be able to do this for me"—he flatters, associates with, and serves that person.
But when there is a loss of benefit for him, when prosperity has departed and he has fallen into decline, [the other] abandons him in his various affairs.
Some fools abandon this person who has supported them—this "otthibyādhi" (a burden)—just as they would a discarded piece of bone.
"One who has performed good deeds" means one who has performed meritorious actions for oneself by another. "One who has accomplished his purpose" means one whose duty has been fulfilled.

"He does not recognize" means that later, even when the other has rendered such assistance, he does not remember it at a time of old age or when he is incapacitated; [he forgets] what was done for himself by another.
Even the fame that has been given back, he takes up again. "They perish" means they break apart and vanish.
"Whatever things are desired" means whatever aims are called for or wished for—all these perish; this is what he demonstrates.
For whatever is desired by a person who betrays his friends perishes like a seed cast into fire. "Having accomplished his purpose, he wakes up."
"One who has done good understands"—the letter *ma* is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*byañjanasandhi*).
"I tell you this": for that reason, I speak to you. "You shall stand firm": having become grateful, you will remain established for a long time, experiencing divine prosperity in heaven.
Thus the Great Being gave this exhortation to all those assembled, beginning with the king. Having heard it—
The king restored Yaśas’s health from the disease of *oṭṭhī*. Abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and became destined for heaven.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Bhaddavatikā was the one with the *oṭṭhī* disease; the king was Ānanda; and the minister was none other than myself.”
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Daḷhadhamma Jātaka.
[410] 5. The Commentary on the Somadatta Jātaka.
"He who formerly rose up for me..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain elderly man.
He related the story. It is said that he had ordained a novice, and that novice, having been his benefactor, passed away from such an illness.
When the novice had died, the elder wandered about weeping and lamenting.
Seeing him, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Friends, this certain elder, because of the death of a novice..."
“Wailing and lamenting, he wanders about; surely he is devoid of the meditation subject of mindfulness of death.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he wept over this dead man. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was exercising the office of Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
At that time, a wealthy brahmin householder living in a village of Kāsi abandoned sensual pleasures and entered the Himalayas.
Having gone forth as an ascetic, he made his dwelling there, subsisting on forest roots and fruits gathered through the practice of gleaning. One day, for the sake of gathering fruits...
Having gone out and seen a young elephant calf, he brought it to his own hermitage, treated it as a son, gave it the name Somadatta, and tended to it by feeding it grass and leaves.
When it reached maturity and had grown into a large-bodied animal, one day it took much food and became weak due to indigestion.
The ascetic, having placed it within the precincts of the hermitage, went out for the sake of gathering fruits and roots.
When he had gone, even before his return, the young elephant calf passed away. As the ascetic was returning, carrying various fruits, he lamented, saying the first verse:
"On other days my son used to come out to meet me; today he is not seen. Where indeed has he gone?"
“He who formerly used to go out to meet me in the distant forest—now that elephant Mātaṅga is not seen; where has Somadatta gone?

In this context, *pure* means “formerly. *Paccuḍḍeti* means “he goes out to meet. *Araññe dūraṃ* means “in this uninhabited forest, he used to go out to meet me at a great distance. *Āyato* means “endowed with great stature.”
Lamenting thus, he came and saw him fallen at the edge of the walkway; seizing him by the neck and lamenting, he spoke this second verse:
“Is this one dead who lies here, like a calf with wet horns?
He lies prostrate upon the ground; alas, the elephant is no more!”
In this context, the word *vā* has the sense of clarification (*vibhāvana*). He spoke thus in order to clarify that "this is indeed that, not something else.
*Allasiṅga* refers to the tip of a sprout of the *māluva* creeper. *Vacchito* means cut;
what is meant is that it is like a shoot of the *māluva* creeper which, during the heat of midday in the summer season, has been cut with a fingernail and cast down upon a sandy bank of hot sand.
“From earth to earth. “Amarā vata” means “O, he is dead indeed”; there is also a reading, “amarī.
At that moment, Sakka, surveying the world, saw him and thought: “This ascetic went forth having abandoned his wife and children;
now, regarding this young elephant calf as his son, he is lamenting. I shall stir his heart and cause him to regain mindfulness.”
Having arrived at his hermitage, standing in the air, he spoke this third verse:
“Since you have entered the homeless life and are fully liberated,
it is not fitting for you, an ascetic, that you should grieve for the deceased.”
Having heard his words, the ascetic spoke this fourth verse:
“Indeed, Sakka, through living together, affection arises in the heart of a human or a beast; it is impossible not to grieve for that.”
In this context, the term "deer" (*miga*) refers to all animals. "Him" (*taṃ*) refers to the beloved being.
Then Sakka, exhorting him, spoke these two verses:
"They weep for the dead and for those about to die; they weep and lament."
Therefore, O sage, do not weep; the virtuous say that weeping is in vain.
"O Brahmā, by means of lamentation, could a dead spirit be raised up?
Let us all gather together and weep for our respective kinsmen."
In this regard, O Brahmā, as for those beings who weep and lament—those who weep and wail for one who has died or for one who will die—they weep for them;
for those who thus weep, there is no end to the drying of their tears.
Therefore, O Seer, do not weep. For what reason? The virtuous say that weeping is in vain, for the wise declare that "weeping is fruitless."

They said: "If this one who has passed away and has entered the reckoning as a *peta* could rise up because of our weeping, then let us all gather together and weep for one another’s kinsmen; why should we remain idle?
Having heard Sakka’s words, the ascetic regained his mindfulness, was freed from grief, wiped away his tears, and spoke the remaining verses by way of praising Sakka.
“While I was burning, like a fire fed with ghee,
you have sprinkled me with water as it were and extinguished every dart.
You have indeed pulled out the arrow that was lodged in my heart.”
“He who dispelled the grief for my son while I was overcome by sorrow—
having heard from you, O Vāsava, I am one whose arrow has been pulled out,
free from grief and undisturbed; I do not grieve, nor do I weep.”
These [details] have already been explained above. Thus Sakka, having given this exhortation to the ascetic, returned to his own abode.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the young elephant was the novice monk, the aged ascetic was the Elder, and Sakka was none other than myself.
This is the fifth commentary on the Somadatta Jātaka.
[411] 6. The Commentary on the Susīma Jātaka.
"The hair was black in former times"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation.
At that time, the monks, having sat down in the Hall of Truth, were discussing the departure of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
They praised [him]. The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?

When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "It is not surprising, monks, that I—having fulfilled the perfections for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons—should now undertake the Great Renunciation;
for even in the past, I abandoned my sovereignty over the kingdom of Kāsī, which extended three hundred leagues."
Having said, “He has indeed gone forth,” he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of that king’s domestic priest.
On the very day of his birth, a son was also born to the King of Bārāṇasī. On the day of the naming ceremony for these two...
They gave the name Susīma Kumāra to the Great Being, and Brahmadatta Kumāra to the prince.
The King of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "He was born on the same day as my son," sent for the Bodhisatta, provided him with nurses, and had him raised together with his own son.
When they both reached maturity, having become handsome and possessing the appearance of celestial youths, they went to Takkasilā.
Having mastered all the arts, they returned. The prince, having become the viceroy, ate, drank, sat, and slept together with the Bodhisatta.
Upon the death of his father, he attained the kingship;
he bestowed great honor upon the Mahāsatta, appointed him to the position of high priest, and one day, after having the city adorned, [he thought: "Sakka..."
Adorned like a king of the gods, he sat upon the back of a superb, intoxicated elephant resembling the decorated Erāvaṇa;
having seated the Bodhisatta behind him on the elephant's back, he circumambulated the city.
His mother, standing at the lion-window thinking, "I shall look upon my son," watched as he completed his circumambulation of the city and returned.
Seeing the chaplain seated behind her, she became infatuated with him;
entering her bedchamber, she thought, "If I do not obtain this man, I shall die right here," and having cut off all food, she lay down.
Not seeing his mother, the king asked, "Where is my mother? and hearing that she was ill, he went to her side.
Having gone and paid his respects, he asked, "What is it, mother? Are you unwell? Out of shame, she did not speak.
He went and sat upon the royal couch; then, having summoned his chief queen, he sent her forth, saying, "Go and find out what is wrong with my mother.
She went and, while massaging her back, asked; for indeed, women do not [reveal] the secrets of other women.
She concealed it, but she reported that matter to her [friend]. The other, having heard it, went and reported it to the king.
The king said, "Very well; go and comfort her. Having made the chaplain the king, we shall make her his chief queen.
She came and comforted her. The king also summoned the chaplain, informed him of this matter, and—
“Friend, give my mother her life; you shall be king, she shall be the chief queen, and I shall be the viceroy,” he said.
He refused, saying, “It is not possible to do this,” but when he was entreated by him again and again, he consented.
The king had the chaplain made king and his mother made chief queen, while he himself became the viceroy.
While they were living in harmony, at a later time the Bodhisatta, becoming weary of the household life, abandoned sensual pleasures,
and with his heart inclined toward the going-forth, remained alone— neither clinging to the delight of the defilements; he stood alone, sat alone, and lay down alone,
like one bound in a prison or like a cock cast into a cage.
Then his chief queen thought, "This king does not take delight with me; he stands, sits, and lies down all alone.
Moreover, this youth is young and I am old; grey hairs are already appearing on my head.
What if I were to deceive the king by means of a stratagem, uttering a falsehood, saying: 'O King, a single grey hair is seen upon your head'? Thus she devised a plan.

Thinking, "Having gained his trust, I shall make him take pleasure with me," she one day acted as if searching for lice on the king's head and said, "Your Majesty, you have grown old; a single grey hair is visible upon your head.
"In that case, my dear lady, pull out this grey hair and place it in my hand. She then pulled a single hair from his head.
Having plucked out a grey hair from his own head, he placed it in the king’s hand, saying, “This, O King, is your grey hair.
As soon as the Bodhisatta saw it, the Bodhisatta—terrified and trembling—broke into a sweat upon his forehead, which was like a golden plate.
Admonishing himself, he thought: “Susīma, though you were young, you have become old; for so long a time you have remained in the mire of excrement.”
"Like a village pig submerged in the mire of sensual pleasures, you are unable to abandon that mire.
Is it not time for you to renounce sensual pleasures, enter the Himalayas, go forth into homelessness, and dwell in the holy life?
Having thought thus, he spoke the first verse:
“Black were the hairs that formerly grew upon your head in their proper places;
seeing them now turned white, Susīma, practice the Dhamma—for this is the time for the holy life.
In this context, “in their proper places” means in those various locations on your head that are suitable for hair, which previously were black.
He says that his hair has grown with the color of a bee’s wing. "Practice the Dhamma" means he commands himself to practice the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
"'It is time for the holy life' (brahmacariyassa)" means it is time for you to abstain from sexual intercourse.
When the Bodhisattva had thus praised the virtues of living the holy life, the other [wife] thought, "I shall cause him to fall into this."
