Being terrified and trembling, they replied, “We shall do exactly as you say. Then, thinking, “Now I shall describe the beauty of his body so that he will not go forth,” she spoke these two verses:
“O King, it is my hair that has turned grey, not yours; it is my head, my very crown, that is thus.”
“I spoke falsely, thinking ‘I shall do you a service’; forgive this one offense, O best of kings.
You are young and handsome, O King, like a young bamboo shoot just risen from the ground;
rule the kingdom and look after me, O lord of men—do not let the time pass you by.”
In this context, "gray hair has grown on my very head" indicates that gray hair has appeared upon my head; the other phrase is a synonym for that same thing.
"The matter" means I spoke falsely, thinking, "I shall bring about my own advancement. "A single offense" means this one offense of mine.
"Risen in the first stage" means risen in the first period of life; "be so" means you are, you are established in the first period of life.
The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, the reading is simply “hosī.

Just as a *kaḷīra*—just as a tender, smooth-skinned young bamboo shoot shines exceedingly when stirred by a gentle breeze—so too do you appear; this is what he shows. There is also the reading “paṭhamuggato hotī,” the meaning of which is:
just as a young bamboo shoot that has first emerged is beautiful to behold, so too are you beautiful to behold. And for me...
"Look upon me"—the meaning is: "Behold me; do not leave me as one who is protectorless and widowed. Regarding "timely" (*kālika*):
the practice of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) is called "timely" because its ripening is granted in a second or third existence;

however, sovereignty is "not timely" (*akālika*) because it produces the pleasure of the strands of sensual desire in this very existence. Thus he says: "Having abandoned this which is not timely, do not pursue that which is timely."
The Bodhisatta, having heard her words, said: "My dear lady, you speak as if this were inevitable;
for as my age advances, these black hairs must surely turn white, becoming like coarse hemp-fiber.
For I have seen youths who resemble golden statues, adorned with garlands of blue lotuses and other flowers, and endowed with the splendor of supreme youth."
“I see that when the daughters of the khattiyas and others have reached old age as their years turn, they undergo both disfigurement and the breaking up of the body.
Thus, Bhaddā, this world of living beings ends in misfortune. Having said this, he spoke two verses while teaching the Dhamma with the playful grace of a Buddha:
“I see a young maiden, slender-limbed and well-proportioned, with skin like refined gold;
she moves among men as if to entice them, swaying like a dark coral branch.
Yet later I see that same woman, eighty or ninety years of age.”
"Taking up a staff, they move about trembling like a rafter that has become crooked.
In this context, *vo* is a mere particle. *Sāmaṭṭhapassaṃ* means "with well-polished sides. Or rather, this is the reading itself;
the meaning is "with skin-color polished on all sides. *Sutanaṃ* means "of beautiful body. *Sumajjhaṃ* means "with a well-proportioned waist."

“Like a black creeper or coral swaying”: just as a young black creeper or coral, having fully emerged in its prime, sways here and there when stirred by a gentle breeze, so too does a young girl, displaying her feminine charms and as if enticing men, move about.
The locative case is used in the sense of proximity; that is, in the presence of men.
She goes along as if enticing those men by means of the defilements.
At one time I see that woman; at another time I see that same woman reached by old age, her beauty and excellence vanished.
Having thus spoken of the gratification in form in the first verse, the Bodhisatta now demonstrates its danger.
He spoke thus: "Eighty or ninety years of age" means eighty or ninety years from birth.

"Bent like a rafter" means bent like a rafter; the meaning is that his body was broken in the manner of a rafter, and he moved about as if searching for a lost coin while leaning over. And although it was indeed [the case] by the Bodhisatta...
"Having seen [her] in childhood, she was not previously seen again in her nineties"; however, this was said with reference to the state of being seen by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Thus, having shown the disadvantage of form (*rūpa*) with this verse, the Great Being now spoke two verses to manifest his own lack of delight in the midst of the household life:
"Reflecting upon that very [fact], I lie alone in the middle of my bed."
“Perceiving, ‘I too am thus,’ one should not take delight in the household life, for it is time for the holy life (brahmacariya).
This delight of one dwelling at home is like hanging by a rope;
having cut even this asunder, the wise go forth, free from longing and having abandoned sensual pleasure.”
In that regard, *sohanti* means "I am he. *Tamevānuvicintayanto* means reflecting upon that very thing—the gratification and the danger of forms.
*Evaṃ iti pekkhamāno* means observing thus: "Just as this [body] has changed, I too shall reach old age and become one whose body is broken.
*Na gahe rameti* means "I do not delight in the house"; I do not take pleasure in the home. *Brahmacariyassa kālo* means, "O Bhaddā, it is the time for the holy life."
"It is the time for my holy life; therefore, I shall go forth"—this is what he indicates.
Regarding the phrase "and like a rope for support" (*rajjuvālambanī*): the word *ca* is merely a particle; the meaning is "it is like a supporting rope. Which [rope]?
It is the delight in dwelling in the household; the meaning is the sensual delight in objects such as forms for one living in the household. By this—
It shows the meager gratification found in sensual pleasures. This is the intended meaning here:

just as they might tie a support-rope for a sick person who is unable to turn over by his own strength, saying, "Grasp this and turn over," and as that person turns over by grasping it, he experiences a slight degree of physical and mental pleasure.
Thus, for those beings afflicted by defilements who are unable to turn toward the bliss of seclusion,
the objects such as visible forms that provide sensual delight— placed within the midst of the household— are,
at the time of the fever of their defilements, [the basis] for physical and mental pleasure consisting of the experience of sexual intercourse when they turn toward them.
That which is called "delight in sensual pleasures" arises for only a moment and is insignificant; thus, sensual pleasures have little gratification.

Having cut even this as well—because sensual pleasures involve much suffering and much despair, and because the danger therein is even greater—the wise, perceiving that danger, abandon them just as a man submerged in a cesspool would cut his rope.
"Like those who, being indifferent, abandon this trifling sensual pleasure that leads to much suffering and go forth, having renounced the world,
they enter the delightful life of a wanderer. Thus the Great Being,
demonstrating both the gratification and the danger in sensual pleasures, taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha.
Having summoned his companion and entrusted the kingdom to him, and while his kinsmen, friends, and associates were still weeping and lamenting,
he cast aside his royal splendor and wealth, entered the Himalayas, went forth as a seer (isipabbajjā),
and having attained the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges (jhānābhiññā), became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths, caused many people to drink the drink of the Deathless, and then identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the chief queen was Rāhula’s mother; the companion king was Ānanda;
and I myself was King Susīma."
The sixth: The Commentary on the Susīma Jātaka.
[412] 7. The Commentary on the Koṭasimbalī Jātaka.
"I am ten hundred leagues in height"—the Teacher related this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the subduing of the defilements.
The background story, however, will be revealed in the *Pānīya-jātaka*.

Here too, the Teacher, seeing five hundred bhikkhus at Antokoṭisanthāra overcome by sensual thoughts, assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and said: "Bhikkhus, it is proper to be wary of that which is worthy of wariness;
for defilements, when they increase, [destroy] a person just as the *nigrodha* and other trees destroy a tree in the forest."

“They are being destroyed; for that very reason, in the past, a deity reborn in a *koṭasimbalī* tree became seized with fear upon seeing a bird eating *nigrodha* seeds and dropping its excrement among the branches of her own tree, thinking, ‘From this, the destruction of my mansion will come.
Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a *koṭasimbalī* tree.
Then, a certain king of the *supaṇṇas*, having assumed a body one hundred and fifty *yojanas* in height, split the waters of the great ocean in two with the wind from his wings;
he seized a king of the *nāgas*, who was a thousand *vyāmas* in length, by the tail, and—
Having caused him to abandon the food he had taken in his mouth, [the bird] set out through the forest toward a *koṭasimbali* tree.
The Naga king, thinking, "I will free myself by hanging down," thrust his coils into a banyan tree (*nigrodha*), entwined the banyan, and seized it.
Due to the great strength of the Supaṇṇa king and the massive body of the Naga king, the banyan tree—
[The conflict] reached its conclusion. The Naga king did not let go of the tree; the Supanna king, having seized the Naga king along with the banyan tree, reached the Koṭisimbalī mountain.
There, he laid the Naga king down on his back, slit open his belly, ate the Naga’s fat, and cast the remaining carcass into the ocean. As for that banyan tree—
There was a certain female bird that, having flown up from a banyan tree where she had been resting, perched upon a branch of a *koṭasimbalī* tree.
Seeing her, the deity of the tree thought: "This female bird will drop excrement upon my tree trunk;
from that, either a banyan grove or a *pilakkhu* grove will spring up and grow, completely covering the entire tree."
“Then my celestial palace will be destroyed! she cried, trembling with fear and terror.
As she trembled, even the *koṭasimbalī* tree shook down to its very roots. Seeing her trembling, the king of the supaṇṇas asked for the reason and spoke these two verses:
“I have come here bringing a serpent a thousand cubits long;”
“Even when bearing that large-bodied one, you did not tremble.
But now, bearing this small bird, which has even less flesh than I do, you are agitated with fear. For what purpose, Koṭasimbalī?”
In this context, "ten hundred byāmas" means a length of exactly one thousand byāmas.
"Having brought a serpent and come" means he has come here having taken such a large serpent. "And that bed" refers to that serpent on the bed.
"They hold" means they are supporting it. "You tremble" means you shake. "For what purpose?"—he asks for what aim or for what reason; or, "for what benefit? (kaṃ vā atthaṃ).
"Beholding" (*sampassamānā*) is also the meaning. "Koṭasimbalī" is an address to a son of the gods by means of the name of a tree.
For that *simbali* tree receives the name "Koṭasimbalī" because of the great size of its trunk and branches; the son of the gods residing therein has that same name.
Then, explaining the reason for this, the son of the gods spoke four verses:
“You, O King, are an eater of meat, while this brahmin is an eater of fruit.
Having eaten the seeds of the *nigrodha*, the *pilakkhu*, the *udumbara*,
and the *assattha* trees, he will hang them upon my trunk.”
“Those trees grow up on my side, sheltered from the wind;
they will envelop me and turn me into a treeless place.
There are other trees as well—rooted and trunked trees.”
“By this species of bird, the seeds are brought and destroyed.
‘The creepers grow over even a vast forest tree;
therefore, O King, I tremble, foreseeing the danger that has arrived.’”
In that context, "he will void" means he will discharge excrement. "Those trees" refers to the *nigrodha* and other trees grown from those seeds.
"They will grow" means they will sprout and increase. "Within my sight" means within the space between my branches and so forth.
"Born in a windless place" means born in a windless spot because the wind has been shielded by my branches. "They will envelop me" means these very [trees] will thus...
"They will grow and overwhelm me"—this is the intended meaning here. "They will make me" means that, having thus overwhelmed me, they will make me like a treeless wasteland;
they will utterly break me down. "Rukkhā" is a synonym for trees.
"Mūlino khandhino" means those endowed with roots and those endowed with trunks. "Dumā" is likewise a synonym for trees. "Having brought the seed" refers to the seed.
"Having brought [them]. "There are other trees in this forest that have been struck down and destroyed.
"The secondary growth increases" means that trees such as the *nigrodha* (banyan), having become secondary growth (*ajjhārūha*), grow surpassing even a great other forest tree;
this is what he shows. In this context, however, all three readings—*vanapati*, *vanassa pati*, and *vanappatī*—are indeed correct. "O King! is an address to the *supaṇṇa*.
Having heard the words of the tree deity, the Supaṇṇa spoke this concluding verse:
“One should suspect what is to be suspected, and guard against future danger;
by being wary of future dangers, the wise man looks out over both worlds.”
In this context, "future danger" means that one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth guards against future danger, both pertaining to the present life and to the future life.
Furthermore, by not associating with evil friends or hostile persons, one guards against future danger.
In this way, one should guard against future danger. "On account of future dangers" means for the sake of the causes of future danger.
Perceiving that danger, the wise one surveys and looks upon both this world and the world beyond.
Having spoken thus, the Supaṇṇa, by means of his own supernatural power, caused that bird to fly away from that tree.
After the Teacher had delivered this Dhamma teaching, he said, "It is right to be wary of what is worthy of suspicion."
Having proclaimed the Truths, he identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, five hundred bhikkhus were established in the fruit of Arahatship.
At that time, the king of the Supaṇṇas was Sāriputta, while the tree deity was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Koṭasimbalijātaka.
[413] 8. The Commentary on the Dhūmakāri Jātaka.
"The King asked Vidhura..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the King of Kosala’s hospitality toward newcomers.
It is said that on one occasion, he [the King] was honoring the ancient warriors who had come down through his lineage.
Without having shown honor and respect to the newly arrived guests, he went forth to fight because the border regions had risen in rebellion.

When he was gone, the veteran warriors did not fight, thinking, "The guests who have received honors will fight," and the guests also did not fight, thinking, "The veteran warriors will fight. The bandits defeated the king. The king—
Having been defeated, and realizing his own state of defeat through the fault of failing to welcome the newcomers,
he returned to Sāvatthī and thought, "Is it only I who am defeated for acting in this way, or have other kings also been defeated before? Thinking,
"I shall ask the One of Ten Powers," he went to Jetavana after breakfast, paid his respects, and having performed the honors, bowed down to the Teacher.
He asked about that matter. The Teacher said, "Great King, you are not the only one; in the past, ancient kings also were defeated after showing hospitality to newcomers.
Being thus requested, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, in the city of Indapatta, there was a king of the Koravyas named Dhanañjaya, of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan, who ruled the realm."
He had [this] made. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn into the family of his chaplain;
having reached maturity and mastered all arts at Takkasilā, he returned to Indapatta and, upon the passing of his father, obtained the position of chaplain.
He became the advisor to the king in matters of welfare and righteousness, and they gave him the name Vidhura Paṇḍita. At that time, King Dhanañjaya, disregarding the veteran warriors—

He showed favor only to the newcomers. When he went to the frontier to fight because it had risen in rebellion, the old residents did not fight, thinking, "The newcomers will know [how to handle this]," and the newcomers did not fight, thinking, "The old residents will fight.
The king was defeated and returned to Indapatta, saying, "I have been defeated because of my practice of showing favor only to the newcomers."
He thought: "Is it only I who have been defeated by failing to provide hospitality to a guest, or have there been other kings defeated before?
I shall ask Vidhura the Wise. Having reflected thus, he approached the king while the latter was seated in attendance and asked him about that matter.
Then, revealing the manner of his inquiry, the Teacher spoke this half-stanza:
“King Yudhiṭṭhila, desiring the Dhamma, questioned Vidhura.
In this context, “desiring the Dhamma” means one who loves the Dhamma of good conduct.
“Do you know, O Brahmin, who alone grieves much?”—thus [he asked].
As for the meaning of the remaining half-verse: "O Brahmin, do you perhaps know who it is in this world that alone grieves much, grieving for various reasons?
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta said: "Great King, what is this so-called grief? Is it your own grief? Formerly, there was one named Dhūmakārī..."
A certain cowherd brahmin, having taken a large herd of goats and established a pen in the forest, settled there with them.
Having provided fire and smoke, he lived there tending the herd and consuming their milk and other products.
There, seeing golden-colored *sarabha* deer arrive, he felt affection for them; disregarding the goats, he devoted himself to honoring the deer.

"Having done so for the deer, when the autumn season arrived and the deer fled to the Himalayas and were lost, and even the goats having perished, he—seeing no deer and becoming pale with grief—met his end. This is the illustration:
by showing hospitality to strangers, you have come to ruin after grieving and suffering a hundredfold and a thousandfold more than they did."
Having brought them forward and showing them, he spoke these verses:
“The brāhmaṇa Vāseṭṭha, possessing great majesty, dwelt in the forest with a herd of goats;
untiring by day and night, he produced smoke.”
“By the smell of that smoke, the cranes, harassed by gadflies,
entered the rainy-season residence in the presence of the one who made the smoke.
Focusing his mind on the cranes, the goat did not realize [the danger].”
Whether coming or going, those does of his perished:
“In the autumn season, at Sarabhū, in the forest where the mosquitoes had departed,
they entered the mountain fastnesses and the sources of the rivers.”
“Having seen that Sarabhā had gone away and that Ajā had met her end,
you, O brahmin, have become emaciated, discolored,
and afflicted with jaundice. Thus, he who, having rejected what is his own, makes affection for a stranger— ”
“Thus, alone, he grieves greatly, like the smoke-making brahmin.
In this context, *pahūtejo* means having abundant fuel. *Dhūmam akāsi* means he produced both fire and smoke for the purpose of clearing away the obstacles caused by flies.
*Vāseṭṭho* is his clan name (*gotra*). *Atandito* means being untiring and diligent. *Tandhūmagandhena* means by the scent of that smoke.
By that scent of smoke. *Sarabhā* refers to the sarabha deer. *Makasaḍḍitā* means afflicted and oppressed by mosquitoes;
the other types of flies are also included by the mention of mosquitoes. *Vassāvāsaṃ* means they dwelt for the rainy-season retreat.
*Manaṃ katvā* means having generated affection. *Nāvabujjhathā* means that while returning from wandering in the forest toward the village, they did not realize [the danger].
And as she was going to the forest, she did not know how many had arrived and how many had not yet arrived.
"They were lost to him" means that while he was thus failing to reflect, those goats—being unprotected from dangers such as lions—were lost to him by those very dangers;
they were all destroyed.
"And the sources of rivers" means he entered the places of origin of the mountain rivers.
"They disappear" means they reach non-existence. "Having seen that the goats had met with destruction" means having perceived it.

"Emaciated and discolored" means that, having abandoned the goats who provided milk and so forth and instead gathering in with the deer, and then no longer seeing even them, he was deprived on both sides; overcome by sorrow, he became emaciated.

"And he became ill-favored. Thus, O Great King, 'he who, having cast out his own ancient internal kin and abandoned them, does not count anyone [as his own] but cherishes a newcomer'—such a person, like you, alone grieves much.
This man is like the smoke-making brahmin I have shown you; he grieves greatly."
Thus the Great Being spoke, persuading the king. Having been thus persuaded, the king gained confidence in him and gave him much wealth.
From that time forward, practicing internal integration alone and performing meritorious deeds such as giving, he became destined for heaven.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Koravya was Ānanda; the smoke-maker was Pasenadi of Kosala; and the wise Vidhura was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Dhūmakāri-jātaka.
9. The Jāgara-jātaka (The Story of the Watchman)
"Anger is the sleep of the watchful"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower.
For that noble disciple, a stream-enterer, set out from Sāvatthī on a caravan road through the wilderness together with a merchant caravan.
There, the caravan leader unyoked five hundred carts at a place convenient for water.
Having provided hard and soft food, he entered the camp.
Those people lay down here and there and fell asleep, but the lay follower, in the presence of the caravan leader, resolved upon a walking meditation at the foot of a tree.
Then five hundred thieves, desiring to plunder the caravan, took various weapons and surrounded the caravan.
They stood about. Seeing that lay follower walking back and forth, they thought, "We shall plunder him when he is asleep," and so they remained stationed here and there.
He, however, continued to walk for three watches of the night.
At dawn, the thieves abandoned the stones, clubs, and other weapons they had seized, and said, "O caravan leader, it is because of this man who is guarding with such diligence..."
"Having regained your life, you have become the master of what belonged to you; you should show honor to him," they said, and then they departed.

The people rose early in the morning, and seeing the stones, clubs, and other weapons discarded by them, thought, "It was because of this man that we regained our lives," and they paid honor to the lay devotee (upāsaka). The lay devotee also [went] to his desired destination...
Having gone and accomplished his task, he returned again to Sāvatthī, went to the Jeta Grove, and after honoring and bowing to the Tathāgata, sat down.
When asked, "Lay follower, why do you not appear? he related that matter. The Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only you who have attained distinction by remaining awake and vigilant;
in the past, wise men also attained distinguished qualities by remaining vigilant."
Having said, "They obtained [them]," when requested by him, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family;
having reached maturity and mastered all arts at Takkasilā, he returned home and lived in the midst of household life. Later on—
Having gone forth and taken up the ascetic life of an *isi*, he soon attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Dwelling in a region of the Himalayas, maintaining the postures of standing and walking, he did not succumb to sleep but walked in meditation (*caṅkamati*) throughout the entire night.
Then, a tree deity who had manifested at the end of his walking path, being delighted, stood upon the branches of the tree and asked him a question.
He spoke the first verse:
“Anger is sleep for those who are awake; anger is wakefulness for those who are asleep.
Who understands this of mine? Who will answer me?”

In that context, "Who? means "Who here? "Who knows this of mine? means "Who understands this question of mine? "Who will answer it for me? means he asks, "Who will be able to answer this question put by me?
Having heard her words, the Bodhisatta said:
"I am awake among those who sleep; I am awake among those who sleep."
“I understand this; I shall give you an answer.
Having spoken this verse, she was then addressed by her [with the following]:
“How is one sleeping while those who are awake? How is one awake among those who sleep?”
“How do you know this? How do you respond to me?
Being asked this verse, he explained the meaning as follows:
“Those who do not understand the Dhamma—what is called restraint and what is called self-control;”
While they are sleeping, O deity, I am awake.
But while those whose passion, hatred, and ignorance have been extinguished are awake, O deity, I am asleep.
“Thus one who is awake among those who sleep, thus one who is awake among those who are asleep—thus do I understand this, and thus do I respond to you. These were the verses he spoke.
Therein, as for “how one is asleep among those who are awake”: how is it that you are called “asleep” in the midst of beings who are awake?
...you shall be. This method applies everywhere. "Those beings" refers to those who do not understand the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.

Regarding "restraint" and "taming": they do not know that "this is restraint" and "this is taming," nor do they know the virtue and the restraint of the sense faculties that have come through the Path.
For the restraint of the sense faculties consists in the taming of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
It is said: “*dama*. Regarding the phrase “while they sleep”: while those beings are sleeping due to the slumber of the defilements (*kilesa*), I remain awake through heedfulness (*appamāda*).

In the verse beginning with “Those whose passion...,” for those great ones who have destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*), that which is designated by one hundred and fifty lines—namely, craving and greed consisting of one thousand five hundred types—is [described].

Lust, which arises from the nine grounds of malice, and hatred, as well as ignorance—which consists of non-knowing regarding the eight grounds such as suffering—these defilements have been shunned and abandoned.
While those Noble Ones are awake in every respect, I am "asleep" in comparison to them;
this is the meaning, O deity. Thus, "being awake," O deity, for this reason I...
“The sleeper among those who are awake. This same method applies to all the verses.
When the Great Being had thus spoken these questions, the satisfied deity, offering him praise, recited this concluding verse:
“Excellent is the sleeper among those who are awake; excellent is the one who is awake among those who sleep.”
“It is well that you understand this; it is well that you have answered me. Therein, “well” means:
“Having made this question auspicious, you have spoken it; we too shall speak it in just this way. Having thus offered praise to the Bodhisatta, she entered her own celestial palace.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the goddess was Uppalavaṇṇā, but the ascetic was none other than myself.”
The ninth is the commentary on the *Jāgarajātakavaṇṇanā*.
[415] 10. The commentary on the *Kummāsapiṇḍijātakavaṇṇanā*:
"Indeed, there is no need..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Queen Mallikā. For she...
In Sāvatthī, the daughter of a certain chief florist—possessing supreme beauty and great merit—was once going to a flower garden with other young girls when she was sixteen years old.
Taking three lumps of sour gruel and placing them in her flower basket, she departed from the city; at that moment, the Blessed One emitted a radiance from his body.
Seeing him entering the city surrounded by the community of monks, she offered three lumps of sour gruel.

The Teacher held out the bowl given to him by the Four Great Kings and accepted it. She too, having bowed her head at the feet of the Tathāgata and experienced joy directed toward the Buddha, stood to one side. The Teacher, looking at her, manifested a smile.
The Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One, “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the Tathāgata’s smile?
Then the Teacher explained the reason for his smile: “Ānanda, by the fruit of these balls of sour gruel, this young girl shall this very day become the chief queen of the King of Kosala.”
The maiden also went to the flower garden. On that very day, the King of Kosala, having been defeated in battle while fighting against Ajātasattu, fled and was returning mounted on his horse;
hearing the sound of her singing, his heart became bound to her, and he urged his horse toward the garden.
Endowed with merit, the maiden, upon seeing the king, did not flee.
Having arrived, he seized the horse by its nose-string. While still seated on the horse's back, the king asked, "Is this horse owned by someone, or is it ownerless?
Upon learning that it was ownerless, he dismounted; though exhausted by the wind and sun, he lay for a moment in her lap to rest.
Then, seating her upon the horse's back, surrounded by his army, he entered the city and [proceeded] to his own...
Having sent her to her family home and dispatched a carriage at eventide, he had her brought back from her family home with great honor and respect.
Placing her upon a heap of jewels and bestowing the royal consecration upon her, he made her his chief queen.
From that time forth, she was dear and pleasing to the king, and she was endowed with the five virtuous qualities beginning with rising before him.

A devoted wife, Mallikā was dear even to the Buddhas. Having given three lumps of *kummāsa* (sour gruel) to the Teacher, the fact that she had attained such prosperity spread throughout the entire city.
Then one day, in the Hall of Truth, they raised this discussion: "Friends, Queen Mallikā [gave alms] to the Buddhas..."
“Having given three lumps of millet, they attained the consecration on that very day as a result of those gifts; oh, how great is the virtue of the Buddhas!
The Teacher returned and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, it is not surprising that Mallikā [attained the consecration] for a single All-Knowing Buddha.”
“By giving three lumps of millet, she attained the status of chief queen to the King of Kosala. Why? Because of the greatness of the Buddhas’ virtues.
However, in the past, certain wise men gave saltless, oil-less, and sugarless millet to Paccekabuddhas;

by the fruit of that deed, in their second existence, they attained the glory of sovereignty over the kingdom of Kāsi, which extended for three hundred yojanas. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family.
Having reached maturity, he earned his living by working for wages in the service of a certain merchant.
One day, thinking, "This will serve as my breakfast," he took four lumps of coarse meal from a shop and went to his place of work.
While traveling, he saw four Paccekabuddhas approaching toward the city of Bārāṇasī for the purpose of almsround.
Thinking, “These men are going to Bārāṇasī for the sake of alms; I have these four lumps of boiled rice myself;
what if I were to give them to these men? he approached them, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sirs, ...”
"These four lumps of millet porridge are in my hands; I give them to you.
It would be well, venerable sirs, if you would accept them, so that this merit may be for my long-term welfare and happiness.
Having spoken thus and perceiving their consent, he swept away the sand, prepared four seats, and spread branches over them.

Having had the Paccekabuddhas sit down in order, he brought water in a leaf-wrapped vessel, poured it as the water of honor (*dakṣiṇodaka*), placed four lumps of sour gruel into the four bowls, and after bowing, said:
"Venerable sirs, by the result of this merit, may there never be a birth in a poor household; may this be a condition for the penetration of omniscient knowledge."
The Paccekabuddhas partook of the meal; at the conclusion of the meal, having offered words of thanksgiving, they rose up and returned to the Nandamūlaka cave.
The Bodhisatta, having raised his hands in reverent salutation and taken upon himself the joy directed toward the Paccekabuddhas, went to his own work after they had passed from his sight.
Recalling the gift throughout the remainder of his life, he passed away, and by the fruit of that deed, [he was reborn] as the king of Bārāṇasī.
He was conceived in the womb of the chief queen, and they gave him the name Prince Brahmadatta.

From the time he began to walk on his own feet, he thought: "Having been a hired laborer in this very city, I went to work and gave four lumps of sour gruel to Paccekabuddhas; it is by the fruit of that gift that I have been reborn here."
With the knowledge of recollecting past births (*jātissara-ñāṇa*), he made all his actions in previous lives manifest as clearly as a face seen in a mirror by a faithful servant;
thus he saw them. When he reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā and, having mastered all the arts, returned home.
After showing his father the skills he had learned, his father, being well-pleased, established him in the position of viceroy. Later, upon the passing of his father, [he ascended] to the kingship.
He was established [on the throne]. Then, having brought the daughter of the King of Kosala, who possessed the most excellent beauty, they made her his chief queen.
On the day of the auspicious parasol ceremony, they adorned the entire city so that it resembled the city of the gods.
Having circumambulated the city and ascended the decorated palace, he stood in the middle of the great terrace beneath a raised white parasol.
Having ascended his throne and sat down, he was surrounded by ministers standing on one side;

on another side were brahmins, householders, and others, resplendent with various ranks and the splendor of royal luxury; on another side were the city-dwellers with various kinds of gifts in their hands;
and on another side was a troupe of sixteen thousand dancing girls, like a host of adorned celestial nymphs—this scene was exceedingly delightful.
Beholding his glorious majesty and recollecting his own past karma, he thought:
"This golden pedestal, this golden canopy, and this white parasol; these many thousands of mounts consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots;
this inner chamber filled with gems, pearls, and other treasures; this great earth filled with various kinds of grain; and these women who resemble celestial nymphs—all of this..."
"This glory and wealth of mine do not belong to anyone else; they belong only to that gift of four handfuls of broken rice given to the four Paccekabuddhas.
It is by depending on them that I have obtained this," he said.
Recalling the virtues of the Paccekabuddhas, he made his own deed manifest. As he recollected this, his entire body was filled with rapture (*pīti*). With that rapture...
With his heart filled with joy, singing an inspired song in the midst of the great multitude, he spoke these two verses:
“Indeed, there is no service rendered to the Buddhas, those of peerless vision, that is too small;
behold the fruit of a mere lump of sour, saltless gruel!”
“These many elephants, cattle, and horses, wealth and grain, and the entire earth;
these women who resemble celestial nymphs—behold the fruit of a ball of boiled rice.
In that context, “Anomadassī” refers to those Paccekabuddhas because they have seen the peerless, flawless knowledge of Paccekabodhi.

[The Buddha] was named Anomadassin. "Service" (*pāricariyā*) refers both to acts of courtesy— such as prostrating, rising to greet, and joining the palms— and to the act of relinquishment, which occurs when,
upon seeing [the Blessed One] arrive, one clarifies the mind, perceives his virtues,
purifies the three types of volition, and, with faith in the fruit [of giving], performs the act of renouncing whatever gift is available, whether small or great, coarse or refined.
“Among the Buddhas” means among the Paccekabuddhas. “There is none meager” means there is none dull or limited, it is said. “Dried up” means devoid of moisture. “Saltless” means lacking molasses;
for because it is free from boiled-down sugar (phāṇita), it is called “saltless. “A lump of boiled rice” (kummāsapiṇḍiyā):
he spoke thus referring to the boiled rice taken after having combined four lumps of boiled rice into one. Of those possessed of virtues...

Having observed the virtues of recluses and brahmins and having gladdened the mind, for those who expect the arising of fruit, there is no such thing as a small meritorious gift once the three types of volition have been purified;
rather, it bestows great prosperity in every place of rebirth—this is what is meant. And on this point, there is a verse:
“When one has faith in the mind, even a small gift is called no small gift—
whether given to a Tathāgata, a Perfectly Enlightened One, or to his disciple.
Whether [the Buddha] is still living or has attained Nibbāna, if the mind is equal, the fruit is equal.”
"For it is by reason of a mental aspiration that beings go to a happy destination.
To illustrate this meaning:
"I gave milk-rice to a bhikkhu wandering for alms;"
“Behold my celestial mansion! I am a nymph of lovely form.
I am the most excellent among a thousand nymphs; behold the ripening of my merits!
It is because of this that I have such beauty, and it is because of this that I prosper here.”
“Riches arise for me, whatever is dear to the mind;
therefore my power blazes forth thus, and my complexion shines in all directions.
Passages such as these from the *Vimānavatthu* should be cited.
"Riches and grain" refers to wealth such as pearls and the like, as well as the seven types of grain. "The entire earth" means this whole great earth;
speaking thus, he imagines that the entire earth has come into his hands. "Behold the fruit of the ball of sour gruel" was said by him while showing the fruit of his own giving to himself.
Indeed, it is said that the fruit of giving belongs only to Bodhisattvas and omniscient Buddhas.
And they do not know it. Therefore, when the Teacher was speaking the Itivuttaka Sutta, he said:

"If, monks, beings knew the ripening of the fruit of giving and sharing as I know it, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of stinginess remain obsessing their minds. Even that..."
“Even their very last morsel, their very last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing it, were there recipients for them.
But because beings do not know the ripening of the gift and sharing as I know it, they eat without giving; and the stain of stinginess remains, having taken possession of their minds.”
On the auspicious day of his own birth, the Bodhisatta, filled with joy and gladness, sang this song of exultation in these two verses.
From that time forth, it was known as "The King’s Beloved Song.

Consequently, the female dancers of the Bodhisatta, as well as the other actors, musicians, and so forth, the people of the inner palace, the inhabitants of the city, and those living outside the city—even in taverns and among the circles of ministers—[all sang it].
Thinking, “This is our king’s favorite song,” they sang that very same song.
When a long time had passed in this manner, the chief queen desired to know the meaning of that song, yet she did not dare to ask the Great Being.
Then, having become pleased with her for a certain virtue, the king one day said, “My dear, I shall grant you a boon; choose a boon. “Very well,” [she replied].
“Your Majesty, I accept them. “What shall I give you from among the elephants, horses, and so forth?
“Your Majesty, by depending on you, there is nothing that I lack; I have no need for these things. But if you wish to grant me a boon, please give it after explaining the meaning of your song.
“Lady, what use have you for this boon? Choose something else. “Your Majesty, I have no need for anything else.”
“I have no need [for anything else]; I shall take this very thing. “Very well, lady, I will explain it;

however, I will not explain it to you in private alone. Rather, having had a drum beaten throughout the twelve-league city of Bārāṇasī, and having had a jeweled pavilion constructed at the palace gate and a jeweled couch prepared, I will do so in the presence of the ministers, brahmins, and others, as well as the citizens and the sixteen thousand women.”
"And surrounded by them, sitting in the midst of them upon a jeweled couch, I shall speak. She consented, saying, "Very well, Your Majesty.
The king, having had it prepared accordingly, sat upon the jeweled couch surrounded by a great multitude of people, like Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by hosts of immortals.
The queen also, adorned with every ornament, having spread out a golden auspicious seat, [sat] to one side with the corner of her eye—
Having observed [the king] and sat down in such a place, he said, “Your Majesty,
please explain the meaning of this song of auspiciousness sung out of satisfaction with you, making it as manifest as the full moon rising in the sky,” and then he spoke the third verse:
“O elephant among kings, Lord of Kosala, you constantly recite these verses;”
“I ask you, O increaser of the realm: why do you speak with such intense joy?
Therein, “lord of Kosala” does not mean that he is the ruler of the kingdom of Kosala; rather, he dwells having made wholesome qualities (*kusala-dhamma*) his sovereign.
Thus, addressing him, she spoke these words; the meaning is: “O lord of the wholesome, O one whose inclination is toward the wholesome. “With intense joy” means...
"You speak with a mind exceedingly filled with joy; therefore, please tell me the meaning of these verses.
Then, revealing the meaning of the verses to him, the Great Being spoke four stanzas:
"In this very city, I was born in a certain family;..."
I was a hired laborer, supported by wages and restrained by virtue.
As I was going out to work, I saw four ascetics,
endowed with proper conduct and virtue, who had become cool and were free from taints.
“Having inspired confidence in them and sitting upon a mat of leaves,
I gave the Buddhas sour gruel with my own hands out of faith.
This is the fruit of that wholesome deed, such as this, for me.”
"I experience this kingdom, this most excellent and prosperous earth.
In that context, "in a certain family" means in one particular family, whether it be unknown by name or by clan. "I was born" refers to my birth.
"I was a laborer for others" means that, having been born into that family, I lived by performing work for others due to my poverty.
"Working for others," means I was a hired laborer. "A servant" means one supported by another's wages. "Restrained by virtue" means established in the restraint of the five precepts;
this indicates that even while living on wages, he abandoned immorality and remained endowed with virtue.
"Setting out for work" means I had gone out on that day for the purpose of performing the duties to be done. Four...

"O Bhaddā, I am going forth, my lady. Having departed from the city and ascended the great highway, as I was proceeding to my own field of action, I saw four renunciants who had stilled their evil deeds entering the city of Bārāṇasī for alms.

'Endowed with conduct and virtue'—non-conduct (*anācāra*) refers to making a livelihood by means of the twenty-one improper modes of seeking; it is by way of its opposite [that they are so described]."
"Endowed with conduct and with the virtue that has arrived through the paths and fruits.

"Become cool" means having attained a state of coolness through the subsiding of the fevers of passion and so forth, and through the extinguishing of the eleven fires. "Free from taints" means devoid of the taints of sensual desire and the rest.
"Having sat down" means having caused him to sit upon a spread of leaves laid over the sand seats. For here, "spread" (*santhato*) refers to the bedding (*santharo*).
It was said: "Having given them water to drink, I respectfully gave them boiled rice with my own hands.
"Of the wholesome" means in the sense of being healthy and blameless. "Fruit" refers to its outflowing result (*nissanda-phala*). "Prosperous" means blossoming with all forms of excellence.
And having heard the Great Being thus recounting in detail his own karmic fruit, the queen’s mind became serene.

“If, O Great King, you thus know the fruit of giving through direct experience, then from this day forward, having obtained even a single morsel of food, you should eat only after first giving it to righteous recluses and brahmins. Thus praising the Bodhisatta, she said:
“Give and then eat, and do not be negligent; turn the wheel, O Lord of Kosala!”
“O King, do not be unrighteous; protect the Dhamma, O Lord of Kosala!”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “giving and enjoying” means that you should enjoy [wealth] only after giving to others. “And do not be negligent” means do not be heedless regarding meritorious deeds such as giving.
“Turn the wheel, O Lord of Kosala” means, O Great King, [turn the wheel] through wholesome inclinations, dwelling in a suitable locality, and so forth.

Set in motion the fourfold Wheel of Dhamma. For while an ordinary chariot moves by means of two wheels, this body goes to the world of the devas by means of these four wheels; therefore, they have come to be designated as the "Wheel of Dhamma.
Set that wheel in motion. "Unrighteous" means that just as others, following the course of favoritism, [crush] the world like sugarcane in a mill—
Those who, like squeezing [a plant], merely amass wealth become unrighteous; likewise, you must not be unrighteous. "Guard the Dhamma" means:
"Generosity, virtue, renunciation, uprightness, gentleness, austerity, non-anger, non-harming, patience, and non-opposition."
"But protect and guard these tenfold duties of a king; do not abandon them.
Accepting her words, the Great Being said:
"O beautiful one, I shall practice that very path again and again."
"O beautiful Kosala princess, it is pleasing for me to see those who practice the noble way"—thus he spoke this verse.
In this context, *vaṭumaṃ* means the path. *Ariyācaritaṃ* means practiced by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others.

*Sukosale* means "O beautiful one," being the daughter of King Kosala. *Arahanto* means "Worthy Ones" because they are far removed from defilements (*kilesa*), and because they have slain the spokes (*ara*) and the enemies (*ari*).
Because they have attained the state of being worthy of offerings, the Paccekabuddhas are thus named. This is what is meant:

"O Bhaddā, daughter of the King of Kosala, I, not making satisfaction with the thought 'I have given this gift,' shall practice again and again that very same path of giving which is the conduct of the Noble Ones.
For because they are the foremost recipients of offerings, the Arahants are pleasing to behold; and because of my desire to give them robes and other requisites..."
"I wish to see them as they truly are.
Having spoken thus, the king looked upon the queen’s splendor and said, "Bhadde, I have already related in detail my own wholesome kamma from previous existences;
however, among these women, [none can compare] in beauty or in graceful charm."
"Since there is not even one woman equal to you, what deed did you perform to obtain this prosperity?
Thus questioning her, he spoke again in verse:
"Like a goddess, with the form of an *accharā*, you shine in the midst of this host of women."
"What auspicious deed did you perform, by what means have you become so beautiful, O Sukosala?"—the meaning of which is:

"O Bhaddā Sukosala, daughter of the King of Kosala, you shine in the midst of this assembly of women like a certain divine maiden of Sakka, the king of the gods, in the city of the Thirty-three, being like a celestial nymph (accharā) through the perfection of your form. Previously...
“What indeed was that auspicious and wholesome deed you performed, and for what reason were you born so beautiful?
Then, explaining the wholesome deed he had done in a previous existence, she spoke these two further verses:
“O Khattiya of the Ambaṭṭha clan, I was once a slave girl, employed by others.”
“Self-restrained, living according to the Dhamma, virtuous, and of blameless vision—
when I was wandering for alms, I then gave a portion of food to that bhikkhu.
Cheerful and joyful myself, such is the fruit of that deed.”
She too, it is said, possessed the knowledge of past lives (*jātissara*); therefore, having determined [the matter] by means of her own knowledge of past lives, she spoke.
In that context, "of the Ambaṭṭha family" means of a householders' family. "I was a slave-girl" (*dāsyāham*) means "I was a slave"; there is also a reading, "I was a slave" (*dāsāham*).
"One to be sent by others" (*parapesiyā*) means one who must be dispatched by others for the purpose of performing various tasks; one who acts as a messenger. "Restrained" (*saññatā*)—
As for "slave-girls," they are immoral; however, I am restrained in the three doors and endowed with virtue.

"Living by the Dhamma" means maintaining one's livelihood through the Dhamma and justice, without practicing deception against others or similar acts. "Virtuous" means being perfected in conduct and possessed of good qualities.
"Of blameless appearance" means having a beautiful appearance and being dear in her character.
“*Uddhaṭabhattaṃ*”: food obtained by setting aside one’s own allotted portion of the meal.
“*Bhikkhu*”: a Paccekabuddha whose defilements have been destroyed. “*Vittā sumanā*”: satisfied, joyful, and filled with gladness, having faith in the fruit of kamma.
“*Tassa kammassā*”: of that single act of giving alms-food to a monk. This is what is meant: I—
"Great King, formerly in Sāvatthī, while I was a maidservant in a certain household, I took my allotted portion of food and, as I was going out, saw a Paccekabuddha wandering for alms.
Suppressing my own craving, endowed with virtues such as self-restraint and having faith in the fruit of kamma, I gave that food to him; and for as long as my life lasted,"
"Having passed away after staying there, I was reborn in Sāvatthī in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Kosala;
now, while serving at your feet, I enjoy such prosperity as this. This is the fruit of that deed of mine.
In this context, it is for the purpose of showing that a gift given to those endowed with virtues yields great fruit:—
And the opening verses should be recited in detail: “Truly,
for those with faith, [it is] foremost,” and “This is the treasure that grants all desires for gods and humans.”
Thus, having both related their own past deeds in detail, they built six halls for almsgiving— at the four city gates, in the center of the city,
and at the door of their residence— and from that time forth, having made the whole of Jambudīpa free from want,
they distributed great gifts, guarded their virtue, and observed the Uposatha rites; at the end of their lives, they became destined for heaven.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the queen was Rāhula’s mother, and the king was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the *Kummāsapiṇḍa Jātaka*, the tenth.
11. The Commentary on the *Parantapa Jātaka*
“Evil will come to me,” [said the Teacher]. This was spoken by the Teacher while staying at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s attempts to bring about his own destruction.
For at that time, they had raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying: “Friends, Devadatta is striving solely for the sake of killing the Tathāgata;
he has employed archers, hurled a stone, and released the elephant Nāḷāgiri.”
“He is even now employing a means for the purpose of destroying the Tathāgata. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that he has striven for my destruction;
in the past as well, he sought to kill me, but being unable to do even so much as that, he brought suffering upon himself.”
Having said, "You have experienced it," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity, he studied all the arts at Takkasilā and mastered the incantations for knowing all languages.
Thus, having given his instructions to the teacher, he returned to Bārāṇasī, and his father appointed him as viceroy.
Although he placed him in the position of viceroy, being desirous of having him killed, he did not even wish to see him.
Then, one night while the people were in seclusion, a female jackal carrying two cubs entered the city through a drain. To the Bodhisatta—
And not far from the bedchamber of the palace there was a hall;
in it, a certain traveler, having removed his sandals and placed them on the ground at his feet, lay down upon a wooden plank and had not yet fallen asleep.
At that time, the lion cubs, hungry, were crying out. Then their mother said, "Dear ones, do not make a noise."
"In this hall, there is a man who has taken off his sandals, placed them on the ground, and is lying on a wooden plank;
he has not yet fallen asleep. When he falls asleep, I will bring these sandals and have you eat them," she said in her own language.
The Bodhisatta, through the power of his spells, understood her speech and emerged from the bedchamber.
Opening the window, he asked, "Who is there? "I am a traveler, Your Majesty," he replied.
"Where are your sandals? "On the ground, Your Majesty. "Lift them up and hang them [on the door]," he said. Hearing this, the female jackal became angry with the Bodhisatta.
Again, one day, she entered the city in the same manner. At that time, a certain intoxicated man, thinking, "I shall drink water..."
As he was descending into the lotus pond, he fell in, submerged, and died from lack of breath.
He had two garments on, and between his waist-cloth and his body there were a thousand kahāpaṇas, as well as a ring on his finger.
Even then, while his children were crying out, "We are hungry, mother!", she said, "Sons, do not make a noise; a man has died in this lotus pond. Regarding him—
“This and that is here; however, he has died and is lying right there on the steps.
We shall have you eat this man,” he said. Having heard this, the Bodhisatta opened the window and asked, “Who is in the hall?
When one stood up and replied, “It is I, Your Majesty,” he said, “Go, [take] the cloth and the thousand kahāpaṇas from the dead man in this lotus pond.”
"Take his finger-ring and sink his body into the water so that it does not rise again," she said. He did exactly as he was told.
She became angry once more and said, "On the previous day you would not even let my children eat your sandals;
today you will not let me eat a dead man. Very well, from now on, on the third day..."
“A rival king will come and surround the city. Then your father will send you forth for battle;
there they will cut off your head. Having drunk the blood from your throat, I shall release my enmity.
You are forging an enmity with me!”—having cried out thus and threatened the Bodhisatta, he took his two little sons and departed.
On the third day, a rival king arrived and surrounded the city.
The king said to the Bodhisatta, "Go, dear son, and fight with him. "Your Majesty, there is something I have seen;
I do not dare to go, for I fear for my life," he replied. "What does it matter to me whether you live or die? Go at once! he said.

Saying, "Very well, O King," the Great Being took his retinue and, instead of exiting through the gate where the rival king was stationed, he opened another gate and departed. As he went, the entire city became as if empty;
everyone followed along with him. Having established his camp at a suitable location, he settled there.
“Alas! the king thought: “The viceroy has abandoned the city empty and fled with his army;
the rival king, too, stands surrounding the city. Now there is no life for me.
Thinking, “I shall protect my life,” he took the queen, the chaplain, and a servant named Parantapa who was at his feet, and in the middle of the night, disguised as a stranger—
Having fled, he entered the forest. The Bodhisatta, knowing that he had escaped, entered the city, waged war, drove his enemy away, and took possession of the kingdom.
His father also built a leaf-hut on the bank of a river and lived there, subsisting on various fruits.
Both the king and the court priest would go there for the sake of gathering fruit. Thus ends the *Parantapadāsa*.
She was staying right there in the leaf-hut together with the queen. There too, a fetus took root in the queen’s womb on account of the king.
Through their frequent association, she committed adultery with Parantapa.
One day she said to Parantapa, "If the king finds out, neither you nor I will have life; therefore, kill him. "How? [he asked].
"Shall I kill him? "He is going to bathe after having you take his sword and bathing robe;
there, at the bathing place, once you have recognized his negligence, cut off his head with the sword, cut his body into pieces, and bury it in the ground.
He consented, saying, "Very well."
Now one day, the chaplain himself went for the sake of gathering fruits and climbed a tree near the king’s bathing place to gather fruit.
The king, thinking, "I shall bathe," had his sword and bathing cloth brought by a servant and went to the riverbank.
There, while the king was at the moment of bathing and had become negligent, [the chaplain thought], "I shall kill him."
Parantapa seized him by the neck and drew his sword. Out of fear of death, he cried out.
Hearing that sound and looking around, the chaplain saw King Parantapa about to kill him;
terrified and trembling, he let go of the branch, descended from the tree, entered a thicket, and hid himself. Parantapa, hearing the sound of the branch being released—
Having killed the king and dug him into the ground, he searched about, thinking, "There was the sound of branches being snapped at this spot;
who could it be here? Finding no one, he bathed and departed.
When he had gone, the chaplain emerged from his seat, and having realized that the king’s body had been cut into pieces and buried in a pit, he bathed.
Out of fear of being killed, he took the guise of a blind man and went to the leaf-hut. Seeing him, Parantapa asked, "What have you done, brahmin?
Acting as if he did not know, he replied, "Your Majesty, having had my eyes destroyed, I have come here.
In a forest thick with venomous snakes, I stood by the side of a termite mound; there, by one venomous snake..."
"He will be released from my grasp," he said. Parantapa thought, "He does not recognize me; he calls me 'Devā.
I shall comfort him. Having comforted him, saying, "Brahmin, do not worry, I shall look after you," he gave him various fruits and satisfied him.
From that time on, Parantapa's slave brought the fruits, and the queen also gave birth to a son.
As her sons were growing up, one day while sitting comfortably at dawn, she spoke slowly to Parantapa:
"Were you seen by anyone while killing the king? "No one saw me," he replied, "but I heard the sound of a branch being released;
I do not know whether that branch was dropped by a human or by an animal."
"But whenever fear comes upon me, it will come from the place where I am suspended by the branch," he said,
conversing with her, and spoke this first verse:
"Evil shall come upon me, fear shall come upon me."
"For then the branch was shaken by a human or by a deer.
In this context, "evil" means base, undesirable, and unpleasant. "Fear" means that even the fear of mental terror will come upon me;
it is not possible for it not to come. Why? Because at that time, when the branch was shaken, it was not perceived whether it was by a human or by a deer.
"Therefore, danger shall come to me from that.
They thought, "The chaplain is sleeping," but he, though not actually sleeping, overheard their conversation.
Then one day, when the Parantapas had gone out to gather fruits, the chaplain, remembering his own Brahmin wife, lamented and spoke this second verse:
“Surely my desire is for one who is timid, living not far away;
she alone will make me thin and pale, O scorcher of foes.
In this context, a woman indeed fears even the slightest thing, and therefore she is called “timid.”
"Not far away" means that she dwells only a few *yojanas* from here;
this shows that the desire which has arisen in me for that timid Brahmin woman will surely make me thin and pale.
With the words "that very branch," however, he shows a simile: the meaning is that just as a branch makes the enemy scorcher thin and pale, so too [will my desire].
Thus the brahmin spoke only the verse and did not explain its meaning; therefore, the purpose of this verse was not apparent to the queen.
Then she said to him, "What are you saying, brahmin? He replied, "I have observed it," and on another day he spoke a third verse:
“The beloved one, dwelling in the village, blameless and praised, will cause me to grieve;
she alone, O scorcher of foes, will make me thin and pale.

In this context, “will cause me to grieve” means she will wither me by producing sorrow. “The beloved” (kantā) refers to a desired wife. “Dwelling in the village” means residing in Bārāṇasī; this is the intended meaning. “Blameless” (aninditā) means irreproachable, possessing supreme beauty.
On another day, he spoke the fourth verse:
“O you with the dark-browed eyes, those smiles spoken by you— how will they make me thin and pale? Just like that branch, O scorcher of foes.”
In that regard, "by you, with darkened eyebrows" means by you, with eyebrows made dark. This is what is meant:

O lady, those gentle smiles and sweet words uttered by you—with your eyebrows darkened by applying collyrium-sticks drawn from the corner of the eye—have made me, like a withered branch crying out, emaciated and pale, like one who has been scorched by an enemy.
"He will do it. By changing the letter *pa* to *va*, the reading is also simply "Vaṅgī.

Later, when the prince had reached maturity and was about sixteen years old, the brahmin had him take hold of the tip of his staff, went to the bathing ford, opened his eyes, and looked at him. The prince said, "Is it not you, brahmin?"
“Are you blind? he asked. He replied, “I am not blind; I protect my life by this means,” and then said, “Do you know your father?
When [the son] said, “This is my father,” [the other] said, “This is not your father. Your father is the King of Bārāṇasī.
This man is your slave; having behaved improperly toward your mother, he killed your father in this place.”
“Dig them up,” he said, and having dug them up, he showed the bones to the prince. A powerful anger arose within the prince.
Then he asked him, “What shall I do now? [The father] explained the entire sequence of events, saying, “Do exactly what your father did at this very same ford.
He then instructed the prince for several days in the art of archery. Then one day, the prince—
Taking his sword and bathing-cloth, he said, “Let us go to bathe, dear father. Parantapa replied, “Very well,” and went with him.

Then, as they had descended into the water to bathe, [the prince] took the sword in his right hand and his father’s hair-tuft in his left, saying, “It seems that at this very bathing place, you seized my father by the hair-tuft while he was crying out...”
“He killed him, and I too shall do the same to you,” he said. Terrified by the fear of death and lamenting, he spoke these two verses:
“Surely that sound has come from him; surely he has spoken to you;
surely it was told by him who caused that branch to shake.”
“Having come together with this, it was thought by me, a fool:
‘Surely that branch has been shaken now by a human or by a deer.
In this context, *āgama* means that sound surely came to, or reached, him. *Asaṃsi nūna so tava* means that sound surely belonged to you.
"I imagine you have informed him. "Surely that was told by him" means that the being who then shook that branch surely told him the reason:
"In this way your father was killed. "Having come together" (*samāgamma*) means having gathered, having assembled. [He thought:
"When that branch shook for me, a fool, then fear will arise in me from a human or a wild beast."
"What was thought and reflected upon has come to pass: that you have met with me," this is what was said.
Then the prince spoke the concluding verse:
"In that very way you have experienced it; you have deceived my father."
"Having killed him and covering [the body] with branches, my fear will depart.
Therein, "you understood it exactly thus" means you knew it exactly so.
"You deceived my father" means that you, having reassured my father by saying, "Let us go to bathe," killed him while he was bathing and cut him into pieces.
Having buried him, he deceived him by saying, "If anyone were to find out, such fear would come upon me as well," but [the other] knew,
"This very fear of death has now come upon you.
Having said this, he brought about his end of life right there, buried him, covered him with branches, and [took up] his sword.
Having washed themselves and bathed, they went to the leaf-hut and informed the chaplain that he had been killed.
After reviling their mother, the three men said, "What shall we do here? and returned to Bārāṇasī itself.
The Bodhisatta, having given the vice-regency to his youngest brother and performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, fulfilled the path to heaven.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the father-king was Devadatta, the chaplain was Ānanda, and the son-king was none other than myself.
This is the eleventh story, the Commentary on the Parantapa Jātaka.
The second chapter, the Gandhāra Vagga, is concluded.
The Summary of the Jātakas:
Kukku, Manoja, Sutano, Gijjha, Dabbhapuppha, Paṇṇaka, Sattubhasta,
Aṭṭhisena, Kapi, and Bakabrahmā— these are the ten.
Gandhāra and Mahākapi, Kumbhakāra of firm virtue;
Somadatta and Susīma, Koṭisimbalī and Dhūmakārī;
Jāgara and Kummāsapiṇḍa—these are the eleven who scorched their enemies.
The commentary on the Sattaka-nipāta is finished.
8. Aṭṭhaka-nipāta [417] 1.
Kaccāni-jātaka-vannanā (Commentary on the Kaccāni Birth Story)
“Clad in white robes, pure, with clean hair”— this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower who supported his mother.
It is said that this young man of good family in Sāvatthī, being endowed with virtuous conduct,
became a deity to his mother after his father passed away, performing services for her such as washing her face, providing tooth-sticks, bathing her, and washing her feet.
And he tended to his mother with rice gruel, cooked rice, and other provisions. Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, you have other duties pertaining to the life of a householder;
take a young girl from a family of similar status. She will support me, and you too can attend to your own work.
He replied, "Mother, without seeking my own welfare or happiness, I am attending upon you."
“Who else will serve you in this way? “Father, one ought to perform the duty of increasing the family.
“I have no need for the household life; having served you, I shall go forth into homelessness at the time of your funeral smoke.
Then his mother, though she entreated him again and again, not obtaining his consent and unable to take hold of his desire, [sought] one of similar birth...
He brought home a girl from a noble family. Without having rejected his mother, he lived in cohabitation with her.
She too, thinking, "My husband attends upon my mother with great devotion;
I too shall attend upon her, and in this way I will become dear to him," served her with great care. He [said], "This woman [is attending] my mother..."
“Serve her with due respect. From that time on, whatever sweet foods and other delicacies he obtained, he gave them only to her.
Later, she thought: “He gives me all the sweet foods and delicacies he obtains;
surely he must intend to have my mother removed. I shall devise a means to have her removed. Thus...
Having emerged from improper reflection, one day she said, "Master, when you go outside, your mother reviles me.
He remained silent.
She thought, "I will cause this old woman to be despised and make her repulsive to my son. From that time forth—
When giving rice gruel, she gives it either too hot or too cold, or too salty or not salty enough.
When told, "Mother, it is too hot," or "It is too salty," she fills it up and adds cold water.
Then, when told, "It is too cold" or "It is not salty enough," she says, "Just now you said it was 'too hot' and 'too salty,' and now you say it is 'too cold' and 'not salty. What is this?"
“Will she be able to satisfy me? he cried out with a great clamor. He made the bathing water too hot and poured it over her back.
When she said, “Mother, my back is burning,” he filled it again and added cold water.
When she said, “It is too cold, Mother,” he thought, “Just now she said it was 'too hot,' and now she says it is 'too cold'; what contempt does she have for me?”

She told her neighbors, "He will not be able to endure it. When she was told, "Mother, there are many bugs on my bed," she removed her own bed, placed it over his, and having brought it back saying, "It has been cleaned for me," she prepared it for him.
The Great Laywoman, being bitten by twice as many bugs, spent the entire night sitting there.
“Mother, we have been bitten by insects all night long,” she said. The other replied, “Yesterday your bed was crushed;

who is capable of managing this woman’s affairs? Thinking, “Now I shall have her reproached by her son,” she scattered saliva, mucus, and other such things here and there, saying, “Who is it that makes the whole house impure?”
When he had said this, she replied, "Your mother does such things; though told 'do not do it,' she engages in quarreling.
I cannot live in one house with such an ill-omened woman as her; either let her stay in the house, or me.
Having heard her words, he said, "My dear, you are young and can go and live anywhere you wish."
"But my mother is weak with old age; I alone am her refuge. You should go forth and return to your own family home," he said.
Hearing his words, she was afraid and thought: "It is not possible to cause a rift between him and his mother;
his mother is dearly beloved by him in every way. But if I go to my father's house, I shall live as a widow."
“Living here, I shall become afflicted; therefore, having propitiated my mother-in-law just as before, I will look after her.
From then on, she looked after her in exactly the same manner as previously. Then one day, that lay devotee went to Jetavana for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma;
having paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side. “What is it, lay devotee? Are you [neglecting] meritorious deeds?”

When he was told, "Do not be negligent; fulfill your duty of attending upon your mother," he replied, "Yes, venerable sir, but that mother of mine brought home a young woman from a family against my very will, and she committed all manner of improper acts.
Having related everything to the Teacher, [he added], "Thus, Blessed One, that woman was not able to cause a rift between me and my mother..."
"Now she attends upon him with great care," he said. Having heard his words, the Teacher said, "Upāsaka, for the time being you did not follow her word;
however, in the past, because of her word, you cast out your mother and, relying on me, brought her back home again and looked after her. When requested by him, he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the son of a certain family, upon his father’s death, became a guardian deity to his mother and attended to her according to the same procedure already described;
all this is to be detailed in the manner explained below. [He thought: "I cannot live with such an ill-omened woman; either she must leave the house..."
When she said, "Live here, or let me go," he took her words to heart and said to his mother, "The fault is yours alone.
He said, "Mother, you constantly cause quarrels in this house; leave here and live wherever else you please.
She replied, "Very well," and weeping, she departed. Relying on a prosperous family, she worked for wages.
She made her living with great hardship. When she had departed from her mother-in-law’s house, her daughter-in-law became pregnant.
Thinking, “While that ill-omened woman lived in the house, I could not even conceive;
now I have conceived,” she went about telling her husband and her neighbors.
Later, having given birth to a son, she said to her husband, "While your mother was living in our house, I did not obtain a son;
now I have obtained one. By this reason also, you should know her ill-omened nature.
The other woman, hearing that she had indeed obtained a son at the time she was being expelled, thought, "Surely the Dhamma must have perished in this world."
"For if Dhamma were not dead, those who beat their mother and cast her out would not obtain a son, nor would they live in happiness;
I shall give a funeral meal for Dhamma. One day, taking sesame flour, rice, a cooking pot, and a ladle, she went to the raw charnel ground and built a hearth with three human heads.
Having prepared the fire and kindled it, he went down into the water, bathed including his head, put on a lower garment, rinsed his mouth, and went to the hearth.
There he loosened his hair and began to wash the rice. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of the gods.
For Bodhisattas are indeed vigilant; at that moment, he surveyed the world.
Seeing him fallen into suffering and wishing to give the funeral meal for the Dhamma under the impression that "the Dhamma has died," [the Bodhisatta] thought, "Today I shall show my power.

Acting as if he were traveling along the high road in the guise of a brahmin, he saw him, stepped off the path, stood before him, and said: "Mother, there are no such things as people cooking food in a cemetery."
Addressing her thus, "What will you do here with this cooked sesame-rice? and initiating the conversation, he spoke the first verse:
"Clad in white garments, with pure and wet hair, Kaccānā, why are you leaning over the pot?
Why are you washing husked sesame seeds and rice? For what reason will there be sesame-rice?"
In this context, "Kaccānī" is an address by means of her clan name. "Having placed it on the oven" means having set it upon a cooking pot shaped like a human head.
"Hehi" means: "For what purpose will this sesame-rice be? Will you eat it yourself, or is there some other reason?"
Then, explaining it to him, she spoke this second verse:
“O Brahmin, this is not for the sake of food; this sesame-rice is well-prepared.
Today there is an abundance of the Dharma for one who has died; I shall prepare it in the midst of the cemetery.”

In this context, "Dhamma" refers both to the duty of honoring one's elders and the Dhamma of the threefold good conduct. "Tassa pahuttamajjā" means: "I shall perform this funeral meal for that Dhamma.
Then Sakka spoke the third verse:
"Having investigated, Kaccāna, do what ought to be done. What Dhamma has passed away? Who indeed has instructed you?"
“The thousand-eyed one of incomparable power—the excellent Dhamma never dies.

Therein, *anuvicca* means having investigated and understood. *Ko nu taveva saṃsī* means “Who indeed has told this to you? By saying *sahassanetto*, he spoke thus while presenting himself as the excellent Dhamma, the supreme Dhamma.
Having heard those words, she recited the other two verses:
“O Brahmā, my confidence in this matter is firm; the Dhamma is known to me, and I have no doubt here.
Those who were indeed wicked have now become happy.
For my daughter-in-law was barren; she killed me and gave birth to a son.”
"She is now the mistress of the entire family, while I am cast out alone.
In this context, "firm authority" (*daḷhappamāṇa*) means: "O Brahmin, my authority here is firm, stable, and beyond doubt," she says.
"Whosoever" (*ye ye*)—she speaks thus, pointing out the reason for his state of mind. "Having struck" (*vadhitvāna*) means having beaten and driven out.
"Cast away," she said, "I dwell here alone, having been abandoned and left without a protector.
Then Sakka spoke the sixth verse:
"I live, I am not dead; I have come here for your very sake."
“Having killed her, I shall bring forth a son; together with that son, I will reduce her to ashes.
In this context, *vo* is merely a particle.
Having heard this, the other said: “Shame on me! What have I said? I shall provide the means for my granddaughter not to die,” and she spoke the seventh verse:
“If this is what pleases you, O King of Gods, it is for my sake alone that you have come here;
may I, my son, my daughter-in-law, and my grandson dwell together in our home in mutual harmony.
Then Sakka spoke this eighth verse to her:
“And if this is pleasing to you, Kātiyāni—even though you have been struck, you do not abandon the Dhamma.
You, your son, your daughter-in-law, and your grandson—may you dwell together in the home in harmony.

Therein, “even though you have been struck” means: even if you were beaten or driven out, if you do not abandon your loving-kindness toward your children, then let it be as you wish; for I am pleased with this virtue of yours.
Having spoken thus, Sakka, adorned and prepared, stood in the sky by his own supernatural power and said, "Do not fear;
through my power, your son and daughter-in-law will come, apologize to you on the way, and take you with them.
Be heedful. Having said this, he returned to his own abode. And they too, through the power of Sakka—
Recalling her virtues, they asked the people within the village, "Where is our mother?
Upon hearing that she had gone toward the cemetery, they set out on the path to the cemetery, crying out, "Mother! Mother!
As soon as they saw her, they fell at her feet and asked for her forgiveness, saying, "Mother, please forgive our fault. She too took her grandchildren [into her embrace]. Thus, they were reconciled.
