Having gone home, from that time forth they lived in harmony.
“Kātiyānī lived in her house in mutual affection with her daughter-in-law;
her son and grandson waited upon them, for she was protected by Devānaminda.”
This is the verse of the Fully Enlightened One.
Therein, "Sā Kātyāyanī, O monks," means she was of the Kaccāna clan. "Taken up by Devānaminda" means being supported by Sakka, the Lord of Devas; through his power, they lived in harmony.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths—
Thus that lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the one who supported his mother was the present supporter of his mother;
his wife at that time was indeed his wife; and Sakka was none other than myself.
This is the first commentary on the Kaccāni-jātaka.
[418] 2. The Commentary on the Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka.

"This was formerly called a low-lying place," etc. While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher spoke this concerning the terrifying, indistinguishable sound heard by the King of Kosala at the hour of midnight. The story is found below in the Lohakumbhi Jātaka.
It is exactly as previously described. Here, however, when the king said, "Venerable sir, having heard these sounds, what will become of me?", the Teacher replied:
"Do not fear, Great King; no obstacle shall arise for you because of hearing these.
For it is not only you alone, Great King, who has heard such terrifying, inseparable sounds; kings of the past also [heard them]."
"Having heard such a sound, and having accepted the advice of the brahmins who desired to perform the sacrifice of all fourfold animals,

they released the beings previously seized for the purpose of the sacrifice after hearing the words of the wise men, and caused the proclamation of the festival drums (māghātabheri) to be sounded throughout the city.
Having said this, being requested by him, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family possessing a wealth of eight hundred million.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the arts at Takkasilā;
and after his parents passed away, he performed the "jewel-inspection" ceremony, distributed his entire fortune through acts of generosity, renounced sensual pleasures, and entered the Himalayas.

Having gone forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*) and attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), he later traveled through the inhabited world for the sake of partaking of salt and sour gruel.

Upon reaching Bārāṇasī, he stayed in the royal park. At that time, while the King of Bārāṇasī was seated upon his magnificent couch at the hour of midnight, he heard eight sounds: first, those from the vicinity of the royal palace within the park.
One heron made a sound; while that sound had not yet ceased, a female crow living in the gateway of the elephant stable made a sound;
thirdly, a wood-boring insect dwelling in the pillar of the royal palace made a sound;
fourthly, a cuckoo being raised in the royal palace made a sound; fifthly, a deer being raised right there made a sound.
The sixth time, right there, the monkey Posāvaniya made a sound; the seventh time, right there, the kinnara Posāvaniya made a sound;
and the eighth time, while that sound was still continuing, a Paccekabuddha passing by the royal palace on his way to the park made a sound while uttering an udāna.
Having heard these eight sounds, the King of Bārāṇasī was terrified and trembling; on the following day, he questioned the brahmins.
The brahmins said, "A calamity will befall you, Great King; we shall perform a sacrifice of all fourfold animals.
When the king gave his permission, saying, "Do as you please," they departed from the royal palace in high spirits and began the sacrificial rites.
Then a young brahmin student, wise and competent, who was a pupil of the eldest of those sacrificers, said to his teacher:
"Teacher, do not perform such a cruel, harsh, and unpleasant act that will bring destruction upon many beings.
"Dear son, what do you know? Even if there is nothing else at all, there is fish and meat."
“Then we shall be able to eat as much as we like. “Teacher, do not perform an action that will cause you to be reborn in hell on account of your belly,” he said.
Upon hearing this, the other brahmins became angry with him, thinking, “This man is creating an obstacle to our gain.
Out of fear of them, the young man said, “In that case, you yourselves must find a way to eat fish and meat.”
Having spoken thus and departed, he went to the royal park seeking a righteous ascetic or brahmin capable of dissuading the king outside the city.
Finding the Bodhisatta there, he paid homage to him and said, "Venerable sir, do you have no compassion for living beings?
The king is having many beings slaughtered to perform a sacrifice; why do you not release the great multitude from their bonds?"
“It is not proper to do so,” he said. “Young man, in this matter the king does not know us, nor do we know the king.
“But, venerable sir, do you know how the sounds heard by the king were produced? “Yes, I know. “If you know, why did you not tell the king?
“Young man, what can be done? One cannot tie a horn upon one’s forehead and say, ‘I know.’”
“I shall go; if he comes here and asks me, I will explain.
The young brahmin went quickly to the royal palace, and when asked, “What is it, dear son?
he replied, “Great King, there is a certain ascetic who knows how sounds are produced; he is sitting on the auspicious stone in your park, thinking, ‘If he asks me, ...’”
"I shall tell you," he said; "it is fitting to go and ask him. The king went there in haste, paid homage to the ascetic, and after exchanging greetings, sat down and asked:
"Is it true, venerable sir, that you know the origin of the sounds I have heard?
"Yes, Great King," he replied. "In that case, please explain it to me. "Great King,..."
"Because you have heard this, no obstacle whatsoever exists for you;
however, in that ancient park there is a certain crane who, not finding food and overcome by hunger, uttered his first cry.
Having discerned that action of his through his own knowledge, he spoke the first verse:
“This place was formerly said to be sloping toward the water, abundant with fish and full of great waters;
it was the dwelling of the king of crocodiles, my ancestral home.
Let us now subsist here on frogs; let us not abandon our own abode.”
In this context, "this" refers to the Mangala lotus pond. For formerly, when water was poured in with water-pots, it was full of water and abounded in fish;
but now, because the supply of water has been cut off, it has become devoid of much water.
"We shall live today on mere frogs"—thus we, not finding any fish today, shall subsist on nothing more than frogs. Thus they spoke.
"Even though we were oppressed by hunger, we did not leave our dwelling place.
Thus, Great King, that crane, oppressed by hunger, made a sound.
If you wish to free him from that hunger, have that park cleaned and fill the lotus pond with water. The king commanded a minister to have it done accordingly.

"But regarding the elephant-stable archway, O Great King, a single female crow living there raised a second cry out of grief for her own offspring; even from that, you have no fear," he said, and spoke the second verse:
"Who, having eyes, will break the bonds of the unvirtuous one?
Who will bring safety to my chicks and my nest?"
Having said this, he asked, "Great King, what is the name of that young elephant in your elephant stable?
"His name is Bandharo, venerable sir. "Is he blind in one eye, Great King? "Yes, venerable sir.
"Great King, a female crow has built a nest on the gate-arch of your elephant stable and laid her eggs there. Those eggs have hatched, and there are now young crows."
Having gone out, the elephant-keeper, mounting his elephant, would strike even her with a goad as she was entering and leaving the stable, and he would even destroy her nesting place.
Oppressed by that suffering, she spoke thus, entreating him to spare her eyes:
"If you have a heart of loving-kindness toward this female crow, release her."
“Summon him and forbid him from destroying the nests. The king summoned him, rebuked him, stripped him of his rank, and gave that elephant to another.
“Furthermore, O Great King, a certain wood-boring insect dwells in the pinnacle of your palace. It eats the softwood there, and—”
"When that [food] was exhausted, he was unable to eat the heartwood; finding no food and being unable even to depart, he uttered lamentations and made a third sound.
You have no fear from that either," he said, and having discerned his actions with his own knowledge, he spoke the third verse:
“All the softwood has been consumed, as far as its extent reached;
O Great King, when its food is exhausted, the wood-boring beetle finds no delight in the heartwood.
In this context, “as far as its extent reached” means that all of that softwood, up to the point where it ended, has been eaten away.
“He does not find delight,” [the monk] said. “Great King, that creature, having emerged from there and seeing no place to go, is lamenting;
have him taken out. The king gave orders to a man and had him removed by a stratagem.
“But in your residence, Great King, is there a female cuckoo that lays eggs? “There is, venerable sir. “Great King, [that creature is she].”
"Remembering the grove where she had previously lived, she became longing and uttered a fourth cry, saying:
'When indeed shall I be released from this cage and go to that delightful grove? Therein too, you have nothing to fear.
Having said this, he recited the fourth verse:
“Surely, having gone from here, released from the king’s residence, I shall delight myself, dwelling in the branches of trees.

In this context, “dwelling in the branches of trees” means making her own home among the well-flowered branches of the trees. Having spoken thus, he said, “The cuckoo is weary, Great King; release her. The king did so.
“But in your residence, Great King, there is a deer that must be raised,” he asked. “There is, venerable sir,” he replied.
“Great King, that leader of the herd, longing for his own mate due to the influence of defilement, uttered a fifth cry;
even from that, you have no fear. Having said this, he recited the fifth verse:
“Thus, having departed from here and being released from the king’s dwelling, I shall drink the first water and go at the head of the herd.

In this context, *aggodakāni* means *agga-udakāni*: the first water, not yet drunk by other deer, the water that has not been left behind—thinking, “When indeed shall I drink while going at the head of the herd?”
The Great Being, having released that deer as well, asked, "But do you have a pet monkey in your residence, Your Majesty?
When he replied, "There is one, Bhante," he said, "That one too, Your Majesty, was a leader of a troop wandering in the Himalayan regions, infatuated with sensual desires;
he was brought here by a hunter named Bharata, and now—"
“Having become weary [of this life], you wished to go back to that very place and uttered a sixth cry; even from that, there is no fear for you.
Having said this, he spoke the sixth verse:
“Me, who am completely devoted to sensual pleasures, addicted to desires and infatuated with them...”
“The hunter Bharata has brought him;
may it be well with you, O Bahika!”—therein, “Bahika” means one who dwells in the Bahika country. “May it be well with you”—the monkey spoke these words, meaning, “May it be well with you;
please release him. Having had that monkey released, the Great Being said: “But in your palace, O Great King, there is a Kinnarī to be raised…”
Having asked, "Is there?", and being told, "There is," [the king said], "Great King, he, distressed by defilements, cried out as he recollected the virtues his kinnarī had performed for him.
For one day, he had climbed with her to the peak of a lofty mountain.
There, while they were gathering and adorning themselves with various flowers endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor, the sun set."
They did not notice it, and as they were descending after the sun had set, darkness fell.
Thereupon the Kinnarī said to him, “Lord, darkness prevails; descend with care so that you do not stumble,” and taking him by the hand, she helped him down.
He made a sound because he remembered her words, but even from that there was no danger for them.
Having determined that cause through the power of his own knowledge and making it manifest, he spoke the seventh verse:
“In this blinding darkness, upon the high mountain peak;
May she, with her soft and gentle voice, not let my foot stumble on the stone.”
In that context, "in the blinding darkness" (*andhakāratimisāya*) means in the gloom that causes blindness. "Tall" (*tuṅge*) means sharp.
"With gentle and soft words" (*saṇhena mudunā*) means with polished and mild speech. "Do not stumble on my foot" (*mā pādaṃ khali yasmani*):
the letter *ya* is included here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*byañjanasandhi*). This is what is meant: that Kinnarī addressed me with gentle and soft words, saying, "Master, be heedful..."

"Be careful; do not let your foot slip on the stone. Descend in such a way that your foot, having stepped out, does not stumble upon the rock," he said, and taking him by the hand, he helped him down.
Thus, after the Great Being had explained the reason for the sound made by the Kinnara and caused him to release it, [he said], "Great King, the eighth..."
A cry of exultation arose. It is said that in the Nandamūlaka Cave, a certain Paccekabuddha, knowing that the constituent forces of his own life were exhausted, thought:
"I shall go to the path of men and attain final Nibbāna in the royal park of the King of Bārāṇasī;
there, people will perform the enshrinement of my remains, hold a great festival, and by making offerings to my relics, they will fulfill the path to heaven."
“Coming by means of the power of psychic success (*iddhi*), when he reached the summit of your palace,
he set down his physical burden and uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) illustrating his entry into the city of Nibbāna,” he said, reciting the verse spoken by the Paccekabuddha:
“Without doubt, having seen the end of birth, I shall not again enter a womb.”
“This is my final, last lying-in; my wandering-on in saṃsāra for renewed existence has been exhausted.
The meaning of this is: because I have seen Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the end of birth, I am a seer of the end of birth;
without doubt, I shall not again enter a lying-in chamber. This is my final birth, my last lying-in.
“The cycle of existence, consisting of the succession of aggregates that leads to renewed becoming, has been exhausted for me.
Having uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), the Great Being arrived at this park-grove and attained final *parinibbāna* at the foot of a single, beautifully blossoming *sāla* tree.
“Come, Great King, let us perform the funeral rites for him,” he said to the king.
Having taken [the body], he went to the place where the Paccekabuddha had attained final Nibbāna and showed the physical remains to him.
Upon seeing the remains, the king, together with his army, honored them with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.

Relying on the Bodhisatta’s words, he abolished the sacrifice, granted the gift of life to all beings, caused the proclamation of the *māghāta* drum throughout the city, and for seven days held a grand festival of celebration.
Having played and honored the body of the Paccekabuddha with great ceremony upon the pyre of all kinds of perfumes, he enshrined the relics at a crossroads and erected a stupa.
The Bodhisatta, too, having taught the Dhamma to the king and exhorted him, saying, “Be heedful,” entered the Himālaya mountains;
there, having practiced the preliminary exercises for the sublime abidings (brahmavihāras), he remained without falling away from his meditative absorption.
He became one whose ultimate goal was the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Great King, there is no obstacle for you whatsoever on account of hearing that sound.
He then had the sacrifice withdrawn and caused the gift of life to be granted, saying, "Give back the lives of the great multitude!"
Having caused the drum of the Dhamma to be beaten throughout the city and having taught the Dhamma, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda;
the young brahmin was Sāriputta; and the ascetic was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka.
[419] 3. The Commentary on the Sulasā Jātaka: "This golden armlet.
This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a female slave of Anāthapiṇḍika.
It is said that on a festival day, she was going to the park together with a group of female slaves.
She asked her mistress, Queen Puññalakkhaṇā, for an ornament. The queen gave her an ornament worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Having adorned herself with it, she entered the park together with a group of female slaves.
Then, a certain thief, conceiving a greedy desire for her ornament, thought, "I shall kill this woman and take the ornament," and [approached] her.
Conversing with her, he went to the garden and gave her fish, meat, liquor, and other such things. Thinking, "He gives these out of defilement," she accepted them.
After they had enjoyed themselves at the garden festival, she rose during the evening when the group of female servants was lying down, and for the sake of testing him, she went into his presence.
He said, "Bhadde, this place is not secluded; go a little further ahead."
"Let us go," he said. Hearing this, the other thought, "It is possible to perform a secret act in this place;
however, this man will undoubtedly wish to kill me and take my jewelry. Very well, I shall teach him a lesson.
Having thought this, she said, "Husband, my body is parched with intoxication from the liquor; give me some water to drink first."
Having led him to a well, she said, "Pour water for me from here," and gave him a rope and a jar. The robber lowered the rope into the well;

then, as he leaned over to pour out the water, the very powerful female slave struck him on both sides with a mallet and threw him into the well, saying, "You will not die by this much alone," and placed a large brick upon his head.

She struck him. He met his death right there. She too, having entered the city and giving the jewelry to her mistress, said, "Today I have died because of this jewelry," and related the whole incident.
She in turn told Anāthapiṇḍika, and Anāthapiṇḍika told the Tathāgata. The Teacher said, "Indeed, not..."
“Householder, it is not only now that this slave girl is endowed with situational wisdom (*ṭhānuppattikā paññā*); she was endowed with it even in the past.
And it is not only now that she killed him; she would have killed him even before. Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past:
“In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there was a city beauty named Sulasā, who had a retinue of five hundred beautiful slave girls.”
He would travel at night with a thousand [men]. In that very city, there was a thief named Sattuka who possessed the strength of an elephant;
entering noble houses during the night, he plundered them according to his whim. The citizens gathered together and complained to the king.
The king, having ordered the city guardian to station troops here and there, had the thief captured.
“Cut off his head! he said. They bound him hand and foot, lashed him with whips at every four-way intersection, and led him to the place of execution.
Hearing that “a thief has been captured,” the entire city was thrown into commotion.
At that time, Sulasā, standing at a window looking down the street, saw him; her heart became bound to him, and she thought, “If this man who has been seized as a thief...”

Thinking, "I shall be able to release him; without committing this defiled deed, I will live in harmony with him," she sent a thousand pieces of money to the city watchman in the same manner as described below in the Kaṇavera Jātaka.
Having released him, she lived in harmony with him, exchanging friendly greetings. After three or four months, the robber—
After some time, he thought: "I will not be able to remain in this very place; it is also impossible to flee empty-handed.
Sulasa’s jewelry is worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]; I shall kill Sulasa and take this. Then, one day, he said to her:
"My dear, when I was being led away by the king's men, on the summit of such-and-such a mountain..."
“I promised to perform an offering for the tree deity; since she has not received that offering, she makes me afraid.
Let us make an offering to her. “Very well, my lord; prepare it and send it,” [she replied]. “My dear, it is not right to simply send it.
Both of us, adorned with all our ornaments and accompanied by a large retinue, shall go and give it to her. “Very well, my lord; let us do so.”
Then, having had her do so and reached the foot of the mountain, he said: "My dear, when the great multitude sees us, the deities will not accept the offering;

let us both ascend together and present it. Having been agreed by her with the words "Very well," he had her lift up that offering-bowl, and himself, equipped with his five weapons, ascended to the summit of the mountain.
Having climbed up, he stood leaning against a tree at the foot of a *jātaka* tree near a precipice one *sataporisa* high.
After having a sacrificial vessel set down, he said, "Bhadde, I have not come for the sake of a ritual offering; rather, I have come thinking that I shall kill you, take your ornaments, and depart.
Take off your ornaments and make them into a bundle with your upper garment. She replied, "My lord," and so on.
"Why did you kill me? "For the sake of wealth. "My lord, remember the service I performed for you:
when you were being led away bound, I exchanged you for the merchant's son and gave him much wealth so that you obtained your life.
Even though I receive a thousand pieces daily, I do not look upon another man. Do not kill me, who has been so helpful to you!"
“I will give you much wealth, and I shall become your slave,” she said, requesting with the first verse:
“This golden armlet, and many pearls and beryl gems—
take all of it, O blessed one, and declare me to be your slave.”
In this context, *kāyūra* refers to an armlet, an ornament worn on the neck. *Sāvaya* means that he makes her announce it in the midst of the great crowd and takes her as a slave.
Then Sattuka said:
“Take it off, O auspicious lady; do not lament so bitterly.”
"And I do not recall bringing wealth here without having killed [someone].
When she had spoken this second verse in accordance with her own inclination, Sulasā, finding the immediate opportunity, thought:
"This thief will not spare my life; by some means I must throw him into the precipice first, so that he meets his death."
Thinking, "I shall cause him to fall," he spoke these two verses:
"Since I can remember myself, since I have attained the state of discernment,
I do not recall anyone dearer to me than you."
“Come, I shall embrace you and perform the circumambulation;
for now there will never again be a meeting between me and you.
Not understanding her intention, Sattuka said, “Very well, my dear, come and embrace me. Sulasā—
Having circumambulated him three times and embraced him, she said, "Now, my lord, I shall pay homage to you from all four sides.
Placing her head upon the back of his feet, she paid homage at his side;

then, having gone to his rear side as if still paying homage, the courtesan Nāgabalā seized the thief by both hind legs, turned him upside down with his head below, and [threw him] a hundred cubits high.
He threw him into hell. There, having been reduced to a mere pulp, he died.
Seeing that deed, a deity reborn on the mountain peak spoke these verses:
“Not in all places is a man wise;”
A woman, too, can be wise, discerning in every circumstance.
For it is not the case that a man alone is wise in all situations;
a woman, too, can be wise, quickly considering what is beneficial.
“Swiftly and quickly indeed, Sulasā aimed her weapon at what was near;
she slew Sattuka as a hunter slays a deer with a full-stretched bow.
But he who does not quickly realize a matter that has arisen—”
Thus the dull-witted one is slain, like a thief in a mountain cave.
But he who quickly understands a matter as it arises is released from the oppression of his enemies,
just as Sulasā was from the enemy Sattu.
"In this matter she is wise" means that the woman is wise and discerning in various respects;
or rather, the woman is both wise and discerning in various respects. "Quickly considering the meaning" means quickly and swiftly considering the meaning.
"Truly without delay" means indeed not slow. "And quickly" means in no long time. "In what is near..."
"She thought" means that while standing right there, she contemplated a means for his death. "With a full bow" means with a bow drawn to its full extent.
This is what is meant: just as a skilled deer-hunter quickly kills a deer when his bow is drawn with an arrow, so did Sulasā kill Sattuka.
"A warrior" refers to one who [fights] in this world of beings. "He understands" means he knows. "As if toward Sattuka" means...
"Like *sattuka* flowers; just as the *sulasā* jasmine is released, so too is he released—this is the meaning.

Thus, having slain the thief and descended from the mountain, Sulasā went into the presence of her own attendants. When asked, "Where is my noble son? she said, "Do not ask about him," and mounting her chariot, she entered the city itself.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, those two were these very same persons, while the deity was none other than myself."
The third *Jātaka* commentary, the *Sulasājātakavaṇṇanā*.
[420] 4. The *Sumaṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā*:

"When one is greatly provoked..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, concerning the *Rājovādasutta*. At that time, however, being requested by the king, the Teacher related a past event.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity, he ascended the throne upon his father’s passing and distributed great alms.
He had a park-keeper named Sumaṅgala. Then, a certain Paccekabuddha, having departed from the Nandamūlaka mountain cave, set out on a journey.
While wandering, he reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in a park; on the following day, he entered the city for alms.
The king, seeing him, with a mind full of faith, paid homage to him, escorted him up to the palace, and had him sit upon the royal throne.
After serving him with various kinds of choice foods and delicacies and hearing his words of thanksgiving, the king, being inspired with faith, [invited him] to dwell in his own park.

Having obtained his promise and led him into the garden, the king himself went there after breakfast, arranged the night-quarters, day-quarters, and other facilities, and appointed a park-keeper named Sumaṅgala as an attendant; then he entered the city.
From that time on, the Paccekabuddha resided there for a long period, eating regularly at the royal palace, while Sumaṅgala served him with great care.
Then one day, the Paccekabuddha addressed Sumaṅgala, saying, "I shall stay for a few days depending on a certain village and then return;
inform the king. Having said this, he departed. Sumaṅgala also informed the king.
After staying there for a few days, the Paccekabuddha returned to that garden in the evening when the sun had set.
Sumaṅgala, unaware of his arrival, went to his own home.
The Paccekabuddha, having put away his bowl and robe and walked a short distance for exercise, sat down on a stone slab. On that day, however, guests had come to the gardener’s house.
For the sake of curry and condiments, he [said to them], "In the garden there is a deer who has attained fearlessness..."
Thinking, "I shall kill him," he took his bow, went to the park, and while searching for game, he saw the Paccekabuddha.
Mistaking him for a large deer, he fixed an arrow and shot him. The Paccekabuddha uncovered his head and said, "Sumaṅgala.
Overcome with spiritual urgency, he prostrated himself and said, "Venerable Sir, not knowing that you had come, I thought [you were] a 'deer'..."
Having said, "I pierced you through ignorance; forgive me," and being told, "Let it be now, what will you do?
Come, pull out the arrow and take it," he prostrated himself and pulled out the arrow. Great pain arose.
The Paccekabuddha attained final nibbāna right there. The park keeper, thinking, "If the king finds out, he will destroy us," took his wife and children and departed from that very place.
He fled. At that very moment, through the supernatural power of the deities, the entire city broke into a single tumultuous outcry, crying, "The Paccekabuddha has passed away!
On the following day, people went to the park, and seeing the Paccekabuddha there, they told the king, "The park keeper killed the Paccekabuddha and fled.
The king, accompanied by a great retinue, went to the park and [remained] for seven days.
Having performed the funeral rites for the body with great honor, he cremated it, took the relics, and having erected a cetiya, he ruled the kingdom righteously while making offerings there.
Sumaṅgala, too, after spending one year, thinking, "I shall learn the king's mind," returned;
seeing a certain minister, he said to him, "Find out the king's mind regarding me. The minister then went into the presence of the king.
Having gone there, he spoke of his virtues. The king acted as if he had not heard him. Without saying anything further, he described the king’s displeasure to Sumaṅgala.
In the second year, he came again and did exactly the same, yet the king remained silent.
In the third year, he came bringing his wife and children with him. The minister, perceiving that the king’s mind had become softened, [placed him] at the palace gate.
He told the king everything except for his own role in the matter.
The king summoned him, offered him hospitality, and asked, "Sumaṅgala, why did you kill my field of merit, the Paccekabuddha?
He replied, "Your Majesty, I did not kill the Paccekabuddha with the intention of killing him; rather, for this specific reason, I did this..."
He related that occurrence, saying, "He did it. Then the king, having comforted him with the words, "In that case, do not be afraid," made him the garden-keeper once again.
Then that minister asked him, "Your Majesty, why is it that although you heard of Sumaṅgala’s virtue on two occasions..."
“Why did he not say anything at all, yet upon hearing him for the third time, summoned him and showed him compassion?
The king replied, “Dear son, it is not fitting for a king who is angry to act impulsively; therefore, I remained silent before.
On the third occasion, however, Sumaṅgala perceived the softness of my heart and had him summoned. Thus he explained the king’s conduct.
While speaking, he uttered these verses:
“Reflecting, ‘I am greatly provoked,’ a lord should not yet inflict punishment;
for it is improper for him to cause intense suffering to another for what is not a fit occasion.”
“When one knows that confidence resides within oneself, one may apply another’s transgression for the sake of their welfare;
having personally considered, ‘This is for their benefit,’ one should then impose a punishment proportionate to it.
One who, being free from delusion, guides what is right and wrong, neither burns others nor himself.”
He who wields the rod as a lord in this world, protected by his reputation, does not fall from his glory.
But those Khattiyas who act without reflection, who mete out punishment impulsively and deludedly—they, joined with ill-repute, lose their lives;
even when released from here, they go to a state of misery.
“Those who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones are unsurpassed in speech, mind, and deed;
established in peace, gentleness, and concentration, such as these traverse both worlds.
‘I am a king, the lord of men and princes; even when I am angry, I restrain myself.’”
“Restraining such people, I impose punishment out of reasoned compassion.
In this context, *avekkhiyāna* means having looked upon and understood. This is what is meant:
“Dear one, a king who is a lord of the earth, knowing ‘I am greatly enraged and overcome by powerful anger,’ [imposes] punishment consisting of the eight bases and so forth.”
One should not be deferential toward another, nor should one act [in such a way]. Why is that?

For when angry, having made [the matter] eightfold or sixteenfold, and without cause or reason, he would incite intense and powerful sufferings for another—sufferings unbecoming of his own royal status—by saying, "Bring this much! or "Do this to him!"
"Yato" means when. This is what is intended: when the king should perceive that confidence has arisen in another toward himself, he should then direct and examine the other's transgression.
Directing it in this way—having personally verified for himself, "This indeed is the matter here; this is his fault"—he [should deal] with that offender.
If one takes eight coins as the basis for the offense, there are eight [denominations]; if one takes sixteen coins as the basis for the offense, there are sixteen.
For one who takes [the coins], he should impose, establish, and carry out a punishment that is equal and appropriate to the fault committed.
"Uninfatuated" means being uninfatuated and unsubdued by the defilements such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth, and thus one who leads [others] according to what is right and what is wrong.

He investigates; thus he neither burns others nor himself. For one who, through desire and other such motives, inflicts punishment without cause, burns, consumes, and oppresses others with that punishment, and likewise burns himself by the evil resulting from that source.
But this person neither burns others nor himself. He who, being the wielder of the rod here, is the lord—this is the one who [investigates].
The king, lord of the earth, who here in the world of beings administers punishment appropriate to the offense, is a wielder of the rod.
He is "protected by his fair reputation" (vaṇṇagutta), meaning he is guarded and protected by the reputation for his virtues and the reputation for his glory;
thus, through his majesty, he does not fall away nor does he decline. "Those joined with ill-repute perish" means that unrighteous, greedy kings, being possessed of ill-repute, lose their lives.

"And those who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones" refers to those kings who take pleasure in the tenfold duties of a king (rājadhamma) as proclaimed by the noble ones who are themselves righteous kings.
"They are unsurpassed" means they are supreme—the eldest—in respect of these three: speech, mind, and action.

"They are established in peace, gentleness, and concentration" means that through the abandonment of wrong courses, they are established in the peace of the defilements [through tranquility] and in what is termed virtuous conduct.
Dharmic kings are established and grounded in both gentleness and one-pointed concentration.
Having ruled their kingdom according to the Dharma, they proceed from the world of humans to the world of devas, and from the world of devas to the world of humans;
thus they proceed only between these two worlds, and are not reborn in the hells or other lower realms. *Narapamadānaṃ* means of both men and women.

“I establish myself” means: even when angry, I do not act out of anger, but rather I establish myself in the very Dhamma established by former kings as the principle; I do not violate the law of legal judgment.
When the king had thus described his own virtues with these six verses, the entire royal assembly was delighted, [saying]: “This perfection of virtue, conduct, and qualities...”
“They are indeed worthy of you,” they said, praising the virtues of the king.
But at the conclusion of the assembly’s speech, Sumaṅgala rose, paid homage to the king, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke three verses in praise of him:
“O Khattiya, lord of men, may glory (*sirī*) and fortune (*lakkhī*) never forsake you at any time! ... [the rest of the verses follow] ...”
Free from anger, with a mind always serene and free from affliction, may you protect [the earth] for a hundred years.
O Kṣatriya, endowed with these virtues—established in the conduct of the noble, easy to speak to, and free from anger—rule the earth happily and without oppression;
and even after departing from here, go to a happy destination.

“Thus, by means of well-guided, well-spoken Dhamma, through the method of the right way, one should extinguish the agitated masses of people, just as a great cloud extinguishes the earth with its water.
In this context, *sirī* and *lakkhī* refer to the excellence of one’s retinue and wisdom, respectively. *Anīgho* means being free from suffering.

"Endowed with the khattiya [virtues]" means one who is endowed with the khattiya; or this reading may be "upeto khattiya. "Abiding in the conduct of the noble ones" means established in the conduct of the noble ones (*ṭhitāriyavatti*);

"conduct of the noble ones" refers to the ancient royal conduct known as the ten duties of a king (*dasarājadhamma*). Because he is firmly established therein, the meaning is "having become one who abides in the duties of a king.
"Rule the earth without oppression" means rule the earth without causing oppression; or this reading may be *anuppīḷa pasāsa mediniñ ca*.
By *sunītena*: by a good policy, by a proper means. By *dhammena*: by the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).

By *ñāyena*: this is a synonym for the preceding term. By *upāyena*: by skill in means (*upāyakosalla*). A king who rules righteously, leading and guiding [his people], is a "righteous king" (*dhammikarājā*).
He "quenches" (*nibbāpeti*) by removing physical and mental suffering and distress through this practice.

He spoke thus to show that even a great multitude agitated by physical and mental suffering could be extinguished—just as a great cloud extinguishes the earth with its water—and that you, too, should extinguish it in the same way.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching as an exhortation to the King of Kosala, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Paccekabuddha who had attained Parinibbāna was Ānanda; Sumaṅgala was I myself, and the king was none other than I."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Sumaṅgala Jātaka. [421] 5.
The Commentary on the Gaṅgamāla Jātaka. "Aṅgārajātā" (Born of Embers):
This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the performance of the Uposatha ceremony. For one day...
The Teacher addressed the lay followers observing the Uposatha: “Lay followers, it is well done by you who observe the Uposatha;
you should give gifts, guard your virtue, refrain from anger, cultivate loving-kindness, and dwell in the observance of the Uposatha.
For in the past, ancient wise men attained great glory by relying on even a single half-Uposatha practice.”
Having spoken thus, being requested by them, he related a past event.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there lived in that city a merchant named Suciparivāra, who possessed a fortune of eight hundred million and delighted in meritorious deeds such as giving. His sons, wife, and attendants—even down to...
In that house, all the cowherds observed the Uposatha on six days of every month.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family and lived in hardship, working for wages.
Thinking, "I shall go to work," he went to that man's house, paid his respects, and stood to one side. When asked, "Why have you come? he replied, "To work for you in your house."

“...for the purpose of working for wages,” he said. On the very day other wage-earners arrived, the merchant told them, “Those who work in this house must observe their virtue; you may work provided you are able to guard your virtue.
However, without giving any indication regarding the Bodhisatta’s observance of virtue, he said, “Very well, dear son, [work] for your own wages.”
“Having understood this, perform your work,” he said. From that time forth, becoming obedient, he gave his breast [as a pledge], disregarded his own exhaustion, and performed all of his duties;
going to the workplace at dawn, he returned in the evening.
Then one day, they proclaimed a festival in the city. The great merchant addressed a female slave, saying, “Today is the Uposatha day.”
“Cook food for the workers early in the morning and give it to them; having eaten at an early hour, they will observe the Uposatha.
The Bodhisatta rose early and went to his work, but no one informed him that today was the Uposatha day.
The other workers, having eaten early, observed the Uposatha. The merchant, too—
Together with his wife, children, and retinue, he observed the Uposatha.

All those observing the Uposatha went to their respective dwelling places and sat reflecting upon their moral precepts (*sīla*). Having worked all day long, the Bodhisatta returned at the time of sunset.
Then, the cook gave him water for washing his hands, increased the portion of rice in his bowl, and presented it to him.
The Bodhisatta asked, "On other days there is a great noise at this hour; where have they gone today?
"They have all undertaken the Uposatha and gone to their respective dwelling places," he was told. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought:
"I shall not continue to live as the sole immoral one among so many virtuous people. Now—"
"Once the factors of the Uposatha have been resolved upon, does the Uposatha ritual take place or not? He went and asked the merchant.
Then the merchant said to him, "Dear son, because it was not resolved upon early in the morning, the entire Uposatha ritual does not take place; however, half of the Uposatha ritual does take place.
Thinking, "Let even this much suffice," he undertook the moral precepts in the presence of the merchant and resolved upon the Uposatha ritual.
Having entered his own dwelling place, he lay down reflecting upon his moral virtue (*sīla*).
Then, because he had gone without food for the entire day, immediately following the final watch of the night, pains like the thrusting of a knife arose within him.
Although the merchant brought various kinds of medicine and said to him, "Eat," he replied, "I will not break my *uposatha* vow; having made it a limit unto life..."
He said, "I have undertaken [the precepts]. A powerful sensation arose, and at the time of sunrise, he was unable to establish mindfulness.
Then, thinking, "He will die now," they carried him out and laid him down on a couch.
At that moment, the King of Bārāṇasī, mounted upon an excellent chariot and accompanied by a great retinue, was performing a circumambulation of the city when he reached that spot.
He attained [the throne]. The Bodhisatta, having observed his glory and conceived a longing for it, aspired to the kingship.
Having passed away, by the result of half a *uposatha* ceremony performed [in his previous life], he took rebirth in the womb of that king’s chief queen.
When she had received the necessary care for her pregnancy, at the end of ten months she gave birth to a son; "Udayakumāra" was his name.
They gave him a name. When he reached maturity, he attained perfection in all arts;

then, recollecting his own past karma through the knowledge of recollecting former births (*jātissara-ñāṇa*), he frequently uttered this inspired exclamation (*udāna*): "This is the fruit of a small deed for me.
Even after his father’s passing and his accession to the throne, he looked upon his own great glory and wealth and uttered that very same exclamation.
Then one day, a festival was prepared in the city, and the great multitude became intent on sport.

At that time, a certain laborer living at the northern gate of Bārāṇasī, having performed water-labor and received half a māsaka as wages, placed it between bricks of a wall while performing his work;
having reached the southern gate, he performed water-labor there as well, and while he was still alive—
He lived in cohabitation with a certain poor woman. She said to him, "Husband, there is a festival going on in the city;
if you have anything, we too would like to enjoy ourselves. "Yes, I have," he replied. "How much, husband? "Half a māsaka. "Where is it, husband?
"It was placed inside a brick wall at the northern gate; thus, I have a treasure within twelve yojanas from here."
“But do you have anything in your hand? “Yes, I have,” he replied. “How much? “Half a māsaka.
“In that case, your half-māsaka and my half-māsaka make one whole māsaka.
Taking one portion of it for a garland, one portion for perfume, and one portion for liquor, we shall enjoy ourselves. Go and fetch what you have set aside.”
"Bring half a māsaka coin. Thinking, "I have received a message from my wife," he departed, joyful and delighted, saying, "My dear, do not worry;
I will bring it. Having traveled six leagues, the laborer Nāgabala, out of greed for wealth, was trampling through sand that was as hot at midday as if strewn with glowing embers.
Exceedingly joyful, dressed in a garment dyed with kasāva, and having fastened a palm-leaf ornament to his ear,
he proceeded through the royal courtyard singing a song accompanied by a single stringed instrument.
King Udaya, standing with the window-lattice open, saw him passing in that manner and thought, "What indeed is this?"
Disregarding such wind and heat, he went along singing, joyful and delighted.
Thinking, "I shall question him," the king sent a man to summon him. When that man had gone and said, "The king summons you," he replied, "What does the king have to do with me?
I do not know the king. Though taken by force, he stood to one side.
Then the king, questioning him, spoke these two verses:
“The earth has become a mass of embers; the world is filled with glowing coals.
Yet you sing your songs; the heat does not distress you.”
“The sun burns above, the sands burn below;
yet you sing your songs, and the heat does not scorch you.
In this context, “covered with embers” means, O man, that this earth has become heated like glowing, incandescent coals. It is “followed by hot ashes.”
She was followed by hot sand like a pit of glowing embers known as *kukkuḷa*. "Having undertaken the duties" means she sang while performing her assigned tasks.
Having heard the king’s words, he spoke the third verse:
“The sun’s heat does not burn me; it is the [fires of] heat that burn me.
For there are various matters, O King, that burn, not the sun’s heat.
In this context, “heat” refers to sensual objects and the defilements of sensual desire. For these burn a person; therefore, they are called “heat.”

“‘Various matters,’ O Great King, means that there are various matters consisting of diverse duties to be performed by me in reliance upon material objects and the defilements of sensual pleasure; these burn me, they do not heat me.
Then the king asked him, “What indeed are those matters? He replied, “My lord, at the southern gate, for a destitute woman...”
I lived together with her, and she asked me, "We shall play on the festival day;
do you have anything in your hand? Then I told her, "My treasure is kept behind the wall by the northern gate.
She sent me, saying, "Go and fetch it; we both shall play together. That conversation of hers does not leave my heart.
“The heat of sensual desire torments me as I remember him; this, O King, is my purpose.
Then [the king asked], “Disregarding such wind and sun, what is the cause of your satisfaction that you go along singing?
“O King, it is because I am satisfied with the thought, ‘Having brought back that treasure, I shall enjoy myself with her,’ that I sing. “But what, sir, is your—”
“Man, is there a treasure deposited at the northern gate worth a hundred thousand? “There is not, Your Majesty.
The king said, “In that case, fifty thousand; forty, thirty, twenty, ten, one thousand, five hundred, four, three, two, one, a hundred, fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, ten, five...”
He asked, "Four, three, two, or one kahāpaṇa? Half, a quarter, four māsakas, three, two, or one māsaka?
Having rejected all these, when he was told, "Half a māsaka," he replied, "Yes, Your Majesty, this much is my wealth;
having brought it, I shall go to enjoy myself with her. With that joy and that gladness..."
"This wind and heat do not distress me," he said.
Then the king said to him, "O man, do not go there in such heat; I will give you half a māsaka coin.
[The man replied,] "Your Majesty, I shall abide by your word and take that, and I shall not let my other wealth perish."
“Without missing my departure, I shall take that as well. Even when he was told, “O man, turn back! I will give you a māsaka;
by increasing it from two māsakas in this way, I will give you a crore, a hundred crores, immeasurable wealth—turn back!
he replied, “Your Majesty, having taken that, I shall take the other as well. Then, [the king spoke] regarding his status as a merchant prince and so forth...
Tempted by successive positions up to the rank of viceroy, he spoke in that same manner; when it was said, "I will give you half the kingdom, so return," he accepted.
The king commanded his ministers, "Go, have my friend's hair and beard trimmed, bathe him, adorn him, and bring him back.
The ministers did accordingly. The king divided the kingdom in two and gave it to him.
He gave him half the kingdom. But it is said that even after receiving it, he went to the northern region with an affection for it no greater than that for half a māsaka coin;
thus, he became known as King Aḍḍhamāsaka. Ruling their kingdom together in harmony and mutual affection, they once went to a pleasure garden.
Having played there, King Udaya lay down with his head resting on the lap of King Aḍḍhamāsaka.
When he had fallen asleep, his attendants went here and there to enjoy their pastimes.
King Aḍḍhamāsa thought, "What use have I for half the kingdom forever? Having killed him, I alone shall rule over the entire kingdom.
Drawing his sword and thinking, "I will strike him," he then reflected, "This king [has treated] me, a poor and wretched man..."
"Having treated this human being as my equal, I established him in great sovereignty;
yet the thought arose in me, 'I shall kill such a bestower of fame and rule the kingdom myself. Alas, what an improper deed I have intended!
Having regained his mindfulness, he withdrew the sword. Then, for a second and a third time, the same thought arose in him. Thereupon, he reflected: "This..."
“Furthermore, my mind, arising again and again, might lead me to commit evil deeds.
He threw his sword upon the ground, raised the king up, and fell at his feet, saying, “Forgive me, O Lord!
“My good man, do you not have no ill-will toward me? “There is, Great King; I have done such-and-such a thing. “In that case, my good man, I forgive you.”
“But if you wish, O King, rule the kingdom; I shall serve you as your viceroy.
He replied, “I have no need for kingship, Your Majesty. For this craving will cause me to be reborn in the states of woe.
You take the kingdom yourself; I shall go forth into homelessness. I have seen the root of sensual desire: it increases through conceptual thought, not otherwise.”
"Now, from this point on, I shall restrain my intentions," he declared, and uttered the fourth verse:
"I have seen the root of desire, O Desire; you are born from intention.
I shall no longer intend [for you]; thus, O Desire, you shall not exist."
In that context, *evaṃ* means "thus"; *na hehisi* means "you will not arise.
Having spoken thus, and further teaching the Dhamma to the great multitude who were still devoted to sensual pleasures, he spoke the fifth verse:
"Even few sensual pleasures are not enough; one is not satisfied even by many."
“Alas! The prattle of fools—let the watchful one avoid it.
Herein, “alas” (ahahā) is an expression indicating spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). “The watchful one” (*jaggato*) means one who is awake. This is what is meant:

“O Great King, for these people of the world, even a small amount of sensual pleasure derived from material objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasure derived from the defilements (*kilesakāma*) is not sufficient; nor indeed are they enough, even when abundant.”
They indeed burn because of the prattling, “Oh, these forms are mine! These sounds are mine!”; thus sensual pleasures are the "prattle of fools.
A clansman who is awake, devoted to the practice of developing the factors conducive to enlightenment by increasing his insight, should avoid them;
having fully understood them through the clear realizations of full comprehension and abandonment, he should abandon them.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the great multitude and having entrusted the kingdom to King Udaya, he left the weeping, tearful crowd behind,
entered the Himālayas, went forth into homelessness, and dwelt there after having attained the jhānas and the higher knowledges (abhiññās).
At the time of his going forth, the king, reciting that inspired utterance (udāna) in its entirety, spoke the sixth verse:
“This is the fruit of my small deed; through its arising, I have attained greatness.
What a great gain for this young man, who has gone forth into homelessness, having abandoned sensual desire!”—in this passage, he speaks of himself as “the arising” (*udayo*).
“Attained greatness” (*mahattapattaṃ*) means having reached a state of vastness and abundance.
He attained sovereignty. "Of the young man" means: "It is a great gain for me, his companion, that he has gone forth after abandoning sensual lust"—this was the intention with which he spoke thus.
However, no one understood the meaning of this verse. Then, one day, the chief queen [spoke] the verse...
He asked for a boon, but the king did not speak. Now, he had a barber named Gaṅgamāla who performed auspicious baths;
while shaving the king, he would first perform the work with the razor and only afterwards take up the hair with the tweezers.
At the time of the razor-work, the king felt pleasure, but at the time of pulling out the hair, he felt pain. [The barber] first gave him a boon.
He desired to give [the gift], yet afterwards he longed for the cutting off of his head.
Then one day, having informed the queen of that matter by saying, "My lady, our barber Gaṅgamālakappa is a fool," and when she asked, "But what, O King, ought to be done?
he replied, "First, let the hair be grasped with tweezers, and afterwards let there be the work of the razor. She then had that barber summoned.
“Father,” he said, “on the day the king has his beard trimmed, you should first take the hair and afterwards perform the shaving work.
And when the king says, ‘Choose a boon,’ you should say, ‘Sire, I have no need for anything else;
please explain the meaning of your inspired verse. I will give you much wealth.”
Having agreed by saying, "Very well," on the day for the grooming of his beard, he first took up the tweezers.
When the king asked, "What is this, my man Gaṅgamāla? Are you doing something unprecedented? he replied, "Your Majesty, barbers indeed do things that have never been done before.
Having first plucked out the hair, he then performed the work with the razor. The king said, "Choose a boon."
He said, "Your Majesty, I have no need for anything else; please explain the meaning of the *udāna* verse for you.
The king, feeling ashamed to recount what he had done during his own time of poverty, said, "Dear son, what use have you for this boon? Choose something else.
"Give me this very thing, Your Majesty," he replied. Out of fear of telling a lie, the king consented, saying, "Very well."
Having made all the necessary arrangements in the same manner as described in the *Kummāsapiṇḍi-jātaka*, he sat upon a jeweled couch and declared his entire past conduct, saying:
"I am Gaṅgamāla; in a previous existence, I was in this very city. Having related everything, he said:
"For this reason, [he recited] the first half-verse: 'But my friend has gone forth, while I, having become negligent, continue to rule the kingdom.'"
"For this reason, I speak the latter half-verse," he said, explaining the meaning of the *udāna*.
Having heard this, the barber thought: "It seems this prosperity was obtained by the king through even a half-uposatha observance; indeed, what is wholesome must certainly be done.
What if I were to go forth and establish my own refuge? Having thus reflected, [he left] his relatives, wealth, and circle of attendants...
Having abandoned the king and obtained his permission for the going forth, he went to the Himālaya mountains, where he took up the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Developing insight by applying the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), he attained the enlightenment of a *paccekabuddha*.

Wearing robes and a bowl produced through supernormal power (*iddhi*), he dwelt on Mount Gandhamādana for five or six years; then, thinking, "I shall look upon the King of Bārāṇasī," he traveled through the air.
He sat down upon the auspicious stone in the park. The park keeper, having recognized him, went and informed the king:
"Your Majesty, Gaṅgamāla, having become a paccekabuddha, has come through the air and is sitting in the park.
Upon hearing this, the king set out in haste, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the paccekabuddha. The queen mother also departed together with her son. The king [reached] the park.
Having entered and paid homage to him, he sat down to one side together with his retinue.

Engaging in polite conversation with the king, he addressed the king by his family name, saying, "How is it, Brahmadatta, are you diligent? Do you rule according to the Dhamma? Do you perform meritorious deeds such as giving? Upon hearing this, the king’s mother—
“‘This man of low birth, a bath-attendant’s son who is filthy and foul-smelling, does not know his own status;
he addresses my son, a world-renowned kshatriya by birth, by the name ‘Brahmadatta’!”—having spoken thus in anger, he recited the seventh verse:
“Through austerity one abandons evil karma; through austerity [one abandons] the state of being a bath-attendant or a potter.”
"O Gaṅgāmāla, having overcome [all things] by means of asceticism (tapas), address me by the name Brahmadatta.
The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, these beings abandon evil karma through asceticism—that is, through the quality of asceticism performed by themselves;
but can they, by means of asceticism, even abandon their state of being a potter who has been washed [by the river], you who are Gaṅgāmāla, by your own asceticism?
"You address my son, named Brahmadatta, with such contempt; is this indeed appropriate for you?
The king, having restrained his mother and proclaiming the virtues of the Paccekabuddha, spoke the eighth verse:
"Behold, mother, this very visible fruit of forbearance and gentleness."
“Whoever has been honored by all people, him we honor, together with the king and all our ministers.

In this context, “of patience and gentleness” means of both patience as endurance and of gentleness. “Him we honor”: now, together with the king and all our ministers, we all honor him; behold, mother, the fruit of patience and gentleness!
When the king had thus forbidden [the salutation] toward his mother, the rest of the great multitude rose up and said: “It is indeed improper, O King, for such a person of low birth...”
“Do not address him by name,” he said. The king, having warded off the great multitude, spoke this final verse to recount his virtues:
“Say nothing to Gaṅgamāla, who is training in the paths of silence of the sages;
for he has crossed the ocean, crossing which they wander, free from sorrow.”
In this context, "the sage" (muni) refers to the Paccekabuddha among the categories of householders, non-householders, those in training (sekha), those beyond training (asekha), and Paccekabuddhas.
"Training in the paths of sagehood" (monapatha) means training in the paths of sagehood known as the preliminary practice and the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma).
"The ocean" (aṇṇava) refers to the great ocean of saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus, the king paid homage to the Paccekabuddha and said, "Venerable sir, please forgive my mother.
"I forgive you, Great King," he replied. The king's retinue also asked for his forgiveness. The king then requested permission to dwell there, relying upon him;
however, the Paccekabuddha, without granting the request, while the royal assembly was looking on—
Standing in the air, he gave counsel to the king and returned to Mount Gandhamādana.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "And thus, lay followers, should one dwell in the observance of the Uposatha," and then identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the Paccekabuddha passed away; the half-month king was Ānanda."
“Queen Mahāmāyā was the king’s mother; Rāhulamātā was the chief queen; and I myself was King Udaya.
Thus ends the fifth commentary, the Gaṅgamālajātakavaṇṇanā.
[422] 6. The Commentary on the Cetiyajātakavaṇṇanā.
"The Dhamma, when violated, destroys"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Devadatta’s sinking into the earth.

On that day, the monks had raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, Devadatta, having uttered a falsehood, has sunk into the earth and become one whose destination is the Avīci hell. The Teacher came and...
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked. When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he entered the earth. Having said this, he related the past.
In the first aeon of the past, there was a king named Mahāsammata who had an incalculable lifespan. His son was Roja.
His son was named Vararoja; his son was named Kalyāṇa;
Kalyāṇa’s son was named Varakalyāṇa; Varakalyāṇa’s son was named Uposatha; Uposatha’s son was named Varauposatha;
Varauposatha’s son was named Mandhātā; Mandhātā’s son was named Varamandhātā; Varamandhātā’s son was named Vara...
He had a son named Upavara, also known by the name Uparicara.
He reigned in the city of Sotthiya in the kingdom of Cetiya; he was endowed with the four royal powers and could travel through the sky.
Four sons of gods, bearing swords in their hands, protected him from the four directions, and sandalwood fragrance issued from his body.
A lotus fragrance issued from his mouth. He had a brahmin chaplain named Kapila.
Now, Kapila’s younger brother, named Korakalamba, was a childhood friend who, having learned his craft in the same teacher’s household as the king, had promised him during their youth:
"When I attain the kingship, I shall give you the position of chaplain."
Thus, having attained the kingship, he was unable to displace his father’s chaplain, the brahmin Kapila, from his position as court priest.
However, whenever the chaplain came to attend upon him, the king showed him signs of respect out of reverence.
Observing this, the brahmin thought, "The office of royalty is indeed easy to manage when shared with those of equal age; I—"
Thinking, "I shall go forth after taking leave of the king," he said to the king, "Your Majesty, I am old;

I have a son at home, so appoint him as the chaplain (purohita). I shall go forth. Having thus obtained the king's permission and established his son in the position of chaplain, he entered the royal park, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Relying on his son, he took up residence right there.
Korakalamba, however, harbored resentment toward his brother, thinking, "Even though he has gone forth into homelessness, he did not grant me a position.
One day, while they were sitting together engaged in pleasant conversation, the king asked, "Korakalamba, why have you [not taken] the position of chief priest?"
When he was told, "Do you not do it? he replied, "Yes, Your Majesty, I do not; my brother does.
"Has your brother not gone forth [into the religious life]? "Yes, he has gone forth, but he has caused a position of authority to be given to his son. "In that case, why do you not do it yourself?
"Your Majesty, it is not possible for me to remove from my brother a position of authority that has come down to him through our lineage."
“...to do. “If that is the case, I shall make you the elder and make your brother the younger.

“How so, Your Majesty? “By telling a lie. “What, Your Majesty? Do you not know that when my brother, who is a master of the sciences (vidyādhara) endowed with great miraculous power, deceives you with his miraculous power, the four [great kings]...”
“He will act as if the son of a god has vanished; he will make his body and mouth smell like a foul odor;
he will make you feel as if you have been brought down from the sky and are standing on the ground; and you will feel as if you are entering the earth.
At that time, you will not be able to establish yourselves in your own discourse. “You yourself—”
"Do not worry; I shall be able to do it," he said. "When will you do it, Your Majesty? "In seven days from now.

That news became known throughout the entire city: "The king, it seems, having committed a falsehood, will make the great man small and the small man great; he will grant a high position to the lowly. What kind of..."
"Is this so-called 'false speech' blue, or is it one of the other colors such as yellow?"—such was the reflection that arose among the great multitude.
At that time, it is said, it was an age when people spoke the truth; they did not know that "false speech" was of such a nature.
Having heard those words, the son of the family priest went to his father and told him, "Father, it seems the king intends to speak falsely."
“Having made you the minor ones and making us the major ones, he will give our position to my younger uncle.
“Dear father, even if the king were to tell a lie, he will not be able to take away our position. On which day, however, will he do it?
“It is said, on the seventh day from now. “In that case, inform me then. On the seventh—
On that day, the great multitude, thinking, "We shall witness the lying," gathered in the royal courtyard and stood there having set up tier upon tier of platforms.
The prince went and informed his father. The king, having prepared himself in full regalia, came out and stood in the air over the royal courtyard in the midst of the great multitude.
The ascetic arrived through the air and spread out a sitting-skin before the king.

Sitting cross-legged in the air, he asked, "Is it true, Great King, that you have committed an act of falsehood by making the junior [monk] senior and wishing to grant him his position? "Yes, Teacher, I spoke thus," he replied.
Then, admonishing him, he said, "Great King, falsehood is indeed a grave matter; it destroys one's virtues and leads to rebirth in the four states of misery."
"He causes [the truth] to arise. For a king who speaks falsehood destroys the Dhamma; having destroyed the Dhamma, he himself is destroyed.
Having said this, he recited the first verse:
"The Dhamma, when destroyed, indeed destroys; the Dhamma, when not destroyed, destroys nothing at all."
"Therefore, do not destroy the Dhamma; let it not be that the Dhamma, once destroyed, destroys you.
In this context, "Dhamma" refers specifically to the duty of honoring one's elders.
Then, further exhorting him, he said, "If you, Great King, should speak falsehood, the four psychic powers will vanish," and spoke the second verse:
“The deities depart from one who speaks untruth;
his mouth smells foul, and he falls from his own station— he who,
when questioned about a matter, knowingly answers it otherwise.”
"Regarding that, 'the deities depart,' O Great King: he says this with the intention that if you speak falsely, the four sons of the gods will abandon their protection and vanish.
'And a putrid smell blows from your mouth' means he says it referring to the fact that both your mouth and your body will emit a foul odor. 'And you fall from your own place' means from the sky."
Having spoken thus, he said this while pointing out that [the king] would enter the earth.
Upon hearing this, the king became terrified and looked toward Korakalamba. Then he said to him, "Do not fear, Great King;
did I not tell you this very thing at the very beginning? Although the king heard Kapila’s words, he paid them no heed.
Placing what he himself had said before him, he said, "Venerable sir, you are the younger; Korakalamba is the elder.
At that moment, along with his lie, four sons of the gods thought, "We will not provide protection for such a liar," and casting their swords at his feet, they vanished;
his mouth became as foul-smelling as a broken hen's egg.
The body emitted a foul odor like that of an open latrine; having fallen from the sky, it landed upon the earth, and all four of his psychic powers (iddhi) vanished.
Then the Great Purohita said to him, "Do not fear, O Great King!
If you speak the truth, I shall restore everything to its natural state," and he spoke this third verse:
“If indeed you speak the truth, O King, remain as you were before;
but if you speak a lie, O King, stay upon the ground at the shrine.
In this context, “stay upon the ground” means that he remains firmly established on the ground itself; the sense is that he will no longer be able to leap back into the air.
Thus, having been told, "Behold, Great King, it was by your first lie that those four psychic powers vanished;

consider this, for even now it is possible to restore them," he replied, "By saying this, you wish to deceive me," and uttering a second lie, he sank into the earth up to his ankles. Then the brahmin spoke to him again: "Consider..."
"Great King, it is still possible to restore things to their natural state," he said, and then spoke this fourth verse: "He for whom it rains out of season,
and for whom it does not rain at the proper time— this is the one who,
when asked about a question while knowing the answer, explains it otherwise."

In that context, "of him" means: of that king who, knowing the answer yet speaking falsely when asked, explains the question otherwise, the rain does not fall in the proper season within his realm but falls out of season—this is the meaning.
Then, saying to him, "Observe this, Great King," as he had previously entered the earth up to his shanks due to the fruit of his lying, he spoke the fifth verse:
"If indeed you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before."
“If you speak falsely, O King, enter the earth at Cetiyā.

For a third time he spoke only a falsehood, saying, “Venerable sir, you are the younger brother; Korakalamba is the elder,” and he entered the earth up to his knees. Then, addressing him again with the words, “Observe well, Great King,” he recited two verses:
“His tongue becomes split in two, like that of a serpent, O Lord of the Earth;”
“He who, being questioned about a matter he knows,
answers it otherwise— ‘If you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before;
if you speak a lie, O King, enter even deeper into the shrine.’”
Having spoken these two verses, he said, "Now you may restore him to his natural state.
Although the king heard his words, he disregarded them and, having uttered a fourth falsehood—saying, "Venerable sir, you are the younger brother;
Korakalamba is the elder"—he entered the earth from the waist up. Then the brahmin said to him, "Observe, Great King! and...
He further spoke two verses:
“O Lord of the Earth, that man has no tongue, just like a fish, who,
when asked a question while knowing the answer, explains it otherwise.”
“If you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before;
if you speak a lie, O King, enter the shrine even deeper.
In this context, “like a fish” means that the tongue of a liar is incapable of speaking in every place where it might arise, just like a fish; the meaning is that he becomes like a mute.

Thus, for the fifth time, having uttered the falsehood, "You are the youngest, Korakalamba is the eldest," he sank into the earth as far as his navel. Then the brahmin said to him again, "Observe well, Great King," and spoke these two verses:
"Only females are born in that family, not males, Of him who, when asked about a question he knows, Explains it otherwise."
“If indeed you speak the truth, O King, become as you were before;
if you speak a falsehood, O King, enter further into the cetiya.
In this context, “only daughters” means that for one who speaks falsehood, only daughters are born in every place where they are reborn, and sons are not born.

The king, disregarding his words, uttered a sixth false statement in the same manner and sank into the earth up to his breasts. Then the brahmin said to him again, "Take heed, Great King," and spoke these two verses:
"His sons do not remain, but depart in every direction, For he who, though knowing, answers a question falsely when asked."
“If indeed you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before;
if you speak a falsehood, O King, enter the shrine even deeper.
In this context, “they depart” means that if they become the sons of one who speaks falsehood, they flee away, failing to be of service to their mother and father.

Thus, due to the fault of associating with evil friends, he disregarded the sage’s words and committed a lie for the seventh time as well. Then the earth opened up for him, and flames from the Avīci hell rose up and seized him:
“That king who formerly moved through the sky, now struck down by the seer, has fallen into the earth like a wretched man who has reached his end.”
Therefore, indeed, the wise do not praise the approach of desire;
one should speak with a mind free from malice, uttering speech endowed with truth.
These are the two verses of the Fully Enlightened One.
In this context, "that king," monks, refers to King Cetiya, who, having previously been a wanderer in the sky, was later struck down by a seer and thus lost his natural state.
"Having reached his turn" means that having reached his own appointed time, he entered the earth;
such is the meaning. "Therefore" means because King Cetiya, through following his own desires, became one whose destination was the Avīci hell; therefore.
"With a mind free from hatred" means that one should speak only the truth, having ensured the mind is not defiled by desire or other such passions.
The great multitude became seized with fear, thinking, "The King of Cetiya, having reviled the seer and uttered a falsehood, has entered Avīci.
Then the king’s five sons came, fell at the feet of the brahmin, and said, "Be our refuge!"
They said: "Sirs, your father, having destroyed the Dhamma, committed falsehood, and reviled the seer, has been reborn in Avīci.
This Dhamma, once destroyed, destroys; you cannot remain here. Having said this, he spoke to the eldest among them:
"Come, dear son, go out by the eastern gate and proceed straight ahead until you see a completely white..."
“You shall see the elephant-treasure with its seven-fold foundation;
having established a city there by that sign, dwell there, for that city shall be known as Hatthipura. Having addressed the second son, he said:
“My dear, going out through the southern gate and proceeding straight ahead, you shall see the all-white horse-treasure; by that sign, [establish a city there]...”
"Build a city and dwell there; that city shall be named Assapura," he said. Addressing the third son, he said:
"Dear son, having gone out by the western gate and proceeding straight ahead, you will see a maned lion.
Build a city there at that sign and dwell there; that city shall be named Sīhapura."

He said: "Addressing the fourth, he said, 'My son, having gone out by the northern gate and proceeding straight ahead, you will see a wheel-fence made entirely of jewels; having established a city there according to that sign, dwell there;
that city shall be known as Uttarapañcāla. Addressing the fifth, he said, 'My son..."

"It is not possible to dwell in this place. After building the Mahāthūpa in this city and departing, as you go straight toward the northwestern direction, you will see two mountains striking against each other repeatedly and making a loud crashing sound.
Establish a city there at that sign and dwell there; that city shall be called Daddarapura."
"so shall it be named," he said. Those five men, each according to his own perception, went and established cities in those respective places and dwelt there.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Devadatta spoke falsehood."
Having said, "Having made [the earth] thus, he entered the earth," he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Devadatta was the King of the Cetiya, while I myself was the brahmin Kapila.
This concludes the commentary on the Cetiyajātakavaṇṇanā, the sixth.
[423] 7. The Indriya Jātaka Commentary.
"He who [guards] the faculties..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction of his former wife.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain son of good family, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, thought: "It is not possible for one living in the midst of a household..."
“Having gone forth in the teaching that leads to liberation, I shall lead the holy life (brahmacariya) which is entirely fulfilled and entirely pure, and I shall make an end of suffering.
Having thus entrusted his wealth at home to his wife and children, he departed and requested ordination from the Teacher.
The Teacher granted him the going-forth. Together with his preceptor and teacher, he went for alms.
Because they travel constantly and because there are many bhikkhus, they do not obtain a seat in the families' homes or in the assembly hall;
at the very end of the row for the junior members of the Saṅgha, they obtain only a stool or a wooden plank.
As for food, they receive either broken rice gruel touched by the rim of a ladle, or putrid dry snacks, or boiled rice that has become moldy and dried out.
It was not enough for his sustenance. Taking what he had received, he went to his former wife.
Then she took his bowl, paid him homage, and having removed the food from the bowl, gave him well-prepared rice gruel, boiled rice, curry, and condiments.
Bound by craving for flavors, the old man was unable to abandon his former wife. She thought:
"I shall investigate whether he is bound or not.

Then one day, having had the country folk bathe with white clay and seated them in his house, and having commanded several other attendants to serve him, he had them given small portions of food and drink. As they were eating and consuming it—
They sat down. Having had oxen tied to the wheels at the door of the house, he also had one cart stationed there;
he himself, however, sat in the inner chamber and baked cakes. An old man arrived and stood at the door.
Seeing him, another old man said, "Madam, an elder is standing at the door. "Worship him and bid him farewell," she replied.
Thus, although she said again and again, "Please enter, venerable sir," seeing that he would not go, she said, "Noble lady, the elder is not going.
