She came forward, lifted the curtain, and looked out; saying, "Oh, this is my child's father!
she went out, took his bowl, led him into the house, served him, and at the conclusion of the meal, paid her respects.
“Venerable sir, please attain final nibbāna right here. For all this time we have not taken another family;
however, a household life does not endure in a house that lacks a master. We shall take another family and go to a distant province.
Be heedful, and if there has been any fault on our part, forgive us,” he said. To the elder—
It was like the moment of his heart being torn asunder. Then he said to her, "I cannot bear to abandon you;
do not go. I shall disrobe. Send my undergarment to such-and-such a place; I will return after having my bowl and robes returned.
She consented, saying, "Very well. The elder went to the monastery and, while having his preceptor and teacher return his bowl and robes—
When asked, "Friend, why do you act thus? he replied, "I cannot abandon my former wife; I shall disrobe.
Then, even though he was unwilling, they led him into the presence of the Teacher. When the Teacher asked, "Monks, why have you brought this man here against his will?
they said, "Venerable Sir, this man has become dissatisfied and wishes to disrobe. Then [the Teacher addressed] him...
The Teacher asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are disenchanted? "It is true, Venerable Sir," he replied.
"Who has caused you to become disenchanted? "My former wife, Venerable Sir," he said. The Teacher said, "Monk, this woman has not only now acted to your detriment;
in the past as well, because of her, you fell away from the four meditative absorptions and experienced great suffering."
"Having relied upon me and been freed from that suffering, he regained his lost jhāna," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born from the womb of the king’s brahmin wife, having depended upon him as his family priest.
On the day of his birth, weapons throughout the entire city burst into flame.
Therefore, they gave him the name "Prince Jotipāla.
When he reached maturity, having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and demonstrated his skill to the king, he renounced his sovereignty;

without informing anyone, he departed through the main gate, entered the forest, and in the Kaviṭṭhaka hermitage belonging to Sakka-dattiya, he went forth as an ascetic (isipabbajjā) and attained the meditative absorptions and supernormal powers.
He was reborn there. While he was dwelling there, many hundreds of seers attended upon him, and a great assembly gathered.
He became known as the teacher Sarabhaṅga, and he had seven chief disciples.
Among them, the seer named Sālissara departed from the Kaviṭṭhaka hermitage and went to the eastern country of Surāṣṭra, to a place with pleasant waters.
The seer named Nāma lived on the bank of the river Nāma, surrounded by many thousands of seers.
The seer named Meṇḍissara lived near a town called Kalabbacūḷaka within the kingdom of King Pañcāla Pajjota, surrounded by many thousands of seers.
The seer named Pabbata lived near a certain forest district, surrounded by many thousands of seers. The one named Kāḷadevila...
In the eastern and southern regions of Avanti, a seer named Kisavaccha lived with a retinue of many thousands of seers, dwelling by a solid rock mountain.
Another seer, also named Kisavaccha, lived alone in a park near the city of Kumbhavatī belonging to King Daṇḍaki.
Furthermore, the ascetic Anupiya, who was the attendant of the Bodhisatta, lived in his presence. And a seer named Nārada, the younger brother of Kāḷadevila, [also lived there].
In the Middle Country, on Mount Ārañjara, within a mountain thicket, he dwelt alone in a single cave-dwelling.
Not far from Mount Ārañjara there was a market town crowded with people;
between them there was a great river into which many people were descending. Even women of excellent form and beauty, acting as courtesans, were enticing men.
They sat down on the bank of that river. Seeing one among them, the ascetic Nārada became infatuated;
his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) vanished, and becoming emaciated from fasting, he fell under the power of the defilements (*kilesa*). After staying there for seven days, he lay down.
Then his brother, Kāḷadevila, perceiving this situation through his supernormal knowledge, arrived through the air and entered the cave.
Nārada saw him and asked, "Why have you come, sir? He replied, "Sir, I have come to attend upon you because you were unwell.
Then he rebuked him with false speech, saying, "What is this unreal talk? You speak what is false and empty!
Thinking, "This must not be abandoned," he brought Sālissara, he brought Meṇḍissara, and even a mountain.
He brought him. The other three also tried to restrain him with false speech.
Kāḷadevila, thinking, "I shall bring the teacher Sarabhaṅga," came through the air and brought him.

Having arrived and seen him, and knowing that he had fallen under the sway of the senses, he asked, "Nārada, have you perhaps fallen under the sway of the senses? Upon hearing this, the other rose up, paid homage, and said, "Yes."

When he said, "Teacher," [the Buddha] replied, "Nārada, those who have fallen under the sway of the sense faculties wither away in this very life, experience suffering, and are reborn in hell in their second existence. Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
"O Nārada, he who goes under the sway of the sense faculties through desire..."
“Thus, having abandoned both worlds, he withers away even while still living.

In this context, “he who [is under the sway] of the faculties,” O Nārada, refers to that person who, having grasped at the aspect of beauty in forms and so forth, falls under the power of the six faculties by way of defiled desire (*kilesakāma*). “Having abandoned both worlds” means having abandoned both the human world and the divine world.
The meaning is that, having abandoned both worlds, they are reborn in the hells and other such realms.
"While living he withers away" means that while still alive, failing to obtain the objects of defilement he desires, he withers away with grief and encounters great suffering.

Having heard this, Nārada asked, "Teacher, the pursuit of sensual pleasures is indeed happiness; with reference to what kind of happiness do you say it is suffering? Then Sarabhaṅga said to him, "In that case, listen," and spoke the second verse:
“After happiness comes suffering, after suffering comes happiness;
you have passed from happiness to suffering—it is to be expected that happiness will follow.
In this context, “after happiness” means that immediately following sensual pleasure comes the suffering of hell. “Of suffering” refers to the suffering of guarding one’s virtue (*sīla*).
Immediately after that come both divine and human happiness, as well as the happiness of Nibbāna. This is what is meant:
"Nārada, for these beings, at the time of indulging in sensual pleasures, die and are reborn in the exclusively painful hell;
yet those who guard their virtue and perform the work of insight meditation undergo weariness. Having guarded their virtue through hardship, by the power of that virtue—"
“They obtain the kind of happiness already described; it is with reference to this suffering that I speak thus. “You have fallen,” means:
O Nārada, you have now ruined the bliss of *jhāna* and have fallen from that happiness into a great mental suffering dependent on sensual desires.
“You may expect” means: having abandoned this suffering of the defilements (*kilesa*), desire and aspire once again for that very same excellent and supreme bliss of *jhāna*.

Nārada said, “Teacher, this suffering is unbearable; I am not able to endure it. Then the Great Being, saying to him, “Nārada, suffering that has arisen must indeed be endured,” spoke the third verse:
“In a time of hardship, he who endures hardship and does not yield to it—that wise man, through his endurance of hardship, attains happiness and achieves spiritual union.”
In this context, "does not exceed" means "does not follow after"; or rather, this is the reading itself. This is what is meant:
O Nārada, he who, when suffering—consisting of bodily and mental pain—arises, remains heedful and, by applying the means for its removal, becomes one who endures that suffering;
he does not follow after that suffering, nor does he come under its sway, but [remains firm] through various...
“By means of skillful methods, one overcomes and destroys that hardship;

that wise person attains the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna-sukha), which is reckoned as the end of hardship and is called non-worldly happiness, or he attains that very happiness of yoga despite the hardship, reaching it without weariness.

Then he said, “Teacher, sensual pleasure is indeed the supreme happiness; I am not able to abandon it. Thereupon the Great Being, saying, “Nārada, the Dhamma must not be destroyed for any reason whatsoever,” spoke the fourth verse:
“Not for the sake of sensual pleasures, nor for the sake of harm, nor for the sake of doing what is harmful, nor by rejecting what has been done, should you depart from the Dhamma.

In this context, “for the sake of sensual pleasures” (*kāmāna kāmā*) means for the sake of the desire for sense-objects; that is, for the longing for material objects. “Nor for the sake of harm, nor for the sake of doing what is harmful” (*nānatthā nātthakāraṇā*).

"Not for the sake of what is harmful, nor for the sake of what is beneficial. "Nor by repudiating what has been done" means: having repudiated the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) that has already been produced and accomplished.
This is what is meant: "O Nārada, you ought not to fall away from the Dhamma merely through longing for sensual objects;
nor, when some harm has arisen and you wish to ward it off, ought you to fall away from the Dhamma either because of that harm or because of the benefit which serves as the motive."
“Even for the sake of some purpose thinking, ‘Such-and-such a need will arise for me,’ you ought not to fall away from the Dhamma;
moreover, having accomplished and produced the bliss of jhāna, you ought not to cast it aside or destroy it by falling away from the Dhamma.
When Sarabhaṅga had thus taught the Dhamma with these four verses, Kāḷadevila, advising his own younger brother, spoke this fifth verse:
“Skillful, O householder, is it good; sharing food with others;
being free from pride when gaining wealth; and remaining unperturbed when wealth is lost.
Regarding this, “skillful, O householder” means, Nārada, for the sake of generating wealth for householders living in the life of a householder...
"Dexterity" (dakkha) means being skillful, clever, and proficient; such dexterity is good, and the state of being dexterous is auspicious.
"Sharing food" means making use of wealth acquired through hardship by sharing it with righteous recluses and brahmins;
this is the second good thing. "Absence of pride when gaining wealth" refers to remaining free from conceit due to heedfulness even when great power has arisen.
"Freedom from laughter and lack of agitation is the third good thing.

As for 'the ruin of one's welfare'—when there is the ruin of one's own welfare and the loss of glory, then freedom from distress and lack of dejection is the fourth good thing. Therefore, Nārada, do not grieve thinking, 'My jhāna has vanished.
If you do not fall under the power of the sense-faculties, even though your jhāna has been lost, it will [be recovered]."
"It will become as it was before.
Then, knowing that Kāḷadevila had again exhorted Nārada, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke the sixth verse:
"To this extent is his wisdom, even though that Devila says so;"
“There is nothing worse than this: he who falls under the power of the sense-faculties.
The meaning of this is: “Monks, this much is wisdom,” said that Devila. But there is no one worse than him who, through the influence of the defilements, falls under the power of the sense-faculties.

Then Sarabhaṅga addressed him, saying: “Nārada, listen first to this: for he who does not do what ought to be done at the very outset grieves and laments like a young man who has entered the forest. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in a certain Kāsi village, there was a young brahmin who was handsome, endowed with strength, and possessed the power of an elephant.
He thought: "What is the use of performing agricultural work and such for my parents? What is the use of having sons and a wife?
What is the use of performing meritorious deeds such as giving? Without supporting anyone and without performing any merit, I shall enter the forest and [hunt] deer."

"Having killed [others], I shall nourish myself alone. Thus, equipped with his five weapons, he went to the Himalayas and, having slain various wild animals and eating them, he reached a great mountain range surrounded by hills on the bank of a river called Vidhavā within the Himalayas.
There, having slain deer and eating meat cooked over coals, he made his dwelling.
He thought: "I shall not always possess such strength; when I am weak, I will not be able to roam the forest.

Therefore, right now, having caused deer of various colors to enter the mountain range and secured the gate, I shall not wander the forest but will kill and eat the deer according to my desire. He did exactly so. Then, when his time had passed—
That karma reached its culmination and became manifest in this very life;
he was unable to move by his own hands and feet, nor could he turn over from side to side. He saw neither any solid food, nor soft food, nor drink;
his body withered away, and he became a hungry ghost (*manussapeta*). In the heat of summer, his body cracked open like the earth.
He showed the streaks [of his body], and being deformed and misshapen, he experienced great suffering.
When a long time had passed in this way, in the kingdom of Sivi, a king named Sivī, thinking, "I shall eat meat roasted on coals in the forest," handed over the sovereignty to his ministers.
Clad in armor with the five weapons, he entered the forest, killed deer, and [took] their meat.
While eating, he gradually reached that place; seeing the man, although terrified, he established mindfulness and asked, "Who are you, good man?
"Sir, I am a *manussapeta* (a ghost of a human); I am experiencing the fruit of my own past actions.
But who are you? "I am King Sivi. "Then for what reason have you come here? "For deer meat..."

“For the purpose of eating. Then he [the ghost] told him everything in detail, saying, “Great King, I too have come for this very reason and was born as a *manussapeta*,” and spoke the remaining verses while explaining his own state of suffering to the king:
“Sivi fell into the hands of his enemies, just as I have;”
“Skill in craft, learning, and discernment, marriage, virtue, and gentleness—
having lost these and my reputation through my own deeds, I have been reborn thus.
Though I live for a thousand years, I am friendless and without refuge.”
“Having departed from the noble Dhamma, I am just like a peta.
Having caused those who desire happiness to suffer, I have fallen into this state;
thus I find no happiness, remaining as if in the midst of a blazing fire.”
In this context, "as if into the hands of enemies" means as if into the hands of enemies for one's ruin or destruction. "Sivi" is an address to the king.
"He meets [it] like me" means that one such as I meets it through evil karma; what is meant is that one meets with destruction through one's own karma.
"Kamma" refers to the activity that accomplishes a livelihood, divided into types such as agricultural work and so forth. "Vijjā" refers to various kinds [of knowledge].
The craft refers to elephant-riding skills and so forth. Skillfulness (*dakkheyya*) means proficiency in generating various kinds of wealth.

Marriage (*vivāha*) refers to the connection of giving and taking in marriage. Virtue and gentleness (*sīlamaddava*) refers to the fivefold virtue, as well as gentle speech, the desire for others' welfare, the warding off of evil, and association with virtuous friends;
for it is this that is intended here by "gentleness. And "having lost these [qualities] in fame" refers to these very things.
"And having failed in the duties that bring glory. "Reborn through my own deeds" means reborn by virtue of my own karma.
This is what is meant: "Great King, I did not perform in this world the appropriate work that bestows sovereignty;
I did not train in a craft; I did not acquire wealth through skillful means; I did not arrange marriages; and I did not guard my virtue."
"Without associating with virtuous friends capable of warding off evil while I was committing an improper act,
and having lost and discarded these worldly phenomena— which are reckoned as 'glory' because they bestow such fame— I entered this forest; now,
due to the evil deeds I myself committed, I have been reborn as a hungry ghost."
"Sahassajīnovā" means "like a man who has won a thousand"; the meaning is that by practicing rightly, I would acquire wealth, and thus I am "conquered" (won over) by those many thousands of riches.
"Aparāyaṇo" means without refuge; the meaning is without support. "Ariyadhammā" means from the dhamma of the true person (sappurisa).
"Yathā peto" means just as one might arise after having died and become a peta, even while still living...

Likewise, "I am born as a *manussapeta*" means that I have been reborn as such. "Having caused those who desire happiness to suffer" means having caused sentient beings who desire happiness to undergo suffering.

There is also the reading "sukhakāmo," which means: being myself desirous of happiness, I have caused another to suffer. "I have fallen into this state" (*āpannosmi padam idam*) means I have reached such a portion [of existence]. There is also the reading "patham," meaning this which has become the path to suffering.
The meaning is: "I have attained a [new] personal existence. Regarding the phrase "standing like Bhāṇumā": Bhāṇumā is said to be fire;
he says that, as if surrounded on all sides by glowing embers, being consumed by a great burning arising within his body, he does not experience any bodily or mental pleasure.
Having spoken thus, he said: "Great King, desiring happiness myself, I caused another to suffer and was born as a human peta even in this very life.
Therefore, do not commit evil; having gone to your own city, perform meritorious deeds such as giving.
The king did so and filled the city of heaven. The Teacher Sarabhaṅga, having brought forward this account, [addressed] the ascetic...

He instructed him. Having gained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) through that discourse on the Dhamma, he paid homage to him, asked for forgiveness, and by performing the preliminary exercises for the meditation objects (*kasiṇaparikamma*), restored his lost meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Since Sarabhaṅga would not allow him to remain there, he took him with him and went to his own hermitage.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.
At that time, Nārada was the despondent monk; Nagarasobhinī was his former wife; Sālissara was Sāriputta;
Meṇḍissara was Kassapa; Pabbata was Anuruddha; Kāḷadevila was Kaccāyana; Anupiya was Ānanda; and Kisavaccha was [the Buddha].
Mahāmoggallāna was [the other], but Sarabhaṅga was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Indriya Jātaka.
[424] 8. The Commentary on the Āditta Jātaka.
“In the burning” (Ādittasmiṃ): this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the peerless gift (asadisadāna).
The peerless gift should be explained in detail from the commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta.
On the day after that gift was given, they raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: “Friends, the King of Kosala has indeed searched for a field of merit...”
“Having understood this, she gave an incomparable gift to the Noble Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?

When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not surprising that the king, having investigated, established a foundation for giving in the unsurpassed field of merit; for even the wise of old did so.”
Having said, “They gave a great gift after searching [for the recipient],” he related a story of the past:

In the past, in the city of Roruva in the kingdom of Sivi, there was a great king named Roruva. Without violating the ten duties of a king (*rājadhamma*), he won over the people through the four means of attraction (*saṅgahavatthu*).
Standing in the place of a mother and father to the masses, he [provided for] the poor, the destitute, the indigent, beggars, and others.
He established a great distribution of alms. His chief queen was named Samuddavijayā, who was wise and endowed with discernment.
One day, while surveying the pinnacle of his charity, he thought: "Beings of immoral conduct and lustful nature consume my gifts; this does not please me.
I, however, desire to give to the Paccekabuddhas, who are virtuous and the foremost recipients of offerings."
“They dwell in the region of the Himālayas; who indeed will invite them and bring them here? Whom shall I send?
Having reflected thus, he informed the queen of this matter. Then she said to him, “Great King, do not worry.
By the power of the gifts we have given, the power of our virtue, and the power of truth, let us send flowers and invite the Paccekabuddhas.”
“When they have arrived, we shall give them a gift complete with all requisites.
The King, accepting this with the words “Very well,” had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming, “Let all the inhabitants of the city undertake the precepts of virtue!
He himself, together with his retinue, resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha, distributed a great almsgiving, and [prepared] a golden casket filled with jasmine flowers.

Having caused [the people] to take hold [of him], he descended from the palace and stood in the royal courtyard. Placing his five limbs upon the ground, he paid homage facing the eastern direction and said:
“I pay homage to the Arahants in the eastern direction. If there is any virtue in us, out of compassion for us, please accept our alms.
Having spoken thus, he threw seven handfuls of flowers toward the eastern direction. In the eastern direction...
Due to the absence of the Paccekabuddhas, they did not come on the following day. On the second day, he paid homage to the southern direction, but they did not come from there either.
On the third day, he paid homage to the western direction, but they did not come from there either. On the fourth day, he paid homage to the northern direction;
and having paid homage, [he thought]: "The Paccekabuddhas dwelling in the region of the Northern Himalayas..."
"Please accept our alms," she said, and released seven handfuls of flowers.
The flowers went and fell upon five hundred paccekabuddhas in the Nandamūlaka cave.
Knowing through their supernormal power that they had been invited by the king, those [paccekabuddhas] addressed seven paccekabuddhas on the following day.
“Friends, the king invites you; please show him favor,” they said.
The seven Paccekabuddhas arrived through the air and alighted at the king’s gate. Seeing them, the king was filled with joy;

he paid homage to them, escorted them up to the palace, and having rendered great honor and given a gift, at the conclusion of the meal, he invited them for the following day, and again for the following day.
Having thus invited them for six days, on the seventh day he prepared a gift of all requisites;
having arranged beds, seats, and so forth inlaid with the seven precious gems, and having placed all the monastic requisites such as the three robes before the seven Paccekabuddhas,
he said, "We give these requisites to you," at the conclusion of their meal.
Both the king and the queen stood there paying homage. Then, offering them words of appreciation, the Elder of the Saṅgha spoke these two verses:
“When a house is ablaze, whatever vessel one carries out, that is for one’s own benefit; but not that which is consumed by the fire therein.”
“Thus the world is set ablaze by old age and death;
one should indeed carry out goods with gifts, for what is given is well carried out.
In this context, “set ablaze” means ignited at that very moment. “Vessel” means an implement. “And not that which is burning there” [refers to the fire itself].
But whatever is burned there—even down to a layer of grass—is entirely useless to him.
The mention of "by old age and death" is merely a heading for the teaching; in actual fact, however, he is said to be set ablaze by eleven fires.
"One should carry it out" means that from this world ablaze with those eleven fires, one should remove each of those various tenfold bases for giving.
The gift of requisites is indeed extracted by the intention itself. "It has been given" means that whatever has been given, whether little or much, that alone is what is called "well-bestowed.
Having thus offered the blessing of thanksgiving, the Elder of the Saṅgha gave this exhortation to the king: "Be heedful, O Great King."
Leaping into the air, he split the pinnacle of the palace in two and went, descending right at the Nandamūlaka Cavern.
The requisites given to him also leapt up along with him and descended right at the Nandamūlaka Cavern.
The entire bodies of both the king and the queen were filled with rapture. When he had thus departed, the rest also—
“The person who gives a gift obtained by righteous means, acquired through exertion and energy, that mortal, having crossed over Yama’s Vetaraṇī River, attains divine abodes.
They say that giving and battle are alike: even those who are few conquer many.”
Even if one gives with little faith, by that alone one becomes happy in the next world.
"Giving after careful discernment is praised by the Sugata—those who are worthy of offerings here in the world of the living.
What is given to these yields great fruit, like seeds sown in a fertile field."
“He who wanders without harming living beings, and commits no evil through reviling others—the timid man they praise there, not the hero;
for it is out of fear that the virtuous refrain from evil.
Through inferior conduct, one is reborn among the Khattiyas.”
Through moderate [generosity] one attains the state of the gods, and through supreme [generosity] one is purified.
"Indeed, giving is praised in many ways; yet the footprint of the Dhamma is better than giving.
For the wise ones of old, even earlier still, having been virtuous, attained nothing other than Nibbāna."
Having thus expressed their appreciation with each verse, they departed together with their requisites.

In this context, "one who has acquired through the Dhamma" (dhammaladdha) refers to a person beginning from one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) down to a practitioner of dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka), so called because they have acquired the Dhamma.
Precisely that same person is [also] so called because that Dhamma was attained through the energy of exertion (uṭṭhāna-vīriya).
"Attained through initiative and energy" means: whatever person gives a gift to that individual; or alternatively, it means:

whatever person, having taken the best portion of the gift-property acquired through initiative—which is to say, through energy—and which was obtained in accordance with the Dhamma, gives that gift to those possessed of virtue.
Or else, here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
The meaning should be understood. "Vetaraṇī" is merely a heading for the teaching; the meaning is that one has passed beyond the eight great hells and the sixteen sub-hells.
"He attains divine abodes" means he is reborn in the world of the devas.
"They call it equal" means they say it is the same. For there is no giving for one who fears destruction, and no battle for one who fears fear.
There is none. One who has abandoned attachment to life is able to strive as one truly striving;
one who has abandoned attachment to wealth is able to give as a true donor. For that very reason, both of these are called "equal.

Even when they are few—meaning even those few who have sacrificed their lives—conquer the many; in the same way, even a small volition of relinquishment overcomes a great deal of a mind of stinginess.
Or it conquers the dense thicket of defilements such as greed. “Even if it is little” means that even if one gives a small amount of a gift while having faith in both the action and its fruit.
“By that very [act]” means that by means of that gift, even though its material basis is limited and the act of giving is small, he becomes happy in the next world, O Great King.
"Discerning giving" means giving after having investigated both the gift and the recipient.
In this regard, one who gives by selecting the most excellent and refined object of offering, rather than giving just anything, is said to "discern the gift.
One who gives by selecting those endowed with qualities such as virtue, rather than giving to just anyone, is said to "discern the recipient."
[The word] *nāma*. "Praised by the Sugata" means such a gift is praised by the Buddhas.

In that context, the passage beginning with "those who are worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyā*) was stated in order to show the selection of those worthy of offerings. Therein, "worthy of offerings" refers to the Buddhas and others who are suitable for offerings (*dakkhiṇā*).
"Living beings" (*pāṇabhūtāni*) refers to beings counted as living creatures. "They move about without harming" means moving about while not causing harm out of compassion.
"Out of fear of slander" means that one does not commit evil out of fear of being slandered.

"One who is afraid" refers to one who fears slander. "The brave therein" refers to one who, through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), becomes bold regarding such slander; the wise do not praise him.
"Indeed, out of fear" means that it is indeed out of fear of slander that the wise do not commit evil.
"By a low holy life": first, in the external sectarian systems, the mere virtue of abstaining from sexual intercourse is called a low holy life;
by that, one is reborn in a kṣatriya family. The mere access concentration of jhāna is middling;
by that, one is reborn in the world of the devas. The eight attainments are supreme; by that, one who is reborn in the Brahma-world is said to be "purified."
Within the Dispensation, however, the holy life lived by one who possesses virtue alone while aspiring for a single class of deities is called "inferior.

The production of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) by one whose virtue is completely purified is called "middling. And the arising of Arahantship by one who, standing on a foundation of completely purified virtue, has increased insight (*vipassanā*) is called "superior.
This is the meaning of the concluding verse: "O Great King, although giving is praised and extolled in many ways with absolute certainty,"
But as for giving, the very word of the Dhamma—consisting of the categories of the Dhamma known as serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and Nibbāna—is far superior.

Why is that? Because even prior to this eon, the Great Seers and Wise Ones, such as the Seven Buddhas beginning with Kassapa and those even earlier beginning with Vessabhū, having developed serenity and insight, attained Nibbāna itself.
"They have attained" means they have reached [the goal].

Thus, after the seven Paccekabuddhas had praised the King with verses of appreciation regarding the great Nibbāna of the Deathless, and had exhorted the King to heedfulness, they departed for their own respective abodes in the manner already described. The King, together with his chief queen—
Having given the gift, he remained [in that state] for the rest of his life; then, passing away from there, he filled the city of heaven.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, even in the past, the wise gave gifts with discernment," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the Paccekabuddhas attained Parinibbāna; Samuddavijayā was Rāhula’s mother."
“Ahosi was indeed myself, while Roruvamahārāja was also myself.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the Ādittajātakavaṇṇanā.
[425] 9. The Commentary on the Aṭṭhānajātaka.
"Gaṅgā, Kumudinī"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.
The Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?
When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "For what reason? When he replied, "On account of the defilements," the Teacher said, "Monk, as for women..."
"Ungrateful and treacherous toward friends, a woman is not to be trusted. In the past, even though wise men gave her a thousand coins every day, they were unable to satisfy a woman.
Failing to receive even a single day’s worth of a thousand, she had them seized by the neck and driven out.
Thus ungrateful is a woman; do not fall under the power of defilement for her sake. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there was his son, Prince Brahmadatta, and the son of the chief merchant of Benares, named Mahādhanakumāra.
Both of them were companions who played together in the dust, and they learned their craft in the very same teacher’s school.
When the king passed away, the prince was established in the kingdom, and the merchant’s son remained right in his presence.

In Benares, there was a courtesan named Nagarasobhinī who was beautiful, lovely, and possessed of the highest charm. The merchant’s son gave her a thousand pieces of money every day and constantly took his pleasure with her alone.
Even after he had obtained the position of treasurer upon his father’s death, he did not abandon her;
rather, giving her a thousand pieces of money daily as before, he continued to enjoy her company. Thus the merchant’s son [lived].
He went to wait upon the king three times each day.
Then, one day, as he was conversing with the king while on his way to the royal court, the sun set and darkness fell.
Having departed from the palace, he thought, "Now there is no time to go home; I shall go instead to the house of Nagarasobhinī."
Having dismissed his attendants, he entered her house all alone. When she saw him, she said, "Noble son, the thousand has been brought.
He replied, "My dear, it became very late today; therefore, instead of going home, I dismissed the people and entered by myself.
However, tomorrow I shall give you two thousand."
She thought, "If I grant him an opportunity today, he will come with empty hands on other days as well, and thus my wealth will diminish; I shall no longer give him an opportunity.
Then she said to him, "Master, we are known as 'courtesans'; for us, there is no play without giving a thousand [pieces of gold]. "Lady, tomorrow..."
“I shall bring back double,” he said, and he begged her again and again. Nagarasobhinī commanded her female servants:
“Do not let him stand here and look at me; seize him by the neck, lead him out, and close the door!
Hearing this, the servants did exactly as they were told. Then he thought: “I [have] eighty crores of wealth together with her...”
"I ate it. One day, seeing that my hands were empty, she seized me by the neck and had me driven out.
Oh, how women are indeed wicked, shameless, ungrateful, and treacherous to their friends! Recalling these faults of women, he became dispassionate;
he perceived the repulsive nature of things and grew weary of the household life, thinking, "What use have I for the household life? I shall go forth this very day."
Thinking, “I shall go forth,” he did not return home again; and without even seeing the king, he departed from the city, entered the forest,
established a hermitage on the bank of the Ganges, and having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*),
making his dwelling there while subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
Not seeing him, the king asked, "Where is my companion? The deed committed by Nagarasobhini became known throughout the entire city.

Then, having explained the matter to him, they said, "Thus, O King, out of shame your companion has not even gone home, but having entered the forest, he must have gone forth into the religious life. When the king heard this, [he sent for] Nagarasobhini.
Having summoned her, he asked, "Is it true that one day, failing to obtain a thousand [pieces of gold], you had my companion seized by the neck and driven out?
"It is true, Your Majesty," she replied. "You wicked, vile woman!
Go quickly to the place where my companion has gone and bring him back; if you do not bring him back, there shall be no life for you. At the king's word, she—
Having heard this, she became terrified; mounting her chariot with a large retinue, she departed from the city and, seeking out his dwelling place, learned of that location through her hearing.
Having gone there and paid homage, she entreated him, saying, "Noble sir, forgive the fault committed by me through my foolishness;
I shall never do so again. He replied, "Very well, I forgive you; there is no [fault]."
When she said, "I have no ill will toward you," he replied, "If you will forgive me, mount the chariot with me and let us go to the city;
when we have arrived, I shall give you all the wealth that is in my house.
Having heard her words, he said, "My dear lady, it is not possible for me to go with you now; however, when [the time comes] in this world..."
"What must not come to pass will come to pass; perhaps then he might go," he said, and recited the first verse:
"The Ganges, the night-lily, the swan, the conch-colored cuckoo, the rose-apple tree, and the palmyra fruit—only then, indeed, would it be so."

The meaning of this is as follows: "O Bhaddā, just as lotus ponds remain covered with white water-lilies, even so, if the entire great Ganges River were a bed of white water-lilies, having abandoned its swift current and become still and tranquil;
and if all cuckoos were the color of conch shells; and if the entire Jambu tree were to yield the fruit of the palmyra—only then, indeed, would it be so."
“Then, at such a time, surely there would be a meeting for us too; it might indeed happen,” this was what was meant.

Having spoken thus, when she said again, “Come, noble sir, let us go,” he replied, “We shall go. When she asked, “At what time? he said, “At such-and-such a time and such-and-such a time,” and then recited the remaining verses:
“When a cloak made of tortoise hair should come into being in three varieties;”
“A winter cloak would surely be needed then.
When a watchtower for gadflies has been well-constructed—
firm and unshakable— then indeed it would be needed.”
“When a ladder well-constructed for those with horns should exist,
for the purpose of ascending to heaven— only then, indeed,
would that be possible. When mice, having climbed that ladder, should devour the moon;”
They might even strike down Rāhu; only then would it truly be so.
When flies that wander in swarms, having drunk from a jar of liquor, should settle to dwell upon burning coals—only then would it truly be so.
“When a donkey might possess lips as red as the *bimba* fruit and have a handsome face,
and be skilled in dance and song— only then, indeed,
would it be so. When crows and owls might hold counsel together in secret;”
They would surely envy one another, and only then would it truly be so:
"When a parasol made of muñjagrass leaves becomes more durable,
for the purpose of warding off the rain, only then would it truly be so."
“When a *kulaka* bird might carry Mount Gandhamādana in its beak and fly away—
only then would it be possible. When one might sleep upon a ship at sea, complete with its mast and rudder— only then would it be possible.”
"A servant might take it and go; then, surely, at that time it would exist.
In this context, "threefold" means one [type] made of flower-cloth from tortoise hair, one from cotton, and one from both; thus it is of three kinds.
"A winter cloak" (*hemantika-pāvuraṇa*) refers to that which is capable of serving as a cloak during the season of falling snow. Then...
"Surely at that time there would be"—that is, at that time, my association with her would be absolute.
In this way, the final phrase should be applied in every instance. "A well-constructed watchtower" means it is constructed such that it can support a hundred men fighting while mounted upon it.
"They would cause to fall" means they would cause them to flee. "In embers" means on a bed of glowing, charcoal-free embers.
"May they dwell together" means that having drunk each a jar of liquor, they might remain intoxicated.
"Endowed with bimba-like lips" means possessed of lips resembling the *bimba* fruit. "With a beautiful face" means a face like a golden mirror.
"They would envy" means that, desiring one another's excellence, they would envy and long for it. "Of *muḷāla* leaves" means of the tender leaves of the *muḷāla* reed.
*Kulakoti* is a certain small bird. *Sāmuddikaṃ* refers to a great ship that sails upon the ocean.
*Sayantaṃ savaṭākaraṃ* means together with its machinery and its rudder, equipped with all its necessary parts.
*Ceṭo ādāya* means when a small village boy were to go along, having grasped such a ship with his hand; this is the meaning.

Thus, by means of this contemplation on what is impossible, the Great Being spoke eleven verses. Having heard them, Nagarasobhini asked forgiveness of the Great Being, went to the city, and having reported the matter to the king, she begged for and regained her own life.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, said, "Monk, thus indeed women are ungrateful and treacherous to friends," and after proclaiming the Truths, he identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent attained the fruit of Stream-entry.
He established himself. At that time, King Ānanda was he, but the ascetic was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Aṭṭhāna Jātaka.
[426] 10. The Commentary on the Dīpi Jātaka.
"It is bearable; it is tolerable"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning a certain ewe.
For on one occasion, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling in the Giribbaja monastery, which was surrounded by mountains and had but a single gate.
His walking path was right near that gate. At that time, some shepherds said, "Let the sheep graze here."
Having entered Giribbaja, they lived there sporting together.
One day, as they were returning in the evening after taking their sheep, one ewe, wandering far off, did not see the other sheep coming out and remained behind.
A leopard, seeing her as she was coming out last, stood at the gate of Giribbaja thinking, "I shall eat her. She too, looking here and there, [saw him].
Seeing him, he thought, "He stands here desiring to kill and eat me; if I turn back and flee, I shall have no life left.
Today it is right for me to exercise my manly prowess.
Thinking thus, he raised his horns and rushed with speed toward the leopard, while the leopard quivered, thinking, "I will seize him from this side! I will seize him from that side!"
Without allowing herself to be captured, she fled with speed and entered among the sheep.
Then the Elder, having seen their actions, went on the following day and informed the Tathāgata, saying, "It is so, Bhante;
through her own skill in means and by exerting effort, that ewe was released from the leopard. The Teacher said, "Moggallāna, now—"
"Even so, that leopard was unable to seize him; however, previously, he killed and ate him while he was crying out.
Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a family of great wealth in a certain village, and having reached maturity..."
Having abandoned sensual pleasures and gone forth into the ascetic life, he developed the meditative absorptions and supernormal powers.
After dwelling for a long time in the Himalayas, he went to Rājagaha to partake of salt and sour gruel; there, he constructed a leaf-hut on the very same Giribbaja mountain and made his residence.
At that time, while the sheep were grazing among the *eḷakapāla* shrubs according to their usual custom, one day, in exactly the same manner, one—
Seeing a she-jackal emerging from behind, a certain leopard stood at the gate, thinking, "I shall eat her.

She too, seeing him, thought, "Today my life is at an end; by some means, I shall establish a friendly greeting with him, soften his heart, and thus preserve my life. Having thought this, even from afar she [approached] him...
As she approached, offering her greetings, she spoke the first stanza:
“Is it bearable? Is it sustainable? I hope you are well, my maternal uncle.
Your mother said you were well; we too desire only your welfare.”
In that context, "Is it well with you, mother? means that my mother said to me today, "You should ask after their welfare. "And us" means, "O uncle, we too desire only your welfare.
Hearing this, the leopard thought, "This cunning woman wishes to deceive me by calling me 'uncle'; she does not know my harsh nature," and he spoke the second verse:
"Having thrust your tail into my mouth, And having struck me, O little goat,..."
"Do you think that today you should be released by the title 'uncle'?
The meaning of this is: "You have come after treading upon and crushing my tail-tuft; do you think, 'Today I ought to be released by the title "uncle"'? Do you think so, do you think so?
Having heard that, the other said, "Uncle, do not act thus," and spoke the third verse:
“You are seated facing east, and I have come before your face;
your tail is behind you—how indeed could I have entered?
In this context, “face” means directly in front. “How indeed could I have entered? means: how could I have entered while standing behind you?
Then he said to her, “What are you saying, Eḷikā? There is no place where my tail is not covered with hair,” and he spoke this fourth verse:
“As far as the four continents extend, together with the oceans and the mountains, even that much of my tail is covered; how then could it be otherwise?”
"There, for now" means he says, "this much place has gone around my tail.
Hearing that, the she-goat said, "This wicked one does not yield to sweet talk; having become his adversary, I shall speak to him," and she spoke the fifth verse:
"Even before this, my mother, father, and brothers told me:"
“The tail of the wicked one is long; I have come through the air.
Therein, “they told me” means that previously my mother, father, and brothers had told me this.
“I am she” means that I, having heard from my kinsmen about the length of your tail, was protecting your tail.
"You have come through the air, through the sky.
Then he said to her, "I know that you have come through the air; however, by coming in this manner, you have destroyed my food," and he spoke the sixth verse:
"O Eḷikā, seeing you coming thus through the atmosphere..."
“The herd of deer has fled; my food has been destroyed by you!
Hearing this, the other, terrified by the fear of death and unable to provide any other excuse, lamented:
“Uncle, do not commit such a cruel deed! Give me my life! Even as she was thus lamenting, the other [struck her] on the shoulder.
Having seized and killed her, he ate her.
As the ewe was thus lamenting, the wolf-devourer crushed her throat;
there is no well-spoken word for one who is wicked.
“There is no method for one who is corrupt, neither Dhamma nor well-spoken words;
one should apply oneself with diligence toward the corrupt, yet such a person does not delight in the company of the virtuous.
These are two verses of perfect enlightenment.
In this context, *ruhagghaso* means one who feeds on raw flesh, a drinker of blood, a violent leopard.
*Galakaṃ anvāvamaddī* means he crushed the neck; the meaning is that having bitten it, he tore it apart.
*Naya* means cause. *Dhamma* means intrinsic nature. *Subhāsitaṃ* means well-spoken words; the meaning is that all of this is absent in a wicked person. "Bhikkhus, apply effort toward the wicked."
One should apply oneself only to making an effort against wicked persons.

And as for the phrase "he does not delight in the virtuous," the meaning is that such a person does not take pleasure in, nor does he cherish, the beautiful and well-spoken words of the virtuous. The ascetic saw all their actions.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the female jackal was the female jackal of today; the leopard was the leopard of today; and the ascetic was none other than myself."
The tenth: The Commentary on the Dīpijātaka.
The Summary of the Jātakas (Jātakuddāna): Kaccānī, Aṭṭhasadda, Sulasā, and Sumaṅgala;
The Gaṅgamāla Cetiya, the burning faculties,
the impossible, and the deer— these ten [cases] belong to the Chapter of Eights.
The commentary on the Chapter of Eights is finished.
9. The Ninth Chapter [427] 1.
The Gijjhakūṭa Jātaka Commentary:
Regarding the one named “The Path Thrown into Confusion,” this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak to.

He related [the story]. It is said that a certain son of good family, although having gone forth into the liberating dispensation, was instructed by his teachers, preceptors, and fellow-celibates who desired his welfare:
"In this way you should advance; in this way you should retreat; in this way you should look forward; in this way you should look around;
in this way you should bend [your limbs]; in this way you should stretch them; in this way you should put on your lower robe..."
One should wear the robes; the bowl should be taken up in this manner; having taken a meal of sufficient size for sustenance, one should consume it only after reflecting upon it;
one should guard the doors of the sense faculties, be moderate in eating, and be devoted to wakefulness—this is what is known as the duty for a visitor;
this is what is known as the duty for one departing; these are the fourteen duties of the Khandhaka.
“There are eighty great duties; therein you must conduct yourselves properly. These are called the thirteen qualities of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga);
having undertaken these, you must live accordingly. While being thus exhorted, he was difficult to speak to, impatient, and unwilling to accept instruction.
“I do not speak to you; but why do you speak to me? I alone [decide] my own welfare or non-welfare.”
“I shall know [the truth] myself,” he made himself unadmonishable. Then, having learned of his ill-natured character, the monks sat in the Dhamma hall discussing his faults.
The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what talk are you sitting here gathered now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he had that monk summoned and said, “Is it true, as it seems, that...”

Having asked, "Monk, are you difficult to speak to? and being told, "It is true," he said, "Why, monk, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, do you not act according to the words of those who desire your welfare?
Previously too, by not acting on the words of the wise, you were ground to dust in the mouth of the Veramba wind.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, on Vulture Peak Mountain, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a vulture.
His son, named Supatta, was a king of vultures who possessed great strength and was surrounded by many thousands of vultures. He supported his parents;
however, because of his great strength, he would fly up to an exceedingly great distance. Then his father said to him, "Dear one, such a place as this..."
“You must not go beyond [this point],” he advised. Although the bird replied, “Very well,” one day, when it had rained, it flew up together with the vultures;
but leaving the others behind, it went too far and, having encountered the mouth of the Verambha wind, was reduced to dust and fragments.
The Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke these verses to illustrate that matter:
“There was a path known as Parisaṅkupatha, an ancient vulture track.
There lived a mother and father who were aged vultures whom he supported;
he repeatedly brought them the flesh of pythons.”
And the father spoke to his son, who knew how to fly high, possessed of beautiful wings,
endowed with strength, radiant, and capable of traveling far:
“When you perceive, my dear, that the earth is overflowing— ”
"Surrounded by the ocean, it is perfectly circular like a wheel;
therefore, dear father, turn back from there—do not go further beyond this.
"You have flown up with great speed, O powerful bird, best among the winged ones!"
Surveying the mountain peaks and forests,
Vakkaṅga saw the earth— just as his father had described it—
encircled by the ocean, perfectly round like a wheel.
“Having transcended that, he reached the supreme state beyond all turning back;
yet even that sharp crest of the wind the twice-born Bali could not surpass.
No person who has gone beyond can ever return again.”
The brahmin met with disaster, having fallen under the power of the Verambha winds.
His sons, his wives, and all those others who depended on him—
all met with disaster because they did not heed his advice.
“Even so, one who here does not understand the words of the elders—
proud, transgressing the bounds, like a vulture whose instruction has passed him by—
he indeed meets with disaster for having failed to follow the instruction of the elders.”
In this context, *parisaṅkupatha* means a "stake-path. People traveling there for the sake of gold and bullion would drive stakes into that place, tie ropes to them, and proceed;
therefore, that footpath on Mount Gijjha is called a "stake-path" (*saṅkupatha*).
*Gijjhapantha* is the great road at the summit of Mount Gijjha. *Sanantano*...
"Of old. "There was" means that on that path of spikes at the summit of Vulture Peak, there was a vulture who supported his aged parents.
"Fat of pythons" means the fat of pythons. "He brought excessively" means he brought it in great abundance. "Frequently" means many times.
"Knowing [him] to be leaping to a high place" means that having heard, "Your son is jumping to a very high place," [he thought], "To a high..."
"Thinking, 'This one will fall,' they know. 'Possessed of splendor' means endowed with human majesty. 'Far-reaching' means far-reaching by that very splendor.
'Leaping about' means floating upon the water like a lotus leaf. 'Know' means you understand.
'Like a wheel, perfectly round' refers to Jambudīpa as it appears, delimited by the ocean, from the position where you stand."
"It appears like a wheel-circle; therefore, my dear, turn back"—thus he spoke, advising him.
"You have flown up" means that one day, having failed to follow his father's advice, he flew up with the vultures and, leaving them behind, went to the place mentioned by his father.
"Looking down" means having reached that place, looking downward. "Vakkaṅga" means...
"Vaṅkagīvo" (crooked-necked). "Yathāsāsi pitussutaṃ" means he saw exactly as it had been heard from his father;
there is also a reading, "yathāssāsī. "Paramevaccavattatha" means he indeed overstepped the place declared by his father.
And "tañca vātasikhā tikkhā" means that sharp crest of the Verambha wind [struck] that twice-born bird, even though he was powerful and beyond admonition.
He overstepped and transgressed; he reduced [him] to powder and fragments. "He was unable to go beyond" means he was not able to pass over.
"A person" means a sentient being. "To one who does not accept advice": while that brahmin was not following the advice of the wise, they all fell into great suffering.
"Without having acted upon the instruction of the elders" means that, by not acting upon the words of the elders who desire their welfare, such is indeed the calamity [that follows].
“He incurs great suffering. Therefore, monk, do not be like the vulture; act upon the words of those who wish you well.
Having been thus exhorted by the Teacher, from that time forward he became easy to speak to.

When the Teacher had delivered this Dhamma teaching, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the ill-behaved vulture was the present ill-behaved monk, while the father of the vulture was none other than I myself.”
The First: The Commentary on the Vulture’s Peak Birth Story (Gijjhajātakavaṇṇanā).
2. The Commentary on the Kosambī Birth Story (Kosambiyajātakavaṇṇanā): "A Great Crowd.
This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Ghosita’s Monastery near Kosambī, concerning those who were quarreling in Kosambī.
He spoke concerning the bhikkhus. The background story is already recorded in the *Kosambaka-kkhandhaka*; this, however, is the summary here.
At that time, it seems, two bhikkhus were living together in one residence: a master of the Vinaya and a master of the Suttantas.
One day, after the master of the Suttantas had performed his bodily ablutions, he placed the remainder of the water used for rinsing in a vessel at the water cistern.
He went out. Later, the master of the Vinaya entered there, and seeing that water, he went out and asked the other, "Friend, was the water set aside by you?
"Yes, friend. "But do you not know that this constitutes an offense?
"Yes, friend, I do not know. "There is an offense here, friend. "In that case, I shall make amends for it."
"No," [he replied]. "But if, friend, it was done by you unintentionally and through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense.
Thus, he held the view that there was no offense for that transgression.
The holder of the Vinaya also informed his own dependents, "This master of the Suttantas does not even know when he incurs an offense. When they saw his dependents, [they said], "Your preceptor..."
"Even after committing an offense, he does not recognize its nature as an offense," they said. They went and reported this to their own preceptor.
He replied, "This master of the Vinaya previously said it was 'no offense,' yet now he says it is 'an offense';
he is a liar. They went and told one another, "Your preceptor is a liar. Thus they spoke to each other.
They increased their quarreling. Then, having obtained the opportunity, the Vinaya-master performed an act of suspension against him for his failure to acknowledge an offense.
From that time on, the lay devotees who provided them with requisites were divided into two factions.
The nuns who received their exhortations and the guardian deities were also divided into two factions. Even the deities dwelling in the sky who were their close friends and companions [were divided].
As far as the Brahma-world, all the worldlings were divided into two factions. This clamor even reached as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm.

Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Tathāgata and reported their view: "This one was suspended by a legitimate act, while those who follow the suspended one were suspended by an illegitimate act," even though they were being restrained by the suspenders.
Having followed them, he reported their conduct to the Teacher. The Blessed One, thinking, "Let them indeed be reconciled," sent word twice;
but hearing, "Venerable Sir, they do not wish to be reconciled," on the third occasion, thinking, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split," he went into their presence.
Regarding the suspension of those who had suspended others, and regarding the other [accused] who were acting unintentionally—
Having spoken of the danger in not acknowledging an offense, he departed.

Later, while they were performing the Uposatha and other rites within that very same boundary, he established a rule for the dining hall (*bhattagga*) for those who had fallen into quarreling, stating: "One must sit with a seat between oneself and another.
Hearing that they were still living in quarrel even then, he went there and said: "Enough, monks!"
After saying, "Do not quarrel," and so forth, when a certain monk who speaks according to the Dhamma, not wishing to cause trouble for the Blessed One, said:
"Let the Blessed One come, O Lord, the Master of the Dhamma; let the Blessed One, O Lord, dwell at ease, devoted to the pleasant abiding in this very life;
we shall be known by that quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute."
"Once upon a time, monks, there was a king of Kāsi in Bārāṇasī named Brahmadatta.

Having thus related how Brahmadatta, after refusing to hand over the kingdom to Dīghīti, the King of Kosala, was killed while living in disguise, and how Prince Dīghāvu gave him his own life, and how from that time forth they lived in harmony; [he spoke].
“Bhikkhus, it is indeed remarkable that those kings—who have taken up the rod and taken up the sword—should possess such patience and gentleness.
It would truly befit you, bhikkhus, that having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, you should likewise be patient and gentle.
Having thus exhorted them, for a second and a third time he said: “Enough! …”
Having restrained them, saying, "Monks, do not quarrel," and seeing that they would not desist, [the Blessed One thought], "These foolish men are obstinate;

it will not be easy to convince them. He departed. On the following day, having returned from his almsround and rested for a short while in the Fragrant Chamber, he tidied his lodging, took his own bowl and robes, and appeared in the midst of the Saṅgha in the air.
Standing there, he spoke these verses:
“The crowd is loud and the people are gathered; do not think that anyone here is a fool.
While the Saṅgha is being split, they did not think of anything else as more important.”
“Those who are utterly deluded, though appearing wise, speak only within the range of mere words;
they utter whatever comes from their mouths, not knowing that by which they are led away.
‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me’—”
And for those who harbor resentment toward him, their enmity is not appeased.
“He reviled me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me”—
but for those who do not harbor such resentment, their enmity is appeased.
“Indeed, hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world;
it is appeased by non-hatred alone. This is an eternal law.
But others do not understand that we are practicing restraint here.”
And those who understand this therein, from that their quarrels are stilled.
Even for those who break bones, take away life, and carry off cattle,
horses, and wealth— for those plundering the kingdom, there is still association.
Why should it not be so for you?
“If one should find a prudent companion who walks together, a wise person living virtuously,
one may travel with them, overcoming all dangers, mindful and contented in heart.”

“If one does not find a prudent companion to walk with—one who is virtuous, steadfast, and lives rightly—then like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom, one should wander alone, like a lone elephant in the forest.
Wandering alone is better; there is no companionship for a fool.”
"One should wander alone, committing no evil deeds, free from concern, like a great elephant in the Mātaṅga forest.
In this context, "puthusaddo" means one who has a widespread, great noise; "samajano" means people who are equal or similar;
that is, all these people who engage in quarreling are both "puthusaddo"—due to the emission of noise from all sides—and "sadiso" (similar). Thus it is said.
“No fool at all was there who thought so”: in that situation, not even a single person thought, "I am a fool";
everyone considered themselves wise, and this entire group was indeed quarrelsome. "No one else thought more":
not even a single person thought, "I am a fool," nor did anyone else think more [of themselves] while the Saṅgha was being split; furthermore, regarding another [thought], "In my..."
The meaning of “the Saṅgha is split by a cause” is that they did not consider this to be the cause.

“Forgetful” means those whose mindfulness is lost. “Appearing wise” means resembling the wise due to their own conceit of being wise. Regarding “those who speak within the range of speech”: the long vowel *rā* has been replaced by its short substitute;
they are those whose range is speech—that is, they do not have the Noble Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness as their range—and who are speakers.
And how do they speak? As far as they wish to open their mouths, as far as they wish to stretch their faces, so far they stretch them, stand on their tiptoes, and speak.
The meaning is that not even a single person, out of respect for the Saṅgha, contracts his mouth [to hide his words].
"By which they were led" means by which quarrel they were led to this state of shamelessness. "The wise do not see that" refers to the danger [of such behavior].
They do not know "this.
And those who harbor resentment toward it means those who harbor resentment toward such forms as "He abused me," and so forth.
"Sanantano" means ancient. "Others" refers to those other than the wise—those who create quarrels; they are called "others" here in the midst of the Saṅgha.
Making a clamor, they do not realize: "We are being subdued, we are being overcome, we are perishing;
we go constantly and continuously into the presence of Death. And those who understand therein—those wise ones there—who understand:
"We are going into the vicinity of Death. Then, monks, their quarrels subside; for it is by knowing thus that they apply proper attention.
Having generated [compassion], they apply themselves to the pacification of disputes and quarrels.
The verse beginning with "Those who have cut through the bones" was spoken with reference to Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu;
even for them there was a meeting [of minds]. Why is it not so for you? For you, the bones of neither mother nor father have been cut asunder.
No living beings were seized, nor were cattle, horses, or wealth seized. This is what is meant:

"Monks, even those kings who have taken up the rod and taken up the sword—such is their assembly and gathering, having formed bonds through marriage and alliance, that they share food and drink together;
yet you, having gone forth in such a teaching as this, [have not even committed] a mere personal act of enmity."
"If you cannot abandon [them], what is your status as monks?
The verses beginning with "If one should obtain... are spoken for the purpose of illustrating the praise and blame of a wise companion and a foolish companion.
"Having overcome all dangers" refers to all manifest dangers (*pākaṭa-parissaya*) and concealed dangers (*paṭicchanna-parissaya*).
And having overcome [them], one should dwell with him, contented and mindful.
"Like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom" means that just as King Mahājanaka and King Arindama abandoned their own conquered kingdoms and wandered alone, so too should one wander;
this is the meaning. "Like an elephant in the Mātaṅga forest" means like an elephant (*nāga*) in the Mātaṅga forest. *Mātaṅga* means an elephant.

It is said that "nāga" is a designation for greatness. For just as the Mātuposaka elephant-king wandered alone in the forest and committed no evil deeds, and just as the virtuous elephant-king [did], and just as Pālileyyaka did—thus it is meant:
"one should wander alone and commit no evil deeds."
Although the Teacher had spoken thus, being unable to bring those bhikkhus into harmony, he went to the village of Bālakaloṇaka.
There, having explained the benefits of living alone to the elder Bhagu, he then went to the dwelling place of three clansmen and spoke to them on the benefits of living in concord.
From there, he went to the Pālileyyaka forest grove and, while staying there—
Having stayed for three months, instead of returning to Kosambī, he went directly to Sāvatthī.
The lay followers living in Kosambī thought, "These venerable monks from Kosambī have caused us much harm;
the Blessed One departed because he was oppressed by them. We shall neither pay homage to them nor offer almsfood to those who come to us."
"Let us give [them this punishment]; thus they will either depart, or cease their enmity, or else they will inspire confidence in the Blessed One.
Having deliberated thus, they did exactly so. Oppressed by that disciplinary measure, they went to Sāvatthī and asked the Blessed One for forgiveness.
After delivering this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "The father was the Great King Suddhodana, the mother was Mahāmāyā, and Prince Dīghāvu was none other than I myself."
The second *Kosambiya-jātaka* commentary.
[429] 3. The *Mahāsūva-jātaka* commentary:
"When the tree..."—this was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu.
It is said that after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, he dwelt in a forest near a certain frontier village in the Kosala country.

People prepared resting places for him by night and by day, and having constructed a dwelling in a location convenient for coming and going, they attended upon him with great care. While he had entered the rains retreat, even in the first month, it happened thus:
That village was burned down, and not even a seed’s worth remained for the people. They were unable to give him choice almsfood.
Exhausted by the lack of almsfood, even though his lodging was suitable, he was unable to produce either the path or the fruit.
Then, when he had come to pay homage to the Teacher at the end of the three months’ residence, the Teacher greeted him with words of welcome.
Having done so, he asked, "I hope, monk, that you are not distressed by lack of almsfood, and that the lodging has been suitable for you?
He reported the matter to him. The Teacher, knowing that the lodging was indeed suitable for him, said:
"Monk, when a recluse has a suitable lodging, he should abandon greedy conduct and, having consumed whatever little he has obtained, [should remain content]."

It is fitting for one who is content to practice the duty of a recluse. Long ago, even after being reborn in the animal realm, the ancient wise ones—though eating the dust on the very tree where they lived—abandoned greed, remained content, did not break the bond of friendship, and did not go elsewhere;
why then do you say, "The alms-food is meager and coarse," and [seek] a comfortable dwelling?
Having said, "Give it up," when he was requested by him, [the Buddha] related a story of the past.
In the past, on the banks of the Ganges in the Himālayas, there lived many hundreds of thousands of parrots in a certain Udumbara forest.
There, a king of the parrots, when the fruits of his own dwelling-tree were exhausted, [saw] whatever sprout remained.
Whether it was a leaf, bark, or a strip of wood, he would eat that, drink water from the Ganges, and being supremely content with few desires, would not go elsewhere.
By virtue of his quality of contentment with few desires, the palace of Sakka trembled.
Sakka, reflecting and seeing him, used his own supernatural power for the purpose of testing him, [transforming] that tree—
He dried it up. The tree, reduced to a mere stump and riddled with holes, stood there as if being struck by the wind.
From its holes, fine dust emerged. King Suva, having eaten that dust and drunk water from the Ganges, did not go elsewhere;
disregarding the wind and heat, he sat upon the Udumbara stump. Sakka...
Knowing his state of supreme fewness-of-wishes, one king of swans said, "I shall speak of the virtue of the duty of friendship, grant him a boon,
and having turned the udumbara fruit into the fruit of the Deathless, I will return. Having placed the Asura maiden Sujā before him,
he went to that udumbara grove and sat upon the branch of a tree not far away, and engaged in conversation with him.
While giving rise [to this thought], he spoke the first verse:
“When a tree has come into fruition, birds flock together and eat from it.
But knowing that the tree’s fruit has been exhausted, the birds then depart from there in every direction.”
The meaning of this is as follows: O King, when a tree is laden with fruit, birds consume it while flying from branch to branch;
but knowing it to be exhausted and the fruits having ceased, the birds depart from that tree in every direction.
Having spoken thus, he then uttered a second verse in order to dismiss him:
“Wander on your journey, O red-beaked one; do not die! Why, O bird, do you brood upon this withered tree?
Pray tell me, you who resemble the springtime, why, O bird, do you not abandon this withered tree?”
In this context, "you meditate" means: for what reason do you stand there, meditating and brooding upon the top of a dry stump?
"Iṅgha" is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. "Resembling springtime": during the spring season, a forest grove possesses a green luster as if crowded with flocks of beautiful birds;
therefore, he addresses him as "resembling springtime. "You do not neglect" means you do not abandon it.
Then Suva-rāja said to him, “O swan, out of gratitude and thankfulness for what has been done for me, I shall not abandon this tree,” and he spoke these two verses:
“Those who indeed become helpers to their friends, O swan, in times of danger, in suffering or in happiness—
whether their own merit be exhausted or not exhausted— they do not abandon them, being virtuous and mindful of the way of the good.”
“I am one among the good, O swan; this tree is my kinsman and my friend.
I cannot bring myself to abandon it for the sake of a livelihood, for knowing it to be exhausted, [I think]:
‘This is not the right way. In that context, “those who are helpers to their friends” means those who are companions to their companions. “Exhausted or even unexhausted” means...
The wise do not abandon their companion even when that companion is exhausted by the depletion of wealth, as if it were not exhausted at all.
"Recalling the Dhamma of the virtuous" means recollecting the lineage of the wise.
"And my kinsman," O King of Swans—this tree is my kinsman in the sense of being a source of affection, and it is my friend because of the practice of mutual association. "For the sake of livelihood."
“Desiring a livelihood, I am unable to abandon him.
When Sakka heard his words, he was pleased and, having praised him, spoke two verses, wishing to grant him a boon:
“Excellent! A witness has been made; there is friendship, intimacy, and association.”
“If you approve of this Dhamma, you are praiseworthy in the eyes of the wise.
“O beautiful one, O bird who travels on wings, I grant you a boon.
Choose a boon, O Vakkaṅga, whatever you desire in your heart.”
In this context, "good" (*sādhu*) is an expression of encouragement. "Friendship has been made" means that there is friendship, intimacy, and socializing in the midst of the assembly;
thus, the friendship you have established is good, well-acquired, and truly auspicious. "If this is the Dhamma" means if this is the duty of a friend.
"By one who understands" means: since this is so, you are worthy of praise by the wise.
"Meaning. "So te" means "that [gift] for you. "Varassu" means "choose. "Yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi" means "whatever you desire in your mind; I grant all that boon to you.
Having heard this, King Suva, choosing a boon, spoke the seventh verse:
“O swan, if you would grant me a boon, let this tree regain its life;
let it stand forth resplendent, fully grown, with branches and laden with fruit, for I am one who longs for honey.
In this context, *sākhavā* means endowed with branches; *phalimā* means possessed of fruit; and *saṃvirūḷho* means having leaves that have grown out on all sides.
Having become endowed with young leaves, "madhutthika" means that he became one whose fruit was as sweet as honey placed upon sweet fruits already existing; such is the meaning.
Then Sakka, granting him a boon, spoke the eighth verse:
“Behold that noble fruit-bearing [tree]; let it be together with you, right here with the udumbara.
Bearing branches and laden with fruit, having grown well, let it stand there, beautiful and longing for honey.
In this context, “let it be together with you, right here with the udumbara” means: let its dwelling be with you, together with the udumbara tree, as one and the same.
Having spoken thus, Sakka abandoned that physical form and, displaying his own majesty and that of Sujā, took water from the Ganges with his hand and struck the Udumbara stump.
At that very moment, a tree rose up, covered with branches and foliage and bearing sweet fruit; it stood there, full of beauty, like Mount Muṇḍamaṇi. King Suvaṇṇa—
Seeing him, filled with joy, he uttered the ninth verse in praise of Sakka:
“Thus, O Sakka, may you be happy together with all your kinsmen,
just as I am happy today, having seen this tree bearing fruit.”

Sakka, having granted him the boon and turned the udumbara tree into one bearing the fruit of immortality, returned to his own abode together with Sujā. To illuminate this matter, the following verses of the Perfectly Enlightened One are placed at the conclusion:
"Having granted the boon to Suvā and having made the tree bear fruit, he departed with his wife to the Nandana grove of the gods."
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Thus, monk, even though they were reborn in the womb of animals, the ancient wise ones were free from greed for gain.
But why do you, having gone forth in such a dispensation as this, behave with greed for gain?
Go and dwell right there! Having thus assigned a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to him, he identified the Jātaka.
Thus, having gone there, the bhikkhu developed insight and attained arahantship.
At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha, while I myself was King Suvīra.
This is the third commentary, the Mahāsuvajātaka-vaṇṇanā.
[430] 4. The Commentary on the Cūḷasuvajātaka.
"There are trees," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, concerning the Verañjakaṇḍa.
When the Teacher had spent the rains retreat at Verañjā and had gradually arrived at Sāvatthī, the monks were in the Hall of Truth.

How did they report it? "Friends, although the Tathāgata is a delicate Kṣatriya, a delicate Buddha, and endowed with great supernormal power, he was invited by the brahmin Verañjā and stayed for three months;

yet, because of Māra’s enticement, he received not even a single day’s alms from him, and having abandoned the pursuit of greed, he lived for those three months on water mixed with the flour of parched grain."
“Sustaining himself thus, he did not go elsewhere; oh, how great is the state of fewness of desires and contentment possessed by the Tathāgatas!
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is no wonder that the Tathāgata has now abandoned greedy conduct; even in the past, while in the womb of an animal...”
"Even after being reborn, he abandoned the practice of greed," he said, and then related a story from the past. The entire narrative should be expanded upon in the same manner as before:
"There are trees with shimmering leaves, many trees with abundant fruit;
