why then is your mind so devoted to a withered, hollow *koḷāpa* tree?"
“For many numerous years we have enjoyed its fruit;
yet even knowing it to be fruitless, our friendship remains just as it was before.
[We regard] the tree that is withered, the hollow trunk, the leafless and fruitless tree.”
"Leaving him, the birds depart; what fault do you see, O twice-born one?
Those who flock together for the sake of fruit abandon him when he is fruitless;
those of dull wit, intent on their own self-interest, are thus partial."
“Excellent! A witness has been established; friendship flows from familiarity.
If you approve of this Dhamma, you are praiseworthy among those who understand.
Therefore, O beautiful bird, having reached me, I grant you a boon.”
“Choose a boon, Vakkaṅga, whatever you desire in your mind.
“May I indeed see him, my enemy, like a tree bearing fruit;
like a poor man who has found a treasure, may I rejoice again and again.”
“Then, taking the nectar, he sprinkled the tree;
its branches grew forth, providing cool shade and delight.
‘In this way, Sakka, may you be happy together with all your kinsmen.’”
"Just as I am happy today, having seen the tree bearing fruit.
Having granted a boon to Suvassa and having made the tree fruitful,
I departed with my wife for the Nandana grove of the gods."
The questions, the counter-questions, and the meaning should be understood in the same manner as before; however, we shall explain only those words that are not [already] obvious.
"Haripattā" means covered with blue leaves. "Koḷāpe" refers to a sapless tree that, when struck by the wind, emits a sound like that of being beaten.
"Suvassa" means: why did the Venerable Suva’s mind delight in such a tree? "Phalassa" means...
The fruit of this tree. "In many groups of years" means in several groups of years. "Many" means that even though there are many hundreds, they are not merely two or three, but rather numerous.
"Having known" means: O King of Swans, having now known that this tree of ours is fruitless, we nevertheless maintain the same friendship as before with him; indeed, we do not break that friendship.
He spoke thus to show that those who destroy [their own welfare] are indeed called ignoble and base persons.
"Opatta" means leafless, stripped of leaves, or fallen-leaved. "What fault do you see? means:
other birds abandon this place and go elsewhere; what kind of fault do you see in going in such a manner? "Those who seek fruit... [and so forth].
Those birds that flock together and approach for the sake of fruit, knowing it to be fruitless, abandon it.

"Wisdom for one's own benefit" (attatthapaññā) means wisdom for one's own sake; it is called "wisdom for one's own benefit" because their wisdom stands only within themselves, without regard for others.
"Partisans" (pakkhapātino) refers to those who hope only for their own prosperity.
They are called "partial" (*pakkhapātino*) because they cause their own faction to fall and destroy it; or alternatively, they are called "partial" because they fall only toward their own side.

"Perhaps," O King of Swans, "if my wish should be fulfilled, if the boon granted by you should come to pass, perhaps I might again see this tree with its leaves and its fruit; then, as a poor man, [I would find] a treasure."
"Having obtained this again and again, I would rejoice; having seen it, I would be glad.
"Taking the Deathless" means that, standing by his own supernatural power, he took water from the Ganges and sprinkled himself.
In this Jātaka, there are two verses on the Perfectly Enlightened One (Abhisambuddha) along with this one.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Anuruddha was Sakka, and I myself was King Sūra.
This concludes the commentary on the Cūḷasuvajātaka, the fourth.
5. The Commentary on the Haritacajātaka.
"I have heard this from Mahābrahmā"—this was said by the Teacher while staying at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who had become despondent.
For that monk, having seen a well-adorned woman, had become despondent;
with his hair, nails, and beard long, he desired to leave the order, and was brought back against his will by his teachers and preceptors. The Teacher said, "Is it true, monk?"
Having asked, "Are you distressed? and being told, "It is true, Bhante," he said, "For what reason?

When it was replied, "Because of the defilement [arising] from seeing a woman adorned with ornaments, Bhante," he said, "Monk, that which is called 'defilement' destroys one's virtues, yields little gratification, and causes rebirth in hell. How then will this defilement not distress you? For it is not as if Mount Sineru..."
"Having struck it, the wind of the blow feels shame toward the old leaf; for, relying on this very defilement,
even those Great Beings who have attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, while walking in the footsteps of the knowledge of Enlightenment,
were unable to maintain mindfulness and caused their jhāna to vanish," he said, and then related a story from the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family of eighty million in wealth in a certain town.
Because his skin was the color of gold, they gave him the name "Haritacchavikumāra.
When he reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā, mastered the arts, established a household, and after the passing of his parents...
Having surveyed his wealth, he thought, "Only wealth is seen here; those who produced this wealth are not seen.
I too must be ground to dust in the mouth of death. Terrified by the fear of death, he gave a great gift, entered the Himalayas, and went forth as an ascetic.
On the seventh day, he developed the supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the meditative attainments (samāpatti).
Having sustained himself there for a long time on a diet of forest roots and fruits, he descended from the mountain in order to seek salt and sour condiments.
Traveling by stages, he reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park. On the following day, while wandering for alms in Bārāṇasī, he arrived at the king’s gate.
Upon seeing him, the king, with a mind full of faith, had him summoned and seated him upon the royal couch beneath a raised white parasol.

Having had him seated and fed various kinds of exquisite foods, and having become even more deeply inspired with faith at the conclusion of the expression of thanksgiving, he asked, "Venerable sir, where are you going?
When it was replied, "We are seeking a place for the rains residence, Great King," he said, "Very well, venerable sir.
Having eaten his morning meal, he took him and went to a pleasure grove; there, [he prepared] places for staying by night and by day, and so forth.
Having had [the palace] built, he appointed the park-keeper as his attendant, gave him [the gift], paid homage, and departed.
From that time forth, the Great Being resided there for twelve years, eating regularly at the king’s house.
Then one day, as the king was departing to pacify a rebellion on the frontier, he said: “Our field of merit...”
"Do not neglect him," he said, and having entrusted the Great Being to the queen, he departed. From that time forth, she served the Great Being with her own hands.

Then one day, after she had prepared the meal, while he was taking a long time [to eat], she bathed herself in scented water, put on a fine, smooth garment, opened the window-lattices, and fanned the air against her body.
He lay down upon a small couch. The Great Being also, having dressed and clad himself well at an early hour, took his alms-bowl and arrived through the air, reaching the lion-window.
As the queen heard the sound of his bark-garment and rose up in haste, her smooth robe slipped off;
it struck against the eye of the Great Being, which was repelled by that disagreeable object.

Then, within the span of many hundreds of thousands of millions of years, the defilement that had resided within him arose like a venomous snake lying in its basket and caused his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) to vanish.
Unable to establish mindfulness, he went and took the queen by the hand;
at that very moment, they surrounded her with a curtain. Having indulged in worldly pleasures with her and having eaten, he—
Having gone to the park, he continued to act in that same manner from then on.
His indulgence in worldly pleasures with her became known throughout the entire city. The ministers sent a letter to the king stating, "The ascetic Harita acted in this way.
The king, not believing them because they intended to alienate him, went to Bārāṇasī after pacifying the border regions.

Having returned to the city and circumambulated it, he went into the presence of the queen and asked, "Is it true, my lady, that my noble friend, the green-hued ascetic, indulges in worldly pleasures with you? "It is true, Your Majesty," she replied.
Not believing her either, thinking, "I shall question him myself," he went to the park, paid his respects, and stood to one side.
Having sat down, he asked him this first verse:
“I have heard this, Great Brahmā: ‘Hārita enjoys sensual pleasures.
Is this statement false? Are you living in purity?”
In this context, *kaccetaṃ* means: "Is this report we have heard—that 'Hārita is enjoying sensual pleasures'—empty and untrue? Do you live and conduct yourself in purity? He thought:
"Even if I say, 'I do not enjoy them,' this king will still believe me;
for in this world there is no foundation equal to truth. Indeed, those who have abandoned untruth, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, attained enlightenment."
“They are unable to reach it; therefore, it is fitting that I speak only the truth.
For in certain instances, the Bodhisatta indeed commits killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors;

however, there is no such thing as lying when it is preceded by a deliberate intent to deceive for the sake of breaking up an alliance. Therefore, speaking only the truth, he uttered the second verse:
“Just so it is, Great King, as you have heard my words:
I have set out upon a wrong path, infatuated by things that lead to delusion.

In this context, “things that lead to delusion” refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). For the world is deluded by the strands of sensual pleasure, and they in turn delude the world; therefore, they are called “things that lead to delusion.”
Having heard that, the king spoke this third verse:
“What is the purpose of that wisdom, so subtle and well-reflecting,
by which the mind would not dispel the passion that has arisen?”
In this context, *adū* is a particle. This is what is meant: "Venerable sir, medicine is indeed a refuge for one who is ill, and water for one who is thirsty;

but what is the purpose of this subtle wisdom of yours, which considers the welfare of the virtuous, by which you might not again dispel arisen lust? Why was it that your mind was unable to dispel it?"
Then, showing the power of the defilements, Hārita spoke the fourth verse:
“O Great King, these four in the world are exceedingly powerful:
lust, hatred, pride, and delusion, wherein wisdom finds no footing.”
In that context, "where" means in those [states] where, when they have reached their full manifestation, wisdom finds no foothold or support, as if one has fallen into a great flood.
Having heard this, the king spoke the fifth verse:
"The Arahant, endowed with virtue, pure, moves about like Hārita."
"May you be wise and learned; thus may you be esteemed by us.
Therein, "thus esteemed by us" means: "may you, sir, be so esteemed and honored by us.
Then Hārita spoke the sixth verse:
“Even the wise they harm, O King— the seer who delights in the virtues of the Dhamma—
those evil thoughts associated with passion, though beautiful in appearance.
In this context, “beautiful” means they proceed by way of grasping at signs of beauty.
Then, encouraging him to strive for the abandoning of the defilements, the King spoke the seventh verse:
“O Blessed One, this passion born within you, which defiles your complexion—abandon it!
May prosperity attend you; you are renowned as one of great wisdom.”
In that regard, "the destroyer of your beauty" means the destroyer of both the beauty of your body and the beauty of your virtues. "Bahunnāsī" means he was renowned as one who was wise among many.
Then, having regained mindfulness and perceived the danger in sensual pleasures, the Great Being spoke the eighth verse:
"These sensual pleasures are darkness, full of much suffering and great poison."
“I shall seek their root and cut off passion along with its bonds.

In this context, *andhakārake* means that which causes blindness by destroying the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). Regarding *bahudukkhe*, one should demonstrate the great suffering inherent in sensual pleasures by citing such suttas as “Sensual pleasures offer little gratification,” and so forth.
*Mahāvisa* refers to the poison of the defilements (*kilesa*) associated [with those pleasures].
And because of the greatness of both the poison and its ripening, they are called "great poisons. Their root:
I shall seek and search for the root of those sensual pleasures of the aforementioned kind, in order to abandon them. But what is their root? Unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
"I shall cut off lust along with its bond," O Great King—having just now struck it with the sword of wisdom, [I shall sever] the bond of the sign of beauty.
"I shall sever the passion that binds.

Having said this, he requested, "Great King, please grant me leave," and having obtained leave, he entered the leaf-hut, gazed at the *kasiṇa* disk, and once again attained the lost jhāna. Then, emerging from the leaf-hut, he rose into the air.
Having sat down cross-legged and taught the Dhamma to the king, he said, "Great King, because I lived in an improper place, I have incurred reproach in the midst of the great multitude;
be heedful! Now, once again, I shall go to the Anitthigandha forest grove.
While the king was weeping and lamenting, he departed for the Himālayas and, without falling away from his meditative absorption, attained rebirth in the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, knowing the reason for this,
said: “Having spoken thus, the seer Hārita, who was devoted to truth,
having abandoned sensual lust, went to the Brahma-world.”

Having become fully enlightened, he spoke this verse, proclaimed the Truths, and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was weary of the world was established in Arahatship.
At that time, King Ānanda was [the king], while I myself was the ascetic Haritaca.
This is the fifth narrative, the Commentary on the Haritaca Jātaka.
[432] 6. The Commentary on the Birth Story of the Boy Padakusala.
"One who is learned"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain boy.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, this son of a householder became proficient in the *pada* texts even at the age of seven. Then his father [thought]: "This..."
Thinking, "I shall investigate," he went to his friend's house even while the father was unaware of it.
Without asking where his father had gone, he followed his footprints and stood in his father's presence.
Then one day his father asked him, "Dear son, even though I went without letting you know, do you know the place where I went? He replied, "Father, I recognize your footprint."
“I am skilled in the steps,” he said. Then, in order to test him, his father left the house after breakfast, went to the house next door, then entered the second and the third houses;
having emerged from the third house, he returned to his own house, exited through the northern gate, and turned left toward the city.
Having gone to Jetavana and paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to listen to the Dhamma.

The boy asked, "Where is my father? When they replied, "We do not know," he followed his father's footprints, starting from the house of the immediate neighbor and proceeding along the very path his father had taken until he reached Jetavana.
There, having paid homage to the Teacher, [he stood] in the presence of his father.
He stood there. When his father asked him, "How did you know, my son, that I had come here? he replied, "I recognized your footprint and followed it.
The Teacher asked, "What are you saying, lay follower? and [the father] replied, "Venerable sir, this boy is skilled in footprints;
I came by this very means while testing him, and he also [recognized me] at home."
When it was said, "Having seen [them], he has come following my footprints," [the Buddha] replied, "It is not surprising, lay follower, that one should perceive footprints on the ground;
in ancient times, wise men perceived footprints even in the sky. Being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, his chief queen committed adultery. When she was questioned by the king, she said:
“‘If I transgress against you, may I become an ass-faced yakkhinī,’ she swore this oath.
Then, having passed away, she was reborn as an ass-faced yakkhinī on the slope of a certain mountain.

Dwelling in a rock cave, she would seize and devour men traveling along the road from one end of the great wilderness to the other as they wandered back and forth. It is said that she [lived] for three...”
Having served Vessavaṇa for years, she obtained permission to devour humans in a place thirty yojanas long and five yojanas wide.
Then one day, a wealthy, affluent, and prosperous brahmin of handsome appearance, surrounded by many people, set out upon that road. Seeing him, the yakkhinī was delighted and sprang forward.
Seeing him, her attendants fled. She went with the speed of the wind, seized the brahmin, laid him on her back, and as she was going toward the cave, she experienced the touch of a man;
through the power of defilement, she conceived an affection for him and, instead of eating him, made him her husband. From then on, they lived together in harmony.
From that time on, the yakkhinī, seizing men and taking their clothes, rice, oil, and so forth, would bring him various kinds of choice food while she herself ate human flesh.

When it was time for her to depart, out of fear that he might escape, she would block the entrance of the cave with a massive rock before leaving. While they were thus living together in mutual affection, the Bodhisatta—
Having passed away from her place of rebirth, she took conception in the womb of that brahmin.
After ten months had elapsed, she gave birth to a son; having developed a powerful affection for both her son and the brahmin, she nourished them both.
Later, when her son had reached maturity, she placed both the son and the father inside the inner cave and closed the door.
Then one day, the Bodhisatta, knowing that she had gone out, removed the stone and placed his father outside.
When she returned and asked, "By whom was the stone removed? he replied, "Mother, it was removed by me; I cannot sit in the darkness.
Out of affection for her son, she said nothing. Then one day, the Bodhisatta questioned his father.
“Father, my mother’s face is one way, and your faces are another; what indeed is the reason for this?
“Son, your mother is a *yakkhinī* who eats human flesh; we both are humans. “Father, if that is so, why do we live here?
Come, let us go to the path of men. “Son, if we were to flee...”
“Both of us, your mother and I, will be eaten by you. The Bodhisatta comforted his father, saying, “Do not fear, dear father;
it is my burden to bring you to a path frequented by humans. The next day, when his mother had gone out, he took his father and fled.
The yakkhinī returned, and not seeing them, she rushed forward with the speed of the wind, seized them, and cried, “Brāhmaṇa, why do you flee?”
"What is it that you lack here? she asked. When he replied, "Bhadde, do not be angry with me;
your son has taken me and is fleeing," she said nothing out of affection for her son, but after comforting them, she took them to her own dwelling place.
In this way, she brought them back again several days later whenever they attempted to flee.
The Bodhisatta thought: "There must be a limited space for my mother;
what if I were to ask her the boundary of her domain of authority, and then escape by overstepping it?
One day, taking his mother aside and sitting with her, he said: "Mother, that which belongs to a mother indeed falls to her sons; please tell me—"

“This much is the extent of my own land,” he said. She described the landmarks of mountains, rivers, and so forth in all directions, and having told her son that it was thirty yojanas in length and five yojanas in width, she said, “Son, take note of this much ground.
After two or three days had passed, when his mother had gone into the forest...
Having placed his father upon his shoulder, he leaped with the force of the wind at her command and reached the bank of the river Paricchanda.
She too came along, not seeing them, and pursued them. The Bodhisatta, taking his father, went into the middle of the river.
She arrived and stood on the riverbank; realizing that she had exceeded her own boundary, she remained right there.
Stopping there, she entreated her son and her husband, saying, "Dear one, take your father and come; what fault is there in me?
Because of me, what is it that you do not succeed? Turn back, my lord! Then the brahmin crossed the river.
She, entreating only her son, said, "Dear one, do not do this; turn back! "Mother, we are human beings..."
“You are a female spirit; it is not possible to live in your presence for all time.
“You will not turn back, my dear? “Yes, mother. “My dear, if you do not turn back, life in the human world is indeed suffering;
those who do not know a craft are unable to survive. I know a spell called the Cintāmaṇi; by its power—”
"Even stolen goods can be identified by following them step by step over the course of twelve years;
this shall be your livelihood, my dear, so learn this priceless mantra. Though overwhelmed by such suffering, she gave him the mantra out of affection for her son.

The Bodhisatta, while still standing by the river, paid homage to his mother, received the mantra with the utmost reverence, and having paid homage to her again, said, "Go now, mother. She replied, "Dear son, if you do not return, I shall have no life left.
He said, "Come, my son, let us return; do not leave me without a protector."
“Today, not seeing her son, the ogress has died.
The ogress beat her breast; at that very moment, her heart burst from grief for her son.
Having died, she fell right there. Then the Bodhisatta, knowing she was dead, called his father and went to his mother’s side.
Having prepared a funeral pyre, cremated [the body], extinguished the funeral fire, and honored him with various kinds of flowers, he paid homage, wept, and lamented.
Taking his father’s remains, he went to Bārāṇasī and stood at the royal gate.
Announcing to the king, “A youth skilled in foot-racing stands at the gate,” and when the king said, “In that case, let him enter,” he went inside and paid homage to the king.
When he was asked, "Father, what craft do you know?", he replied, "Your Majesty, I know how to go step by step and recover goods that have been taken away within the space of twelve years.
"In that case, attend upon me," [the king said]. "Your Majesty, I shall attend upon you while receiving a thousand [pieces of money] daily," he replied.
"Very well, father, attend upon me," [the king said]. The king then had a thousand pieces given to him every day.

Then one day the chaplain said to the king: "Great King, because we have performed no work by virtue of that young man's mastery of his craft, we do not know whether he possesses such skill or not; let us first put him to the test.
The king agreed, saying, "Very well," and both men gave notice to various jewel-keepers.
Taking a basket filled with the essence of jewels, he descended from the palace and, having shaken it three times within the royal residence, set up a ladder;
then, descending by way of the top of the wall, he entered the hall of justice and sat there.
Returning once more, he set up the ladder, descended by way of the top of the wall, and [stood] by the lotus pond in the inner apartments.
Having gone to the bank of the lotus pond, they circumambulated it three times clockwise, descended, placed their bundle inside the pond, and ascended the palace.
On the following day, a great clamor arose: "They have reportedly stolen a treasure from the royal residence!
The king, acting as if he did not know, summoned the Bodhisatta and said, "Dear son, from the royal residence..."
"A great quantity of precious goods has been stolen; come now, it is necessary to search for them," he said.
"Great King, it is no marvel for me—that I am capable of recovering stolen goods by following the thieves' tracks—even to recover goods stolen this very night at the end of twelve years.
I shall bring them back; do not worry. "In that case, bring them here."
Saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," he paid homage to his mother, recited the incantation, and while still standing on the great terrace,
said, "Great King, the footprints of two thieves are visible. Following the tracks of the king and the chaplain,
he entered the chamber of honor, emerged from there, descended from the palace, and circled three times through the vicinity of the royal residence.
Following the very footprints, he went near the wall; standing upon the wall, he said, "Great King, here at this spot, footprints are visible in the air, having been released from the wall.

Have a ladder set up! Having descended the ladder over the top of the wall, he followed the footprints right along to the Hall of Justice, and then, returning again to the royal residence, [he took] the ladder...
Having had it spread out, he descended along the top of the wall, went to the lotus pond, circumambulated it three times to the right,
and said, "Great King, thieves have entered this lotus pond. Then, as if taking it from his own place, he brought forth the bundle,
gave it to the king, and said, "Great King, these two thieves are notorious great thieves who [entered] the royal residence by this path."
“He has climbed aboard,” he said. The great crowd, thrilled and overjoyed, snapped their fingers and waved their garments.
The king thought, “This young man seems to know only the location where the goods were placed by the thieves by following their footprints, but he is unable to capture the thieves themselves.
Then he said to him, “First, [show us] the goods carried off by the thieves...”
“[The goods] were brought by her, but the thieves were not brought. “Great King, the thieves are right here; they are not far away. “Who is a thief? Who is a thief?
“Great King, whoever desires [the goods], he himself becomes a thief. Therefore, since you have already obtained your bundle from them, what use have you for thieves?
Do not ask about them. “My dear, I give you a thousand [pieces of gold] every day.”
“I will give it; seize the thieves and bring them to me. “Great King, once the wealth is obtained, what is the use of the thieves?
“We need the thieves even more than the wealth, dear father. “In that case, Great King, I shall not tell you who these thieves are by name;
however, I will relate to you the events of the past. If you are wise, then...”
"Know the cause," he said, and having spoken thus, he related a story from the past.
In the past, not far from Bārāṇasī, in a village on the riverbank, there lived a dancer named Pāṭali.
On a festival day, taking his wife with him, he entered Bārāṇasī; having danced, played the lute, and sung, he obtained wealth.
At the conclusion of the festival, having had much liquor and food taken [for him], he was going to his own village;
upon reaching the riverbank, seeing the fresh water coming in, he sat down eating the food and drinking the liquor.
Having become intoxicated and being unaware of his own strength, he said to his wife, "I shall tie a great lute around my neck, cross the river, and go."
Taking him by the hand, she descended into the river. Water entered through the holes of the lute, and then that lute caused him to sink.
His wife, perceiving his state of sinking, let go of him, and having crossed over, stood on the bank.
Naṭapāṭali emerged once and sank once; having entered the water, he became bloated in his belly. Then, for him—
His wife thought, "My husband will die now; having requested one song from him, I shall maintain my livelihood by singing it in the midst of the assembly.
Having thought this, she said, "Husband, you are about to submerge yourself in the water;
give me one song, and with that I shall maintain my livelihood," and she spoke this verse:
“The Ganges carries away the *pāṭali* tree, though it is full of sap and a skilled speaker;
O Blessed One, as you are being swept along, give me even a single little verse.
In this context, “a little verse” (*gāthaka*) means a short verse.
Then Naṭapāṭali said to her, "Bhadde, how shall I show you my song? Now this water, which has become a refuge for the great multitude, is killing me," and he spoke this verse:
"That with which they sprinkle the suffering one, that with which they sprinkle the afflicted one—in the midst of it I shall die; fear has arisen from what was once a refuge."
Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta said, “Great King, just as water is a refuge for the multitude, so too are kings;
when fear arises from them, who will ward off that fear? Then he added, “Great King, this matter is hidden;
however, I have explained it by making it intelligible to the wise. Understand this, Great King.”
He said, "Father, I do not understand such cryptic speech; seize the thieves and give them to me.
Then the Great Being brought forward another reason, saying, "In that case, Your Majesty, having heard this, you shall know.
"Your Majesty, formerly, in a village near the gate of this very Bārāṇasī, a certain potter, while bringing clay for the sake of making vessels—"
Having fixed it in one place, he dug a large pit inside the mountain slope.
Then one day, while he was taking the clay, an unseasonable great cloud arose and let fall a heavy rain.
The water, overflowing, filled the pit, and by that his head was broken. Lamenting, he spoke this verse:
“Where seeds sprout, where beings are established—that [earth] presses down upon my head; born from a refuge, there is fear.
In this context, *nipīleti* means that having fallen upon it, it oppresses and crushes.
"Your Majesty, just as the great earth, which serves as the refuge for the masses, split the head of a potter, even so, when a lord of men—
who is like the great earth and the refuge of the entire world— rises up and commits acts of theft, who can restrain him? O Great King,
will you be able to recognize a thief described to you in such a concealed manner?"
“Father, I have no reason to conceal anything; ‘This man is a thief,’ so take this thief and give him to me.
Protecting the king, he did not say, “You are the thief,” but instead cited another example:
“Great King, formerly in this very city, the house of a certain man caught fire. He said, ‘Enter inside and bring out the goods.’”
He gave another order. When [the man] had entered and was being led out, he closed the door of the house.
Blinded by smoke and unable to find the way out, suffering from the pain of a rising fever, he lamented while still inside and spoke this verse:
“By which the meals are cooked, by which one is afflicted by cold;”
"So it burns my limbs; fear has arisen from what was a refuge.
Regarding that, "So maṃ ḍahati" means "it burns me," or this very reading [so me ḍahati] is the text.
"O Great King, just as fire is a refuge for the multitude, a certain man carried away a bundle of jewels."
"Do not ask me about the thief. "Father, give me the thief indeed!

Without saying to the king, "You are the thief," he brought forward another illustration: "Your Majesty, formerly in this very city, a certain man, having eaten far too much and being unable to digest it, fell into agony and, lamenting, spoke this verse:"
“The food by which the many brahmins and khattiyas sustain themselves—that very food, when eaten, destroys me; fear has arisen from that which was my refuge.
In this context, “that food, when eaten, destroys me” means that the boiled rice, once consumed, kills me.
“Great King, there was once a man who stole a single article of merchandise that served as the sole refuge for the multitude, like food.
Now that it has been recovered, why do you ask about the thief? “My dear son, if you are able, give me the thief,” he said.
To convince him, the king brought forth another illustration: “Great King, in the past, in this very city, a wind arose...”
His limbs broke. Lamenting, he spoke this verse:
“In the last month of summer, the wise desire a breeze;
but it breaks my limbs—fear has arisen from that which was my refuge.”
"Thus, Great King, know that fear arises from taking refuge; understand that to be the cause. "Dear father, give me a thief," he said.

For the sake of convincing him, he brought forward another illustration: "Your Majesty, in the past, in a region of the Himalayas, there was a great tree endowed with branches and foliage, rich in flowers and fruit, a dwelling place for many thousands of birds. Of that tree, there were two branches..."
They struck one another, from which smoke arose and sparks of fire fell. Seeing this, the chief of the birds spoke this verse:
“Since even this tree upon which you depend emits fire, O Vakkaṅga birds, seek other directions;
there is danger born from that which provides refuge.”
"In that regard, 'jagatiruha' means a tree.
For just as a tree, O King, is a refuge for birds, so too is a king a refuge for the great multitude;
if he commits theft, who will restrain him? Please consider this, Your Majesty. "Dear father, for me, it is only a thief..."

"Give it," he said. Then he brought another illustration to him: "Great King, in a certain village of Kāsi, on the western side of a certain household, there was a harsh river inhabited by crocodiles. That family had only one son.
When his father passed away, he looked after his mother. His mother, against his will, [brought] a daughter of a noble family..."
She brought her back. Previously, she had been affectionate toward her mother-in-law, but later, as her own sons and daughters grew up, she desired to have her removed.

Her mother also lived in that very same house. [The daughter-in-law], speaking of various faults of the mother-in-law to her husband and causing a rift between them, said: "I am unable to support your mother; kill her!"
When it was said, "Killing a human being is a grave matter;
how shall I kill him?", he replied, "We will take him along with his bed at the time he goes to sleep and throw him into the Susumāra River; then the crocodiles will devour him.
[The other asked: "But where is your mother? "She sleeps right there beside him. "In that case, go to her..."
“Having tied a rope to the bed where you are lying, give the signal. She did so and said, “I have given the signal.
The other replied, “Wait a little while; let the people sleep first,” and then, as if falling asleep, he lay down.
Having gone there, he tied that rope to his wife’s mother’s bed, woke his wife, and both of them departed.
They lifted him up along with his bed and threw him into the river. While he was sleeping there, crocodiles tore him apart and devoured him.
On the following day, having realized that his mother had been turned over, he said, "Master, my own mother has been killed; now it is your turn."
Having said, "Kill your mother," when he replied, "In that case, very well," she said, "Let us build a funeral pyre in the charnel ground, place her upon it, and kill her with fire.
Then, while he was sleeping, they both led him to the charnel ground and set him down there.
There, the husband said to his wife, "Has the fire been brought? "I have forgotten it, husband. "In that case, go and..."
“Bring it! [he said]. “I cannot go, Master; even if you go, I will not be able to remain behind. We both shall go.

When they had gone, the old woman was awakened by the cold wind; realizing she was in a cemetery and reflecting, “These men have gone for the sake of fire, wishing to kill me,” and thinking, “They do not know my strength,” she [seized] a corpse.
Having taken her, he laid her down upon a couch, covered her with a cloth, and fleeing himself, entered that very rock cave.
The others, having brought fire and thinking she was "old," cremated the corpse and departed.
A certain thief, who had previously deposited a bundle in that rock cave, came there thinking, "I shall take it."
Seeing an old woman, [the man] thought, "She must be a female spirit (yakkhinī); my bundle has been seized by a non-human being," and so he brought a physician who treats spirits.
While the physician was reciting a mantra, he entered the cave.
Then she said to him, "I am not a female spirit; come, let us both divide this wealth. He asked, "How can this be believed?"
“Place your tongue upon my tongue,” she said. He did so. Then, having bitten his tongue and cut it off, she made it fall out.
The spirit-doctor, thinking, “This is certainly a female *yakkha*,” fled wailing as blood flowed from his tongue.
On the following day, the old woman dressed herself in a polished robe and [carried] a bundle of various precious gems.
Having taken it, she went home. When her daughter-in-law saw it, she asked, "Mother, where did you get this?
She replied, "Daughter, in this cemetery, those who are cremated on a wooden pyre receive such things as these. [The daughter-in-law said,] "Mother, I too can obtain one.
[Her mother-in-law said,] "You will obtain one if you become like me. Out of greed for the goods she could obtain, she told her husband.
There she burned herself. Then, on the following day, her husband, not seeing her, said:
"Mother, you have arrived at this time, but your daughter-in-law has not come. Hearing this, she rebuked him, saying, "O wicked man, how can one who is dead come back? and spoke this verse:
“I brought her joy, Mālinī, adorned with sandalwood paste;
yet she casts me out from my home—fear has arisen from that which was once a refuge.
Therein, *somanassaṃ* means having produced joy. The reading *somanassā* also exists, meaning “having become one possessed of joy.”

The meaning is this: "She whom I brought home with joy—having adorned her by anointing her with garlands and sandalwood paste, thinking, 'By relying on her, my son will increase through sons and daughters, and he will support me in my old age'—she today casts me out from the house;
indeed, fear has arisen in me from that very refuge."
“Great King, just as a daughter-in-law is to her mother-in-law, so is the king the refuge for the multitude; therefore, when fear arises, what can be done?
Observe this, O Lord. Having heard that, the king said, “Dear son, I do not know the reasons you have brought forward;
give me the thief himself. He, thinking, “I shall protect the king,” brought forward another illustration.
"Your Majesty, formerly in this very city, a certain man made an aspiration and obtained a son.
At the time of his son's birth, filled with joy at the thought, 'I have gained a son,' he raised him; and when the boy reached maturity, he provided him with a wife.
Later, having fallen into old age, the man was unable to attend to his work. Then his son said to him, 'You are no longer able to do the work.'"
“Come out from here! he said, and he was driven out of the house. Finding his livelihood with great difficulty and hardship, he lamented and spoke this verse:
“The very one by whose birth I would have rejoiced, and for whom I desired existence—that very one now casts me out from my home; fear has arisen from that which was my refuge.”
"In this regard, 'he' refers to that son who casts me out from the house and drives me away. Thus, I live in misery by wandering for alms; indeed, fear has arisen for me even from my own refuge.
"Great King, just as a father, being elderly, must be protected by a capable son, so too must the entire realm be protected by the king.
And this fear that arises [is a threat] to the king who protects all beings."
“O King, because it arose from his very presence, know by this reason that ‘such-and-such a person is the thief.
“Dear son, I do not know whether there is a reason or no reason; either give me the thief, or you yourself must be the thief.
Thus the king questioned the young man again and again. Then he said to him: “But, Great King, why is it that the apprehension of a thief is absolute?”
“Do you approve? “Yes, father. “In that case, I shall announce in the midst of the assembly:
‘Such-and-such a man and such-and-such a man are thieves. “Do so, father. Having heard his words, [the thief thought], “This king will not allow me to protect myself;
now I shall seize the thief! Then, addressing the great crowd that had assembled, he spoke these verses:
“Listen to me, O people of the countryside, and you citizens gathered here:
where there was water, there is now fire; where there was safety, there is now fear.
The king plunders the realm, as does the brahmin court priest.”
“Dwell guarded within yourselves; for from what is born comes fear.
In this context, “where there is water, there is fire” means that very same water is ablaze.
“Where there is safety” means that from the king, by whom safety ought to be provided, fear has arisen. “Dwell guarded within yourselves” means that you are now without a protector.
"O people, do not destroy yourselves! Being guarded by yourselves, protect your own wealth and grain.
A king is indeed the refuge of the great multitude; therefore, this fear has arisen among you.
Both the king and the chaplain are plundering thieves. If you wish to apprehend thieves, seize these two and have them punished."

Having heard his words, they thought: "Even though this king is one who ought to provide protection, he now casts the blame upon another and, having placed his own bundle by the lotus pond himself, has him search for the thief.
From now on, we must kill this wicked king so that he will never again commit such thievery. With clubs and mallets in their hands, they...
Rising right there, they beat the king and the chaplain to death, bringing them to their end, and having consecrated the Great Being, they established him in the kingdom.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "It is not surprising, lay follower, that one should perceive footprints on the earth."
"Only the ancient wise ones perceived footprints in the sky," he said, and having proclaimed the Truths, he identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, both the lay follower and his son were established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti).
At that time, the father was Kassapa, and the youth skilled in footprints was none other than myself.
The Sixth: The Commentary on the *Padakusala-Māṇava-Jātaka*.
7. The Commentary on the *Lomasakassapa-Jātaka*:
"That king was like Indra," this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain monk who was disenchanted with the religious life.
He related it. For the Teacher, having asked that bhikkhu, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are disenchanted?
and being told "It is true," said: "Bhikkhu, will the wind that shakes Mount Sineru not shake even old leaves?
Even noble persons endowed with glory encounter misfortune; these defilements make even perfectly pure beings defiled."
Having said, "How much more so one such as that," he was requested by him to relate a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares,
two friends— the prince of Brahmadatta named Brahmadattakumāra and the son of the royal priest named Kassapa— studied all the arts under the same teacher’s family.
They mastered them. Later on, when Prince Brahmadatta was established in the kingdom upon the passing of his father, Kassapa thought:
"My friend has become king; now he will grant me great power. But what use have I for power?
Having asked leave of my parents and the king, I shall go forth into the homeless life. He then [approached] the king and his parents...
Having taken leave [of his family] and entered the Himālaya mountains, he went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.

On the seventh day, having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he dwelt subsisting on gleaned food. Because he had gone forth, they knew him as "Lomasakassapa.
He became an ascetic of fierce austerity with his faculties perfectly conquered. By his spiritual power, the palace of Sakka...
He trembled. Sakka, perceiving this as he reflected, thought: "This ascetic possesses such exceeding fierce power that he might even displace me from my status as Sakka.
Joining forces with the King of Bārāṇasī, I shall shatter his asceticism.
By means of his Sakka-power, at the hour of midnight, he entered the royal bedchamber of the King of Bārāṇasī and filled the entire chamber with the radiance of his body.
Having illuminated the area, he stood in the air before the king and woke him, saying, “Arise, Great King!
When asked, “Who are you? he replied, “I am Sakka. “For what purpose have you come? “Great King, do you desire sole sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa, or not?
“Why would I not desire it? Then Sakka said to him, “In that case, [go to] Lomasakassapa...”

"Having brought [them], perform a sacrifice of animal slaughter; becoming equal to Sakka and free from old age and death, you shall rule over the whole of Jambudīpa," he said, and spoke the first verse:
"O King, may you be like Indra, forever free from old age and death; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“If you were to perform a sacrifice, [bring] the seer Lomasakassapa.
In this context, *assa* means “you will be. *Yājeyyāsi* means “if you were to bring the seer Lomasakassapa from the forest region and perform a sacrifice.
Having heard his words, the king accepted it, saying, “Very well. Sakka said, “In that case, do not delay.”
Having said this, he departed. On the following day, the king summoned his minister named Seyya and said, "Friend, go to my dear companion Lomasakassapa and speak these words on my behalf:

'It is said that after you have caused the sacrifice of animals to be performed, the king will become the sole ruler of the whole of Jambudīpa; therefore, whatever territory you desire for yourselves..."
“He will grant you that much; come with me to perform a sacrifice,” he said.

“Very well, Your Majesty,” [the king] replied, and having had a drum beaten in the city to find the ascetic’s dwelling place, when a forest-dweller said, “I know it,” the king placed him in front and went there with a great retinue. Having paid homage to the seer, he said:
Seated to one side, he reported that message.
Then, saying to him, "Seṭṭha, what is this you are talking about?", he spoke four verses in refusal:
"The earth, bounded by the ocean, with the sea as its earrings;..."
One should not desire association with blame; know this to be superior.
"Fie on that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O Brahmin, which is obtained through a downfall or by practicing unrighteousness!"
“Even if one goes forth as a homeless wanderer, taking up the alms-bowl,
that very livelihood is better than seeking by unrighteous means.
Even if one goes forth as a homeless wanderer, taking up the alms-bowl...”
“Better than sovereignty over this earth, bounded by the ocean, with its garland of seas—that is better.

In that context, “bounded by the ocean” means surrounded by the ocean. “With the ocean as its earrings” means it is endowed with oceans situated around the four continents like earrings placed upon the lobes of the ears. “Together with blame” means: “By this...”
With this reproach, "The act of slaughtering animals has been committed," he says, "I do not desire even the great earth as far as the limits of the world-system.
By the phrase "the way of life through falling away," he indicates: "Fie upon that way of life which exists through the karma of falling into hell;
I condemn that way of life. "That very livelihood" refers to the clay bowl of one who has gone forth.

The meaning is that a life of seeking food and maintaining one's livelihood by visiting the houses of others is a hundredfold and a thousandfold more excellent than the acquisition of fame and wealth;
even sovereignty is considered inferior to that state of homelessness for one who does not harm others while wandering—
the meaning is that it is superior even to the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.
Having heard his words, the minister went and informed the king. Upon hearing this, the king remained silent, thinking, "What can be done if he does not come?

Then, at the hour of midnight, Sakka returned, stood in the air, and asked, "Great King, why have you not had the sacrifice performed after bringing Lomasakassapa? [The king replied,] "Even though I sent for him, he does not come."
“In that case, Great King, have your daughter, Princess Candavatī, adorned with ornaments and sent to her bed as before, and have it said:
‘If you come and perform the sacrifice, the King will give this maiden to you.
Surely, having his heart bound by the maiden, he will come. The King accepted, saying, “Very well.”
On the following day, he gave his daughter into the hand of Seyya.
Taking the king’s daughter with him, he went there, paid homage to the seer, and after exchanging greetings, showed the king’s daughter—who resembled a celestial nymph—to him and stood to one side.
Then the seer, having broken his sense-faculties, gazed at her; at the very moment of that gaze, his mind became bound by passion for her.
Having performed the sacrifice, he fell away from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*). A minister, perceiving that the king’s mind was bound to her, said:
"Venerable sir, if you should indeed perform the sacrifice, the king will give this girl to you as a foot-attendant.
Shaking with the power of defilement (*kilesa*), he said: "They will indeed give her to me? [The minister replied: "Yes, they will give her to you when you perform the sacrifice."
Saying, "Excellent! Having obtained this, I shall perform the sacrifice," he took it and, mounting the decorated chariot together with his matted locks, went to Bārāṇasī.
The king, having heard that he was coming, began the work at the sacrificial enclosure.
Then, seeing him arrived, [the other said]: "Perform the sacrifice tomorrow; I shall become equal to Indra at the conclusion of the sacrifice."
“I will give you my daughter,” he said. Kassapa accepted, saying, “Very well.
Then, on the following day, the king took him along with Candavatī and went to the sacrificial enclosure.
There, all four-footed creatures—elephants, horses, bulls, and so forth—had already been arranged in rows. Kassapa began to perform the sacrifice by killing and slaughtering them all.
Then the great multitude gathered there, seeing him, said, "Lomasakassapa, this is improper and unseemly for you;
what is it that you are doing? and lamenting, they spoke these two verses:
"The moon has power, the sun has power, and the recluses and brahmins have power."
"The ocean's strength is its tide, but women are stronger than the strongest.
Just as Candavatī, for the sake of her father, caused the Vājapeyya sacrifice to be performed for the seer Lomasakassapa, who was peaceful and possessed of fierce asceticism."
In this context, regarding the dispelling of great darkness, there is no power other than that of the moon and the sun;

the meaning is that the moon and the sun alone are powerful here. "Ascetics and brahmins" refers to those who possess the power of patience and the power of knowledge in enduring the force of desirable and undesirable sense objects—ascetics and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil. "The power of the shore..."
"Of the ocean" means that the shore is called "strength" because of its capacity to block the waters of the great ocean and destroy them by not allowing them to cross over.

"Women are stronger than strength" means that women are called "exceedingly strong" even compared to all those other strengths, because they are capable of bringing even those with sharp wisdom who have not yet abandoned passion under their own control and destroying them. [They are] stronger than all strengths.
The meaning is: "The power of women alone is great. "Yathā" means "because. "For the sake of the father" means for the sake of the father's prosperity.

This is what is intended: because this Candavatī, while he was an *isi* (sage) possessing such intense asceticism due to his pursuit of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), has rendered him devoid of virtue and is causing him to perform the Vājapeyya sacrifice for the sake of her father's prosperity; therefore, this must be understood.
“Women possess power beyond measure.
At that time, Kassapa, intending to perform a sacrifice, raised his sword-jewel, thinking, “I shall strike the auspicious elephant on the neck.
Upon seeing it, the elephant, terrified by the fear of death, let out a great cry. Of him—
Hearing that sound, the rest—the elephants, horses, bulls, and others—also cried out in terror, agitated by the fear of death. The great multitude likewise cried out.
Having heard that great outcry, Kassapa was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and looked upon his own matted hair, beard, and body hair.
Then his matted hair, beard, and body hair became visible [as coarse]. Feeling remorseful, he thought: "Alas, this is indeed unbecoming!"
Proclaiming his sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, "I have committed an evil deed," he spoke the eighth verse:
"That deed fashioned by greed, bitter and caused by sensual desire—
I shall seek its root and cut off passion along with all its bonds."
The meaning of this is: Great King, that evil rooted in sensual desire which was committed by me toward Candavatī after I had aroused greed in her—its ripening is bitter and sharp.

I shall seek its root, which is called unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*); enough for me with this sword; having drawn forth the sword of wisdom, [I shall sever] the bond of the sign of the beautiful.
“I shall sever passion along with its bonds.
Then the king said to him, “Do not fear, my friend; I shall now give you Princess Candavatī, the kingdom, and a heap of the seven treasures;
perform the sacrifice! Having heard this, Kassapa replied, “Great King, I have no need for this defilement.”
Having said, "It is enough," he spoke this concluding verse:
"Fie on the many sensual pleasures in the world! Asceticism, O King, is better than the strands of sensual pleasure.
I shall practice asceticism, having abandoned sensual pleasures; let the kingdom and Candavatī remain yours alone."
In that context, "even though very many" means even though there were exceedingly many. "I shall perform asceticism" means he will perform only the asceticism of moral discipline and self-restraint.
Having spoken thus, and having focused his mind on the *kasiṇa* (meditation device), he produced a state of distinction;
sitting cross-legged in the air, he taught the Dhamma to the king, exhorted him with the words "Be heedful," caused the sacrificial enclosure to be demolished, and [for] the great multitude...
Having caused the gift of fearlessness to be given, even as the king was still entreating him, he flew up and went back to his own dwelling place.
Remaining there for the rest of his life, at the end of his lifespan, he was destined for the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka; and at the conclusion of the Truths, [The identification follows: "The king who requested the gift of fearlessness was Ānanda. The one who gave it was myself."
The discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the chief minister Seyya was Sāriputta, while I myself was Lomasakassapa.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Commentary on the Lomasakassapa Jātaka.
[434] 8. The Commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka.
"In saffron robes"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain greedy bhikkhu.
It is said that he was greedy and covetous of requisites; having abandoned his duties toward his teachers and preceptors and so forth, he would go to Sāvatthī every morning.
Having entered and drunk rice-gruel accompanied by various kinds of hard foods in Visākhā’s house, and having also eaten fine rice and meat with various superior flavors, he was still not satisfied;
he then wandered from there to the residences of Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, Mahā-Anāthapiṇḍika, and the King of Kosala, visiting those respective dwellings.
Then one day, concerning his greed, [the matter arose] in the Dhamma Hall.
How did they originate? The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, about what talk are you sitting together here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he had that monk summoned and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are greedy?
When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, why are you greedy? Even in the past, because of your greediness..."
"Having wandered about in Bārāṇasī eating elephant carcasses and such, being unsatisfied with those,
he departed from there and wandered along the banks of the Gaṅgā until he entered the Himālaya," he said, and then related a story of the past: "In the past,
while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a certain greedy crow [was wandering] in Bārāṇasī eating elephant carcasses and such..."
Wandering about after eating, not yet satisfied by those things, he went thinking, "I shall eat dead fish on the bank of the Ganges.
Having stayed there for several days while eating dead fish, he entered the Himālaya mountains.
Eating various fruits and berries, he reached a great lotus lake abounding in fish and turtles; there, he saw two golden-colored cakravāka birds.
Having eaten moss during the springtime and seeing [the birds], he thought: "These are exceedingly endowed with beauty and have attained great fortune;
their food must be delightful. Having asked what their food is, and having eaten that very same thing myself, I too shall become golden-colored.
Thinking thus, he went into their presence, exchanged greetings, and [stood] at the end of one branch.
Having sat down and engaging them in conversation concerning their praise, he spoke the first verse:
“I speak of two birds wearing saffron robes, moving about together in delight.
Among humans, which egg-born creature do they praise as being born from an egg? Pray, tell me that.”
In that passage: "in saffron-colored clothing" means as if in saffron-colored garments of golden hue. "Two by two" means in pairs.
"Rejoicing" means with a joyful mind. Regarding the phrase "O egg-born ones, which egg-born birth do you praise among humans?":
"O egg-born ones," [the meaning is] when you praise humans, which egg-born birth do you say and praise—namely, what kind of egg-born one?
"Which bird? he said; the meaning is: "Which one among humans do you praise? There is also a reading: "Kaṃ aṇḍajaṃ aṇḍajamānusesu" (Which egg-born one among the egg-born and humans?).
Its meaning is: "Having asked 'Which egg-born one [is it]?', you praise [it] among both the egg-born and humans.
Having heard that, the cakravāka bird spoke the second verse:
“They call us human-harmers among humans, though we are Cakkavāka birds;
we are esteemed for our auspicious nature among the birds, and we wander beautiful upon the great lake.
In this context, “human-harmer” means that the crow harms and harasses humans; therefore, he addresses him thus. “Anubbate” means...
Living together in mutual harmony and affection, they dwell in close association. Regarding the *cakkavāka*, they praise, extol, and speak of them as being of the egg-born species.
Among the birds—that is, among all those known as winged creatures—we are recognized by humans as being "of noble nature.
According to the second interpretation of the meaning, humans call us "cakkavākas" among themselves, and [we are so called] among the birds.
But we are considered "of noble nature" (*kalyāṇabhāva*); the meaning is that our fellow-birds call us "of noble nature.
Regarding the word *aṇṇave*: in this place, a lake is called "aṇṇava"; the meaning is that in this lotus lake, we two alone wander about beautifully because we do not harm others.
However, the fourth line of this verse is: "Not even for the sake of food... [The rest of the verse follows].

"We do not commit evil," they recite. The meaning of this is: "Since we do not commit evil even for the sake of food, therefore we are esteemed among humans and birds as being 'of noble nature' (*kalyāṇabhāva*).
Having heard that, the crow spoke the third verse:
“What fruits do you eat in the ocean? From where do you eat meat, O cakravāka birds?
What food do you consume, O Anomā, that you possess such strength and beauty, so wondrous in form?
In this passage, *kiṃ* is an address by way of inquiry; it means, “What, O cakravākas? *Aṇṇave* refers to this [ocean].
*Sare*: "Eat, eat! What do you eat?"—the meaning is, "From where do you eat meat?
From whose bodies do you eat the flesh of living beings? *Bhuñjatha vo*—the particle *vo* is merely an expletive, or it is connected with the following word:
"strength and beauty, of immeasurable form."
Then the Cakkavāka bird spoke this fourth verse:
“O Dhanka, there are no fruits in the ocean; how could there be meat for us Cakkavākas to eat?
We subsist on water-moss and feed on nothing that has life; we do not commit evil even for the sake of food.”
Therein, "cakkavāke" means "of the ruddy sheldrake. "Apāṇabhojanā" means those whose food is water devoid of living creatures;
he thereby shows that for us, both moss and water are food. "Not for the sake of food" means: "We do not commit evil for the sake of food as you and others do.
Then the crow spoke two verses:
“Cakravāka, this does not please me: that there should be the presence of food in this existence.
Formerly it was otherwise for me, and thus has this doubt arisen in me regarding this matter.
‘I too shall eat meats and fruits, and foods with salt and oil.’”
“I obtain the taste to eat among humans, like a hero who has conquered at the front of battle;
yet my complexion is not such as yours, O Cakravāka.
Therein, “this” refers to this food of yours that you eat, which does not please me. “In this existence, a likeness to food”—that is, it resembles food.
"In this existence, you were a companion in food"—that is, in this life as a cakravāka bird, you were a companion, similar to it, and corresponding to it;

the meaning is that your body was exceedingly radiant. "Therefore, my state has become otherwise"—meaning that previously, upon seeing you, [I thought], "These birds eat various kinds of fruits and fish and meat here."
The meaning is: "By that very [practice], she attained such great beauty; now, for me, it has become otherwise than that. "It is for this very reason" (*icceva me*) means:
for this reason of mine, doubt has arisen regarding the color of your bodies, as in:
"How indeed have these come to possess such beauty while eating such coarse food? "I too" (*ahampi*)—for I am [the one who knows]; or rather, *ahampi* is simply the reading. "Eats" (*bhuñjeti*).
"I eat. "And foods" means various kinds of meals. "Salty oils" means those mixed with salt and oil. "Flavors" refers to superior tastes enjoyed by people.

"Having plundered" means: just as a brave warrior, having conquered the front of a battle and plundered [the spoils], enjoys them, so too do I enjoy them after plundering; this is the meaning. "Just as yours" refers to such excellent food.
He indicated: "Even while eating, I do not possess such a complexion as yours; therefore, I do not believe your words.
Then, explaining the reason for his own lack of excellence in complexion and the reason for his own possession of it, the Cakravāka bird spoke the remaining verses:
"You feed on impure things and are dependent on the moment; food and drink are obtained by you with difficulty.
“O vulture, you do not find satisfaction in the fruits of trees, nor in the flesh found in the midst of a charnel ground.
O vulture, when one who has acquired wealth through violence consumes it, seeking only the immediate moment, his true nature reproaches him;
thus reproached, he loses both his complexion and his strength.”

“Even if one enjoys but little of the state of peace (nibbāna), provided it is without violence and without harming others, that person possesses both strength and beauty; for not all beauty consists merely of physical nourishment.
In this context, “you are one who eats impure food” means that you are an eater of impure food because you eat by means of stealing and deceiving.
"Following the moment" means having the habit of following after the moment of negligence. "By you it is obtained with difficulty" means that food and drink are obtained by you through hardship.
"Or whatever meats" refers to those meats found in the midst of a charnel ground; you are not satisfied even with them. "Thereafter" means subsequently.
"His own nature reviles him" means that his very self censures that person. "Rebuked" means rebuked both by himself and by others.
Being censured, you lose both your complexion and your strength due to remorse. "If he enjoys the bliss of extinction" means:

if, however, without harming others, he eats even a small amount of the food of extinction obtained in accordance with the Dhamma, then "that belongs to him"—at that time, strength and complexion arise in the body of that wise man. "By means of various kinds of food" refers specifically to food of many different types.
This is what was meant: "O crow, this thing called beauty arises from four causes; it does not arise from food alone, but also from the elements, the mind, and kamma.
Thus, in many ways, the ruddy goose reproached the crow. The crow, feeling ashamed, cried out, "I have no need for your beauty! Ka ka! and flew away.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:

at the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy bhikkhu was established in the fruit of Non-Returner. At that time, the crow was the greedy bhikkhu, the female cakravāka was Rāhula’s mother, and the male cakravāka was none other than myself.
The eighth is the commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka.
[435] 9. The commentary on the Haliddirāga Jātaka:
"Enduring with patience..."—this was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the seduction of Thullakumārikā.
The background story will be made clear in the Cūḷanāradajāta of the Terasakanipāta. However, regarding the past event:
that young woman, having broken the ascetic youth’s virtue and knowing that he was under her control, thought, “I shall deceive him and lead him to the human world.
Then, [she said], “In a forest devoid of the objects of sensual pleasure such as forms, one’s virtue is truly protected.”
"It does not bear great fruit; it bears great fruit when forms and other objects are present on the path of men.
Come, go there with me and guard your virtue; what use have you for the forest? Having said this, he spoke the first verse:
"In the forest, in a remote lodging, one should endure hearing [the sounds]."
“And those who endure within the village are even more exalted than you.
In this context, *sutitikkhanti* means thorough endurance. They “endure” by enduring cold and other such hardships.
Having heard that, the young ascetic thought, “My father has gone into the forest; when he returns, I shall ask his permission and depart.”
She said, "He has a father; if he sees me, he will strike me with the tip of a hoe and bring about my destruction.
I must go first. Then she said to him, "In that case, I will go ahead, making the way known; you follow after," and she departed. He [followed] her...
When his father had departed, he did not fetch firewood, nor did he provide water or food; he sat there merely brooding.
When his father returned, he did not go out to meet him. Then his father, realizing that "this boy has fallen under the sway of women," asked him:
"Why, my son, did you neither fetch firewood, nor provide water, nor prepare food?"
"But you were sitting there just meditating," he said. Then the young ascetic replied to him, "Father, it is said that guarding one's virtue in the forest does not yield great fruit;
it is on the path frequented by people that it yields great fruit. I shall go there and guard my virtue.
My companion went on ahead, saying to me, 'Come after me,' and I shall follow right along with him."
Then, asking, "Living there, what kind of man should I serve?", he spoke the second verse:
"Having come from the forest to the village, O dear one, what kind of character and what kind of conduct should I have in the man whom I, being asked, should serve? Tell me that."
Then his father, as he spoke, recited the remaining verses:
“O dear one, go from here and associate with him who would inspire confidence in you,
who would forgive your lack of confidence, who is attentive, and who is patient.”
“He who has committed no wrong by body, speech, or mind—
go from here and seek him out, as one would seek a treasure resting upon the breast.
And he who lives according to the Dhamma, yet does not conceive pride while so living;”
Go from here and associate with one who acts with purity and possesses wisdom.
“O dear son, do not serve a man who is like turmeric in color, whose mind is like a monkey, and who has lost his passion for sensual desires— even if such a person were to be more than human.”
“Like an enraged venomous snake, like a great highway smeared with filth—
avoid it from afar, as one would avoid a rugged road.
O dear one, misfortunes increase for the fool who serves excessively.”
"Do not associate with a fool at any time, as if with an enemy.
"Therefore, my dear, I entreat you: do as I say;
do not associate with a fool, for association with fools is suffering."
In this context, "he who would inspire confidence in you" means one who would place trust in you. "He who would forgive you" means one who would forgive the confidence placed in him by you.
"One who is desirous of hearing and patient" means he should be endowed with both a desire to hear your words and the endurance of those words;
such is the meaning. "As if established upon his breast" means just as a child is established upon a mother’s breast.
Having thus established himself, he says that one should associate with such a person, regarding them as if they were one's own mother.
"And he who conducts himself according to the Dhamma" means one who conducts oneself by means of the Dhamma of the threefold good conduct.

"He does not conceive [pride]" means that even while conducting himself in that way, he does not form the conceit, "I am practicing the Dhamma. "One of purified conduct" means a doer of the ten paths of wholesome action which are purified.

"Those who have passion and those who are dispassionate" means both the passionate and the dispassionate, whose very nature is to become dispassionate at that very moment after having been impassioned.
"Even if it should be devoid of men" means even if the entire surface of Jambudīpa were devoid of men, and only that one person remained;
even so, one should not associate with such a person. "Like a great path" means like a road smeared with excrement. "Whatever [vehicles]" means by means of a vehicle.
"As if walking" means as though one were actually walking. "Uneven ground" refers to the uneven terrain consisting of depressions, elevations, stumps, rocks, and so forth.
"Associating excessively with a fool" means for one who associates too much with a person lacking wisdom (*appañña*). "Always," my dear, association with a fool is like association with an enemy;
it is painful at all times, at every moment. "Therefore, I [say] that" means for that reason, I say that.
Thus, having been exhorted by his father, he said: "Father, having gone to the human world, I shall not find wise men like you;
I am afraid to go there. I will remain right here in your presence.

Then, after giving him further instruction, he explained the preparatory exercises for the *kasiṇas*. Not long after, he brought forth the superknowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Together with his father, he became destined for the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.
At that time, the young ascetic was the despondent monk, the young woman was Thullakumārikā herself, and the father-ascetic was none other than myself.
The ninth is the commentary on the Haliddirāga Jātaka.
[436] 10. The commentary on the Samugga Jātaka:
"From where indeed do you come?"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a bhikkhu who was despondent.

The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are disenchanted? When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Why, monk, do you long for women? Women are indeed unrefined and ungrateful;
even when the *dānavarakkhasas* of old swallowed them and carried them about in their wombs, they were unable to protect a woman who was dependent on a single man."
"Since they were unable to do it, how will you be able? Having said this, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having abandoned sensual pleasures, entered the Himalayas and went forth as an ascetic.
Having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he sustained himself on wild fruits."
He dwelt there. Not far from his leaf-hut lived a certain *dānava-rakkhasa*. From time to time he would approach the Great Being and listen to the Dhamma;
however, standing on the path frequented by people in the forest, he would seize whoever came along and devour them.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kāsi, there was a daughter of a noble family who possessed unsurpassed beauty. In a certain...
She lived in a border village. One day, having gone to visit her parents and returning, she saw her attendants;
then that *dānava* sprang forth in a terrifying form. The people, struck with fear, cast away their weapons as they fled.
Seeing the beautiful woman seated in the carriage, the *dānava* became infatuated with her.
Having sacrificed him and led him to his own cave, he made him his wife.
From that time forth, he brought him ghee, oil, rice, fish, meat, and other such things, as well as sweet fruits, and nourished him.
Having adorned him with garments and ornaments, he placed him in a casket for protection, swallowed the casket, and carried him within his belly.
Thus, one day, desiring to bathe, he went to a lake, vomited up his basket, took it out from there, bathed it, anointed it, and adorned it.
Then, saying, "Let your body take on some warmth for a moment," he placed it near the basket and himself descended to the bathing place;
not looking back at it, he walked a short distance away and bathed.
At that time, a Vidyādhara named Vāyussa-putta was traveling through the air, equipped with armor and sword.
Seeing him, she made a hand gesture saying, "Come! The Vidyādhara quickly descended.
Then, having placed him inside a basket, she sat upon the basket while waiting for the Dānava to arrive; and seeing him approaching, she—
Having revealed herself, before the Dānava had even reached the basket, she opened it, entered within, and lay down upon the Vidyādhara, covering herself with her own garment. The Dānava arrived;
without inspecting the basket, and perceiving "It is only a woman for me," he swallowed the basket and went to his own cave.
As he was traveling, he thought on the way: "I have not seen this ascetic for a long time; today I shall go and pay my respects to him.
He went into his presence. The ascetic, seeing him approaching from afar and knowing that two beings were in her womb, spoke the first verse as they conversed:
“From where have you come, O three men? Welcome! Come and sit upon these seats.
Is it well with you, sirs, and are you free from illness? For it has been a long time since your arrival here.
In this context, *bho* is a form of address. *Kaccittha* means “are you,” “do you exist,” or “are you present. *Bhonto* is used again as a form of address.
He said: "I ask after your welfare; is it well with you? Is there health?
For it has been a long time since your arrival here.
Having heard this, the Dānava thought, "I came into the presence of this ascetic alone, yet this ascetic says, 'Three...'"
People say, "He speaks of 'people'"; what indeed is he saying? Does he speak having understood their true nature, or is he merely lamenting like one who has gone mad?
Having thus reflected, he approached the ascetic, paid homage, sat down to one side, and while conversing with him, spoke the second verse:
“I alone have arrived here today; not even a second person exists for me.
With what intent, O seer, was this spoken by you? From where indeed have you three people come? In this passage, *idha majja* means “here today.
Regarding the phrase *kimeva sandhāya te bhāsitaṃ ise*: “Venerable sir, O seer, with what intent was this spoken by you? Please explain it clearly to me.”
The ascetic asked, "Friend, do you truly wish to hear? When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the ascetic said, "Then listen," and spoke this third verse:
"You alone and your beloved wife were placed together within a closed box;
she was guarded by you always even while still in her womb, yet there she took delight with the son of the wind."
In that regard, "you alone" means first of all that you are a single person. "Placed and scattered within" means placed and scattered within;

the meaning is that she was kept there by one desiring to protect his wife, always placed in a casket and scattered together with the casket, that is, deposited inside the belly. "Together with Vāyussa-putta" means together with the one who has such a name.
"With a master of magic" means: "Delighting there" means you delight in the passion of the defilements right here within your own womb.
Now, you, who carry a woman even in your womb with the thought, "I shall make her dependent on a man," go about having cast out her paramour.
Hearing this, the Dānava thought, “Those called *vidyādharas* are full of many illusions; if that sword has indeed come into his hand, he will escape even by cutting open my belly.
Terrified and trembling, he quickly disgorged the casket and placed it before him.
Having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher, explaining this occurrence, spoke the fourth verse:
“Filled with agitation, having been thus prophesied by the seer, that Dānava opened his mouth wide there and swallowed him.
He saw his wife, who wore a beautiful garland, rejoicing there together with Vāyussa’s son.
In this context, “he saw” means that he opened the basket and looked inside.

But as soon as the Karaṇḍaka casket was opened, the Vidyādhara recited his spell, took up his sword, and leapt into the sky. Seeing this, the Dānava was pleased with the Great Being and spoke the remaining verses, beginning with a hymn of praise:
