“By one who has clearly seen the true form and follows the path of the Awakened, those base men who have fallen under the sway of women are shunned;
for just as life itself must be protected here, so too did I, though wicked, find delight in another.”
“Day and night I attended upon you, O ascetic, dwelling like a light in the forest;
yet you, having abandoned the Dhamma, practiced what is not Dhamma—engaging in non-action and intimacy with women.
Thinking ‘she stands within my body,’ they approached me while I was heedless and unrestrained.”
She practiced what is contrary to the Dhamma after having abandoned the Dhamma; her nature was one of non-action, and she was intimate with those who are heedless.
How can one trust her, saying, "She is well-guarded"? For among women whose minds are manifold, there is no such thing as guarding.
Indeed, they are like a precipice falling into the abyss; he who is heedless here meets with disaster.
“Therefore, indeed, those are happy and free from sorrow who move about detached from women;
aspiring to this auspicious and supreme state, one should not cultivate intimacy with women.
In that regard, [the Buddha said]: “O Bhante, you have clearly seen the true nature of one who follows Uggata-pāna. Thus spoke the seer (isi) who followed Uggata-pāna.
This is the reason. "Base" means lowly. Just as one would protect one's own life here, so was she protected by me while dwelling within my womb as if she were my own life.
"She is ill-disposed toward me" means that now, having committed an act of treachery against me, she is ill-disposed and delights in another man.
Like a fire dwelling in the forest, [she is like] one dwelling in the forest with an ascetic.
She was attended upon and served by me like a fire. "She has transgressed the Dhamma" means she has stepped beyond and overstepped the Dhamma.
"Of an inactive nature" means of a nature that ought not to be done.
"I thought she stood in the midst of my body"—[referring to] this one who is heedless, unrestrained, possessed of the qualities of a non-noble person, undisciplined, and immoral.
“I think, ‘She is situated within my body,’ and ‘She is mine. How could one place trust in her, thinking, ‘She is well-guarded by me’?
How could a wise person trust her, when even someone like me, guarding her within my own belly, was unable to guard her? She is like a precipice falling into the underworld.”
Because they are difficult to satisfy with worldly pleasures, they are like the precipices known as the Pātāla abysses in the great ocean.
"He who is heedless therein"—a person who is negligent regarding such meritless things incurs a great calamity.
Therefore—"because those who have fallen under the power of women meet with great ruin—therefore, those who live having escaped from the influence of women..."

They are happy. This is called "peaceful": this wandering apart from and dissociated from women is the very bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), which is peaceful, secure, supreme, and worthy of being aspired to;
aspiring to this, one should not cultivate intimacy with women.
Having spoken thus, the Dānava fell at the feet of the Great Being and praised him, saying: "Venerable sir, it is by depending on you that I have regained my life;
I was about to be put to death by this wicked woman through the power of a master of magic.
The Great Being, having taught the Dhamma to him as well, said: "Do not commit any evil toward her; receive the precepts," and he [established] her in the five...
He established him in the precepts. Dānava thought, "Even while carrying him in my womb, I was unable to protect him;
who else will protect him? Having dismissed him, he went back to his own forest.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dejected monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, I myself was the ascetic possessed of divine vision.
The Tenth: The Commentary on the Samugga Jātaka.
[437] 11. The Commentary on the Pūtimansa Jātaka:
"It does not please me"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning lack of restraint over the sense faculties.
On one occasion, many bhikkhus were not guarding the doors of their sense faculties.

The Teacher, thinking, "It is fitting to exhort these bhikkhus," spoke to the Elder Ānanda and, having summoned the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in an informal gathering, sat upon a magnificent, well-adorned couch.
Addressing the bhikkhus, he said: "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu must not, by way of the sign of beauty, take up a mental sign in regard to forms and so forth."
It is not proper to grasp [them], for if one should die at that moment, one is reborn in the hells and other such realms;
therefore, do not take the sign of beauty in forms and so forth.

A monk indeed should not have forms and so forth as his range of activity, for those whose range of activity consists of forms and so forth meet with great ruin even in this very life. Therefore, monks, it is better—than a red-hot iron ball...
Having explained in detail, "The eye-faculty has been utterly consumed by an iron rod that is burning, blazing, and glowing," he said:

"There is a time for you to look at forms and a time when you do not look. At the time of looking, rather than looking through the aspect of the beautiful, you should look only through the aspect of the unattractive;
in this way, you will not fall away from your own proper domain. But who..."
"Is this your sphere? "The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the noble eightfold path, and the nine supramundane states.

For while you are walking in this sphere, Māra will find no opportunity; however, if you fall under the sway of the defilements and look out through the sign of beauty, you will become like a jackal for putrid meat."
"Your own range of pasture will diminish," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, several hundred goats lived in a mountain cave in a forest region in the Himalayas.
Not far from their dwelling place, in a certain cave, there was one named Pūtimansa (Foul Meat).
A jackal lived with a wife named Veṇī. One day, while wandering about with his wife, he saw those sheep and thought, "It would be right to eat their meat by some means.
Having devised a plan, he killed one sheep at a time. As they both ate the sheep's meat, they became strong and fat-bodied.
Gradually, the sheep were brought to exhaustion. Among them, there was one ewe named Meṇḍamātā who was clever and skilled in expedients.
Unable to kill her, the jackal one day consulted with his wife:
"My dear, the sheep are exhausted; it is fitting that we eat this ewe by some means. This, however, is the method for doing so:"
"You go alone and become friends with her; then, when confidence has arisen between you two, I will make my bed in the cemetery and lie down.
You should approach him and say: 'Eḷikā, my husband is dead and I am without a protector;
I have no other relative except for you. Come, weep and wail, and perform his funeral rites.'"
"Having said, 'I will do so,' you must take her and come back; then I shall spring up, bite her by the neck, and kill her," she said.
She agreed, saying "Very well," and having established a friendship with her, once confidence had arisen, she spoke thus to the female jackal.
The female jackal said, "Āḷi, Siṅgāli! All my kinsmen have been eaten by your husband; I am afraid."
“I cannot go,” she said. “Āḷi, do not fear; what can a dead man do? “My husband is harsh in his speech; I am indeed afraid.

Although she spoke thus, when she was entreated again and again, she agreed, thinking, “He must surely be dead,” and set out with her. But as they were going, she thought, “Who knows? What might happen?”
Out of apprehension, she went along placing a jackal in front of her while pretending to seize the jackal.
Hearing the sound of their footsteps, the jackal thought, "Has the doe come? and lifting his head, he rolled his eyes and looked around.
Seeing him acting in that manner, the doe thought, "This wicked-natured one wishes to deceive me and kill me."
Having shown her the dwelling place of her mate, she lay down. Then, as the female jackal was turning back to flee, [the male] asked, "Why do you flee?
As she explained the reason, she spoke the first verse:
"O Āḷi, I do not relish the sight of putrid flesh."
“One should avoid such a companion from afar.
In this context, *āḷī* is a form of address; it means “friend” or “companion. “Such a companion” means that one should depart and avoid such a friend from afar.
Having spoken thus, she turned back and went to her own dwelling place. [The jackal] was unable to turn her back.
Unable to do so, she became angry with her and went back to her own husband, where she sat brooding.
Then a jackal, reproaching her, spoke this second verse:
“This woman is truly mad; she praises her friend’s husband.”
"She grieved for the ewe returning home, who had come as 'Meṇḍamātā'.
In this context, *veṇī* is her name. Regarding the word *vaṇṇeti*:

thinking, "My husband's friend will come to my presence out of affection and trust," she first [addressed] her own friend, the ewe, in the presence of her husband, saying, "Make a burial mound for me."
She praises her. Then she broods over and laments for the mother of the rams, who has now returned without coming into her presence.
Hearing this, the female jackal spoke the third verse:
“You are indeed mad, my friend, foolish and lacking insight, you who have made a dwelling for the dead and look about at the wrong time.
In this context, “lacking insight” means devoid of the wisdom of investigation. “Looks about at the wrong time” means that he looked while the female jackal had not yet come into his presence.
“A wise person should not look at things out of season; he should look at them in due season.
He who looks at things out of season burns like rotten meat. This is the verse of the Fully Enlightened One (*abhisambuddhagāthā*).

In this context, “out of season” refers to the time when the mind arises with regard to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) by way of their attractive appearance. For this [is what happens] to a bhikkhu regarding form...
“Improper time for looking” means: at the time when one is grasping a form by way of the foul, by way of recollection, or by way of the kasiṇas.
For this is indeed the proper time for a bhikkhu to look at a form.

In that regard, it should be illustrated by such Jātaka stories as the *Haritacaja*, the *Lomasakassapa*, and others, that those who look at a form at an improper time—that is, at a time of lust—meet with great ruin. At the proper time, by way of the foul...
"One who looks [upon forms] becomes established in Arahatship"—this should be explained by the story of the Elder Tissa, the practitioner of foulness meditation (*asubha-kammatthāna*).

"He brooded like a dog with putrid meat": monks, just as a dog with putrid meat, having sighted a stray goat at an improper time, broods because he has been deprived of his own food, even so a monk, having looked upon a form through the lens of beauty at an improper time, [is deprived] of his range of practice such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"One who has fallen away grieves, broods, and becomes exhausted both in this present life and in the future.
Then the female jackal Veṇī, having comforted the dog with the rotten meat, said, "Master, do not worry; I will bring you back again by some means.
When he returns, you must take him carefully. Having said this, she went to her side and said, "Āḷi..."
“Only at the very moment of your arrival has our purpose been fulfilled;
for it was at the very time of your coming that my husband regained his senses and now lives. Come, exchange greetings with him,” she said, and spoke this fifth verse:
“O Āḷi, may you be dear to me; give me a full bowl.”
“Give me a full bowl, you who speak pleasant words;

give me that which brings joy to my heart. “In this matter, ‘give me a full bowl’ means: give me that which bestows satisfaction upon me, you who speak pleasant words. “My husband has been restored to life”: the meaning is that my lord has been revived, arisen, and is free from illness. “Come”: come together with me.

The female jackal, thinking, “This woman of evil character wishes to deceive me; however, it is improper to act against her directly; I shall deceive her by means of a stratagem,” spoke the sixth verse:
“May it be dear to you, Āḷi; I give you this full bowl.
With a great retinue, you should prepare food for my arrival.
In this context, *essaṃ* means “I shall come. And as she comes, she will ensure her own protection and arrive with a large retinue.
Then the female jackal, asking about his retinue, spoke the seventh verse:
“What is the nature of your retinue, for whom I shall provide food?
What are their names, all of them? Tell me when you are asked.”
Explaining this, she spoke the eighth verse:
“Māliya, Caturakkha, Piṅgiya, and Jambuka—such is my retinue; provide them with food.”
In that regard, he informed me of his retinue, saying, "They are mine. *Māliya* and so forth are the names of four dogs.
Having said, "In that place, five hundred dogs accompany each one;
thus, surrounded by two thousand dogs, I shall come," [he added], "If they do not receive food, you two people..."
“Having killed her, they will eat her,” she said.
Hearing this, the female jackal was terrified and thought, “Enough of her going there; by some means I shall ensure she does not go at all. Having reflected thus, she spoke the ninth verse:
“When one has gone forth from the home, even the household goods are lost;”
“Health is a blessing for Āḷina; stay right here, do not go away. The meaning of this is:
“Āḷina, there is much property in your house; if you leave home, that property will perish unprotected.
I myself shall speak words of health and blessing to your friend Āḷina; you—”
"Stay right here; do not come back!
Having spoken thus, terrified by the fear of death, she went quickly to her husband's side, took him, and fled. They were unable to return to that place again.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I was the deity reborn in the chief tree of the forest in that place."
The eleventh: The Exposition of the Pūtimamsa Jātaka.
[438] 12. The Exposition of the Daddara Jātaka.
"He who is your son..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Vulture Peak regarding Devadatta’s plotting for his own destruction.
He spoke with reference to this. At that time, in the Hall of Truth, they raised a discussion, saying: "Oh, friends!

Devadatta is shameless and ignoble; having allied himself with Ajātasattu against the Perfectly Enlightened One who possesses such supreme qualities, he employs means for his destruction by means of archers, the *payojana* stone, the *nāḷāgiri* elephant, and the hurling of rocks."
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?

When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, Devadatta plotted for my death, yet now he was unable to do even so much as a scratch against me. Having said this, he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a world-renowned teacher who was instructing five hundred young men in their craft thought one day: "While I am living here, there are many obstacles;
the students' mastery of their craft will not reach completion. I shall enter a forest region in the Himalayan foothills and dwell there."
"I shall teach them during the spring. Having spoken thus to the young brahmins, he had them take sesame seeds, rice, oil, cloth, and other provisions;
then, having entered the forest and built a leaf-hut in a place not far from the road, he made his dwelling there, while the young brahmins also built their own leaf-huts.
The relatives of the young brahmins sent oil, rice, and other supplies, and the inhabitants of the kingdom as well.
“Word spread that a world-renowned teacher, living in such-and-such a place in the forest, was teaching his craft.
People brought him rice and other provisions; even those traveling through the wilderness gave to him. One man, moreover, gave a cow with its calf for the purpose of providing milk.
Near the teacher’s leaf-hut, there was one [cow] together with two calves.
A monitor lizard lived there, and lions and tigers would come to attend upon it. A single partridge also resided there permanently.
Hearing the sound of his teacher reciting the mantras to the young brahmin students, he mastered all three Vedas.
The students became very intimate with him.
Later on, before the young brahmins had even attained proficiency in their studies, the teacher passed away.
The young brahmins cremated his body, built a stupa of sand over it, and after worshipping it with various flowers, they wept and lamented.
Then the partridge asked them, "Why do you weep? They replied, "Our teacher has died before we had completed our training in the arts; therefore, we weep."
“This being so, do not grieve; I shall teach you a craft. “How do you know?
“When my teachers were teaching you, I heard the sound and mastered the three Vedas. “In that case, let us know your proficiency.
The partridge said, “Then listen,” and from the mountain peak, he [recited] right from the difficult passages...
He recited it as if descending into a river. The young brahmins, filled with joy and satisfaction, began their craft in the presence of the wise partridge.
He, standing in the place of the world-renowned teacher, taught them the craft.
The young brahmins constructed a golden cage for him, fastened a canopy above it, and placed honey, parched grain, and other offerings upon a golden platter.
Offering various kinds of flowers and paying great honor, they worshipped him.
The news that "the partridge (Tittira), it is said, was teaching the mantras to five hundred young brahmins in the forest retreat" became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
At that time, they proclaimed a great festival throughout Jambudīpa, like a mountain-top carnival. The parents of the young brahmins—
"Let them come for the sake of seeing the festival," they sent word. The young men informed Tittira;
having entrusted the wise Tittira with the entire hermitage and the monitor lizard (godhā), they each returned to their own cities.
At that time, a certain merciless and wicked ascetic, wandering here and there, arrived at that place. The monitor lizard—
Having seen him, she offered him hospitality and said, "Rice is in such-and-such a place, and oil and other provisions are in such-and-such a place;
cook a meal and eat," and then she went out for her own almsround. The ascetic cooked his meal early in the morning and killed and ate two young antelopes;
at midday he killed and ate a wise partridge and a calf; and in the evening, [he waited for] the cow as it returned.
Having seen him, he too killed it, ate the flesh, and lying down at the foot of the tree, fell asleep while snoring.
In the evening, the iguana returned; not seeing her two little ones, she wandered about searching for them.
Seeing the iguana trembling because she could not find her young, the tree deity stood within the trunk and branches by means of his divine power and said:
“O cow, do not tremble! This wicked man has killed both your calves—the partridge and the heifer—and now you too.
Bite him by the neck and bring about the end of his life! Thus she spoke, and recited the first verse:
“He who ate your two innocent calves, for whom food had been provided—”
"Set your fangs upon him; let them not escape you while he yet lives.
In this context, "one to whom food has been given" means one to whom you have given food, saying, "Cook and eat.
"Innocent" means blameless and without fault. "Set your fangs upon him" means set all four of your fangs upon that wicked man.
This is the intention: "May he not escape from you while living" means that while still alive, being possessed of life, may this one of evil nature not escape from your hand;
may he not obtain liberation, but rather bring about the destruction of his life.
Then the lizard spoke two verses:
“A man who is full of cruelty is like one smeared with a nurse’s garment;
I see no place where he would not set his fangs.
For a person ungrateful and always looking for a flaw,”
"Even if one were to give the entire earth, one could not satisfy such a person.
In this context, "one who is crowded with greed" means one who is intensely greedy. "One who looks for a flaw" means one who seeks out a defect or an opportunity for attack.
"One could not satisfy him" means that even if one were to give away the whole earth, one would not be able to please a person of such a nature.
"How much less, then, could I be one who gives even a mere morsel of food? Thus she showed.
Having spoken thus, the lizard, thinking "He will wake up and eat me too," fled to protect her own life.
But those lions and tigers were indeed friends of the partridge; sometimes they would come and see the partridge.
Sometimes, after he had gone and taught them the Dhamma, he would return;
on that particular day, however, the lion said to the tiger, "Friend, we have not seen the partridge for a long time—it has been seven or eight days now.
Go, find out his whereabouts and then return. The tiger agreed, saying, "Very well," and [went] at the moment the iguana was fleeing.
Upon reaching that place, he saw the wicked man sleeping.
Within his matted hair, the feathers of the wise partridge were visible, and the bones of the cow and her calf were also visible.
Having seen all this, and not seeing the wise partridge in the golden cage, the tiger king thought, "These have been killed by this wicked man."
Thinking, "They will become [like this]," he kicked him and made him rise up. Seeing him, the other became terrified with fear.
Then the tiger asked him, "Are you going to kill and eat these? He replied, "I am neither killing them nor eating them.
The tiger said, "O you of evil nature, if you do not kill them, who else will? Tell me the reason first; for one who does not speak, there is no life."
“They do not exist,” he said. Terrified by the fear of death, he replied, “Yes, sir;
I kill and eat the young lizard, the calf, and the cow, but I do not kill the partridge. Although the man spoke much to him, he did not believe him.
He asked, “Where have you come from? and [the other] replied, “Sir, I am coming from the kingdom of Kaliṅga, carrying the merchandise of merchants.”
“Having performed this and that work for the sake of a livelihood, I have now come here,” he said.
When the tiger had thus related all the work he had done himself, [the lion] said, “O you of evil character, if you do not kill the partridge yourself, who else will kill it?
Come, I shall take you into the presence of Siha, the king of beasts. Leading him along and frightening him, he went forward. King Siha saw the tiger bringing him.
Questioning him, he spoke the fourth verse:
“Subāhu, why have you returned in such a hurried manner together with the young brahmin?
What business or purpose do you have here? Being asked, tell me this matter.”
In this context, "Subāhu" is an address to the tiger by name; for the tiger’s forebody is pleasing, and thus he speaks to it in that way.
"What service or purpose is there here for you? means: "What duty, designated as a 'purpose,' is there here for you with this young brahmin?
There is also a reading, "What service or purpose is there for you," which has the same meaning.
Having heard that, the tiger spoke the fifth verse:
“The Daddara, your friend of noble form, I suspect will meet his death today;
having heard of the spheres of human action, I do not consider the Daddara to be safe today.”

In that context, *daddara* means a partridge. Regarding "his slaughter": today I suspect the slaughter of this partridge-sage from this man. "I do not think he is happy" means: today I do not consider the *daddara* to be happy or free from illness.
Then the lion spoke the sixth verse to him:
"What spheres of action would there be for this man, through the accomplishment of his livelihood?"
“Having heard what promise from the man, do you suspect the *daddara* by means of the young brahmin (*māṇava*)?
In this context, “heard” (*assu*) means he listened. “By the convergence of livelihood” (*vuttisamodhānatāya*) means by the convergence of the means of subsistence;
the meaning is: “What indeed were his own deeds that he told you? Regarding “by the young brahmin”: having heard what, do you suspect that it was killed by this young brahmin?
Then, as he was speaking, the tiger-king recited the remaining verses:
“The Kaliṅgas have been traversed, trade has been practiced, and the Vettācara and Saṅkupatha regions have also been traveled.
I have performed with actors and dancers, and even fought with a staff in the midst of a fair.”
“Bound by his family ties, he has overcome measured dwellings; the dice have been won, self-restraint has been transcended.
At the early hour of midnight, his former wealth was lost; his hands were burned by the acceptance of alms-food.
These were the spheres of his action, due to the man’s accumulation of livelihood.”
"Just as this tuft of hair is seen, what then [is there] for the Daddara bull?
Therein, "The Kaliṅgas were traversed" means that while carrying the merchandise of merchants, he is said to have traversed the Kaliṅga kingdom.
"Commerce was practiced" means that trade was also carried out by him. "To be traversed by means of canes" means it must be traveled using canes. "A path of stakes" also...
“Traversed” means even a path of stumps was frequented. “Even with actors” means even together with actors solely for the sake of a livelihood.
“Traversed along with dogs” means he traveled together with dogs while carrying a dog. “A fight with a staff” means, it is said, that he even fought with a staff.
"Kulīkā was bound": it is said that even a certain bird-catcher was bound by him. "The measuring-floor":
it is said that he also performed the work of measuring grain. "The dice were won": while performing service for gamblers, the dice were taken away by him. "Restraint has passed away":
by one who goes forth into homelessness for the sake of a livelihood, the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*) is already transgressed. "It has been carried away."
"Exuding" means flowing out. "Old" refers to blood. This is what is meant:
it is said that, for the sake of his livelihood, this man would go at midnight to the hall where the hands and feet of royal offenders had been cut off;
having brought them there and laid them down, he would apply *kuṇḍaka* smoke to the wounds and leave them. "The hands were burnt."
When he went forth into the Ājīvika order, it is said that even his hands were burned when receiving hot alms-food.
"Those are his spheres of action" means those are his deeds. "I heard" means I have heard.
"Just as this" means that because even a tuft of partridge-feather down is seen within his matted hair, by this reason it should be understood: "By him alone..."
"He was killed. "The cows were killed—what then of Daddara? [The meaning is: The cows were indeed killed by him, but what about Daddara that he should not have been killed? Why would he not kill him?
The lion asked that man, "Was the wise partridge killed by you? "Yes, sir," he replied. Then [the lion] [tested] his word of truth...
Upon hearing this, Sīha wished to release him; however, the tiger king, saying, "This one is fit to be killed," struck him right there with his fangs, killed him, dug a pit, and threw him in.
The young men returned, and not seeing Tittira Paṇḍita, they wept and lamented, then turned back.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past Devadatta strove for my death," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Kūṭajaṭila was Devadatta; the iguana was Uppalavaṇṇā;
the tiger was Moggallāna; the lion was Sāriputta; and the world-renowned teacher was Mahākassapa."
"But I myself was the wise partridge.
This concludes the twelfth narrative, the Commentary on the Daddara Jātaka.
The summary of the Jātakas:
Gijjha, Kosambī, and Sūva, Cūḷasūva, and Harittaca;
Kusala, Lomakassapa, Cakkavāka, and Haliddi.
Samugga, Pūtimansa, and Daddara—these are the twelve.
In the *Jātaka*, in the Ninth Chapter, the authors of the verses sang [these verses].
The commentary on the Ninth Chapter is finished.
(The third part is finished.)
